Mr. D. Flynn, of Mandan, returned home, last Saturday.
Messrs. Sleeper and Kerr returned yesterday morning from a trip to Helena.
Lawyer Carpenter, of Dickinson, has been in town for several days on legal business.
Mr. Richard Gray, who represents the Co's. interests at Fargo is in town on business.
Gustave Stoltze, who is in the employment of the N. P. R. C. Co., as draughtsman, is in town for a few days.
It is the unanimous opinion of our oldest settlers that the cold snap is almost gone and that it will be the last one of the season.
Frank Coughlan started this morning for the Indian camp, forty miles down the river. Wm. Vandriesche takes his place in the post-office.
The remainder of the Marquis' cattle which were to be taken to the Ox-Bow ranch will be held at Matthew's camp until milder weather.
We would like to hear from "How" often. We are not talking politics now but refer to our correspondent who sails under that suggestive "nom de plume."
Geo. F. Porter, store-keeper of the company's store, has returned from a five weeks' visit to New York and Chicago. He reports having thoroughly enjoyed his vacation.
The outfit which put up the ice here and afterward went to Miles City to build the ice-house and put up ice there have returned. The foreman is Charles Ellison, of Dubuque.
The wolves seem to have left the Bad Lands. None have been poisoned lately and no cattle have been harmed by them. The absence of buffalo thus turns out to be a blessing in disguise to the stock men.
One of Pennell & Robert's bears was untied Wednesday and the boys had a lively time lassoing it. When caught, it held a pig in a loving embrace, which was only loosened after considerable difficulty.

We have twice been offered $5 for the first copy of THE COW BOY that was printed, but we can scarcely see it in that light. If it is worth $100 to any one as a memento, it is worth twice that amount to us.

It was pretty rough work taking care of cattle during the high winds of Sunday and Monday, but the "cow girls" all attended to their duty, and as yet we have not heard of the loss of a single head, except some young calves.

The immigration edition of the Mandan Pioneer, reached us this morning. For thoroughness in editorial work, typographical neatness and general make-up it is a model paper. It foreshadows the future prosperity of the city which is destined to be one of the best in Dakota.

Trains both east and west have been badly delayed by snow drifts. Two engines with a snow plow precede every passenger train, but even this is not sufficient to overcome the drifts immediately. It is a curious fact that in the Bad Lands there are no difficulties from drifts as the wind cannot get enough of a sweep. All delay is east and west of us.

Transient trade at the hotels is rather light, but every one is making preparations for the influx of tourists that is sure to come with the summer. This point is the best one in the Bad Lands from which to see its curiosities, and tourists seem to appreciate the fact. The principal ones, of course, are Cedar Canon and the Burning Mine. They have a national reputation and the large majority of tourists passing through the Bad Lands will stop off to see them.

Mose Ryder, "Moody and Sankey" and Jones started Tuesday on a trip up the river to cut posts. A mile or two out of town their wagon upset and pinned Ryder and Jones down into a snow drift. It was said to be very animating to see Jones draw his pocket pistol from his pocket, allow some of the contents to gurgle down his throat, pass it to Mose, who did likewise, and then both would struggle to get the load off, and quote scripture like a Missouri steamboat mate. "Moody and Sankey" meanwhile were conducting select religious exercises in another drift, and at last accounts the whole outfit seemed to have the "power" or something else that was evidently the work of the spirits.

Last Sunday morning Deputy Sheriff Townley, from Miles City, came down and arrested Wm. Baupre, alias Bird, for stealing a team of mules at that place about six months ago. There are a number of stories afloat, but as near as we can find out the truth is about as follows: Bird worked last summer for a man at Miles City, and in settling up Bird claimed that he was not paid in full. He then stole a team of mules from his former employer, drove them through to Deadwood, and sold them for $300. He then came here, and after engaging in several occupations, commenced working for Mr. J. J. Fitzgerald in his restaurant. He continued here until last Sunday morning, when the Miles City deputy inquired of Bird if he knew of such a person. Bird said he did and would call him, and started for the river. The deputy procured the assistance of Mr. Wm. Vandriesche and went in pursuit. Bird was overtaken at Smith's ranch, about five miles up the river, brought back and taken to Miles City on the next train. Further particulars will be furnished as soon as they arrive.
The train from the west ran off the track this side of Glendive this morning and has not yet arrived. No one was injured.

Messrs. Hohnick and Duryea, surveyors of the N. P. road, have been in town several days. Their instruments have not yet arrived, but as soon as they come they intend surveying up the river for about twenty miles. The work is to be done so that the Marquis will know where his lines run.

Mr. Frank Keeler, who has been occupying Mr. Porter's place in the Co's. store during the latter's absence will probably leave in a few days. There is not an acquaintance of Mr. Keeler's who is not his friend and they will all regret seeing him go. A more popular and deservedly liked young man we have rarely known.

Mr. C. W. Van Slyck, of Mandan, was in town on business the first of the week, and made us a pleasant call. There is not a town on the N. P. between Mandan and Miles City in which he does not sell goods from his Mandan house. He intends advertising his business still more thoroughly. He showed his appreciation of THE COW BOY by subscribing.

Mr. Z. Hyde, foreman of the abattoir here, and who was the first cash subscriber to THE COW BOY, took us over the abattoir yesterday and explained its mysteries. Everything is reduced to a system and is done after the most approved manner. Many additions will be made in the spring, however, and facilities for slaughtering a hundred cattle a day will be added. The premises will also be thoroughly cleaned up and thus do away in a great measure with the disagreeable smell. Mr. Hyde intends going to Chicago soon and bringing his family back with him.

Subscriptions keep coming in, but not as fast as they should. We wish as soon as possible to reach every man in the Bad Lands, and we can only do this by the united action of our subscribers. There is not one of them who cannot hand in the name of from one to ten additional subscribers. If every subscriber will remember this and speak of the matter to his neighbor our subscription list, as far as the Bad Lands is concerned, will soon be complete. What is a small matter for all would be an almost insurmountable task for one. Let each subscriber then make a point of gaining at least one new name to add to THE COW BOY list.

Game has had a hard time of it this winter. So many buffalo hunters were thrown out of employment by the absence of their favorite game, that they had to kill deer, elk and mountain sheep or give up hunting. The Sioux have held the buffalo down on the reservation closely but it seems that one bull was unwilling to die there. He strayed toward Little Missouri and was shot within twenty rods of the Custer Trail home ranch. We expect to live on fat hump, buffalo tongue and tender steaks for some time, as Howard Eaton knows we have a vacuum that yearns to be filled with just that kind of "poi," and he must be a mighty mean man if he does'nt try to satisfy that yearn. Send down a saddle, old boy.

The editor of THE COW BOY has recently been appointed agent for the Studebaker Bros.' wagons and will hereafter represent their interests in the Bad Lands. Studebaker Bros. have always occupied a warm place in our hearts as they were the heaviest advertisers in our earliest journalistic venture, a county fair daily. We also lived for many years near South Bend, Ind., and no other wagon is thought of for a moment in that region besides the Studebakers'. They as well as their father, are practical wagon makers, understanding every detail of the work. There isn't a dishonest point in their characters any more than there is a dishonest stick of timber in their wagons. We speak from personal experience when we say that it is the best wagon made.

It is not yet decided whether John Nelson has failed or not. Certain it is that his goods have disappeared. The affair is at present involved in mystery. It seems that the cause of the whole business was that Nelson was led to believe that his creditors were about to close in on him. As a matter of fact this was entirely untrue. One of his heaviest creditors has since said that he would even have trusted him for a larger amount. At any rate, John for some reason believed that he was to be closed out and the goods were secreted somewhere. Nelson has heretofore borne a good reputation in town. He has been thoroughly honest in all his transactions and has the good will of every one. In this instance, however, he allowed his fears to get the better of his judgment. It is to be hoped that the matter will be straightened out satisfactorily.

A man stopped off here on his way back to Michigan from the Cœur D'Alene mines yesterday morning, and his account was anything but rosy. He was utterly disgusted with the mines, claiming that it was a huge swindle. There is very little gold in paying quantities, he claims, and the whole plan is a gigantic speculation for the purpose of gulling people out of their money. That it will be a success there is not much doubt. The excitement is at fever heat everywhere, and thousands will hurry into the mines in the spring and will soon not have money enough to hire a mule to kick them out. The trouble with gold mining is that it is not a legitimate business. With just as good sense one might as well expect to win a fortune in a lottery. There are a thousand chances to one against winning. But as long as a fortune is subjected to these odds there will be found men to risk them. And not only once will they do this but again and again, urged on by the phantom fortune that seems to be just ahead. It is the unvarying history of even the best mining countries that thousands are disappointed where one is fortunate. This will not deter many, however, as to gold miners especially that line applies:

"Distance lends enchantment to the view."

All indications and recent developments point to the speedy opening of the freight route between this point and Deadwood. It is now almost as good as a settled fact. Whether a route is established from Dickinson or not is a matter of small importance, except for the short-lived opposition it will offer. Recent articles in the Dickinson Press and Minnesela Boomer state that the contemplated route from Dickinson to Deadwood runs through Minnesela. This fact alone proves that the route from Dickinson will either never be started or else will be short lived. During wet seasons forty miles of this route is absolutely impassable. All along the Moreau and to Minnesela is one vast bed of gumbo. There is no bottom to this, and wagons will mire over the axles. At the present writing it is impossible to ride a horse over part of the route. Great cracks are found everywhere and horses are in constant danger of stepping into them and breaking their legs.

As we have before stated, the route from Dickinson is at best a poor one. For a large part of the distance it must cross the head waters of the Heart, Cannonball and Moreau rivers. These will require many bridges, and, in fact, almost the whole route from Dickinson to Deadwood would have to be bridged to escape the gumbo. The route from here, on the other hand, is entirely clear of these head waters and traverses the level, grassy divide between them and the Little Missouri valley. Very little gumbo is encountered and the route from beginning to end presents no serious obstacles. The worst part of the road is right here in the Bad Lands, and this morning a gang of men was set to work to make a good road out to the divide. This will soon be completed and the route will be in condition.

This route is for summer, but in winter the Little Missouri river and valley furnish a route that would be a delight to any freighter. Two routes, each vastly superior than the one from Dickinson, would really seem to indicate that no serious opposition will be felt in that direction.

Geo. Weaver, who represents transportation for 250,000 pounds of freight, was in town a day or two since, and is now waiting word for the completion of the route to bring all the horses, mules and wagons to this point. Indeed, some have already started and will be here in a few days. T. G. Jones of Deadwood, will also be in town in a few days. He has over four hundred head of horses and a hundred mules that he will bring here as soon as preparations can be made. The Jones Bros. have already contracted for hauling all the bullion of the Homestake mine, which will in itself support a large freighting outfit. Many Deadwood merchants have also been consulted in reference to their freight and have guaranteed it to our line as soon as it is started. The popular opinion seems to be that in some way the freight line is connected with the government or railroad. This is entirely false. It is merely a private enterprise and one could be started from every town on the N. P. if it had sufficient backing. This is the reason why our route is next to a certainty. The Marquis has written from Washington that the freight route must be established here at all events, whether there is opposition at Dickinson or not.

The mail route is entirely an outside matter. This is one of the principal reasons for the Marquis' Washington trip, however, and we will doubtless soon have that also.

Pennell & Roberts are enthusiastic over the prospect and consider the route as a question of only a very short time. As before stated, they have already sent out men to grade the road and in our next issue we hope to chronicle its successful completion.

LITTLE MISSOURI, Feb. 19, 1884.
EDITOR COW BOY:

Your brisk little sheet struck in on the quietness here as a "bile" ointment would have affected Job in olden times.

Geary Paddock was so wrought upon that his tears flowed freely, and he remarked, "This will boom my lots in Little Missouri and make the Marquis down in the mouth."

Joe Pennel said he hadn't felt so happy since he presented Capt. Baker with two nice mules.

Bob Roberts mixed something with a spoon and said "How!"

Baron von Steiger broke for the old garden left by the soldiers and took a homestead at once.

Old citizens like Frank Moore remember well when this country was made, and can give any scientist pointers on geology.

It is strange to an old-timer to look at the "Senate," smell the slaughter house, and think of the many changes here within a year.

Many of the pioneers here have died with their boots on.

In the days of old, a famous hunter and scout spent his spare time and cash at the old post-trader's store. There he enjoyed life during the intermission of scalping Sioux, hunting and trapping. Old men will remember the brave man we refer to. His public name was "Bloody Hand"—few indeed knew his true name. Once a drunken butcher attacked the post-trader in his private room and would have killed him but for the bold scout. Peace to his soul. He has now retired from the battlefield and is only remembered here as the man who could pour five glasses of beer from one bottle. He has retired from the rush of civilization and lives quietly on his ranch near the Kill-Deer Mountains, building up a fortune for himself and nursing a wound in his foot, where Frenchy shot through the door and hit him hard. Private Jim unfeelingly said that "Frenchy would have obliged him by holding the pistol about three feet higher."

But those days are past, the cheerful crack of the pistol is no longer heard through the land, and men now shed their boots before dying.

Paddock has grown stout and takes "sugar in his."

Pennell & Roberts resist the march of time and set 'em up for the boys at the old price.

Next week we'll post you on the doings of "Bigfoot" Ryder.

HOW.

The refrigerator cars of the N. P. R. C. Co. are marvels of neatness and simplicity. They are considered equal, if not superior to any other refrigerator car made. The cars are very solidly built and are air-tight except for ventilation. They are of double thickness and are built for heavy use. The ice boxes are at either end, the capacity of both being from three to five tons. The boxes are elevated from the floor and are provided with waste troughs and pipes. Under the boxes is room to pack hearts, livers, etc. Long iron rods, running lengthwise of the car, are used to hang the beef on. It is first cut into quarters, and all the quarters numbered. The quarters are then separated, for instance, the quarters of No. 1 occupy the four corners of the car; the quarters of No. 2 come next, and so on till the car is filled. A load consists of the quarters of from thirty to forty dressed beef. There are now twenty-four refrigerator cars belonging to the company, and doubtless others will be needed before long. The car is the invention of Mr. C. W. Sleeper, now vice president of the company.
STOCKMEN Who Have Gathered Here To-Day Consider Well The Benefits of the Following Article And Act Accordingly.

Why not make this point the Territorial cattle headquarters? The opportunity is within your grasp, if you will only make an effort for it. We have here every natural and artifical advantage that could be asked. The cattle interests east of the Bad Lands are small and this point is virtually the farthest east and consequently the nearest to a market. The bulk of the cattle business of Western Dakota is on or tributary to the Little Missouri river. These two facts would alone be sufficient for establishing the Territorial headquarters here. But in addition we have the only railroad outlet for the cattle interests of Dakota. Beside these reasons the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co. furnishes a ready market for many cattle right at home. Any one of these facts would be sufficient to bring the headquarters here, but the four present an array of arguments that is unanswerable. Beyond all these facts no other place has made active efforts to be the headquarters. All seem naturally to look here as the best place. This meeting could easily organize as a Bad Lands association, pass all the legislation required, and then resolve itself into a preliminary meeting to issue a call for a Territorial convention to be held here on March 27, for instance. This will give sufficient time before the general round-up to let every one interested know of the project and also to pass any motions they may wish to have acted upon by the Montana association, which meets soon after. Many Montana, Wyoming and Colorado cattle men would undoubtedly join the association, and, then, what is to prevent this place becoming, in the course of time, the cattle center of the whole Northwest, with a huge association having its headquarters here. Both the above plans are reasonable and feasible. A very little effort will secure the first and time will be sure to bring the last.

THE COW BOY merely places these facts before the attention of the cattle men. It is for your and our own interests to take vigorous action upon them. Don't let this opportunity go by, but strike while the iron is hot and the prize is ours.

We wish to say a word or two in reference to the Bad Lands as a sheep country. The report of the death of many of Marquis de Mores' sheep has been widely published and heralded abroad as an evidence of the unfitness of the Bad Lands for sheep raising. Let us examine the facts. The Marquis came here last May and in the fall, judging this to be a good sheep country, sent men east to buy a large herd. Right here we must mention that the whole thing was an experiment. No sheep had ever been raised here, there was no data to be governed by, and naturally there was a mistake made. The mistake in this instance was in buying merino sheep, shipping them here late in the fall, and providing no buildings for their protection. Any one of these reasons, viewed in the light of the experience of the last two months, would have been sufficient to make the project a failure. The total loss, however, has been greatly magnified. It is not at all likely that it will reach $5,000, and the experience gained is an ample return for the loss. On the other hand, look at some of the successful sheep raising in the Bad Lands. Howard Eaton has some of the large, long-wooled variety that also labored under the disadvantage of being driven upon new ranges late in the fall, but they have done as well as cattle. This winter has been a severe one on all kinds of stock, and the above amply proves that the Bad Lands is a sheep country, if the right kind of sheep are bred. Sheep cannot stand as much exposure as cattle and they need to get acquainted with the range earlier in the season. With protection from storms, and hay during the worst winter weather sheep will undoubtedly prove as remunerative in the Bad Lands as cattle. In the Red river valley, where the cold and exposure to storms are far greater than here, common Minnesota sheep do well. The same is true of Montana. Why, than, should not the Bad Lands, which has every natural advantage, make a better sheep country than either of them?

The cedar with which the Bad Lands abounds is the regular lead-pencil variety and makes excellent firewood. It is easily cut, close grained, burns readily and for a long time, and gives off an intense heat. In spite of the fact that coal is so plenty many here prefer to burn the cedar. If one has a team the cedar costs nothing beside the labor of cutting it.

Never was there a more delightful or welcome chinook than that of Sunday and Monday. As if by magic the grip of Boreas was broken and the snow begun disappearing from the buttes in roaring torrents of water. The ice of the Little Missouri river, three feet thick, was soon covered with two to three feet of water, and Tuesday, although it was again freezing, four feet of water. A sigh of relief has gone up from every cattle man in the Bad Lands. Now all possible danger is past. It is altogether likely that not a solitary head in the whole Bad Lands will die of exposure this winter or spring. This is the record that “the most God-forsaken country on earth, the tail-end of frozen-up Dakota,” publishes to the world. It speaks for itself.

One of the most sensible things done for a long time by a railroad is that of the Northern Pacific officials in concluding to lower emigrant rates. The difference in rates between the roads is almost the exclusive reason for the larger settlements in Southern Dakota. All those who have been in both sections readily appreciate the vast superiority of Northern Dakota. Up to this time, however, emigrants who had but little money have been almost compelled to go to Southern Dakota. We have never heard the right idea expressed better than by our genial Register at Bismarck, Mr. Rea. He says: “If I was running this thing I would conduct it like a church festival. Nothing to get in and five dollars to get out.”

“The Deadwood merchants are determined to make the Northern Pacific route a freight route, as quite a number of them are ordering their stocks from the East via Dickinson. There is, however, an opinion among them that Dickinson will not long remain the point of transfer of goods from the cars to wagons, as Little Missouri station is much nearer the Hills.”

The above clipping from an article published in the Black Hills Journal gives a very good idea of the opinion of Deadwood merchants in respect to the relative merits of the Dickinson and Medora routes.

It is very seldom that an appointment is greeted with less opposition than was that of Judge Palmer to the vacancy on the bench caused by the death of Judge Kidder. There seems to be no doubt as to the eminent qualifications of Judge Palmer, but some of our exchanges would rather have had a Dakota man.

We hear of a few cases of black leg among calves on the range, though no one range reports more than half a dozen cases. Without going into a scientific discussion of the disease, or indulging in any big words, we want to say to ranchmen that there is very little trouble in getting rid of the plague. After the disease once takes hold of an animal it is all the same as a carcass, for it works rapidly. But the moment one of your calves dies with it, round all of the balance up and give them a sharp run for two or three miles and back, driving fast enough to get up an active circulation of the blood. Keep this up for a week and you will have no more black leg. No losses will occur from the time you commence this process. Should the disease break out again weeks later, repeat and keep it up until grass comes. It is sometimes difficult to get the calves together, but it is the only sure way of saving them that can be well resorted to on the open range.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

At the regular annual meeting of the Chicago Academy of Homeopathic Physicians and Surgeons, a paper was read by Dr. T. C. Duncan on “Dakota as a Health Resort.” Premising that the essentials of a health resort are in its sources productive of diversion, deep respiration and vigorous digestion, the doctor showed that Dakota furnished such in a marked degree, the water, air and other favorable conditions contributing to the cure of dyspepsia, diseases of the kidneys and bladder, catarrh, bronchitis and consumption in its early stages, though in its advanced stages the patient should seek a warmer and less bracing air. Asthma is also markedly affected by Dakota air, which, moreover, is more beneficial than that of Colorado, or other elevated regions, in cases of heart disease, complicated by asthma, bronchitis or indigestion. The large amount of soda in the soil makes the wheat of Dakota especially healthful, while from its large amount of nitrogenous elements the use of this staple supplants the demand for meat.—[Chicago Daily news.

The friends of Mervine Thompson, the Cleveland slugger, are ready to back him for $25,000 against Sullivan. Thompson easily knocked out Stewart, champion of Canada, and Welch, champion of Pennsylvania. Sullivan was challenged some time ago by Ross, Thompson's backer, but nothing has been heard from the “culchahed” slugger.

A Russian noble recently lost $400,000 at cards in a single night at Paris. He lost the money at the Parisian club and it is thought he was cheated out of the amount as recent discoveries of marked cards have been made there, and some of the members have been incontinently “fired.”

A total of 1,450 live cattle, [316?] live sheep, 10,566 quarters of dressed beef, 2,125 carcasses of mutton and 50 dressed pigs were exported from New York last week.—[Stockman.

The numerous inquiries for good stock ranches by men who are looking for locations in the new West would indicate an active business in all kinds of stock the coming season.—[Boomerang.

There is a perfect unanimity of opinion among all our exchanges relative to the condition of stock on the range. The report comes from all sides that cattle have never been in better condition at this season of the year.

Several subscribers ask for a remedy to keep lice off cattle. One ounce of crude carbolic acid mixed in one quart of water and applied warm is recommended as a sure cure. It also possesses healing properties—[Colorado Farmer.

Stock in this section is wintering splendidly, and we hear of no losses in the immediate neighborhood. We learn however, that parties on the Upper Poudre have lost considerably, the loss occurring entirely among herds that have recently been brought from the East.—[Loveland Leader.

The River Falls Cattle Company, whose range is on Powder river, will make a heavy shipment of stock cattle to this country early in the spring. Several members of the company are now in the East making purchases, and it is their intention to ship no less than 2,000 head.—[Miles City Press.

Parties in from Cherokee strip report cattle in good shape and well scattered out over the ranges. Plenty of good grass, water and appetites are taking the old sisters and families through in good shape. The boys would not give one per cent to have any one insure them ninety per cent of calves from their entire cow herds this spring.—[Caldwell Journal.

The grazing lands of Dakota, Montana, Colorado, Nebraska, Wyoming, Eastern Oregon and Idaho are estimated at 1,000,000,000 acres. The Northern Pacific railroad is now opening up a region capable of supporting 5,000,000 cattle and 10,000,000 sheep, which when it shall be fully occupied, can export yearly 600,000 cattle, 1,500,000 sheep and 10,000,000 pounds of wool.—[Northwest.

A Dallas, Tex., dispatch of the 7th says that information has been received here to the effect that George B. Loving, of this State, who is now in England representing the Texas Improvement Company, has sold a large amount of ranch property situated in four adjoining counties, on Double Mountain fork of the Brazos river, for $2,500,000. This is said to be the largest live stock transaction ever made.

It takes eleven pounds of milk to add one pound of live weight to a calf, and an ox that weighs 1,300 pounds will consume twenty-two pounds of hay in twenty-four hours to keep from losing weight. If he is to fatten he must have just twice that quanty, when he will gain two pounds a day. This is one pound live weight to eleven pounds of good hay. To obtain fifty cents a hundred for his hay a farmer must sell fat steers at $5.50 per hundred pounds.—]N. W. L. S. Journal.

We received a call last week from a young Mexican residing at Monclova, Miguel Arguindegui, who is interested in ranching in the state of Coahuila. He reports a good season and says stock are doing well. Speaking of selling cattle or other stock under estray laws, he says they are sold whenever it is found that the brand has not been recorded and no owner appears. At any time within six months the money may be reclaimed, but after that time it goes to the public. Brands should be recorded at the capital of a state, whence they will be forwarded to the different municipalities for general recording.—[Texas L. S. Journal.

The one thing our Northwestern cattle growers seem to be a “little off” in is the placing of strange cattle upon their ranges late in the season, so late that they do not become familiar with their surroundings until the winter is upon them. During the warm, pleasant days of the late spring and early summer animals will at once go to work on the inviting green sward, and very soon become as if to the manor born. But late in the season they have a disposition to wander in search of other and perhaps better ranges. They are restless and nervous, and do not take on fat preparatory for nature's trial season. In order to withstand the rigors of our northern climate, range animals need to be at home. Dumb animals have nerves and temperaments just as men have. They don't want any cheap “boarding house” experience. They want a regular home table, at which they are masters of ceremony. In order to acquire that contented feeling, they must be on the range in time to learn all the characteristics of their surroundings. Then they are contented and happy. Under such conditions will they take on fat and develop rapidly. If our herd owners would get all their cattle on the range by the middle of July each year the mortality of the range would be almost entirely overcome. Who ever heard of a native dying in this country from the vicissitudes of the climate? Of course, there is an occasional cow dies in the early spring from the effects of calf-dropping, but the bulk of the losses are confined to “rawhides,” or late arrivals.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.
James Hannigan took in Bismarck and Mandan last week.
George Smith made ye typo “smile” in the absence of the editor last week.
W. G. Hollins, one of Mandan's most prominent lawyers, was in town last week.
Jos. Pennell has gone to St. Paul to meet the Marquis and complete arrangements as to the freight route.
Hayes Moore is in from the Killdeer mountains country where he has a first-rate ranch. He expects to stay but a short time.
We will doubtless surprise our readers by the early appearance of THE COW BOY this morning, but a glance at our editorial page will disclose the reason.
The Tongue river bridge at Miles City was washed away by the flood of Sunday, and no passenger train came through from the west until yesterday morning.
It is a magnificent sight to see the torrents of water rushing along on the ice of the Little Missouri river. When the ice breaks, however, the present spectacle will fade into insignificance.
Messrs. Jones, of Deadwood; Meeks, of Sully, and Avery, of Augusta, Me., called during our absence. We regret not having seen the gentlemen and hope they will call again when we are “to hum.”

We made a trip to Bismarck and Mandan last Friday and Saturday and did not meet a person who had not read and liked THE COW BOY. Without a solitary solicitation on our part we received eleven cash subscribers.

Frank Smith, not to be outdone by his brother, yesterday brought in a petrifaction of a piece of cottonwood which seems to have petrified after the wood had dried and the veins separated slightly. It is a very curious specimen.

Messrs. Paddock and Roberts will soon do something for which the citizens will rise up and call them blessed. They propose to haul fifty or seventy-five loads of scoria and distribute it along the streets, thus forming a good road-bed even in the muddiest times.

Daniel Friedman started for Minnesota last Friday to buy cattle for Wm. Dantz. The latter will also start soon for the same purpose. They expect to buy 700 or 800 head, perhaps more. They return about April 1, and will drive the cattle to Mr. Dantz' present ranch.

Subscriptions are coming in from places where we least expected them. From Minnesota especially we have received many subscriptions. A total stranger to us writes: “THE COW BOY suits me so well that you can count me as a subscriber until it gets to be an old man.”

Lloyd Boberts started East last week to buy cattle. As we stated in a previous issue, Mr. Roberts is the pioneer cattle man of the Bad Lands. He has a good ranch about ten miles up the river and will stock it with first-rate cattle from Minnesota and Iowa. He will return in about a month.

E. G. Paddock has gone into partnership with Frank Moore to run the Pyramid Park Hotel. Many improvements will be made in the building, especially in the way of cutting up the second floor into rooms. The rush of tourists in the summer will undoubtedly repay the outlay abundantly.

Geo. Fitzgerald's wounded hand presents an appearance that a surgeon would call beautiful. Since the time of the accident the wound has not presented an unfavorable symptom and is now almost entirely healed. The action of the third finger may be enfeebled, but there is no danger of losing it.

Stockmen readily appreciate the value of inserting their brands in THE COW BOY and several have come in lately. In the near future we will get new cuts much superior to those we now have and put our stockmen's brands on them without extra charge. It will be expensive, but as we will pay particular attention to this branch of advertising we propose to have the best.

Messrs. George Smith and Edwin Bulpin are the two latest contributors to our museum of Bad Lands curiosities. Mr. Smith donated two splendid specimens of scoria with a perfect impression of a leaf on each. Mr. Bulpin's gift was several fine specimens of gypsum and agate. Our collection seems to have awakened an active interest and although it will take a long time to obtain a complete collection its ultimate success is assured.

We will make a specialty of our “Sporting Notes” and in the same column will answer any question addressed to us on the subject. All questions that we cannot answer immediately we will get authority for before publishing the answer. We also make a specialty of records made in all sports and in the course of a season a careful perusal of our “Sporting Notes” will enable a reader of THE COW BOY to decide almost any question relative to sports.

The last report we heard about the men who stole the horses at Matthews' camp was that a posse had started in pursuit with every prospect of capturing them. It is very probable that if the thieves are caught it will occur to the captors that Mandan is altogether too far to take them for trial, and an impromptu necktie festival will be held. The Bad Lands has been wonderfully free from the depredations of horse thieves, and a dose of the above kind of medicine will tend to discourage any future attempts of the kind.
OUR FREIGHT ROUTE. With a Big “OUR.”

Now that the matter is decided and only the final preliminaries to the opening remain to be settled concerning our freight route, things wear a rosy aspect that causes that “quiet smile to percolate about our features” in a manner wonderful to behold.

The gang of men that started out a week ago to-day, staked out the road to the level ridge east of the Little Missouri valley and found that there was only one place where the teams would have to be doubled. Grading will remedy this and after the ridge is reached, no difficulty at all is experienced clear to Deadwood. There is an abundance of wood and water and the route as a whole is a model one, better even than the old Bismarck-Deadwood route except for the few hills encountered before leaving the Bad Lands.

Mail stations have been picked out and the petitions have been forwarded to Washington. By this time probably, they have official sanction. They are three in number, the first at Grand river, Billings county; the second at Moreau, Harding county and the third at Belle, Butte county.

As we prophesied in our last issue, the route is now a question of a very short time. The trial trip will be made as soon as possible.

Mr. Clark, of Little Falls, Minn., who has been with us several days has concluded to stay and make this his home. He will certainly find that he has used good judgment in coming to this decision and he will undoubtedly make us a valuable citizen.

To the land of the Dakotas,
To the region known as Bad Lands,
Came a festive lightning jerker,
“Which his name” was Edwin Bulpin.
Quick he was with ear and finger
To receive or send a message,
But his telegraphic learning
Helped him none in going hunting.
On the balmy day of Monday
When Chinook was softly blowing
Melting all the winter's snow-fall
Till the brooks were turned to rivers
And the creeks to mighty torrents,
Making mellow all the butte sides
By the death blow to the frost king,
Edwin started forth a hunting.
Tramped he with a stubborn purpose
Up and down the sloping coolies
On the buttes and in the canons
Till he saw a bird of omen
Of the Accipitres order
And the family Strigidae
In other words a common night owl,
Solemn-looking, blinking, staring,
Wishing for the we'come night-time
When it might pursue its booty.
Edwin saw it at distance
And he crept and crawled and wiggled
Till the muzzle of his rifle
Almost touched the owl's tail feathers.
Shut he both his optics closely!
Held his breath and pulled the trigger,
Then he looked at where the owl was,
Looked and wondered where he could be,
Till at last he thought that he had
Blown him out of all existence,
Stepped he forward to examine
And the treacherous butte-side yielded,
Giving way beneath the pressure
Of the No. 12's of Edwin.
Down he rolled with wild gyrations
To the bottom of the coolie.
Full two hundred lengthened paces
Was the depth where he had fallen
And the earth, soft with the melting,
Closed around him like a mantle,
Lying flat in this position
Edwin saw the bird of omen
Far above him on a cedar,
Thoughtful-looking and a wond'ring,
What the—skip it—was the matter.

We wish to call the especial attention of our readers to the advertisements of M. Kline and Mahar & Drury, of Mandan. Mr. Kline, by the excellence of his cigars has controlled that trade since his arrival at Mandan and he now proposes to put out a new and first-class brand, for sale exclusively at this point. We are expecting a box every day and our friends will then have a treat, as we never were known to use the naughty weed. Every one who has been in Mandan knows Tom Mahar and Ed Drury and will be pleased to know that the new firm is enjoying unbounded prosperity.

Messrs. Geo. Blankenberg and R. H. Montgomery, of Belfield, made Medora a visit Tuesday. They report good prospects for their town. Indeed, there is no reason why Belfield should not be one of the best towns in Western Dakota. It possesses many natural advantages and men of energy and capital are calling the attention of emigrants to it. What is Belfield's gain is our gain and we hope that it will be all its most sanguine friends wish.

Since our first issue we have not seen an article in any of our exchanges relative to lawlessness in Little Missouri. We do not know whether our articles had the effect of stopping the scurrilous attacks or not. Certain it is they have ceased. The future of both Medora and Little Missouri is assured and the attacks referred to will soon be only a matter of remembrance.

Messrs. Pennell & Roberts have kindly offered their large room over the “Senate” for the use of the stockmen for the meeting to-day. It is the only available room of sufficient size to be had. All reports from above show that a full meeting will be held, as every cow-man on the river takes a deep interest in the matters to be discussed.

The Cœur D'Alene mines craze seems to have abated considerably. A man who has wintered here and will leave just as soon as the worst part of the season has passed and such bright prospects are constantly opening, should have a keeper appointed for him.

LITTLE MISSOURI, Feb. 27, 1884.

EDITOR COW BOY:

Another week is here, and more good things with it. Among them will be the coming meeting of the stockmen and the always welcome COW BOY.

Howard Eaton, must be frozen up and afraid that the visitors will be likewise afflicted, as he has chosen a place where hot water with some other stuff in it can be had.

We're informed that he is credited with the authorship of our last letter, but he hasn't any “savvey” as the Greasers say, about writing for a newspaper and is an innocent cuss in this matter. Frank Moore is also blamed, but the smarties are just as far off about him. “How” is a man who could just about fill Geary Paddock's clothes.

Many distinguished guests have come to the metropolis lately. Among them we noticed Charlie Mason, Nitche, Boland and other bloods.

Jack Bullion rides a good horse when he shows up in town.

Billy Paddock has come out as a hunter and guide since he quit cow punching. He intends to open an office and give all tourists the “proper steer” to the happy land. His last trip was with Weeks, of New York, and Hampton, of Columbia, S. C. Billy showed them the burning mine and then they rode down Custer's trail to Eaton's cow camp. Here the boys took in the eagle, wild geese, deer and buffalo, then came back here, and he kindly showed them how to oil their saddles so they wouldn't wear out the leather on a hunting trip of that kind.

A long man is apt to wear out a good saddle, especially if he has not ridden for a few months and is out of practice. Weeks and Hampton left here “very sore” but well pleased with their vist to this wonderful place. They hope to return in the hunting season.

Mose Ryder, with the gospel crew Moody and Sankey, is still up-river making his everlasting fortune. Nitche says that they had been very successful at the time he passed. They had only been at work four days and had almost one hundred posts cut. Senator Jones lends an airy dignity and respectabilty to the gang Mose says that he can't work as he used to do before he fell in the ditch near the railroad. He hurt his leg and caught “Jessie” generally.

If Steiger had been there a great contest would have occurred, as Mose wanted that claim sure.

Capt. Moore and John Nelson didn't tumble in time to join the gang, so had to climb up to the old garden.

It's tough on a Christain to read all we've written, but your patience is like Job's “biles,” slow to come to a head.

Some day we'll write again, until then

HOW.

LITTLE MISSOURI, FEB. 24, 1884.

EDITOR COW BOY:

In your last issue some pilgrim who signs his name “How” had a lot of stuff about the old times in Little Missouri. He gives himself dead away. It was Frank Moore who nearly killed the drunken butcher, when the fight occurred in the back room. I was there and know about that. So does Paddock, Henry Hudson and lots of the other folks who were here then.

There never was such a man as “Bloody Hand” here. The party referred to was called “Stug” or “Guitar Strings” or some such name. I know for I was there and knew all the parties well.

“How” had better dry up on things he don't know anything about.

Will write soon again.

POST T. RADER.

LITTLE MISSOURI, Feb. 26.

EDITOR COW BOY:

In your paper of last week, I noticed a line about the buffalo shot here and a request for some hump and tender steaks. I would be a mighty mean man to impose on a “tenderfoot,” who wore a four-dollar set of store teeth, by sending him a steak that would “bust his gums” as well as his teeth. Wait until you become a “tough” and hold the garden claim, old boy, then I'll fire hump at you for a week right along. It's better to do so than to ring in any veteran of the herd on you now. If you got outside ten or twelve pounds of that steak you would pass in your chips, and some vandal would plant a tent and stake (steak) a claim on your grave.

Sadly yours,

HOWARD EATON.

Dispatches from St. Paul state that Messrs. Pennell and Jones have signed contracts for 17,000,000 pounds of freight from Chicago, St. Paul and Minneapolis via Little Missouri crossing to the Black Hills. Jones will put on seventy-five teams, Pennell forty-five and Larson forty as a starter. Immediate arrangements will be concluded, however, to enlarge the transportation facilities. The stage and mail line will also be put on as soon as possible. Most of the bullion product of the Black Hills mines has also been contracted for and will be taken over our line instead of the old Pierre line as formerly. Last year Deadwood's carrying trade was 40,000,000 pounds. This year it will doubtless go over 50,000,000 pounds.

We wonder if our citizens fully realize what the success of this route means. It means success for the town and every person in it. It means a large number of new citizens. It means new houses and new stores. It means one of the largest circulating mediums of any town on the line. In itself it means all this. Were it not for the freight route, there would surely have been a large and flourishing city here. With it, it means a flourishing city from the start. The capital and labor will be here first and these will draw a large number of citizens. The start given it by the freight route will receive a fresh impetus by its being made the cattle headquarters of a large extent of territory and doubtless in a short time the headquarters of the whole Northwest.

At the present time there is no point on the line between Mandan and Helena, and we think can safely say between Minneapolis and Portland, which has as large a cash backing as this point. There is an abundance of money and Marquis de Mores has shown that he is not all afraid to spend his share in anything to increase the general welfare. We do not need to create a boom here. It is already upon us. The next year will witness such an improvement as will astonish even the most sanguine. At least twenty-five letters have been received at The Cow Boy office alone from persons thinking of settling here. The success of our freight route will be the deciding point. They and hundreds of others will see the advantage of coming here and our little town will soon be alive with the bustle of incoming citizens.

The proceedings of the meeting held at Little Missouri in Pennell & Roberts' hall, Thursday afternoon, Feb. 28, are as follows:

The meeting was called to order at 2 o'clock by Howard Eaton, who nominated Mr. B. Barr for chairman. There being no other nominees, Mr. Barr was declared unanimously elected. In the same way A. T. Packard was elected secretary.

Appropriate remarks were made by the chairman as to the purpose of the meeting. He showed plainly the need of organization, and his words met the approval of all present.

Mr. J. L. Truscott stated as the reason for the absence of several cattle men that they thought it was only a meeting to organize for the round-up and also that the river having risen so much it was almost impossible to get here.

The secretary moved, and Mr. Eaton seconded the motion, that a committee of four, including the chairman, be appointed to draw up an order of business. The chair appointed Messrs. Packard, Eaton and Truscott. Pending their report a recess of ten minutes was held.

The meeting being again called to order, the report of the committee was read by the secretary.

The first article was, "That this meeting be considered as only preliminary to a meeting held on a date to be decided by a call committee." Carried.

"The object of this article is that no definite steps should be taken at this meeting for a Bad Lands organization. Many of the most prominent cattle men are absent owing to the impossibility of getting here, and all should fully understand the object of the meeting beforehand and have a voice in its organization."

The second article was, "That a committee of five be appointed to call a meeting for the organization of the Bad Lands cattle men, to report at that meeting a constitution and by-laws and any other business to come up for consideration for the governing of the above association when organized." Carried, with an amendment by Mr. Eaton that the chairman of this meeting be appointed on the committee. The chair appointed Messrs. Eaton, Packard, Merrifield and Paddock four members of the committee, himself constituting the fifth.

The third article was, "That a committee of three be appointed to draw up a call for the organization of a Territorial association. Carried, with the understanding that the chair should appoint three influential men on the committee and notify each man of his appointment, and instruct them to draw up the call.

The last article was that a list of names should be prepared of the men interested in cattle anywhere in this vicinity. The following list was obtained: Dickey Bros., Stoneville; Clark & Plum, Spearfish; Driscoll & Son, Spearfish; Hughes & Simpson, Stoneville; Continental Cattle Co., Stoneville; Towers & Gudgell, Keith, Mont.; Berry, Boice & Co., Keith, Mont.; Gregor Lang, J. L. Truscott, Wm. Dantz, Bullion & Marsh, D. K. Wade, J. L. Roberts, Ferris & Merrifield, E. W. Casey & Co., Marquis de Mores, E. G. Paddock, Wm.
