Little Rock Special: Advices from the Texas border represent that stockmen are making an effort leading to congressional action in the matter of establishing a permanent cattle trail running from the line of that state via Kansas and Indian Territory to the west. Some time ago the cattle men addressed a memorial to Secretary Teller asking him to use his authority to prevent the closing of what is known as the Western trail, which runs through lands belonging to the Cheyenne-Arapahoe agency in Indian Territory, and which lands have been leased for a term of years to a syndicate of sotckmen and inclosed with fences. It is understood that Mr. Teller has given the memorial consideration and that the trail will be kept open this season at least. The lessees state that the fence is so arranged that herds can be passed through the lands without trouble. However the question of a permanent trail is a serious one to to the stock-growing interest of the south-west. The shipping of stock to the western markets and ranges is owing to the high freight charges and distance from railroads, impracticable in most cases The difficulty in passing herds over the present trail is likewise great in Kansas and elsewhere. Settlers have taken up lands along the trail and given herdsmen trouble by claiming damages for trespass and for water. The drive this year is expected to foot up many hundred thousand head and next season will probably double that number. In view of the immense pecuniary interest involved, it is deemed advisable to have congress locate a permanent trail, thus giving a guarantee to stock growers that there will be no obstacle in the way of getting stock to western markets. It is believed that all the stock associations in the country will take action in the matter, and that a vigorous and concerted movement will be made on congress to secure the desired trail.

The worst storm of the season has been raging here for the past three days, and poor stock will no doubt feel the effects severely. A fierce wind has been blowing from the north and northwest since Monday, accompanied by snow, with hail occasionally for a variation. Tuesday morning the thermometer showed three degrees below zero and yesterday — degrees. While the snow is a stem-winder and no mistake, we do not anticipate any considerable loss of stock from the fact that the bulk of the stock is still strong and able to endure a very hard racket.—[Medicine Lodge, Kan., Cresset.

The Idaho Register says that stock in that part of the country is as fat as butter and requires no feeding.

At a meeting of the stockholders of the Converse Cattle Company, held last Saturday, all the shares being represented, the capital stock was increased from $550,000 to $1,000,000. The calves on the range grow so rapidly that it keeps the owners busy to keep up with them.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

Mr. Charles Wheeler has sold to E. Johnson and Wm. Parker his ranch and about 3,000 head of stock. The property is among the finest in Colfax county and includes a fine range. The purchase makes the parties owners of about 10,000 head of stock. The price paid is understood to be $85,000.—[Colorado Live Stock Journal.

A delayed correspondence from Fort Laramie, dated the 4th, which reached here the 9th, says the snow has all gone and the grass is green. Cattle on the range are looking well. The Laramie river is open and cattle get plenty of water. The only fatalities heard of are three or four calves dying from black leg. The outlook is very promising.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

The calf crop will be an average one—neither light nor heavy in numbers, a trifle better though on account of more and better bulls being on the range than heretofore. To inquiring minds wishing to know how stock are wintering in Texas we can safely say they are doing well, better than average. Losses none to speak of. Certainly not from bad weather or shortness of range.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

The Durbin Land and Cattle Company filed articles of incorporation at the office of the secretary of the territory and county clerk yesterday. The incorporators and officers are: John H. Durbin and Thomas F. Durbin, of Cheyenne; Godfrey Snydacker, Morris Rosenbaum and Joseph Rosenbaum, of Illinois. The principal office will be in Cheyenne. Capital $750,000, paid up in full.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

Stockmen in the northern part of the State fear the late heavy snow and cold weather will result in the loss of cattle. The ranges around Pueblo, and in fact anywhere south of the divide, are exempt from this danger. We sometimes lack sufficient moisture during the winter and spring to insure good grass, and stock does not take on flesh so fast as in colder localities, but we never lose any cattle by heavy snows and cold weather.—[Pueblo, Colo., Star.

The Messrs. McDowell, of Hunnewell, have taken the safe plan this winter of carrying their poor cattle through. They drove their cattle from below last summer, held them on the range till after frost, then cut out all the poor ones and drove them into the State, where they are feeding them hay and millet and running them in stalk fields. By this plan they are safely carrying their herd through with very slight loss. They expect to save the lives of enough cattle to pay all expenses of the feeding, etc., and have all their cattle in good shape for the summer.—[Caldwell, Kan., Journal.

Hon. J. B. Grinnell, of Iowa, recently prepared and sent on to the press an extensive paper on "Legislation for the Suppression of Contagious Diseases Among Animals." The document was lengthy and well loaded down with arguments and statistics which were calculated to show the importance of maintaining cleanliness and purity of our meats. He gave the following "head-line" facts, which give one some idea of the magnitude of our cattle interests:

1. There is an investment of $1,008,000,000 in cattle, as estimated by the department of agriculture, representing 41,171,000 animals. That of swine is $291,000,000, representing over 43,000,000 animals.

2. The losses annually on exportation of cattle and beef, consequent upon restrictive regulations and the decreased relative consumption of our beef, aggregate many millions of dollars. We reach an approximate estimate by these facts relative to our foreign trade as follows:

The exports of 1880-81 were 368,463 animals; those of 1882-83 were 212,551—a loss of 155,000 animals, and in value a loss of $11,506,000 in two years.

The exports of fresh beef for two years were less by 50,071,167 pounds and by value $2,191,190. The value of pork products decreased in the same time to the extent of $35,679,093.

This shows a falling off of about $25,000,000 per annum for two years, as compared with the receipts for the preceding years.

No nation has so large a relative portion of its wealth in domestic animals, and none can show such strides in material advancement during the present century. But what is our foreign trade? The exports of provisions from the United States during the last fiscal year were in value about $107,000,000; those in 1882 amounted to $120,000,000, equal to a falling off in a single year of $13,000,000. Our exports of manufactured articles for the last year aggregate $211,000,000 against $103,000,000, a gain of $108,000,000 in a single year. It was a reasonable expectation that our animal exports would have increased in like ratio as the manufactures, which would have enhanced the value of all domestic animals and furnished, instead of a mortifying fact, a proud exhibit.

The causes of a decline are not found in high prices at home nor in inferior products; rather in suspicion of diseases and the clamor of interested parties, which led to arbitrary restrictions, oppressive quarantine regulations and forbidding beeves which were ripened for the highest markets to pass beyond the shambles, and the egress of young premature cattle on the English pastures. Pork products up to the Chicago meeting were prohibited by France, and they are inhibited now from Germany, our long-time valuable customer. It was their whims, caprices, jealousies, commercial restrictions and bans which decreased our exports and led the commissioners of agriculture to call the Chicago meeting of November.

That convention developed facts and was fruitful in results. That there were solitary cases of pleuro-pneumonia and limited to the eastern border states, that western herdsmen had just cause of alarm on account of the shipment of young stock west from the narrow pastures and dairy districts of the east. It was shown that across the ocean there was a morbid appetite for suspicions and facts that would justify severe restrictions and an absolute inhibition of our products.

The cattle commission formed by the treasury department gave decided opinions and imparted valuable information, but were constrained to admit that they were powerless in an emergency to stop the spread of contagious diseases, and that it was a vain hope there would be an increased foreign demand for our cattle and meat without radical congressional enactment.

Who can be indifferent in the face of our great perils and recounting the losses by foreign restrictions? We are emphatically a nation of beef eaters, and by the extent of our domain and beautiful climate are justly entitled to the honored designation of the first producer among civilized nations. It is the question of healthful food for the masses, of profitable tonnage for the railways and of deep concern in cultivating fraternal relations abroad, not less than a question for the political economist in maintaining a good trade balance sheet. If we can impress our congressional delegation with the necessity of early and decisive legislation we shall have accomplished a noble work and have earned the warm commendation of millions of citizens whose interests have been neglected and whose vocation and property have been imperiled.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

The hide and pelt business of Colorado and New Mexico last year amounted to $2,500,000. Colorado had by far the greater number of hides, while New Mexico excelled in the matter of pelts. The goat skins of New Mexico alone amounted to $300,000.

The Ogalalla Land and Cattle company have just purchased the Bosler herd of cattle, numbering from thirty-five to forty thousand head, paying $1,250,000. The Ogalalla company is a new outfit but has unlimited capital and is now one of the largest outfits on the range. [Sidney P.-Telegraph.
Marquis de Mores will return in about a week.
Read the report of the cattle meeting and send in your list of cattle men.
Howard Eaton has been shipping in lumber for a large stock barn which he will soon erect on his ranch.
Mrs. McNanny, sister of E. G. Paddock, has gone to Minneapolis to have her eyes treated. She expects to return soon.
Frank Chase, of the Killdeer mountains region, was in town and will start back to-morrow with Mr. Clark, who intends visiting him for a short time.
Large preparations have been made for the dance at the Pyramid Park hotel to-morrow evening and it will doubtless be largely attended. All are invited.
Edwin Bulpin has resigned from the region of owls and man-slides for one of jack-rabbits, in other words, for Idaho. Hugh Flynn, of Mandan, takes his place.
Wm. Smith, cattle inspector for Montana, was here last Sunday. He had been in pursuit of some thieves and came here to see about the Marquis' ponies stolen recently.
As many of our friends can testify, Mr. Kline sent that box of cigars and the "De Mores," as the new brand is called, is already an established favorite. The cigars will soon be on sale.
Rev. Cooke, of Gladstone, held two services last Sunday at the Cantonment. His preaching was able and well received. We hope Mr. Cooke will make it convenient to come here often.
A cow-boy here was being catechised by a minister and gave some rather unique answers. In reply to the question "What is the noblest work of God?" he replied, "THE BAD LANDS COW BOY."
The best specimens of gypsum we have yet seen were brought in and added to our collection by Frank Smith. The Smith Brothers alone, if they keep on, will give us a splendid collection by fall.

Frank Coughlan started for New York last Saturday. He is firmly impressed with the advantages this country possesses for young men and will return as soon as possible. He left two Indian arrows with us as mementoes.

J. H. Rising, who has filled the position of night operator for some time past, has gone home to Hillsdale, Mich. Mr. Rising was a general favorite, and we are sorry to lose him. Mr. Harris, of Dickinson, takes his place here.

John Keefer handed us a rib of a beef that is certainly an anatomical curiosity. The rib has been broken and over-lapped but it is almost impossible to see the line of knitting on one side. On the other the bones are separated half an inch.

The "Sankey" part of the gospel firm came in yesterday for repairs or something. He says that the "Big-foot" Ryder gang have cut 1500 posts and hauled them to the bank of the river. Their "everlasting fortunes" are just in sight.

Several visitors called during our visit to Belfied the first of the week. Our sorrow at this fact, however, is wonderfully tempered by the remembrance of the pleasant evening spent with Mrs. Fred Ertel and Miss Nellie Dailie, at Belfield.

If the Northern Pacific road is noted for one thing more than another, it is for the good qualities of the hotel men along its line. One of the best of them is Max Bass, of Belfield. Max is a thorough hotel man and is also a boomer from way back on the beauties of Belfield.

The boarders at the Hotel de Mores all unite in thanking Mr. Z. Hyde for the prairie chicken dinner for which he furnished the chickens this noon. That all of them were shot with a rifle, some of them being on the wing, sufficiently testifies to Mr. Hyde's skill as a marksman.

J. A. Ferris started for Mandan last Saturday to buy a stock of dry goods. He will open soon and will doubtless be successful in his venture. Mr. Ferris is widely known as a reliable man and under his administration there will not be a repetition of the "Wall street failure!"

The sad news came in yesterday morning that J. L. Truscott's father had died the day before in New York. Mr. Gibbs started immediately for Mr. Truscott's ranch. The news, though not personal to any one here, will strike all with a feeling of sadness as Mr. Truscott has endeared himself to every cattle man in the Bad Lands.

Mr. W. E. Bean, of Mt. Sterling, Ky., writes us a valuable letter concerning blooded stock and also encloses copy for an advertisement which will be of interest to our cattle men, and is found in another column. Mr. Bean is an old and experienced breeder and an enthusiast on blooded stock. Questions addressed him by our stockmen would probably bring out many valuable points.

For any tourist who has visited the Bad Lands to say that he does not know Frank Moore and the Pyramid Park hotel is to argue himself unknown. In view of the certain boom which has already struck this point, every effort is being made to receive the influx of visitors which will come during the warm season. The Pyramid Park hotel will receive a thorough overhauling and every convenience will be added for the comfort of visitors. Many additions will be made, new rooms added and everything will be strictly first-class. Mr. E. G. Paddock will run a livery stable in connection with the hotel and every facility for viewing the wonders of the Bad Lands will be at hand. We are glad to notice this new departure and do not doubt that it will have every success.
Joe Pennell is still in St. Paul.
Bob Roberts went to Bismarck on the early train yesterday morning.

W. B. Milne, of the popular dry-goods house of Wyman, Mullin & VanDyke, of Minneapolis was in town yesterday and to-day. Mr. Milne is one of the boys and has made many friends since his arrival. He has the "cinch" on the dry-goods trade here. We hope he will come this way often.

It was more fun than a basket of monkeys to hear Arthur Smith yell: "By the bald-headed Mackinaw," as he took a header off his wagon and struck out for a bale of hay that had fallen into the Little Missouri and was floating toward the big Muddy amid the drifting ice at the rate of [ten?] miles an hour. He got the hay but haysn't dried out yet.

More than one heart will be struck with sorrow at the bereavement that Mr. and Mrs. Osterhaut have just endured. The little baby which had made itself a general favorite by its infantile beauty, died this morning. As Mr. Osterhaut moved up the river last week, it was impossible to learn more than the mere fact of the death and that it was entirely unexpected.

Our citizens have labored under one disadvantage which they will endure no longer. There has been no insurance agent here and great difficulty has been found in obtaining insurance. We wish to state that we have just received a commission as agent for the old reliable Springfield Ins. company, one of the best if not the best in the U. S. All insurance matters will be promptly attended to by writing to or calling at the Cow Boy office.

Jack Simmons, better known as "Black Jack" made Medora a flying visit yesterday. He is fresh from the Coeur D'Alene gold region. He reports great scarcity and costliness of provisions and much suffering on account of the snow. The gold regions as yet, are an experiment but he thinks the prospects are good. At any rate so many people will go in this spring and summer that it will be a good point for merchants and lumbermen. He has a saw-mill near the mines and will get to work with it as soon as possible.

The list of names published in our report of the cattle meeting is doubtless very incomplete. We wish every reader of The Cow Boy who knows any additional names would send them in immediately. It is necessary to get a full and complete list of all cattle men in the territory and those who will be actively interested in a Territorial organization. This would include many in Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, Minnesota and Iowa. All who know additional names will facilitate the work of the committee and confer a favor on the editor by sending them to The Cow Boy.

The meeting of stockmen held last Thursday did all that a full attendance of every man in the Bad Lands could have accomplished. It started the ball rolling that will eventually make this point the cattle headquarters of the Northwest. We do not care to go over the arguments again to proove this, for it is so manifest on its face. There is no argument against it and everything is in its favor. The bulk of the work now rests with the two committees. Upon these rests in a great measure the responsibility of making this point what it should be. Every member should realize the importance of his position and let no personal matters interfere with the performance of his committee duties. The report of both committees will probably be published in our next issue.

A Miles City special says that it is reported there that a remarkable death rate prevails among Marquis de Mores' sheep in the Little Missouri Bad Lands in Dakota, the result of poison. The Marquis has some enemies. Sheep on Montana ranges are healthy. The Marquis lost 6,000 out of 12,000. It can be accounted for on no other ground than that poison was administered by enemies of the Marquis, on account of the killing of O'Donnell last year.

The above article, clipped from The Evening Missourian, is too foolish even to contradict, were it not for the fact that it has been extensively copied and commented on by editors who should know more than to give it credence. The only and true reasons for the death of the sheep, as we stated in our last issue, were that they were fall-clipped, belonged to the Merino breed, were shipped in late in the fall and were entirely unacquainted with the ranges till after the snow flew. These are the reasons and none other for the death of the sheep. The long-wooled variety, shipped in at the same time, are doing as well as cattle.

Mr. Gregor Lang's herd of cattle, fifty miles up the river, are a standing advertisement for the Bad Lands and the best one they have ever had as a cattle country. They are mostly young cattle and were brought in here during the intense cold of January. On the way here they suffered severely from the effects of a railroad accident, many being hurt badly and all bruised more or less. On the day of their introduction to this country the thermometer was 48 degrees below zero. For about three weeks they were close-herded and fed on hay about five miles down the river. At the end of that period they were branded deeply and driven to the ranch up the river. Since that time has come some very cold weather, enough to test the endurance of old range cattle. These were mostly young cattle entirely unused to range life. They have not had a spear of hay fed them, they were driven upon a new range and branded deeply during the worst weather we have had, and not a solitary head has died from exposure. More than that, they are all fat and in good condition. There is no cattle country under the sun that can show a record like this. It is simply wonderful. When the cattle were driven on the range bets were freely offered that before spring was over half the herd would be dead and there were no takers. Do our readers wonder now why we desire to advertise the Bad Lands by our name and that we are proud to do so?

BELFIELD, Dak., March 4, 1884.
EDITOR COW BOY:

As Belfield has not yet been represented in The Cow Boy, will you permit your humble scribe to transmit the following few pointers in regard to this rising young town:

Belfield, although in its incipiency, is one of the most thriving and picturesque towns of the West Missouri country. Its population to-day numbers about 200 persons, which will double ere spring has fully set in. It is the center of as truly handsome an agricultural country as any portion of the "great and glorious Northwest" can boast of. In regard to productiveness it stands pre-eminently without a superior. Its close proximity to the Bad Lands admirably adapts it to successful stock raising. Lignite coal, of a very superior quality, is obtainable on almost every claim merely for the digging. One of the marked features of the town is the substantial manner in which its buildings have been erected, it sporting the finest residences of any town on the line.

The business community is composed of a fine hotel, general store, lumber yard, real estate office, saloon, postoffice and grocery. Among other improvements contemplated is a furniture factory, brick yard and elevator.

Our citizens have received the very pleasing information from Louis Hay, of the Townsite Company, that their agent in Sweden has organized a colony of 500 persons who will settle in Belfield and its immediate vicinity.

Mr. Ed. Gallien and family are expected to arrive from the east this evening, whither they were called by the death of Mr. Gallien's father. Mr. Brace Gallien will also return soon. These gentlemen have extensive interests here, having 100 head of cattle and about 1,500 acres of land, two or three hundred acres of which will be put under cultivation the coming season.

Belfield, unlike many other small towns, has not suffered for want of hotel accommodations. The Riverside Hotel, under the management of the enterprising and genial Max Bass, is one of the best on the line and figures very prominently as one of the important features in the development of the town.

Mr. Robt. Montgomery, or Bob. as he is familiary called, is on the sick list and his early recovery is hoped for by his many friends.

Jno. R. Thayer & Co., the popular lumber firm and contractors, will soon commence the erection of several business houses, among which will be a real estate office for Ertel & Houk.

Mr. T. J. Sharkey, traveling auditor of the Northern Pacific railroad, is in town inspecting the accounts of Mr. Frank B. B. Holmes, our accommodating station agent. Mr. Holmes' ability as a railroad man is unquestionable, and, of course, everything was found in first-class order.

Mr. F. H. Ertel is expected home from St. Paul the latter part of the week.

It is very amusing to see how enthusiastic the Dickinson people are over the proposed freight line, and our friend Scott says they are determined to push the road to completion as rapidly as time and money will permit, when we have it on good authority that they can't raise money enough to build a little bridge to enable the freighters to get out of their town. We think our sister city will soon put a damper on their enthusiasm.

The Bad Lands Cow Boy is meeting with great favor here, and the already large number of subscribers secured at this place will bear me out in this statement.

More to follow. SADIE.

The Miles City Journal has the first principles of journalistic courtesy yet to learn. It not only stole an article of ours in reference to the Bad Lands as a cattle country, but added a few lines making it applicable to the country about Miles City and published the whole as an original article, giving us not a particle of credit. Had the article appeared without any additions being made to it and no credit given to us, it would have been passed over as it might readily be an excusable mistake. The additions, however, showed that there was no mistake about the matter. It was a theft pure and simple. If the country about Miles City is so poor that it needs the aid of outside help to puff it, we would urge the cattle men to move down here. This crime of stealing articles to make up for a paucity of brains we believe should be punished by law as well as any other theft. What an editor writes is his stock in trade as much as are the goods of a merchant. The stealing of a stock in trade or any part of it is a punishable offense. Even in the short time we have been here we have repeatedly had our articles stolen, but never have we seen a more brazen-faced attempt than the one quoted above. A repetition of the offence may lead us to make a mild remonstrance. This article is merely a warning.

An illustration of the stir a newspaper can make, in calling attention to the place in which it is published, is seen in the case of The Bad Lands Cow Boy. The editor of that journal, together with others who are interested in Medora, have made up their minds that the route from the Black Hills to the Northern Pacific is best which has one terminus at Medora. The Dickinson people have made up their minds that it is from their town that the most reliable, best and quickest route must start. Not until The Cow Boy started and proclaimed to the world that Medora was to be the coming headquarters of a freight to the Hills, did any one outside the little town itself dream of such a project. Now Medora is getting a deal of advertising, not merely as a point at which beeves are slaughtered, but as a point of divergence to the Hills. Concerning the merits of the two routes—that via Dickinson and that via Medora—The Pioneer has nothing to say. If our correspondents who live up the road find that we decline to publish partisan statements which they may send in to us, it is to be hoped that they will realize that The Pioneer desires to steer clear of all the rocks of discord that it can.—[Mandan Pioneer.

We will now state the principal object of our making a collection of Bad Lands curiosities. We intend inside of a year to exhibit it at the Chicago exposition and perhaps at others. It will make a most interesting exhibit and will be the best possible advertisement of the Bad Lands.

This part of the country has been visited in the past few days with the most severe storm on range stock of the season. It began on Sunday morning with a slow, misty rain, which turned to ice as soon as it fell, covering ground, grass and every thing with a coating that was anything but pleasant for cattle to tackle. Sunday night and Monday it continued, changing to snow on Monday night, which continued during Tuesday and Wednesday until 10 A. M. About three inches of snow fell during that time. A strong wind Tuesday night drifted the snow into the low places, leaving the high places on the ranges covered by sleet. Yesterday about 10 o'clock the sun came out bright and shone nicely all day, melting the sleet off the high grass and making it possible for the range stock to get something to eat, the first since the storm began on Sunday morning. It is early yet to predict the result of the storm on the range below, but it is safe to say that the loss by this storm will be greater than all the previous losses this winter. Stock have suffered terribly in the last three days, and it is useless to deny the fact; but a few days of blue sky and warm south breezes will brighten up matters on the range amazingly.—Caldwell, Kan., Journal.

At the meeting of the committee of five held last evening at THE COW BOY office for the purpose of drafting by-laws and other business to come up before the Bad Lands organization, all the members of the committee were present, consisting of Messrs. Barr, Paddock, Eaton, Merrifield and Packard. It is, of course, understood, that all the by-laws and general business proposed by the committee are subjected to approval, rejection or amendment by the association. The by-laws are founded upon those of the Wyoming association as they are as near perfect as possible.

Every cattle man in the Bad Lands should carefully consider every point made by the committee [and?] come to the meeting with his mind [made?] up as to how he shall vote.

The committee is enthusiastic over the prospect of a successful organization and every stock man in the Bad Lands should take the personal interest in the association which alone means complete success.

It will be noticed that the meeting for organization includes all stock men, whether owning cattle, horses, mules or sheep, and that it is to be held the third Monday in April. This date does not conflict with other meetings and gives plenty of time before the spring round-up. It was also the unanimous opinion of the committee that all classes of stock men should join the association.

The following is the list of by-laws and other matters to come up for consideration when the association is organized:

BY-LAWS.

SECTION 1. This association shall be known as the Bad Lands Live Stock Association.

SEC. 2. The object of this association is to advance the interests of the stock growers and dealers in live stock of all kinds within the Bad Lands, and for the protection of the same against frauds and swindlers, and to prevent the stealing, taking and driving away of horned cattle, sheep, horses and other stock from the rightful owners thereof.

ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

SEC. 3. The affairs of this association shall be conducted and managed by a president, vice-president, secretary, treasurer and an executive committee, consisting of five members.

All permanent officers of the association shall be ex-officio members of this committee.

These officers and above-named committee shall be elected at the annual meeting of each year and shall serve until tne annual meeting following their election, or until their successors have been elected.

Written proxies, approved as genuine by the executive committee, may be voted at elections.

The executive committee is empowered to fill any vacancy that may occur by death or otherwise in their own body or among the officers of this association and the person so appointed shall hold his office until the next regular election.

DUTY OF OFFICERS.

SEC. 4. The president shall preside at all meetings of the association. He shall see that all the laws and regulations thereof are faithfully executed and perform such other duties as may be required of him in these laws, as well as such as may be necessary to secure the objects and best interests of this association not herein otherwise provided for.

SEC. 5. The vice-president, in the absence of the president, shall perform the duties of the latter and if both be absent at any meeting a president pro tem. may be elected.

SEC. 6. The secretary shall keep accurate minutes of the transactions of this association. He shall keep a roll of members and a correct account of all moneys received and shall pay the same to the treasurer. He shall write and send all communications as directed by the association. He shall draw all orders on the treasurer when directed by the executive committee and shall make a full report of all the transactions of his office at each annual session. He shall deliver to his successor all books and papers and other property in his possession belonging to the association and shall perform such other duties as may be required by these laws and regulations or by the association. He is authorized to employ a collector at a reasonable rate of compensation at such time as he may deem necessary.

SEC. 7. The treasurer of this association shall receive all moneys belonging to the same from the secretary and pay the same out only on the order of the executive committee, attested by the secretary as hereinbefore provided. He shall keep a correct account of all such moneys received and paid out. He shall make a report at each annual meeting of the association and at such other times as the association may direct, of all the transactions of his office, producing therewith vouchers for all moneys paid out. He shall deliver all books, papers, moneys and other property in his possession, belonging to the association, to his successor in office and shall give bond to the association in such sum and with such sureties as may be required by motion or otherwise, conditioned that he will faithfully perform all acts and things required of him in this section.

SEC. 8. The executive committee shall meet immediately after their election and appoint a chairman and secretary. This committee shall have entire control of the inspectors and all the business of the association during its adjournment. It shall audit all accounts and order vouchers for their proper payments to be drawn by the secretary on the treasurer. They shall represent the association before the board of county commissioners and the legislature and in other similar positions during adjournments of the association.

At each annual meeting, this committee shall make a report to the association in regard to matters requiring their attention and shall recommend such measures as they deem necessary.

MEETINGS.

SEC. 9. The annual meetings of this association shall be held on the third Monday in April at 10 a. m., at the Little Missouri crossing of the N. P. R. R. Place to be selected by the executive committee and proper notice published.

Special meetings may be called at any time by the president, or in his absence, by the vice-president, and shall be called whenever requested by five members.

Eleven members shall constitute a quorum for business at all meetings.

The call for a special meeting shall state the object of such meeting and no other business shall be transacted at such meeting.

ORDER OF BUSINESS AT MEETINGS.

1. Calling the roll.
2. Reading minutes of last meeting.
3. Election of new members.
4. Unfinished business.
5. Reports of officers.
6. Election of officers.
7. Election of executive committee.
8. Election of brand inspection committee.
9. General business.

MEMBERSHIP.

SEC. 10. No person shall be a member of this association except a stock grower as defined by the executive committee. To become a member of this association, any person must be proposed at an annual meeting by a member, each proposition shall be accompanied by the fee for admission hereinafter stated and shall be referred to a committee of three members who may report immediately. A ballot shall then be taken on the application and three black balls shall reject.

All persons admitted members bind themselves and their employes to the observance of all by-laws and resolutions of the association that are now in force or that may hereafter be adopted, on a penalty of forfeiture of membership.

Membership shall be personal. No firm as such shall be admitted, but any number of partners may become members by election and payment of entrance fee in each case.

ENTRANCE FEE, DUES AND ASSESSMENTS.

SEC. 11. The admission fee shall be fifteen (15) dollars payable at time of election, and no one shall become a member without such payment.

The dues shall be ten (10) dollars, payable at the annual meeting for the year following.

Any member failing to pay his dues before the next annual meeting when the same became due, shall cease to be a member.

Any member who has been dropped for non-payment of dues, shall before he can be re-elected pay to the secretary all dues and assessments for the period from his last payment to the date of his new application, as though he had remained a member.

All members shall be subjected, not oftener than once per annum, to an assessment not exceeding one cent per head for all cattle, horses, mules and sheep of which each man may at that time be the owner and no resignation shall be accepted until all dues and assessments are paid.

The assessment may be levied in the discretion of the executive committee and shall be payable when called for. Failure to pay on or before the annual meeting following date of such assessment, shall work a forfeiture of membership.

The fund so produced shall be collected by the secretary and paid to the treasurer, and shall become a part of the common fund of the association subject to such regulations as before provided.

SEC. 12. Any member who shall divulge the proceedings of, or any action taken in any meeting of the association to any person or persons, or do any act calculated or that may injure or defeat any proceeding or action of this association or officers thereof, that may be instituted for the purpose of its protection or that of any of its members under the laws of this Territory, or of these rules and regulations, or that may be subversive of the interests generally of the association shall have a fair and impartial hearing at a special meeting called for that purpose, or at the annual meeting, and if found guilty by a majority of the members present shall be expelled.

SEC. 13. Any member of the association who shall be expelled therefrom as aforesaid, shall not again be received as a member thereof, and stock growers generally shall be notified of such expulsion.

SEC. 14. Whenever it shall come to the knowledge of any member of the association that any person or persons are engaged in stealing or killing stock of any kind, he shall immediately notify the executive committee of the association, who shall be empowered to act in such manner as will, if possible, bring such person or persons to justice and recover said property.

SEC. 15. These laws, regulations and resolutions shall not be annulled or amended except at an annual meeting, and then only by a vote of two-thirds of the members present.

There is a limit to all things and the limit to the cattle business in the Bad Lands will be reached in three years at the farthest. Although many good ranges still remain, the most of them have been taken. New men are constantly coming in, old cattle men are re-stocking and soon the Bad Lands will have its quota of cattle. This fact annihilates the only argument that can be brought against the fabulous profits of cattle raising. The territory which can be used for the raising of cattle is limited. The demand is practically unlimited and constantly increasing. It is utterly impossible that there shall ever be an over-supply. The only question for social economists is: If cattle are worth from $40 to $60 a head with fifty millions of people to supply, what will they be worth and where will the cattle be raised to supply a hundred million persons?

Still Holds the Fort for the Freight-Route Is Ours,

The latest information settles the freight route question beyond all peradventure. Contracts have been made with the railroads for rates, with merchants for goods, and, alas, for the route that is "sunk in a gumbo slough," for the freight now at Dickinson, which will be shipped here and freighted to Deadwood from this point. Marquis de Mores has sent word from New York that a freight depot should be erected here immediately, not waiting either for his return or for the break in the weather. Six residence houses are also to be built at the same time.

The route from here is selected and needs almost no grading. It seems incredibly that such a good road exists right through the heart of the Bad Lands. We went out on it several miles, however, and with the exception of one little stream, which does not even need bridging, the road was as level as any street in a city. Of course, it is winding while in the Bad Lands, but except for this it is as good a road as can be found anywhere. We ask skeptics to not take any one's word for it, but go and be convinced for themselves.

It seems that John Cranston, the agent for the route, turned traitor and tried to sell out to the Pierre route. His scheme was nipped in the bud, however, and only the intervention of friends of Mr. Jones kept the latter from putting Cranston's skin in a very leaky condition with a six-shooter.

Mr. Roberts here has ordered all his stock to be in readiness to come in, and expects to start with full loads next week. Only one bridge is necessary and that will be built in a day or two.

Our citizens can now rest assured that in two weeks at the most the route will be in full operation. The first freight will consist partly of that which is now at Dickinson and there is plenty of bullion at Deadwood for the return trip.

A telegram was received this morning from Mr. Jones, dated at Deadwood, that the train should start from here as soon as possible.

On reading the last copy of The Dickidson Press we were surprised at either the inefficiency of the people who have the matter in hand there or the buncombe of The Press itself. Contrary to all our expectations, not a solitary thing has been done for the route from that place. In The Press account of the citizens' meeting the reports of two committees were heard. We quote:

"The committee appointed to confer with the Northern Pacific officials reported that the business entrusted to it had not yet been completed. The committee appointed to carry on correspondence with the boards of trade of St. Paul and Minneapolis reported that they had written to said boards of trade, but had as yet received no reply."

From previous issues of The Press we supposed that the road was decided upon and bridged in a great part at least. Again we quote:

"Under the head of new business, after some time spent arguing different points of interest, a motion that a committee of three be appointed to view the road and estimate the cost of constructing the necessary bridges on the route from this point south was appointed, consisting of John D, Barnes, L. W. Granteer and Wm. Walton. They will make the trip as soon as practicable, after which the work of bridging the streams will be commenced."

This needs no comment. The first thing they ought to have done was to see whether they had a good all-weather route. The Dickinson freight route then dwindles down to the bare fact that "as soon as practicable" the route will be "viewed." Oh, Scotty, thou hast given thyself away.

The Press in another article tries to prove that Dickinson will be the end of the freight route. But what are arguments compared to the hard, cold fact that "We've got there, Eli." A fair exchange is no robbery, Bro. Scott. You take the argument and we take the cake.

It seems almost incredible that there should be any opposition to organizing Billings county, but we know of two or three such cases. They are all either small or non-property holders, however, but lest their objections have some weight, it seems fitting that a few reasons should be advanced in favor of county organization.

In the first place, a failure to organize is an advertisement to the world that we are too poor to support a county organization. No one who knows this county and its capabilities would for an instant hold such a view, but to the prospective settler a lack of county organization would be prima facie evidence of its sterility.

As long as the county is unorganized we can do nothing toward bringing its advantages before the world. The greatest argument in favor of Billings county is the very fact of its becoming so rapidly settled in spite of itself.

The most potent reason for county organization, however, is that the laws may be applied by officers elected here at home. We are now under the jurisdiction of Morton county and when any case is to be tried or the application of the law in any way is wished for we must go to Mandan, one hundred and fifty-six miles east of us.

Take the case of a tenderfoot who comes here intending to go into the cattle business. He hears all sorts of lies about the desperate deeds of cow-boys and by the time he gets here is more than half inclined to turn around and go back. Suppose right on top of this he learns that the county is not organized, and that if any law is broken here, a telegram must call the sheriff from one hundred and sixty miles before the law-breaker can be arres[illegible] We have received, addressed to THE COW BOY, at least fifty letters from persons who think of coming here. At least a quarter of the writers wished to know about the county officers and whether they were well able to uphold the laws. The rest of the writers said nothing about it for the manifest reason that they thought the county was organized and the machinery running smoothly.

About the only reason urged against county organization is that the taxes will be so heavy. Of course, this reason has little or no weight with our best citizens as they know its falsity, those who do not know it we ask to consider for a moment the resources of Billings county. If all the rest of the world were shut off from us we could live as well as we do now, except for manufactured articles. We have as good agricultural, stock and mining land as there is on the face of the globe. There is no county in the United States that furnishes so many necessaries of life as does Billings. Consequently none can better afford organization.

SADIK.

To our cattle men the fact is so well known that the Bad Lands furnish the best cattle country in the world that there is no need of mentioning the subject. To our outside readers, however, this may need proof. We ask, then, what are the prime requisites for a cattle country? The answer is as plain as the question, food, water and shelter. The best of food is rich, nutritious hay. It is here in the Bad Lands in greater abundance than anywhere else. There never has been and there never can be a snowstorm in the Bad Lands sufficient to cover the grass. On account of the broken nature of the country there are always bare spots affording excellent grazing to new cattle. The old cattle which know how to rustle will paw away a foot of snow to get at their feed and be as fat as a mole all winter. This standing hay cures so well that it is actually superior to that which is cut and stacked. We have seen cattle turn away from a stack of hay, apparently in disgust, and commence grazing on the dry grass.

The falsity of the idea that the alkali in the water is any detriment has long since been proven. It is, in fact, one of the greatest helps. Cattle actually refuse to touch salt when they have access to alkali water, and thus the ranchman is relieved of a large expense for salt. There is water in abundance, but the cattle in the winter can get along almost as well on snow. The herd of cattle owned by Mr. Lang, which we spoke of in our last issue as contending with so many difficulties, has not had a drop of water for over two months, and yet is as fat as any herd on the range.

For shelter, however, the Bad Lands is unsurpassed. The force of the wind coming over the buttes is greatly broken and a few steps at any time will take a person into a coolie where the wind is absolutely unfelt. The sun is shining almost all the time, and in the coolies during the coldest days it is perfectly comfortable.

There are now in the Bad Lands many cattle men who have had experience in every cattle country in the United States and who own from one thousand to fifty thousand head of cattle. We have questioned many of them and the invariable answer has been that nowhere in the United States is there a better cattle country than the Bad Lands.

An inspection of several herds of cattle in Lyons county, Kan., shows the prevalence of foot and mouth disease in its most terrible and deadly form. The report tells of animals still alive but slowly falling to pieces. It is difficult to understand why they should be suffered to live and spread the disease, instead of being killed at once. Strong measures should be taken, and that without delay, to quarantine the infected district and prevent a wider dissemination of the scourge.—[Pioneer-Press.

By the law of Dakota the following property is exempt from execution for debt. Homesteads, one acre if within a town plat, and 160 acres if not, with house and appurtenances, unlimited in value. Exemption is absolute except as to taxes, mechanics' lien for work on the homestead, and debts created for the purchase thereof. Personal property exempt, $150, besides wearing apparel, books to the amount of $100, provisions for one year, family pictures, etc. Real estate or personal property is liable for its purchase money, otherwise the exemptions are as above stated. Married women retain their real and personal property, and may make contracts, sue and be sued, as if single. Neither husband nor wife has any interest in the property of the other. Dower and courtesy are abolished.—[The Northwest.

"Are there no real good Injuns?"
The cow-boy raised his head,
And glancing at the tenderfoot,
He turned to him and said:
"I rode the prairies, pardner,
Ten years in rain and sun,
But as to 'real good Injuns,'
I haven't met more nor one,
A swig o' that hoss liniment,
And then I'll try to place
This A 1 virtuous redskin
That for goodness trumped the ace,
'Twas at the bar at Mack's Ford,
A lot o' boys one day
Got to making things quite lively
In a ball and cartridge way,
I banged around about me,
And didn't count the odds—
I'd been soaking electricity
Like fifty lightning rods:
When suddenly the sheriff
And his gang came bounding down,
And the boys took to their cattle
And dusted outen town.
But suthin' was the matter
With my head works, I dare say,
For I stumbled by the roadside,
And I couldn't find my way;
And the next I can remember,
It was night, and pitchy black,
And I tried to strike the trail from there,
But couldn't hit a track,
And I was mighty dizzy
And felt I should have died,
When standing just before,
An Injun's shape I spied,
He held his hands out to me,
But I didn't say a word;
And when I tried to hail him,
He neither spoke nor stirred,
And then I slipped in somehow
Between each sturdy arm,
And then he let me down so gently,
Without a bit o' harm;
And I lay there quite contented,
And slept until 'twas day,
And woke to find him watching
At my side the same old way;
So I climbed upon my uprights,
And a word I couldn't say,
But I looked the red man in the face,
And then I sneaked away.
We parted. But, as years passed by,
I wonder more and more
If still that real good Injun stands
At Mack's tobacco store."
—[The Northwest.

The weakest article of all the maudlin trash that has appeared against our freight route emanated from a Dickinson numskull and was published in the Pioneer-Press of the 14th. The article says: "We claim, and with justice, that the best road to that point (Deadwood) is from Dickinson." How does this sound when taken in connection with the statement of The Dickinson Press that a committee was appointed to view the road as soon as practicable? The article goes on to say: "We claim, also, that this is the proper place from which to ship the freight, as it is the end of the Missouri freight division of the railroad." Does the writer have any idea that a railroad in such a case as this looks at the "proper" side of the case? A railroad is built and run to make money. The Northern Pacific can make more money by having a freight route start[?] from this point. Ergo, it will start from here. The article adds to the above quotation that to have the route start from here "will necessitate the expenditure of vast sums of money by the railroad company for additional side-tracks, freight houses, etc." Were this even a fact, a practical view of the matter settles it. If it pays the railroad company to go to any additional expense they will do it, otherwise they will not. The fact of the matter is, however, that the Marquis de Mores stands all the expense of extra buildings, and if the freight route had never been thought of, our growing trade would have compelled the railroad company to put in a side-track.

The article further states: "The road from Little Missouri (or Medora, as it is now called) is through an almost impassable series of buttes or Bad Lands." The writer here displays his ignorance of even the starting point of our route and states a willful lie in reference to the road in the Bad Lands. We call the lie willful because no writer has any business describing a thing of which his own utterances display his utter ignorance. We would willingly pay our share toward the expenses of an unbiased committee to view the merits of the two roads. Our road is as level as a floor and will not need a bridge, and only a little grading in one place while in the Bad Lands. The writer is informed that our road is decided upon. The road which their committee will "view as soon as practicable" he is, of course, as ignorant of as he is of ours. For his benefit we will state that the road from Dickinson that is free from gumbo consists of what are called "buffalo wallows." That is, there is a space, say of ten feet, where the ground is as bare as a floor. Then comes an equal space of turf about six inches higher than the general level. In the lightest buggy it is impossible to go over this land on a trot. With heavy freight wagons the jar will be sufficient to tear the horses' shoulders to pieces. Also, Mr. Ignorance, we would like to know if you have figured on "the vast sums of money" it will take to bridge your route? Of course, you haven't, for your committee has not yet found it practicable to view your route.

But right here is where the most laughable ignorance of this writer is displayed. The very thing which condemns the Dickinson route beyond all peradventure. He says their route "crosses the head-waters of the North and South Cannonball rivers, the Grand river (north and south forks)" and then goes further out of his way to condemn the route by saying that "it crosses a number of small streams known by various names, whereas the more western route from Little Missouri heads some of them, thus missing a number of watering places." We should say our route did "miss some of the watering places." Almost from the Heart river to the South Moreau on the Dickinson route is one vast "watering place." But we never heard gumbo called a "watering place" before.

The rest of the article is a mass of drivel that only reminds one of a spoiled child blubbering because a valuable toy that it does not know how to handle has been taken away from it. And, now, we want to ask this writer of what good was his production? If any one wants a freight route they must work for it personally. A mass of rot such as this article is can do nothing but injury. The falsity of most of the statements and the pusillanimity of the rest condemn the article as the route is already condemned. We dislike to fight men of straw such as the writer of this article has proved himself to be, as it scarcely furnishes the needed exercise. For the good of Dickinson we hope this effervescent individual will be effectually corkedup or he may slop over again.

Following a time-honored custom with newspapers we publish below a few of the many favorable comments we have received at the hands of the press. We don't believe much in a paper blowing its own trumpet, but like crumpets, we find these extracts "werry filin' at the price."

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY is the name of a new paper in Little Missouri, Dak., and is owned and edited by A. T. Packard, '83. A handsome, wide-awake weekly paper called THE BAD LANDS COW BOY has been started at Medora, formerly Little Missouri, Dak., by A. T. Packard. It will have a good field in representing the cattle and sheep industries of one of the best grazing regions of the West, and in chronicling the growth and doings of the new town founded by the Marquis de Mores.—[The Northwest.

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY of which A. T. Packard, a former Chicago reporter, is the editor, tells each of the 600 what the rest have been doing during the week, and to the public at large details the many natural and acquired advantages of the new city as a place of business and residence. It has done this since February 4, a day that will therefore long be remembered in Medora.—[New York Sun.

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, a new newspaper published at Little Missouri has reached our table. It is filled with fresh news and is of neat makeup. THE COW BOY is published in the heart of the Bad Lands of Western Dakota which are becoming famous as the best stock ranges in this country, if not in the world, and will devote considerable of its space to the stock industry.—[Kansas City Live Stock Indicator.

This week brings to our editorial table the initial number of THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, published by A. T. Packard, Medora, Dak., not for fun (as he says) but whereby to make a living. The paper starts out well, and we trust will keep up its lick, as The Northwestern Live Stock Journal (the daddy of all stock journals in the Northwest) wishes to see its children succeed. THE COW BOY is a four-page, seven-column paper, ably edited and representing well the interest for which mission it has started in.—[Cheyenne, Wyo., Northwestern Live Stock Journal.

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, published at Little Missouri, Dak., is a surprisingly good paper.—[Minneapolis Hotel Register.

The first issue of THE BAD LAND COW BOY, published by A. T. Packard, at Little Missouri, is full of interesting matter to stock men. It aims to be the best cattle paper in the Northwest, and we trust the long-felt want among the ranchmen is filled by this paper.—[Dickinson Press.

Little Missouri has a newspaper which sails under the significant name of THE BAD LANDS COW BOY. Typographically it is excellent. It is ably edited by A. T. Packard.—[Glendive Times.

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY is the unique title of a thorough cattle paper, published at Medora, Dak., which is fast becoming a noted cattle point. It gives all the cattle and general news of the Bad Lands and advocates Medora as the cattle headquarters of the Northwest. The name of the paper calls attention to the two things concerning which the editor, A. T. Packard wishes to change public opinion, as the Bad Lands are not bad but very good and produce mints of money; and the cowboys, as a rule, are good citizens. The exceptions have formed public opinion against them.—[Pioneer-Press.

The Cattle buyers of Eastern Washington Territory are paying $12 for calves, $18 for yearlings, $25 for two-year-olds and $40 for cows.—Kansas City Live Stock Indicator.

A correspondent writing from LaCueva, Mora Co., N. M., says: "Cattle in this part of the country are fat enough to ship. I hear of considerable losses in Colfax county, north of this, and also out on the other side of Red river.

Yearling steers are worth from $11.50 to $12.50 and twos from $14.50 to $17. We refer to steer cattle. Better classes of yearlings sell from $12 up. Beeves are in good demand, but scarce at any price, if fat.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

E. E. Crawford, Miles City, Mont., writes: "Stock of all kinds has wintered well thus far. On the range the horses and native cattle are fat; state cattle, late arrivals last fall, are a little thin. Loss, nothing to speak of. Unless we should have some very rough weather this month they will pull through all right."

The winter is over, if we know ourselves. Warm weather and the grass-growing rains have blessed a large portion of the country and the prospect is good. Our correspondents refer to the last spell of weather, which was threatening bad, but let up easily. Texas stock, on the average, wintered exceedingly well.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

We notice many papers of late printing the names of parties prominent in rounding up cattle crooks. This is not advisable. The thieves know who are hunting them and keep out of the way. It exposes stock detectives and parties assisting to unnecessary danger. Thief-takers are not grateful for gratuitous advertising of their business.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

One of the largest sales of property ever made in the far west took place Friday, by which the Swan Land and Cattle Company purchased for a consideration of $2,588,825 upward of 88,000 head of cattle, besides ranch improvements, horses and other kinds of personal property and immense tracts of land, all of said property being in this county.—[Cheyenne Sun.

Mr. F. P. Ernest sometime last season bought a bunch of cattle of the Prairie Cattle Company, in the southern part of the state. Without handling a beef or looking at a single animal he had purchased, Mr. Ernest sold the cattle to the outfit known as the Mill-Iron Company, which was formerly the John Hitson Company, at an advance over the purchase of $32,000.—[Pueblo, Colo., Chieftain.

There was, perhaps, never a brighter outlook for the stock interests of Texas than at present. The nippers have been prohibited, made a deadly weapon, so to speak, the stock have wintered in good shape, those who have no land are arranging to secure it, those who have land are fencing or preparing to fence it, and, indeed, it begins to look as if the new era in the stock business of Texas, that we have been all along predicting, is about to be ushered in.—[Texas Stockmen.

Fifteen years ago people who had small herds of cattle, and when the state did not contain more than 100,000 head, proclaimed the thing overdone, and wanted the gates closed. They said there was room for no more. But despite this discouragement the increase has gone on until now we have 1,500,000 and there is room for more. Five years from now there will be as many cattle grazed west of the Continental Divide as there are east of it at the present time.—[Colorado Live Stock Record.

Plenty of food and enough exercise to keep the muscles firm is the best treatment of horses in winter. It is quite common for many farmers to underfeed in winter, because they have little or nothing for horses to do. But a horse thus managed soon loses his capacity for hard service. Such a horse may be fed so as to make a good show in spring, but it will be fat, not muscle, and a few days in plowing or harrowing will bring him down. Horses worked continuously are less liable to [gall?] from the harness, as the skin is always firm and hard.—[Journal of Agriculture.

Mr. Bennett, who is employed by the Colorado Cattle Growers' Association to inspect the cattle killed by the railroads, is just in from Wallace, Kan., and reports large numbers of Republican river cattle suffering and dying on account of the large pasture fences on North Smoky river. These cattle are dying on both the outside and inside of the pastures. On the outside they die from want of water. Some hundreds of them have broken through the fence to get water, and the pastures having all been eaten out last fall and the cattle that were in them turned out south before winter set in, leaves them on the inside with no grass and they are dying in as great numbers as those on the outside.—[Denver Republican.

Effective measures have already been taken to prevent the spread of the foot and mouth disease in Kansas. Gov. Glick, himself a large cattle owner, is personally interesting himself in the matter and a strict quarantine has been effected. The disease has undoubtedly spread from cattle that have been imported. Hereafter it is probable that the health of all imported stock will be strictly inquired into. The disease itself is a very contagious eruptive fever. It is communicable not only between animals of the same species but between those of species entirely different. For instance, it spreads from cattle to sheep, pigs and fowls and vice versa. The symptoms according to Prof. Law are, roughness of the coat or shivering, increased temperature, dry muzzle, hot red mouth, teats, and interdigital spaces, lameness, inclination to lie and shrinking from the hand in milking. The second or third day blisters arise on any part of the whole interior of the mouth, one-half to one inch in breadth, or on the teats and digits about one-half inch across. Saliva drivels from the mouth, collecting in froth around the lips and a loud smacking is made with the lips and tongue. Swine champ the jaws. Sheep and swine suffer more especially in the feet, often losing the hoofs or even the digital bones, a contingency not unknown in neglected cattle. We do not need to enter into a description of the prevention and cure of this disease, as it will probably never trouble any of our cattle men. It is sufficient to say that the quarantine is so effective that it is not at all likely to spread out of the five or six miles of infected district in Kansas.
