Smoke the Far West cigar, sold only by Roberts & Co.
In this climate and weather it is sufficient enjoyment to exist.
The dance at the Hotel de Mores Monday night was a very pleasant affair.
The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.
Gill Kennedy went to Belfield Saturday. He has a claim adjoining the townsite.
The Marquis started for St. Paul the 17th and will doubtless be here inside of a week.
J. M. Cook sold his team and outfit Tuesday, to A. T. Packard, to be used on the butte farm.
Will McNaughton, running for Dan Eisenberg, of Bismarck, put in a profitable day here last Saturday.
The Northern Pacific bridge gang went up the road Monday. The pile-driver will soon start on its spring trip.
Abe Goodkind, travelling for Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, was in town Saturday. He had good success here.
Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
"Doc" Pennell has gone to Deadwood via the Medora route. Part or all of Mr. Jones' teams will doubtless return with him.
C. A. Williams, of Bismarck, was in the city yesterday. He showed his appreciation of THE COW BOY by subscribing and advertising.
Pennell & Roberts drove their transportation outfit in from their ranch last Saturday and went into camp south of the railroad track.
The latest reports from all along the river for fifty miles up state that the cattle are in prime condition, many being fat enough to kill.
Only two head of the Marquis' cattle have died this winter. These were pure-bred Durhams that died from accidents. Out of about fifteen hundred head this is a splendid showing.
Johnny Goodall, Frank Smith and Rev. Silas Cheval are the latest contributors to our Bad Lands museum. The latter "held up" a passing freight and secured a good specimen of galena.
Moody and Jones, of the "Big Foot" Ryder outfit came in for supplies this week. When not "tired" they reported 5,000 posts cut. The increase, however, was about 1,000 posts to the "smile."

Howard Eaton will probably have the largest barn in the county when it is finished. It is a "ready-made" barn, every piece being cut to fit its proper place. Several teams are busy hauling the parts to Howard's ranch.

If any one doubts that the cattle are in good condition, let them go to the company's meat market or cold-storage room here and look at the cattle slaughtered Tuesday. They are rolling in fat and have had nothing to eat but the grass they rustled.

The river was on a big boom Monday. A gorge forming a few miles up the river and breaking about 12 o'clock. For two or three hours it was a grand sight to see the broken ice shoot down stream. The current for a while was fully twelve miles an hour.

The Northern Pacific, in connection with the new fast mail from New York to Chicago and St. Paul, will soon change their time from St. Paul to Portland to ninety-two hours instead of one hundred and four. The trains will then run through the Bad Lands in daylight, and two each way will be put on probably the first of the month.

Work is progressing in good shape on the Packard-Steiger butte farm. As soon as the frost is out of the ground, plowing will commence. All sorts of vegetables will be planted to see which will do the best. The most of the ground, however, will be planted with potatoes. It will be an interesting experiment to find out what the summits of the buttes are good for.

Reduced rates on emigrant movables have been issued by the Northern Pacific R. R. The term "emigrant movables" is meant to apply to any part of the outfit of an intending settler. This includes second-hand household goods, farming implements and tools and vehicles, trees, shrubbery, fowls and not to exceed ten head of live stock per car. It does not include merchandise, provisions, grain (except for feed in transit and fifty bushels for seed), or any article intended for sale. Twenty-five hundred feet of lumber and 500 fence posts, and portable houses may also be shipped. The rates are proportionate for any amount and are $71 per car of 20,000 pounds from St. Paul to Little Missouri.

John Doulisch met with a serious accident yesterday. He was excavating the dirt next to Michael Knott's saloon for a new building, when a number of large lumps fell on him. Joe Pennell and two or three others happened to be passing and stopped on hearing the noise. A slight groan convinced them that some one was hurt, but nothing could be seen except the frozen blocks of displaced earth. It took the combined strength of three men to roll the blocks off of Doulisch. It is not thought that he has received any internal injury, but it is difficult to tell at present. He was resting much easier last night. The victim would not have lived five minutes had he not been relieved from the pressure as he was squeezed so hard that it was impossible for him to breathe.

Let dogs delight to bark and bite,
For God hath made them so;
Let bears and lions growl and fight,
For 'tis their nature too.

But, Sandy, you should never let
Your angry passions rise,
Your hands were never made
To scratch out Jones' eyes.

Messrs. Boice and Towers arrived in town this afternoon to make arrangements for a round-up meeting to be held in Pennell's Hall, Little Missouri, April 5. This notice will take the place of a call, as enough cattle men are already interested to insure the success of the meeting. Turn out, stockmen.

The latest thing in reference to the freight route is that the Northwestern and Milwaukee roads have pooled and lowered rates to meet the Rock Island schedule. These rates apply to Medora, Dickinson and Belfield. Every town has a fair show and that is all our route wants. On account of the superiority of our road, none other can possibly compete with it.

In reply to our "preposterous remarks about the freight line," the Press claims that it is not a fact that freight now in Dickinson is to be shipped here and freighted from this point. Up to date, this is the first "claim" emanating from Dickinson that is substantiated by facts. We were misled into stating it by reading orders from Messrs. Jansen & Bliss, Blum, Zeipp and F. B. Smith, of Deadwood, for all freight at Dickinson to be turned over to Cranston; also orders from Cranston to turn over the freight to Jones & Pennell. Upon inquiry, however, it was found that there was only a car-load or two at Dickinson and the firm here wouldn't ship such a small amount, and this very freight that we don't want is what Dickinson has gone so wild over!

The Press further states that eleven loaded freight outfits had started for the Black Hills last week. Your vocabulary needs enlarging, Bro. Scott. In speaking of outfits, one does not call every team an outfit. Mr. Jones' outfit will haul 200,000 pounds, Pennell & Roberts' 100,000 and Larson's 75,000.

The Press goes on to say:

"We will now give the facts as they exist at the present time. Keyes & Bramble, heavy freighters, have made contracts with the railroad to have all of their freight delivered at Dickinson and at no other point. Jones & Pennell have made contracts to have their freight delivered either at Dickinson or Little Missouri."

As food for thought on the part of The Press we will "give the facts" in the shape of a telegram from Mr. Jones to Mr. Pennell:

DEADWOOD, March 16, 1884.
JOE PENNELL, Little Missouri, Dak.:
Have made contracts with many merchants. Have consolidated with Bramble in favor of Medora route. (Signed) JONES.

Read, Bro. Scott, and then go out and weep a spring freshet into the Heart river.
A trial of the Far West cigar is its best recommendation.

BELFIELD, Dak., March 19, 1884.
EDITOR COW BOY:

Belfield is much pleased with the efforts of THE COW BOY in urging prompt organization of the county. Billings county is one of the richest of Dakota and for its age, most densely populated. We are entitled to organization and the executive should recognize the fact.

Two dozen buttons came off when the Dickinson freight-line article was read in The Pioneer-Press.

Will Houk celebrated his twenty-third birthday on Sunday last, and hilarity reigned supreme upon this festive occasion.

The Galliens, who were expected to return last week, have not arrived yet and it is feared that their little child, which was sick at St. Paul, has grown worse.

The first new settler, Mr. Schurke, of Chicago, arrived last Monday, and will be followed by six families within a week.

The snow is disappearing fast and it is beginning to be unsafe to venture through the many creeks with ordinary ponies.

Quite a traffic in relinquishment papers has commenced here. Many excellent claims were filed on by speculators last season who are now trying to unload. Such proceedings are utterly unlawful and suggest food for a special agent of the U. S. land department.

Quite a number of Indians passed through here a few days ago.

A somewhat interesting case of horse stealing came to light this week. A party of Indians recognized among some ponies belonging to our citizens, one which they claimed had been stolen from them three years ago and were going to take it from their present owner. After considerable parleying they were induced to seek redress by legal process, and will likely recover their animal to-day. The pony has passed through three different hands here and was originally purchased from the Townsite Company for $60. The moral attached to this item is that no one should ever purchase any kind of stock without taking a bill of sale for his money, or run the risk of being arrested for horse stealing.

Boomer Kennedy was down from Little Missouri this week and thinks of erecting a two-story store this season.

Senor Bass, the Delmonico of Billings county, entertained a number of guests royally on St. Patrick's day.

The anniversary of the Emerald Isle's noted saint was the occasion of a lavish expenditure of green ribbon, flags, etc.

Ertel & Houk have received a large supply of all kinds of garden seeds to furnish the million settlers around here.

Several large herds of antelope were seen here the last few days, likely attracted by the fact of some young travelling men stopping over. The antelope have lots of fun with the latter.

SADIE.

The effectual way in which the ice-dam, built last fall, protects the western bank of the river has called the attention of several to the fact that at a very trifling expense the channel could be turned so that the river will run as close to the abattoir as necessary. If this is done it will be a great benefit in two ways, in carrying away the debris from the abattoir and in saving the western bank, which threatens to wash away and dump several houses into the river. The matter will probably be attended to soon.

EDITOR COW BOY:

The recent effusion of a Dickinson correspondent in The Pioneer-Press prompts me to say a word in behalf of Belfield, which proudly looks to your aggressive journal as its champion, as long as it has not reached the stage where it can support a paper of its own.

Belfield possesses none of the "dog in the manger" element and congratulates Medora upon having scored "first blood" in the Black Hills freight-line contest. If its superior energy, unity of action, backed by the necessary cash, has secured for it a large share of this valuable freight, Belfield, who has made a gallant fight, cheerfully echos "amen." But what of Dickinson? Years before Belfield or Medora were dreamt of, Dickinson's wonderful advantages regarding the Black Hills freight route were or should have been known as well as now, and the very idea that its citizens should have permitted this fact, if such it be, to escape recognition augurs badly for a town, whose main brag is the imaginable halo surrounding the end of a freight division. Do the merchants of that hamlet, and they have some of the most wideawke in the country, begin to see that a few side tracks and a very modest freight-house are a mere myth, when it comes to the handling of fifty million pounds of freight? Would they grasp the idea that any village, even so humble, would gladly duplicate these accommodations for the terminus of a freight line and throw in a handsome bonus besides? Would they believe that the heavy freighters of the Hills are among the most intelligent, wide-awake men of the country, who are sure to select the shortest and best route where the hauling would be best, provided the rates of the railroad company would permit an option? Would Dickinson expect to come out victorious and carry off the trophies, when other towns, that happen to be blessed with better natural advantages, fight for it?

Dickinson is one of the most promising towns along the line, but it made a sad mistake when it allowed itself to be inflated with the erroneous idea that it could play a bluff game on other and younger places. Though its home journal had misled its own people by making them believe the freight line was theirs, the wail to the St. Paul Chamber of Commerce and The Pioneer-Press smacks too much of long clothes, and if no stronger efforts are put forth the freight line, as far as Dickinson is concerned, will remain and look best on paper.

In conclusion, Belfield trusts that Dickinson has not bankrupted itself in building stations and bridges, but if it has they will find ready purchasers for the same at Belfield, which will have use for them.

WORKER.

LITTLE MISSOURI, March 20, 1884.
EDITOR COW BOY:

In several German newspapers, The Extrablatt and The Mecklenberger Wachrichten, there is an article warning emigrants against the Northwest, especially Dakota. The writer of the article, Mr. Anton Milde, of Bismarck, seems to be entirely unacquainted with the country in which he is living. In his article he says that emigration speculators buy a section of land of 160 acres and lay it out in town lots, sell these as quick as possible and skip the country. Poor man, go to the U. S. land office and ask how many acres a section contains before you write another article.

Then he says that the winter is so severe, with continual lasting storms, that it is impossible to keep cattle except in heated stables. Where do people sometimes get the rage for writing about things they do not understand? If you would like to see cattle in winter-time, come out to the Bad Lands of Dakota and here you will find them neither stabled nor fed, but running free during the whole winter grazing.

Another sentence says nobody takes care of the emigrants after they are here, but have to seek their way alone to get enough to live on in winter. Well, let them bring wetnurses to lead these poor fellows who cannot find their way alone.

At the end of the article the writer wishing to prove his statements about Dakota says: "I will give an illustration of one case. A former Vienna lawyer, T. Kratky, has to make his living in New York by washing dishes in a restaurant." Old friend, what has your lawyer in New York to do with Dakota. Let him wash dishes. I hope he will do less damage than as a lawyer. The less lawyers there are the more peace there is in a place, and the less doctors and druggists the better the health of the people. This can be proved by Little Missouri, where there are no fights and only two children have died; they grow up as well or quick as calves.

To this ridiculous article of Mr. Anton Milde (in plain English Anton Softness) I can only reply that it is true both your article and your name are soft, much too soft for Dakota. Go East!

A.

WM. F. VAN DRIESCHE.

Up where the snow shines clear and white
On the peaks that point to the summer sky,
Up in the gulch by the evening light
I saw, as we travelled slowly by,
A claim deserted and left alone,
A shaft sunk in the mountain side,
A roofless cabin of logs rough hewn,
Where some one had labored till hope had died.

And later on, when our camp was made,
And the white tents pitched for another night,
While the pine trees wildly tossed and swayed,
In the cheerful glow of our camp-fire light,
When merry voices rang in the air,
And smiling faces flashed in and out—
I thought of the cabin, rude and bare,
Of its owner who labored in hope and doubt.

He had come, perhaps, from some eastern home
For speedy wealth, to this western clime.
And homesick, and weary, and all alone,
He had faithfully toiled for some friendly sign.
Cold moans the wind through the canon deep,
And the coyote cries the night hours drear;
There are unknown footsteps that softly creep,
No comrade to help, no loved one to cheer.

Still he dreamed, as others had done before,
As others shall do in the days to come,
Of finding wealth in unbounded store,
And joyfully bringing the treasure home;
But fortune is chary when all is told—
Her smiles are hardest on earth to gain,
And where one is favored with shining gold,
A thousand others may toil in vain.

Thus I sit and muse in the camp-fire glow,
While the welcome evening meal is spread,
And the sound of the brook comes soft and low,
And the stars shine brilliantly overhead;
For my heart is saddened, as day by day
We pass in sunshine or dripping rain,
That frequent sod-mark on our way,
A deserted, desolate mining claim.
There is danger of a flood at Mandan as water from the Missouri is already backing up into the Heart. The river broke at Mandan yesterday, however, and what danger there is will soon be gone.

A mass of ice six miles long and frozen solid passed Glendive yesterday, floating down the Yellowstone. If in its present condition it should strike the piers of the Bismarck bridge, short work would be made of it.

A little squib in the Mandan Pioneer to the effect that a travelling man from Bismarck was braced up against a bar and forced to warble a few select tunes to the accompaniment of six-shooters in the hands of Win Roberts and friends is creating considerable comment here. Such articles may do well enough to fill up when located in imaginary places, but they easily give a place a hard reputation even when they are as devoid of foundation as was the article above referred to. The Pioneer is assured that there was no truth in the article and for the future we hope to see no more of them.

Johnny Goodall is at the Ox Bow ranch to bring in beef cattle for slaughtering. The cattle are in splendid condition and are covered with great layers of fat. No eastern man would believe that range cattle which have not been fed a spear of hay or any grain and which have had no protection except that furnished by the buttes and coolies would be in any condition except the worst. On the other hand they are as fit for butchering as any stock-fed cattle in the States. The Refrigerator Car Company are constantly receiving orders for beef. All the cattle killed have been these range cattle and every order has given perfect satisfaction.

Messrs. Boice and Towers came in too late last Thursday for us to make any comment on the round-up meeting to be held here April 5. In fact, we had to take the forms off the press to insert the notice published in last week's Cow Boy. Since our last issue, however, we have spoken with a number of cattle men and there is no doubt that there will be a large turnout to the meeting. The meeting for the Bad Lands association can be thoroughly canvassed at this time and thus serve a double purpose. It is not only a privilege, but a duty of every cattle man in the Bad Lands to attend the meeting of April 5. Upon the initial meetings will depend in a great measure our future success in making this point a cattle headquarters. Every man is interested in round-up meetings for his section, and every one who attends this meeting must be made to fully appreciate the value of the Bad Lands and Territorial associations.

The Southeast Dakota Live Stock and Breeders' Association has been organized, with headquarters at Mitchell. Representatives were present from sixteen counties and everything points to a very successful organization. The avowed purpose of the association is to develop the quality and facilitate and encourage the raising of all kinds of live stock in Southeastern Dakota. The list of members includes most of the prominent live-stock men of Southern Dakota. Right here is the explanation of the difficulty brought forward in our last stock meeting—How to get all Dakota cattle men interested in a Territorial organization? The enthusiasm displayed at the Mitchell meeting seems to prove conclusively that the association would join with the Bad Lands and other associations to form a Territorial association. There is no need in arguing the advisability of this plan. Stock growers' interests are getting so strong in Dakota that they demand a Territorial organization so that their rights may be effectually laid before the legislature and citizens at large. Especially for the reason that considerable legislation must be passed by the Territorial legislature, it is necessary to embrace all classes of live-stock men in the Territoral organization. Of course, the raising of range cattle is unknown in Southeastern Dakota, but an interchange of views between breeders and range-stock raisers will be wonderfully beneficial to both. To a great extent the interests of both classes would be identical and the united action of such a list of men as will compose the Territorial association must have great weight in carrying a measure for the general interest of all. The territorial organization will soon be a matter of vital interest and every means should be tried to induce all cattle men of the Territory to join it. The success of the Mitchell meeting is a guarantee of the success of the larger organization.

We have received notice of the annual meeting of the Dawson County Live Stock Association, to be held at Glendive, April 7 and 8. All stockmen are cordially invited to attend. Business of importance will be transacted, such as appointing of foreman of round-up committees, place of round-up, etc. On the evening of the 8th there will be a grand stockmen's ball and banquet. Those wishing to join the association are requested to send in their names to the secretary, C. J. Neal, of Glendive, some time before the 8th.

We want credit for items taken from this paper. We are getting tired of furnishing brains for a number of territorial papers, and if the practice is continued those papers which transgress will be dropped from our exchange list.—[Yellowstone Journal.

The above is the undiluted essence of an unspeakable gall. All the time The Journal is wishing and wanting, has it ever entered the mind of the editor that perhaps other papers want credit for their articles. Coming, as the above extract does, from a paper that stole bodily a half-column article from The Cow Boy and only changed two words, to make it apply to Miles City instead of the Bad Lands, and added a few lines at the end so that the readers of The Journal might recognize the editor's bungling work—in the face of all this we certainly desire to know if the editor wants the earth fried on both sides and served with cream gravy, or will he just take it raw if a part of the solar system is thrown in?

The official call for the election of delegates to the Territorial Republican convention to be held at Huron, April 23, has been issued. This convention will elect two delegates and two alternates to the National Republican convention to be held in Chicago, June 3. The apportionment of delegates to the different counties has been decided and Billings county is entitled to one. As this is a matter about which our citizens have thought but little, we would suggest that some consideration be given as to who shall represent our county at the Huron convention. The Territorial central committee recommended that on Saturday, April 12, primaries be held to elect delegates to the county conventions, and that on the following Wednesday the county conventions elect delegates to the Territorial convention. Our county is as yet unorganized, but before April 12 it is hoped that some one will be appointed with authority to call the meetings. The first thing then to be done is to select a county central committee which shall hereafter have such things in charge.

Spalding's base-ball guide for 1884 is out.

Jem Goode and Sheriff, the Prussian, will box for $1,000 a side.

The Ross-Courtney scull race takes place May 25, at Oak Point.

Jay-Eye-See and Phallas will take their spring training in Louisville.

Phil Dwyer would not sell his stables and retire from the turf for $500,000.

New professional and amateur ball clubs are being organized every day.

Base-ball players all over the country are reporting for April's preliminary practice.

Lynn, Mass., and Akron, O., will run base-ball nines on the co-operative plan this summer.

Jem Mace will start for America April 10. He hasn't any idea of tackling Sullivan, however.

The great and only base-ball manager, Dan O'Leary will manage the Cincinnati Unions this season.

The American Association clubs will travel [88,704?] miles in filling their league engagements this season.

A large number of professional oarsmen and ball-players are employed as trainers by college organizations.

Duncan C. Ross was considerably surprised last week when an amateur in Chicago named Whitmore laid him on his back after a hard struggle.

There is now no doubt but that Sullivan and Thompson will meet before three months are over. A match has been made for $5,000, each side depositing $500.

Matsada Sorakichi, the Japanese wrestler, is claimed to be the strongest man in this country at present. He is learning our style of wrestling and expects to make matches with Ross, Thompson, Bibby and McLaughlan. The Japanese style of wrestling consists in shoving the opponent out of a six-foot ring.

W. H. Edwards, president of the Cleveland Association, says: "This will be a rousing season of trotting. There is more public interest than ever. The record will go down, I think, to 2:10, possibly 2:07, or between 2:08 and 2:10 somewhere. What we want most is good square trotting and no foolishness. We are buttoning them down pretty close to that with the rules now in force."
All Bad Lands cattle men and those having any interest in a Bad Lands round-up are requested to meet here on the morning of April 5, to arrange for an annual round-up of this region.

There will be a meeting held at Little Missouri crossing, the third Monday in April (the 21st) for the purpose of forming a Bad Lands Association. All raisers of live stock are requested to attend. Upon its organization, business of much importance will come before the association and it is to the interest of every man interested in live stock to attend. The Committee.

Best American cattle are quoted at 15½c, dressed weight, in Liverpool; best sheep at 18c.

The bill granting $50,000 for the suppression of the foot and mouth disease has passed the senate. It was introduced by Senator Plumb.

The Swan Land and Cattle Company has sent to England for 200 full blooded bulls for use on their ranches.—[Cheyenne Democratic Leader.

Stock reports from the north side of the Yellowstone are very favorable. The only losses occurring so far have been from wolves. Wolves are quite numerous in that locality and have occasioned considerable loss on young cattle.—[Helena, Mon., Independent.

Out of over 8,300,000 head of live stock received at Chicago last year only 273 cattle, 758 hogs, 332 sheep and 21 calves were condemned by inspecting officers at the stock yards. This shows wonderful sanitary soundness or very poor inspection.—[Cheyenne Democratic Leader.

An exchange gives the following as a means of detecting glanders: A bucket half full of water should be held under the animal's nostrils and the mucous allowed to drop into the water. If the substance remains on top or spreads or dissolves the disease is not glanders, but if the drop remains undissolved and sinks to the bottom the horse should be killed.

A letter from north of the river says cattle are looking fine and horses doing well. The winter has not been as hard on cattle north of the river as in this vicinity. We hear of some outfits close to Sidney that have lost a good many "dogies" that were put on the range late in the fall. The railroad has not killed as many cattle as it did last year, the number on the main line between Antelope and North Platte being about two hundred and fifty.—[Sidney, Neb., Plaindealer.

The department of state has received information from the United States consul at Birmingham, Eng., that the foot and mouth disease is raging among the cattle in almost every county in England. The secretary of the treasury has requested the secretary of state to notify the United States consuls in Great Britain not to certify to invoices of cattle unless, after an examination of the animals by a veterinary surgeon, they are satisfied no disease exists.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

The New Mexico stock growers have requested the legislature of that territory to enact a law requiring butchers to give a bond of $1,000 to keep a record, open at all times to public inspection, containing a description of all the animals they slaughter and the names of parties from whom purchased; also to keep the hides of slaughtered animals for a reasonable length of time, thus enabling parties to identify their property. The request is a reasonable one and a law to that effect would materially aid in the detection of thieves, while a compliance with its provisions would entail no hardships on the butchers.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

White & Moulton, of the Lochuquilla ranch in Crockett county, are lambing 6,000 to 7,000 ewes by loose herding or line riding, with only two or three extra hands. This is no new plan, but it is very rarely practiced, especially in open range, and we know of no large ranch in Texas that has heretofore had the courage to adopt it. So far it is a success and will end successfully, from the common-sense fact that an animal left to itself will take care of its young. The only objection to the mode is the presence of wild animals, but it costs considerable less to keep a pack of good dogs and buy an ounce or two of poison than it does to put seven or eight Mexicans with each band through the lambing season. The demand is imperative for a law against wild animals. If a fair price was allowed for their scalps, the sheep's natural enemies would soon be extirpated.—[Texas Wool Grower.

Mr. John Snodgrass, general foreman of the Bay State Live Stock Company, was in town last evening and from him we learn of the purchase by the Bay State Company of the herd of John F. Coad, ranging on Pumpkin creek and the North Platte river. The price paid was $730,000 and the number of cattle given in was 23,000 head, the outfit to be run by Mr. Coad until July first when the final transfer will be made. The Bay State Company now controls about 75,000 cattle and is the second in size if not the largest in the country. It is the expectation of the company to brand about ten thousand calves this spring, the Creighton herd which was purchased last spring being largely composed of breeding stock. This company now has two ranches on the Lodge Pole, near Antelope, one on Horse creek and the Coad ranches, their range covering the western half of the county south of the river, including the heads of Pumpkin and Horse creeks and the Lodge Pole. The principal brand of the company will be the half circle block, originally the Creighton brand, and all the young stock will be branded with that brand.—[Sidney, Neb., Plaindealer-Telegraph.

A. H. Swan, of Cheyenne City, is not only the cattle king of Wyoming Territory, but probably the leading cattle king in the entire West, having control of as much stock as any single individual on the continent. His present possessions amount to between $2,000,000 and $3,000,000, while the amount of stock of which he has the exclusive control and management is over 200,000 head, and valued at over $6,000,000. He was the organizer, is directly interested in and is president and general manager of no less than five different stock organizations in Wyoming, having the personal superintendency and entire management of the same. One of these cattle ranges is 100 miles in length by from 50 to 100 miles in width, and hence contains an immense acreage of grazing surface, including the best land in the territory, and lying along the Laramie, Medicine Bow, North Platte and other rivers. Beside the large amount of capital invested in stock, of which this individual has full control, some of the companies have made large purchases of land on which they have completed extensive improvements and which were done by this cattle king's suggestions and directions, so that he has the entire credit of accumulating, massing and controlling this immense congregation of wealth.

The career of this person has been remarkable for its brilliant success financially. At twenty-two years of age he travelled from his native place, Green county, Pa., to Iowa, locating in the latter state on some wild land when everything in that commonwealth was comparatively free from the intrusion of civilization. This was in 1853. At that time he had $1,000 in his pocket as his stock in trade. After making some improvements on his land he sold out at an advance, and then pushed still further on to the frontier, again investing in land. Two years after his first entrance into Iowa, he returned to Ohio, where he purchased a farm, remaining in the latter state seven years, at the end of which time he again returned to Iowa, and began dealing in sheep and cattle, buying and selling. Taking his brother as a partner they began turning their attention to the cattle business exclusively, beginning with a herd of 3,000. This herd was increased at various times as follows, naturally and purchase: In 1874 to 5,000, in 1875 to 7,000, in 1876 to 10,000, in 1877 to 11,000, in 1878 to 14,000, in 1879 to 19,000, in 1880 to 24,000, in 1881 to 28,000 and in 1882 to [33,000?]. Most of the increase was natural.

By this time the profits of the two brothers in the stock business had been so great, not including the stock on hand, that the next year (1883), with several other stockmen they purchased 31,000 more cattle on a range west of the Black Hills, merging their two herds into one, and with other parties forming a land and cattle syndicate company, with an invested capital of $2,555,000, A. H. Swan being made president of the same at a salary of $10,000 per year, the amount of cattle numbering 115,000. Negotiations are now pending for the sale of Mr. A. H. Swan's interest in this company at the princely sum of $750,000. Mr. Swan next organized four other companies on a similar basis, to all of which he has been given the direct management. One of the companies, known as the Ogallala Land and Cattle Company of Nebraska, owns 85,000 head of cattle. The latest enterprise in which this cattle king has been engaged was the organization of a land syndicate and stock yards company, which purchased 2,000 acres of land adjoining the city of Omaha, Neb., a portion to be sold in lots and the balance to be reserved for this land syndicate and stock yards company for the slaughtering and shipping of dressed beef in refrigerator cars to eastern markets. This latter establishment is to be ready for operation by July, 1884, and its capacities are placed at 1,000 head per day. Among the cattle king's private possessions are 150,000 acres of land under fence, with ten houses, eight barns and fifty corrals for the branding of stock. He is also the owner of land in Iowa, forty miles from Des Moines, valued at $350,000.

He claims to have never had any litigations about contracts, never having forfeited his word to any person with whom he has had any business transactions, either in buying or selling. In appearance he is tall, but well proportioned and his countenance bears the imprint of modesty, frankness and intelligence, and though naturally easy in his bearing, yet he is free from the suavity and independence of action so common among frontier stockmen.—[Pioneer-Press.

A Mr. Terry, of England, has invented a tricycle which is capable of being converted into a boat. When used on the road the machine is an ordinary rear steerer. The operation of converting it into a boat is very simple and takes but half an hour. All mounted, the apparatus forms a decked canoe, combining all the conditions necessary for proper buoyancy, even at sea. The buoyancy is, moreover, increased by two air bags, which are attached to the two sides at the upper part of the open space.—[Mirror of American Sports.

Woodside and Morgan on May 1 will start on their trans-continental bicycle trip from New York to San Francisco. Two thousand dollars is up that they will cover the distance in seventy days.

At last the names of the St. Paul nine have been published. It is long odds that they will bring up the rear in the Northwestern League race.

The first consignment of freight via the Medora route came yesterday. It is destined for Lead City.
Pennell & Roberts and their men are busily engaged in the bridging and grading of the freight route.
One of Pennell & Roberts' mules was shown the last Dickinson Press and it immediately sickened and died.

Let every cattle man remember the date of the meeting to be held for arranging the Bad Lands round-up—April 5th.

Dr. A. R. Duncan, surgeon of the N. P. R. R., and H. S. Davis, both of Glendive, made us a call last Friday. It is probable that Dr. Duncan will arrange for weekly visits here.
A number of the boys are interested in base-ball and practice daily for a while after dinner. A nine will be organized soon, which will result in considerable sport, if not in glory.
Again has Frank Smith come to the front with valuable additions to our Bad Lands curiosities. If we don't have a collection to be proud of it won't be the fault of the Smith brothers.
It is the unanimous opinion of men here from all parts of the world, that they have never experienced more delightful weather than we are having at present. It is simply perfect.
Jos. Doulisch, an account of whose accident we published in our last issue, is rapidly recovering. It was feared for a time that his pelvis was injured, but his rapid recovery contradicts that idea.

Adolph Eyraud, the Marquis' gardener, is hard at work on his garden, getting hot-beds in order. Owing to this being the first year, there are many difficulties to overcome, but Mr. Eyraud's hopes are high.

Considerable sport has been had here lately over a number of races. Several of the ponies have exhibited extraordinary speed at two hundred yards, but none can take away the championship for that distance from "Old Tex."

The bears are a great curiosity and are let loose occasionally for the delectation of passengers on the cars. The bears always take a shoot for the dining-car and their confidence is usually rewarded by a liberal donation of scraps.

T. A. Matthews was appointed to represent the Little Missouri ranges on the round-up committee of the Eastern Montana Live Stock Association, whose last annual meeting was held at Miles City the 15th of the present month.

The train due here night before last was fifteen hours late and the first train from the east for two days will be in some time to-night on account of the washing out of the Green river bridge, a mile or two this side of Gladstone.

Some of as good ruled work as can be done in the Territory was recently furnished by The Cow Boy for the N. P. R. C. Co. We wish it distinctly understood that we take a back seat for no office in the West on job work of all kinds.

There will be fun for the boys on April 5, when Pennell & Roberts' bears and Paddock's boar get at each other. Fifty dollars a side is up, but as the stockmen will be here on the day of the fight, considerable money will change hands.

Ned Hager and H. H. Gove, of Mandan, were in town Tuesday on business. They report business as picking up at Mandan and that all the merchants are confident of a good trade this season. Their confidence certainly has a good foundation.

J. A. Ferris, who has opened a dry goods and notion store in the building formerly occupied by John Nelson, is too well known to need any introduction. The cattle men and others will consult their interest by dealing with Mr. Ferris.

A dance will be given at the Pyramid Park hotel the evening of the round-up meeting, April 5. All our young men are interested in the event and it will certainly be a success. Music will be procured at Glendive and everything will be provided for a good time.

Mr. B. Barr has returned from J. A. Beaumont's sheep ranch and reports that all danger of further deaths is at an end. Those now alive are in poor condition, but are rapidly picking up. Next winter they will be acclimated and it is confidently expected will do well. The valuable lessons of the past are a guarantee of success in the future.

J. Slatcher, of Dickinson, is making a gun stock for Vick Smith which is the prettiest thing of the kind we have ever seen. It is made of English walnut, the veins showing out beautifully. It is worth a trip to Dickinson to see. Mr. Slatcher appreciates the value of The Cow Boy as an advertising medium and comes out in a good advertisement this week. We can personally recommend him as as a skillful and honest workman.
THE LAST SQUAWK Of the Dickinson Dying Duck Reminds Us of the Man Who Never Opened His Mouth, but He Put His FOOT INTO IT.

The last issue of The Dickinson Press was a chromo edition. It was intended to reassure its readers in reference to the Dickinson freight route, but as the bald-headed facts were known there as well as here, it must have utterly failed in its intention. The editor of The Press, however, was astute enough to put two and two together and reasoned that his chromo edition was the last or next to the last time he could hold even a bob-tail straight in his bluff game and so he went his whole stack on the last deal. At least, the above is the explanation we received from a friend. We like facts, in fact, we are stuck on them, so we packed our spare suit in a handker—grip, we mean—and started for Dickinson last Friday, bound to know something more than hearsay about the merits of the two routes. We found Dickinson to be a lively, bustling place, very well calculated to predispose anyone in its favor. In company with a friend we rode out several miles on the proposed Dickinson route. The ground was frozen so that it was hard to judge of the nature of the soil, but there was considerable gumbo grass and frequent indications of quicksand. The country was rolling, but the first few miles of the route are level enough, with the exception of one steep hill. We very much doubt, however, if the gumbo will be passable during wet weather. In fact, several of the Dickinson citizens admitted as much. It must be borne in mind also that this is the best part of the Dickinson route.

The next day, in company with Messrs. Keyes, Pennell and Hyde, we took a long trip over the Medora route. It must also be remembered that right here in the Bad Lands is the only poor part of our route. Outside of the Bad Lands, every one unites in saying that there is not a more perfect route in the country. In the Bad Lands it is, on the whole, more level than the Dickinson route but there are more hills. Only the Sully creek hill would compel teams to double, however, and the bridge does away entirely with this difficulty.

Summing up, we believe the first twenty-five miles of the Dickinson route is preferable to ours, if the gumbo can be avoided. Otherwise our twenty-five miles in the Bad Lands are vastly preferable. For the remaining hundred and sixty miles, there is no question but that our route is far superior.

As the matter has gone beyond argument now and the success of our route is assured, there is no need of mentioning these facts.

Whether there is to be a route from Dickinson or not, we neither know nor care. What we do know is that contracts have been signed with Black Hills merchants for the hauling of their freight that will test the four hundred teams on our route to the utmost.

Up to the date of the publication of the chromo edition, not a merchant had made a contract specifying that his goods were to be shipped by the Dickinson route. Not a contractor had decided to ship via Dickinson. Not a stroke of work had been done on their route. And oh, tempora, the route hadn't even been "viewed" by the enterprising committee appointed for that purpose.

Belfield, Dak., March 26, 1884.
Editor Cow Boy:

Louis C. Hay, the Grand Guy of the Belfield Townsite Company, returned home Saturday morning. Louis spent several months in New York and Washington in behalf of our town, and comes back to us the Boomer, of Boomerville. In the language of our lamented chum Napoleon, "There is music in the air."

Sheriff Cuskelly came up from Dickinson to replevin the pony which an Indian claimed was stolen from him several years before J. Christ's, Esq., birthday. As the Indian had the trademark and the sheriff on his side, the animal was turned over to him in the presence of the whole town and tears have flowed freely since. Moral—Don't buy or steal an animal with a trademark.

Bill Tuttle, the manager of the Gallien ranch in the Bad Lands, is hot and liable to crawl upon the paper collar of a couple of noble red men, who stole two valuable horses from him. It appears Bill befriended these men, who sought food and shelter at his place. After enjoying the most liberal hospitality, these copper-colored knights of the lasso departed during Mr. Tuttle's absence in town, taking along a couple of ropes on the ends of which these two horses unfortunately happened to be appended. Should they be sighted a mineral claim will be located on both of them.

Breaking and seeding will commence this week and a fine crop is surely expected.

Three men fainted dead away when The Dickinson Press reached here last week. They mistook the sickly rooster for the editor-in-chief of The Press.

Mr. Gilchrist, our end-man who keepeth watch during the darkest hour of night at the depot, has left us to accept a more lucrative position at Sully Springs. All the girls in town are praying that he will follow the valuable example of Hamlet's ghost and semi-occasionally return—when the spirit moves him, so to speak.

A. Goodrow represents Wisconsin and the night operator all at the same time at this point. He seems to be a clever boy, though the atmosphere got very dry since his arrival here.

Mr. W. M. LeMoyne, of the Belfield Townsite Company, came in Tuesday morning.

Several new bridges and houses are going up and everything indicates that the spring poet should have his life insured, if he would venture upon these pastures green.

Mine host Bass is spending a small fortune, with the accent on the first syllable, in paint and oil and in getting plans made for an addition to his popular hotel. Verily, the world moveth.

Your correspondent does not venture to church often and only when "Mamma dear" threatens to envelope us with a new bonnet. Such was the case last Sunday, and the sermon ran as follows: "And it came to pass in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and eighty-four that some good merchants from a far away country called the Black Hills got lost in a town called Dickinson. And upon their arrival the people gathered around them and looked at each other and in silence spake, 'Blessed be those who strike Dickinson, for they will see the way to the Black Hills.' But, alas, the freighters got frightened, for the crowd's manners were wild and the spokesman had not wherewith to grease the wheel. They got. And upon their journey toward the setting sun they struck two places, recorded in the great book of the Northern Pacific as Belfield and Medora, and here the merchants seemed full of hope, faith and charity. They took kindly to the people of that locality, who slaughtered the fattest rooster in their behalf, and immediately decided upon these points for their journey home. And it is recorded in the archives, more commonly known as Scott's Dickinson Press that the fine words, 'Gold and silver have I none, but such as I have I will give thee,' are quoted superlatively N. G.
Sadie.

Enough has already been said about the round-up meeting to insure a full attendance, but lest there may be any forgetfulness, we wish to state again that it will be held day after to-morrow at 2 o'clock in the afternoon, in Pennell & Roberts' hall. Let every cattle man attend.

Some men, like things "no fellah can find out." The editor of The Mandan Pioneer referred to us as "The handsome and fearless editor of The Bad Lands Cow Boy," and then refused the loan of our cash capital, consisting of eleven cents, two used postage stamps and a shirt and overcoat button, the latter in good condition and almost new. As he scorned our base lucre, it must be that he is working some political scheme. Look out for a dark horse.

The last article in our Dickinson correspondence is a "ringer." The bare truth is sufficient about this country, and in time will bring plenty of men and capital here. We are decidedly not an adherent of the Pat Donan school and think it altogether better to at least mildly insinuate that perhaps there may be a better banana country in the world. In the course of time every lie about this country will be found out and thus "booming" is, to a large extent detrimental. We really believe that we have better natural advantages in the combined production of grain, cattle and coal than any state or territory in the Union. Any one who is cognizant of the fact admits this. Our facilities are rapidly becoming known and they need no exaggeration. Tell the truth and shame Pat D—we mean His Satanic Majesty.

In to-day's issue of The Cow Boy we publish a call for a convention to select a delegate to represent this county at the Territorial convention to be held at Huron, the 23d inst., and to select members for a Republican county central committee. Our citizens should turn out at this convention and see that a good man is elected to represent the county at the Territorial convention. We are young yet and prompt and judicious selection will do as much as anything else to bring us to the front. There are many good men here who would well represent the county, but we think the man best fitted in all respects is Mr. Fred Ertel, of Belfield. He is a good business man and will see that the interests of our county do not suffer. As there has been no caucus to decide the matter, we have taken it upon ourselves to fix the date and place for the convention, and have chosen Medora as the most convenient place and April 12 as the day.

The recent riots in Cincinnati are but the outbreak at the sense of wrong every city experiences in the dispensation of justice (?). A cold-blooded, premeditated murder was committed and the jury only sentenced the murderer to imprisonment. A popular outbreak was the result and the bummer element took advantage of this to indulge in wholesele depradations. Justice in cities is getting to be a perfect by-word. One of the most noted criminal lawyers in Chicago told us that if a man had money he would guarantee to free him from any crime. This has also been the case in Cincinnati, and the people determined to put a stop to it and run the shyster lawyers out of town. The result has been that the court house, together with the second-best law library in the United States and many valuable records have been almost totally destroyed. A few more lessons like this and lawyers and juries will learn not to tamper with and pervert justice.

Telegrams from Miles City state that Deputy Sheriff King and posse have returned from the Upper Rosebud and brought with them thirteen Cheyenne Indians who were participants in the burning of Alderson's ranch. The facts in the case are about as follows: A drunken cow-boy, named Henry Talford, thought it would be extremely funny to shoot a hole through the hat of Black Wolf, a Cheyenne chief. The result was that the Indian received an ugly wound in the head. Returning to his camp Black Wolf's warriors, of course, wanted revenge and started for Alderson's ranch where Talford was working. When the Indians arrived he had skipped the country and no one being at the ranch they vented their rage on the buildings. In connection with these facts it should be known that these Indians have been peaceful, that they were on their reservation and supposed to be supported by the government, when they were nearly starving to death not receiving one-fifth rations, and the attention of the secretary of the interior had to be called to their deplorable condition by the recent meeting of stockmen at Miles City. Also that Black Wolf is one of the best of Indians and that the attack on him was entirely unprovoked.

We must confess that we have no consuming love for Indians, but justice is justice the world over and any infraction we believe should be punished. The Indians knew as well as any of our readers that they would not have obtained justice by recourse to law and they took the only means obtainable to get revenge. Reverse the circumstances and let the unprovoked attack come from an Indian and the matter would never have ended with the burning of a few buildings. Talford tacitly acknowledged his guilt by skipping the country, and he is the man who should have been pursued and brought back for punishment. Because a man is an Indian it does not mean that he has no rights that a white man is bound to respect. Get at the facts in the matter and let punishment fall on the guilty alone.

Dickinson, March 31, 1884.

Dickinson matters have quieted down since the anxiety about eastern communications has subsided. While the four train loads of passengers were delayed here our streets looked much as we expect to see them when spring business has begun.

A new livery, feed and sale stable is one of the assured additions to the business life of this place.

Mr. Jerry Russell, one of the proprietors of the old stable, is now in the East on a business trip, and is expected soon to return with a car load of horses.

The old coal shed, containing about [1,000?] tons of coal, collapsed Sunday and let several hundred tons of coal fall upon the main track. No damage was caused by the accident.

The resident agent of the Northern Pacific land department has issued a glowing hand-bill setting forth the manifold advantages of this region and calling special attention to the brick yards and freight route, employing a thousand teams, all of which radiates from Dickinson. We should greatly enjoy seeing the realization of these projects, but such references seem a trifle too previous in view of the facts. One trouble, if trouble it be, which embarrasses the boomer class, is the apparently reckless and easy habit of misrepresenting the actual condition of their wares.

The American, and particularly the American of the Great West, is deleriously optimistic; everything is touched with the rose-colored light of his hopeful and imaginative nature. Wherein lies the secret of the great disgust most new settlers feel before they have become mentally, morally and physically acclimated. The simple truth about this country, when it becomes known, will bring men and means to develop it quite as rapidly as consistent with a healthy growth. Do not let us enable some future Dickens to regale the world with a revival of Mark Tapley's Egyptian experience.

Anthropos.

There will be over 800 entries at the Chicago Driving Park's midsummer meeting.

One hundred and nineteen horses have scored 2:20 or better and twenty-five have beaten 2:17.

Next to the New York dog show the one now open at Toronto is pronounced the best ever held in America.

Whistler and Muldoon wrestled for three hours at San Francisco, the evening of the 20th, neither gaining a fall. It was one of the most exciting contests ever witnessed.

The postponed six-days' go-as-you-please contest will probably commence April 28, at New York. The entries so far are Noremac, Fitzgerald, Vint, Harland and Rowell.

Matsada Sorakichi and Duncan C. Ross will have a wrestling match in Cleveland, April 7. One fall Japanese style, one catch-as-catch-can and the choice of the third will be decided by lot.

Record breaking began early this season. This time it is the hop, skip and jump record, which was raised from 28 feet, 3½ inches to [29?] feet, 2½ inches by M. W. Ford, at a meeting of the New York atheletic club last week.

The Baltimore Union Club intends to have band music before games and between innings this season. It is an unmitigated nuisance and we will guarantee that the players will have the band fired before the first week's play is ended.

From the make-up of the clubs it now looks as though Minneapolis would win the Northwestern league championship; the Chicago's that of the league; the Athletics that of the American league, and the Chicago Unions that of the Union league. St. Paul seems destined for a place near the foot of the Northwestern League.

The Milwaukee management has decided not to play Sunday games of base-ball and thereto the Grand Rapids Democrat howls its violent opposition. We heartily concur with the Milwaukee management in their decision. Base-ball is just rising to the position it should rightfully occupy—the king of American sports. As long as Sunday games are allowed, so long will its old reputation cling to it. In the past, it has been a gamblers' game. Owing to the efforts of Mr. Hulbert in doing away with Sunday games, it received its first lift toward respectability, and now we are surprised to see a paper supporting a measure that will inevitably lower the standard of base-ball. If for no other reason than as a day of rest, ball-players should not play on Sundays. They are worked hard enough during the week.

The prize fight between Sullivan and Thompson now seems to be an assured fact. It will be fought according to the rules of the London prize ring in either Louisiana, Texas or Kansas, with or without gloves at Sullivan's option. The forfeit is deposited, articles signed and the fight will be for $5,000 a side and the championship of the world. Only six persons on a side will be allowed as witnesses.
On the Range. Call for Bad Lands Association.

There will be a meeting held at Little Missouri crossing, the third Monday in April (the 21st) for the purpose of forming a Bad Lands Association. All raisers of live stock are requested to attend. Upon its organization, business of much importance will come before the association and it is to the interest of every man interested in live stock to attend.

The Committee.
All Bad Lands cattle men and those having any interest in a Bad Lands round-up are requested to meet here on the morning of April 5, to arrange for an annual round-up of this region.
A hog raiser in this county, four years ago started with two sows. During that time he has sold $400 of hogs and his stock now on hand is worth $350; all from two sows.—[Minneapolis Messenger.
Eastern Montana stockmen have wisely decided to take all bulls from the herds on the 1st of November and keep them separated therefrom until the 1st of July of each year.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Stockmen continue to arrive daily in this city from the ranges, and all report that the cattle and stock generally are in splendid condition. They are predicting an unprecedented influx of stockmen into this section of the country this spring and summer, and one and all claim this country to be without a peer.—[Yellowstone, Mont., Journal.

Montana beeves have stood as high or higher than those of any other grazing region, owing in part to the presence of good blood; but this large introduction of blooded animals into the herds south will be likely to change this and place Montana beef in the background, unless our herds are improved by the same process.—[Helena, Mont., Independent.

Two or three hundred new cattle ranches will not overstock the bunch grass ranges of the Bad Lands and Montana but from the number of cattle companies and individuals getting ready to take stock in this spring, we doubt whether there will be much vacant grazing territory left next spring. People who think of going into this safe and profitable business should be up and doing.—[Northwest.

Cattlemen of the northwest must be active and positive in their policy to prevent the introduction of infectious diseases into their herds. They must provide unquestioned security and leave no act undone for the good of the industry. Great care and sound discretion must guide every step. There should be no mistakes in a matter that involves the wealth of half a dozen states and territories.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

There are thirteen crooks lingering behind the bars of the Bent county jail, all of whom can trace the cause of their arrest to the effective work of a successful stock growers' association. With stockmen, forbearance has ceased to be a virtue and "iron bars" will be brought into requisition in other counties before the season of 1884 is over, unless the "stray stock pullers" take a timely warning.—[Hurricane, Colo., Cactus.

Windgalls are produced by sprains of the tendons and these may occur in many ways. The treatment of the puffy swellings consists in reducing the inflammation by cold applications, as pounded ice or a solution of saltpetre and salt in cold water, and then favoring absorption by blistering. Rest is necessary during the treatment. Sometimes the blister may need repeating two or three times, but always after a sufficient interval to permit the effects to pass off. After every effort the trouble will return whenever excessive strain is brought upon the weakened tendon.—[Kansas City Live Stock Indicator.

There is a wide difference of opinion among Texas men who claim opportunities for making an estimate as to the number of cattle likely to take the trail for the north the coming spring. The highest estimates we have heard, place the number at 350,000, while the lowest is 150,000. From all the information we have been able to gather it is doubtful, in our opinion, if the drive amounts to more than a quarter of a million head, and even this, we think, is a very liberal estimate. Double that number of Texas cattle will change hands but about half of them will be sold in connection with Texas ranges, or to ranchmen owning herds on neighboring ranges.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

We hail with pleasure the birth of a new Dakota paper, The Bad Lands Cow Boy. Its proprietor and editor is the Marquis de Mores, son of the Duc de Vallombrosa, who is well known in France as the leader of the social world at Cannes. The Cow Boy is really a neat little journal, with lots to read in it, and the American press has every reason to be proud of its new baby. We are quite sure it will live to be a credit to its family. The Cow Boy evidently means business. It says in the introductory notice in its first number that it intends to be the leading cattle paper of the Northwest and adds that it is not published for fun but for two dollars a year.—New York Herald.

No comments; no cards.

It is now quite certain that Marquis de Mores, who has engaged very extensively in the beef trade at Medora, will create a branch business at Deadwood just as soon as a railroad from any point reaches us. He has taken a contract to furnish New York with forty cars of dressed beef, and to do this kills 200 head each day. He buys large numbers from Wyoming and all sections, taking them to Medora. The dressed meat is placed in refrigerator cars and shipped through to that city in as fresh a condition as when first slaughtered. He has indicated his intention to establish a branch at this place just as soon as he can be afforded steam transportation.

It is needless to comment upon the impetus, such an industry would lend to the business of the Hills, but alone is of sufficient importance to elicit every effort of our people to encourage the completion of a road to this point. It would make a steady market for the fatted cattle of this section and throw large sums of money into circulation here that now is captured by other places so far distant from us that its stimulating effects are not experienced by our people. Such an enterprise, aside from the financial benefits, will afford ample employment for a large number of men, and would form one more substantial and lasting feature to the Hills.—[Minnesela Boomer.

I have yet to find any stock raiser dissatisfied with his efforts to improve his stock, provided he has given care and attention to his business. Of course, there are plenty of men in Texas, as elsewhere, who carelessly start into any business and neglect it, that grumble at their want of success. Some of these cry down blooded stock. Let us briefly consider the question of which pays the best to keep, a blooded bull or a Spanish scrub? Take the Spanish bull, turn him out to rustle for himself; spring finds him poor and weak, when he is old enough for service, his fight with poverty has left him a poor subject to breed from, if he gets one-half the calves of cows served he will have done remarkably well, and these calves are generally thriftless little fellows that develop into small beeves at maturity and sell at low figures. Take the blooded bull, pasture and care for him until he reaches the proper age for duty. Expend cotton seed, corn, oats and millet upon him. When he is put to service the result is ninety per cent of good strong calves that will mature a year younger and weigh full 300 pounds more than our Spanish bull's produce, and sell for at least $15 a head more in market. Say the Spanish bull gets 25 out of 50 cows, and these calves at four years old sell for $25 a head or $625. The shorthorn gets 45 calves, which at three years old sell for $40 per head or $1,800. Now the loss from the failure to produce of the 25 cows bred to the Spanish bull, will amply cover all the expense of feed and extra keep of the blooded bull. A merchant's rule is to handle the goods that is the quickest sale and bring the best returns. Stockmen should follow suit.

The above illustration I know to be true for I have seen them sell together on the market. Three years ago I was at the Stock Yards at Chicago and had some very good native steers (Missouri cattle) for which I obtained $4.75 per hundred, thinking I had made a pretty good sale. Mr. Hall, of Hall, Greer & Co., called my attention to a car-load of Colorado half-breed Herefords in a pen opposite my stock that a purchaser was just closing the trade for at $5 per hundred. I asked, "How does it come that those range cattle bring more money than my natives?"

"Well," said he, "I will explain it to you. Those cattle are no better than yours as far as flesh is concerned, but in the long run makes the shrinkage heavier and they kill better than your cattle for they come such a long distance there isn't anything but beef in them when they get here, and being wild and unaccustomed to being penned they won't eat or drink to do any good, while your cattle are quiet and gentle, will eat all they want and take a big fill of water, etc., making [quite a difference?], you see."

Then he said: "Now, I have just given you a minor reason; here is a load of cattle off of the same ranch, but are nothing but scrubs. I only sold them for $4.25 per hundred, and they are just as good in flesh as those over there, but don't you see these half-breeds are of a uniform color. All look very nearly alike!"

There is the beauty of breeding blooded stock. If you get a bull that has been bred a solid color, he will make seven calves out of ten just like him. I think that load of cattle the finest I have ever seen. They had been sorted out and put in a load to themselves, and they well paid the owner for his trouble, for the buyers were two to one for that load of cattle to any other in the yard. They had been shipped from Colorado to Nebraska and corned about three months, and they were perfect beauties. These were not all the grade cattle I've seen knock the socks off of scrubs. I have seen numbers of them. I followed shipping to Chicago for three years and it very often came under my notice. You can ship two loads of cattle to St. Louis any day, one of the Spanish and the other half-breeds, and your half-breeds will bring from twenty-five to fifty cents per hundred over your scrubs every time.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

A trial of the Far West cigar is its best recommendation.
Mr. J. C. Beekman Fish, a New York banker and broker, is visiting the Marquis.
Mr. Geo. Roderick has claimed the butte north of town and is now "holding it down."
A. J. Monroe, of Junction City, an old friend of Frank Keeler, is in town for a few days.
F. G. Sikes, travelling for the Gilmore Furniture Co., of Minneapolis, is in town securing orders.
F. B. Allen, the secretary of the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co., is expected to-day or to-morrow.
There were two sections of No. 1 this morning, both very heavy trains. The first section had eleven coaches.
Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
Now that spring is fairly upon us, the cleaning up season commences. Every one who can rustle a rake is hard at work.
The company's hides were all packed and shipped Saturday. Such a favorable impression was made on both sides that Mr. Hample will doubtless be the future buyer here.
A visit to the store of Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, is rather an eye-opener on the way business is done in the West. They carry a stock that would do credit to any city firm.
The gang of men who are putting up the through telegraph wire between St. Paul and Portland arrived here yesterday. They are making from twelve to twenty miles a day.

M. J. Mahon, of Mandan, is on deck this week with an advertisement of his restaurant. From personal experience we can assert that he gives perfect satisfaction. Mike's is certainly the place to make your "Headquarters" while in Mandan.

Mr. John Nye, a Livingstone and Deadwood capitalist, was in town Tuesday and thinks strongly of interesting himself in the Medora freight route. He has formerly been a forwarding agent and understands the freight business thoroughly.

M. G. Hall, assistant superintendent of the Northern Pacific Express Co., came in this morning on the second section of No. 1. He expects to make Medora an express station very soon, which will be a great convenience to the citizens on this side of the river.

A visit to the furniture rooms of Duncan & Hillis, in Mandan, disclosed the fact that for the future there will be no more going to St. Paul to buy. Their stock compares favorably with that carried by any city firm, and one who cannot be suited there is certainly hard to please.

Mr. M. L. Kramer, of Pueblo, Colo., has been in town for several days to attend the round-up meeting, to be held next Saturday. He owns about 15,000 head of cattle in Colorado and will perhaps drive up a number of beeves to fatten in the Bad Lands. He is much pleased with the country.

Mr. Flynn, of Mandan, is intending to start a boot and shoe store here. As yet he is undecided whether he will give it his personal attention or make it a branch store. In either event it will be a needed addition. Mr. Flynn is well known throughout this whole country and has hosts of friends who will patronize him.

It has just been learned that Mr. Matthias, the superintendent of this, the Missouri division, has resigned to take effect in a few days. The cause of his action is unknown, but we will certainly be sorry to see him go. No word can be said against his management and in private he is one of the most courteous gentleman we have ever met.

Could our subscribers read some of our letters from the East it would surprise them to know the general interest and in a good many cases the ignorance of eastern persons in reference to the Bad Lands. In nearly every letter some reference is made to intended visits and all express a decided curiosity to see the wonders of the Bad Lands. The number of last year's sight-seers will be doubled this summer. The most of these are persons of capital and many will be induced to stay.

A visit to Mandan and Bismarck has disclosed to us the fact that every one there is interested in Medora. Eleven lots have been spoken for in those two places, and they will doubtless go off like hot cakes. First come, first served is the rule, and our citizens should see to it that all the choice lots are not gobbled by outsiders. We have only space to say to-day that the deeds arrived this morning and prices may be learned by a visit to The Cow Boy office.

Some crank at Dickinson has issued a luminous circular advertising the town and speaks in glowing terms of the thousand teams on the Dickinson freight route. We wonder if said crank has ever thought of the result of one of these circulars falling into the hands of an intending settler there and the sense of disgust he will have when he finds out the bare-faced lie. For the sake of Dickinson and this whole country, such a nuisance as this agent has proved himself to be should be abated. Will the sensible citizens of Dickinson cork him up?
Smoke the Far West cigar, sold only by Roberts & Co.
A new barber has taken the place of the bold soldier boy who has gone back to the defence of his country.
Mr. Sam English, well known to many of our citizens, is on his way to Medora to engage in business. He will be a welcome addition.
We are anxious to hear from "How" again, and if he doesn't show-up soon we will give him away and let the wrath of the community down on his devoted head.
The smiling countenance of "Big Foot" Ryder has been beaming on our citizens for a day or two. "The gang" is resting from its arduous labors until the June freshet.
Again has Frank Smith placed our Bad Lands museum under obligations to him. One specimen has the plain print of water flags upon it, although it was found on the top of a high butte.

The immigration edition of The Mandan Pioneer has had the good effect of influencing several persons to write us in reference to the Bad Lands. From recent letters we are convinced that one at least will settle here.

The following is an extract from a letter written in Paris, France, to a friend of ours in Medora: "The Bad Lands Cow Boy is a favorite of mine. Be sure and send it to me regularly. Give my kindest regards to the editor and wish him every success." She is the right kind to stick to, William.

The knight of the curry-comb tackled a cotton pie April 1, and in his herculean efforts to swallow it and not give the thing away to his fellow boarders, his eyes rolled out on the bridge of his nose until they gazed into each others countenances, and the boys never "smiled," oh, no!

One of the strangest displays of aurora borealis it has ever been our lot to witness was seen last Friday night. The usual flickerings were greatly magnified, but the climax was reached with a broad band of light looking exactly like a dense mist extending across the heavens from the eastern to the western horizon. The greatest display of lights was also from the eastern horizon.

Messrs. Hyde and Wilkes left Tuesday night for Chicago to visit their families for a week or two. Mr. Hyde will bring his family back with him and live at the Cantonment until his residence is completed. Mr. Wilkes, though strongly urged by a number of would-be sons-in-law, could not be prevailed upon to bring his family back with him. Oh, George, how could you be so cruel?

The stockmen's ball Saturday night bids fair to eclipse anything of the kind held in Little Missouri. Every preparation has been made. First-class music from Glendive will be in attendance and supper will be served at a convenient hour. The best of order is guaranteed and everything will doubtless pass off pleasantly. Messrs. Keeler and Goodall are well known enough to insure this. Tickets, including supper, are only $2.50 each, and no one can afford to miss the good time.

We received a call from Mr. Gregor Lang last week, and he reports that his cattle are in prime condition. Only a few head have died, and as a jelly-like substance was found about the joints of each one, there is no doubt that the deaths were due to the bruises the cattle received in the railroad accident. Mr. Lang has a first-rate ranch about fifty miles up the river and will put a thousand more cattle on it this spring. He will soon begin to erect a brick house and when completed will bring out his family.

It will be a matter of interest and news to the most of our readers that a new road has been found out of the Bad Lands to the divide, for our freight route. It is even better than the old one and at least five miles shorter, the distance to the divide being now eighteen miles or less. There was no serious need of bridges, but five have been put in so that the road in the Bad Lands is now almost as good as that on the divide. Very little grading was required. A gang of men under Joe Pennell have been at work for several days and by to-night or to-morrow, at farthest, our route will be finished and be then the most perfect one that there has ever been or will be west of the Missouri. Considerable additional freight has come and a trip will soon be made. A large number of additional contracts have been made by Mr. Jones, at Deadwood, guaranteeing an abundance of freighting for the whole 400 teams that will start from Medora.

The Marquis and Mr. Sleeper returned early this morning. They came in on the first through train that has run from Bismarck for nearly a week. The old track has been washed away for two miles and a temporary track was laid on the prairie. Mr. Sleeper, on being "held up," stated that every thing in regard to the company's business is working in the most satisfactory manner. An abundance of ice has been put up at all the places where cold-storage houses have been or are now being erected. Most of the cold-storage houses are near completion and will be ready for business as soon as the summer killing begins. Large contracts have been made in New York for dressed beef and this trade alone will keep the abattoirs busy. The retail merchants up and down the line have already signified their intention of purchasing almost wholly from the company's cold-storage houses and a prosperous business season will open almost immediately. In addition to the buildings now being erected, it was found necessary to add one to the already large St. Paul facilities of the company. The Marquis intends going on to Helena almost immediately and Mr. Sleeper will return to St. Paul.
