The boys always manage to enjoy themselves here, but a little the most uproarious time we have had lately was at the expense of Mr. Hample, who has lately bought the company's hides. It seems that when Mr. Hample cannot get hide quotations he makes his rates from the other market reports, especially on wheat and corn. Last Friday evening Mr. Fisher became apparently very much interested in reading a paper, and finally laid it down with the remark that the market seemed wonderfully depressed. Mr. Hample became deeply interested at once, and taking up the paper turned eagerly to the market reports. Wheat, 52c; corn, 27c, was the first thing he saw and his hair began to raise like the fur of an angry Sir Thomas cat. By comparison, the hides that he had just bought and made a first payment of $10,000 on, were worth but little if any more than the $10,000. Vain efforts were made by him to buy off from his contract. A more thoroughly "broke up" man we have never seen until a kind friend showed him the date of the paper—March 23, 1840.
The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.

At last we have found some one who realizes the money there is in such a venture and a brick-yard and pottery works will soon be in active operation here. Mr. Peter Book, of Mandan, is the gentleman to whom we refer. He is one of the best known masons and contract- there, that he built the People's block being a sufficient recommendation. Mr. Book will be here next week, as he is only waiting in Mandan to close up his business. The clay with which our buttes abound he says will make brick of a beautiful dark red color, exactly similar to the famous St. Louis brick. It is also the very best quality of pottery clay, and as Mr. Book has had long experience in making both brick and pottery he has every hope of being completely successful in their manufacture here. He also expects to make pressed brick exclusively, as aside from the cost of the presses they can be made as cheaply and will command a far readier sale. There will be a splendid market for both the brick and pottery, and Mr. Book is to be congratulated on his foresight in entering into the business at this point.

Now that many intelligent observers have gone over our freight route, it is being made known that a very valuable country will be developed by it. The riches of the Bad Lands are spoken of in another article. When the road strikes the ridge, some of the best agricultural land in the territory is found and with few exceptions extends clear to the Hills. Besides the precious metals found here, there is at least one vein of pure hard coal which is now mined extensively and found to equal Pennsylvania coal in every respect. A vein of the purest mica has been found and is now being sold at the mine for $90 a cubic foot. The supply seems inexhaustible. These reasons, besides many others, make it almost certain that a railroad will soon be built. It has been under consideration for some time and as for almost half the distance the road will require no grading whatever and will be immensely remunerative we feel safe in predicting that the road will at least be commenced before six months are passed.

A person scarcely thinks he is becoming acquainted with the resources of the Bad Lands when something new is discovered of which he had no previous conception. We have yet to hear of a man who was posted, who did not place the Bad Lands at or near the top of all the cattle countries in the United States. Here the productiveness of the Bad Lands was and still is supposed to stop. On the contrary, it scarcely begins here. By repeated experiments the soil has been found extremely productive and it will raise vegetables in profusion. The strangest thing about the soil is that the tops of the buttes, from two to four hundred feet high, have been found far more productive than the bottom lands. Beyond gardening, however, agriculture will never be a success here on account of the broken nature of the country. To the east and southeast, however, no better land can be found anywhere. The buttes which have hitherto been considered worthless, except for their wealth of coal and the shelter they furnished stock, are now found to be regular gold mines. Red and white brick and potter's clay abound and of a quality unsurpassed in the world. Fire clay, cement, molder's sand and sandstone, all of the very best quality, are in almost every butte. The coal, one to five veins of which can be seen in every [raw?] butte, is the best quality of lignite to be found in Dakota. Beyond all this it is certain that there is a large amount of petroleum in the Bad Lands, as many streams are so thickly covered as to be unfit for drinking. Whether it will pay to sink wells for it is a question which will soon be decided. A great future is certainly in store for the Bad Lands.

The following memoranda were handed us by Dr. J. M. Louthan. As our readers will notice it is a very interesting account of a trip made from Deadwood and Spearfish over the now completed Medora freight route to Medora by a party composed of Thos. G. Jones, H. M. Jorgens, E. Deffebach, Dr. J. M. Louthan and Doc. Pennell:

"We started April 1 from Spearfish at 3 P. M. Traveling over the new road to Red Water we found an outfit busily at work on the bridge. The stream was down and we forded it easily. B. Deffebach and myself went over the grade with saddle horses and found the work almost complete on the Red Water hill. The road was dry and dusty from that point to Belle Fourche, where we arrived at 5 P. M. Here we found A. Burnham with a force of ten men and five of Mr. T. G. Jones' teams, constructing a bridge across the Belle Fourche river. The bridge will be finished by April 10 at a cost of $1,500. Fording the Belle Fourche on a good rock bottom, we pulled for Crow creek, where we arrived at 5:30. Here we made an early camp for the night, having plenty of wood and water. After supper, beds were quickly made and we were soundly asleep in the open air.

Daylight of April 2 broke without a cloud. At 6:30 we were on the move. Before reaching the divide between Crow creek and Owl creek a beautiful phenomenon was seen. Looking toward the east we could see a perfect rainbow on the blades of grass, caused by the frost crystals resolving themselves into dew drops. The road was good and perfectly dry between Crow creek and Owl creek where we arrived at 8:30. This will be bridged in a few days, as there is an abundance of wood immediately alongside the trail. At 10 o'clock we headed for Indian creek, arriving there at 12:20 and encamped for dinner. Continuing our course directly north we went into camp for the night on the south fork of the Moreau.

At 8 o'clock of April 3, we crossed the Moreau and found the freight road to Medora. Stopping for dinner near Nash's ranch in the Short Pine hills. One great beauty of the whole road we found was that everywhere there was an abundance of wood and water. At 5:30, we arrived at John Gallop's, where we were hospitably entertained for the night.

At 6 o'clock of April 4 we started on, but Deffebach's Arabian steed, better known as a broncho, concluded to roll. In so doing he turned the saddle, became scared and started for the Cœur D'Alene mines. Rassie, having no faith in that section of the country, concluded he would round the brute up and strike for the Bohemian settlement on the Northern Pacific R. R. All this took up much valuable time of those who were anxious to locate the road from Spearfish to Medora. At 5:30 we arrived at Eagle springs, better known as Foot & Beckett's ranch. This place was located upward of two years ago, and the firm have since kept a hunter's supply store. Buffalo used to be here by the thousands, but now they are all gone. We saw the carcasses of hundreds strewn over the prairies, in some instances neither hide nor meat being taken. Being a sportsman myself, I keenly felt the inevitable fact, as I looked into the dim future, that the time was fast coming when the buffalo, antelope, deer and beaver would pass into the long catalogue of animals that had become extinct. Yet while taking a philosophical view of this seemingly wanton destruction, we could still see before the sunset of our lives great herds of cattle roaming over this vast domain, more profitable to the white man than game of any kind. Taking into consideration that this country, wonderful for its agricultural and grazing resources, is in close proximity to the Sioux reservation, the sooner game is destroyed the less danger there is to the pioneer, who will soon find for his wife and little ones a good home and open up a new country, which will earn himself an independency and lay the foundations for railroads, towns, schools, churches and colleges.

At Eagle springs we found Mr. Palmer and wife in charge of Foot & Beckett's store and eating house. The first person we met being Mr. Jas. Elliott, bookkeeper of the VVV outfit. Mr. Palmer and wife soon had a good supper for us which was heartily enjoyed by the entire party. Mr. Elliott accompanied us for a distance on our way to the railroad.

At 6 o'clock of April 5 we started over a beautiful rolling prairie, and after ten miles pulled up at Mr. Maddox' ranch, located on one of the head streams of the Cannonball river. Here we saw a vein of coal forty feet thick, exposed to view. After making some investigations we found that the whole country was underlaid with coal. After spending some time here, Doc, the scout, misled us to the extent of about eight miles, owing to the fact that the road had been shortened by the locators from Medora some ten or twelve miles.

In the afternoon, when within eight miles of Medora, rain and snow began falling. We soon arrived at Eaton's ranch, however, and were cordially entertained by Mr. Eaton, who told us that his sons were at Little Missouri, attending the stock meeting. In the morning, bidding good-by to Mr. Eaton, who is one of God's noblemen, we soon arrived at our destination—Medora, the future great.

During our whole journey we did not change horses and the time actually consumed in travelling was a little less than three days and a half. Nearly the whole way the road was dry and dusty, and the distance from Medora to Spearfish is not an inch over 160 miles."

The meeting to arrange for the round-up of the Little Missouri river and tributaries was held, in accordance with the call, last Saturday, April 5, in Pennell & Roberts' hall, at Little Missouri, Dak.

The meeting was called to order at 2:30 by H. S. Boice, who nominated B. Barr for chairman. No other nominations being made, Mr. Barr was declared unanimously elected. Howard Eaton nominated A. T. Packard for secretary, who was also unanimously elected.

C. W. Sleeper moved that the chair appoint a delegate from each range to arrange for a round-up, seconded by G. Grisy. Mr. Boice moved to amend by having the chair appoint a committee of seven; J. L. Truscott seconded. Carried. The committee as appointed was: G. W. Towers, C. W. Sleeper, H. S. Boice, M. Wadsworth, Howard Eaton, Wm. Merrifield and G. Grisy. Howard Eaton resigning, W. L. Eaton was appointed in his stead.

Howard Eaton moved for a recess until the committee made their report. Carried.

After an adjournment of half an hour the meeting was called to order and listened to the following report:

"Your committee would recommend that the round-up for this district commence on May 25, at the crossing of the Northern Pacific R. R. of the Big Beaver at Keith, and hunt down to the mouth of the Big Beaver. Thence move up the Little Missouri, working tributaries to the mouth of the Little Beaver, sending a small party over to the headwaters of the Knife and Green rivers. Thence up the Little Beaver and cross over to the head of the Big Beaver, working tributaries, and thence down to the point of starting at the railroad crossing of the Big Beaver. We would also recommend that John Goodall be appointed captain or foreman of this round-up and that Wm. Jones be appointed assistant, and that the foreman have full control of this round-up with authority to discharge any men who refuse to obey orders.

THE COMMITTEE.

It is a significant fact that meetings are being held in various parts of England to protest against the severity of the restrictions relative to the importation of foreign cattle contemplated in the contagious disease act, now before parliament.—[Western Rural.

R. M. Sparks, Lexington, Mo., a prominent breeder and owner of a cattle ranch at Medicine Lodge, Kan., who has considerable practical experience with diseased cattle, informs The Kansas Farmer that he has read everything published concerning the new cattle disease in that state and is confident that it was nothing more than grease heel.

Great mortality prevails among the horses in different sections of Oregon. The disease prevalent seems to be blind staggers. A large percentage of cases result fatally, and the disease baffles the skill of the most experienced veterinary surgeons. Soon after contracting the disease the animal becomes partially or totally blind, is unable to walk, swells up and dies. The greatest mortality prevails in Chicamas and Yam Hill counties. Over 500 valuable horses have died recently in these counties. The disease is seriously interfering with farmers' seeding. It is contagious and at our latest accounts it was spreading.—[Western Farmer.

This time last year a Barber county cattleman was a most abject and miserable appearing being; his face was long and sour; his words were few and doleful, and he appeared to have lost his last friend. How different now! He capers nimbly on sleek fat horses; his face is wreathed in smiles; he luxuriates in ten-cent cigars and fine-cut tobacco; takes hot hotel dinners when he comes to town and would as soon talk of selling his family as his cows. Last year he was wondering if he would have cattle enough to pay the round-up expenses, and this year he is wondering if he can get hands enough to brand all his calves. This has been a remarkable easy winter on cattle, and the grass will be here in a few more days. Last year the sun appeared to have formed a lasting partnership with the northern icebergs and agreed to send out no more warm rays. Let us hope that our stockmen will always feel as good as they do now.—[Barber Co., Kan., Index.

DICKINSON, April 9, 1884.

The presence of Messrs. Bramble & Keyes on Monday gave our townspeople renewed interest in the proposed freight route, and we expect to see before long a few, at least, of the thousand teams that are said to be at work on the line.

Private teams have been loaded out for the Hills right along and more freight on the way.

Large quantities of nursery goods in the shape of orchard and garden fruit trees from New York and Illinois nurseries are lying in the freight house.

It is said that steps will be taken during the week looking toward the erection of a capacious warehouse at this point to accommodate the Black Hills freight.

Dickinson is growing. Several men have come here during the week past who expect to remain. One of them has bought a lot and a bill of lumber, and will put up his house himself immediately. Another gentleman, Dr. Pelton, of Frederick City, Md., looking up land and investments in his own interest and eastern parties, has written for them to come on. The doctor is a practical man and proposes to employ steam to break the Dakota sod, also to grind feed, bale hay and in various other ways make the invisible giant useful. He expects to use a convertible traction engine instead of the cable system in use elsewhere.

We observed the polite reference to our former notes in The Dickinson Press of the 5th inst. In the spasm of courtesy that agitated the worthy editor, he entirely forgot to say that our note was untrue. We fail to see the motive that actuated him, but probably he thinks he knows the side upon which his bread is buttered, and since The Press has appropriated the issue, we will say to him that it knows the truth of the note criticised. The example of misrepresentation selected for our text is only one of many such which will some day rise in condemnation of their author. Of course, if the authors alone were the ones who would suffer, no one would care to stay the coming retribution, but they are not; this whole country and the people who are misled are the ones to suffer. Intelligent selfishness alone ought to instruct thinking men better. The very lax ideas of business morality indicated by such methods must be corrected, otherwise they will correct themselves in a fashion not altogether to the fancy of such business men. And when a so-called newspaper prostitutes its pages to support and intrench what it knows to be false, it simply shows the depth to which the disease of commercial immorality has burrowed.

Mr. Alex. Metzger, of Bismarck, was in town Wednesday. His genial grip is ever welcome.
Mr. Joy, of Livingston, returned this morning to become connected with the freight route.

D. K. Wade has received a car-load of household goods and is freighting them to his future home on Tepee bottom. His family will be here soon.
Up to the present time only one car load of freight has arrived, but enough is on the way and daily expected to load the outfit now here, about 100,000 lbs.
An impromptu dance was held Monday evening at the Western House, which was thoroughly enjoyed by all participators. It was gotten up on short notice, but the affair was a complete success.

Our readers will be greatly interested in the communication of Dr. J. M. Louthan. He is an old campaigner, has the best practice in Spearfish, is a thorough gentleman, and all his statements can be relied upon.

The plans and specifications are all made and the contract for the new billiard hall has been awarded to Mr. Thos. McClung. A large amount of lumber is here and the building will begin almost immediately.

Mr. Boice, of the well-known firm of Berry, Boice & Co., says that although many weak pilgrims were brought into this country late last fall, the total loss of cattle for the Bad Lands will fall considerably under three per cent.

Mr. G. Grisy, of Grisy and Wibaux, is enthusiastic over this as a cattle country. He has only been here a year but his herd is in splendid condition and his loss will fall under one per cent. We doubt if a better showing can be found anywhere.

Jos. Doulische, who was considered almost well from the injuries he received from the caving in of a foundation, died last Thursday. His death was entirely unexpected and was a great blow to the family. He was buried Saturday afternoon on the coal mine butte.

Gregor Lang had a valuable horse stolen from the Cantonment last Saturday night, but it was tracked and recovered thirty-five miles up the river, the first of the week. We profess to be a law-abiding citizen but we wish to state here and now that the most effectual way of ridding the country of horse thieves is to hang them when caught, to the nearest tree. We have been remarkably [free?] from such depredators and harsh measures will insure immunity for the future.

Two hundred and sixty head of yearlings and two-year-olds, belonging to W. N. Thompson & Co., came in yesterday morning. They were under the charge of Wm. Dantz and Lloyd Roberts, who brought them through from Minnesota. They were in prime condition, although they had a long run from Jamestown. Yesterday afternoon they were started toward the home ranch. Messrs. Dantz and Roberts will return soon to Minnesota after another bunch. Meantime, the former will go into the upper country after horses.

Another good citizen will soon be lost and gained, Mandan being the loser and Medora the gainer. Mr. Book came last Friday and was satisfied far beyond his expectations. The supposition was that good brick clay was here in abundance, but we confess that we were surprised to find the value of our buttes. Clay for making the best red and cream-colored brick in the world is here in the greatest abundance. Mr. Book says that he can compete [in every?] way with St. Louis and Milwaukee brick, pressed or moulded. Besides these kinds of clay, Mr. Book discovered the best quality of fire clay. This will be extremely valuable, as it is and has always been costly. Beyond this, too, was the discovery of cement and a vein of pottery clay that surpasses anything found anywhere. At last the Bad Lands are coming to the front as being something besides the best cattle country in the United States, and Mr. Book proposes to help develop them to their utmost. He is now in Mandan getting his outfit ready and will soon be here and at work. His first contract is for 500,000 brick for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co., but others will soon keep him busy. In the fall he will start an extensive pottery works, thus furnishing employment to many men the year round. Mr. Book is thoroughly in earnest in this matter and is sure of great success.
J. C. B. Fish left last Saturday to continue his trip to Portland.
Messrs. T. G. Jones, C. W. Sleeper, Jos. Pennell and H. M. Jorgens started for St. Paul Tuesday night.
Twenty-three freight cars on one side-track and seventeen on another made it look like business yesterday.
C. A. Wood, of The Northwestern Live Stock Journal, made us a pleasant call last Saturday. He is a fit representative of the best stock paper in America.
Mr. R. S. Richardson, of Sully, brought us in some fine specimens of crystallizations this morning. He found them near Sully Springs.
An intelligent eastener on the train Tuesday evening, asked a group of Bad Lands enthusiasts if the Bad Lands were visible or did a person have to dig for them. Such is fame.

A large cinnamon bear, weight about 1,200 pounds, was killed lately near J. A. Beaumont's sheep ranch. "Scotty" has promised us the claws and if they don't materialize pretty soon, we intend starting after them.

With ten changes of horses, it took the last mail on the Pierre line nearly seven days to get into the Hills. Messrs. Jones, Louthan, Jorgan and Deffebach came through in three days and a half with no change of horses. Our route is dry and dusty. The Pierre route is a perfect quagmire of gumbo.

Of all the dismal failures we ever saw, the bear and boar fight last Saturday was the worst. The two bears and boar being put into a cattle car, the only sign of hostility between them was a sigh of satisfaction on the part of the boar as he nestled down in the soft fur of one of the bears, who had previously curled up into one of the corners and gone to sleep.

Dr. Louthan added materially to the value of our Bad Lands museum by presenting us with some fine specimens of petrified eels and the petrified coccyx of a human being, probably an Indian woman. He also gave us a specimen of coal from a mine on our freight route which is pure anthracite of a quality very nearly, if not quite, equal to Pennsylvania coal.

The western line of Dakota, running due south forms the eastern Wyoming line. Medora and Deadwood are both almost exactly fifteen miles from this line. Medora, therefore, is almost if not directly on a line drawn directly north from Deadwood. Except for about four miles in the Bad Lands and another short turn near Spearfish, our route goes almost as straight as the flight of a bullet. Accurate judges estimate the distance at one hundred and seventy-two miles.

Let every Republican heed the call published elseywhere and attend the convention to be held day after to-morrow in Medora, at the Hotel de Mores, at 2 P. M. For many reasons a full attendance is necessary, to express the will of the majority of the Republican voters, to elect a good delegate to Huron and a good county central committee, to have every voter's political status decided, to form a union so that concerted action can be taken and to consider many other items of interest that will turn up.

The most complete success in the amusement way we have ever had was the stockmen's ball last Saturday evening, given by Messrs. Keeler and Goodall. The music was furnished by Messrs. R. A. Dickinson and R. D. Owen, of Glendive, on violins, and T. J. Kerr on the piano. No one could possibly pick a flaw in the music and all three of the gentlemen showed that they were finished musicians. They can consider themselves engaged for future events of the kind. The ladies turned out in full force and joined in the good time as heartily as the gentlemen. The climax was reached, however, when the company seated themselves to as fine a supper as could be gotten up in the west. Everything that heart could wish was provided in abundance and keen appetites soon made large inroads on the choice viands. No expense was spared to make the ball a success, which it was in every sense of the word.

A Connecticut emigrant standing on the platform of a train yesterday began to remark that "This seems to be a pooty slim kentry," when seeing the Senate sign he started with a comrade after an invigorator. Placing ten cents on the counter, the clerical Jim remarked, "Fifteen cents more, please." The wooden nutmegger said: "What, fifteen cents for two glasses of beer?" Jim then explained that it was fifteen cents for one drink, but owing to the flush times and on account of the customer's good looks, he would break over a life-long custom make it two for a quarter, as nickels did not pass here. And then the emigrant wrapped his arms around his stomach and is probably hugging it yet to get his money's worth out of that beer. We wonder what he will say when he bumps up against "a quarter a smile" in Montana.

BELFIELD, Dak., April 9, 1884.

EDITOR COW BOY:

May!

May she never!

May she never return!

Breaking, seeding and backsetting are now in full blast, and it now looks as if mother earth would be afforded every opportunity to distinguish herself this season.

Wm. LeMoyne returned east Sunday morning in company of a Mr. C. Taylor, who spent several days in the village.

Postmaster Harbison left for his former home in New York a few days ago. He intends to go into a limited partnership (for life) bringing with him Mrs. J. W. Harbison upon his return. All the available tin cans, pans and such will be brought into requisition to properly serenade the happy couple upon their arrival at Belfield!

The "cause celebre" of the stolen pony was settled by the Townsite Company paying costs and furnishing a good substitute for the replevined animal.

Several couples prepared to attend the ball at Little Missouri Saturday, but the long delay of a freight train finally kept many at home who now deeply regret their change of base. Those who were fortunate enough to attend pronounce the affair the most enjoyable ever held west of the Missouri and sincerely hope for a repetition of the good time.

Bob Montgomery has just finished his spring cleaning and those who knew his place before will have visions of Arabian nights when they enter it again. A very liberal and judicious expenditure of paste, brush and paper coupled with Mr. Day's artistic skill have transformed his neat resort into one of the cosiest places on the line, and the vicious buffalo who holds the fort, more loudly than words proclaims "Get there, Eli."

Bob Tuttle has had word sent him from the Indian agency that he can have his stolen horses returned to him by calling for them at the agency. Bob will go, and if he meets the fellows who took accidentally, there will be some more good Indians added to the list.

Quite a heavy delegation of Belfielders will likely attend Saturday's first convention of Billings county.

Ed. Gallien proved up on his valuable homestead a few days ago, making the third homestead proved up on at Belfield within four months.

United States Government Surveyor Austin visited the town on Saturday and the result will be that three new townships will be surveyed in a few weeks. This land comprises some of the very finest in the county and will not go begging a minute.

SADIE.
The Foot and Mouth Disease Scare.

The Texas Live Stock Journal publishes a complete exposure of the Kansas foot and mouth disease scare. Some of the best veterinary surgeons of the United States and Canada who have had much experience with the disease in England and who have made careful examinations in Kansas, have been interviewed and they all state positively that there has not been a symptom of the foot and mouth disease. The whole trouble was caused by allowing the animals to stand in filth and decaying vegetation, which generated large amounts of ammonia. This inflamed the hoofs and made them freeze easily. Much of the hay fed was wild rye upon almost every stalk of which ergot was clinging. This generated a disease called ergotism which draws the blood from the extremities. This disease further increased the tendency to freeze the feet, and to the above causes, the whole shameful scare can be attributed. With good cause we can say the scare was shameful, for it has done the live stock of the United States infinite pecuniary damage, and was the result in the first place of gross ignorance both of the disease itself and how to take care of cattle.

This leads us to speak of a subject which we have had in mind for a long time. It is that the government should appoint a competent corps of veterinary surgeons who should immediately take charge and have under complete control infected cattle. In Germany, for instance, every hamlet almost has a veterinary surgeon to whom every head of infected stock must be reported. He is the supreme arbitrator in all cases, and if he considers the disease contagious or the animal beyond recovery, he immediately orders it killed and the body disposed of in such a way that infection is impossible from the carcass. A fund is established by the German government and for every animal thus killed the owner receives about two-thirds the value. Long experience has proved that this is the only sure way to prevent contagion, and that the plan is eminently successful.

On the other hand, in the United States, the owner suffers a complete loss in case the animal dies and by keeping it until the last hope of its living has expired many others are liable to be infected. Should the government take hold of the matter and establish a fund and a corps of competent veterinarians all danger of a repetition of the Kansas scare would be over.

We call the attention of stockmen to this idea and hope that future meetings of the different associations will take immediate measures to have the project pushed. It is the only effective way in which our stock can be protected from groundless rumors of infection.

There has been considerable comment of late among stock papers as to the advisability of shipping dressed meat to Europe. They one and all approve the idea. It does, in fact, seem hard to bring any objection to the plan, and we hope soon to see the matter thoroughly tested. The Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co. has already demonstrated that there is a large profit in killing cattle and shipping the dressed meat to market. This is owing to the fact that all the shrinkage, which live stock experiences in being taken to market alive, is saved by the refrigerator plan, there is much less trouble and expense in handling and from a third to a half is saved in freight charges. Exactly the same reasons will make it profitable to kill cattle in or near the range and ship the dressed meat to Europe. It has been satisfactorily demonstrated that meat dressed in New York can be shipped to Europe at a large profit, so that it is absolutely certain that a much larger profit could be realized by killing the cattle on the range. In fact, the additional profit would be exactly the profit that is now made by shipping dressed instead of live meat to New York. The Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co. is one of the most enterprising as it will soon be the largest concern of the kind in the world, and we hope to see it take the initiative in this new departure.

This will be the last issue in which we can call attention to the meeting for forming a Bad Lands stock association to be held here next Monday. Since the call was framed several other and very important reasons have arisen in addition to all those presented before, why we should have a first-rate organization here. Perhaps the most important one is that the Glendive association has been abandoned. This makes the nearest association that of Miles City, too far away for members to take particular interest in Bad Lands stock. After we are started, however, we can easily join forces with Miles City and thus form a very strong association. In addition to this, is the fact that the Bad Lands stockmen need some special legislation which only concerns themselves and would be of no interest to another association. Starting now, too, we would be the only association of the kind in Dakota, and it would be a very easy matter to make this point the headquarters for Dakota stockmen. The greatest point of all, however, when it comes to a realization, will be found in the new Medora-Black Hills railroad. This will make Medora the market for the immense stock interests of the Black Hills and all the Bad Lands south of here. For these reasons, in addition to the patent advantages a good association confers upon its members we confidently look forward to next Monday for the inauguratson of one of the best stock associations in the whole west. Every stockman who consults his own interests will be present. The meeting will be held at 2 P. M. at the Hotel de Mores.

Were it not for the fact that our Dickinson correspondent is abundantly able to take care of himself in his spat with the editor of The Press, we would be tempted to make a few remarks. As it is we will merely state that in the first place our correspondent took exception to an advertisement of Dickinson which stated that a thousand teams were employed on the freight route from that point. From the mass of school-boy drivel that this article occasioned in The Press we extract the meaning that the advertisement concerning the thousand teams was truthful. We don't propose to argue the question, but would say that common sense should teach any one that such a baseless fabrication would only react as a boomerang on the town. There is such a thing as legitimate booming, but it should not be confounded with downright lying. Our correspondent had the interests of Dickinson at heart when he took exception to the senseless statement of the advertisement. Its purpose was certainly to gain settlers for Dickinson. Suppose it succeeded in getting them there, who can doubt that they would be utterly disgusted at the outset. Our correspondent was exactly right when he said: "The simple truth about this country when it becomes known, will bring men and means to develop it quite as rapidly as is consistent with a healthy growth."

The Republicans of Billings county met pursuant to call last Saturday afternoon at the Hotel de Mores. The meeting was called to order by A. T. Packard, who nominated J. C. Fisher for chairman. The motion was seconded and carried unanimously. Fred Ertel moved that A. T. Packard be elected secretary. Carried unanimously.

By request of the chairman, Mr. Ertel stated the object of the meeting, to elect a delegate to the Huron convention and a county central committee.

A. T. Packard moved that Fred Ertel be appointed delegate to the Huron convention. Carried unanimously.

The county central committee was then elected as follows: J. C. Fisher, Max Bass, A. T. Packard, Geo. Blankenberg, H. Gilbert.

Fred Ertel then offered the following resolutions, which were unanimously adopted:

WHEREAS, The time for filling the vacancy caused by the expiration of Gov. Ordway's term is drawing near and it is important that an executive who is fully conversant with the needs and wants of the people of Dakota be appointed.

Resolved, that in Col. C. A. Lounsberry, of Bismarck, the Republicans of Billings county see a man in every way qualified to assume the high responsibilities of said office; a man in whom the greatest confidence can be placed, a man whose long residence in the territory and past honorable career entitle him to the unqualified confidence of every citizen in the same. Col. Lounsberry is a recognized leader among leaders and has at all times been found foremost when the welfare of the territory has been at stake. The Republicans of Billings county recognize in him a thorough representative of the territory, a staunch Republican, a wise and experienced legislator, a gentleman of highest character and heartily endorse his candidacy for the honorable office to be made vacant.

Resolved, That a copy of these resolutions be transmitted to the president of the United States for his most careful consideration.

WHEREAS, The territory of Dakota is and for some years has been badly handicapped by the government discriminating against the purchaser of public lands within the railroad limits by charging him $2.50 per acre against only $1.25 when outside said limit.

WHEREAS, The completion of the N. P. R. R. has opened up for settlement a vast area of public domain, consisting of the most fertile soil, which suffers under this apparent unjust discrimination, especially at a time when the eyes of emigration are particularly directed to this section.

WHEREAS, A bill has been introduced in congress by Maj. Strait, of Minnesota, to reduce the price of public lands within the railroad limits from $2.50 to $1.25 per acre, be it

Resolved, That the Republicans of Billings county, in convention assembled, heartily endorse the bill as introduced by Mr. Strait.

Resolved further, That the delegate of Billings county to the territorial convention, to be held at Huron, April 23, 1884, be hereby instructed to use his utmost endeavors to urge upon the members of said convention the great benefit derived by the passage of said bill, and if possible secure their aid to direct the attention of congress to the importance of this bill and pray for an early passage of the same.

A. T. Packard moved that the county central committee be empowered to collect money to defray the expenses of the Huron delegate. Carried.

Fred Ertel moved that the thanks of the meeting be tendered to G. W. Fitzgerald for the use of his room. Carried.

Adjourned.

J. C. FISHER, Chairman.
A. T. PACKARD, Secretary.

The cattlemen of the Hills ranges whose headquarters are in Rapid City, met at that place on April 1 and organized for the round-up, by electing two foremen, Wm. Moses and H. Hood, and Jones, Driskill, Coleman and Criswell as assistants.

Stockmen who do not belong to the association, and ranchmen who own cattle that have gone off to the herds should be ready and join with the boys when they start out. They can by so doing, not only get their cattle, but at the same time have a good time.

The following is the programme agreed upon, and that will be followed out to the letter:

No. 1. On June 1, to commence at the mouth of Elm creek on the Belle Fourche, work up the Belle Fourche and all its tributaries to the mouth of Cabin creek. Wm. Moses, foreman; Jones and Driskill, assistants.

No. 2. On June 1, to commence at the head of the Box Elder, work to the mouth of the Box Elder on the Little Missouri; thence up all its tributaries to the head of the Little Missouri. H. Hood, foreman; Coleman and Criswell, assistants.
—[Black Hills Times.

THE COMMITTEE.

The fright about the foot and mouth disease has about subsided, but reports that have gone to England and other countries can never be recalled, and it is undoubtedly true that damage to the extent of hundreds of thousands of dollars has been done to Kansas, and the live-stock trade of the whole country has suffered incalculable loss on that account. The matter has served a good purpose in arousing the country to the need of taking ample measures for the suppression and prevention of any calamity that might arise in future.

There are 50,000 head of cattle in the Comanche County Pool, Kansas.

There are now 4,000 head of cattle on the Cantrell ranch on the Gila. This herd was purchased and put upon the range last year, and no increase was expected until this spring. There has been however, 800 head of calves belonging to this herd branded. Of this large increase only two have been lost.—[Colfax, N. M., Stockman.

Lately we made some inquiries as to the experiment of breeding Polled Angus and Galloway bulls to our range cows, scrubs and high grades, and are agreeably surprised to learn that in every instance the ranchman has been successful and is preparing to further test the virtues claimed for the black muleys. Perhaps the most extensive tests being made are by the firm of Hunter & Evans, who have a large fenced range in this county, well stocked and carefully looked after, and the Comanche Pool, with its 50,000 head of cattle. Hunter & Evans have on their place about fifty head of heifers, coming two years old this spring, bred from high-bred Short-horn cows and Polled Angus and Galloway bulls, and many of these are in calf from a thoroughbred imported Galloway bull, and will this spring drop three-quarter bred calves. Besides the heifers mentioned above, this firm also raised about sixty bulls, the same as the heifers, and these were sold to the Comanche Pool last year and turned loose on their range. From the time these calves were dropped until now they have done well every day, readily taking to the range diet, adapting themselves to heat and cold as though neither was objectionable, "rustling" by the side of Texans, and still maintaining flesh, strength and energy. They were nearly every one black and in every instance hornless, showing that the stronger blood was in their sires and predominated. The heifers are well filled out and promise a good crop of calves. The bulls turned in the Comanche Pool pasture are wintering in splendid shape, are no trouble whatever and even now are more active than their Short-horn cousins. It is confidently expected that quite a sprinkling of black muley calves will be discovered following the cows on this range even this season, and by next spring the result of these sixty industrious animals will undoubtedly be an attraction. Those gentlemen in the east who are handling either the Galloways or the Polled Angus cattle need not hesitate to warrant these breeds will stand the range under all circumstances with any horned breed, and that a cross from them with a Texas or grade cow will be as good an animal as can be bred for the range.—[Barber County, Kan., Index.

It is estimated that there are at this time fully 2,500 head of horses on this market. The demand for cow ponies has fallen off and prices range from $25 to $40. Most of the heavy buyers have been supplied. There will probably be from ten to twelve thousand stock horses and mares driven this season, the bulk of which will go to Dodge.—[San Antonio Cor. Texas Live Stock Journal.

As the time draws near when preparations begin for the calf crop of 1885, we would again call the attention of our range cattlemen to the necessity of having with their herds a full supply of vigorous bulls. Bulls that have size, form, constitution and merit. High grades we believe to be the best, but if these cannot be had in numbers and condition sufficient to meet the entire demand of the herd, then get the best native bulls to be had, and above all things be careful to have enough on the range to serve every female old enough to produce a calf. Do not emulate the custom so many have indulged in of depending on roving bulls of neighboring ranchmen to make calves for you, but talk to all holding near your ranch, and by united effort put on the ranges as many bulls as are required. We are assured that more than [90?] per cent of calves can be annually secured in any part of Texas, if the cows are all served. Then see to it, now, before breeding begins that your herds are fully supplied with good bulls, lusty fellows and vigorous animals. You will find the money expended in this way will pay better than in any other.—[Texas L. S. Journal.

DICKINSON, April 16, 1884.

The examination of Joseph McClung, which attracted much attention from the gravity of the charge against him, resulted as was expected, in his discharge.

Asa Fisher has bought the Seaman corner and R. L. Wright will occupy the place. Mr. Fisher is to be congratulated upon having secured a valuable property.

Jerry Russell arrived from St. Paul last week with a car-load of stock and farm implements. He also brought furniture for his livery stable.

The stable and office erected by Matt. Kincaid are nearly ready for business and will form an acquisition to the business interests of the town.

Mr. Anderson opened his new place last week. The bowling alley will be reported for business in a few days.

There has been a little talk of organizing a base-ball nine among the young men here. It is thought that Dickinson could produce a fair team.

A large quantity of Black Hills freight was side-tracked here on Monday.

While we do not wish to prolong a fruitless controversy, at the same time being in, we would not appear to shrink from the contest. Therefore, we will say to The Press that vituperation is not argument. Instead of touching our position on the question of commercial ethics, it dives to the bottom of a putrid inkwell, stirs up a vile cloud and hides like a cuttle fish under cover of its own excretion. Aside from the manner, the matter of The Press criticism is equally ineffective, irrelevant and insincere. We have to charge it with publishing an intentional untruth in its hopeless attempt to distract attention from the real point. It is unfortunate that our E. C. is not willing to advocate the cause of honesty in business methods.
ANTHROPOS.

Smoke the Far West.

City lots for sale at this office.

A trial of the Far West cigar is its best recommendation.
The Marchioness de Mores is expected here in a week or ten days.
Bob Roberts has gone to Miles City to attend court, now in session there.
The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.
Geo. Roderick began breaking yesterday afternoon on the butte east of town.
Maj. Snider and Doc Pennell left for Spearfish Monday.
A. J. Rich and G. W. Randall came in Monday evening for a week's visit to Howard Eaton.
Dr. Duncan, of Glendive, last evening passed through on his way west. He will be here to-morrow or Saturday.
Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
A telegram from Mr. Peter Book, as we go to press, states that he will be here Saturday with his men and machinery.
Several cattle were killed by a freight last Saturday morning west of town. The Northern Pacific is good for them.
A number of coal miners have arrived and it is expected that the mine will be in full operation by the first of next month.
We hope all our stockmen will heed the call for the meeting next Monday. It will be held at 2 P. M. at the Hotel de Mores.
Rev. Wm. Cooke preached very acceptably last Sunday at the Cantonment. He will hold regular services there every Sunday evening.
Mr. A. H. Morrison, N. P. R. R. auditor, was here Monday looking over Mr. Spurrier's accounts. It is needless to say that they were all right.
The thanks of the Republican convention to Geo. Fitzgerald for the use of his room were very fitting. A better place could not be found.
Howard Eaton's usual happy smile was wonderfully augmented last Saturday. We didn't blame him when we saw his mother and sister step from the cars.
"Ox-Bow Jack," alias Johnny Goodall, started west last evening to buy about a hundred head of horses to be used on the round-up. His first stop will be at Terry.
Two young gentlemen of the west side are breeding a violent sickness. They are assured that the next pies they rustle won't have near as an agreeable effect on them.
The petition for the survey of this township which was circulated recently, met with almost unanimous approval and we hope the surveyor general will act upon it immediately.

We doubt if more business will ever be done more quickly or harmoniously than at the Republican convention last Saturday. There was not a hitch in the proceedings and the meeting augered well for concerted action of the party in the future.

The recent rains have gladdened the hearts of the stockmen. The grass started up beautifully about two weeks ago, but the dry weather had a depressing effect on it. The rains of the last few days have given it a fresh and sufficient start so that it is now growing rapidly.

Mr. R. E. Spurrier, agent of the N. P. R. R. at this point, has resigned his position to take effect May 1. He expects to go to Spokane Falls as operator, and was led to make the change in order that his daughter's education might not be neglected. His many friends will regret seeing him go.

The Mandan Pioneer publishes the following as though it were a fact: "The Dickinson Press says that there are about 400,000 pounds of freight lying there for transportation to the Black Hills, and that Medora has not a pound yet." We see that you are not acquainted with the editor of The Press, Bro. Tuttle.

Mrs. Samuel English arrived Saturday night. For the present Mr. and Mrs. English will live at the Cantonment. Mrs. English is not in very good health, but this climate is sure to bring her health back. Mr. English will soon open a general commission store, selling fruit, fish, etc. It will be a needed addition.

That we will have a stage line in addition to our freight line is now beyond all question. Mr. Nye, of Livingston, Mont., was here the first of the week and is eager to at once enter upon the preliminary steps toward putting on a line of stages. The only question is, whether Mr. Nye or the company will put them on.

As the season approaches for the annual awakening to duty of the deadly massasauger, or prairie rattlesnake, whose bite is almost certain death, Mr. James Hannigan is about to confer a boon on an appreciative public. He has a cure which is warranted in every case to destroy all evil effect on the person bitten. The cure comes in liquid form in pint and half-pint bottles.

Lots are going off in good shape. They have only been on the market a few days but already over fifty have been bought or reserved. As soon as word comes that final arrangements have been made to build the railroad to the Hills, the lots will start on a boom that will soon take away the choicest bargains. Come to THE COW BOY office, examine the plat and invest before it is everlastingly too [illegible]

Messrs. Hines & Casey, of Glendive, left yesterday for home. We are pleased to state that before leaving they made arrangements to open a drug store here within a week or two. For the present they will rent the room now occupied by the N. P. Ref. Car Co. as a meat market. They will soon erect a building of their own. We are glad to welcome the new firm and predict for them a successful future. Mr. Casey will probably have charge of the store here.

Three car-loads of Black Hills freight arrived Tuesday morning and the first trip will doubtless be made as soon as Joe Pennell returns from Deadwood. Telegrams have been received from nearly every large dealer in the Hills that every pound of their freight shall be shipped from here. Deadwood merchants are greatly interested in our railroad and will do anything in their power to bring it to completion. Their first action was a concerted movement to have all their freight shipped via Medora, which assures the complete success of our freight route.

G. W. Racek, the well-known saddler and harness maker of Bismarck, came in last evening. His intention is to start a harness shop here and he will make a specialty of cow boy outfits. There is not a better opening on the line and Mr. Racek has shown his energy and foresight by taking the first chance. He bought one lot of us and reserved three others, which also goes to prove his level-headedness. He will erect a substantial brick building as soon as Mr. Book can get the brick ready for him. He returned to Bismarck to-day to settle up his business there.

M. Adolph Eyraud, the Marquis' gardener, is making many improvements in the bottom south of the Marquis' house. A large number of hot beds are doing well and the work of transplanting has just begun. Ten acres have been broken and twenty more will be soon. Two experienced New Jersey gardeners, the Sigler brothers, arrived lately and are lending valuable aid. M. Eyraud expects in addition to the garden, to grow a large number of grapes. If the season is not too short they will be a success, as the bottom land will certainly be warm enough.

It would have melted the risibilities of Sitting Bull to have seen Mr. Paddock fit Mr. Allen to a pair of "chapps" last Monday evening. It wouldn't have been in consonance with Bad Lands human nature if such an opportunity for fun had been allowed to escape, and the look of intense earnestness on Mr. Paddock's face as he carefully pulled the "chapps" over Mr. Allen's "dips" wrong side to, would have broken the heart of a stoic. Every one was "on" except the victim, who thought that the hip pockets were rather unhandy. At last the "chapps" were put on right, Mr. Paddock carefully tied one of Mr. Allen's feet to the stirrup and as Messrs. Jones and Allen dashed off in the direction of Deadwood in the rain and darkness, the voice of the latter was heard calling back: "Well, boys, if you've had any fun with me, I'm glad of it."

Marquis de Mores and Joe Pennell started yesterday morning at 4:30 for Deadwood. There were three relays of horses sent on ahead, and they expect to make the 185 miles in thirty-six hours. Messrs. Allen and Jones started the night before, and at Deadwood they will complete arrangements for the railroad. There is no doubt whatever that they mean business as the plan is entirely feasible and will certainly be a very paying investment. Plenty of capital is already guaranteed and the only question is as to an agreement on the final arrangements. The railroad will tap the best mining, agricultural and stock country in the United States, and it will probably pay from the send-off. We hope to chronicle the fact that all arrangements have been completed, in our next issue.

Monday morning we sold four $250 lots to the Merchant's National Bank, of Deadwood. As soon as brick can be received a substantial brick building will adorn the corner of Third street and Broadway. Meantime it is expected that the bank will do business in some of the company's buildings. The bank firm, Stebbins, Mund & Co., is known as the largest and soundest banking firm in the whole Northwest, and our citizens can be congratulated on having such a sound institution start here. With Mr. Fox as another partner, this firm has banks at Deadwood, Spearfish, Lead City, Billings and Livingston, Mont. The bank here is its latest venture and its establishment will speak in the loudest terms, the future of Medora. This firm is too careful and experienced to invest thousands of dollars in real estate and buildings unless there was a certainty of success.

Major Wm. R. Snider, editor of the Spearfish Register, made us a pleasant visit Monday. He comes direct from Washington, where he has been on business. He reports that, contrary to general opinion, the Northwestern road never has been granted the right of way across the Sioux reservation and that as the bill for the opening of the reservation is so far down on the calendar there is no chance whatever that it will be acted on at this session of congress. Even when the reservation is opened it will be very doubtful if the Northwestern will build into the Hills, as their policy, although liberal, is against building a line through such an extent of, at present, unproductive country. This leaves an open field for a railroad from Medora and it will undoubtedly be begun very soon. Men are at present interested in the project who have plenty of money and who mean business. The cost of building the entire road from here will not exceed twice the amount that it will take for a Chicago road to bridge the big Missouri and Cheyenne. About half the way there is such a level grade that absolutely no more work will be required than to lay the track. Our readers can rest assured that a railroad from here to the Hills is a thing of the very near future.

BELFIELD, Dak., April 16, 1884.
EDITOR COW BOY:

Quite a delegation from Belfield attended the Republican convention at Medora on Saturday last. They report a pleasant time and a harmonious meeting.

Rev. R. H. Fulton held divine services in the Presbyterian church last Sunday. The probabilities are that he will be permanently located at this place; at any rate it is sincerely hoped so.

Brace Gallien has returned from the east and is now making preparations to do farming on a large scale.

Two good and substantial settlers arrived this morning from Chicago, bringing with them a car-load of household goods, stock, farming implements, etc., and are exceedingly well prepared to endure the hardships characteristic of the settler's first year's residence.

Mr. Max Bass is having plans made for an addition to his popular hotel and otherwise making preparations for the large immigration which Belfield is soon to witness,

Louis C. Hay has been sojourning in Mandan the past few days. He is expected home this evening.

Parties are looking over the ground for the establishment of a brickyard here, and numerous brick buildings will undoubtedly decorate our town in the near future.
SADIE.

Now that the era of prosperity is fairly inaugurated, Medora is destined for some time to be the liveliest town on the Northern Pacific. Numerous buildings are in contemplation, many of them, however, waiting for the brick which will soon be manufactured here in large quantities. The present season is not the time when the Hills merchants receive the most freight, but large quantities will be handled from here all summer. As the Northern Pacific doubles freight rates Nov. 1, the busiest season will be from Oct. 1 clear on into the winter, a vast quantity being shipped to arrive here before Nov. 1. The freight-house will be begun soon and the Marquis will probably build it of brick. Besides putting in an additional side-track the railroad company will make many other improvements. City lots are going off rapidly, eight being sold yesterday.

The best part of our growth is that there is no boom in connection with it. It is all legitimate growth. From its site alone, Medora was destined to be a good-sized town. As it would have been a cattle town, it would probably have been the richest for its size in Dakota. Then came the Marquis de Mores, establishing the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co., the largest thing of its kind in the world. This would also, of itself, make a good town, as many industries are bound to spring up therefrom. Now comes the freight, stage and mail routes of which we have the complete control. Not a pound of freight will be shipped from any point on the Northern Pacific R. R. except from Medora. The stage route will be in full operation as soon as stages and horses can be procured and the mail route will be established as soon as an appropriation passes congress. Less than these three made Bismarck so successful for a time with ten dollars to where there is one there now. Consequently, if analogy goes to show anything, we will have a better town than was Bismarck in the heyday of its prosperity. In addition to all this, there is almost a certainty that inside of a year a railroad will be completed between Medora and the Hills. It can be built at less than an average of $5,000 a mile and will be a paying institution from the send-off. It will make the whole southern Bad Lands and the Black Hills country tributary to Medora and make probably the largest city in the territory. These are facts, not fancies, and all our conclusions are logical deductions which are proved by ample experience.

Medora is assuredly the coming town of Dakota.

We wish all the emigrants who are passing through Dakota at the rate of from three to five hundred a day, bound for Washington and Oregon, could speak with returning emigrants who are coming back at the rate of two to three hundred a day. Monday morning, for instance, there were about two hundred and fifty emigrants on the train returning east, and a more disgusted lot of people it has never been our lot to see. They were all returning from Washington, Oregon and the Cœur D'Alene mines, where they had been lured by circulars stating that there was plenty of work for all and fortunes were waiting every arrival.

The amount of the matter is that in all those places it is harder for a laboring man to get a job than it is in overcrowed New York and Chicago. Of course, the reports of the returning emigrants are rather highly colored, but they report that there are thousands there who do not know where their next meal is to come from. These reports will be scattered all over the east and do incalculable damage to the west.

The moral of this whole matter is that for a temporary success the railroads and town-site owners are killing the goose which would in the future lay the golden eggs. If we could makee very one in the east know that "booming" is almost a synonym for lying we think it would be an immense benefit to this whole country. What a useless and wholly damnable scheme the lying circulars are, a little thought will show to any one. We have never seen one yet that did not enlarge the facts far beyond what they warrant. They are all issued for the purpose of inducing settlers and speculators to invest. Suppose, as is generally the case, that they are successful in their aim. Settlers come and find nothing more than they could find in fifty other places. Will any reasonable man claim that this is legitimate, or in the end, profitable way in which to gain citizens? If there is such a man, let him go to any eastern-bound train and interview the emigrants. We must again quote the statement of our Dickinson correspondent: "The simple truth about this country, when it becomes known, will bring men and means to develop it quite as rapidly as is consistent with a healthy growth."

The reader may notice that our remarks have been directed to points far west from here and think they do not apply to Dakota. We have taken the far west because the emigrants we have seen are returning from there and because the swindle is greater as they have to pay more to get there. The whole of Dakota is and has been cursed with a set of men who make "booming" their livelihood. Every settler who is misled by their false statements should be able to and we think can sue and recover damages. A boomer is a liar every time. If a man comes to Dakota with enough money to get a start and a willingness to work as hard as he would east, he can do no better than to come. There are fortunes for that kind of men. For men who expect to make money easier here than they could in the east we have no use. They are a clog on the rest and are the class of easily discouraged men who do far more harm than good. Happy Dakota and happy west when the boomer is no more in the land!

The Marquis de Mores and Jos. Pennell returned yesterday morning from their Deadwood trip. From the Black Hills papers and interviews it is very manifest that the trip was a great success. They started a week ago yesterday morning and made the trip in forty-eight hours, passing on the road Messrs. Allen and Jones who had thirty-five hours the start.

According to Mr. Pennell they had a parrot and monkey kind of a time on the way down. They were caught on the open ridge in a driving storm of snow and rain without even a blanket to cover them and for six hours were compelled to walk around their horses to keep alive. Their only protection from the storm was their saddle blankets thrown over their heads. Between Spearfish and Deadwood they were met by a delegation of the principal citizens of Deadwood and there was a perfect ovation. The principal mines and points of interest were visited and everywhere the party met with an enthusiastic reception. Several banquets were given, and aside from the business done, many warm friends were made.

The return trip was made in much better time. Starting Monday they arrived here yesterday morning, being in the saddle just twenty-six hours. This fact alone prevents all argument as to the "practicability" of our route. If any one doubts it, there is $500 to $10,000 here that says the trip can be made in twenty-four hours. That is, in twenty-four hours after leaving Medora the rider will be in Deadwood.

The merchants of the Hills to a man are interested in our route and there is now no doubt that every pound of Black Hills freight will be shipped via Medora. At a meeting of the Black Hills Shippers' Association it was decided to send all freight by our line and a telegram was sent to Keyes & Bramble to that effect and offering them the position of forwarders. Mr. Keyes went through here Tuesday evening and reported their acceptance of the offer and that there were 40,000 pounds of freight at Belfield that would be shipped here immediately. In addition to this, Marquis has agreed to put on a tri-weekly line of stages, which will be running as soon as the stages can be procured. The railroad is perfectly feasible and before fall it is expected that at least fifty miles will be built.

The route itself is even better than was reported. It is thought, that if anything, to be under 180 miles and of this 150 miles is absolutely devoid of gumbo. For the remaining thirty miles it only appears in places and will be no trouble except when the frost is coming out of the ground in the spring. At this season there will be very little freighting so that the gumbo question is not worth consideration.

The route has now repeatedly been pronounced one of the best, if not the best, in the country and there seems no doubt on the subject.

We don't believe in kicking a man when he is down and we hope our citizens will join with us in dropping a tear to the ephemeral dreams of freight routes held by some of Medora's suburbs down the road.

It was deemed best by many interested to put off the organization of the Bad Lands stock association till next fall. Several reasons led to this result, among them the following: That there is no business of immediate importance to come before the meeting; that at the present season it is impossible for all interested to attend a meeting, many of them being away, and finally that the subject has not received as thorough a canvass as it should have. Altogether it seems better to put off the organization, as a poor association is little better than none at all and will prevent the establishment of a good one. It is also better to wait for the reason that we can draw members as far as the Black Hills, and very soon a steel highway will afford ready access to Medora for all Hills stockmen. It is merely putting off the day for the purpose of forming a far more important organization.

DICKINSON, April 23, 1884.

In spite of frosty mornings our farmers are rushing seed into the ground and before the next issue there will be several hundred acres sown here. The ground is reported to be in first-class condition and prospects are bright for good harvests.

The county convention select Mr. Campbell to represent the Republicans at the territorial convention to select delegates to the national convention at Chicago.

About 2,000 head of young stock cattle passed through en route for Montana Saturday and Sunday. The manager reported serious losses resulting from inadequate accommodations at feeding stations along the N. P. There are over one hundred car-loads yet to come on. The cattle were nearly all yearlings and none were more than two-year-olds.

Editor Scott, of The Press, has betaken himself to the old Ohio scenes for a brief season.

Freight continues to arrive for the Black Hills and is forwarded as rapidly as it comes.

ANTHROPOS.

D. A. McPherson, cashier of the First National bank of this city, is a man who is silent on all subjects unless he has something to say, and he now speaks to the point: "The Northern Pacific will extend fifty miles of their line from Medora toward the Black Hills this summer." The above statement was made in public on Wednesday evening last. The Pioneer made the statement over a week ago that the signs of the times pointed to the building of the portion of a line from the above point, and that T. G. Jones had gone to the headquarters of the company to bid on the work of grading. These threads followed up lead to the discovery of facts, which will eventually be of great benefit to this country. It is sufficient to state that the lea[ven?] is working, and in less than sixty days we shall see developments that will confirm all rumors. It is now almost a settled conclusion that the reseravtion will not be opened at this session of congress and the granting of the right of way to the Milwaukee & St. Paul and Chicago & Northwestern railways may be delayed. Therefore, a movement by the Northern Pacific to capture the trade of this country is opportune and will be pushed with all possible vigor. Before snow flies next winter we may take a hack to the terminus of the Medora and Black Hills railroad. It is not a fanciful dream, but an easy project that can be accomplished with the assurance of a paying business from its completion.—[Black Hills Pioneer.

Beckwith & Quinn, ranchmen from Western Wyoming, branded 90 per cent. of calves last year and there were no mavericks in the count. How high is this?

Telegraphic reports from Austin, Tex., say that a cattle syndicate is negotiating for the 3,000,000 acres of land in the Panhandle of Texas, known as the capital lands.

Renewed confidence in the outlook is everywhere manifest among stockmen as the news from the outlying ranges comes in. The losses are reported small and cattle generally in fair condition.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

Reports from Nevada, Idaho, Montana and Dakota as to the range cattle are very flattering. In Oregon, Washington Territory and Utah, cattle as a rule have done well, but in a few small areas considerable loss has been sustained on account of deep snow.

All kinds of stock are very weak at this time and when they get into soft ground many die from dampness, getting mired down and unable to get out. A great many cattle will die within the next two weeks, as there is just enough green grass to weaken them and when once down a large per cent never get up.—[Cheyenne Transporter.

The Dominion Cattle Company, which has now nearly 97,000 cattle on 284,000 acres of the Cherokee Reservation, which is leased for two cents an acre from the United States government, has thus far proved a decided success. Last year its capital stock, amounting to almost $250,000, brought a net profit of $100,000 out of which a dividend of 20 per cent has been declared.—[Texas Stockman.

The different associations, composed of owners of cattle on the western and southwestern ranges, have within the past six weeks held their annual meetings and from these meetings a general idea can be obtained as to the feeling existing among cattte owners. The business of these associations have been conducted in a systematic member, and no loop-hole left unguarded by which the interests of the members may be infringed upon. The attendance at these meetings has been unusually large, showing the interest taken by the members. This, however, is hardly to be remarked upon, from the fact that among range cattle owners there is a community of interest which they cannot fail to appreciate without affecting the value of their property. The Colorado Cattle Growers' Association was the first of the kind in the west and from it has grown these other associations, which have been found by those interested to be a necessity. The amount of capital represented at these different meetings is large and the investment having been made in many cases by capitalists whose interests are entrusted to others, causes the business to assnme a position quite different from what it was five or six years ago. Now the investment is made upon a basis from which certain returns are expected, whereas six, ten or fifteen years ago there was a speculative character in the ownership of range cattle which does not exist at the present day. Now there are breeding ranches and steer ranches, and the conclusion is arrived at that to raise cattle in the south and let them mature in the north is the proper way in which to conduct the business of raising cattle on the range. The reports as to the manner in which the cattle passed through the winter are to the effect that with the exception of one or two localities the losses have been light. The calf crop promises to be fair and upon this question we have a few words. It is false economy to buy less than one bull to every twenty-five cows, or to give the preference to yearling bulls, when they should be guaranteed yearlings, or two-year-olds. There is one question upon which range cattle owners appear to be unanimous and that is in endeavoring to protect their herds from contagious diseases. They realize the importance of avoiding the appearance of a contagious disease which would be ruinous in its effects. The outlook for the prices of range cattle the coming summer is not discouraging, but at the same time the expectation of inflated prices should not be encouraged.—[Live Stock Indicator.

One of the striking developments of the cattle business in the west in the last few years has been the wonderful increase in the value of female stock. In the earlier days of ranching, when stockers could be obtained with ease from sources which then seemed inexhaustible, cows were considered of little value. Indeed, no more than three or four years ago they were a drug in the frontier market. But with the giving out of stocker supplies in Oregon, Montana and elsewhere, ranchmen began to see that they must raise their own stockers and cows commenced straightway to increase in value. No longer ago than in 1880 purchasers of ranch property often attempted to throw the cows aside altogether and if they were taken into the trade at all it was at a paltry figure. It was considered quite a good thing in those days to get from $20 to $25 straight through for a herd of good cows, with calves thrown in without valuation. For two or three years past, however, the stock has been in increased request and corresponding scarcity, until now, [in the?] northwest, prices range from $35 to $[illegible], according to locality and quality, with a supply insufficient for the demand. The limit of prices will, of course, be reached when cows can be taken out freely from the states at the same figures. It will only be a matter of a short time, too, until the demand for cows for ranching purposes will be as great in the states lying along the Missouri river as it now is for stockers in the same region—[National Stockman.
