C. W. Sleeper will return in a day or two.
Geo. Fitzgerald is having a large ice-chest built.
Smoke the Far West cigar, sold only by Roberts & Co.
Father Cassidy, of Mandan, is visiting Geo. Fitzgerald.
A trial of the Far West cigar is its best recommendation.
Mr. Avery, who has been visiting A. M. Sinnott for some time, has returned east.
The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.
T. J. Houlahan, formerly clerk of the Merchants' Hotel, of Mandan, is in town.
The summer birds are arriving fast. Many kinds have already put in an appearance.
Painting is now the order of the day and THE COW BOY office is glistening in a new coat.
Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
T. J. Kerr after the first of the month will spend the most of his time in St. Paul, in charge of the company's books.
There is nothing in the job printing line that we cannot do in the best and most satisfactory manner at THE COW BOY office.
E. G. Green, superindendent of the Northern Pacific stock yards, is in town. He purchased forty tons of hay for cattle at Glendive.
Four freighting outfits are on their way here from the Hills. They were passed on the road by the Marquis and Jos. Pennell.
Several new carpenters have arrived and work on the new billiard hall is being rapidly pushed. Thomas McClung has the contract.
A large quantity of Black Hills freight has arrived and with the 40,000 pounds at Belfield will be enough for a light load for Pennell & Roberts' outfit.
Dr. Duncan, of Glendive, made us a call last Friday. He has arranged matters to be down every week. He has a first-class practice in Glendive and will doubtless do considerable here.
The devotees of Terpsichore will be rejoiced to know that a dance is to be given by Geo. Fitzgerald at the Hotel de Mores, Saturday evening. There will doubtless be a large attendance.

A hundred car-loads of stock have gone through here the last two days. Eastern capitalists are beginning to realize that there is no more profitable business than cattle raising and are investing largely.
Moody and Sankey, our gospel firm, are going on a tear—no, tour, we mean. They will join a mastodonic agglomeration of primeval aborigines and hirsute cowboys, which will travel through the east.
Lloyd Roberts and Daniel Friedman started Saturday morning for St. Cloud, Minn., where they expect to stay all summer buying cattle. As both are experienced cattle men their trip is sure of success.

More miners have arrived and it is expected that work will soon begin in the N. P. shaft here. The Sims vein besides being vastly inferior in quality to that here is nearly worked out. As soon as the boom subsides there the mine here will doubtless be worked to its utmost capacity.

A piece of the clay that will be used for the brick was molded slightly by hand and left in the sun to dry for several hours. At the end of that time it was almost as hard as a stone, much harder for instance than the Sims pressed brick. The piece is now in our office where it can be seen by visitors. There is no doubt whatever that sun-dried brick could be used successfully. The price is so low though that it is hardly worth while to try the experiment.

A great commotion was stirred up last Saturday by the report that thirteen horses and mules had been stolen. A man named Martin had followed the trail several miles and then returned. A party was immediately made up, consisting of Messrs. Paddock, Roberts, Jolly, Packard and Martin, to go in pursuit. Preparations were made to follow the thieves a month if necessary, and the pursuing party certainly meant business as all but Roberts and Martin had stock missing. The pursuit came to a successful but rather ludicrous termination by running across all the stock about seven miles from town. Whether they were driven there or simply wandered off is still a question.

Peter Book and family arrived last Saturday, together with five experienced brick-makers. Lumber was bought immediately and work begun on the grounds, which are located south of town where the Deadwood trail separates from the river. Two machines and all the implements necessary are on the ground and the work of clearing and digging wells is going rapidly forward. Mr. Book is enthusiastic over the clay, stating it to the best he has ever seen. The same view is taken of it by all the men. The first kiln will be done in less than three weeks. Several kinds of clay will be used so as to find out as much as possible about the varieties abounding here. There will be a number of brick buildings erected as soon as the brick is ready and we will soon have a city of which to be proud. The brick work could not possibly be in better hands, as Mr. Book is an experienced contractor and builder as well as a brick-maker.
Mr. Bramble is in town making preparations to ship his freight here.

Howard Eaton has made application for a policy of insurance for the Custer Trail ranch property. It is an example that should be universally followed. Insurance can be furnished at THE COW BOY office.

W. T. Kennedy is the latest arrival to minister to the comfort of the inner man. As he carries a hatchet all the time, we can believe him when he says that he has as good goods for the money as can be bought anywhere.

A number of good ball-players have materialized and if any town up or down the line wants a game a communication to that effect will receive a favorable answer. Several old buttons and things could be raked up that say Medora can down any local nine on the Missouri division.

Mr. C. D. Edick, of the Bismarck firm of Edick Bros., cigar makers, has been in town for a day or two. He is much pleased with Medora's prospects and reports numerous sales of his goods. From the samples he left at THE COW BOY office, we don't blame our merchants for investing.

We sold and reserved fourteen lots last week. As this was when the public was uncertain about the freight route, we expect a large increase now that the matter is settled. We would especially urge citizens to invest at once as the lots are sure to go off rapidly and the bargains will soon be gone.

The lots on the south side of the track have been priced and are now for sale at THE COW BOY office. We don't think there is any need of booming them as they will go off very rapidly. Anyone knows, however, that it is for his interest to be among the first to buy and secure the choicest location.

Mr. Duncan, of the new Mandan furniture house of Duncan & Hilles spent Monday and Tuesday in town. He is well known all along the road and was very successful in obtaining orders. The advertisement of the firm appearing in this issue, will for the future call the attention of our citizens to the best place to buy furniture.

If the person who stole the card-case from THE COW BOY office thinks it a joke, he must understand that it has lasted too long to be funny. It has been found out who took it and if it is not returned by to-morrow night, there will be some serious explaining to be done. There is no reward offered, but some very embarrassing questions will be asked unless it is returned on time.

Howard Eaton will soon receive a number of registered pedigreed Holstein cattle, recently imported. The two-year-olds are worth $250 or over and altogether it will be the most valuable lot of cattle ever brought into the country. It is principally for their reception that the large barn is to be built at the Custer Trail home ranch. The Holsteins were bought by Mr. Huidakoper in Holland.

The Marchioness de Mores, her friend, Miss Wright, and a relative, Mr. Liebre, arrived last evening in the Marquis' private car, Montana. The party were not at all fatigued by their trip and immediately started on a tour of inspection over Medora. THE COW BOY office was examined and had ye editor not forgotten how, he would have blushed at the encomiums heaped upon it and the paper To-night, together with the Marquis, they will go on to Helena where an extended stay will be made.

Messrs. G. F. Randall, of Horicon, Wis., and A. J. Rich, of Ontonagon, Mich., returned this morning to their homes. They have already sent Messrs. Roberts and Friedman to Minnesota to buy cattle and as soon as possible will put 1,000 head on the range, under the charge of Howard Eaton. Messrs. Randall and Rich are lumber men and having just closed out a big deal, are doing the most sensible thing possible—putting their money into cattle. Nor could they have chosen better hands than Howard's in which to place their investment.

The old timers will have to take a back seat. A tenderfoot has come to town and broken the record on rustling. He started last Sunday morning on a visit to one of Medora's suburbs. Finding a check on a seat he put it in his hat and although the conductor knew him, the tenderfoot's gall knocked him out so that he couldn't muster courage to say a word about the ticket. Arriving at his destination he reports having an elegant time, which was undoubtedly the case. Of course, it cost something so he made expenses by inveigling his host into a quiet game of draw. Having seduced a brakeman from the path of rectitude into a state of inebriety he was permitted to ride back on the bumpers of a freight train. The old timers will have to rustle a while longer to beat this.

There are still a number of subscribers to THE COW BOY who have not paid up. To these we would say that we propose to adhere strictly to our three-months' rule. Notice will be sent to each one and if the delinquency is allowed to run a quarter, the name will be dropped and we will charge the amount to profit and loss. On general principles a subscriber who will not pay before the end of the first quarter does not mean to pay at all and the sooner we get rid of him the better. There will be some who have neglected the matter meaning to pay. A failure to receive THE COW BOY will notify these anew. No business can be run without money and printing is no exception to the rule. If anyone wants THE COW BOY they want it badly enough to pay two dollars a year.

A request has been forwarded to us, coming from Mr. John Hager, of Mandan, to call a convention for next Saturday, for the purpose of electing a delegate to the Democratic convention at Pierre, on the 14th of the present month. Morton county intends sending a delegrte to Pierre and Billings county can appoint a delegate and send the proxy to the Morton county delegate. Although our political preferences are for the Republican party, we take pleasure in publishing this call as both parties should be organized here. Billings county is entitled to one delegate and it will be a simple matter for several Democrats to take the lead in deciding the place of meeting, etc. If the delegate does not wish to attend the Pierre convention the proxy could be sent to Mr. Hager, who would doubtless see that it is put into the hands of the Morton county delegate.

An editor who perverts the meaning of another is as guilty as one who steals articles without giving proper credit. In last week's issue we used the words, "There is now no doubt that every pound of Black Hills freight will be shipped via Medora," meaning the words, as every sensible person can see, by the use of the word "will" to apply to the future, say a week or two hence. The present editor of The Dickinson Press, with a bungling use of tenses says: "The truth is contrary to his statement," meaning that it is not the truth at the present time. If the editor pro tem will go back to "first principles" and brush up his grammar he will see that he has either misstated himself or that he has said what he knows every one even in Dickinson believes to be false. If a solitary ray of hope had existed in Dickinson of shipping any freight after we get started why was it not brought out in the consolation meeting held by the citizens of Dickinson on the evening of April 22? The Press stated only the fact that the meeting was held, when it is known as well here as in Dickinson, that all hope was then given up of shipping any further freight from there. As is well known here and also in Dickinson, every merchant in the Hills, except three, have pledged themselves to ship via Medora. These three will stick to the Pierre route. We can hardly see what is left for Dickinson to ship except wind.

F. B. Allen, attorney for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co., returned Monday morning from his Black Hills trip in company with E. Deffebach, of Spearfish. The return trip was made in a leisurely manner, with no changes and occupied three days. Mr. Allen has delayed his return till this time as he wished to thoroughly examine the mineral wealth and other resources of the Hills. The following interview is especially interesting reading, as it shows what a valuable country can be made tributary to Medora through the means of a railroad from this point:

Mr. Allen states that after reaching the divide, clear to the Hills is a first-class agricultural country. This has been so well described by Dr. Louthan in a former issue, that but little more need be said on the subject. From a point twenty-five miles north of the Belle Fourche to the base of the mountains is already very well settled. In former years the whole country was irrigated, but during the last few years the ditches have been useless as there has been ample rain. This is doubtless due to the well-demonstrated fact that much more rain will fall on the same ground after cultivation than before. In the district above mentioned more than enough grain is raised to supply the wants of the Hills, and here especially will an outlet be valuable, as it will furnish a ready market at advanced figures to these farmers. To illustrate the abundance of grain, oats are now selling at twenty-five cents and wheat at forty-five cents a bushel.

The Hills themselves are noted only as a mining region and they may well be as the half cannot be told of their fabulous resources. Mr. Allen has been in a large number of mining camps, but all of them are vastly inferior to the Hills. The gold ore is mostly of low grade but easily worked. The Homestake Co., the largest in the world, can work ore yielding only $2 a ton at a profit. The monthly clean-up of this mine averages over $3,000,000 and millions of dollars have been declared in dividends. There are hundreds of mines as valuable as the Homestake, but they are undeveloped as the cost of transporting machinery is so great. Among the undeveloped mines are those of the Carbonate Co., said to be very rich.

The silver mines are situated at Galena, the principal one being the Sitting Bull. According to the testimony of experts, brought out in the trial now going on between the Richmond Mining Co. and the Sitting Bull, there is exposed ore to the value of $500,000. All indications point to the existence of numerous other mines equally as valuable in the immediate vicinity. The Sitting Bull mine is the only one that is worked to any extent and is the sole property of Mr. Davy. He began the work and the ore was freighted to Cheyenne. By this costly method enough money was obtained to develop the mine. Competent authorities state that the mine is capable of clearing $1,000 a day.

The coal region is in Wyoming, about twenty-five miles from Deadwood. It is owned by the Philadelphia Coal Co. and as far as developed shows two veins four and six feet thick. It is similar to the Bull Mountain coal and is the best lignite yet found. The coal beds are supposed to cover about 3,800 acres.

Tin ore has been found in Bear gulch and other localities. The specimens assayed show about five per cent. The mines, owing again to the cost of transporting machinery, are as yet undeveloped, but there is no doubt tin exists in paying quantities.

Adjacent to the coal fields are situated the largest salt wells, capable of furnishing 200 tons of salt per diem. The Sitting Bull mine now derives all its salt from these wells.

Springs here also show evidences of petroleum. Mr. Allen now has a bottle of the oil and a piece of sandstone so strongly saturated with the oil that it readily blazes when a lighted match is applied to it. Oil springs are also found in the southwestern part of the Hills, beyond the located wells.

The gypsum mines of the Hills are also very valuable. The mineral is extensively used for lime and plaster of paris. Large deposits are found in the foot-hills, the veins being fifteen to twenty feet in thickness.

Veins of mica are also found in the southern hills and are being worked as extensively as is allowed by the poor facilities afforded.

From the above it can be readily seen that the Black Hills country is probably the richest in the world and all it needs for full development are better facilities for transportation. With a good railroad the country would rapidly settle up and the Medora & Black Hills R. R. is waited for even more anxiously by the people of the Hills than it is here.

The Northern New Mexico Stock Growers' Association, which met recently at Springer, represents 600,000 cattle and $25,000,000 to $30,000,000 capital.—[Western Rural.

During the winter a great many cattle from the Yellowstone range strayed across the river on the ice to the Crow reservation. Stockmen complain that the Indians kill the cattle and wantonly destroy more than they can eat, generally taking only the tongues and unborn calves.—[Billings Post.

Several persons have mentioned the fact that especially at Fargo the stock yards are entirely unfit for the reception of cattle, unloaded for feed and water. The mud is six to eight inches deep and scores of cattle die in the pens. This is a condition of things that should be remedied immediately. The stock interest is too valuable to the railroad to be allowed to suffer thus.

The shipments of live stock over the Northern Pacific R. R. the last two weeks have been greater than at any time in the history of the road. Although not many cars have unloaded at Medora, a large number will arrive during the summer and be driven upon the ranges in the Bad Lands. The Custer Trail Cattle Co., W. N. Thompson & Co., Wadsworth & Co., Niemela Cattle Co. and several others will increase their herds from 1,000 up. Several new men will also come in with large herds.

An exchange says of lambs that although they are supposed to be tender things there is no young animal that has so much vitality as a lamb, if it only has plenty of food and can get it. Very often it needs help to reach the teat and to get the milk. The ewe's teats are often closed with a gluey, sticky substance, which should be forced out and the milk started; then, if the lamb is held to the teat it will come to, when it has seemed past hope, and in a day or two will skip, if it can get but a ray of sunshine to start it.

The committee on foreign relations has agreed to report favorably to congress several amendments to the bill providing for the inspection of meats for exportation. One amendment provides that when in the president's judgment it shall be necessary for the protection of animals in the United States against infectious or contagious diseases, he may by proclamation suspend the importation of all or any class of animals for a limited time, and may change, modify, revoke or renew such proclamation as the public good may require.—[Western Rural.

The tendency of thoroughbred stock to deteriorate when turned upon the range to rustle for their feed is well understood. This suggests a point that stockmen must decide upon sooner or later. Will they buy fine stock from the breeding farms of the old states, turn them loose upon their ranges till they have survived their usefulness and then replace them with others from the same source, or will they breed their own sires and care for them as they should be cared for—that is, make a proper provision for them in the way of food and shelter?—Exchange.

The Stockman thinks there are but few, if any, industries that are more promising at the present time than breeding and raising horses. There is no danger whatever of an over-supply and prices have held firmer for the past five years on horses than on any other class of live stock, that is, for anything like first-class animals. The horse, of any merit, if placed upon the market now, need not want long for a buyer at a good round price. Nothing need stand in the way of any farmer making his horse stock yield him a good income each year, if properly handled. One advantage in having an income from a source like this is that the time when horses sell the best and when they naturally come into the market is in the spring time of the year, just the time when farmers need the money the worst and when they generally have but little of the products of the farm to sell. A few young horses can be ready for the market each spring with but little extra cost.—[Glendive Times.

Since the hides taken from the dead cattle on the range in the vicinity of Sun river have begun to come in, cattle men have concluded the loss will be somewhat larger than anticipated. Hon. R. S. Ford, who is one of the largest stock owners, thinks the loss will not fall much below ten per cent. but that the fine weather which we are now having will more than make up that loss by adding to the crop of calves, many of which die from cold, snow and wind storms, usually during March and April and this spring there will be no loss from that source.—[Livingston Enterprise.

[Not transcribed in full: clipped national sporting paragraphs.] Items concern bicycle clubs, a Hanlan sculling match in Australia, St. Paul lacrosse, Stillwater and St. Paul base-ball, a Hart–Edwards six-days go-as-you-please match, the pacer Little Brown Jug, Higham's 230-mile bicycle ride, roller-skate polo at Minneapolis, Duncan C. Asel Keyes, one of the Northern Pacific forwarding company which controls the recently established freight route from the Northern Pacific to the Black Hills, was on the Pacific express to-day bound for Missoula and will return in a few days and visit Livingston. He says, reports to the contrary notwithstanding, the freighters have centered upon Medora as the point from which all freight for the Black Hills will be received from the railroad.—[Livingston Enterprise.

Dakota has more post-offices than Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Idaho, Indian Territory, Louisiana, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Utah, Washington Territory or Wyoming, more than Delaware, Nevada, Rhode Island and Montana combined.—[Cooperstown Courier.

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY is the best paper west of Fargo, except Kit Adams' daily. The editor of THE COW BOY goes out and kills a bear every morning before he attacks his raw steak.—[Minneapolis Hotel Gazette.

The editor of The Gazette doesn't appreciate the "odorousness" of comparisons and exceptions in some cases.

C. W. Sleeper returned from St. Paul last night.
Smoke the Far West cigar, sold only by Roberts & Co.
The work of overhauling and enlarging the abattoir will soon begin.
The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.
R. J. Jewell has returned from his eastern trip. As yet, he is undecided about his future occupation.
C. F. Ellison, who put up the company's ice here and at Miles City, has been in Medora for several days.
The outfit which Moody and Cummings will accompany on an eastern trip is expected here this evening.
Harriman, who is on his walk from Duluth to San Francisco, will probably pass through here Saturday.
Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
Part of the office furniture of Keyes & Bramble has arrived and the forwarding firm will be ready for business in a few days.
Although it has not been measured, a trip over our route will convince anyone that it is not over fifteen miles to the divide.
About one hundred tons of hay were sold the last week by the company to E. G. Green, superintendent of the N. P. R. R. stock yards.
The work of grading Main St. began this morning. It will be levelled and filled in. It will vastly improve the appearance of the town.
We have heard nothing as yet from outside nines wanting to play us a game of base-ball. There is a good nine here just spoiling for the fray.
E. Deffebach, of Spearfish, is still with us and it is to be hoped that his stay will be a permanent one. "Bassie" makes the kind of a citizen we need here.
The dance given by Geo. Fitzgerald last Saturday night was a complete success. Every thing passed off pleasantly, and we hope to have more of such entertainments.
W. B. Milne of the Minneaplis firm of Wyman, Mullin & Van Dyke, made us one of his periodical visits last Saturday. As he is a good salesman, he is building up a large trade.

Disgusted Cœur D'Aleners still continue to pass through on their way east. A few of them go in the cars, but the most of them, on account of the beautiful weather, prefer riding on the bumpers or trucks.

Mr. Allen returned to Bismarck Tuesday morning. He is a welcome visitor and we hope to see him often. He says that the only thing about his trip to the Hills that he didn't like is that he could only spend four cents while there and that was for postage.

Mr. Gunn, of Colorado, left for the east Tuesday. He will return soon and probably go into the cattle business in the Bad Lands. He has been a cattle man for nearly thirty years and is abundantly able and experienced to handle a large herd successfully. We hope soon to number him among our ranchmen.

We never knew a paper that didn't contain a notice stating that old papers were for sale at the office. As we dislike following a practice that never yields a dollar a year, we wish to state that we have several bundles of papers at our office which we will give to our subscribers, if they will take the trouble to take them away. Don't think you are imposing on us by taking them, as they are of more use to any one else than to us.

M. J. Conners, of Spearfish, has been in Medora for several days. He is on the way to his Beaver creek ranche, where he has about 9,000 head of cattle. Some time ago in riding all through the heart of his range he found only one carcass. His cow-boys state that more cattle died last summer than during the winter and place the total loss at less than one per cent. Mr. Conners himself said that two per cent is an outside figure. This is a remarkably fine showing, the best we have yet heard. All cattle men unite in saying that the loss in the Bad Lands especially has hardly been large enough to account for deaths from natural causes.

This is the last issue of THE COW BOY that will be sent to any but paying subscribers. We have given ample notice to all delinquents and we propose to have a list upon which there is not a solitary deadhead. As we have said before, a failure to receive the paper will be the best kind of an intimation that it takes money to subscribe for THE COW BOY. Three months is a long enough time for any one to pay up in. We will give this time to subscribers who are reliable, but beyond this we won't trust Vanderbilt or Gould. We are prompted to this decision by several reasons. First, cash or short credit is the only business way of running a paper. Second, we consider a money equivalent is received by subscribers just as much as if a person has a $2 bill changed into small coin. Third, we don't propose to deadhead or be deadheaded. Cash both ways will give far better satisfaction. Lastly, we can do far better with our papers than by sending them free to the same person continually. Lists of names are obtained from exchanges, of the principal men in western towns and a copy of THE COW BOY is sent to each one. As a consequence we have already reached thousands of people and made THE COW BOY at least as well known as any paper in the northwest.
The Marquis, his wife and party returned from Helena and Miles City Monday evening. After a stop of a few days they will go to St. Paul.
Justice Mark Bateman, H. G. Voss and Pat Cuskelley, all of Mandan, came up Tuesday to hold the inquest on the remains of John Magranahan.
The site for the freight warehouse has been selected. It is on the south side of the track near the bluff. Work will begin as soon as the brick can be supplied by Mr. Book.
The frame to the new billiard hall is almost ready to raise, but work has been interrupted by the storm. An increased force has been put on and the work will be prosecuted as fast as possible.

The N. P. Ref. Car Co., in consonance with their advertisement, are now selling corn-fed beef. As a rule, range cattle are now too poor to kill, it paying better to delay killing till they increase in weight.

W. B. Wright and Mr. Baird arrived from New York Tuesday evening. Mr. Wright will soon leave for the east and Mr. Baird will remain and take charge of the Little Missouri Land and Stock Co.'s interests.

George Wilkes returned last Friday evening from Chicago. He has brought along a number of tools and can now do the company's repairing, instead of having it sent way. That Mr. Wilkes is an able machinist, his work here abundantly shows.

Had it not been for the snow, Pennell & Roberts' outfit would now be loaded with Black Hills freight and on the road. There are now about 60,000 pounds here, which will make heavy enough load for the first trip. The outfit will start as soon as the weather permits loading.

Z. Hyde returned from Chicago Saturday evening, accompanied by his wife and children. They are now keeping house at the Cantonment. Mr. Hyde will soon be in his glory handling the immense business that will be done at the abattoir this summer. The works will begin on full time very soon.

The friends of T. J. Kerr will be happy to know that he has been promoted. Since his arrival, he has shown his bookkeeping ability so thoroughly that he has now been appointed traveling auditor for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co. At present, sets of books will be kept at twelve different places and he will have a general supervision over the whole. His headquarters will be here with those of the company.

The present snow-storm is a perfect blessing to the cattle men. Almost every particle of it will melt into the ground and give the grass the moisture it so much needs. The perfect weather of the last three weeks has dried out the ground too much and the present snow in this warm weather will do as much good as twice the amount of moisture in the form of rain. "'Tis an ill wind that blows nobody good."

We publish this week the price-list of lots. The plat can be seen at THE COW BOY office. It will be seen that the prices are low, both because of the assured future of Medora and because of the limited number of lots. The prices are subject to change without notice and as the prices are at rock bottom an early investment before a raise in prices will pay the prospective purchaser. Terms will be made known at THE COW BOY office.

Wm. Huggins, of Scotland, has made up his mind to stay with us and go into business. He will go into some mercantile business with McNeave Nally in charge, and besides will go into the business of raising horses. He cannot possibly find a better location for both. The growth Medora is bound to undergo will make the first profitable and there is a constant demand for cow horses here that the home market cannot begin to supply.

Last Saturday Messrs. Pennell, Roberts and Packard went out to the divide to stake the route through the Bad Lands. The completeness and perfection of the road are astonishing. The only hill worth mentioning is about two miles from Medora and at no season of the year will teams have to be doubled on it. The whole route is now complete and it only needs one bull-train to mark it thoroughly. Stakes were put up by the party on Saturday, but owing to illiteracy or something the plain direction, "Keep to the right and avoid the washout," was read by Messrs. Allen and Deffebach "Keep straight ahead and camp in the washout." Tuesday, at the request of the former, ninety large guide-boards were painted to be distributed along the route, and it now looks as though one could walk on them from here to the divide.

Last Sunday morning as the train from the west was on the point of starting out, the dead body of a man was discovered on the north side of the track about a thousand feet east of the depot. Investigation showed that the head and arms had been severed from the body. The head lying on the opposite side of the track and about twenty feet west of the body. The man's name was John Magranahan and he had been cutting wood the past winter. He was a wanderer and no one seems to know where his home was. At present it is on the coal-mine butte. Tuesday evening a coroner's jury was impanelled, consisting of H. G. Voss, R. J. Jewell and M. M. Coleman. The evidence was heard before Justice Bateman, of Mandan. Not much farther testimony was brought out than the above except the manner of death. Geo. Fitzgerald's testimony was the clearest on this point and had most weight on account of his extended railroad experience. As there were almost no bruises on the body and the head and arms were cut off so smoothly it seemed manifest that the deceased was riding between the cars and falling off was run over by the wheels. There were no marks about the body to indicate that he had been struck by the pilot of an engine. Besides that the body was almost touching the rails when found. Had he been struck by the pilot he would have been thrown off the embankment. It was brought out in the evidence of the witnesses that the deceased had been seen as late as 10 o'clock Saturday night in an intoxicated condition. The body was buried Monday on the coal-mine butte.

We congratulate our citizens beforehand on the acquisition of one and perhaps two of the best citizens of the Hills. We allude to Messrs. Louthan and Jorgens. Dr. Louthan has the best practice in the Hills, but realizing that more money can be made here than by practicing anywhere, he will come. Mr. Jorgens does the largest drug business in the Hills and will open up a drug store here as soon as possible. They are both old timers and will make valuable citizens.

The Northwest will after this be published in St. Paul. It has done much toward building up this country and we welcome its advent to a point closer to its field of operations. The last issue contains a handsome cut of the mammoth hot springs in Yellowstone Park.

The Chicago Tribune gives an anxious public the weighty views of Eli Perkins on the question of who is to be the nominee of the Republican party for president. Eli is for Blaine. Now if The Tribune will only consult Geo. Francis Train and Private Dalzell and J. N. Free and the ghost of Emperor Norton, the matter may be settled in advance of the convention.

Some years ago when Gen. Schenck, then a member of the house of representatives from Ohio, had the management of a tariff bill before the house it was amended till he was compelled to vote against it himself, and in his last speech on it he said the epitaph on its tombstone would be "Nibbled to death by pismires." Mr. Morrison, of Illinois, may say of his short-lived bantling, "Beheaded by the congressional guillotine."

The case at Miles City against Black Wolf and followers for burning Zook and Alderson's ranch has ended in the acquittal of Black Wolf and the conviction of four of his followers, who plead guilty and were sentenced to five years each. It will be remembered that all this trouble arose from the foolishness of a man named Telford. who plowed a furrow in Black Wolf's scalp while shooting through his hat. It seems too bad that the only guilty one has not been found and that the Indians are the only ones to suffer.

"Little Red Riding Hood," the Allard correspondent of The Glendive Times, needs to brush up his (?) zoology a little. Three Mrs. Partingtons in one sentence is a little too bad. He (?) speaks of the "inveterate" order and family insecta. Insecta are a class, not a family, and all insecta are articulates, not invertebrates as is doubtless meant by "inveterate." If L. R. R. H. means "family insectivora" she—beg pardon—he is again wrong as all insectivora are mammals and hence vertebrates and not "inveterates." Future zoological lessons will be charged full rates.

Twenty years ago a person who advocated cremation was almost considered a criminal. Ten years ago he was considered a crank or monomanic of the first water. Within the last five years, however, there has been a great change in opinion concerning cremation. Thinking men everywhere are joining the ranks of cremationists and in the very near future we look for legislation on the subject, requiring the incineration at least of persons dying from contagious diseases. Experience has amply demonstrated that the most fruitful source of contagion, especially in the south, is directly owing to the germs arising from infected bodies. How long shall the living suffer because of the foolish prejudice against cremation? It is time the law stepped in and protected its living citizens. In this part of the country where we are not crowded for room and where there are no contagious diseases to speak of cremation is not so much of a necessity. In the crowded cities, however, the living are constantly surrounding and overriding the homes of the dead. That this leads to the spread of any contagious disease whose victim may be buried there is now beyond all doubt. Here, then, is where the reform should begin and where it doubtless will very soon. Every country in Europe now has legalized cremation and any legislation passed in this country can find plenty of foreign precedents. We are heartily in favor of the movement which has lately received a fresh impetus and our columns will be always open to communications on the subject.

As an illustration of downright ignorance Dickinson justice carries the banner. As a display of legal learning it is a pitiable farce. That any man or set of men must be governed by the law as interpreted by Dickinson methods is a burning shame. To an outsider it might seem better in a case of this kind to particularize, but we will save that till some future time, merely stating the fact, of which every one having legal dealings at Dickinson is cognizant, that the most of the expounders of the law there are so ignorant of the rules, that even if they erred wilfully they do not know enough to cover up their tracks. We might be satisfied to let the dead bury its dead in Stark county, but that Billings county should be under the judicial jurisdiction of such a mass of ignorance is more than we can bear with equanimity. It is time we roused from our lethargy and demanded a county organization so that we can decide our own cases here. We cannot possibly be in a worse condition and any change will be for the better. We are much stronger and wealthier and better able in every way to support a county organization than is Stark county. The time is coming, and we hope very soon, when we will have an efficient county organization in Billings county. As long as THE COW BOY is published we can promise our readers that no such ignorance can gain power in Billings as now holds the reins in Stark. Dakota has again and again been disgraced by a corrupt county organization and as far as Billings county is concerned this will cease. We are bound to have a county organization and to have a good one.
Stock trains continue to pass over the N. P. in rapid succession. Large numbers for the Bad Lands have been unloaded at Keith.
Towers & Gudgell of the OX ranch, will soon drive in 5,000 head of cattle. They were all taken from their home ranch in Nebraska and will be fattened in the Bad Lands.
Reports from Southern Utah say that over half the cattle on the ranges are dead from starvation and exposure because of such deep snows during the winter.—[Pioneer-Press.

A branding machine has been invented by which the work has been considerably lightened. The animal is driven into a machine and suspended in such a way as to render struggling impossible. It is thought that it will come into general use.

Gregor Lang returned from St. Paul Tuesday evening. To-day or to-morrow about six hundred cattle will arrive for him and as many more will soon follow. These will be added to his present herd on the Neimmela ranch, situated about fifty miles up the river.

That any of our stock men should put in scrub bulls on the score of economy is past all understanding. A moment's thought should convince any one that a graded bull pays for itself every year in the increased value of his progeny. In four or five years the herd will be twice as valuable as it would be if scrub stock were used.

The increase of the cattle family of Colorado from the calf crop and from importations from abroad, will be quite half a million the present year.—Twenty years ago big fat oxen sold in the streets of Denver for forty and fifty dollars a pair. To-day the beef brutes that would have gone fifty dollars in those early times, would bring hard on to a hundred and fifty.—[Denver Journal of Commerce.

M. Wadsworth is in town awaiting the arrival of a thousand head of cattle, coming from Minnesota. H. B. Wadsworth who owns the reversed L herd, is with them. These cattle will be added to the herd at present on the home ranch. Mr. Wadsworth reports that out of the herd of sixteen hundred head only twenty-five have died, hardly enough for natural loss. Not an animal died on account of the cold although a number of them were pilgrims.

If competition gives life to any enterprise it certainly does to breeding and raising horses, says The National Stockman. The man who is afraid to go into this business simply because there are others at it in his community, certainly does not look at the matter in the right light. The greater the number in any community the better it will be for each one thus engaged and the best thing a man can do who is breeding any kind of horses is to persuade his neighbors, if he can, to join him in his work.

On the 17th inst., the committee appointed by the Wyoming Stock Growers' association to go to Washington to advocate the passage of the pleuro-puenumonia bill, invited the stock men and commission merchants of Chicago to meet them at the Grand Pacific Hotel. The committee men then argued to convince them that the bill was essential for the absolute protection of the immense stock interests of the west, pointed out to them that every stock association had passed resolutions urging its passage, and appealed to the commissien men to withdraw their opposition. According to published reports of the conference, no favorable progress was made and the committee went on to Washington.—[New Mexico Stock Grower,

The cattle men of the Shonkin range sent a force of eight or ten men a few days ago to drive the cattle out of Arrow creek country this way, where the grass is better, and they have just completed the task. Tom Martin, who superintended the work, reports that a great majority of the cattle are in fine condition, and a large number of young calves are already to be seen, with every prospect of an unusually prolific crop of calves. They have ridden all over the country frequented by the cattle during the winter and found only twenty-five dead animals, which is less than one per cent of the whole. This is scarcely the loss expected in summer by casualties, etc., so that the loss on the Shonkin range this winter on account of the severe weather has hardly been anything.—[Benton River Press.

The enormous cattle possibilities of New Mexico have been known for a long time throughout the west, and Colorado capital has taken hold of an immense stock enterprise in that section of the country. Grant and Socorro counties contain within their limits some fine ranges which are unoccupied, part of these lands lying in the Black Range and the Mogollon mountains and running across the border into Old Mexico. For the last several months a representative of a Denver syndicate, whose name need not at present be mentioned, has been down in this country buying land and taking it up under the desert land act, until the company has obtained 85,000 acres of range in Old Mexico and 180,000 in Socorro and Grant counties. These ranges are said to be well watered and grassed. The company, which has been waiting for the report of its agent, has not yet formally organized, but will do so shortly as the White Oaks Cattle Co., and the capital stock will probably be placed at $6,000,000. The present intention is to place 25,000 head of Texas cattle on the ranges as soon after the organization as they can be driven in.—[Ex.

A company has been formed for the purpose of stocking a ranch in Dakota with pure bred cattle and good mares. The latter will be mated with Percheron stallions. All the cattle on the ranch will be pure bred. The profits from such a venture will no doubt be very large, as the company will be able to sell the increase of its herds for $150 to $500 each, as soon as the calves can be taken from their dams, or at least at a very early age, where they would have to wait three years for a market for ordinary beeves at $30 to $45 each. The cost of raising the pure bred stock will be but little more than that of scrubs and even if this should be made double the cost of the scrub, the profit would be enormous, says a cotemporary.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

The Illinois and Indiana duck hunters are in clover.

Girofle has become blind in one eye since going to England.

Several English bicyclists will visit the United States this season to engage in contests.

Bicyclists all over the United States will test the legality of different laws prohibiting the use of highways to them.

The weather is always so poor in Chicago during April that hereafter the preliminary base-ball practice will be done further south.

The six-days' go-as-you-please match at New York ended with two scores, the best on record. Fitzgerald made 610 miles and Rowell 602. Poor Eo was badly left.

Slosson and Schæfer are said to be making higher averages in their preliminary play for their coming billiard contest than have ever been made before. Betting is slightly in favor of Schæfer.

The base-ball season is now in full blast. Championship games between the nines of all the leagues and associations are taking place daily. It is impossible, as yet, to name with any certainty the positions of the nines, but we will keep our readers posted.

Harriman, the man who passed through here on on his walk from Duluth to San Francisco, has made a blooming set of chumps of the reporters who have interviewed him. Among other things, he claims to be the champion six-days' pedestrian and also the only man who ever defeated O'Leary. We don't know whether to wonder more at Harriman's nerve or the gullibility of the reporters. Harriman has no best on record of any kind for any distance. He is a fair walker, but knew he stood no show in the recent Madison square six-days' contest and showed his good sense by keeping out. The further density of the reporters is shown by the fact or their not knowing that in a contest like the one alluded to, every man who stays out cannot style himself champion until he defeats the victor. Ths worst statement, though, is that Harriman is the only man who has defeated Dan O'Leary. Will some of these aforementioned reporters rise up and name a single race in which O'Leary has been successful the last five years? In all Dan's numerous contests for this time he has found none so poor but they have done him up to the queen's taste. We can't blame Harriman much, however, for taking advantage of the tenderfoot reporter's gullibility.

DICKINSON, Dak., May 7, 1884.

Harriman, the walkist, spun his yarn for the boys Monday evening. Coming so close upon the heels of Fitzgerald's wonderful work, it elicited more interest than was perhaps justified. Although a fair heel-and-toe walker, Harriman is off color as a pedestrian, having no record that we remember.

Six car-loads of young stock were unloaded here last week. They belong to Mr. Crosby, a LaCrosse lawyer, who is going to make an experiment on the Killdeer ranges.

Quite a little breeze was caused in some circles here by the report that Mr. Messersmith had brought in a specimen of quarts from the Killdeer mountains which shows good color as gold-bearing rock. It is said that parties have already departed for the neighborhood with a design to see what there is in the country of that nature. Meantime Mr. Messersmith continues the even tenor of his way and is not excited by his find.

Mrs. Messersmith and her daughters left for St. Paul last week where the young ladies are to remain in school for some time.

Considerable interest was manifested in the trials here Monday and Tuesday. Little Missouri indulges in more litigation than many larger places.

There remains little or no seeding to be done in this vicinity and the early sowing is up and looking finely.

We notice that a few parties are setting out trees. This is a practice that should be much commended. In ground deeply cultivated young trees will do well, provided there is some other crop sown with them that will closely shade the ground. Parties living in town ought to plant trees on their lots, as they can counteract the drouth by a liberal use of the force pump.

Quite a large lot of freight has been sent to the Hills during the past week. Messrs. Seaman & Davis will start in a day or two with another outfit.

Ox-Bow Jack has returned, but "where, oh, where is she?"
One of the side-tracks has been undergoing needed repairs.
The work of cleaning up around the abattoir has commenced.
A force of men has been at Beaver putting in a side-track at that point.
E. G. Paddock has gone to his old home in Minnesota for a short visit.
Mr. and Mrs. James Hannigan will begin keeping house to-day at the Cantonment.
Sheriff Cuskelley, of Dickinson, was in town Sunday corralling witnesses on the Moody-Malloy trial.
J. C. Fisher will soon begin the erection of a block for business purposes. It is a needed addition.
Mr. Bramble came in Monday and immediately began superintending the work of loading the freight for the Black Hills.
The beatific smile we have attached to our countenance is all owing to the unexpected appearance of the author of our being in the city.
The Moody-Malloy case was tried at Dickinson Monday and Tuesday and resulted in the defendant being bound over in the sum of $300.
Wm. Huggins has gone to St. Paul to buy some kind of a stock with which to engage in business here. His intentions are not yet public.
Peter Malloy has gone to St. Paul to purchase about a thousand head of cattle for his brother-in-law, who will go into the stock business here.
The deserted camp where Pennell & Roberts' outfit has been for several weeks presents a scene of lonesomeness and tin cans that is really touching.
The gospel firm have left us and are now on their starring expedition, showing the denizens of the east how to subdue wild horses and throw riatas.
No greater improvement could have been made for the money than that done on Main street by grading. The leveling and ditching were much needed.
C. F. Ellison left Monday for his home in Dubuque. The company is well satisfied with his labors here and at Miles City and expect to employ him in the future.
We have just received a select assortment of new type and are better prepared than ever to do job printing of all kinds. Remember we take a back seat for no one in this line.
Several teams have arrived here for Black Hills freight besides the large outfit already here. More are on the way and they will be needed, as the freight is arriving rapidly.
The river has been encroaching too much on its eastern bank here and to guard against this a dam has been built below the railroad bridge which throws the current toward the western bank.
Mr. Conners started for his Beaver creek ranch Saturday. He may conclude a large cattle deal with the company soon. His cattle although in excellent condition, are not yet fat enough to kill.

John O'Sullivan has bought a lot and will soon begin the erection of a barber shop here. Mr. Sullivan is a young man of ability and besides making a success in his business will be a valuable citizen.

Any one wishing to subscribe for any paper or periodical in the world can be accommodated at THE COW BOY office. Subscribers will find this the easiest and best way of renewing or beginning subscriptions.

The freight house will be built as soon as brick can be procured. It will stand on the south side of the track, as near as possible to the butte. For the present, freight will be stored in the company's cold-storage rooms.

Johnny Goodall returned yesterday from his western trip after cow-horses. He brought back forty-seven head and more will soon follow. They were taken out to Wal. Osterhaut's ranch to be put into condition for the round-up.

We have received a letter from G. W. Racek, of Bismarck, containing substantial proof of his belief in Medora's future. In other words he has bought a business lot and will soon open a large harness and saddlery shop here,

A letter to us from T. G. Jones, of Deadwood, conveys the intelligence that a friend of his is coming here and desires a good lot, as he intends going into business. Word like this is coming from all quarters and Medora will be transformed before fall.

We received an interesting letter Sunday evening to which no name was appended. Although it was for publication we must, of course, refuse to print it as publishing anonymous correspondence is a thing no editor can do, We should be pleased to publish it or anything else from the writer, provided he sends his name also.

Messrs. Louthan and Jorgens, of the Black Hills, have decided to locate here. and go into business. They say that they know of no place which has the prospect for the future that Medora has and they intend helping make her prosper and benefit by her prosperity. As is the case with Mr. Deffebach, these gentlemen have lived on the frontier a long time, have had numerous and profitable experiences in prosperous new towns and their action in coming shows more than anything else that Medora is going to be a first-rate town.

The billiard hall has now assumed nearly its true proportions, the walls all being up and both floors in. There will be a hard finish inside and a thickness of brown paper and clapboarding outside, making a very warm and substantial building.

Sam English received a large supply of fish a day or two since. From the way he has sold them he is certain of success in his business of dealing in fruits, fish, game, etc. He expects to go into one of Mr. Fisher's buildings when they are completed.

The butte farm is being rapidly seeded. Considerable more ground will be broken and planted principally to potatoes. The old ground has been fenced and a large part seeded. All kinds of vegetables will be planted and it will be interesting to note the success of the different kinds.

Howard Eaton started for Chicago last Friday morning to receive the Holstein cattle to be put on the range of the Custer Trail Cattle Co. The Holsteins were described in a previous issue and will be the most valuable cattle in the west. Besides these, he will ship about a thousand head of yearlings and two-year-olds.

The article in "Sporting Notes" relative to Harriman, written last Monday, makes interesting reading now that he is so thoroughly exposed. He is nothing more nor less than a tramp who is endeavoring to gain a little notoriety by beating freight trains and calling it pedestrianism. His ignorance concerning leading sporting men is absolutely painful and a conversation with him should convince anyone that he is a fraud.

George Wilkes brought to our office two beautiful blackbirds that he shot near the abattoir. One of them was a freak of nature. The feathers on and around its neck and extending down on its breast were a rich golden yellow and some of the wing feathers were a pure white. This is the first time we have ever seen or heard of a yellow-white blackbird. It has gone to Ann Arbor, Mich., to be added to the large collection at the University there.

T. J. Kerr left last week for St. Paul, where he has gone to arrange for new sets of books for the company. As before stated, Mr. Kerr is now the company's auditor and will have complete charge of all the books. Twelve sets of books, one each for the present cold-storage houses, will be ordered. They will all be of the same ruling, which will be of special form, to accurately accommodate the company's business. Mr. Kerr will return in about ten days.

Tom Creighton and "Liver-Eating" Johnson passed through Friday morning to arrange for their outfit which went through early Saturday morning. It consists of about fifty Crow Indians, several cow-boys including Moody and Sankey, and two car-loads of wild broncos and steers. It is said that "Liver-Eating" Johnson earned his title by actually eating the liver of an Indian whom he had killed and who with his friends had kept Johnson under cover for several days without food.

Messrs. A. and E. Fox and Fred Hartman, of Minnieska, Minn., and Rev. J. W. Klepper, of Mandan, Dak., started Tuesday afternoon on a unique trip. They brought a boat from Mandan and are going to Bismarck in it via the Little and Big Missouris. They will hunt and fish on the way and expect a thoroughly enjoyable time roughing it. All showed their appreciation of THE COW BOY by subscribing. The party made numerous friends while here and all join in wishing them a pleasant journey.

Pennell & Roberts' outfit loaded with about 70,000 pounds of freight last Monday and by this time are many miles on their road to the Hills. All the wagons were loaded light and slow time will be made as it is not deemed economy to load heavy or hasten on the initial trip. Bob Roberts is conducting the outfit. New orders have been issued by the Northern Pacific railroad to have all Hills freight shipped to Medora and as stated in previous issues, this will be the only place from which freight is to be carried to the Black Hills.

Wm. Shriver, of Deadwood, in company with Dr. Ralfe's sons, of the Minnesela mills, arrived Monday. He is en route for his home in West Virginia, to receive a legacy coming from his father's estate. He expects to return soon and invest his money in stock and help to build up this country with whose interests he has been identified for twenty-one years. Coming overland on our freight route he had good opportunities of judging of it and says it is "one of the finest" and presents a splendid route for a railroad. He intends booming the country on his eastern trip.

Mr. Deffebach started the first of the week on his return trip to Spearfish. He is thoroughly impressed with the future of Medora and intends returning soon and starting a first-class livery stable. Arrangements have been made by which he will use the company's barn and corral and additional stable room will be built. Mr. Deffebach is an experienced horse man and will be a valuable addition to Medora. He has been on the frontier a long time and his choice of Medora as a location to open business is a large straw showing the prosperity the wind is blowing this way.

The brickyard is now running on full time, ten thousand or more being turned out every day. A visit to the yard found Mr. Book surrounded by his assistants all hard at work. Still more of the good qualities of our clay are becoming manifest. No sand whatever is required, either before the brick are molded or for sprinkling after they are laid in the yard. Not a crack has appeared in a single brick, the clay being extremely cohesive. Dried in the sun, they are almost hard enough for building purposes. For the first kiln only fifty thousand will be burned. Coal will be used as fuel and Mr. Book is now making clay grates to burn it. The work is rushing forward as rapidly as possible and Mr. Book says that we will have the best brick in the country. The clay bed is almost indefinite in area and twenty-five feet deep. A nine foot coal vein furnishes the fuel. With the good facilities and cheap material, Medora is destined to be a brick city.

The Pioneer thinks it would be a good idea for the Mandan base-ball nine to come here and "whip the nine that is spoiling for a fray." The motion is open to a large and decided amendment. Although several of our best players are on the freight route or temporarily out of town, we can still scare up a nine that will beat any strictly local nine on the road, for fun, money, marbles or chalk.
Smoke the Far West cigar, sold only by Roberts & Co.
The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.
Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
A trial of the Far West cigar is its best recommendation.

We have before spoken of Medora's future, but it is a subject of which we cannot say too much. We never have and never will indulge in the boom-fizz-Pat-Donan style of literary architecture, but now and at all times will deal in facts and from them gain our conclusions.

It is a well-known fact that a cattle town is livelier and wealthier than an agricultural town. Medora is not and never by any possibility can be an agricultural town. That she will be a great cattle town is beyond all question. We state boldly and without fear of successful challenge that the Bad Lands are the best cattle country in the United States. This is readily proved by the greater per cent. of increase and less per cent. of loss that we enjoy, in comparison to any other cattle region. The cattle country tributary to Medora is already more than a hundred by fifty miles and the extent that will be tributary is almost unlimited. This is for the reason that Medora is the only place that has east, west, north and south outlets. In addition to this, we have the one thing that would force a town to grow here even if we had not the location. That is, a market. In the course of time, the N. P. R. C. Co. will buy for killing or shipping, every animal on the river. From this will arise the inevitable factories that the extensive abattoirs soon to be built, will amply support.

Almost without the cattle the location itself is enough to build a town, or it is an exception to a rule, hitherto invariable. Take any east and west rail-road in the country, follow its course and it will be found that at the crossing of every stream that has a supply of water the year round, there springs up a good town. This is the case whether the stream is navigable or not. Take the N. P., for instance, to this point. St. Paul and Minneapolis are virtually at one crossing of the Mississippi and Brainerd is at the other. Moorhead and Fargo are on the Red river, Jamestown on the James and Bismarck and Mandan on the Missouri. Although these are all larger rivers than the Little Missouri, the rule still holds good in all cases.

We will not stop here however, for the freight route and coming rail-road place the Black Hills and southern Bad Lands tributary to us and makes Medora the capital of a larger and far richer country than any of the cities mentioned. This will also make Medora a great jobbing point and to this, the cattle industries and the freight route we will owe a prosperity as phenomenal as it is sure.
The new agent, Mr. Brinker, came yesterday to relieve Mr. Spurrier.
A large number of sheep pelts were brought in yesterday from Beaumont's ranch.
There is not a better opening on the line of the road for a shoemaker than Medora.
Mr. Morrison, who has a fine lot of young cattle on Beaver creek, has been in town for several days.
Mr. Weatherby, of Mandan, travelling for Charlie VanSlyck, was in town yesterday. He started east this morning.
Dr. McIntosh, of Glendive, was in town Tuesday, attending Mrs. Fitzgerald's baby, which was quite sick the first of the week.
The billiard hall is rapidly approaching completion. In fifteen days at the farthest, Pennell & Roberts expect to open it with a grand ball.
A good deal of work is being done toward the establishment of the stage route and we expect to see it in full running operation in less than a month.
We are reliably informed that the plan of building the rail-road to the Hills is being energetically pushed and that in all probabitity work will begin this summer.
Wm. Jones returned the first of the week from his hunt after Charlie Jolly's horses. He corralled three of them and heard that the fourth had been seen on the way to the Hills.
Freight is coming in on almost every train and the freight house will soon be badly needed. The brick will soon be ready however, and the building will begin immediately.
We have sold a number more valuable lots this week and purchasers will begin to come in rapidly, judging from the letters we are receiving from prospective purchasers and business men.
Smith & Graham's outfit loaded yesterday and will start to-day or to-morrow for the Hills. One of the wagons is an immense affair, the hind wheels being six feet high and the tires are an inch thick.

Over four thousand pounds of deer and antelope hides came in from Spearfish this morning, for McFarland & Kyes. They came over the new freight route and the freighters report the road in splendid condition.

In addition to the large lot of cattle brought in by Gregor Lang, another lot will arrive soon. As stated in a former issue, Mr. Lang will soon build a substantial dwelling on his home ranch and bring his family here.

J. C. Fisher and Wm. Vandriesche will soon begin the erection of a building for business purposes. It will contain three store rooms and as tenants are waiting already, it will not only be a needed but a profitable improvement.

The lumber is now on the way for three dwelling houses, which will be built immediately on its arrival. The reason for the haste is that families are already here awaiting the buildings. The rest of them will probably be built of brick.

The lettering on the COW BOY roof is a subject of profound meditation and anxious inquiry on the part of emigrants passing through. One emigrant was heard to remark that it must be a pretty tough cow-boy that they put on exhibition in this country.

T. J. Kerr will be here to-morrow or Saturday. His duties as auditor of the N. P. R. C. Co. will keep him on the road until the books of all the cold-storage houses are started, after which he will be found at the Medora headquarters the most of the time. As soon as he gets settled he will bring his family out.

Additions will be made to the abattoir as soon as work is finished on the billiard hall. Facilities for slaughtering a hundred more head a day will be added to satisfy the large contracts entered into by the Marquis in New York. Full work will not begin much before June 1, as the cattle are not yet in prime condition.

We are afraid that after all we are destined not to have Dr. Louthan as a citizen, for a time at least. He fully intended coming from Spearfish with Mr. Jones and had taken his seat in the buckboard for that purpose, when almost the whole town turned out and actually forced him to stay. Better luck next time, Dr.

W., May 22; Malone at pool in New York; bicycle polo at Washington; roller skating and roller polo; John Hughes and Fitzgerald; cricket clubs in the east; a collar-and-elbow wrestling match at Chicago May 3; the League of American Wheelmen meeting in Washington; Woodside & Morgan's trans-continental bicycle trip ("It is a good thing for them that the Bad Lands are not in their route"); single scull races; a grand-stand accident at the Cincinnati Union base-ball grounds; Victor Martin's proposed Paris-to-Rome walk; and the Union League's contract suits, including Tony Mullane.

DICKINSON, Dak., May 13, 1884.

About 25,000 pounds of freight were forwarded from here over the new freight route Tuesday.

The party engaged in laying out the road have passed the north Cannon Ball and report a good road to and beyond that point.

The delegation selected to confer with the Black Hills merchants, returned Monday and report progress. Prospects for freight are looking favorably at this point.

The R. R. Co. is replacing the dam on the Heart river, which was damaged by the ice last winter. The substantial structure in process of erection, together with the new pump started last week, will insure a permanent water supply at this point.

The funeral of Mrs. Robt. Fuller took place on Saturday, after which Mr. Fuller left with the body for his former home in New York. Mr. and Mrs. Hayes received the sad intelligence Saturday that their son, a promising boy of seven years, had died suddenly of brain fever. Both Mr. Fuller and Mr. and Mrs. Hayes have the sympathy of the entire community in their afflictions.

Lieut. Varnum, of the 7th U. S. cavalry, in command of the force detailed to survey the freight route from Ft. Mead to Dickinson, arrived Monday morning. The party was delayed at the Belle Fourche by storms for some days. The Lieut. reports a very direct and practicable route and will officially report one of less than 190 miles. The party will remain here till late in the week, awaiting supplies from Ft. Lincoln, after which they will proceed to Medora in order to view a road from that point.

ANTHROPOS.

Press dispatches from various points in Texas show a large increase in the number of fine bulls being placed on the ranges.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Indications point to the removal of a good many herds of cattle from Indian territory to northern ranges the coming season. Grass in that country is still abundant, but legislation is averse to the stock interests.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Mr. Burke, of Burke & Jackson of Dallas, started a herd of 3,000 two-year-old steers from Hillsboro, Texas, on the 15th for the Yellowstone region in Montana. They go by way of Greer county and the Panhandle.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

J. W. Snyder left last week for Texas and will start six to ten thousand head of two and three-year-old steers from the company's Stonewall ranch for the L F range in South park. They hope to leave the 15th to the 20th of June.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

A St. Louis dispatch says that advices from western Texas are to the effect that cattle are suffering, and large numbers are dying for want of water and grass, the drouth having been very severe in that section. Myriads of caterpillars have appeared and are destroying all kinds of vegetation.—[Black Hills Times.

The papers of New Mexico are happy over the great influx of Texas cattlemen. They are going in by the dozen and in a very short time that country will be filled with live, progressive men, who will join hands with the older ranchmen and make the grazing fields of that territory productive to their fullest capacity.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

In district No. 10, which is the largest round-up cattle district in the State, there are estimated to be about 3,500 bulls. When they are all gathered together in one pasture, as they will be the coming fall, there will be music in the air. Nine of every ten of these bulls are graded Short-horns, with a sprinkling of Herefords, Holsteins and Polled-Angus.—[Colorado Live Stock Record.

Jos. Cuenin, Gunnison. Colo., writes: "I note an article in the last number of your paper that the Montana stockmen propose to adopt the plan of taking bulls off the range at certain seasons of the year. This agrees with the view I have entertained for some time past and I think the proposition, if carried into effect, will prove to be of value in the interest of stock growing.—[Breeder's Gazette.

An exchange says that young horses should never have shoes imposed upon them until it is well proved that they cannot do without them. He predicts that the day is not far off when some humane benefactor of his kind and horse-kind will procure a breed of horses having such firm, tough feet, in addition to all other good qualities, that shoeing will be unnecessary.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

The fact that should be borne in mind by those engaged in horse training is that the horse has a very acute faculty for understanding and interpreting the tone of the voice. If you talk confidently the animal acquires confidence, if your voice shows fear he notices it and is afraid. Talk kindly to your horse and be sure that he understands the meaning of the tone if not of the words.—[Exchange.

The loss among cattle during the past year is the greatest for several years. Mr. Longendyke and also Mr. J. H. Baker estimate their loss at about ten per cent. Their winter losses will probably reach as high as six or eight per cent. These are fair representaitons of losses among ranch herded cattle generally in this locality. They have resulted principally from the fact of the late fall rains destroying the nutritive qualities of the grass and are confined, to a very large extent, to cattle that were brought in here in the late summer or fall from eastern Kansas, Missouri and Iowa. Notwithstanding these great losses, stockmen are by no means discouraged. They say that the profits arising from increase in young stock and increased growth of the same will yet give them a good round profit for their year's work and investment. Some say that the loss may amount to as much as fifteen, twenty or even twenty-five per cent. and still a profit can be realized.—[Kansas Cowboy.

Never in the history of Montana did the horse interest look so encouraging as now. A larger number of well-bred stallions and mares will be brought into the territory this year than any previous season and never did our people manifest such an interest in the equine race as now. So great is the progress that we feel assured that the time is not far distant when our oft-repeated assertion that Montana roadsters and flyers will eclipse the world, is near at hand. This is no idle boast; on the contrary, it is based upon a train of facts that can scarcely fail to lead to such results. In the first place, we have a hilly country and the soil of our pastural lands is rocky and sandy and grows the clear, tough-hoof, ivory-like bone, powerful muscle ligaments and tendons that are an [illegible] on with the horses grown upon that soft, rich soil of the states. This, coupled with the rarity of our atmosphere, so improves the endurance and action as to warrant our conclusions. Even the horse bred in the states improves greatly by a few years' residence here, and after we have grown a few generations of high blood, if we have not a race of horses that will be sought for and [nerve?] for service, long endurance and superior achievements, and if they do not step away from anything grown elsewhere, we miss our guess and the low lands can walk away with our money.—[Husbandman.

BAD LANDS COW BOY, BY A. T. PACKARD. THURSDAY, MAY 15, 1884.
