R. E. SPURRIER, Agent.
Peter Malloy returned last Friday night from his eastern trip.
Geo. Fitzgerald has been making some improvements in the Hotel de Mores.
Geo. Smith was bitten severely last Saturday by the Kentucky stallion.
Al. Gifford stopped over a train Tuesday on his way to New York. He will return in two weeks.
Geo. Porter started for Chicago last Saturday to buy a $10,000 general stock of goods for the company.
Lee Eisenberg, of Bismarck, travelling for Dan Eisenberg, was in town Monday and secured a number of orders.
There has been good fishing in the river for some time. Cat-fish and suckers are the principal ones caught.
Smith & Graham's freight outfit arrived Monday from Montana. It consists of nine wagons and thirty-six mules.
The COW BOY is feeling the effects of Medora's prosperity and job work is coming in as fast as we can take care of it.
Ford's freighting outfit is on the way here from Helena. It is composed of twenty wagons and seventy-five mules.
There was great danger for awhile that the river would wash in too close to the slaughter-house but the building of the dam has averted it.
Wm. Byrd, the man who stole the team at Miles City, and who was arrested here last winter, was sentenced to five years in the penitentiary on the 7th.
Pat. O'Hara and wife are obeying the scriptural injunction to "multiply etc." to the best of their ability. The latest is a boy and arrived Tuesday morning.
J. W. Reynolds, our printer, left Sunday morning for the east. Whoever employs him may be sure of getting as good a printer as there is in Dakota.
Mr. A. Kyes was in town Saturday. He will soon be here all the time attending to the forwarding, which is now being done by Messrs. Bramble and VanTassel.
Part of the store room formerly used as a carriage house by the company has undergone a number of improvements and will be used temporarily as a meat market.
W. W. Duncan, of Mandan was in town on a business trip, the first of the week. He makes it pleasant for the boys and is in on the ground floor for all furniture orders from here.
We wish we had as dead a cinch on a million dollars as Medora has on the freight route. It seems as though every freighting outfit in the country is heading this way.
J. Juelfs arrived Tuesday from Deadwood. He came on in advance of his outfit, which will probably be in to-day. It is made up of sixteen wagons and one hundred and six oxen.
Ed. Kennedy, brother of Gill, arrived here from Adrian, Mich., last Saturday evening. He will take up his residence among us and engage in some kind of business. He is a welcome addition.

R. E. Spurrier has shipped his household goods to Spokane Falls and will start for that place as soon as a man arrives here to relieve him as agent. We are sorry to lose Mr. Spurrier, but rejoice at his promotion.

Bob. Roberts intends to bring back a number of passengers from Deadwood, paying them a large rebate if he does not make the return trip in six days. This will be fast time for heavy wagons but Bob. can make it if anyone can.

Rassie Deffebach, of Spearfish, has rented the company's stable and will take possession June 1. Ras. is said to be as good a judge of cattle and horses as can be found in the west and he will be the right man in the right place.

An interesting wager was decided the first of the week between Wm. Vandriesche and Frank Keeler. William was to ride the bucker spoken of in another article, for half an hour. He won the bet but at the expense of a tumble or two.

J. O'Sullivan, the barber, has bought a lot and next Monday will begin the erection of a barber shop. He will issue shaving tickets and we bespeak for him the hearty patronage that his skill as a barber and many good qualities as a gentleman demand.

On account of the storm, but a small number turned out to hear Rev. Wm. Cooke's sermon at the Cantonment last Sunday evening. It is to be hoped that larger audiences will greet the reverend gentleman in the future. Both in public and private he is an interesting talker.

The dance at the Western house Monday evening for the benefit of C. E. Blake was largely attended. A snug sum was raised and will be sent to Mr. Blake, who is now in Miles City. Mr. Malloy furnished supper and his house free and Joe Delgie donated his services as musician.

The largest and gumboist comment on the soon-to-be-abandoned freight route from Dickinson to the Hills is furnished by an eight-mule team, which was twenty-five days going from Dickinson to Mattock's, about fifty miles. During the same time Bob. Roberts took an outfit of twenty-seven wagons from Medora to Mattock's in less than two days. This settles the gumbo question. The team from Dickinson started some time before the snow and rain storm of ten days ago and Roberts started a couple of days after it. The time of the Dickinson outfit is vouched for by J. C. Ryan, of Spearfish, and that of Roberts by any one at Mattock's and by several persons here.
Our local page "can't stand the pressure" this week and "slops over" on the editorial page. On this account, the usual amount of editorial had to be omitted.

We feel rather proud of this issue of the COW BOY as every stroke of work both literary and mechanical was done by "ye editor" since Monday morning. During the three days we have also turned out over $25 worth of job work. We are thinking of running a supplement next issue, just for recreation.

Several of the horses brought down by Johnny Goodall have been broken at the Sully Creek ranch. As there are two or three steep embankments near the ranch and the horses take it into their heads to seek tall timber in almost any direction, it was deemed best to do the rest of the breaking at Beaver creek.

T. G. Jones, of Deadwood, arrived last Monday evening. He took it easy on a valuable horse and made the distance in less than three days. Tuesday evening he went to Miles City but expects to return to-morrow. While here he purchased four of our best business lots, showing conclusively the faith he has in Medora.

J. A. Beaumont, better known as "Scotty," is certainly having a streak of hard luck. Late last week his shack at the sheep ranch burned, together with all he owned. Coming to town to get a new outfit he received a letter from Scotland stating that his father was dead. "It never rains but it pours," is little consolation but "Scotty" may be sure that in his present affliction he has the heartfelt sympathy of all his friends.

Particular attention is called to the advertisement of Peter J. Book, appearing for the first time in this issue. Mr. Book wishes it distinctly understood that he is making as good brick as can be made in America and will compete with any one in quality and price. There is a cement in the clay that dries and burns perfectly without a crack or blemish and without the use of sand in any of the processes of making. Both white and red, mould and re-pressed brick will be made, and extensive pottery works will be built in the fall, thus furnishing employment to a large force of men the year round. Besides being a brick-maker Mr. Book is an experienced contractor and is just the kind of energetic business man that makes a valuable citizen.

The cattlemen are all supposed to know that the round-up for this section of the Bad Lands begins May 25, at the Beaver creek crossing of the N. P. R. R. Every stock owner will send enough cowboys to look after his interests, who will all be under the orders of and subject to dismissal by the foreman, John Goodall. Each cattle owner will provide a mess-wagon or make arrangements to mess with some one else. At least six good horses will be needed by every man. There will be day and night herding, in which each man must take part. Branding will be done every day. Every man who wishes his cattle taken care of, must be represented on the round-up. The time taken by the round-up will be from six weeks to two months and the extent of territory is about one hundred by fifty miles. In this district there are about 40,000 cattle.

The cattle belonging to H. B. Wadsworth & Co. came in last Friday. They consisted of 1,333 yearling and two-year-old heifers, all in good condition. They are all Minnesota cattle and from the time they were bought, shipped here, driven to the ranch and up to the present not a head was lost from any cause. Together with the cattle, came several brood mares and a valuable stallion. Before this shipment there were 1,500 cattle on the range and Mr. M. Wadsworth has not seen a dead animal there and knows where all but ten or a dozen of them are. Every cattle paper that we see, estimates the loss at from three to thirty per cent. and we challenge the United States to equal Mr. Wadsworth's record. At the outside it does not equal one-tenth of one per cent. There is not a newspaper in the country but that would rejoice at the smallness of a loss thirty times as great. Bring the banner to the Bad Lands.

Perfecto Fernandez, the Mexican who returned with Johnny Goodall, is a rider from way back. One of the horses is like Mark Train's racer: "warranted to out-buck anything in America." After throwing several riders, the Mexican mounted him. An amused smile began to spread over the bronco's face but it didn't percolate far. His first move was to jump straight into the air and come down stiff-legged, as solid as a brick house. The Mexican never budged but got out his paper and tobacco and began rolling a cigarette. This, the reader will understand, is not always necessary nor, we might add, customary. We have actually seen men on bucking horses who seemed to have their hands full enough without rolling a cigarette. As a general rule we have noticed that the rider seemed, so to speak, to be confining his attention strictly to sticking on. About the time the cigarette got to going, the bronco began to think that his reputatien was at stake. As a preliminary, he jumped into the air, threw down his head and landed on his front legs with a shock sufficient to unseat the throne of grace. Perfecto took a puff at his cigarette, put his foot up by the bronco's ear and rolled him clear to his flank with his stirrup. This was done to encourage the bucker which seemed to think that in some way he had missed the combination. It did put more life into the entertainment for the bronco started on a new deal and began turning forward and back double somersaults with a facility that would put a trained athlete to the blush. Perfecto merely threw his leg over the pommel and rode side-saddle fashion. He really shouldn't have done this for it broke the broncho up in business. He would and could out-buck anything in America but he couldn't buck against fate. He immediately and unanimously soured on himself and since then has never bucked a solitary buck.

The first car-load of Columbia river salmon passed through here Monday morning on No. 2. It was gaudily labeled and will be run through to New York on fast time. The Marquis has a contract to furnish two car-loads a week to a New York house, of which the above is the first shipment.

If we were living eighteen hundred years ago we would return thanks to the immortal gods for the almost immediate answer to our prayer to be deliverd out of the hands of the Philistines, in other words, out of the judicial jurisdiction of Stark county. For the deliverance has come at last and the organization of Billings county is almost complete. It has been a long time coming but we are none the less thankful that it has come.

There is not a county in the Territory that has within its limits more of the elements of wealth than has Billings county. As far as sustaining ourselves is concerned, we could be cut off indefinitely from all the rest of the world. We are an empire in ourselves. Outside of a single vein in the Black Hills, we have the best coal in the whole west, the supply being inexhaustible. There is also an abundance of ash, cedar and cottonwood, thus furnishing fuel for all time to come. The eastern part of the county up to the Bad Lands, is as good agricultural land as there is in Dakota, and altogether the best of anything west of the Missouri. As a cattle country we are unsurpassed by anything in the United States. We have read reports from all cattle districts and none of them compare at all with our small per cent. of loss. Including every loss in the Bad Lands, we are confident that it will fall considerably short of two per cent. The cattle and agricultural territory, moreover, is so well divided that there is but little danger of their interests clashing. For citizens we have a pushing, intelligent class that can and will govern its affairs, with none of the picayuneishness that characterizes too many county governments.

The organization of Billings county will probably be one of the last official acts of Gov. Ordway and in it he shows a judgment that can only receive the highest praise. He had nothing to gain by the organization and the county had everything to lose by delay.

We predict for Billings county, a future that will be a matter of pride to the whole Territory. In the next issue we will publish at least a partial list of the county officers.

If the Mandan and Bismarck papers would be more careful to get at facts, their mission as newspapers would be far better conserved. From the beginning to the end of the long struggle as to which Northern Pacific town should have the freight route, we think we are right in saying that not an original article appeared in any of them, except the Mandan Pioneer, stating the true facts. The truth of the matter is that Medora's prosperity lies heavily on the stomachs of the editors of the afore-mentioned papers, as both Mandan and Bismarck expected a share in the Black Hills trade. Had the freight gone to any other point on the road, a blind man could see that it would be only temporary as a railroad is necessary to hold it and there is no other town on the road besides Medora that has sufficient money to build a railroad, Mandan and Bismarck not excepted. A railroad to the Hills is a certainty of the near future and by our getting it, Mandan and Bismarck will be shut out entirely from the Black Hills trade. It is very easy to see the animus of the slurring articles published in these papers in reference to Medora and the Marquis de Mores and it is an evidence of little, dog-in-the-manger minds which our present prosperity and future prospects put us in a position to view with the contempt they deserve. Mandan and Bismarck can make up their minds that in a very short time, Medora will grow to be a successful rival to either of them. They are both almost entirely agricultural towns depending on crops which at the best, are doubtful. If every crop in Dakota should fail, it would scarcely affect Medora. The increase of Bad Lands cattle never fails, nor will all the jobbing and other industries of which Medora is to the seat.

The Allard correspondent of the Glendive Times again gets his dates mixed. Insectivorous animals and the family insectivora are not by any means synonymous. Almost all animals are to some extent insectivorous but the family insectivora feed exclusively on insects. Little Red Riding Hood will have to try again before he proves that ducks should be milked. This lesson will be one dollar, please.

To the carping critics who prophecied that the name of our paper would kill it, we wish to state that our weekly circulation is now over four hundred copies and outside of a few personal friends we have not a deadhead on our list. When we started we figured on a circulation of three hundred at the end of the year, and as we have already beaten that number the chances are certainly very favorable for the Cow Boy. From letters and other means, we know that our success is due in a great measure to onr name. It describes exactly what our paper is intended to be and the name is striking enough to hold the attention of the stranger until he discovers the mission of the paper and after that, our success or failure depends upon its merits or demerits. That our advertising patronage is liberal a glance will show and the necessity of an enlargement in the immediate future forces itself upon us. Our prosperity is only an index of Medora's substantial future.
We are informed that the stages from Medora will roll across the Belle Fourche bridge in a short time.—[Minnesela Boomer.
Star & Bullock started their bull outfit for Medora on Wednesday last via the Belle Fourche bridge, in charge of John Bowman.—[Minnesela Boomer.
There are seven men from Spearfish out on the new road north from the Belle Fourche bridge, building bridges across Owl, Crow, and Indian creeks and working the freight road.—[Minnesela Boomer.

John Sechler [Arkansas John,] one of the oldest freighters on the Pierre road, passed through our town during the past week, en route to Medora. This is one of the biggest mule trains which comes into the Hills, having a capacity to haul one hundred thousand pounds. John goes via the new Belle Fourche bridge.—[Minnesela Boomer.

The survey of the new town on the Belle Fourche has been completed and the stakes set that outline the limits of the proposed place. It embraces 240 acres of land and the location is reported to be a most desirable site for the erection of a city of several thousand population. The sale of lots will not commence until the plats are completed, at which time they will be offered, and from present indications they will go at a lively rate.—[Black Hills Pioneer.

[The town-site referred to above is the one selected by the Marquis as the Hills terminus of the Medora & Black Hills railroad.—Ed.]

Yesterday morning one of the prominent business men of this city received an important letter from the Marquis de Mores. In it he said that arrangements are completed for the establishment of a stage line from Medora to Deadwood, and from the import it conveyed we are lead to believe that stages will be rolling within the next thirty days. It contained no statement as to how frequent will be their arrival and departure. Of the Medora and Black Hills railroad he expresses much confidence in its ultimate building. More important news of both these enterprises may be expected within a few days.—[Black Hills Pioneer.

Major W. R. Snider, the best editorial writer in Dakota, and editor of the Spearfish Register, is in the city. The Major is a strong believer that a railroad from the Northern Pacific will be built at an early day, and that it will be the first to reach us. He says the country between this place and Medora is the best watered and timbered of any of the prairie soil within two hundred miles of us, and that when it is settled, it will be the most fertile part of Dakota. He was very agreeably disappointed in the lay of the land and the character of the soil, and the numerous streams of living water. The country is now fast settling up by squatters along the anticipated line of the railroad. A stage line is a certainty whether a daily or not, is not yet determined.—[Black Hill Pioneer.

A meeting of the Black Hills Shippers' Association at the city hall last evening was a session of more importance than any of a previous date. The members have awakened to the stern necessity of using all proper means to secure the shipment of freight for the Hills by the Medora route, and give such encouragement to the enterprise as will secure its permanent operation. As there has never been a rate established between the Northern Pacific and Deadwood, and no previous steps taken that would tend to insure transportation, the meeting, upon the motion of S. C. Fargo, voted that $1.75 be admitted as the standard rate, subject to such classification as is made on that road. Two hundred postal cards will be printed and addressed to every member of the association, and merchants of the city, and neighboring towns explaining the action of last night's meeting. It will specify the rate established, and ask all shippers to have their goods shipped via that route.—[Black Hills Pioneer.

DICKINSON, Dak., May 19, 1884.

Considerable building is going on and for the most part they are substantial structures.

F. W. Lawrence, cousin of N. C. Lawrence is in town. He intends being a permanent resident.

A number of prospective residents have been in town lately and all are pleased with our prospects.

Dickinson is soon to have a good school building, as the issuance of bonds will be doubtless voted for that purpose on June 7.

Work is being pushed on the freight route from here and we have by no means abandoned hope of getting the Black Hills freight.

Dickinson promises to be a large shipping point for cattle. The Killdeer mountains and northern Bad Lands are easily reached from here.

A man named Joseph Clifford suffered a severe loss last Friday morning. He had three mules, a mare and colt, besides farm and household implements, valued altogether at $1,200, on the morning freight and the car in which they were contained caught fire, burning everything. The loss will probably be made good by the rail-road company.

ANTHROPOS.

Last week D. C. and A. P. [Rachal?], of Corpus Christi, purchased from Mrs. C. M. Rogers, the Texas cattle queen, her ten-elevenths interest in the Rabb cattle and landed interests, paying $4 per acre and $18 for the cows, with all the calves thrown in. The sale amounts to over two hundred thousand dollars.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

From careful examination of reliable statistics at hand we see that beef cattle are selling at about the same relative prices as a year ago. All other meat are now at lower figures and in view of this fact cattle growers should feel encouraged. There is no prospect of any excitement, but the general outlook for a good healthy trade seems encouraging.—[New Mexico Stock Grower.

Cattlemen report a large number of cattle dying on account of scarcity of water and grass in their pastures and if the drouth continues the loss to stockmen will be great. In some sections the army worm or caterpillar has made its appearance and is eating the buds and leaves of the mesquite trees. The cattle cannot be safely driven, but will have to be shipped by rail to make it pay.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.

The shipment of cattle over the Fort Worth and Denver, on Thursday, was the largest stock shipments ever made in Texas in one day. It required the borrowing of seven engines, and consisted of 12 trains and over 200 cars, transporting 7,000 head of cattle. The work now is immense and on the increase. Hereafter we will give weekly statements of shipments of cattle, receiving them every Monday morning.—[Texas L. S. Journal.

Snider & Drumm have sold all of their she cattle and bulls, to be delivered September 1st, to the Bugbee-Nelson Cattle Company. Every cow with a calf by her side brings $45; dry cows and two-year-old heifers $25; yearling heifers $20 and bulls $45. Snider & Drumm purchased of the Bugbee-Nelson Cattle Company 5,000 head of the Goodnight brand; 2,000 three and four-year-old steers at $35; and 3,000 two year-old at $28; also 4,000 yearling steers of the Bugbee brand, at $22.—[Kansas City Live Stock Indicator.

Cattlemen, do not let the push of your spring work crowd from your minds the bull question. The proper solution of this problem means an increase of twenty per cent. in the gross earnings of your herds. It is of too much importance to be laid aside for future consideration. Now is the time to act. Decide on your course and be ready by the fall season to gather and control your bulls. Seventy per cent. of calves, and we believe ninety per cent., may be annually secured by controlling the drop and fall weaning. Study the matter and get at the bottom facts and experiences of those who have tested the issue.—[N. W. L. S. Journal

King & Kennedy started for their ranch with over 20,000 head of steer cattle. Nine thousand started across a dry belt of country for Cotula, and from the best information 1,800 passed through, while the remainder were abandoned or turned loose to hunt water. About 5,000 have been picked up and brought back. There remain about 15,000 at Pena, where the firm has engaged with the railroad company to ship 1,000 per day. The loss can not be estimated, but a great many have perished for want of water, while many will stray away.—[San Antonio (Texas) Express.

There seems to be a growing disposition on the part of our range cattle owners to mix the Shorthorns and Herefords. The Shorthorn crossed on Texas or common cows rapidly breeds up in size, and gives a frame to take on a large store of fat. But some claim for these a tendency to roughness and lack of rustling qualities. This is overcome by the use of the small-boned, round and compact white faces. Many claim that this will add vitality and rustling ability to the herds. The next few years will settle the question in the minds of most ranchmen, for numerous experiments are being made on this line in all parts of the range.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Although there is not the wild and visionary dream of wealth connected with the live-stock business as in mining schemes, still there is enough in it with its rapid gains and increases, to induce a great many people of the east to invest money in anything that happens to come their way with a brand on it. The purchaser discovers, of course, after it is too late, that the company never existed, except on paper, and that the great and unreasonable dividends promised in the prospectus were but a clever bait with which to catch the sucker. Now these paper companies exist to a great extent throughout the west. A few venturesome and penurious men organize a stock company with a good capital, incorporate it and have it made a matter of record in the Secretary of State's office. They own not a horn nor a hoof, neither do they expect or want to own any. But an agent floods the section he desires to work with prospectuses setting forth what enormous dividends can be derived from investing in the company he represents, the number of cattle now owned by them, and the great and unnatural increase that would surely follow in the number of the herd. Suckers are readily found, and the agent and incorporators are happy. There are numbers of these snide affairs in Colorado, and it would be well for the legitimate companies to begin a tour of investigation, run them down and compel them to cease their nefarious robbing business, as it is bringing discredit on legitimate concerns.—[Denver News.

R. E. SPURRIER, Agent.
George Porter arrived last night from his business trip to Chicago.
Mr. M. C. Conners, of Spearfish, was in town a day or two the first of the week. He will sell some beef cattle to the Co.
Ford's outfit made a pretty large hole in the freight here but enough is on the way to load all teams that come.
Our commission as Notary Public was received yesterday and hereafter we will be prepared to do any business in that line.
The fire was started yesterday in the first brick kiln. Mr. Book has invented a new grate which he is testing in the furnaces.
The vein of coal south of town which was set on fire some time ago bids fair to develop into a rival of our famous Burning mine.
Several quarries of excellent foundation stone have been discovered in the neighboring buttes and will be put to immediate use.
The dance at Ferris & Merrifield's ranch last night was a complete success. Several loads of participants went from here and they all enjoyed themselves hugely.
Western Starr, of Dickinson, and G. H. Spear, of Spearfish, started for Deadwood last Monday morning. They intend to take matters easy and to hunt and have a good time on the way down.

Ford's outfit arrived Tuesday and is the largest that has yet come. It consists of over a hundred mules, about twenty horses and twenty-five large freight wagons. It will finish loading with 120,000 pounds of freight to-day and will start immediately for the Hills.

T. G. Jones returned from Billings where his family is located, last Friday. He is convinced that Medora will make a good town and intends to identify himself with her interests hereafter. He and Joe Pennell are now busy figuring on the mail and stage routes.

Mr. Lorin F. Deland, special correspondent of the Boston Herald and of the large printing firm of Deland & Barta, made us a plesant call Tuesday morning in company with his wife. They are on a pleasure trip along the line of the Northern Pacific and are of the class of people who make the most of their sight-seeing. They are old friends of Messrs. Eaton and Wade and visited them while here.

The Pierre route will soon be practically deserted, almost all the outfits coming on the Medora route. Several already here have had "Northwestern Transportation Company" stamped on their covers and others are on their way. "Arkansas John" will be here in a few days with one of the largest mule trains in the west. Star & Bullock also have a large bull outfit on the road here. Both these outfits, besides several others, have been taken off the Pierre route.

The first step we have taken to improve our paper will be readily noticed in to-day's issue. The new cattle and horse cuts were made expressly for us and "came high but we must have 'em." Gregor Lang's brands are also published for the first time. We owe Berry, Boice & Co. an apology for not publishing their new brand, but through no fault of ours it was engraved backwards and we publish the old brand. We hope to rectify the mistake by next issue. Lloyd Roberts' and Rich, Randall & Co's. brands will also probably appear next issue.

We were pleased to receive a letter from H. M. Jorgens, of Spearfish, saying that he had his drug store fixtures all packed and boxed and would start immediately on receipt of a favorable reply. By this time he is probably on the way. We are also pleased to state that Dr. Louthan will probably accompany him and be a permanent resident of Medora. Mr. Jorgens qualified the remark by saying that Dr. Louthan would come if he could get away. Our readers will remember the forcible manner in which he was detained, as mentioned in our last issue. In Dr. Louthan's own words he "can make ten dollars here to one in Spearfish" and we fully expect that he will be here soon.

Lloyd Roberts, E. G. Paddock and Dan. Friedman returned from Minnesota last Friday with 750 head of cattle for Rich, Randall & Co. The buying was done in a very short time and the cattle were only thirty-one hours on the road from Minnesota. Lloyd has the reputation of being the best and fastest buyer in the west and when seconded by two such men as Messrs. Paddock and Friedman, we do not wonder that quick time was made. Lloyd, Dan and Mr. Rich started back this morning to buy another lot. Besides buying cattle, Lloyd kept the Cow Boy in mind and brought us back eleven subscribers. We hope he will continue to insult us in the same way.

J. L. Bowman, one of the best known mule skinners in the Hills and who has driven over every possible route into Deadwood and almost every freight line in the west, says that the Medora route to the Hills is not only by far the best route into Deadwood, but the best he has ever driven over and at least twenty miles shorter than the Pierre route. The road he came over is the long one and the cut-off made by Bob. Roberts decreases the distance again by twenty miles. Mr. Bowman is on his way through to Montana and has given up driving, having come this far on his way with Wheeler's outfit, which arrived this morning. Such a recommendation as this for our route, coming from such an unbiased source, is final proof of its superiority.

Sergeant Clives, two soldiers and two scouts, an Indian and a half-breed, from Fort Buford, arrived Sunday afternoon. They were in pursuit of the robbers who had waylaid paymaster Whipple, north of Glendive, last Wednesday. Sergeant Clives states that Mr. Whipple, contrary to his usual custom, had the money, $18,000, in two grips in the ambulance, which went ahead of the escort wagon. About three in the afternoon, seven men stepped from the side of the road and began firing immediately. Sergeant Coonrod, an able and well-known soldier, was shot twice clear through the body and died while bravely fighting. In the melee, two of the ambulance mules were wounded and started to run away. This lucky circumstance saved the treasure as it was rapidly taken out of the robbers' reach. The escort wagon was plundered but nothing was taken except a cartridge belt. As soon as word could be sent to Fort Buford, the party under Sergeant Clives was sent out. The trail was struck near the scene of the attempted robbery and followed to Beaver creek. Here it was lost by cattle crossing it. It is exceedingly doubtful if the robbers will be arrested as they were all masked and there is no clue at present. It is the opinion of a number that they belonged to the Axleby gang. The facts seem to bear out this assumption, as the robbers retreated in the general direction of the Black Hills, although they separated into several parties. This and the fact that they tried to kill the mules smacks strongly of professionalism.

[Since the above was put in type it has been found that one of the robbers was Dan. McCarthy, a well-known ranchman living across the river from Glendive. A bloody trail was found and followed, ending in a new grave which contained his body. It is now thought that the others may be captured.—Ed.]

The Dickinson Press atempted recently to make a point in reference to Medora that we would not notice were it not for the fact that the eyes of the Mandan and Bismarck editors caught it and it was forthwith published. The article was in answer to our editorial on Dickinson justice and was to the effect that [illegible] was more in need of jails than [illegible] point on the line and furnished a large proportion of the business for [illegible] justice shops. We do not [illegible] argue the question at all, but [illegible] how utterly baseless the charge we will state that there is not a solitary case on the Dickinson docket from M[edora?]. Up to the present, Medora has [illegible] a case of any kind in any court. [If any]one can show the contrary he can win more money here than he can make running a paper in a town that has soured on itself.

As the round-up now going on is the first one for this section, it will not be surprising if there are some curious developments. No direct case of stealing has yet come to light but that there will as the round-up progresses, is a matter of little doubt. Every stockman in the Bad Lands knows that a number of characters have been living among them, always flush but never apparently doing anything. How some of these men live is as well known as if they had been repeatedly caught in their unlawful acts. The existence of this class of men is not by any means peculiar to the Bad Lands but they are found in every cattle country in the world. The Wyoming Association is making it very warm for this gentry but many more are scared away than are arrested. Of these we will receive our share and it behooves our stockmen to make a start now and cinch every particle of crooked work to the full extent of written and range law. It is astonishing to note the apathy existing in respect to this known criminality. It is as well known as that there are cattle in the Bad Lands. The time to stop this work is now. Delay only increases the evil. The round-up management is in good hands and will doubtless bring to light many eye-openers. Many others will be undiscovered or at least unproven. It has been repeatedly shown that the only way to rid a cattle country of these depredators is united action of stockmen through the means of an association. That the organization of the Bad Lands association was put off until fall, will bring many a loss to our stockmen.

Col. Lounsberry's new paper, the Bismarck Journal, came to hand Sunday. It contains a large amount of interesting reading matter and we see no reason why it should not be a financial success if its present standard is kept up. The Colonel's intimate acquaintance with Dakota affairs will give it great prominence. From the initial number, we are glad to note that the Journal will not join the other Bismarck and Mandan papers in their efforts to injure our town.

Maj. Snider, of the Spearfish Register, is a talented and able writer but he will have to brush up his Latin a little. He heads a recent article: "De Toros—De Mores," referring to the new town on the Belle Fourche. The Major's translation of the title in a joke on the town was: "[Bullocks?] of, from or by death." As the ending "es" cannot follow the preposition "de" and "mores" does not mean death at all but does mean "ways, manners, customs etc.," the Major's wit [illegible] badly.

A perfect matrimonial furore seems to have struck the editors along the line of the Northern Pacific. "Me Lud" Tuttle no sooner kicks over the traces of single blessedness than Bro. Scott also concludes that a faithful helpmeet will do him a world of good, and then the news comes that our old college mate, [Homer?] Hill has gone east on matrimony intent. We don't know whether this thing is catching or not but it looks as though the air here will destroy any contagious properties the disease may have.

The following came in a little too late for our last issue:

BEAVER RANCH, May 20.

EDITOR COW BOY:

The COW BOY continues to come boldly to the front and is perused with interest. Everything in our section is now on the war path to get the cattle in shape and the outfits leave the Little Muddy to meet on Powder river to join in the round-up beginning at the mouth of the Mispah the 25th. Grass is coming along well but we need a little heavenly dew to advance it more rapidly. Cattle have wintered well and are now shaping up nicely. Maj. W. A. Towers is now outlooking over the situation and appears very well pleased with the outlook. Consequently the boys are happy. He will bring in several more thousand this season. He never does anything that is small and is at all times ready to go his length when he receives a little encouragement. We are glad to see him looking so well, the cause being that the summer will bring to him a new partner for life. We think it time and wish him and the unfortunate lady a happy journey through life. Yet we are inclined to doubt him as it has been an old song for years. Mr. W. H. Howell, of Atlanta, Ga., very prominently connected and a most genial gentleman and Mr. G. C. Smart, of Kansas City, also very pleasant, accompany the Major. They are looking out for a chance to locate in business somewhere here, and royal good men they are even if they do saw gourds at night. We simply put a wet sponge in their mouth and lay them gently on their side with a No. 9. We wish them success and hope they may locate in this country.

BAD LANDS.

Every year's experience demonstrates more fully the great benefits derivable from complete organization of range work. Brains are as essential in systematizing the cattle business as in regulating banks or other great enterprises. System wins in any pursuit.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

A gentleman writing from Australia says the big cattle and stock ranches are not all in America, and presents the following as a sample of their extensive operations in that country: "The small run I am on contains 130,000 acres more than Mr. Goodnight's Texas pasture. A friend of mine owns 1,200,000 head of cattle and 500,000 sheep, and his property is valued at $25,000,000. These are facts, so do not boast of your 'potato plots' in future, or you may hear from me again."—[N. M. Stock Grower.

Ranchmen recently returned from New Mexico report the grass and cattle generally in good condition, and the calf crop immense. In Colfax county, however, the losses have been very large, estimated at 15 to 20 per cent, caused by overstocking, the range, and carelessness on the part of the managers of some of the big companies who, instead of driving their stock away from the river when notified that they were perishing, spent their time in the towns enjoying themselves in the usual manner. The Dorsey ranch, we are informed, lost heavily in dead cattle, as many as 300 head being counted in one locality within a range of as many yards.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

Mr. Henry Stewart, who does not write as one without knowledge of such matter, maintains that "there is no contagious disease existing among cattle in America, except as an occasional case may be imported here." He joins The Live-Stock Indicator and other influential agricultural journals in the demand for shutting out foreign animals, which are shipped to our shores principally for speculative purposes. This "putting up the bars" will it is thought be wiser than to take the risk of broadcasting the seeds of infection and then employ politicians and veterinary experts to "stamp out" the laid harvest at government expense.—[New York Tribune.

Prof. Law, Chairman of the Treasury Cattle Commission, has made a report of his investigation of the recent outbreaks of cattle disease, supposed to be Foot-and-Mouth disease, in Illinois and Kansas. After reviewing the circumstances of the cases at eighteen points in Illinois the report states that in the interior of that State the disease was found scattered over an extensive district without any reference to contagion. There was no evidence found of its extension from one herd to another and it was shown that but a small percentage of cattle exposed were infected, while goats, sheep, and swine mingling with infected cattle escaped. The disease was found to continue in the same herds for four months. The report adds that the demonstration of these prominent features of this affection forbids absolutely the idea that it is the European contagious Foot-and-Mouth disease.—[Kansas City L. S. Journal.

The efforts of the New York butchers to boycott the dressed beef of the west is significant as indicating that the experiments in that direction promise to work important results. They show that there is an advantage in slaughtering cattle in the west and shipping the carcasses by refrigerator cars to the consumers over the shipment of the live animals. The butchers are not able to compete with the western dressed beef, and are seeking some restrictive legislation from the New York legislature. But, as in the case of all new processes in business methods, if it has palpable merit it must prevail against all selfish opposition.—[Fargo Argus.

We have often wondered why there is such a large number of bovine breeders and so few of the equine, when the object to be gained is the same in both cases. If we reflect an instant it is quite surprising that a large number of our breeders raise exclusively cattle. True, it does not require so large an amount of capital to breed and raise cattle as horses, and it is just as true that there is more profit in breeding horses than cattle. With the same amount of care and at no greater expense a three-year-old colt can be raised as easily as a three-year-old steer, and if the colt be half Clydesdale it will bring $150, while the steer, if he is half Shorthorn or Hereford, will bring $[55?] or $[60?], and this is figuring him at export prices. In some cases it is a matter of taste, but generally there are as many lovers of the horse as the ox. The industry is on the increase, but it will take years at the present rate to become as wide spread as that of cattle raising. Those who are now in it are rapidly amassing fortunes, and those who enter the field early are the ones who have the best chance. As ever, it is the early bird that gets the worm.—[Iowa Homestead.

Nothing that has been done in the way of national legislation for a long time will be regarded with so much favor by the people of this part of the country as the bill just passed by the senate establishing a Bureau of Animal Industry, having for its object the extirpation of contagious diseases among cattle. The bill is comprehensive in its provisions, having been drafted with the advice of men who have given years of experience to the cattle interests of the country, and aims to cover all that has been suggested either by practice or theory. To the men who have built up the great cattle ranches of Nebraska, Wyoming, Colorado and Utah it will prove a measure the pecuniary advantages of which can not be estimated, while by the feeders of our own state it will be welcomed as something they have long desired.—[McCook (Neb.) Tribune.

The trade in shipping cattle from Pittsburg and intermediate points is now phenomenally small. This is to be accounted for by the additional circumstance that the producers are so located as to labor under great disadvantages in competing with both eastern and western feeders. The feeders of Maryland and eastern Pennsylvania, who, by the way, are apparently extending their business from year to year, have the seaboard markets right at their doors, and possess [special?] advantages in getting their stock [to sale?] in quick time, with none of the evil effects of fatigue in transit, and at a minimum of cost of transportation. Western feeders, on the other hand, have the benefit of low through rates from Chicago, which completely handi[cap] the shipper of the central part of the United States. Hence the weakness of the shipping trade here and elsewhere.—[National Stockman.

Word comes from the round-up in the shape of a letter from the foreman to the following effect: "There are thirty-five or forty men on the round-up, most of them well mounted except a few tenderlegs. The per cent. of calves is very light, but there will be quite a number of late ones. No serious accident has occurred but Thomas Dwire tried to knock down a yearling by running against it with his horse. He succeeded pretty well but by the way he handles his left arm and from the looks of one side of his face one would think he got some strawberry short cake in his. Bony Jake, one of the boys that came down from Miles, tackled a bronco yesterday morning and got thrown so high that he didn't come down till dinner time. He says he is not a pugilist or a pedestrian but he would meet John L. Sullivan in the prize ring or Fitzgerald on the saw-dust track before he would climb Sunfish Browny again. He says when a horse sunfishes both ways, one backstrap won't hold him on."

This new townsite has just been laid off by a company composed of Seth Bullock and Alvin Fox, of this city, Mr. Guild, of New York, and others. It is situated on high ground, at the confluence of the Redwater with the Belle Fourche, and is one of the most natural eligible sites for a town of any in this locality. There is ample room for a city of 50,000 inhabitants, and can be watered from either stream with sufficient pressure for all practical purposes. A Pioneer reporter rode over the new bridge crossing the Belle Fourche on a part of the town yesterday, and we give it as our opinion that it is a substantial structure and will withstand any freshet. It is fully fifteen feet above the present stage of water, has one abutment or crib in the center of the stream which is built of hewn logs filled with rock, that seemingly will withstand any driftwood or ice. The first house in this embryo city will be built by John Mende, who has the lumber piled up on the spot. A hotel will be built as soon as the lumber can be hauled to begin its erection. Messrs. Fox and Bullock met us on the north side of the Belle Fourche and took us across the future town and showed what may be the brief terminus of the Medora and Black Hills railroad. Mr. Bullock offered to wager $1,000 that fall the town would contain fifty buildings. Its close proximity to Minnesela, the county seat of Butte county, will retard its growth until the stage and railroad line make it a point. Its projectors are sanguine of its becoming the largest town in this vicinity in due course of time.—[Black Hills Pioneer.

C. W. Sleeper arrived from the west Tuesday morning and will remain for several days.
J. E. Hample, Oberne, Hosick & Co's. travelling agent, passed through on his way east, last Friday evening.
The night telegraph office, which was on the opposite side of the river, has been moved to this side.
E. G. Paddock is building a residence on his claim, about half way between his shack and the railroad.
Chas. Wilson, of the Mandan Pioneer, was in town to-day on business. He started east this afternoon.
The billiard hall and theatre is nearly ready for the plasterers and will soon be ready for occupancy.
John O'Sullivan will begin the erection of his barber shop and bath rooms as soon as the lumber arrives.
Gosh! Phew!! Gee whizz!!! I thought they were cinnamon drops. This is the reason J. C. has been "setting 'em up" lately.
Father Cassidy, of Mandan, held mass here Tuesday morning. Hereafter he expects to be here every two or three weeks.
All the stock horses from here and Garner creek have been taken to Sully creek ranch. Geo. Smith is in charge at that point.
A large part of the new $10,000 stock has arrived for the general store and is being opened. Additional shelf room has been built to receive it.
Dr E. E. Ball, of Mandan, will be in Medora June 9, 10 and 11; prepared to do all kinds of dentistry. It will be a good opportunity to "have it pulled."
Orrin Kinley, better known as "Nich" received a severe wound in the foot Tuesday from the accidental discharge of his revolver. He will be all right in a week or two.
J. J. Fitzgerald has finished the work of clearing the bottom below the Marquis' residence. M. Eyraud thinks it is susceptible of a high state of cultivation.
Mr. Lorin F. Deland and wife, of Boston, started east Sunday. They expected [illegible line] to go back last Wednesday but they went to Eaton's ranch and that settled it.
John Belding, ex-sheriff of Lawrence county and one of the capital commissioners passed through here Tuesday, on his way east. He was only thirty-six hours from Deadwood.

Orders have come for the erection of three dwelling houses and work has already begun on them. There has been much exasperating delay about getting lumber or four or five other buildings would now be in process of erection.

T. A. Matthews spent several days in town last week. His friends will be pleased to learn that he has a good position as stock inspector for the eastern Montana association. His headquarters will hereafter be in Mandan.

One of Joe Pennell's mules strayed away some time since and a reward of $25 is offered for its recovery. It is a dark brown, weighs over [illegible] pounds and is branded JP monogram on the left shoulder as shown in our brand columns.

Rassie Deffebach and Tom Jones, not T. G., of Spearfish, arrived yesterday afternoon. Mr. Deffebach will immediately take charge of the stables here and turn them into a first-class livery barn. Arrangements have been made by which Mr. Jones will have an interest or partnership in the business.

Several wagons started out yesterday to pick up the buffalo bones with which the adjacent country is strewn. This industry has developed largely during the last few months. The bones are gathered almost everywhere and sell in Bismarck for $8 [?] per ton. Thence they are sent east, where they are pulverized and sold for fertilizers.

Peter Book will open his first kiln of brick to-morrow. Several have already been taken out and the clay will realize the highest expectations. The brick are as good as those made anywhere. The second kiln is now being built and will contain a hundred thousand or more. Immediate use will be made of the first kiln in building foundations etc.

Bob Roberts returned Sunday from the Hills. He was gone nineteen days and stopped three days in the Hills. It will be remembered that he started just after a week's rain and that the outfit was the first that had ever travelled over the road. With all these disadvantages, he made better time than has ever been made on the Pierre road. Perhaps our route has gumbo on it but it seems to be a kind freighters like.

Rev. R. H. Fulton made us a call last Monday and reported the loss of four horses at Belfield, undoubtedly stolen. They were: one black mare about fourteen hands high, weighing [illegible] pounds, right hind hoof white, others black. Some white hair in mane at top of collar. At present there are three small saddle sores on the left side of the back. Long mane and tail, fine traveller, square tripper and five years old. Besides this mare there was a valuable team taken. They were iron-gray geldings, weighing 1400 to 1600 pounds each, and will be easily recognized. The fourth horse was small and white, eight years old and had no special marks. All the horses were unbranded. A liberal reward is offered for the return of the horses or information leading to their recovery. Address Rev. R. [H.?] Fulton, Belfield, Dak.

"Arkensaw John has arriv," at least it is a very good imitation of such an event. He has one of the best outfits in the west and has been freighting for the past twenty-six years. During this time he has freighted over every road from Bismarck to the coast and he wants to be put on record as saying that the road from Medora to the Black Hills is the best one he ever travelled over. We care not what outside parties may say against our route, but such a recommendation as this, coming from John Sechler [?], is sufficient to convince any freighter that our route is all and more than we have ever claimed for it.

The following letter is from one of the party of four that started from here in a row-boat about a month ago via the Little and Big Missouri, to Bismarck. It is interesting and instructive.

MINNEISKA, MINN., May 2[0?].

To A. T. PACKARD, Medora, Dak.

In accordance with my promise I will write you a few lines in regard to our trip down the Little Missouri. It took us a little longer to make it than we expected as the river runs a good many rods to the mile, in other words is very crooked. I think it must be at least [275?] miles by river from Medora to the Big Missouri. We had sport enough, though, to pay us well for our trouble and we feel more than satisfied with our trip. We had no serious trouble in getting through with our boats and the scenery along the stream is very interesting to any one who never saw such a country. We found an abundance of very good timber, much more than we expected to see, enough to supply the country adjacent for many years. But as far as fuel is concerned there is coal enough along the Little Missouri between Medora and the Big Missouri to supply the Territory of Dakota for generations to come. We saw plenty of deer, some mountain sheep, and ducks and geese were plenty. Any one who wishes to see wild scenery and enjoy hunting would have to go a long distance to find a better place for that purpose than along the Little Missouri. Please accept our thanks for your kindness to us while there and we will try and call on you again in about eleven months from date.

Yours very truly,
AARON FOX.

We had intended giving the morning report of the Chicago convention but the wires are not working well and outside of the fact that Gen. J. D. Henderson, of St. Louis, is permanent chairman no further report has been received. Arthur and Blaine are still leading, with Harrison and Gresham as prominent rivals in case the strength of the leaders neutralize each other.

We are glad to see the determined fight that the Glendive Times is waging with the corrupt Custer county ring. That county is now about $120,000 in debt and has scarcely been organized a year and a half. The result is excessive taxation and citizens are getting discouraged and cattle men especially are leaving. There is and can be no excuse for this state of affairs. It is stealing, pure and simple. On top of all this, the ring is preparing to foist a new paper on the citizens of Glendive. It is supposed to be the defunct Fargo Broadaxe outfit and will soon die in Glendive. The reason for its establishment is that an election is coming on and the ring wants an organ. If the citizens of Glendive support the new journal, they will be harming themselves more than they know. Neither Glendive or any other town of its size can support two papers. It is far better to have one live, energetic paper like the Times, than two or more half-starved sheets which are only a drag on the town. As the movement to start the new paper is undoubtedly a piece of spite work to ruin a paper that has refused to quietly stand by and see the county plundered, there is still less reason that any support should be given it. We are the more free in speaking of Custer county affairs as we do not think that there is any danger of such a ring ever gaining control in Billings county. We wish it distinctly understood that any attempt of the kind will be saluted by a broadside in the COW BOY that will open the eyes of the tax-payers. Billings can and will have a clean county administration. Almost invariably a number of bumming place seekers and political shysters get hold of the county reins at first. Billings county is to be an exception or there will be music in the air.

Were there really any danger that Pat Donan would be appointed governor, there would be a popular uprising very much resembling civil war, in Dakota. That such an uncollapsable windbag should even be mentioned as a candidate is a standing disgrace to our Territory.

"Like angels' visits," few and far between, is the meeting of two cremationists. The ideas are too new and their adherents too scattered for much organization. For this reason, it is a real pleasure which we have never experienced but once, to meet a pronounced adherent of the cause. Mr. Julius LeMoyne, of Washington, Pa., referred to in our local columns, is at present the leading cremationist of the United States. The only crematory in this country is now owned by him and was built by his father. We do not now propose to enter into a discussion of the merits of cremation, but wish to say that four-fifths of the cremationists in the United States were made such by a thorough, practical understanding of the subject by the successful operation of the LeMoyne crematory. We are glad to see that the tide of public opinion, as shown by many newspaper articles, is turning in favor of cremation. Leading scientific men everywhere are coming to regard it as altogether the most preferable way of disposing of bodies and the only way to protect the living from contagion by the dead. Before the next generation has passed away, burial will be considered almost as barbarous as was cremation when LeMoyne began his crusade.

Especial attention is called to the notice published in another column in reference to persons setting the grass on fire. The move is one in the right direction and cattlemen mean busines in offering the reward. Grass is their source of profit and no effort will be spared to punish the carelessness or criminality of any one destroying it. There are stringent United States and Territorial laws against setting fire to the grass and any one found doing so can make up his mind to suffer to the full extent of the law.

Considerable comment was caused yesterday by the reported receipt of a telegram that Star & Bullock had telegraphed their intention of shipping by the way of Pierre. The facts in the case are as follows: Star & Bullock have their orders in for goods months ahead. Up to the time when the route was established from here all their goods were consigned by the way of Pierre. Upon the establishment of the Medora route, all their goods were ordered this way. The most of them had already been marked by way of Pierre, and re-marked by way of Medora. The consignment now at Pierre is one of these lots, which was not re-directed. The telegram which was received here was from Star & Bullock to the forwarding company and was to the effect that the lot of goods at Pierre was needed immediately and requested that John Sechler's outfit should be loaded with what freight of theirs was here so that he could go to Pierre. This is all there is to the numerous and conflicting reports circulated yesterday which all seemed to lean toward the opinion that Star & Bullock had abandoned our route. It would be well to examine the reliability of the reports hereafter, before giving them credence.

The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass in the cattle sections of Western Dakota.

Stock and feeding cattle are at least $1 per hundred weight higher, relatively, than they were a year ago. This narrows the margin of feeders. The liberal profits and quick returns of feeding and the great abundance of grass and rough feed have been chief among the causes to bring this about.—[Drovers' News.

The round-up has progressed far more rapidly than was expected and to-day will cross the rail-road at Andrew's creek. Nothing of particular importance has occurred, and the boys seem to be enjoying themselves thoroughly. Some of the Texas cattle from up the river have drifted badly but besides these there are very few ahead of the round-up.

David Neff, near Osborn, O., has a Jumbo of a steer five year old in February; he weighs 2,840 pounds and is far from being fat; in height measures six feet four inches, girths nine feet and is nine feet long from base of horns to root of tail. He is so gentle and kind that the small children play with him, leading him around with an ordinary cow-chain around his neck.—[Exchange.

To a reporter of the New York Herald Mr Bonner said, speaking of the once celebrated trotter, Dexter: "He is now twenty-six years old, and has been kept at my down-town stables during the winter and given only walking exercise, but it is the intention to drive the old horse on the road during the coming season, as he is full of life and vigor and retains a great deal of his old-time speed."

A remedy for worms in horses is given by a writer of experience in an exchange. He says: "Take a lump of rock mineral salt, from one to ten pounds or more, and put it in the horse's manger. In six days the horse or colt will be free of worms. I have used and prescribed this remedy for many years and it has never failed in any one case, and the horse will improve in health and condition at once."—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

An exchange tells how to treat balky horses as follows: Take a good, reliable horse—a good puller—and the balky one. Put similar harness on the two, attach them together and start them in opposite directions. At first the balky horse will allow himself to be dragged backwards, but soon he will tire of this and commence to pull in good earnest, and after that he will never refuse to do his duty.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Dorr Clark, owner of the VVV outfit, and half owner of the E6 brand, is in town, waiting for two hundred head of Short-horn bulls, which will be in Saturday. Mr. Clark is an enthusiastic convert to the thoroughbred bull question and this lot will make about five hundred that he has on his two ranches. He also uses six bulls for every hundred cows. Since his arrivtl here, he has examined the capabilities of the country and thinks, as do all cattle men, that this is the best place in the United states for cattle. To prove his belief, he expects to drive up about 5,000 steers to fatten in the Bad Lands.

The largest cattle herd in Montana owned by one firm or company is that of L. G. Baker & Co., or the Benton & St. Louis Cattle company. Besides the Swett herd recently purchased by C. W. Price and L. G. Baker & Co., Mr. L. C. Baker, of St. Louis, has contracted for the delivery of 2,000 head of two-year-old heifers at the nearest point to Fort Benton, which will make the total owned by this company, estimating the increase for this year, about 25,000 head, of a cash value of not less than $1,000,000. We understand that the company will have $100,000 worth of steers to market this fall. If the Benton & St. Louis Cattle company continue to make purchases as they have during the past two years it will not be long before they can size up with the Swan Land and Cattle company of Wyoming, which is perhaps the largest stock company in the world. The Choteau county company has the advantage of a better range and a better stock country generally, and for that reason will make more rapid progress and earn larger dividends than the other outfit.—[River Press.

Some of our local stock raisers in the southern part of the state, as well as those in the Neutral Strip and Panhandle country, are adopting a new system of handling their local bred cattle which will prevent their home ranges from being overstocked, and protect them from serious loss during very severe winters; which will assure a sufficient amount of grass for winter grazing for all stock left on the local range and prevent the same from being over-crowded. The system they have and are abopting is to have two ranges, one for breeding purposes and the other for maturing their beef cattle on. The last named located in the north, either in Wyoming or Montana, to which they take all steer cattle over the age of one year old, and either drive or ship them to their grazing field in the north and hold them until fully matured before they are marketed. This system not only gives them fatter cattle, but gives them increased weight from two to four hundred pounds to the animal over our local breed steer cattle.—[Ford County (Kan.) Globe.

Messrs. Julius Le Moyne, of Washington, Pa., Joseph U. Rose, Pittsburgh, W. K. Duval, Wheeling, W. V. and Harvey T. Halleck, Washington, Pa., have been in town several days, arranging to put in cattle on Tepee bottom, under the management of D. K. Wade. A company has been formed and as a starter, six hundred graded cattle have been purchased and will be here in three weeks. Mr. LeMoyne, who is a prominent Short-horn breeder and president of the Washington county Thorough-bred stock association, thinks seriously of deserting his first love and using Polled bulls exclusively. The result of such an experiment would be valuable to our stockmen as it is thought that Polled cattle will stand severe weather better and are otherwise hardier than Short-horns.

Teemer defeated Conley by a quarter of a length in their single sculll race at Pullman, Decoration day.

On May 28, for the first time on record, the English Derby ended in a draw. St. Gatien and Harvester were the tying horses.

McLaughlin and Dufur will wrestle collar-and-elbow, best two in three, at Buffalo, June 6. The contest is for $500 and gate money.

The record on 75 yards was broken by John S. Barnes, of St. Paul, May 30. The previous record, made by Myers, Lee and others, was 7¾ seconds. Barnes' time was 7 seconds.

Slosson realized the highest expectations of his friends in his contest with Schaeffer at Chicago last Sunday night, and beat the champion, at the balk-line game of billiards. Betting was $125 to $40 on Schaeffer and large sums were laid at these odds.

F. C. Leethem, the representative of Marder, Luse & Co., type founders, passed through Glendive on Thursday morning's train, cached behind trunks in a baggage car. He sold some goods at Helena when the authorites got after him for not paying the Territorial license. He learned of this and skipped for the east by the first train. At every town he was searched for but by getting off the cars on the opposite side from the platform and waiting until the train started he escaped. As the train pulled out of the Glendive station he was heard to remark: "Well, this is a h—l of a country." Leethem had no love for cowboys and on his arrival at Medora he got off to see Packard, of the Bad Lands Cowboy, but on seeing some of these famous gentry between him and the hotel, he suddenly concluded that Packard was not at home, or at least that he was not anxious to see him.—[Glendive Times.

A Pioneer reporter was on yesterday, permitted to read a letter from one in authority, to a prominent citizen of Deadwood, relative to the construction of the Northern Pacific spur from Medora to this city. The absence of authority from the writer, to publish the letter, alone prevents its appearance in lieu of this article. We do not, however, we think, violate confidence, in stating that abundant assurance is given, not only that the road will be constructed, but that work will begin in a very few days, in fact has already begun if the ordering a survey, and preparing therefor is any portion of the important undertaking. Within a few days at the outside, the project will mature, details will be arranged, and the Pioneer at liberty to disclose full particulars of this most important movement to the entire Hills section. If we can be positive of anything in this world of ours, we may safely count upon all rail communication with the outside world before many moons shall wane.—[Black Hills Pioneer.

At the annual meeting of leading cattle raising associations of Texas in 1882, prompt and very active measures were taken to banish the deadly six-shooter from cattlemen's belt. Resolutions were passed unanimously pledging owners of ranches and cattle not to keep in their employ any hands that would carry deadly weapons. That spring, there was an absence of deadly encounters and shooting sprees observable throughout the range country.

Last year no action was taken by stockmen in convention assembled in regard to the "six-shooter," and since that time serious and deadly shots have been fired. In almost every section of the West murders are on the increase, and cowmen are too often the principal in the encounters. The six-shooter loaded with deadly cartridges is a dangerous companion for any man, especially if he should unfortunately be primed with whisky.

Cattlemen should unite in aiding the enforcement of the law against the carrying of deadly weapons. Lawlessness in any form is hurtful, morally and from a business standpoint, and no business is injured than that of cattle raising, when its employes are allowed to carry deadly weapons. Then we would suggest to the managers of cattle ranches to see that the six-shooter is banished from his outfit.—[Texas L. S. Journal.

A large lot of freight arrived for the Hills this morning.
The plasterers for the billiard hall are expected in a day or two.
Russ Wilson, foreman of the E6 outfit, is in town, with Dorr Clark.
T. G. Jones started for St. Paul last week to consult about rail-road matters.
As we go to press, the rain is descending in torrents. It is exactly what the grass needs.
E. G. Paddock's house is rapidly nearing completion. It presents a first-rate appearance.
The dance at Peter Malloy's Tuesday night was thoroughly enjoyed by the participators.
The Marquis' servants came Monday evening, to set the house to rights for the summer.
Mr. Elder, of St Paul, is in town, making preparations to put in a wind-mill near the Marquis' residence.
Car-loads of salmon, in fulfillment of the Marquis' New York contract, are passing through frequently.
A number of fat cattle are being killed at the slaughter-house and the season will soon begin in earnest.
Tom Tighe came up from Mandan this morning. He will be at Freyburg for some time, working for the N. P.
John O'Sullivan has moved his barber shop to this side of the river and is occupying temporary quarters with John Warn.
The round-up is developing far more fat cattle than was expected. There will be little difficulty in getting plenty for slaughtering.
Mr. Tobin, of Mandan, was in town a day or two last week. He is thinking strongly of entering into a partnership with Tom Stack. It will make a strong partnership and doubtless be successful.
We are in receipt of a number of lithograph bird's eye views of Spearfish, from Dr. J. M. Louthan. It is an excellent view and a good advertisement for Spearfish.
H. H. Parkins has been here several days learning the system of book-keeping inaugurated by Auditor Kerr. Mr. Parkins will have charge of the Duluth cold-storage house.

Several half-breeds were in town Sunday, indulging in unlimited fire-water. One of them was urged to fight the bears on a bet. But the wily half-breed had a level head when he answered: "Liver more wort dan dollars."

A number of persons have taken advantage of our agency and subscribed for outside papers and periodicals. Subscriptions at regular publishers rates will be received for any paper or periodical published in the world.

Notice is again given that Dr. E. E. Ball, an experienbed dentist of Mandan, will be here the 9th, 10th and 11th, prepared to do any work in his line. A call on the dentist at this time is likely to save much suffering when one is not near.

A coal-mine has been located and opened in the bluff east of town. Superior coal has been found in it, the vein being about eight feet thick. The citizens of Medora can rely on getting a fine quality of coal at a cheap rate the coming winter.

Work is going forward rapidly on a new side track. It will run on the south side of the main track, beginning several hundred yards east of the depot. A new freight house for the rail-road company will be built at the same time.

A fatal mistake was providentially discovered Monday by the keen eye of Uncle John. A bone man had nearly finished his load when one of a rather odd shape attracted the attention of the aforesaid eagle eye. It, the bone, was immediate[ly?] dragged out and the voice of our esteemed fellow citizen, Mr. Thomas Stack was heard coming from it, in thanksgiving for his delivery.

The second kiln of brick, which will be ready for burning in a few days, is to contain over 200,000. A permanent kiln is to be erected immediately, thus saving much waste. Specimens of the brick at the COW BOY office have been examined by many competent judges and unanimously pronounced equal to any brick made.

John Bruguier, a well-known scout, is in camp across the track. Johnny is known and liked all over the northwest. To his efficient services, General Miles willingly concedes that he owes his promotion. Strange to say Johnny is as great a favorite with the Indians as with the soldiers. Were it not for him the Sioux would not have come in, and Sitting Bull would still be "bordering" on the Canadian line, making hostile incursions into this country instead of living peaceably with his tribe at Standing Rock. Through his intercession, also Chief Joseph and the Nez Perces surrendered. In these wars he was the constant friend of the white men. During the Nez Perce war he made one of the fastest long-distance rides on record with dispatches from Fort Keogh to Bismarck. The distance is 300 miles and he made it in just thirty-two hours. John's father was French and his mother an Indian. Johnny himself is married to the prettiest squaw in Sitting Bull's tribe.
The American lacrosse team has so far whitewashed its opponents in England.
John England, of England, is the latest arrival who expects to do up our aesthetic John.

A party of Yankton Indians is in camp on the south side of the track. We did not look at the teeth of the patriarch but should judge that he was about four hundred and steen years old, perhaps four hundred and umpty. Conversation was voluble on the Yankton side of the house, between bites at a bone which had seen its palmiest days long before even the pigs had given it up at the slaughter-house. The old man isn't bigger than a minute and he is weighted down with a log chain to keep the wind from blowing him away.

Word has come from Belfield that in addition to the horses already stolen there, two horses and six mules were stolen last Friday evening. The grass raising in the morning, completely hid the trail and it was impossible to tell even in what direction the thieves went. Telegrams were sent in every direction, but no word has been received as yet in reference to any of the stolen stock. The loss falls heavily on some of the citizens of Belfield and it is to be hoped that the stock will be recovered and the thieves summarily punished.

W. M. Farrow, who was with the victorious American team, when they defeated the Irish team at Dollymount in 1880, and who is one of the best, if not the best off-hand rifle shot in the world, gave an exhibition of his skill at 200 yards, in Little Missouri last Sunday afternoon. He used a new Bullard repeating rifle, 40-75. The target was an 8-inch bull's-eye, with circles two inches apart, the count in the bull's-eye being 11, and 12 for the centre.

TO ALL WHOM IT MAY CONCERN: Be it known that on and after this 24th day of May, 1884, the partnership heretofore existing between Chas. Shaffer and John Munroe, under the firm name of Shaffer & Munroe, Plum Grove ranch, on the Little Missouri river, is dissolved by mutual consent.
