The law recently passed increasing the membership of Dakota's Council to twenty-four; and the House of Representatives to forty-eight, is meeting the universal favor of press and people. It had become a matter of necessity, owing to our largely increased population.

Stockmen of Montana, not satisfied with their attempt at trying to keep out all outsiders by the report that the ranges are full, are now buying land of the government and railroad company. They are beginning to realize the fact that their dog-in-the-manger style will not work.

All things considered, it would have been hard for the Republicans to have bettered the ticket. Blaine and Logan will undoubtedly be elected. There is a strong feeling, especially among business men, that the country would be more prosperous under Arthur, but there are few Republicans who will not enter into the campaign with a vim. Blaine will scarcely attempt as President, what he came nearly making a failure of as secretary of State.—his Peruvian scheme.

The mind of the stockman is happy. To say that cattle are looking well does not express it. It is well-known that cattle are by no means at their best during this season but one would think from their looks that they are all stall-fed cattle. The per cent. of calves is smaller than was expected, it not reaching much over 75 per cent. in the most favorable cases. This is made up for in the splendid condition of the cattle and the small per cent. of loss. The latter in no case has reached 3 per cent. and oftener has gone way below that.

A constant source of wonderment is the vast drain of cattle from Minnesota and Iowa to Dakota and Montana and that the supply seems practically inexhaustible. A low estimate would be 50,000 one's and two's that have been shipped to this country from the above mentioned states this season. This movement of stock means far more to our future cattle trade than an outsider would suppose. A grade animal is worth $10 to $20 more as a four-year-old than is native or Texan stock. Almost every one of the Minnesota and Iowa cattle are graded. To be sure some of them are low grade, but blood will tell and tell strongly when the cattle are sold. Our cattlemen have also awaked to the advantage of using full-blood bulls and they are being universally used in the Bad Lands. This will increase the value of the herds very materially and raise the standard of our cattle even above its present high plane.

An article in the Pioneer-Press again calls to mind a subject of which we have before written and which can only be remedied by a united action among the different cattle associations. It is in reference to persons selling diseased stock to avoid a total loss or keeping it until it dies, although it may communicate the disease to fifty others before death. We again wish to call attention to the system practiced in Germany, by which every diseased animal is taken before an inspector and killed if pronounced incurable. The owner in this case receives about two-thirds the value of the animal, while a severe fine is visited upon him in case he conceals the fact of the disease. This plan has worked very satisfactorily and has been found to be the only way by which disease can be eradicated. In conjunction with other stock organizations, this should be one of the first matters toward which to turn our attention. Its manifest feasibility should commend itself especially to stock-raising states and territories and a combined effort of the several associations could get laws passed which would prevent the spread of any disease. The expenses would be light, almost nothing in comparison to the loss should an epidemic start among our cattle. Each district could have an inspector, working in conjunction with an association, who could pronounce on every case of sickness. We hope this matter will be agitated by cattle papers until definite action is taken upon it by the associations and through them, by the different legislatures.

Now that the question of opening the Sioux reservation has been set at rest, for a year at least, there will be no delay in pushing the Medora & Black Hills R. R. to completion. Even were the reservation opened it is extremely probable that no move would be made by the North-Western toward building into the Hills, on account of the expense of crossing the Missouri. The bridge would cost as much or more than did the N. P. bridge, which would be nearly half what the completed road would cost from Medora to the Hills terminus. Already orders have been given for the survey of the road and we are assured by the Marquis de Mores that the stage route, which will be in full operation inside of three weeks is a mere preliminary to the railroad. These matters all take considerable time, but "let patience have her perfect work" and we will soon see the realization of all the present plans toward developing this country. There is an abundance of capital back of all these plans but outside capitalists see their certainty of success and are joining forces with the present company.

At the New York horse show Cyrus W. Field received the first prize for matched pair. Fred. Gebhard's Leo received the first prize for hunters' mare or gelding, also the special prize.—[Black Hills Pioneer.

The grass-feeding animals of Colorado to-day are worth in dollars fifty millions. This will be increased ten millions, at least, the present year, by the calf, colt and lamb crop, and by the importation of animals from other States.—[Live-Stock Record.

The contract for furnishing cattle to the Indians at Standing Rock will probably be awarded to J. B. Martin, of Prairie du Chien, who bid $27. This is a doubtful experiment on the part of the government and will doubtless result in the cattle all being killed during the coming winter.

Cattle are now accumulating flesh so rapidly that the process of growing is fairly visible to the eye. In a short time there will be an abundance of beeves. The survivors of the past winter's hardships have forgotten their sufferings, and are now contented, happy and growing fat speedily.—[Kansas Cowboy.

There is a scheme on foot in Denver to hold a great live stock fair there next year in connection with the mineral, manufacturing and agricultural exposition. If such an exhibition is held, Denver is essentially the point for it, as being nearer the center of the great stock section of the country than any city that could make such an exhibition practicable. It should receive the encouragement of the stock growers of the west and the support of the business men of Denver.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

Tom Sun, of Rawlins, Wyo., with his family, was in the city the past week. He says the Sweetwater, on which his range is located near Devil's Gate, is higher than known for eleven years. The grass on the range is thicker and better than ever known, and the calf crop simply surprising. The extra number of bulls that have been placed upon the range are accountable for the gratifying increase, and have demonstrated the wisdom of the rule requiring each stockmen to fully provide himself with male beasts.—[Cheyenne Live-Stock Journal.

Colts should be halter-broken while following their dams; they never forget it. Once broken always broken. Youngsters may be weaned from their dams at six months old. They should be fed with oats and wheat bran when taken from their mother's milk; it will keep them growing through the first winter, which is essential to early maturity. The good start lays the foundation, in bone and substance, for a good horse. Any check to the growth of the young scion the first winter will seldom be recovered in after years. A colt neglected the first winter never recovers its proper shape, nor does it grow the size and strength of body and limbs which naturally appertain to his breed.—[Kansas L. S. Indicator.

Never, in the history of the live-stock business of Texas, has there been such buying and selling and interchange of stock as there has been for the past month, and likely to continue for at least two weeks to come. It would seem as though every large ranchman and every heavy buyer in the region west of the Mississippi had gone there to buy or to make contracts for the future. The trail is full of moving herds, and for weeks past every railroad in the State has been having a rush. Rolling stock is at a premium, and on some of the roads cars could not be had under any circumstances. It is not that cars are limited in number, but that large lots of cattle are being shipped. The trade in horses has been unusually large also. About twenty car-loads have been shipped to the vicinity of Wichita Falls, Kan., and some east. Most of the cattle go north and west.—[Arizona Live-Stock Journal.

A ranchman named Wilson, of Colorado, now said to be worth some $2,000,000 to $3,000,000, some twenty-five or thirty years ago made the trip to Pike's peak with a team or two of oxen, and which hauled himself and family and all their possessions. A short time since this adventurous settler, through a lawyer in this city, sold one of his ranches to an English company for between $400,000 and $500,000. It was a curious circumstance that first directed Mr. Wilson's attention to the capabilities of Colorado as a stock-raising state. On his way to the peak a yoke of his oxen gave out. He therefore turned them loose, as he thought, to die. A year or so afterward he was passing through the same tract of country, when he came upon his oxen, looking in splendid condition. He at once made up his mind if oxen could stand such a winter as that which this yoke had just weathered in such prime condition that stock-raising would be a profitable business in Colorado. He immediately went into the business, with the result that now "cattle upon a thousanp hills" are his, besides several ranches and a mansion in the city of Denver.—[Chicago News.

Each recurring year Texas more nearly approaches the condition of being the nursery and breeding grounds, from which reservoir the western states and territories draw their main supply of young steers. As to this state being the most prolific breeding section, all agree, while many of our successful cattlemen hold that farther north young steers develop into larger beeves than in this latitude. The cry is often heard, "Texas ranches for cows and calves—the western territories for young steers." Well, we can for an indefinite time supply young steers, and stock cattle too, for less favored breeding grounds. With England opposing the reception of store cattle and Kansas and New Mexico hostile to the reception of Texas cattle, from fear of disease, Texans can still raise and fatten beeves for St. Louis and Chicago markets and for the dead meat markets, both foreign and at home.—[Texas L. S. Indicator.

One of the most niggardly practices of western ranchmen is the failure to provide enough bulls. Each ranchman usually contends that he has bulls enough for his own cows, but that his neighbors are derelict, and that he does not propose to buy extra bulls for his neighbor's herd. There are a good many men mean enough to allow their cows to be served by the bulls belonging to others; not realizing that they are pursuing a very short-sighted policy; not only robbing their neighbor of actual value, but curtailing their own profits by having more cows than bulls to serve them. A bull gets about twenty to twenty-five calves a year with perfect ease. Figure what a calf is worth to you, and multiply it by twenty-five. The calculation will convince any man that he can get three to five improved bulls for the sum he loses in one year by having one bull less than he should.—[Drovers' Journal.

The Calgary Herald is informed by farmers south of there that the Indians are playing sad havoc among the calves. One gentleman says that out of seventy of last year's calves he has only seven left, and that a neighbor who last year had one hundred cattle can only count twenty-five. The other day a butcher, noticing that two cows had calves, and that two Sarcees were eyeing them, went over to the farmer's boy, telling him what he saw, and that he had better go at once and tell his father, who immediately sent him after the calves; and although twenty minutes had not elapsed since the butcher left them, yet when the boy got there one calf was gone and the Indians nowhere to be seen. These depredations are carried on chiefly by the young bucks, who go in parties of five and six. They will not divulge anything, and think that it is only the one who killed the animal who is amenable to the law, and that by going in parties he cannot be so easily caught.

Some of our ranchmen have struck a chord which could have been sounded long since to their great advantage and independence. It is simply the spaying of heifers and old cows. It is just as easy to send off to market a full-grown, fat animal, which will bring more than a steer, as to sell as surplus of the range a sorry yearling to some other fellow who makes all the profit of the growth. And it is just as easy to have an old cow go fat to market as to die poor on the prairie or in the bog. To some extent this expedient was resorted to last year on those ranges whose prolific stock had outgrown the pounds, and with results entirely satisfactory. One of our Panhandle ranches last year spayed 2,000 heifers, and this year the little experiment will be followed by the same ranch as well as others. On those ranges where the selling mania of recent times has caused an enhancement in value of heifers this may be regarded as clear waste, but to those with prospective overstock it is a means of saving grace and profit most apparent.—[Mobeetie (Tex.) Panhandle.

While in North Platte, recently, the editor of the News had a pleasant interview with Messrs. John Bratt & Co., one of the largest and oldest cattle firms in western Nebraska, whose cattle find their range not only in that State, but in Wyoming and eastern Colorado. Mr. Bratt said that for years his firm had practiced putting up all the hay they could. During the last winter and spring they fed 3,125 tons of hay, and some corn; this was to bulls, cows and calves, and although the past season was unusually severe Mr. Bratt estimates the losses of his firm at not more than two per cent. "The stock business," remarked that gentleman, as he signed an order for twenty new branding irons, "has been reduced to an exact system, and as careful judgment should be exercised as that called into use in Wall street, New York. Although most of the big stockmen think it impossible, and like child's play, to feed their range stock, we consider that every ton of hay we feed will bring us back $50, and yet our range is unexcelled. We shall feed all our bulls next winter, and some of our cows and calves." Speaking of the shipments of cattle from Texas by D. Rankin & Company to Brady Island, fifty miles northwest of North Platte, Mr. Bratt said, "I consider that this stock will be worth twenty-five per cent more coming through from Texas in this way, in a few days, than if they were on the trail all summer. Being shipped in the spring, they have all the summer in which to eat, grow fat, and become acclimated." Mr. Bratt expressed himself as not at all afraid of Texas fever.—[Sterling (Col.) News.

Bob. Roberts is in Miles City on business.
Andy Corcoran, section boss at Allard, spent Sunday in town.
The Marquis will return for the summer with his wife, in a few days.
F. B. Allen, attorney for the company, returned to Bismarck this morning.
J. Juelfs is loading his bull teams and will "gee, haw" to-day or to-morrow.
C. L. Brinker's father is dangerously ill and he expects to leave soon to attend him.
John Bruguier and the two families of Yankton Indians left last Saturday for Standing Rock.
One of Dorr Clark's bulls was injured severely while on the way here and died soon after its arrival.
Train-loads of cattle are passing through nearly every day, of from twenty to twenty-five cars.
Messrs. McKenzie and O'Brien have been overrun with work since the removal of the blacksmith shop.
Tom Matthews came up Friday to see the round-up and returned to Mandan Monday, after a trip to Glendive.
Jack Bullion came in Sunday night with about thirty horses, the most of which were for use on the round-up.
Five or six car-loads of freight came in yesterday. This is the dullest season of the year for freight, but it will soon pick up.
Howard Eaton has gone east after another lot of cattle for the Badger Cattle company. He is expected home in a few days.
The pillow-slip dance to be given by the young ladies at the Pyramid park hotel to-night, seems destined to be a gigantic success.
A number of fat cattle have been gathered by the round-up and sent in for slaughtering. Those killed so far are the company's cattle.
While Dorr Clark was here, he partly completed arrangements for the sale of a large number of cattle to the company. He has about 10,000 for sale.
"Arkansas John" loaded and pulled for Deadwood Tuesday. Next to Ford's, his is the best outfit that has been here, having a capacity of about 90,000 pounds.
M. L. Holley, of Minnesota, partner in the cattle firm of H. B. Wadsworth & Co., has been visiting the ranch for several days. He returned home Tuesday morning.
W. T. Kennedy and wife will soon start for New York on a visit. Mrs. Kennedy will stay until fall. Mr. Kennedy's business will be left in charge of John Crosby.
The first load of coal from the new mine in the butte east of town, was delivered Monday. It is the best vein yet opened and will supply Medora for generations to come.
A. von Steiger went to St. Paul Tuesday night to complete arrangements for a stock cattle company that he is organizing. It will be run principally with foreign capital.
Gregor Lang has just received another large lot of cattle. They were all branded with his new and ingenious "triangle JP brand, which appears for the first time in this issue of the Cow Boy.
Mr. Roosevelt, the young New York reformer, who has done more toward exposing the corruptness of New York politics than any other man, is visiting his ranch here, managed by Ferris & Merrifield.

Tom Hardwicke, of the Rocky Mountain show now in Minneapolis, is in town buying horses for his outfit. He reports the gospel firm, Moody & Sankey, as doing a great work among the Minneapolitan tenderfeet.

All the stock horses of the company except the three stallions have been sold to A. C. Huidekoper and H. R. Tarbell. Mr. Tarbell will be manager and has already adopted a new brand that will appear in our next issue.

Persons requiring any papers drawn up, such as acknowledgements, deeds, bills of sale, relinquishments, affidavits, depositions, contracts, protests or any other legal instrument, can be accommodated at the Cow Boy office.

Rev. Wm. Cooke, of Gladstone, made us a pleasant call Monday morning. He is one of the pioneer ministers of western Dakota and knows how to reach his audience. He preaches every Sunday evening at the Cantonment.

It is doubtful if the county will be organized and in running order before July 1st. Mr. Hay, one of the commissioners, has been called east and will be there until about that date. For other reasons also, it has been deemed advisable to put off the organization.

The round-up passed through here last Friday morning and a jollier set of boys we never expect to meet. Their work has been done thoroughly and everything moves with the precision of clock-work. The round-up promises to be satisfactory in all respects.

There are a few chronic kickers here who need to be sat on. A good illustration is the report circulated so freely that we had lost the freight route when at that very time more freight was on the way for our route than at any time before. Another example is the rumor that licenses are to be $400, when the third commissioner has not yet been appointed. These croakers should be spotted and their statements taken for what they are worth.

Experiments with alfalfa will be made in the Marquis' garden, some seed having arrived. Its value for feeding stock and wonderful growing properties will make its cultivation extensive provided the experiments are as successful as there is every reason to suppose they will be.

Dorr Clark started for his ranch last Monday. Saturday, the Short-horn bulls spoken of in our last issue, arrived, and they were as fine looking a lot as we have ever seen. Mr. Clark, before leaving, left the VVV and E6 brands with us for publication and they will appear in our next issue.

The pile-driver left here without orders last Thursday afternoon and ran into the work train at Sully Springs as a result. Several cars were smashed and the engine on the pile-driver was badly wrecked. There was luckily no loss of life but Mr. Gilbert's dining cars were, "considerably shuck up like."

M. Kline, of Mandan, left Monday for home, after a three day's business and pleasure trip here. The boys let him off easy and mounted him on a bronco that only ran away with him four times. He seemed to enjoy the round-up, but his prediction that " the tender-foot will be sore to-morrow," was vividly fulfilled.

We have received a note from Dr. E. E. Ball, of Mandan, stating that on account of sickness it will be impossible for him to keep his engagement here until the last of the month. As Dr. Ball is an excellent dentist, it will be well for those suffering from poor teeth to keep an eye on his dates, which will be published in time.

A serious mistake was made by the N. P. coal Co. in removing the supports from their mine here. The roof is caving in, in many places and repair work will cost more than the original expense of propping. Mr. Thompson asserts that the mine is the best on the road and in view of this fact, the removal of the props was very short-sighted.

John Hager, of Mandan, was in town Saturday. He has concluded to go into the stage line in connection with the Marquis and others. We are pleased to note this fact, as Mr. Hager is exactly the kind of a worker we need here. He has done as much, if not more than any other one man to build up Mandan, and his experience will be a valuable addition to Medora.

The man referred to in our round-up letter as having had "strawberry shortcake in his," made a special trip to town to stop his subscription. As his three months grace was just up, we would have saved him the trouble after the last issue. He is said to "have it in" for the man who wrote the article but if he will take our advice, he will leave him severely alone and pray for a cyclone to strike him instead. We hold ourselves personally responsible for every word that appears in the COW BOY and any complaint will receive proper attention.

Medora Route Impracticable.

A. J. Maxwell, of the Miles City & Spearfish stage line, informed a Journal reporter that he had a dispatch stating that the proposed stage line between Medora, on the Little Missouri, and Deadwood has been given up, and that an order has been issued to pull off the freighting teams. He also hears that much of the freight is now going to Pierre, and it looks as though the Northwestern railroad has made special rates to get the traffic. Mr. Maxwell stated that the route from Deadwood to Medora is a very hard one, there being thirty miles of very bad lands in one stretch and twenty-five in another, and most of these stretches is full of gumbo, through which hauling is very difficult. A very little rain makes the ground so sticky that it soon clogs the wheels of the wagons.—[Yellowstone Journal.

The above would require no answer, provided all the readers of the article were acquainted with the facts. It has been copied several times, however, and we look for a correction in each case.

The stage line between Medora and Deadwood has not been given up by any means. Those thinking it has, can come here and "go broke" a little easier than in any way we know. The stage company has been fully organized and stages will be run in less than two weeks. It will be started as a tri-weekly and increased to a daily as soon as the rail-road is begun.

That freight is going in by the way of Pierre we do not and have not denied. But will the persons who have been so anxious to defame our route, please answer the following question: "Why is it that all but one or two of the fifty outfits that have loaded here, have come from the Pierre route, where they had constant employment hitherto?" It is a matter of no question that more freight is shipped from here than from Pierre.

The article also states that our route is a very hard one and that there are fifty-five miles of Bad Lands. We would like to know whose word should be taken in this case if it is not that of the freighters themselves. Their testimony is unanimous that it is the best road over which they have ever travelled. We care not what freighter's word is taken, provided he is unprejudiced. Again there are but fifteen miles of Bad Lands on the road and if a man could go over this distance, seeing the road only and having the surrounding country shut out from view, he would never know that he was not on the prairie. The route in the Bad Lands is as level and hard as any well-travelled road.

The article further says that these stretches "is" full of gumbo and a very little rain "makes the ground so sticky that it soon clogs the wheels of the wagons." This is a lie, pure and simple and without a mitigating circumstance. All kinds of weather have been experienced since the route was started. We have personally inquired of nearly every outfit that has come in and the invariable answer has been that there was almost no gumbo and that would not delay freighting a minute except for a little while during the spring thaw and then only for a short distance at the Deadwood end of the route. Bob. Roberts started with the first train that ever went over the route, his and Jos. Pennell's, with not even a bridle path to guide him. He started immediately after a week's steady rain and snow and did not even drop a trail wagon on the whole trip. In spite of all these drawbacks, he made the round trip in shorter time than was ever made from Pierre or any other point into the Hills and return. The weather just previous to this trip was the worst of the season and the time made is a sufficient answer as to the "impracticability" of our route.

And now, whence do all these charges emanate? From one Maxwell who is running a one-horse, buck-board, stage-line(?) from Miles City to Deadwood. Of course from such a source the Medora route is worthless. With the beginning of our route Maxwell will have no farther use for his team or two of cayuses, and his buckboards can be chopped up for kindling wood.

In another article, Maxwell states that he will not come to Medora. Of course he won't, but he forgot to mention the reason. It is that he knows as soon as he shows his nose here, he will be arrested for the larceny of a bateau, stolen from Bly & Co. Considering all the circumstances, it would be as well for Mr. Maxwell to put a bridle on his tongue or be sure he is telling the truth when he turns it loose.

A perusal of the statutes calls to light an enactment that is of special interest though comparatively unknown to the farming class of our citizens. It appears that a person planting trees, cuttings or seeds not to exceed twelve feet apart each way on five acres, is exempted from taxes on forty acres of land and improvements not to exceed $1,000, for ten years. The fact of this law should be widely published, as it will do more than anything else to encourage tree planting in Dakota, especially on homesteads.

The question of representation by the Bad Lands, at the New Orleans exposition, is a subject that should call for immediate action among our citizens. The exposition, in all likelihood, will far outshine that of the Centennial and it is a matter of the greatest importance that our products and natural curiosities should occupy a prominent place. The exposition begins the fifteenth of December and lasts until the fifteenth of May.

The per centage of high grade cattle in Kansas is 21, the per cent. for the United States is 18.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
Howard Eaton and Lloyd Roberts came in this morning with a thousand head of cattle for the Badger cattle company.

A cow horn measuring four feet eleven inches in length and eighteen inches around the base is on exhibition at Monticello, Florida, and is supposed to be the largest cow horn in the world.—[N. W. L. S. Indicator.

The colt crop of Colorado will this year number a hundred thousand. Those of thoroughbred will not number a thousand. The large number of this new crop will be of the native variety, and will develop saddle horses on the range.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

Said Mr. Stevens, of Trinidad: "The sheep owners have been getting an unreasonable price for their wool for several years past. From twelve to fifteen cents is a good price for the average quality of the wool produced in Colorado. When the sheep owners were getting eighteen to twenty-two cents per pound, men became so greedy that they sheared their flocks twice a year and then so lazy they left them to freeze and starve through the winter. Prosperity and extortionate prices have spoiled many good men in this country."

At a fair calculation the stock-growers of Colorado have invested in bulls yearly, if not quite, $2,000,000. Nine-tenths of all these animals are grades. This is a very expensive necessity to the stock-grower, since the throughbred animals cost him all the way from $200 to $600 each, and the high-grades about $125, and the low grades, those with but a quarter or an eighth of royal blood, about $60 or $75 each. Now, if all the bulls of the State have cost, on an average, $100 each, then the valuation of these brutes will fall not much short of $2,000,000. The cattle-growers will ship about 100,000 head of beeves the present year, and they will have imported in the cycle of the same 5,000 or 10,000 head of high-priced bulls and at least 200,000 stock cattle.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

Each recurring year Texas more nearly approaches the condition of being the nursery and breeding grounds, from which reservoir the western states and territories draw their main supply of young steers. As to this state being the most prolific breeding section, all agree, while many of our successful cattlemen hold that farther north young steers develop into larger beeves than in this latitude. The cry is often heard, "Texas ranches for cows and calves; the western territories for young steers." Well, we can for an indefinite time supply young steers, and stock cattle, too, for less favored breeding grounds. With England opposing the reception of store cattle and Kansas and New Mexico hostile to Texas cattle, from fear of disease, Texans can still raise and fatten beeves profitable for St. Louis and Chicago markets, and for the dead meat markets, both foreign and at home.—[L. S. Journal.

A very short time ago there was a bad outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia near Pittsburg, according to sensational reports that were flung broadcast over the length and breadth of the land, but as soon as proper examination was made it was found that there was no pleuro-pneumonia in the case. Next we had a bad story about foot-and-mouth disease having broken out among the cattle away up in Montana, but it now turns out that there was nothing worse than frozen feet in this case. Not a great while ago a bull calf was found to be suffering with pleuro-pneumonia in Baltimore, and he was clandestinely shipped to Chicago or some other point in the West, and neither this calf nor the two scotchmen that started the foot-and-mouth disease in Kansas in the early spring have as yet been run down and corralled. The talk about pleuro-pneumonia in New York just now is no doubt a certain kind of filthy stable disease that has been common in and around New York for the past forty years and will be the next forty.—[Drover's Journal.

Mr. [Freuen?] thinks that 60,000 head of cattle from Colorado, Wyoming and the northwest will this year take the northern route; travel through Canada from Duluth, down the St. Lawrence, landing as feeders in England, Ireland and Scotland.—[N. W. L. S. Indicator.

The excitement over the drive is increasing. It is said that Seth Mabry will bet that 650,000 cattle will cross Red river, and there is a man in San Antonio who will put up all he has that 800,000 will leave Texas between February and August.—[Texas Live Stock Indicator.

The live stock interests of the northwest received a wounderful impetus this spring. From many of our exchanges throughout this state and Dakota we note that good blooded stock is being purchased from reliable breeders and importers, and the improvements in grades will be the means of increasing the value of our stock to a very large extent.—[Minnesota Farmer.

Continual improvement in a herd should be the center pillar in the stockmen's temple, and the one upon which all transactions should be based. The secret; it should be no secret; of success is in paying special attention to the steps that will bring about results that will be most durable. Do not be governed by advice that will profit for a little while and finally bring about disaster and ruin to the herd, but unite good, sound judgment with a few good high grade or thoroughbred bulls, and the greatest proof of success will be success.—[Arizona Live Stock Journal.

Cattle raising and agriculture as practiced in the west have about as much affinity for each other as oil and water. It is impossible to have them exist together here in anything like amicable relations, owing to the almost total lack of fences. At present, the herd law in Dakota is oppressive to the cattlemen, although but one or two direct conflicts of interests have as yet arisen. The absence of the herd law would be as oppressive to the farmer. A simple and in fact the only remedy we know, is to set off the western tier of counties or so much of them as is only fit for cattle, as a cattle country and therefore exempt from the herd law. The Bad Lands is not an agricultural country and never will be. It is, however, one of the best cattle countries in the world. Where then, is the justice in having a strictly agricultural law applied to a strictly cattle country. Unless the above plan is adopted, the time is surely coming when serious trouble will arise between the agricultural and cattle interests and the sooner the matter is settled, the better for all concerned. As soon as our cattle organization is effected, this is one of the first and most important matters for it to consider.

Europe is at the present day consuming a very much larger amount of animal food than in former times, while its own means of supplying its population is being considerably diminished. For although the live stock of Europe has in the last twenty years, without doubt, been considerable increased, nevertheless it has been utterly impossible to keep pace with the advance of population and the increasing requirements of the people. The collective amount of horned cattle throughout Europe is estimated at 92,000,000 head, of horses about 36,000,000, of sheep about 200,000,000, and of swine about 46,000,000. While these figures show a decided advance over those of twenty years ago, it must be remembered that the question of European supply does not rest so much upon the amount of live stock as the increase of population and the steadily increasing demand from all classes of the communities.

It appears that Europe's relative strength of live stock, with the exception of swine, has fallen off considerable; that is to say, population has advanced more rapidly than live stock, causing a larger demand to be made on other parts of the world. From this report it appears that the Scandinavian countries and Servia stand in a more favorable position as regards live stock than other parts of Europe. Thus Denmark, ranking first, has 735 head of cattle to 1,000 inhabitants, Servia 609 head, Norway 562 and Sweden 483 head.

As to absolute number of live stock in different countries, Russia stands first as regards all classes of animals, having of cattle, including Poland and Finland, in 1876, no less than 25,000,000 head, 45,000,000 sheep, 10,000,000 swine and 17,000,000 horses. The increase in the last twenty years has been about twenty per cent. in sheep, in cattle and swine only about four per cent, while horses have been stationary. Next comes Germany with 15,000,000 of cattle, sheep 25,000,000, swine 7,000,000, and horses 3,000,000.

Austria, Hungary, France, Great Britain, Holland, Norway and Sweden, follow in the order named with 38,000,000 cattle, 30,500,000 swine, 11,500,000 horses and [61?],000,000 sheep between them.

The object of this valuable report, as the intelligent reader has doubtless observed from these condensed items, is to show the favorable outlook of the future of the live stock industry of our own country, so far as prosperity may be dependent upon foreign demand for animal produce. It shows that, as compared with the increase of population, there has been, in Europe, a decrease in the amount of live stock.—[Henry B. Ryder.

About 165,000 pounds of freight have been shipped from Medora to the Hills so far this week.
Work is progressing fast on the new side-track and inside of a fortnight the steel will be laid.
John O'Sullivan is building a barber shop on his lot next to John Warn's temperance tabernacle.
M. M. Coleman and C. F. Brown have bought a lot and intend erecting a building for a boarding house.
The only and original General P. D. Q. Sheridan will hereafter attend to the cuisine of the Hotel de Mores.
Whitehead's, Thorn's, Gaar's, Dexter's, and Magre's, outfits all loaded this week with time freight and pulled out for the Hills.
The coal in the butte east of town has developed an unexpected superiority and the quantity is sufficient to last for ages.
Rassie Deffebach returned last night from Mattock's ranch, having accompanied Clark's herd of bulls that far on the road.
Ferris & Merrifield have gone to Iowa to purchase a thousand more cattle for their ranch. They expect to return in a month or six weeks.
Thorn's outfit arrived last Saturday at ten in the morning and before three in the afternoon was loaded and pulling back for the Hills.
As we set these lines, No. 2 is pulling in, over sixteen hours late. The cause of the delay was the washing away of the bridge at Gallatin.
Tom Matthews is kept busy in his new position of stock inspector at Mandan. We notice by the papers that he has been testing the tender-footedness of some of the editors.
Graham's mule outfit arrived yesterday morning. Mr. Graham was one of the first to pull over our route and pronounces the cut-off road the best he ever freighted over.
An application for the granting of a charter for the establishment of a Masonic lodge has been forwarded to the proper official and it is thought that the request will be granted.
A number of improvements have taken place at the slaughter house. A large quantity of stone has arrived and a new foundation for the cold-storage end will be built immediately.
The pillow-slip dance given by the young ladies at the Pyramid Park hotel last Friday night was all that was expected. It was a jolly crowd, intent on having a jolly time and they had it.
The freighters who started off to pick up buffalo bones have not had the success they expected. The most of them will make but one load of bones and then return to freighting.
Mrs. T. G. Jones and son George, arrived last night from Billings. They will start on for Spearfish to-morrow or next day. Mrs. Jones will probably invest in several valuable lots before leaving.

Some of these times the railroad company will get itself into trouble by running trains out ahead of time. Every train carrying passengers is obliged by law to wait at each station until the advertised time for leaving.

Peter Book is now making pressed brick and they are as much of a success as the common brick. They are and are claimed to be the best brick made in Dakota and Mr. Book is anxious for competition both as to quality and price.

Some despicable spotter, in order to hold his job, trumped up charges against conductors Clark and Hutton and as a consequence they are laid off. It will be a long while before the road gets two better or more popular conductors.

E. I. Goodkind, of the Bismarck firm of Wise & Goodkind was in town Monday and Tuesday. The firm's advertisement, appearing in this issue of the Cow Boy, shows the liberal spirit that has built them up such a large and profitable trade.

Mr. Rosevelt is still at Ferris & Merrifield's ranch, hunting and playing cowboy. It seems to be more congenial work than reforming New York state politics. He is thoroughly impressed with the profit of raising cattle in the Bad Lands, as his vigorous backing of Ferris Bros. & Merrifield testifies.

A letter from Star & Bullock makes known the fact that the shipping of a consignment of their goods by the way of Pierre, was a straight steal on the part of the North-Western. The whole consignment was billed via Medora, and was switched off to Pierre. There is a great consolation in the fact that the North-Western company did not haul a pound of the freight from Pierre and may in the end have to pay the charges themselves.

W. M. Brewer, late editor of the Minnesela Boomer, came in last Saturday from Deadwood. Mr. Brewer has had a large experience both at freighting and staging and pronounces this route to be altogether the best one running into the Hills. We are pleased to state that Mr. Brewer intends settling in Medora and going into business.

The work on the new billiard hall and theatre building is about completed, the hard-finish coat being the only thing to finish. The house-warming and opening dance will probably be put off until the glorious fourth. Some of the furniture has already arrived and Pennell & Roberts intend sparing no expense in fitting up the building.

The N. P. time table will soon be changed so as to make the trips between St. Paul and Portland and return in six hours faster time. This will make No. 1's time about four in the afternoon and No. 2's about five in the morning. The trains now run just right for free rides across the river but the boys will have to count ties after the change.

Lieutenant Varnum has completed the official survey of a route from Dickinson to Fort Meade and is now working on the survey of the Belfield route. As soon as this is finished he will come to Medora and survey the route from here. Owing to the shortness of our line and the many improvements made upon it, it is not hard to prophecy which route will be finally chosen.

L. H. Palmer, of Deadwood, arrived yesterday. He is an energetic business man, owning considerable property in Deadwood. He has the utmost faith in the future of Medora, and it gives us pleasure to note the fact that he intends settling here and putting up business houses for rent. He says that the freight route is all and more than has been claimed for it, it being the best he has ever seen.

A glance at our cattle-cut columns will prove that the cattlemen appreciate the value of advertising as well as other business men. At no distant date we expect to publish every cattle brand in the Bad Lands. Although the change of cuts necessitated a large expense, we are more than repaid by many congratulatory remarks on the improvement, and the substantial way in which cattle and horse men are bringing in their brands for publication. A number of cow-boys have made clippings of the brands, pasting them in small books for handy reference. It is an excellent thing to do and will soon familiarize anyone with the different brands.

To All Whom It May Concern: Be it known that on and after this 24th day of May, 1884, the partnership heretofore existing between Chas. Shaffer and John Munroe, under the firm name of Shaffer & Munroe, Plum Grove ranch, on the Little Missouri river, is dissolved by mutual consent. All indebtedness of the firm to date will be paid by John Munroe.

Born of the active, rustling life of the west, is an unreasoning impatience at delay, the effect of which is almost wholly evil. Some town, for instance, is boomed in the nervous, energetic way peculiar to the west. No account is taken of the resources a town must have to be successful. A set of men make up their minds that there is to be a good town in a certain place and, seeing the prospect they proceed to make one in advance of the order. Buildings out of all reason are hurried up, stores established and soon a town blossoms out, fair to the eye but consisting only of an outer shell,—an appearance. Like the bodies of some microscopic beings, consisting only of a stomach, they are non-producers; only useful to themselves. As soon as the supply of food or suckers ceases they fairly turn themselves inside out in their search for food or complain bitterly that some good Samaritan does not rescue them from the fire which they have kindled about themselves.

There is no use denying or rather attempting to deny the open secret that the above is the history of a large number of Dakota towns. They are years and years ahead of their surrounding country. We can point to fifty towns which must depend entirely on agriculture for existence and have from ten to fifty per cent more invested in the townsite than in tributary farming improvements. This is getting the cart before the horse with a vengeance. It stands to reason that these towns cannot be immediately prosperous. It is as impossible for them to remain stationary and they will surely retrograde until the surrounding country catches up with them.

Then the silly fool who in search of the almighty dollar, have been decoyed into the embrace of the boomer, sits supinely down and curses the country for not growing faster. The time will surely come when all these towns will be prosperous, but it may be "after many years," at least not until the surrounding country is thickly settled. You must first find your goose before you can get one to lay golden eggs. The boomer's plan of finding a counterfeit goose and selling it to the tenderfoot to kill in search of golden eggs is peach and honey to the boomer but yields only withered leaves for the pilgrims share.

The moral of this whole thing is that there are more consumers than producers in these towns and as long as this state of affairs exists, so long will they be worse than dead.

It might seem invidious in this connection to speak of Medora, but as she is emphatically not an agricultural town, it will be proper to mention her by way of contrast. She depends in no way on the uncertainties of a harvest,—the calf crop is as certain as the everlasting hills. Our growth so far has not been equal to the demand and this is the reason why every business interest here is flourishing. Merely as a cattle town our future is assured. The freight line is now doing much and in the future will do more for our advancement. The stage line, which is hanging fire only because the proper man has not been found to place in charge, will be an entering wedge for the railroad, which will make Medora the distributing point for the whole Black Hills and intermediate country. Without railroad, freight or stage lines, Medora can look forward to a constant, steady and successful growth. With them, she will be the best town in Dakota, west of the Missouri.

But even here the voice of the complainer is heard and there is a constant desire to start a boom. What, we would like to know, would be the permanent advantage derived thereby? There is an abundance of capital ready for investment here and our voice always has been and always will be raised against its use in advance of the needs of the place. We are certain of having enough invested to keep pace with the times. Any invested beyond this will be followed by a corresponding reaction. "Rome was not made in a day," nor will the impression go abroad that Medora's future prosperity can be accomplished in any such short time if we can help it.

We never have and never will claim anything for Medora that we do not believe is absolutely and unqualifiedly true. We don't want a boomed town and won't have it as long as "the voice of the Cow Boy reverberates from butte to butte," as a sap-headed contemporary puts it. "Legitimate growth" is our path to prosperity.

Johnny Goodall and J. L. Truscott came in from Beaver creek yesterday morning, at the close of the round-up. It lasted just a month and was a great success, especially considering the fact that it was the first round-up for this district. No dispute or dissatisfaction of any kind arose and everything moved like clockwork. The district rounded up averages one hundred by fifty miles and contains between 30,000 and 40,000 cattle. The cattle are in excellent condition, most of them being ready for slaughter. The calf crop is lighter than was expected, the highest estimate for the district being 75 per cent. and the lowest 55. This is doubtless owing to the fact that bulls have been allowed to range with the herd the year round. Under an association, this evil will be remedied, as it is a prime necessity in this climate to keep the bulls up from November till July at least, longer would be better.

A number of the outfits represented on our round-up will send cowboys to search Cabin, Glendive and Cedar creeks for stray cattle.
At a fair calculation the stock growers of Colorado have invested in bulls nearly, if not quite, two million dollars. Nine-tenths of all these animals are grades.—[Denver L. S. Journal.

Clark & Plum, of the E6 ranch, will sell several thousand head of fat cattle this year. About 10,000 head of Texas cattle are on the drive for them from their Texas ranches. From conversations with Mr. Clark, we judge that a number of steers will be sent into the Bad Lands near here, for fattening.

A hundred thousand fat steers, four years old and upward will be the beef crop of Colorado the coming fall. Five thousand cars will be required to carry them to market. If the railroads will but give the flock owners double decks and a liberal rate a thousand cars of fat muttons will also go forward.—[Denver L. S. Journal.

Western Colorado is filling up with cattle, and what is noticeable about it is that there are none but the best blooded animals going in. In one year from now the western slope will have more of the Shorthorns, the Herefords, the Galloways and the Polled-Angus cattle than will all the plains country east of the mountains.—[Colorado Live Stock Record.

The Maine governor has been officially notified by the commissioners of contagious diseases that the foot and mouth disease which appeared in one or two places in that state last winter, has been entirely stamped ont. The quarantine was relieved May 16th, just three months from the date of the appearance of the disease. It is believed that there is not now in the United States a single case of genuine "foot and mouth disease."—[N. M. Stock Grower.

It is claimed by some who have had experience, that the hay made from wild prairie grass will not give horses the the heaves, says the National Stockmen. A gentleman who has lived in the West for many years says that he never saw horses affected with this disease until after the introduction of tame grass for meadows. Heaves may not be easily cured, but if farmers will wet the hay a very little and shake it well, it will remove the dust and in most cases prevent heaves. This is more important during dry windy weather of spring.—[Kansas L. S. Indicator.

Not one farmer in five who raises colts from mares that he works appears to realize that with the poor treatment given the colts they only do about half as well as they ought or would do if well kept. They are compelled to chase the mare back and forth over the farm or the roads to town for the half-rations of milk she is unable to exceed, owing to overwork and scant feed, and between the great fatigue and scanty nourishment they receive, the colts make a poor and scraggy growth going into winter quarters dilapidated and hidebound, a proper prey for vermin within and without later on.—[Kansas L. S. Indicator.

Now that the spring season for beef is upon our ranchmen, and grass cattle are moving to market, too much stress cannot be laid upon the class of beef to be sent. The grand demoralizer, the jayhawker, that runs down prices, is the half-fatted, long-legged, distended paunched steer, who has had filling enough from sappy grass to swell his stomach, but whose ribs are bare of fat. He is the boss rascal that fools his owner, hurts his shipment and lowers the price, starting from the ranch looking well, he reaches the shipping-pens the worse for wear and market—a scallawag. Cut such back, and leave him a month or two; send none if not well fatted; half ripe cattle ruin the markets, demoralize trade, and hurt the business. Prices already are none too good; thin stuff will bring them lower; but good, fat steers will always sell. Then wait until ripe before you gather your beef plums.—[Texas L. S. Journal.

The Cherokee Strip Live Stock Association and the Barber County Stock Growers' Association have had bills printed containing a warning to southern cattle drovers to keep on the trail and quarantine grounds, and not infringe on the rights of local stockmen. To be forewarned is to be forearmed, and the drover who knowingly and intentionally intrudes on the rights of the man who is holding wintered or domestic stock should, and undoubtedly will, be made to suffer the full penalty of the law, if nothing worse.—[Medicine Lodge (Kan.) Cresset.

A foreigner who went West a year ago with more money than experience, but who is returning a wiser, albeit a poorer man, recently related to a Chicago reporter the story of his ventures in the cattle business. "Why," he said, in talking of a wicked partner he had met in Denver, "he began to bulldoze me from the very time we went into partnership. We started out on the range to count our cattle—we two—and took only a darkey cook with us. The first night we camped he proposed that we decide who should be the boss, and I said all right. He then called a meeting, consisting of himself, the darkey cook and me, to order and nominated me for chairman. I was elected and sat on a saddle. Then he moved that we proceed to the election of a boss for the firm and that the election be by ballot. The motion was carried, and he handed around his hat, putting in a ballot for himself. I started to vote and he stopped me, saying that the chairman couldn't vote unless there was a tie. Well I thought I'd get a chance to vote anyway when the cook but in his ballot, but when Routt handed him the hat the negro said he couldn't write and I was left without any show at all to get even, and he was elected boss. He is still bossing it."—[Las Animas Leader.

Comparing the business of breeding horses on the range with that of cattle raising, a correspondent of the Texas Live-Stock Journal says: "Horses are thriftier than cattle and require less range for their support. Some cattle men deny this, but the current of stockmen's testimony is to this effect, and it is sustained by the books, and by observation as well. The lips and teeth of the horse adapt it for cropping short herbage much better than those of the cow, and a horse can subsist where an ox would starve. Last winter, in riding over the country, I noticed quite a number of dead cattle but never a dead horse. Horses do not scatter and drift as much as cattle, and it is therefore much less trouble to gather and ranch them. In winter, when cattle are drifting south hundreds of miles, unless held in the face of the northers, a well located herd of horses will not ordinarily leave their accustomed range as much as five miles. Horses are not so branchy as cattle; not so troublesome to surrounding farms, or so obnoxious to farmers. Large numbers of cattle can not be satisfactorily kept in a vicinity interspersed with small farms. It would be folly in any one to think now of raising cattle on a large scale in this section unless held in pastures. Then, as ranges become scarcer, and numbers must be diminished, it is easier to keep the same amount of capital invested in the business by improving the breed of horses than cattle."—[National L. S. Journal.

The Mark Lane Express, London, under date of April 28th, says: "In the 'Meat' columns of this journal last week, the opinions of some high authorities in the United States were cited in favor of the dead-meat trade. The New York Tribune declares that 'if dressed meat can be carried from Australia to England successfully, more than 12,000 miles, and across the tropics, it can be carried from Montana and Wyoming to the Eastern markets, or to England.' The Texas Live Stock Journal says: 'During the past year we have contended that true economy and best financial results, to accrue to our cattle interests, can be secured by building up the dead-meat trade to Great Britain.' The American National Live Stock Journal, and other papers, take the same view, while it is generally admitted that the dressed meat trade from the Western to the Eastern States has completely beaten the cattle traffic, in spite of the opposition of those interested in the latter. Mr. P. D. Armour, probably the largest meat man in the world, says: 'It stands to reason that when a steer has not been subjected to a ten days' feverish journey, and bruised and beaten in a cattle train, his flesh is the better for it. This meat ripens in transit. All this fuss against the fresh meat trade comes from these middle men. No consumer in this wide world has ever said aught against it.' Just so; and what is true about a ten days' journey by rail in America, is still more forcible in relation to a ten days' or a fortnight's passage over the Atlantic, in the stifling hold of a ship, and with the great rollers of the ocean tossing and mauling the wretched cattle for days at a stretch."—[National Live Stock Journal.

C. W. Sleeper arrived last Friday evening.
Coleman & Brown's restaurant is being rapidly completed.
S. Smith's outfit, consisting of two twelve's, came in Sunday morning.
One of Baldwin's mules got his foot caught in his lariat and was found dead.
Jos. Ferris is building a large addition to his store and intends to add a line of groceries.
Claude Ralph's outfit arrived Tuesday and loaded Wednesday, starting immediately for the Hills.
Get ready to trip the "light fantastic" in the theatre building, the evening of July 4th. Every one is cordially invited.
Mr. McNutt, a government contractor at Fort Custer was here last week for a few days and returned home Sunday night.
A car load of nails arrived a few days ago for Star & Bullock. It awaits the arrival of their bull outfit from the Hills.
The N. P. side-track is completed except for a little levelling. It is a great convenience in transacting the freight bnsiness.
Baldwin's mule outfit has been loading about six thousand pounds of freight and will get its complement of 50,000 pounds soon.
Mrs. T. G. Jones started Saturday morning for Spearfish, where she will reside for the future. She was accompanied by her father, Mr. Cable.
Jack Simmons is in town direct from Coeur D'Alene. He likes the prospects but says that of all the mines located, only half a dozen are being worked, all the rest being in litigation.

The cattle for the Badger cattle Co. were branded and driven to the home ranch at the mouth of Beaver, Friday and Saturday. Mr. Woodford, one of the company came with the cattle to make final arrangements.

Major W. A. Fonda has made up his mind to let his legal light shine over our citizens. Although we are a very peaceable community, there will be considerable legal work to be done and we prophecy a successful future for the genial Major.

Vick Smith, one of the best of the hunters, trappers and scouts of the west, called on us Monday morning. Settlers are getting altogether too thick here for Vick, and he intends going to Alaska soon, stopping off awhile at Coeur D'Alene.

Dr. A. J. Morton, of Iowa and his father of South Heart, were in town last Friday. Dr. Morton was so pleased with our place that he intends to locate here. He is a graduate of the College of Physicians and Surgeons, at Chicago, and is undoubtedly an able practitioner.

Pat. Smith of Bismarck and John Belding of Deadwood, got off last night to take our stage line to the Hills, having been informed that it was running. As it was, the cayuse-buckboard line from Miles City received two more of the last few passengers it will have. They will return by our line.

And now Max Bass, of Belfield, has been and gone and done it. The happy capturer of Max's heart is Miss Martha Geissel, of New York. Hereafter "Il Penseroso" will be debarred from the repertoire of the musical Max. May peace and prosperity attend the future of the newly-wedded couple.

B. Welf, a well-known merchant of Deadwood, arrived Sunday morning. He has a large stock of millinery, fancy goods, dress goods etc., and intends to start into business as soon as he can make arrangements for the accommodation of his stock. He is just such an enterprising business man as is needed in a new town.

Owing to the confused looks of Dan Friedman, when he was caught trying to smuggle two side-saddles into town in a cattle car under the head of "Household goods and Furniture," we should judge he was going to commit bigamy, were it not for—but what in the world does he want of two side-saddles anyway?

Now that the new billiard hall and theatre building is so near completion, a detailed description would be appropriate. It is located on lot 7, block 17, and creates a very favorable impression from the railroad, standing as it does in full view. The dimensions of the building are 24x75 and 26 feet high. There are two full stories, each being twelve feet clear. The siding is of rough board, paper and drop siding, giving it a handsome external appearance. The floor is double thickness of 3½ inch hard pine. There are three coats of plaster, the outside being a hard finish coat that makes the rooms extremely bright and cheerful. In the first story is the bar room and two club rooms lead off a hall extending to the rear. In the second story is the theatre, consisting of a large hall, a movable stage and two dressing rooms. There is a snug little balcony in front that adds materially to the fine appearance of the building. The total cost of the structure alone will probably over-run $4,500. The furniture will be in keeping with the building and Roberts & Co. are already receiving it. The opening will take place July 4, to which time all are looking forward for an enjoyable time.
The force-pump in the Marquis' garden is working in excellent shape and no more fear of drought troubles the brain of M. Eyraud.
Twenty-five head and over of cattle are being slaughtered daily. A large number are coming in from the round-up and soon work will begin in earnest.
Dr. Morton's card, published in our card column makes known the fact that we are to have a local physician, an advantage fully appreciated here from its lack hitherto.

As may be seen by their card, Messrs. McKenzie & O'Brien have formed a partnership in the blacksmithing business. It would be hard to find two better workmen and we are glad to state that they are rushed with work.
Ira C. Bellows, of Mandan, was in Medora a few days last week. He has large interests in Mandan and is with good cause a firm believer in her future.

A party of Deadwood prospectors is on a trip north of here, looking for signs of gold. They are in search of the mine said to have been discovered by a man who was afterward killed by Indians while guiding a party of friends to the "find." Although the Bad Lands are liable to contain anything in the mineral kingdom, we are not banking very heavily on getting up a stampede from here.

Messrs. Porter and Ralph, Mrs. John Flaherty and Miss Smith arrived Tuesday morning from Deadwood. Mrs. Flaherty and Miss Smith are going to the Coeur D'Alene to meet the former's husband, Mr. Porter is going to the States, while Mr. Ralph will return to Deadwood. The trip was made in six days and the team was never driven off a walk.

Theodore Rosevelt, the young New York reformer, made us a very pleasant call Monday, in full cow-boy regalia. New York will certainly lose him for a time at least, as he is perfectly charmed with our free western life and is now figuring on a trip into the Big Horn country. He is perfectly non-committal on politics and the alleged interview with him, published in the St. Paul Pioneer Press, speaks more for the reporter's assininity than for his perspicacity.

Lloyd Robert's ranch, twelve miles up the river, was the scene last Sunday of as pleasant a gathering as we have attended for a long time. Lloyd's ranch is a revelation to one supposing that the only level ground in the Bad Lands is found on top of the buttes. There are about a thousand acres of sloping ground and about two thousand acres with a very gentle incline toward the river. Mr. Roberts' family entered into the spirit of the occasion and made every one feel perfectly at home. There was nothing to mar the enjoyment of the occasion although the symmetry of the editorial countenance was slightly deranged, owing to a misunderstanding with the cayuse as to which should stop first, he or the rider.

The building of railroads into the western states and territories is rapidly driving the old time bull and mule outfits out of existence and causing at the same time a feeling of dismay in the heart of the true frontiersman, to whom the crack of the bull whips and stentorian tones of the bull-whacker and mule-skinner are music sweet to hear, because the points to and from which freight is hauled are always lively and hard times never known. Many towns on the Missouri, Platte, Smoky Hill and Arkansas rivers have been virtually built and sustained to a great extent by the old time freighters, who are as a class jovial, generous and extravagant to a fault, who spend their earnings with a lavish hand. In the northwest particularly is this fact noticeable, and when we note all that the freight business has done for Cheyenne, Sidney and Pierre, now right at the present time, before it is too late, the importance of doing all in our power to make Medora a permanent starting point for Black Hills freight presents itself. It can only be for a comparatively short time that any of the present starting points for Black Hills freight can reap the harvest from this industry, because in the near future no less than four railroads will be building towards that Eden of America, therefore the present time is the season for extending every effort and using every influence with the railroad company, the shippers and the freighters to have this point designated as the only one on this line to which Black Hills freight can be consigned. We have such natural advantages as cannot be overlooked either by the railroad officials or freighters, the road is undoubtedly the best ever traveled over by freight teams, better time is made loaded or empty than on the Pierre road, the distance is shorter than that route, instead of traveling over nearly 200 miles of gumbo belt this route only crosses the belt a distance of 33 miles. With these advantages in our favor the course to pursue is patent to any man. Let the railroad company, instead of giving special rates to any point and to any man who may ask it, make a contract with one reliable forwarding company and to this one point. This will encourage the shippers in the Hills, because then they will know exactly what course to pursue and where to look for their freight and to whom to look for damages in case of delay or carelessness, and besides such a course will give full satisfaction to the freighters who to day cannot tell whether to come to Medora, Dickinson or Belfield for freight. The Black Hills freight this year will amount in the aggregate to at least 15,000,000 pounds, and during this month, August and September will the large proportion of this amount be shipped, and right now is the time for all concerned to figure. The most of this freight is shipped in carload lots, and consequently the railroad company can afford to give good rates, the freighters hauling for $1.65 a hundred, are working fully as cheap as they can. If the Northern Pacific railroad wants the Black Hills freight it can undoubtedly get more than a fair proportion, but the forwarding company must be protected by contract and thereby be enabled to protect the teamsters, who will then know from whom and where to make sure of a load. Under the present management apparently no one knows when he can get loaded or where he can load from, and this uncertainty will in the end not only work hardship on the freighter but drive him to other routes where he knows such contracts exist between the railroad and forwarding companies as enable the latter to be always able to tell to within a few days of the time of the arrival of freight. We predict that if such steps are not taken the shippers and freighters will get so disgusted that the railroad will lose this freight entirely.

Col. G. A. Pierce, of Chicago, has been appointed governor of Dakota, vice Ordway, whose term has expired. It has been known for some time that the administration was decidedly opposed to the appointment of any Dakota candidate for this position, for the reason that all prominent Dakota men were supposed to be interested on one side or the other of the capital question, and the appointment of any Dakota man would have placed the administration apparently in the position of bolstering up one side or the other in the Dakota controversy. To preserve neutrality Mr. Ordway was suffered to serve his term, and continued until all legal proceedings against him were disposed of, and then one who has not the slightest interest in either faction was appointed as his successor.—[Bismarck Journal.

In making this appointment the president has made a wise choice. From personal knowledge we predict without fear of contradiction that Col. Pierce will make the best governor this territory has ever had.—[Ed.

The parties who control the ranching business in the Yellowstone region give public notice that there is no room for more ranges and that in the future they will not allow any new comers the privileges of the round-up.[—Western Central Kansas Cow Boy.

The above was evidently written by some tenderfoot with an idea that such a report would cause stockmen to refrain from driving into these ranges. It is too ridiculous to even need contradiction, for every cattle man knows that no such action as barring owners from the privileges of the round-up would be to tolerated on any range. As to the statement that the Yellowstone range is crowded, we do not believe it, but, even if such is a fact, the Bad Lands ranges are not, and to-day no better cattle country can be found in the United States than in these ranges, where there is abundance of water, shelter and feed, and of such quality that cattle are in good beef condition all the year round.—[Ed.
