At Jacksonville, Ill., June 6th J. H. Potts & Son sold 23 females and 6 bulls for $9,420, average $325. So Shorthorns still sell well.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

An exchange says that more than 375,000 head of young cattle will be driven out of Texas this season, and although this is the largest output in her history, stockmen claim that there will be left in the state more young stock than ever before held over.—[Western Central Kansas Cow Boy.

There is no need of bothering about a cow's pulse to find out if she is well or not; simple look at her nose. If well, it will be moist and cold; if feverish, dry and hot. She is like a dog in this respect A staring coat or a hollow eye are also points indicating trouble, and as symptoms of diseases they are more to be dreaded than the dry nose.—[Dairyman.

The advertising columns of The Bad Lands Cow Boy presents a very unique appearance to the eastern reader. One page contains the announcement of thirty-one brands, ranges, ear mark and vint, and the headquarters of nearly all these ranges are at Medora, in Billings county. It shows how rapidly Dakota is becoming a stock as well as a wheat country.—[Fargo Argus.

The use of blood as food for cattle has, it is stated, been the subject of experiment in Denmark by a chemist, who, as a result, has now invented and patented a new kind of cake in which blood forms one of the chief ingredients. This new food is stated to be exceedingly nutritious and wholesome, and is eaten with avidity by all sorts of animals, and even by cows and horses which have naturally a strong dislike to the smell of blood.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

A cow belonging to Mr. George Markham, of St. Mary's crossing, on the Huerfano, last week gave birth to two calves which are alive and doing well. This is the second or third pair of twins which this cow has given birth to and raised. Moreover, she is herself a twin, her mother also having raised several pairs of twins. Mr. Markham says the Herefords, Shorthorns or Polled Anguses may be very good cattle, but this breed is good enough for him.—[Heurfano Cactus.

To run the gauntlet of a sojourn among the Texas cowboys; to prove that frequent predictions of broken limbs and a broken neck as the result of too daring horsemanship were ill-founded; and then to break a leg upon the platform of a London railway station on the way from the Derby, is almost a descent from the sublime to the ridiculous. Yet such has been the fate of Lord Aylesford, and his lordship's mishap, for which we are sincerely sorry, might enable an active emigration agent to score one, and point out that Texas, despite its somewhat doubtful reputation, was the safest spot on earth for members of the aristocracy addicted to horse flesh.—[Industrial and Commercial Gazette.

The President having signed the pleuro-pneumonia bill, the commissioner of agriculture is now besieged on all sides by applicants for the positions created by the bill. It is to be hoped that the commissioner will give those appointments his most careful consideration and attention. In its present form we have not much faith in the bill to do what the cattle industry demanded, but we do not want to see any but first-class men appointed to execute its provisions, that all the good there is in it may be brought out. We don't want any political fossils whose chief merit is the ability to run a caucus, but we want live, progressive business men identified with the great cattle interests of the country.—[Kansas City Drovers, News.

The following is the latest story from Benton: A 16-year old cowboy was driving a steer through Benton the other day. It got scared and dashed through the back door of a saloon and out of the front door on a dead run, followed by the daring boy on a pony. As the steer passed through he jumped clear over a table around which were four men engaged in a friendly game of poker, and when the men saw the boy following they dodged under the table, which made the pony's passage easier in leaping over it. Fortunately the doors were open and were wide enough both front and rear to make a good place of entrance and exit for the frightened steer.—[Tranchant.

H. M. Sloan returned yesterday from the Shields river round-up. It is now working about Flathead and will be through in a week. Stock owners are well pleased with what the spring round-up has developed. The loss during the winter has been insingificant, calves are plentiful, cattle are rolling fat and the grass is more luxuriant than last year this time. The Shields river round-up, though it covers a great deal of ground includes only about 10,000 cattle, and these are principally owned by four concerns—Meyer Bros., Gianniss & Sons, Wright Bros. and Harvey & Treglone. There are many other stockmen in the valley, but they are but beginners and have comparatively small herds.—[Livingstone Enterprise.

The greatest sale of Short Horn cattle that has been made since that of B. B. Groom, several years ago, is reported from the stock farm of A. L. Hamilton, at Lexington, Ky., recently. The Kansas City Live Stock Indicator says. "The highest figures reached was $7,000 for a 2-year-old roan heifer, which was started by Mr. Swope at $3,000, followed by a bid of $4,000 from T. Corwin Anderson. G. L. Chrisman, of Independence, A. C. Briant, of Belton, and R. K. Thomson, of Slater, Mo., also purchased liberally of these, besides taking several of the other families. Counting the calves sold with dams as one animal there were 107 head sold, realizing a total of $87,450—an average of $817,20 per head, and of this large amount of money Missouri paid $35,585, Kansas $7,335, and Colorado $1,600.—[Yellowstone Journal.

Seldom has there been a more favorable season for stockmen than the present one. From all quarters come good reports of the round-ups and the loss of cattle is found to be very light notwithstanding what was called a hard winter. Grass is plenty and the stock is in good condition. It is true that from the mountains the calf crop is reported smaller than in the bad lands and whatever are the conditions of atmosphere or shelter that brings about that difference are yet to be explained. The bad lands affording the most shelter, are more favorable for wintering cattle, and hold the first place in the estimation of stock men. Where bulls have been scarce on the range there has been a consequent diminution in the number of calves, and the stock men of this section appreciating the need of good bulls have been investing heavily in sires this season, particularly in throughbred stock. A large increase of strong, healthy calves cannot be expected where the bulls are scarce or old, and the introduction of fine young males will make a great difference in the number of calves in succeeding round-ups.—[Yellowstone Journal.

While there is no likelihood of it ultimately displacing live cattle in the markets of the country, it must be admitted that the dressed meat trade is gradually extending its field of operations. Conducted with consummate tact, it is steadily widening its scope and gathering new patronage. The results of its growth are especially noticeable as affecting the trade in low grade cattle. It is becoming more difficult, as dressed beef becomes more widely introduced, to dispose of this grade of stock at fair relative prices to butchers who handle cheap stock. It is with these cattle that Chicago beef comes in direct competition. placing the butcher in an independent position as to supplying his wants with stock on the hoof. When he visits the retail market and finds the price of cattle beyond his views, he turns away to the Chicago warehouse and supplies himself at a low figure without the trouble of slaughtering. He can buy dressed beef at only a cent or two a pound above the cost of live cattle, and it is not strange that he takes advantage of this fact to stand off from advancing markets. Butchers in country towns are also handling increased quantities of Chicago beef, and are fitting up refrigerators for that purpose. This trade but slightly affects the sale of good cattle. There is a class of butchers, catering to the best city trade, who under all circumstances slaughter their own stock, and will continue to do so. This insures a continued good market for decent cattle, and ought to stimulate producers to greater pains in looking after the quality of what they grow. The tendency of the times is to run low grade stock out of the intermediate and eastern markets, and place choice cattle at a premium.—[National Stockman.
The coal mine will start up next week.
C. W. Sleeper left for the east on Friday last.
Jim Markley's and Dan McArthur's outfits arrived last Saturday.
Several cars loaded with Black Hills freight have arrived during the past week.
Mr. Barr drove in 200 head of fine beef steers on Monday last, for the N. P. Ref. Car Co.
Some of as fine beef as a man need wish to see in any country was killed at the slaughter house this week.
Bernethy and Deadley's mule and horse trains pulled in this week. They will load with freight for Ryan & Son, Spearfish.
Coleman & Brown's restaurant building is nearly completed, and they promise a good, square meal to the hungry in a few days.
F. B. Allen, secretary of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., accompanied by Fred McKinney, of Bismarck, paid Medora a flying visit last week.
Roberts & Co. have removed their billiard hall from Little Missouri to Medora, occupying the down stairs of the new hall building.
Thomas Matthews, inspector for the Wyoming Stock Association, and Al. Hockett, inspector for the East Montana Associatian, visited Medora this week.
Welf, from Deadwood, has opened out a good stock of notions, dry goods and gents' furnishing goods in a tent nearly opposite this office. He reports a fair trade.
P. D. Cravath, representing the Globe Oil Works, Minneapolis, was a visitor in our town on Sunday and left for Deadwood via the Medora route on Monday afternoon.
John O'Sullivan has his new barber shop and bath rooms completed, and now there is no excuse for any man going dirty, for a bath at John's rooms will only cost 50 cents.

Nick Tiersey, a baker from Jamestown, Dak., arrived here on Wednesday. He is looking up a location for business, and expresses himself as well satisfied with the prospects of Medora. We predict he will stay with us.

Wm. Gay and C. W. Cowgill, of Spearfish, arrived here a few days since and took passage on Saturday's No. 1 for the Coeur d' Alene. Both of these gentlemen are old time Black Hillers and they pronounce the Medora route the chief.

Lieut. Varnum, of the 7th cavalry, with a squad of men passed through last week enroute to Fort Meade via the Medora road. He is viewing the different routes from the Northern Pacific railroad to the Hills by order of the department commander.

The Marquis de Mores returned from St. Paul on Friday night last, but left for the east again on Saturday morning. During his brief visit he expressed himself as well satisfied that the stages would be rolling to the hills from Medora in a short time.

A passenger on Monday's No. 1 let his curiosity overreach his discretion as the train was crossing the bridge. He leaned over so far, in order to see all he could, that his head collided with the bridge. Examination proved that the bridge suffered no damage. The passenger resumed his journey a sorer but a wiser man.

Lloyd Roberts and Dan Friedman will return to Minnesota in a few days to buy another lot of cattle. The satisfaction that they give is amply illustrated by the fact that a Glendive customer of theirs voluntarily counted in a number of calves at full yearling rates, while they are generally thrown in with the purchase.

Roberts & Co. are busily engaged moving into the new hall building, which will be formaly opened on the 4th of July, when a grand ball will be given, including supper. An enjoyable time is assured to every one present, because the gentlemen having charge of the arrangements are among the most popular of our citizens.

William Haley, who drove Pennell & Roberts team to the Hills, which was chartered by Messrs. Guild and Gallop, returned on Saturday evening last. Eight days was the time of the round trip, including a day and a half laying over, and with the same team the entire trip. This is as good time as the Pierre and Sidney coaches make with four horse stock and changes every 15 miles. The Medora route is the chief and no mistake.

On Tuesday evening about dark three strangers were observed loafing around some saddled horses hitched in front of the Hotel de Mores. They apparently had the intention of appropriating some of the animals, but the appearance of George Fitzgerald frustrated their evil designs. This town has, we are pleased to say, so far been neglected by horse thieves, much to the delight of owners of horse flesh; but another break like that made by these strangers and instead of stealing horses it is buckshot the thieves are more likely to carry off.

A. T. Packard, the editor of the Cow Boy, started on Monday last for Deadwood in company with P. D. Cravath, representative of the Globe Oil Works at Minneapolis. They took one of Pennell & Roberts' boss mule teams and expect to be gone about ten days. If the rain and hail storm of Monday night reached them in camp we can imagine how merry a party they were. It is only necessary to say they had one slicker between three of them for the reader to imagine their feelings. The editor's absence will account for any deficiency in the quantity or quality of reading matter in the Cow Boy this week.

The editor, Rassie Deffebach and a friend of the editor's from the east, will always remember last Sunday as one of their red letter days. A magnificent day, a magnificent ride, a view of some of the most wierd and imposing scenery of the Bad Lands, and to crown it all the best of dinners at Wadsworth's ranch served by the most hospitable of ladies, ought certainly to make a day full of pleasure. Mrs. Wadsworth and Mrs. McGregor will always be remembered with most kindly feeling by their visitors. If any hungry citizens of Medora want a good dinner and a drink of the best buttermilk in the Bad Lands we advise them to make a visit to Wadsworth's ranch; but we warn them to stick to the beaten road and not attempt a will o' the wisp jaunt across coolies and perpendicular buttes, where only the fine Italian hand of Rassie Deffebach or a miracle could take them through. If any one aspires to fame as an equestrian acrobat, let him follow our trail from the lower plateau to the higher plateau above Metzen's ranch. Everybody said it couldn't be done, but we did it.

From the Mandan Pioneer of June 30 we clip the following items:

Seventy-seven cars of live stock and about forty cars of freight were temporarily delayed at Mandan by the Marmot washout.

The washout near Marmot will be fully repaired to-day, so as to admit of the passage of trains.

Assistant Superintendent Green will start out to-morrow to pay off on the Missouri division.
Sidney Dillon has a herd of about 8,000 cattle on the trail from North Platte to Powder river. The high water has detained them a little, but they will get through in good season.

The weather for the past week for the most part has been clear, warm and pleasant. The grass is everywhere growing rapidly and the feed is all that could be desired. The abundant rains of the past six weeks were fortunat[illegible] from this time on we can get along without rain. The grass has all the start it needs. Dry weather now will cure it for winter feed.

Mrs. Langtry, while here recently was driven out to see the company's ranch by Manager Oelrich. She was delighted with the trip in the "Tally Ho," and made careful investigation of the ranch and how the business was managed. The result is that she concluded to invest a large amount of money in the cattle business of this country. She has an eye to business and her venture will prove a grand success.—[Northwestern Live Stock Journal.

In the Minneapolis Evening Journal of June 28 we notice an article headed "Rebellious Cow Boys." "The cow boys take possession of stock and refuse to yield control to the owners. Two captured and hanged and a stockman comes to St. Paul to see Gen. Terry to secure aid." This article was written on the information furnished by a Mr. Gallien, and is from beginning to end a lie, and the man Gallien a liar of the first water. In the first place Mr. Gallien never owned but 71 head of cattle and can hardly be counted as "a stockman." This tenderfoot Gallien gives the reporter of the Journal a fine sensational story for publication. The reporter, like a sucker, not only is gulled himself by the liar but gives the sensation to the public as truth, without ever taking the pains to make enquiry as to the responsibility of Mr. Gallien or the truth of his statements. Such a sensational yarn is calculated to work a great injustice to a good country, and an industrious and honest class of men—cow boys. It is only men possessed of but little sense and less experience, men who never traveled outside of their native township, who at the present day believe all the sensational stories told of cow boys. But the Bismarck Tribune and Governor Ordway are led to take stock in liar Gallien's statements, if we judge them by the statement contained in the Tribune of the 4th that Governor Ordway intended to order the Bismarck malitia to quell any future disturbance. This is just too ridiculous, and we advise his excellency to investigate such reports before committing himself in the public press. In a word there has been no disturbances or stock stealing by cow boys. On the contrary they are the first to assist in chasing stock thieves and bring them to justice, and if a man knows anything of the class called cow boys he cannot help but know that as a class they are honest, industrious and fearless; their life is one of hardship and adventure and calculated to remove the polish of civilization from their manners, but they are generous, hospital and extravagant to a fault and abhor a dishonorable action and dispise and hunt down stock thieves with vigor. If the malitia is not called into active service until it is necessary to take the field to fight the cow boys that organization we predict will never smell powder. In the future, Mr. Journal, ascertain the truth before publishing any such sensational stories, for to-day western Dakota is peopled with as law-abiding and peaceable citizens as Minneopolis or any old town in the New England states, and it is an outrage to publish such reports respecting any community without ascertaining first their reliability.

Frank Sperry who was nominated for assoicate justice of Dakota has declined, and the president nominated William H. Francis of Bismarck to that position. Francis is now receiver at the land office at Bismarck, and resigns to accept the justiceship. Mr. Sperry was at once appointed receiver at Bismarck and accepted the office.

Seward Smith, the nominee for associate justice of Dakota, is a native of Massachusetts, well educated, and has been in the law practice in Des Moines for twenty years. He is 53 years old. He was for several years a law partner of Generel Solicitor Withrow of the Rock Island road, and is justly regarded as a thorough lawyer, perhaps rather too amiable to shine brightly before a jury but hard to excel in drawing pleadings.

A cyclone swept over the valley eight miles north of Deadwood at 4 o'clock last Friday, doing great damage. The track of the storm was about three-fourths of a mile in width and extended to a distance of four miles. Thunder and lightning, rain, hail, wind and the ugly funnel were characteristics not to be mistaken. Houses and outbuildings were swept from the face of the earth, fences wiped out, great fields of grain pounded deep into the ground, stock killed and maimed, in short the desolation was rendered complete. Several persons were seriously injured, and one, it is thought, fatally. The storm continued for about fifteen minutes.

We find the following description of the cow boy going the rounds without any credit. It is the best one of many we have read: "The genuine cow boy is worth describing. In many respect he is a wonderful creature. He endures hardships that would take the lives out of most men, and is, therefore, a perfect type of physical manhood. He is the finest horseman in the world, and excels in all the rude sports of the field. He aims to be a dead shot, and universally is. Constantly during the herding season he rides seventy miles a day, and a majority of the year sleeps in the open air. His life in the saddle makes him worship his horse, and, with rifle and six-shooter, complete his happiness. Of vice in the ordinary sense he knows nothing. He is a rough, uncouth, brave and generous creature, who never lies or cheats. It is a mistake to imagine that they are a dangerous set. Any one is as safe with them as with any people in the world, unless he steals a horse or is hunting for a fight. In their eyes death is a mild punishment for horse stealing. Indeed it is the very highest crime known to the unwritten law of the ranch. Their life, habits, education and necessities breed this feeling in human life, and there are less murderers and cut-throats graduated from the cow boy than from among the better class of the east who come out here for venture or gain. They delight in appearing rougher than they are. To a tenderfoot, as they call an eastern man, they love to tell blood-curdling stories and impress him with the dangers on the frontier. But no man need get in a quarrel with them unless he seeks it, or gets harmed unless he seeks some crime. They often own an interest in the herd they are watching, and very frequently become owners of ranches. The slang of the range they always use to perfection, and in season or out of season. Unless you wish to insult them, never offer a cowboy pay for any little kindness he does you or for a share of his rude meal. If the changes that are coming to stock raising should take the cow boy from the ranch its most interesting features will be gone."

Dodge City, Kan., is to have a bull fight.
On the Tongue river round-up, west side, three buffalo calves were driven into camp with the cattle. One was secured by the boys, the other two got away.—[Yellowstone Journal.

An air saddle blanket or pad, is the invention of an Australian stockman, and it is spoken of in the highest terms of praise by those who have used it. We hope it may prove to be a preventative of sore backs.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

While from other localities we hear of crops and grass being scorched by the draught, we have had rain enough to insure a good crop, and the range is as fresh as it was in the spring, and we are losing fortunes by not having cattle to eat the grass that is free to all.

One hundred and forty-six head of horses have been stolen this spring between Tussler's ranch and Billings. If the ranchmen would treat a few horse thieves to a hemp necktie, they might be able to break the business up in a great measure.—[Glendive (Mont.) Independent.

Said Mr. Ratcliff: "I have raised side by side on the Divide, Shorthorn calves and Herefords—treated them just alike—and I will say to you now the Herefords beat the Shorthorns as rustlers all the time. As cattle for a high altitude the Herefords are fifty per cent. ahead.—[Colorado Record.

Round-up captains should be paid by the association. The duties of a round-up captain are many and of a most arduous character. Five dollars a day would be a very reasonable compensation for the responsible position, and we are sure that all association members who have been with the round-up parties this season will heartily concur with us in the opinion that captains should be paid.—[New Mexico Stock Grower.

Mr. Frewen, of Wyoming, the gentleman who has just returned from England, where he has been looking after the practicability of a northern route for cattle to Europe, gives it as his opinion that 50,000 head from Wyoming, Colorado and the northwest will this year take the northern route; travel through Canada, down the St. Lawrence, and finally as "feeders" land upon the coast of England, Ireland or Scotland.—[Denver News.

Our advices from Ogalalla are to the effect that up to date there have been four herds of cattle passed. Two of these, six thousand, were for the Continental Cattle company, and have gone on to the north. J. R. Blocker has also had two herds of three thousand each to pass. These are early arrivals, and will reach their destination in the far north at a date much earlier than has been the case in past years.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The most remarkable convention of the age will be the national cattle convention, which assembles in St. Louis in November next. More than two hundred millions of property will be represented in that convention. Not only will the cattle men of this country, but of the old world be present. Those who raise cattle on the plains will be supplemented by the breeders of choice stock to supply the wants of the growers of cattle. The widest circulation should be given of the proposed meeting, and the largest possible attendance secured.—[Coleman's Rural World.

On behalf of the cattle ranchers of Montana the Canadian Pacific railway authorities have represented to the minister of customs the propriety of allowing cattle from the western states to be carried through the Canadian territory in bond for export. The Montana ranchers propose entering the stock at Fort Walsh; driving them to the Canadian Pacific railway for shipment. The effect would be to make Montreal the cattle market of Montana and other northwestern states. The ministry agreed to the relaxation of the custom regulations so as to bring this trade to Canadian ports.—[New Mexico Stock Grower.

The band of horse thieves who have been committing their depredations in the western portion of the territory were, we learn from the Madisonian Extra, arrested after a hot pursuit and sharp fight, by Ben Burns, Martin Peel, Deputy Sheriff Gloyd and a posse of citizens of Virginia City. One of the thieves named George Munn was killed in the fight. The names of the parties are Albert Edmundson, John Edmundson and Neil Murphy. John Edmundson was accompanied by his wife and two children. This whole band have been captured or killed and the horses they stole recovered.—[Billings (Mont.) Herald.

T. A. Matthews, stock inspector of the Eastern Montana Association, whose headquarters are at Mandan, returned here this morning from a trip up the Missouri to Buford, Poplar River and Wolf Point. He states that he found the Assinnaboine Indians at Wolf Point in a very werk and sickly condition, so that they are dying off very fast. He attributes the mortality to the fact that they were nearly famished last winter and contracted consumption and kindred diseases that are taking them off now. Mr. Matthews recovered on the trip a couple of stolen horses. One belonged to Henry Tusler and the other was from the "T H connected" outfit of Wyoming.—[Yellowstone Journal.

The Kansas Cow Boy says the Kansas Stock Association is raising $100,000 to buy the railroad land in the vicinity of Dodge city for the purpose of keeping the trail and range open, so that shippers can hold cattle and drive in to ship. Would it not be well for the Montana and Dakota associations to take time by the forelock and buy up the land at one or two points along the Northern Pacific road while it can be bought at a nominal figure and locate the government land in the immediate vicinity before settlers get too strong a hold? Already the railroad company is moving the stock yards at Dickinson to a point farther from the town, and business men of Miles City are making an effort to have the stock yards at that place located on the government reservation.

At the annual meetings of leading cattle raising associations of Texas in 1882 prompt and very active measures were taken to banish the deadly six-shooter from the cattle man's belt. Resolutions were passed unanimously pledging owners of ranches and cattle not to keep in their employ any hands that would carry deadly weapons. That spring there was an absence of deadly encounters and shooting sprees observable throughout the range country. Last year no action was taken by stock men in convention assembled in regard to the "six-shooter," and since that time serious and deadly shots have been fired. In almost every section of the west murders are on the increase, and cow men are too often the principals in the encounters. The six-shooter loaded with deadly cartridges is a dangerous companion for any man, especially if he should unfortunately be primed with whisky. Cattle men should unite in aiding the enforcement of the law against the carrying of deadly weapons. Lawlessness in any form is hurtful, morally and from business standpoint, and no business is injured more than that of cattle raising when its employes are allowed to carry deadly weapons. Then we would suggest to the managers of cattle ranches to see that the six-shooter is banished from his outfit.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

Mr. Sleeper left for St. Paul Monday.
Dr. McIntosh, of Glendive, made Medora a short visit on Tuesday.
Two outfits left here for the Black Hills the past week. They were loaded with passengers.
Mr. Cole, one of Montana's cattle kings, was down from Miles City yesterday and spent the day in town.
The prospectors have all returned from an unsuccessful search for the precious in the Bad Lands north of here.
The sheep shearing is progressing slowly on account of the frequent showers. There are about 200 to shear yet.
There was a very pleasant party at Smith's ranch, Beaver Creek, Sunday night, which was attended by some of the elite of Medora.
If this number of the COW BOY seems a little thin or otherwise amiss we hope our readers will lay it to the inexperience of the editor pro tem.
George Porter, manager of the company's store, received about a carload of household furniture this week and will occupy one of those elegant cottages.
The Northern Pacific Forwarding company shipped about 80,000 pounds of freight for the Black Hills this week, and have advices of considerable more which should be here this week.

Pete, the colored cook, had a narrow escape at the depot last evening. As the train was pulling out he attempted to jump on, but making a miscue he fell between the platform and the car steps. He hung on like a good fellow, and with the assistance of others he was pulled out without receiving any serious injury.

C. H. Du Bois, editor of Saturday Spectator and Midland Monthly of Minneapolis, and Prof. T. J. Richardson, artist, were here this week taking notes and making sketches for a series of illustrated articles on the Northern Pacific line. Pictures were taken here at the Cantonment, out on the Bad Lands and at the bend of the river above town.

Drawing room car No. 37 of the Pittsburgh, Cincinnati & St. Louis railroad passed through on train No. 1 Tuesday evening, containing about forty excursionists bound for the opening of the new National Park hotel. The party is from Dayton, Cincinnati and other Ohio cities. They expressed themselves as much surprised and pleased at the wild and weird scenery of the Bad Lands.

A. T. Packard, editer and proprietor of the BAD LANDS COW BOY, and P. D. Cravath, correspondent of the Minneapolis Tribune, arrived here on Thursday evening direct from Medora. They were pleased with the country they passed over, and agreeably surprised with what they saw here. They went to Deadwood this morning and will return the first of the week to remain a day or two.—[Spearfish Register.

The Fourth passed off very quietly in Medora. The day was generally observed as a holiday, but as no programme for celebrating had been decided on everyone passed the day as suited his or her notion, and, although several cow boys visited the town, each and every one behaved like gentlemen. In fact the place presented more the appearance of an eastern town in Sabbath garb than a western town in holiday attire. In the evening the new hall was formally opened with a grand ball, which was a decided success in every particular. There were about fifty couples present, and dancing was kept up till daylight dawned, and every one was unanimous in declaring the ball one of the pleasantest in their experience. Thanks to George Fitzgerald, of the Hotel de Mores, and his well-known and capable chef de cuisine, the old original Gen. Sheridan, the supper was like the ball a success and first-class in every feature. The hall was tastily decorated with flags and evergreens by Jimmy Hannigan, assisted by Joe Pennell, who are artists of no mean calibre whenever a thoroughly æsthetic display is called for.

Three horses were stolen from Sully Springs Sunday night. The picket ropes were cut.

About 10 o'clock the same night Geo. Roderick, at the Cantonment, on going to look after his horses found two men in among the herd, who made off as fast as possible on his approach.

About two hours later Pennell & Jones' herder discovered a man among his horses, who when accosted said he was looking for the brickyard horses, but on advice left forthwith.

Joe Pennell received the following telegrams dated St. Paul, July 5:

Rates only apply to Medora. Come and see me directly.
MARQUIS DE MORES.

Everything lovely. See Marquis' telegram and Pioneer Press. Belfield combination knocked out in one round.
KERR.

Later the Marquis writes that they will give stage and transporation contract rates, and are offering special inducements to a company to stock the line.

Tom Smith, one of Clark & Plum's men, is in from the head of Little Missouri and Boxelder round-up.

This round-up commenced on the head of Boxelder, worked down as far as Stoneville, then leaving part of the men to hold the cattle they went to the head of the Little Missouri and worked down to Stoneville, where the round-up broke up on July 1. The weather was pleasant continually, and, with the exception of two accidents, was very successful.

Theo. Weedon's cook while bathing in the river undertook to dive from the bank and, the water being shallow, his head struck the bottom, nearly breaking his neck and paralyzing him for life. He was taken to Spearfish.

John Leahy, one of the "E6" men, was thrown from his horse, the animal falling on him dislocated his shoulder. He has fully recovered.

The boys roped two bear cubs and brought them to camp. They furnished amusement for many a lonely hour, but 'twas death to the bears.

The farmer's goose, thanks to the abundance of rain, hangs altitudelum.

Rev. Fulton is progressing nicely with a pretty new cottage located in Belfield's most romantic spot.

John R. Thayer has left for the east, and many expect to see him return with a wife.

Belfield is all broke up about the freight route. Men wear clean paper collars, women send for catalogues of hair pins and children frantically shriek for fire crackers in anticipation of it. Nobody knows anything about it, though everybody would bet his last 17th of March hat that the freight route is coming to Belfield. If so, look out for a boom with a big "B," and always remember that it is better to be born lucky than good looking.

Louis C. Hay, the only survivor of the townsite company, arrived home on Tuesday.

Several cases of burglary have come to light, the residences of the Galliens and McBirney being broken into and ransacked. A chain of evidence is fast closing upon the guilty parties, and as soon as all the returns are in they will receive their just punishment. People are tired of getting robbed, and the men implicated will be made an example of.

Quite a trade has sprung up in the bone business here. L. D. Pettit, of Deadwood, the prince of rustlers, who holds heavy contracts for bones, makes Belfield his headquarters, and what is better, pays over to ye hard-working bone pickers the solid cash at the rate of $8 per ton as fast as they can be delivered. In the language of the good old book, "Ye that have bones to pick, prepare to pick them now."

Bob Montgomery's neat addition looms up handsomely, and if Bob will only follow the example of others and take unto himself a partner as good looking as himself there would seem plenty of happiness and counterfeit half dollars in store for Bob.

New potatoes, fresh peas and other tropical vegetables are plentiful hereabouts for those who have the h. k.—hard cash.

To the exclusion of other matter, we will give the main points of the connection of D. T. Bramble with the N. P. and Black Hills freight business.

Going clear back to the beginning, we will commence at the time when Dickinson offered a bonus to the firm of Kyes & Bramble to do their forwarding from there. Immediately after this offer was made, the firm came to Medora and tried to secure an advance in blood money from here. Their errand was profitless as no one would even enter into negotiations with them and they left town on a freight train swearing that they would never come here again, that they were sorry for even the amount they had laid out for dinner and they afterwards declared to Bob. Roberts that: "the Marquis and the whole d—— French army couldn't drag them to Medora." Bob. earnestly assured them that from the looks of things, no one seemed particularly stuck on their coming.

It must be that the Dickinson offer was finally accepted, as Bramble went to the Hills and began taking contracts with the merchants there for their freight via Dickinson.

Meantime, however, the Kyes end of the combination thought he saw a better thing in getting a large bonus of land in Belfield, starting a boom and unloading on tenderfeet. This plan worked to perfection as far as the bonus of land is concerned as, by the terms of the contract, the firm of Kyes & Bramble received a large slice of the Belfield townsite and adjacent country. This put another phase on the matter and Bramble immediately began making contracts via Belfield, pronouncing it far superior to the Dickinson route.

Meantime, considerable work had been done quietly for our route and when the Marquis and Joe Pennell went to the Hills it was agreed by the majority of the merchants to ship via Medora. Here, however, the mistake was made of appointing Bramble forwarder, notwithstanding the fact that he had said and done all he could against us.

Matters went along well enough for awhile, when complaints began coming in from the Black Hills merchants. One of these showed clearly the animus of Bramble toward our route. The regular charge is ten cents a hundred for forwarding and Bramble had agreed to the rate by accepting his position. Without any notice whatever, he began charging fifteen cents, an advance which made considerable difference in a large consignment. The merchants in at least one instance refused to pay the advance draft. This brought matters to such a crisis as Bramble thought was favorable and he went to Deadwood, leaving orders to reduce freighters rates to a dollar and fifty, thus causing all the freighters to strike and forwarding his own ends by thus trying to alienate the traffic of the Hills merchants. Just before leaving, Bramble remarked that there seemed to be some dissatisfaction in the Hills and that he intended to arrange matters satisfactorily, leaving and meaning to leave the impression with a society brother, that he intended to work for the best interests of our route.

For the reason that the Belfield contract was still in force, or that Bramble was intending all the time to sell out the N. P. route to Fred Evans, the latter being probably the case, negotiations had all the time been kept up in favor of some other route than that via Medora, as is shown by a telegram of Bramble's in reference to shipping the machinery for the Homestake 200-stamp mill, amounting to about 1,000,000 pounds. In this telegram he guarantees that he can quote low enough rates to secure she contract but that under no circumstances will he ship via Medora. Immediately after sending this telegram he went to St. Paul, met Fred Evans and it is reasonable to suppose, there concluded a deal with him as it was soon announced that Fred Evans had secured the contract. From this, the assumption was plain that Bramble had sold out the Medora route and nearly as plain that he even went back on Belfield.

This brings matters up to about the date when Bramble went to Deadwood five or six weeks ago, leaving with the promise we have mentioned above, of working for the Medora route. As his actions afterward showed, he intended all the time to betray our route and on account of the lack of explanation of several delays at this end of the line and the seeds of discontent he had sown in the Hills, there was a promising field for his traitorous operations.

Bramble thus had things all his own way in the Hills and for three weeks worked like a beaver convincing merchants that the Belfield route was the best one and inducing many to sign contracts via that point.

This was the state of affairs when the editor of the Cow Boy arrived in Deadwood. Relying on the promise Bramble had made, we were greatly surprised to find that he had been industriously engaged in giving the Medora route a black eye since his arrival. Naturally we inquired the points he had made against our route and found them in almost every instance to be unqualified lies. In the first place, he pronounced the route impracticable, a very favorite expression of his, by the way. In opposition to this we quoted the expressions of Messrs. John Sechler, J. Juelfs, Rassie Deffebach, Billy Brewer, L. H. Palmer, Dr. Louthan, Mr. Spear and many others, all of them well known in the Hills and all experienced in freighting and freight routes and they all say that the Medora route is the best one over which they have ever travelled.

Next, we were met by a direct lie on the part of Bramble. He claimed, and this repeatedly, that there was no depot at Medora and consequently no place to unload freight. Bramble's office is and has been in the depot here and no lapse of memory on his part can excuse the denial of the existence of one of the prettiest depots on the line. He can rest assured that this lie has done him no good in the Hills.

His next tale was more specious but fully as unconscionable. He stated that the Marquis had promised to build a freight house long ago but had failed in his promise. Bramble well knows that he, in company with the Marquis, examined the storage rooms on the slaughter house side-track and pronounced them equal to any demand until the fall freight began coming and to prove the uselessness of building a freight house, said that he had received word from Mr. Hannaford that until fall there need be no hurry about unloading the cars and that the goods could be transferred from them to the freighters wagons and thus avoid a second handling. He undoubtedly advanced these points to prevent the erection of a freight house here for two reasons. First, it would anchor the freight here where there was no chance of securing blood-money and second, because he wished to use the fact of there being no freight house here for the exclusive use of Black Hills freight, as a means to get merchants to ship to some other point where he could get blood-money.

Bramble also stated that the Marquis was financially embarrassed, that he had not the money to put on the stage line, that during his Hills trip the Marquis had fed the merchants on wind, that the Northern Pacific had "tumbled" to him, and that the N. P. officials had assured Bramble that he himself now "stood in" and that the Marquis had to take a back seat. That this is a mass of lies is already proven. The Northern Pacific has pooled issues with the Marquis and Mr. Bramble is "tapped" on the first deal. The N. P. inaugurated proceedings by buying a quarter interest in the Medora townsite and in conjunction with the Marquis have organized the N. P. Stage & Forwarding Co., with termini at Medora and Deadwood. This was accomplished less than a week ago and already the first fruits are visible here. Immense piles have been put in position and the sills laid for a freight house 240x42 feet. The work is being pushed vigorously by a large force of men, five additional workmen were put on this morning and still others will be added as soon as they can work to advantage. The climax of the whole thing, however, and where the N. P. S. & F. Co. hold four aces to Bramble's poor little bob-tail, is the fact of the Northern Pacific having refused rates on any other route than that via Medora.

The careful reader will have observed that we have passed by many disgraceful actions of this man Bramble, notably the one where he apparently joined forces with T. G. Jones in favor of our route, induced Jones to do the outside work of grading and bridging and then perfidiously made all his contracts by the way of Dickinson. But we do not need this and other facts to prove that Bramble has acted throughout, in a thoroughly unprincipled manner, and that he has repeatedly abused the confidence of the Hills merchants when at any time he could serve his ends in the slightest by so doing. That he has been a traitor to Dickinson and Medora is beyond question. That he entered into the whole business with the idea of making as much blood-money as possible and then selling out to Pierre is almost as certain. But the most certain thing of all is that Mr. Bramble's name is D-E-N-N-I-S.

And now that the matter is finally arranged, there will doubtless be no more trouble. In spite of the unavoidable delay in putting on the stages and the disgraceful actions of our thorn(?) in the flesh, the Black Hills merchants look hopefully to the Northern Pacific for relief from the extortionate rates of the Pierre route and for speedy railroad connection. This is bound to come soon and by the way of Medora.

Welcome, N. P. S. & F. Co.

Vale, Bramble!

The stockmen of Mason county, in Texas, have furnished 20,000 cattle to the spring drive at an average of $15 per head, making the handsome sum of $300,000.—[Colorado L. S. Record.

The Denver papers report sales of some Iowa and Missouri heifers, ones and twos, in that city at prices ranging from $30 to $35 per head. Of course they were well graded up, and their off-spring from good bulls, will be valuable.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Kellogg & Co., have the largest horse ranch in Nevada, range 40 by 60 miles, and 2,000 horses grazing thereon.—[Reno Gazette.

A correspondent of the New Mexico Stock Grower reports the stampeding of a large herd of cattle near Devil's river, Texas, and the loss of about 2,000 head.

California breeders claim that they can import Hereford cattle at less cost from Australia than they can from England.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The special dispatch to the Drovers Journal from Liverpool quotes the cattle markets ½c higher; good to choice American steers 15@16c per pound dressed. Sheep weaker; best, 16c.

Two fence cutters were killed in the Territory near Medicine Lodge last week. The parties had been in the habit of going into the pasture, cutting posts, and on leaving would cut the wire or leave the gate open. Finally they were caught in the act, and on being remonstrated with by the cowboys, opened fire, which was returned, and both were instantly killed.—[Indian Chieftain.

It is not likely that many fat beeves will be ready for shipment from this country before August, though a few bunches that were fed until grass appeared may go out in July. Stockmen in this country have learned from experience that it does not pay to ship beeves before they are fat, and it is not likely there will be any mistake made this season. Fat cattle, of the grade this county turns out, always command top prices; if they are but half fat they as invariable sell below their value.—[Barber Co. Index.

The St. James ofttimes entertains among its numerous guests, men who represent great wealth in bovines as well as in mines. In this new West now-a-days a man's personal appearances do not by any means indicate his financial status. During the last few days of the week just passed there were congregated at the hotel a large number of eminent cattle growers from our own State, from Texas and New Mexico, whose combined wealth would represent millions. These cattlemen as a rule are quite unpretentious in their personal appearance. There is no glitter of diamonds about them, no ostentation. As a rule they are plain, practical, every day fellows, who make but little display of their worldly wealth. They buy and sell cattle by the tens of thousands as quickly as would an eastern farmer a single brute. Twenty, fifty, and even an hundred thousand is no gigantic transaction with many of those who come and go at the St. James. Wealth makes less display to-day than it did twenty years ago. The man with slouched hat and faded coat not infrequently has the longest bank account. He with glittering diamonds and the breast-plate too often is the shoddy. These thoughts were suggested on meeting ten or a dozen representative cattlemen in the rotunda of the hotel the other day. There was Mr. Wilkes, of the London Company, he who lately purchased the Wilson cattle and lands on the Republican for a sum of money greater than the worth of all the cattle of Colorado twenty years ago. Mr. Wilkes was a much plainer dressed man than the "roustabout" who tumbled the trunk in and out the hotel door. There was Mr. Pryor, the largest buyer of cattle the present year in Texas, and he whose 45,000 head of cattle now tramp the great trail leading up from the Lone Star state. He would easily be mistaken for a country merchant or a moderate farmer. The stout man with smiling face, whom everybody salutes, is Billy Wilson, the cowboy but yesterday, the cattle king to-day. Colossal fortune has not spoiled him. He is the same jovial fellow he was at the roundup. The plainly dressed man who just remarked to Mr. Pryor, "I'll take five thousand head if you'll shave the price a trifle," is Mr. H. H. Metcalf, whose word in the cattle markets is as good as Jay Gould's on Wall street. These stouter gentlemen on the outer rim of the circle are Messrs. Cranmar and Binkleman, the latter gentleman probably owning more ox-kind than any other man in America. That tall gentleman with a well-brushed hat and dude-like pants, is Captain Anderson, of the Coupalin ranch, in Colfax. He will wear different attire at the round-up. That stoutest of them all, that man who turns the scale beam at 250 pounds, avoirdupois, is Mr. George W. Thompson, of Trinidad. His cattle crop the grasses on a thousand hills, and his sheep are past counting. A shrinkage of one cent on beef might affect Thompson twenty thousand dollars. The young sprig with British look is young Ogilvy, of Greeley, son of the late Earl of Airlie. He is an importer of blooded cattle from the Highlands of Scotland, and a rising man in the cattle business.—[Colorado L. S. Record.

A. M. Sinnott is in town on his way to Butte City.
Mollie Coleman has returned from Andrews station.
The work train which had its headquarters at Sully Springs has gone to Allard.
R. B. Downing, assistant road master has resigned and gone back to his old position on the Manitoba.
The many friends of conductor Clark will be glad to hear that he has resumed his old position on the road.
J. L. Truscott, Johnny Goodall and the cow-boys on the different round-ups are now in and preparations will soon be made for the beef round-up.
Bob Roberts' father died in Wales recently, leaving a considerable property to Bob, who will go over to receive it some time this fall.
Mr. O. C. Green, superintendent of telegraph and R. B. Wilson, special stock agent for the N. P., passed through here Wednesday, enroute for the west.
Joe Ferris returned from the east Monday evening, having purchased a large stock of groceries, which he will open in his new store room across the river.
The prospecting party which went down the river a few weeks ago, has gone back to the Hills, having found no pay gold, but good indications of silver and copper.
A tenderfoot got off the train an evening or two since and picking up a piece of scoria, gravely remarked: "This must be an awful country where the alkali cakes so solid."
School has begun at the Cantonment school-house, with Dan. Williams teacher. Twenty scholars were enrolled the first day and there is every prospect of a successful session.
C. A. Spurling left last Saturday morning for Pierre to accept a position on the Northwestern, at an increased salary. We are glad to hear of his advancement but regret to see him leave.

Joe Pennell started with a car-load of mules yesterday morning for the Canadian Pacific, where some contracts have been taken by Tom Jones. It is not certain that Joe will stay and it is hoped that he will not.

Judging from the success of the dance the evening of the 4th, the one to-morrow evening at the same place will be of a like nature. Roberts & Co. pledge themselves to the maintenance of the best order. All are cordially invited.

P. D. Cravath, of Minneapolis, the editor's travelling companion to the Black Hills, continued his western trip Monday night. An account of the trip will be published in serial form, beginning with the next issue.

Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, held mass here Tuesday morning at Geo. Fitzgerald's, and Wednesday morning at the Marquis' residence. Father Martin takes Father Cassidy's place at Mandan, the latter now having charge of the Jamestown parish.

Thanks to the able services of Messrs. Brewer, Houk, Palmer and Deffebach, there was no delay in issuing the Cow Boy during our absence, and as we have been repeatedly assured that the last two issues were the best since the initial number, our loss of a share of the glory is our subscribers' eternal gain.

Mr. Gallup, of the New York law firm of Johnson, Gallup & Hurry, came through from the Hills with the pilgrims and is now at Wadsworth's ranch with Rassie Deffebach and Billy Brewer who are branding calves there. Mr. Gallup is making a careful study of the profits of stock raising and may conclude to invest.

The coal taken from the Medora mine is pronounced by Geo. Wilkes, the ablest judge here, to be the best Bad Lands coal yet burned at the Company's works. He says it is especially rich in steam-giving properties. Messrs. Coleman & Brown and Mr. Z. Hyde also claim that it is superior to any lignite coal they have hitherto used for cooking. The coal is delivered for $2.50 a ton and considering this low price, business will be conducted on the cash on delivery basis. All orders will be taken at the Cow Boy office.

The team of broncos which has occasioned so much difficulty again showed their untamable spirit last Monday. While George and Arthur Smith were hitching them up, they started to run away, pushing George, who was holding them by the bits, in front of them. He hung on until it seemed certain that they were about to run into the Cow Boy office when he jumped to one side and by great good luck, escaped uninjured. After the broncos were caught, a trot of twenty miles in a heavy lumber wagon, loaded with six men and five hundred pounds of sand scarcely tired them and they were as willing to run as ever. Large broncos, when tamed, make valuable work horses, but no one who is unacquainted with the breed can realize their wildness and the difficulty found in taming them in comparison to States' horses. It is exactly the difference between educating children who have enlightened parents and the children of aboriginal tribes.

Owing to the absence of the editor, the arrival of the Studebaker wagons, buckboards and platform spring wagons has not been chronicled. They are undoubtedly the best wagons manufactured and they will be sold at prices never before touched in this section. The best goods are always the cheapest and these are without question both superior in quality and lower in price than any others hitherto sold in the west. Call at the Cow Boy office and examine wagons and prices.

D. K. Wade finished driving the cattle for the LeMoyne cattle company from Glendive to the home ranch on Tepee bottom, last Monday. The bunch consisted of 500 head of high grade heifers and were purchased from Mr. Mendenhall of Glendive. On his way east, Mr. LeMoyne purchased 200 head of thoroughbred one's and two's and a lot of Shorthorn bulls, which will soon arrive. Mr. Wade had good opportunities of judging the eastern Montana stock ranges and pins his faith stronger than ever to the Little Missouri Bad Lands. The gravel there has a tendency to make cattle foot-sore and numerous quicksands endanger their lives. The grass is also far better here and for protection in winter we are far ahead.

[The following is a rather hap-hazard jotting down of the incidents in the first part of our Black Hills trip. The next issue will contain a longer and probably more interesting article on the resources of the Hills.]

We left the Medora brick-yard at 5 o'clock Monday afternoon in a buck-board barouche, drawn by a pair of Pennell & Roberts' mules and driven by a Spanish nobleman, disgnised under the name of Patrick Devlin. The party consisted of P. D. Cravath, an old college friend, the afore-mentioned nobleman and the Cow Boy ink-slinger.

We went into camp at Ash-coolie at 8:30 after devouring enough grub to feed a regiment, wrapped ourselves in our blankets and by the light of the moon and to the music of a mosquito band, attempted to woo the drowsy god. He wouldn't woo. The mosquitos came without wooing however, and in the morning we carried with us a perfect illustration of the BAD LANDS in the hills and buttes on our neck.

Right here let me stop to say that Joe. Pennell had better seek more congenial climes before we return to Medora. His parting wish that it would rain every day was more than fulfilled. The disguised nobleman was sure Joe. had hoo-dooed us and before we arrived we came to the same conclusion.

Tuesday morning at 3 o'clock we awaked in a drizzling rain. After considerable trouble we got our fire going, boiled and bolted our coffee straight and hot and started on. Had it not been for Mr. Palmer's thoughtfulness in getting a rubber coat we would now be a dead animal by the wayside. It was colder than a defeated candidates reception of his successful competitor and damper tnan the law allows. As the ministsr said: "It was a dam-p cold day." For four hours and a half, until 8 o'clock we rode through the driving rain, when it began to slack, but was cold till 11 o'clock. When 46 1-10 miles from Medora we overtook Lieut. Varnum with his government outfit. After a pleasant chat and an explantion of the odometer by the Lieutenant, we started on and went into camp at Chalk buttes at 11. After dinner we went to sleep and awoke at 1:30 with the rays of the sun shining directly in our upturned faces and the thermometer chassezing up to 130 degrees. Every exposed part of our flesh was "done" "to the queens taste." The mosquitos had also been getting in their work very extensively and the result was a fresh accession of buttes and coolies.

Starting on, we saw many antelope, in fact they abounded the whole way. We put up the 800 yard sight on one and had the satisfaction of seeing it drop. Driving toward it, visions of tender antelope stake filled our mind mixed with the recollection of sundry and divers of Johnson's stories about killing buffalo so far that they had begun to decay before he could reach them. But,

"The beautiful vail is rent in two"

very often. When within fifty yards of the antelope it jumped up and dashed over a butte, making a crack in the atmosphere longer than Mark Twain's jack-rabbit. It was positevily disgusting.

This diversion and several others of a kindred nature delayed us so that we made only fifty miles on Tuesday.

Going into camp at 8 o'clock we made a fire of buffalo chips and then made our bed on them to keep them dry in case of rain.

At three Wednesday morning we were again awaked by a driving rain. This thing was getting monotonous but breakfast was cooked to the tune of college glee songs and we started on in good spirits at four. This was our best day's travelling, amonting to at least seventy-five miles. We made a long stop at the E6 ranch, arriving there just in time to avoid a terrific rain and wind storm. Russ Wilson entertained us royally and after a five hour's stop, we started on, reaching the South Moreau and Macy's ranch at 9:30.

The first gun has been fired and from now until the close of the campaign in November, the political horizon will be eagerly watched by most of our readers. Billings county, at the coming territorial conventions will be entitled to two delegates and therefore have a voice in matters political, to which its rapid growth and great prosperity so well entitle it. For the first time in the history of trans-Missouri politics, representation will be conceded to this section of the country in the coming legislature and the honor naturally falls upon a citizen of Morton, the senior county. The COW BOY has for some time past carefully weighed the merits of the various candidates already in the field and is glad to find a man in every way qualified to come up to the requirements of the occasion. We refer to Mr. L. N. Cary, of Mandan, of the well-known firm of Carpenter & Cary. This gentleman combines to a large extent the essentials of a valuable legislator and his nomination cannot bnt meet with universal approbation by all thinking people. Mr. Cary is a pioneer of the west Missouri country, thoroughly conversant with the needs and wants of its district, pushing, enterprising and has proven his competency and ability by the phenomenal success achieved in his own business. Mr. Cary is in no sense an office-seeker, never having desired nor held one, but that his services in the legislative halls will be invaluable, is beyond successful contradiction. The COW BOY will have more to say on this subject in its later issues, but simply desires to present its candidate to-day, with the firm belief that no possible candidate possesses in a greater degree than Mr. Cary, the elements needed in our legislator.

Reports from all directions are to the effect that cattlemen have awakened to the importance of having plenty of bulls on the range. From the gulf to the northern limit of the range, everywhere, bulls are being turned in by the hundreds, and they are generally of a very fair grade. This will tend to greatly increase the calf crop, and proportionately increase the profits of the business. Let the good work go on. Now if you will keep the bulls up in the winter and spring, and wean your calves in the fall, your cup of success will be nearly full.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

In every flock and herd there will be more or less imperfectly formed or defectively-consituted produce, which, if suffered to perpetuate their defects, will depreciate the value of the breed. These should be thrown out or consigned to the block, and never permitted to breed their kind, to degenerate the blood of their kindred. It is this weeding out practice that has preserved our stock from degenerating. It was by selecting out the most perfect scions to breed from that our stock has been raised to its present high standard of excellence. Grading up is the ladder of promotion; the top round is the summit of perfection.—[Montana Stock and Mining Journal.

To buy a horse, an intending purchaser should have the horse brought out before him, and watch the animal as he stands at rest. If the owner is continually starting the horse in motion, and urging him to "show off," something may be suspected; because it is when a horse is at perfect rest that his weak points are divulged. If the horse is sound he will stand square on his limbs, without moving any one of them, the feet being placed flat on the ground, and all his legs plump and naturally posed. If one foot be thrown forward, and the weight taken from it, disease or tenderness may be suspected.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

There is a disposition on the part of herd owners to become careless about the ages and condition of their bulls. To begin with, bulls should not be put in the herd until they are twenty months or two years old. If yearlings are placed in the herd it should only be for a short time. After a bull has been two seasons with the herd he should be removed. He is no good for service, and as long as you keep him you will figure him in as one of your active partners in the business. Get rid of him and fill his place with a two-year old. These remarks apply to bulls having the freedom of the range. If you are prepared to take them up in the fall and feed them through the winter, and then hold them apart from the herd until July, they will last a couple of years longer and still be valuable. Then will come the question of in and in breeding. If you are satisfied to indulge in that practice you may hold the bulls in the range for four years. But old bulls are a nuisance, viewed from any range standpoint, and the proper method is to abate them.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The total values of the exports of domestic cattle, hogs, and of beef, pork and dairy products in May, and in the five months ended May 31st, also of beef and pork products during the seven months ended May 31st, as compared with similar exports during the corresponding periods of the preceding years were as follows: May, 1884, $7,554,239; May, 1883, $6,473,489. Five months ended May 31, 1884, $34,476,975; 1883, $45,454,041. Beef and pork products for seven months ended May 31st, 1884, $50,278,756; 1883, $61,061,404.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

From all parts of Dakota and Montana come reports of the depredations of horse-thieves. We think we are entirely within bounds in stating that in Dakota alone, there have been at least two hundred head stolen, and scarcely more than a half dozen have been recovered. Several men have also been hung for horse-stealing, but the plague still goes on. In South Heart, Sunday evening, four valuable horses were stolen from Mr Morton's barn, and as the trail has been closely followed, we hope that by this time the horses are recovered and the thieves hung. Mr. Lang writes in reference to his stolen horses that the thieves forgot to take the halters, which he will keep for their personal adornment. We wish to be placed on record as believing that the only way to cure horse-stealing is to hang the thief wherever caught. The end, in this case, fully justifies the means.

The cattle business, the most important industry of the west, is in some respects peculiar. In no other transactions, save those of handling stock, is so much reliance placed on a man's honor and word. Thousands of dollars are often involved and depend on the honer of a single man. It is therefore highly necessary that all cattle trades be conducted on square business principles. If a man engaged in the business wishes to stand well among his neighbors,he must do exactly as he says he will, without regard to the consequences. We might say that in no other businss is one dependent upon his neighbors for assistance so much as in cattle dealing. When a sale is made, care should be exercised that nothing be misrepresented. The temporary profits will not balance the future harm caused by the loss of a good name. Buyers should understand their business, and not say one thing and mean another. A slight mistake may cause a stock grower much trouble. Ranchmen have the cure in their hands. Let them refuse to have any dealings with those whose business conduct is not "straight," and the crooked gentleman will soon find the field lonely and seek pastures new.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

A company has just been organized in New York for the purpose of operating an inmense ranch in the southwest corner of New Mexico. The company is called the Lyons & Campbell Ranch and Cattle company, and has a capital stock of $1,500,000. The president is John C. Barron, of the United Railroads of New Jersey; vice president, Mr. Oliver Sumner Teall; treasurer, Mr. E. Harrison Sanford, treasurer of the Stampfords Manufacturing company; secretary, Mr. Lester M. Clark; manager, Mr. Thomas Lyons: directors, Mr. John C. Barron, Gen. George B. McClellan, Mr. E. Harrison Sanford, Mr. Thomas Lyons, Mr. A. A. Sumner, Mr. George B. Post, Mr. Brayton Ives, Mr. John J. McCook and Mr. Oliver Sumner. The company's property is a combination of a number of ranches along the Gila river and the streams and springs in that vicinity. The ranches are named as follows: the Caves Springs, the White House, the Buck Horn, the Mule Spring, the Harding Cienega and the Lower of Gila ranch. Their range is about forty miles from east to west and sixty miles from north to south, and comprises over 1,500,000 acres of grazing land, at an altitude of from 3,000 to 6,000 feet. The stock consists of 150 horses, 16,000 head of cattle and 200 thoroughbreds.—[Pioneer Press.

The attention of our readers is called to the astonishingly liberal campaign offer of the publishers of the Weekly Pioneer Press. It is proposed to send the Weekly Pioneer Press to any address in the United States or Canada, postage prepaid, for eight months for seventy-five cents. To those who are already subscribers to this excellent journal, it is unnecessary for us to extol its merits; but to those who are unfamiliar with its columns we would say that the Weekly Pioneer Press stands at the head and front of journalism in this country. For full and complete news and miscellany, interesting correspondence from all parts of the world, accurate and complete market reports, it is excelled by no weekly paper, East or West. Those subscribing now will receive the paper during the entire presidential campaign and until after the assembling of congress, next fall. We have made a clubbing arrangement which permits us to offer the Weekly Pioneer Press and the BAD LANDS COW BOY for eight months for $2.00, and confidently expect that nearly every man in the county will avail himself of this opportunity to secure their home paper and a first-class metropolitan paper for the small sum above named. This offer will be open until next September, and in order to cover the full campaign, subscriptions should be made at once.

Gone to get a bonus,
We're free from every care,
Happy is Medora,
Bramble's gone.
F. G. Allen made Medora a flying visit Tuesday.
Gustave Stoltze, the company's architect, was here yesterday.
C. F. Ellison returned Saturday from Dubuque and is now working for the company.
The company will begin putting up hay in a few days. The supply is far less abundant than it was last year.
Lloyd Roberts returned Tuesday morning with several car-loads of Minnesota three-year-old heifers for Wm. Dantz.
The weather lately has been of unmixed perfection. Sun-shine by day and rain by night has a tendency to make everyone happy.
The Eatons have moved to their new home ranch at the logging camp, where they will hererfter reside. Messrs. Tarbell and Bond are now living at the Custer Trail ranch.

Mr. Gallup, of New York, started for home last Monday. Like every other visitor here, he was firmly convinced that the Bad Lands are destined to be one of the greatest cattle raising sections of the United States. He expects to go into the cattle business himself.

Wm. M. Brewer, who has been here for several weeks, left yesterday morning for Bismarck. He will continue on from there to Pierre and thence to his home in Deadwood. "Billy" has made many friends here, but we don't blame him for thinking, "there's no place like home."

A solitary deer stood for a long time on the butte east of town, Tuesday evening, sharply outlined against the evening sky and doubtless wondering at the great change which had come over its old feeding ground in the last year. It is a wonderful change, and one typical of Medora's future.

D. K. Wade finished driving the cattle of the LeMoyne cattle company from Glendive to his range on Tepee bottom last Saturday. The trip was made overland by Mr. Wade and he was accompanied by his wife and daughter. The cattle are all high grades and are as good looking a lot as we ever saw.

One of the quickest jobs we have ever seen, is the building of the new freight house here. A still further force of men was added yesterday and the house will probably be ready for occupancy next week. Then the question as to which town shall be the freighting point, will be brought to a focus immediately. "What will poor Bramble do then."

We are not proud and will walk after this—when our choice is a bucker or no ride. We always thought it very funny to see a bronco buck, but will hereafter watch the wild gyrations with an awe-struck feeling of reverence at the unadulterated cussedness of the brute. It is needless to add that we have been bucked.

About two hundred and fifty teachers from the Madison convention came through here Monday evening, bound for the Yellowstone park and Alaska. The feminine portion of the excursion seemed to have a wonderful curiosity to see some cow-boys and we still have a dark suspicion that some of them were corralled here.

The unanimous report of all who have been down the road is that the crops, especially between here and Bismarck, are better than they have ever been. This is illustrated by specimens of wheat, oats and barley brought by Dr. Morton from his father's farm at South Heart and now on exhibition at this office. Specimens of oats also brought from South Heart by R. J. Jewell have double and triple heads eighteen inches long. Like Banquo's ghost, Dakota will not "down."

Bob Roberts returned Tuesday night from Bismarck, whither he had gone on business. During his absence, he was appointed U. S. commissioner to represent the Bad Lands at the World's fair, to begin at New Orleans next December. No better choice could have been made of commissioner, as Bob has already gone to work gathering petrifactions and other curiosities so numerous in the Bad Lands. Now is the time for each one to step forward and lend a helping hand to lighten the labors of our commissioner. He is thoroughly in earnest about showing the resources and natural curiosities of the Bad Lands to the world and should receive the willing assistance of every one.

The jolliest party that has yet visited the Bad Lands left last Monday evening for the National park and consisted of Mr. M. C. Eaton, of Irvington, N. Y., a relative of the Eatons here, Major O. H. Stevens, New York city and late master of transportation of the N. P. Yellowstone division and Wm. H. Shurtz, a young attorney of Newark, N. J. The party took in the prominent sights of the Bad Lands and were careful inquirers into the profits of cattle raising. It is their intention to put in a large herd soon. They were all confident of the great future of the Bad Lands and of Medora as a cattle centre. Their confidence in the feasibility of the Medora and Black Hills R. R. was backed by the fact that an abundance of capital could be found to complete it. The impression left by these gentlemen will long be favorably remembered, coupled with a hope for a repetion of the visit.

In company with Mr. Gallup, we took a very pleasant ride up the river Sunday. We were hospitably entertained at the Custer Trail ranch by Messrs. Tarbell and Bond and did full justice to Mrs. Lebo's bountiful dinner. At Sloping Bottom ranch we found a jolly company consisting of Mrs. J. L. Roberts and daughters, Misses Ubermann and Friedman and Messrs. Dantz, Friedmar, Tucker and several others. A cavalcade was formed and a ride to Tepee bottom with a pleasant call on Mr. and Mrs. Wade made an agreeable stopping point. The onward journey was through the Prairie-dog bottom and the saucy pertness of its ten thousand inhabitants was as comical as ever. Our journey's end was reached at Will Dantz' ranch, the unanimous opinion being that it was too pleasant and prosperous a home for Will to "bach" it any longer. On the return trip, Mrs. Roberts' "bread and milk supper" was found to consist of all the luxuries of the season and we continued our homeward journey at peace with all mankind.

[Since putting the above in type, we have learned that quite a serious loss has befallen Mr. Dantz. Tuesday, the river was very high and while crossing below Ferris & Merrifield's, the team became entangled in the harness and one was drowned almost immediately, the other dying soon afterward. During the struggle to release the horses, Will himself became entangled in the harness, and it was only by great good luck that he escaped drowning.]
