Thursday morning at four o'clock we started on, with "Spearfish or bust" filling all our minds. From the South Moreau, about twenty miles towards the Belle Fourche is the only gumbo on the route. We got through without any difficulty, however, and camped on Indian creek for dinner.

Soon after starting, a dark cloud began coming up in the west, its toad stool shape and threatening look portending a hard storm. The first couriers came in the shape of huge hail stones, averaging larger than a hen's egg. These were quickly followed by a hurricane of wind, rain and hail that soaked us completely through and in spite of heavy double blankets the hailstones left innumerable black and blue spots wherever they could hit. They came so thick and fast that it was utterly impossible to count the number of times a person was hit. From the size of a hen's egg at first the hailstones dwindled in size to that of a pea. The storm lasted over an hour and was the hardest we ever experienced.

About five o'clock we saw the first signs of human beings, except the E6 and Macy's that we had seen since leaving the brick yard at Medora. Coming to the top of a butte the valley of the Belle Fourche lay below us covered with farm houses and several small towns. We reached the new town of DeMores at 5:30 and were welcomed by D. C. Baker, who has built a good building and stocked it abundantly with grocery and general goods. Messrs. Guild and Gallop, who came to the Hills by way of Medora expect to build a railraod from DeMores to the Hay creek coal mines and it undoubtedly has a good fighting chance to become one of the best towns near the Hills.

Starting on at 7 o'clock we reached Spearfish at 10:30 and putting up at the Spearfish House, enjoyed the luxury of a splendid spring bed. Mr. Rogers, the proprietor, is a very popular hotel man, and he has been forced to build so many additions that he can scarcely tell his original building.

The morning of the 4th of July, all Spearfish had on its holiday clothes and in spite of the inevitable rain-storm, the parade and celebration were great successes.

Under the able guidance of Dr. Louthan and Maj. Snyder, we took in the town and surrounding country and were more than delighted with what we saw. Spearfish is located at the base of the northern Black Hills, near the eastern end of Spearfish valley,--a picture of loveliness. The whole valley is the very best agricultural land and irrigating ditches of magnificent spring water run all over it. Spearfish itself is a beautiful town of about eight hundred inhabitants and is one of the liveliest in the Hills country. The merchants are a wide-awake, generous lot of men, alive to every interest of their town. It is supported largely by stockmen and farmers and is bound to grow with the development of the country.

The morning of the 5th we started for Deadwood in one of Mr. Spear's stages, driven by Hank Monk, a fit descendant of the original. We had the honor of a share of Hank's seat and found him a regular encyclopedia of information. The first part of the ride was over the same agricultural country for which the Hills are famous. Many gypsum beds were seen, practically valueless now, but with railroad facilities it will become a valuable export, for use as a fertilizer and to be manufactured into plaster of paris. Falsebottom is a curious freak of nature that we crossed midway on our ride. It is the wide channel of a river but contains not a drop of water. A few miles above, there is a strong current that sinks gradually into the sand, continues its course underground and "bobs up serenely from below" several miles farther down. Soon we are in the Hills proper and now it is almost a continuous ascent to Deadwood, eight miles distant. The road-bed is a remarkably good one, although winding along at the foot and on the sides of Hills from four to eight hundred feet high. Everywhere, covering the sides and summits of the Hills has grown a dense forest of pine, closely resembling the Norway species. It is rather harder, thus improving its building properties. Except for the brick buildings, every house in the Black Hills region is built from these pine forests. The deep red waters of the streams attracted our attention. The discoloration is caused by the pulverized quartz hammered into powder by the stamps of the immense Homestake mills and others. The Homestake controls the water right of the Hills virtually, conducting it for many miles over mountains and gulches, by a system of ditches and flumes that is a triumph of engineering skill. This water is conducted to other mills than those of the Homestake system and thus a large royalty is made by them.

The trip through the Hills was a jolly one, the echoes fairly shouting back the refrain to "Hark, I hear a voice, way up in the mountain top," and many other college songs. Rounding a bend, we came upon the first miners we had seen, three Chinamen sluicing, at which we afterwards learned that they made, "sometime six bittee, sometime dolllah hap, when dig like hellee." No sooner had we passed these bias-eyed sons of toil than another bend brought Deadwood, the metropolis of the Hills in view.

The Cow Boy is much pleased to note the general satisfaction its legislative nomination is giving in Billings county and the hearty endorsement with which the selection of L. N. Cary is meeting. The Cow Boy is in no sense a political paper although as all our readers know it would be Republican, were there any use in a territorial paper mixing in national politics. We are thus the freer about upholding the candidate of our choice. Long before we had any idea of starting a paper in Medora, we remember that in a conversation with Mr. Cary, he spoke with much intelligence of the magnitude of Dakota's stock interests and of the necessity of fostering such a profitable industry. This conversation was remembered when we first heard Mr. Cary's name mentioned as a candidate and we straightway came out for the man who will certainly do as much as any one we know to look after stock interests. Billings county, as well as the whole west Missouri country can depend upon having an able representative if we send Mr. Cary to the legislature. In view of these facts it behooves Billings county to rally round the Cary flag as one man. Billings, being the junior county, certainly has no right nor desire to dictate to its neighbors, nor in this case will we stand dictation. Our man is straight, honest, politically clean and competent and Billings county's two votes will cheerfully be cast for L. N. Cary.

The stockmen of Mason county, in Texas, have furnished 20,000 cattle to the spring drive at an average of $15 per head, making the handsome sum of $300,000.--[Colorado L. S. Record.

The Missouri Pacific is now running its stock trains in seven sections almost daily. This means that about 4,000 head of cattle go north every evening, the value of which is not far from $125,000.--[Vinita (I. T.) Chieftain.

An enormous ranch in Mexico has just been purchased for $1,000,000 by a syndicate of English and Scotch speculators, of whom Lord Tweedmouth is one. It extends over sixteen hundred square miles.--[Breeder's Gazette.

The Denver papers report sales of some Iowa and Missouri heifers, ones and twos, in that city at prices ranging from $30 to $35 per head. Of course they were well graded up, and their off-spring from good bulls, will be valuable.--[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Wm. Blair, foreman of the Comanche Pool, came in yesterday, July 17th, with his face wreathed in smiles of satisfaction over the splendid outlook on the range. He says the calf crop is showing up equally as well as was ever anticipated, and that about 5,000 calves have been branded. Beeves are taking on fat rapidly, and the Pool will start a bunch of about 600 to Dodge City on the 31st inst.--[Barber Co. (Kan.) Index.

According to the last census two-thirds of the 11,000,000 or more of horses in this country are used for industial purposes, and almost 4,000,000, are employed almost solely to increase the enjoyment of the people. On an average of $250 each these driving horses have an aggregate value of $1,000,000,000--which is quite a sum.--[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The Swan Land and Cattle Company has purchased 450,000 acres of land from the Union Pacific Railroad Company, embracing all the alternate sections between Miser Station and a point near Fort Steele. This purchase will cover a large portion of the country now being ranged over by the company's cattle and give them a most magnificent property.--[Cheyenne L. S. Journal.

A new route for trail cattle is being extensively used this year by herds going to New Mexico, Colorado and the northwestern ranges. Crossing Red river at Doan's, they are driven over the old trail to the North Fork, and thence up that stream and the Sweetwater to a point a little above Mobeetie, where they cross over the ridge to the Canadian, which they follow up to New Mexico. This route furnishes grass and water in abundance and is free from the heavy and exasperating levies of toll on cattle by the Indians.--[Breeder's Gazette.

"Live stock shippers of the country are beginning to realize the fact that few of their number become rich men, and many are in the end impoverished, while with breeders the reverse is the case. No one save themselves seem responsible for this state of things, and if they desire to ruin themselves by overbidding for a chance to lose money on a producer's stock, they have a right to do so. Buying and shipping cattle is an industry closely allied to dealing in futures, and requires both caution and judgment beyond the possession of most men."--[Indian Chieftain.

Another bunch of 3,000 head of Texas ones, to fours, mixed cattle, belonging to the Continental Cattle Company, en route to Montana, passed through Brush last Thursday. This makes 10,000 head of the same grade of cattle belonging to the company, that have passed through Brush within the week. The cattle did look well, considering the fact that they had very short grazing for the first three weeks' drive, and the long march, but they could not be favorably compared with those which rode in the cars from Texas in eight days.--[Brush Lariat.

The present season has been an uncommonly favorable one for the stockmen of Montana. The loss of the past winter, severe as it was supposed to be, is very small, and the crop of calves is a prolific one. The grass and range conditions at this time are excellent, and there is little to worry the cattle kings. But judging by what we were told yesterday by an intelligent stockman, some disappointment is likely to result from the general short-sightedness in not providing a sufficient number of bulls for the range. This is true of all our ranges, and the sooner the matter is remedied the better it will be for the stockmen. Every year the cattle business here is becoming more systematic in management, and this is one of the items that requires some attention at present.--[River Press.

The cattle and horse market is gradually advancing, and to-day Texas cattle and stock horses are bringing better figures than they did thirty days ago. She cattle are in demand, with a very small number offered. Large sales of one and two year old steers have been made in the past few days at good round figures, yearlings selling at from $16 to $17, and two year olds at $19 and $20. A few buyers have been holding off with the expectation that prices would decline, and must now pay higher prices. The depression in the money market is virtually at an end, and money is quite free. New buyers are arriving daily, and large amounts of money are constantly changing hands. Out of the 15,000 horses that have been brought to this market, not over 2,000 are left. Saddle horses are bringing $50 to $60 and stock horses from $27 to $35. About 1,300 horses have been sold since Saturday.--[Colorado L. S. Record.

Miss Maude Reed has been located for five years on the Little Dolores. Coming from Sweden a poor girl, Maude launched out into the far West and started with a few head of cattle, and by strict attention, economy, and braving all the hardships of a frontier life, she is to-day one of the shrewdest and ablest cattle owners in Mesa county. Many is the gallant cowboy that has doffed his sombrero and bestowed his most devoted attentions upon fair Maude, but up to the present writing she is yet heart whole. Miss Maude owns 140 head of good grade cattle and an excellent ranch worth a snug fortune. All this she has accumulated by her own exertions and good business management. Being a fine horsewoman, she superintends the round-up, cutting out and branding of her own cattle each year, markets her beef and attends to her bank account with as much shrewdness as any accomplished cattle dealer. Rumor had it that the fair queen was to bestow her heart and hand on a neighboring stockman this last week, but it must be only a rumor, as she still refuses to bow to cupid's yoke. We sincerely wish her well, with all the success this life affords, and warn all book agents, editors and sky-pilots that travel that way with the idea of picking up a fortune, that the lady is credited with being a capital shot, and an ardent admirer of woman's rights.--[Montrose, Colo., Enquirer.

A large force of teams and men is out putting up hay.
Fred. Ertel and son Fritz, of Belfield, were in town Tuesday.
C. W. Sleeper started Monday for Duluth, on business for the company.
Delegate John B. Raymond passed through Medora on his way west last evening.
We are pleased to state that the team of mules stolen from A. von Steiger has been followed and recovered by him in Canada. Steiger is a stayer.
Mr. Garver, of Bismarck, a practical tin-smith, was here yesterday and this morning returned home. He will probably return soon and establish a tin-shop here.
Doc. Pennell returned last night from the Black Hills, where he had been to get twenty of Jones' Bros. mules. They are to be used on the Canadian Pacific road.
It is estimated that 2,000 cars of stock will be shipped from Beaver this fall. Telegraphic orders have been received to make arrangements for the shipment of this amount.
On account of the success of previous dances, it has been decided to hold one tomorrow evening at the new hall. Every one is invited and an enjoyable time is a matter of course.
Harry Tarbell and Chas. Eaton started for the Hills Monday, to look at a band of horses near Spearfish. If they come up to expectations they will be added to the Custer trail ranch band.
A Mr. Newton, arrived Monday from Ireland, having made the trip from there to Medora in just ten days. He is an acquaintance of Gregor Lang's and will spend some time at the Neimmela ranch.
Geo. Roderick and wife started for the Red river valley Tuesday morning. George has secured remunerative work for his teams there and will work during harvest, after which he will return here.

Chas. Jolly returned last Saturday from Sturgis, where he had gone to recover his horse. This horse strayed about two hundred and twenty-five miles and as Charlie says, would never have been recovered, had it not been for the Cow Boy.

About the quickest job on record of the kind, was that accomplished by Pat. O'Hara, yesterday. He began at eight o'clock to dig a well for the company at the stables and at three o'clock had a pump in, discharging the best water we have tasted for many a day.

Again has the sun risen and set on us. In other words, James Cook, Studebakers' agent for the northwest, has come and gone. "Jim" is one of the best men on the road, and what he doesn't know about making things agreeable, is a lost art. Come again and come often, Jim.

One thousand head of cattle were shipped in Sunday morning by Ferris & Merrifield and driven to their range seven miles up the river. They were one's and two's, half steers and half heifers, and are said to be the best lot of cattle shipped west this year.

The ice has been broken and Medora rejoices at the celebration of her first marriage ceremony. John Kiefer and Mary Jane Corcoran are the chief actors in this domestic drama, which we hope will run along smoothly and close with many recollections of a married life well and happily spent.

Mr. Hohnick, who is with Mr. Duryea's surveying party down the river, came in Sunday night for grub and mail. The party was sent out by the N. P. R. R. for the purpose of finding out what land it really owns and its prospective value. Considerable progress has been made, although the survey of the Bad Lands is attended with many difficulties.

It seems that Mr. Dennis Bramble has again been getting in his funny work on the freighters. Mr. Ford went to Belfield and got the promise of $1.75 for freighting. Yesterday he loaded for $1.50, preferring this rate to lying idle as it was all Bramble would give, after the freighters reached Belfield. "Thus doth the busy little B---- improve each shining hour." It is well for him that he does, for he won't have many more to improve. We wish to prophecy again that in less than three weeks Bramble has handled his last pound of freight over the Northern Pacific.

Vic Smith suffered a peculiar mishap last Monday morning which might easily have terminated fatally. While out hunting, about nine miles northeast of here, he had just killed a deer when his attention was directed to a band of mountain sheep. Just as he started after these the ground gave way and horse and rider were tumbled into an underground wash-out twenty feet deep. Vic was pinned to the ground for several hours but at last succeeded in extricating himself and getting the horse on its feet. Tying his lariat around the barrel of his gun and standing on the horse's back he made a lucky throw and lodged the gun across the apex of the V-shaped hole at the top. A walk of nine miles brought him to Medora, where a party was made up that soon rescued the imprisoned horse.

There are a few croakers in town who will be abated as nuisances if they don't stop their everlasting complaints. We wish it distinctly understood that there are no walls around the town and no string is tied to any resident. They certainly are not in earnest about their complaints or they would leave town. There is not a town on the Northern Pacific in which there is as much money circulating proportionately as in Medora and in which it is so easy to gain a living. The croakers know this but are contented to merely exist on the scraps that fall to their share. This gentry, happily few, had better get up and rustle, or immediately shake the dust of Medora from their feet.

The freight house is very near completion and will be entirely finished inside of a week. The floor is nearly all laid, the siding is on, a pretty and durable cornice has been added and the shingling will be finished in about five days. That this building, which will cost $6,000 and the side-track, costing as much more, have been built for fun, is absurd. Just as soon as preliminary arrangements can be made, the matter will have been settled beyond all doubt, and Medora will be the only point to receive Black Hills rates. Not only this, but we are in a position to know whereof we speak, when we state that the stage line will be on at the same time. A proposition has been made by the Marquis de Mores and accepted to have a stage line running as soon as possible. This we know.

Deadwood! What a flood of articles telling of hardships and affluence, misery and delirious joy, hope and despondency the sight of the city brought to our mind. Like every mining camp, the mines and miners about Deadwood have had their ups and down, but through it all, through fire and flood even, Deadwood, although twice almost swept out of existence, is still the queen city of the Hills, a bright gem sending forth its refreshing rays through the whole Hills country.

Deadwood gulch was discovered in November of 1876, by a number of miners who had come from Custer City to avoid the act of evictment which compelled all miners to leave the Hills by August 15, 1875, as the Hills was at that time a part of the Sioux reservation. The ground upon which Deadwood now stands was located under the name of Lost District and all up and down Deadwood gulch were located placer mines which have yielded enough money for a circulating medium as large as that of the United States. Fortunes of hundreds of thousands of dollars were taken out of a space scarcely larger than a grave, while the claims on either side might not furnish even enough disappointed hopes with which to line it.

In spite of the fact that the Sioux treaty was not ratified until February of 1877, Deadwood city was laid out in April, of 1876. Several curious complications have arisen in respect to the title of the lands, as mining claims everywhere take precedence and the only legal and binding title is a bed rock title deeded to a purchaser from the original locator of the mineral claim. No man without this title is safe for a moment as his whole property is liable to be located at any time and sluiced down stream piecemeal, leaving the house standing on stilts on a quartz vein for instance, which in turn is liable to be located as a quartz claim and a shaft hundreds of feet deep sunk directly under the house. This of course is a hypothetical case but one likely to happen at any time, unless a man has bought a placer title on bed rock, which is known not to contain a quartz lead.

Deadwood deserves a far longer description than we can possibly give it, and our article must in any event be inadequate. No words can do justice to the wonderful enterprise that has built up homes and fortunes in this rugged country. Deadwood is about 185 miles from Medora, the nearest railroad point in the United States. Every solitary article that could not be manufactured in the Hills, had to be shipped this distance or a greater one, on wagons. It would certainly be expected then, that the citizens of Deadwood and the Hills get along with as few of the necessities of life as possible and do not indulge at all in the luxuries. Never was a greater mistake made. The most particular dude of New York can have every want satisfied as readily in Deadwood as he can in his native haunts.

From the narrowness of the gulch, Deadwood can never become a beautiful city, but it would be a monument to the ability of any people. One can never believe that the whole city was virtually hauled in on wagons and almost instinctively listens for the shriek of the locomotive which has so long eluded the hearing of the Hills people, but which must and soon will be heard there.

Deadwood now contains about [4,000?] inhabitants, almost all of whom are prosperous and many have large fortunes. It has all the appearance of a live eastern town, although there is no town of its size in the United States that does an equal amount of business. There are a number of pretentious brick business blocks and many dwellings which would be an ornament to any city. Two daily papers, the Pioneer and Times are ably and successfully maintained. To Dolph Edwards, editor of the Pioneer, we are indebted for much of the pleasure of our stay and no one could have more thoroughly impressed us with the resources of the Hills. He is emphatically the right man in the right place.

Deadwood has as good a system of water works as can be found in the United States, a telephone system extending to every town in the Hills and not satisfied with this, almost every place of business is brilliantly illuminated with electric lights. The sewerage of the city is excellent. Two streams of pure spring water flow in the gutters of Main street, and keep the city in first-class sanitary condition. Much to our surprise, we found Deadwood to be as orderly a city as we ever visited. Not a six-shooter did we see worn openly during our entire stay. Mayor Star and city Marshal Tyler have put a stop to all such foolishness as "painting the town red." With the concluding remark that Deadwood's annual business transactions amount to considerably over $200,000,000, we will leave the subject to some one who has more space at his disposal and more ability to do the subject justice.

The astuteness of some of our exchanges verges on omniscience. The latest we have seen, however, is "the chief." Two or three papers have found out the true reason of Theodore Roosevelt's visit to the Bad Lands—that he will make a strong fight for congress in our present delegate's place. If any common sense had been used by the writers of the articles referred to, they would see that the principal reason for Mr. Roosevelt's presence here is to get away from politics altogether. Other reasons are, that he has a large amount of money invested in cattle here, and that he enjoys hunting more than the dirt of New York's political mud puddle.

We cannot help a feeling of satisfaction over the way in which our nomination of L. N. Cary for the legislature has been received. That he is by all odds the most available man, there is no doubt. That there is a rapidly growing sentiment in his favor is also manifest. Morton county is so full of cliques and factions that it is hard to crystallize the sentiment about any one candidate, but we are assured by a gentleman who is in a position to know, that Mr. Cary is by far the most popular candidate and that he is growing in strength every day. Our informant has personal prejudices in favor of another candidate, but acknowledges that he is engaged in a hopeless fight and that Mr. Cary will win on his merits. It would be hard work to throw a club in Mandan without hitting a candidate's head and the number has been increased by several tenderfeet who think that the voters here will be so dazzled by their glittering intellectuality that their candidacy can only mean success. This gentry will get most beautifully left. It is a matter of surprise that the Mandan papers have not as yet brought out their candidates but we suppose they will in time yield to the popular will, sufficiently to acknowledge the merits of our candidate.

One day last week a commission firm at the Yards received and sold 231 cars of cattle. This unquestionably is the largest number of cattle ever sold by one firm in a single day.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Fat cattle are 50@75c higher than a year ago, while common grades are nearly that much lower. Last year at this time Texans were selling at $3.50@5.00, which is fully $1.00 above present prices.—[Breeder's Gazette.

A pool of all the cattlemen holding between the Cimarron and Canadian river, in Oklahoma, has been formed. It is composed of seven outfits, and will contain, when stocked up to the limits, 50,000 cattle under its control. A board of seven directors was elected, and on August 1st a full set of officers, consisting of president, treasurer, secretary and pool boss. The ranchmen turned all their stock into the pool in their own brands and then put the pool brand on in addition thereto. The pool pays all expenses by assessment pro rata with the number of cattle held by each member. To 1,000 cattle, one man and eight horses are turned in. The annual pay roll and expense bill on the pool plan will be cut down over seventy-five per cent, as under the pool plan twenty-five men and 150 horses will do the work that it now takes over seventy-five men and 500 horses to accomplish. The name is to be Cimarron and Canadian Pool. As the brand has not been decided upon yet, we are unable to give it, but it is very probable that the brand of the pool will appear in these columns soon.—[Caldwell (Kan.) Journal.

W. A. Towers, of Towers & Gudgell, Colorado and Montana ranchmen, was married last week at Decatur, Georgia, to Miss Fannie Hillyer, daughter of Judge Junius Hillyer. Mr. Towers is one of the pioneer Texas cattle drovers, and one of the most popular and well known stockmen in the range country. We extend best wishes and congratulations.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

Year by year mere weight counts for less and less in determining the value of cattle in the Chicago and other great markets. Quality and degree of fatness determine value much more than weight. A farmer or shipper will make a great mistake if he attempts to fix a price on his cattle from the prices made by other lots of about the same weight. Other things being equal, animals of good size command the highest prices, but well-formed and well-fattened steers weighing 1,200 lbs. outsell rough and poorly-fattened ones 200 lbs. heavier. Remarkably large cattle are not preferred by any class of buyers over those of medium weights.—[Breeder's Gazette.

We see by the Texas papers that Mr. Scott, of Colorado, Texas, shipped a lot of about a hundred calves to Chicago, and sold them to the butchers at $5 a hundred, netting to the shipper $7 a head. These calves were taken from old cows on the range so as to allow them to get fat for fall shipment to markets. The cows will bring ready money, but not much of it. It seems to us that these calves, if allowed to run with their mothers until winter would have been worth more to the head than the amount realized from the transaction. Some of the old cows might die, but the chances for their living and raising one to three more calves are fully equal to the chances of death during the winter. We think the policy bad. Hold all your calves and get all you can honestly, if you want to prosper in the cow business.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

There is a mania just now to go into the business of raising stock, and there is danger that it may be over done. Not that the capacity of the pasturage will be unequal to all the cattle that may be brought into New Mexico, but the supply of water may not be sufficient during a severely dry season. The meat question is becoming an important one in the United States, as it has been for centuries in all densely populated countries. The cheap beef of the past will never be known again in America. This does not result alone from the fact that consumption increases, but more particularly because the area of production is constantly diminishing. Lands hitherto devoted to pasture are constantly being taken up for homes and devoted to the production of the necessaries of life other than meat. Hence it has become necessary to occupy and utilize every inch of ground for pasture that is not adapted to growing fruits, vegetables and cereals.—[Santa Fe, New Mexico, Review.

The cowboys are a much misrepresented set of people. It is a popular impression that when one goes among them he must be prepared to shoot. But this is a false idea. I have taken part with them in the rounding up, have eaten, slept, hunted and herded cattle with them, and have never had any difficulty. If you choose to enter rum shops with them or go on drinking sprees with them it is as easy to get into a difficulty out there as it would be in New York, or anywhere else. But if a man minds his own business and at the same time shows that he is fully prepared to assert his rights—if he is neither a bully or a coward and keeps out of places in which he has no business to be, he will get along as well as in Fifth avenue. I have found them a most brave, and hospitable set of men. There is no use in trying to be overbearing with them for they won't stand the least assumption of superiority, yet there are many places in our cities where I should feel less safe than I would among the wildest cowboys of the west.—[Interview with Theodore Roosevelt in New York Tribune.

There is a universal complaint among cattlemen this year about the shortage in the calf crop. This question is a matter of vital importance, and one that should have the first consideration in the minds of our cattlemen. Various reasons have been given to explain the short crop, but there is but one that will explain the reasons, and that is a scarcity of bulls. On the ranges where the number of bulls have been sufficent and in proportion to the number of cows on the range there has been very little complaint, and the calves branded have been up to the usual number. The reason for all this trouble of an insufficient number being on the range is due to cattlemen turning their cows on the range and relying on their neighbor's bulls to bring him his calf crop, thinking he can save money by so doing, and the result is that his neighbor, who has only a sufficent number for his own use, falls short as well as the other. This is nothing more or less than robbery, and the guilty man should be brought up and tried for larceny on the same grounds as if he went to his neighbor's corral and drove off a number of cattle. In Colorado the legislature has seen the evil result of this matter, and has passed a law requiring a man to have four bulls to every hundred cows he possesses. This is a just and equal protection to all men, and a subject to which the legislature of this territory should give attention and pass a like law, and then, and not until then, will this complaint of a small calf crop be at an end.—[Springer Stockmen.

Mr. J. E. Cates, editor of the Mandan Times, dropped in on us Tuesday.
The pay-car has distributed its monthly quota of financial happiness.
R. Grymes, of New York has been engaged by the company to assist in the offices.
Railroad time between St. Paul and Portland is soon to be shortened twelve hours.
Bob. Roberts and E. G. Paddock are building a cottage on the former's lot opposite the new hall.
There will be a dance at the Hotel de Mores, the evening of the 22nd, given by Johnny Fitzgerald. Everyone is invited.
Mr. Turner, of Chicago, arrived here Tuesday evening, to superintend the slaughtering of a bunch of cattle for the Chicago market.
Miss Friedman started for Mandan last Saturday morning, with many regrets at terminating her pleasant visit to Sloping bottom ranch.
Abe Goodkind, of Bismarck, was in town yesterday, attending to the business of Wise & Goodkind. His stops here are always profitable.
All the outfits now making hay report that it is very scarce. There has been an abundance of rain lately, but it was not in time to give the grass a new start.
The Marquise de Mores, Miss Thomas and Mr. and Mrs. Whitmore, of New York and Mr. Harck, of Germany, came in Friday night on the Marquis' car, Montana.
M. T. Smith and H. Gould have taken up several head of horses, branded J on left shoulder. The owner can have the same by proving property and paying charges.
The freight house is nearly completed, the roof looking like a harvest field on account of the bundles of shingles looming up against the vast yellow background of the roof.
Wishart's outfit came in Tuesday with Rassie Deffebach's wife, children and household effects. Rassie has rented the first cottage east of the new hall and will hereafter call Medora his home.

Tommy Jones took two car-loads of cattle to Duluth for the company the first of the week and will continue on to the Canadian Pacific to assist Joe Pennell and T. G. Jones on their railroad contracts there.

There is a prairie fire somewhere near us and we would caution all persons who start them that the advertisement on our first page means business and that a little carelessness is liable to land a person in the penitentiary.

Three hundred and fifty stock cars have been ordered into Dakota and Montana for this and next week's shipment of cattle to the eastern markets. This represents over $300,000, the most of which will be immediately turned into stock again.

We received a very pleasant call from Theodore Roosevelt, of New York, last Monday. He has established another ranch about thirty miles down the river, stocked it and put it in charge of Wm. Seawall and Wm. McDow. He intends soon taking a long hunt in the Big Horn region.

The school is now running in good shape under the direction of Dan. Williams. The funds are all furnished by subscription, however, and some of the subscribers have not come to time. The list is in the hands of Wm. Vandriesche, to whom all subscriptions should be paid immediately.

The dance last Friday night was an occasion long to be remembered by the lovers of a good time. There is no better hall west of Fargo and each participant made the best of the opportunity. Mrs. Ertel and Miss Dallie, of Belfield were present, besides Miss Friedman, Lloyd and Mrs. Roberts from up the river.

Archibald Morton, of South Heart was in town Monday. The two teams stolen from him some time since have not been recovered but hope is not by any means given up. Mr. Morton offers a reward of $150 for their return. A full description of the horses and the men who undoubtedly stole them will be furnished by Dr. Morton, of Medora.

We doubt if there is a paper in Dakota more widely known than the Cow Boy. Since our first issue we have never met a man who has not read it, and there is scarcely a copy sold that does not do double duty here before it is sent to eastern friends. A good illustration of its circulation is furnished by a letter written to George Fitzgerald from an old friend in a small Hills mining camp, who saw his advertisement in our paper. Another illustration is the fact that we figured on two hundred and fifty subscribers at the end of the year and now, before our paper is six months' old, we have a bona fide circulation of five hundred and twenty copies and not a solitary deadhead on our list. This number may seem small to our eastern readers, but we make the assertion now and will compare books at any time with any paper between Fargo and Helena to prove our assertion that we have more cash subscribers than any paper between these points.
James Dilley, of Bismarck, is in Medora and will doubtless make up his mind to stay. He will be a welcome addition to our citizens.
Peter Book has now on hand 100,000 of the best pressed brick in the territory. He can and will sell them at rates that defy competition.

The following extracts from a letter written in Belfield sound rather discouraging when contrasted with the letters written from there to other papers down the line. We hope the Belfield folks will take the advice of one of her fair citizens: "Stick to it and you will wear diamonds—right from Alaska."

"There has been some freight shipped from here to the Black Hills but so far, the freight-line has proven the most over-estimated thing in existence. Stud-tables have been put in at the saloons which are decidedly conspicuous by the absence of players. True, a few new faces are seen hereabouts and even a few town lots have been sold, but that said, all said. There is a something lacking and that something is entire lack of confidence, both in the town-site company and the freight line. Meantime, everyone is watching the movements of the Black Hills freight as one does the thermometer, hoping for the best but fearing for the worst at all times. This is the status of affairs at this writing and though perhaps bad medicine, is the truth."

No account of the Hills is complete without a description of the Homestake mines. Like Deadwood and the whole Hills country, however, the subject is almost beyond description. To the one who has not been in the Hills our account may furnish some matters of interest. To the one acquainted with the Hills our account will be manifestly weak. To the former we would say, go and see for yourselves. To the latter, skip our description.

Lead City, where the Homestake system of mines is located, is three miles south of Deadwood. The road winds through the hills and is a constant ascent of 500 feet to the mile. Everywhere, from the bottom of the gulches to the highest peaks, are seen the inevitable prospect holes, telling of labor lost or fortunes won. One cannot help a feeling of sadness when thinking of the poor devil who has spent his last cent or run into debt for a "grub stake" and then seen it fade away, with no chance of getting another. These very holes, however, are the foundations of the most colossal fortunes ever made in mining. The first man who located on the Homestake vein tried repeatedly to sell out a half interest for a "grub stake," and finally succeeded in selling out for a mere trifle.

The Homestake system now comprises the following locations: The Homestake, Golden Star, Highland, Deadwood-Terra and Father De Smet. Besides these all have mines attached which now belong to the Homestake system. The first mine on the Deadwood-Lead road is the Homestake mine proper, and it, with the tunnels and works attached, will serve as specimens of all.

First, let us get into the car and run along the level track, right into the heart of the mountain, and thank fortune if you can find as good a guide as Dolph Edwards proved to us. The air outside is exceedingly warm, but that of the tunnel is delightfully cool. The car dashes along at a high rate of speed amid a deafening noise and Stygian darkness. Suddenly we come to a halt, couple on to some ore cars and immediately shoot back into the light of day. A careful investigation of the ore at the entrance of the tunnel reveals to our tenderfooted senses the fact that our knowledge of geology is wonderfully deficient. But, as Dolph never lies, we are compelled to believe that this brown, worthless looking rock is the valuable ore out of which the largest gold-mining company in the world is stamping out gigantic fortunes. Next we visit the shaft house, step into a cage, and before we think we have gone twenty feet we are 400 feet down. And now begins an interminable wandering through a dense tangle of props, stopes, drifts and chambers, in which we would have been certainly lost had it not been for Joseph Trewerk, who is as much at home in this underground city as he is on the streets of Lead. This system of propping was to us the most wonderful thing about the whole mine. Imagine logs about eight feet long, built into stories forming a cube of over 300 feet and a faint idea can be gained of a small part of the propping needed in only one mine of the Homestake system. Mile after mile of this wooden tunnelling did we traverse, and then we only saw a small fraction of the whole amount. Coming suddenly to the shaft we again stepped into the cage, and in a trice were again on the ground level.

From the shaft house we went to the stamp mills, guided by the sullen roar that grew louder and louder until when we were fairly inside the mill the crash was so deafening that we could by no possibility make each other hear, except by yelling at the top of our voices directly into the listener's ear.

To retrace our steps a little we will state that under the perfect superintendence of Samuel McMasters everything is reduced to an exactness unparalleled anywhere. The principle of the work is to have as little lifting as possible. Every step in the work takes one to a lower level, and the handling of the ore is done on the dumping plan. After it is blasted out it is loaded on the cars and carried to huge crushers, into which it is dumped, and comes out in chunks about as large as one's fist. Chutes conduct these lumps under the stamps, where it is pounded as fine as powder. A constant stream of water carries this powder through seives and over quicksilver tables that seize greedily upon the gold and let the rest slide over. The water comes thence thick and red, and for the rest of its existence performs no service except to discolor the beautiful running waters of Whitewood creek.

The Homestake railroad is by no means the smallest item in the system. The road is a narrow-gauge, twenty miles long, and was built solely for the purpose of bringing wood to the mines. That it well fulfills its purpose was shown by a modest pile of cord wood at least a 150 high and 300 feet in diameter at its base.

Leaving Lead and walking across the mountain to Terraville, Central and Gayville, we wandered down Deadwood gulch over sluiced mines that had yielded up many fortunes of glittering dust and regaled by the stories of Mr. Edwards, who thoroughly knew and had many reminiscences of every claim clear to Deadwood.

One of the most interesting young men in the West just now is the Marquis de Mores, son-in-law of the New York banker von Hoffman. Two years ago this summer vague little paragraphs began to be seen in the Bismarck and other Western papers about a handsome young Frenchman who was buying vast acreages of grazing land out on the Little Missouri river, and offering in a Quixotic way to furnish everybody who came along a hundred sheep to keep on shares. Everybody thought another Count Joannes had arisen and wandered out here. It took the best part of a year to convince people that De Mores was a sane man with money and purpose. This now needs no argument to prove. The young Frenchman has laid the foundation of a fortune which will rival that of Von Hoffman himself. At first it was his intention to simply raise cattle. He then discovered that there was no systematic shipments of Montana beef to the Eastern markets. Hotels in Fargo and Bismarck, with the fine young Montana cattle right at their doors, were paying 35 or 40 cents a pound for Chicago steaks. The reason of this absurdity was that no one could buy cattle in either of those towns in less than car load lots. Montana steers were shipped on to Chicago, were slaughtered and the dressed meat shipped back. De Mores decided to remedy this by establishing abattoirs along the North Pacific railroads at points where stockmen could drive their cattle in easily from the ranches. To complete the system he would erect refrigerating storehouses in every town where the beef demand warranted it. With refrigerating cars plying between slaughter houses and distributing points fresh meat could be furnished customers regularly at prices 50 per cent. lower than the old way.

De Mores has carried out this plain. He owns a dozen ranches, and has built abattoirs at Medora, Billings, Miles City and Helena. These houses are in full operation. Refrigerators have been built at St. Paul, Duluth and Fargo, and others are being put up at Granger, Mandan and Winnipeg.

Incidentally to the scheme the pretty little town of Medora has been built up at the Northern Pacific crossing of the Little Missouri. A freight line to the Black Hills has been established, which is always a source of rapid growth in these frontier trading posts.

Medora was named after the wife of De Mores, Medora Moffman, who is the namesake of her aunt, the famously beautiful Medora Grimes. Her memory is freshened by the reminiscences of the late Sam Ward, who won her for his second wife when she was already the betrothed of a rich young Frenchman. The Marquise de Mores delights in sharing the wild life of her husband. In St. Paul she is the most richly and tastefully dressed woman you will see. On the plains she rides and shoots faultlessly. Galloping over the prairie, an eagle plume in her hat and a rifle slung from her saddle, she is the picture of a wild beauty. De Mores on the frontier dresses in fringed buckskin shirts, top boots and a cowboy hat. In St. Paul he is a polished French gentleman, openhearted, witty, hospitable. The Marquise has an income of $90,000 a year from a fortune which has been secured by her father beyond all possibility of loss. De Mores has 18,000 acres of farming lands along the Northern Pacific, besides vast estates—in France and Italy.—[Cheyenne Leader.

In the next issue of the Cow Boy will appear a call for a meeting of Bad Lands stockmen for a permanent organization. The need of such an organization is too pressing to need argument. Let each stockman make up his mind that he is personally interested in the movement and we will have an organization that must result in mutual good. We need unity of action on many points, and this is the only means by which it can be secured.

Advices from Cottonwood Aug 3, states that a courier just arrived from near the mouth of the Mussel Shell, reports that Granville Stuart's cowboys have a large band of horse thieves surrounded. The band is too strong to be taken but can be held till help comes. Reinforcements left Cottonwood Sunday. Hot times are expected.—[Pioneer Press.

One or two alleged enterprising western newspaper correspondents have within the past day or two been trying to work themselves and the public into an unnecessary lather over the death of a number of cattle, attributed to the so-called Texas fever. Careful investigation at the stock yards, fails to show any cases of Texas fever or symptoms of the same, nor have there been any. The cattle claimed to have been affected with Texas fever, and which are said to have passed through the Kansas City stock-yards, did not exhibit any symptoms of the disease while here.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

Mr. Charles E. Leonard, a well known breeder of polled cattle, has a theory that in breeding cattle on the range none but throughbred bulls should be used, and that they should not be allowed to run at large except during the few weeks in the mating season. During that time, which lasts not more than six weeks, cow band should be kept "close herded," and the bulls feed daily and cared for. In this manner each cattle-breeder would be compelled to buy his own bulls, and not shirk the expense upon his neighbor. Said Mr. Leonard: "By this method the calf crop would be increased at least ten per cent. in number and twenty-five per cent. in value over the old way of doing."—[Montana Stock and Mining Journal.

And now, referring to the cowboy for the last time, good authority says he is rapidly outgrowing the maliguings of his biographers. "Much if not all the deviltry credited to cowboys should really be charged to refugees from eastern states, who ape the cowboys' free and easy ways, and copy his faults and forget his virtues. These hard cases are being rapidly thinned out. As for the real cowboy, it is only natural, after months on a ranch, often cold, wet and hungry to a degree that would kill a less tenacious individual, that when he comes to town he should seek a little excitement. There is no refined or cultured amusement to be had. He drinks and gambles and dances. He is noisy when drunk, and the gambler cheats him all the time, but, taken when sober, he is industrious, and above doing a mean act. If any of your friends underwent his privations they would nauturally want about the same kind of a frolic."—[St. Louis Globe Democrat.

The Montana Stock-Growers' Association held its annual meeting at Helena, July 29th. The following officers were elected: President, Granville Stuart; treasurer, J. P. Woolman; secretary, R. B. Harrison. Members were present from all portions of the territory representing cattle herds aggregating over half a million head. In view of the ravages of stock thieves, the Association decided to use its influence for the election of members to the Legislature who will work for the passage of a law to afford stock interests better protection from theives. The Association will urge a reduction of the Indian reservations in Montana, which comprise 20,000,000, acres of grazing land or about 6,000 acres to each Indian. They indignantly deny the statement current in Manitoba, the Dominion of Canada, and throughout the United States, that cattle herds of Montana are affected with foot-and-mouth disease.—[Breeder's Gazette

Frequent mention has been made of the large profits realized by some of the companies engaged in the cattle raising business in the west, and the organizers of these companies have in some instances made large fortunes. We find the following in the Tribune of this city: "The Prairie Cattle Company, which has three ranges in Colorado and New Mexico, and owns over $4,500,000 worth of cattle, is a Scotch organization. It was organized by the firm of Underwood, Clark & Co., of Kansas City, Mo., who stipulated with the Scotch stockholders to manage the American business without remuneration on condition that if the stock should pay dividends equal to the capital on or before ten years, then Underwood, Clark & Co. should receive three-eighths of the capital stock of the company. The company has now been in existence for four years, and dividends have been declared equal to 90 per cent. of the capital. It is evident to the Scotchmen that before another year they will be called upon to give up the three-eigths of the stock, according to agreement, and they don't like it. The stockholders don't fancy giving away $1,500,000 of stock which pays a dividend of 20 per cent. per annum and are now kicking and complaining."—[Nat. L. S. Journal.

There will be a convention of the Republican voters of Billings county at Medora, Saturday evening, August 16, at 7 o'clock, in Medora hall, for the purpose of electing two delegates to the Pierre convention.
J. C. [Fisher?], Chairman County Central Committee.

Fred Ertel, of Belfield, was in town Monday.
Mollie Coleman has gone to Sentinel Butte for a short stay.
The Marquis de Mores left for St. Paul yesterday morning in his special car.
Bob Roberts started out yesterday to locate the stations for the stage line.
Several bunches of cattle have been bought for slaughtering at the abattoir here.
Phelix Ingram, of Deadwood, made us a visit Monday. He is on the hay contract at Fort Meade.
Mike Coleman has taken a bunch of the company's cattle to Duluth. He will return in a few days.
It will be a great favor to us if any of our subscribers can return us copies of the Cow Boy of June 26 and July 17.
The N. P. Ref. Car Co. are slaughtering at their Duluth abattoir, having some large contracts to fill from that point.
Dr. W. B. Coyle, of Spearfish, was in town Monday on a prospecting tour. He intends settling somewhere on the Northern Pacific.
James M. Cook is getting to be one of the boys here. His visits are looked for as are summer rains. He left us Tuesday morning after a short visit.
Mr. Kaufman, a contractor of Sims, was in town Tuesday on business. He has the contract for two business houses in Belfield, which will be erected immediately.
Dan McKenzie came up from Belfield last evening, where he has established a [blacksmith?] shop. He will remain here for the [present?], while his partner will run the Be[lfield?] shop.

Baron von Hoffman arrived Monday evening for a [prolonged?] stay at Medora. He is thoroughly [impressed?] with the fact that the Bad Lands ar[e] [illegible] wonderfully good [illegible] lands, and intends to be[come?] more thoroughly acquainted with th[em?].

Frederick Billings, formerly [illegible] president of the Northern Pacific and now [illegible] president of the Oregon Navigation company, came through on a special with his family last Monday. The party made a short stop here as guests of the Marquis.

H. M. Jorgens, of Spearfish, was here the first of the week and returned Monday evening. He will return immediately with a good drug stock, and our citizens can congratulate themselves upon securing another valuable citizen.

T. J. Kerr, traveling auditor for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co., came up from St. Paul last Saturday night. He leaves to-morrow for Helena, when he will return east, auditing the accounts of the various offices on the line.

Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, accompanied by two sisters, arrived in Medora on last evening's train, and held mass at Geo. Fitzgerald's this morning. He called on the Marchioness, who assured him that within three weeks operations will have commenced on the new church.

A contract for the erection of two brick cottages has been awarded by the Marquis to Pete Book. The same contractor has been asked to furnish plans and specifications for a handsome little church 18x40, to be built of brick, on which work will be begun as soon as same are submitted and accepted.

Mr. W. F. Van Driesche, cashier and book-keeper for the company at this point has the consent of the Marquis to establish and conduct a general banking business in connection with his office. This is a private investment of William's, having no connection whatever with the company's affairs, and we would remind our citizens of this fact lest the temptation to ask "charity favors" bear too heavily on our young banker. He expects to be ready for business in about a week.

Mr. C. W. Sleeper, the irrepressible and indefatigable vice-president of the company left for Duluth on the Marquis' special yesterday morning. The editor was also one of the party, as the writer (not said editor) will testify from having seen the porter and train men extricating the Cow Boy from a central position in the double sash window in the end of the car, through which in the exuberance of his feelings he had pirouetted. As the fragments of glass were fortunately not small nor inquisitive he said he experienced no pain from sitting down. As a rule newspaper men are invulnerable in that portion of their anatomy.

Moody and Sankey, two of the best known and most popular cowboys in this section of the country and who are artists that can't be excelled in throwing the lariat, arrived in Medora Tuesday evening. It will be remembered that the boys made an engagement with the Rocky Mountain show in the early part of the season. They have been traveling throughout the east, showing the tenderfeet how to jerk a Texas steer in royal style. The show collapsed a short time ago while they were exhibiting in Chicago. They were doing a big business, but the manager, Tom Hardwick, thought it would be more profitable to bust than to pay the employes their salaries. The Indians and their interpreter were left penniless, and had to sell their stock to secure money to pay their transportation back to the reservation. This same individual is now in Bismarck endeavoring to organize another company.

The Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company is about to indulge in a series of improvements that is destined to almost revolutionize the meat trade of the west. Besides the magnificent buildings at Duluth, St. Paul and elsewhere, many additional ones will be built. What interests us most, however, is the improvement that will be made here at Medora. The present abattoir and cooling rooms are entirely insufficient for the needs of the company, and will be torn down to make room for buildings capable of containing the operations of killing and cooling five hunhred head of cattle a day. It will be one of the largest, if not the largest, slaughter-house for cattle in the world, and will be built entirely of brick. The old house will be left standing for the fall trade and the new one will be in full running order for next summer's trade. In addition to this, the company will drive up 20,000 head of cattle into the Bad Lands and fatten them for their own use. There is no question that range beef does and will sell equal to corn-fed beef, aud from our slaughter-house it can be laid down in Chicago at from three-quarters to a cent a pound cheaper than any other beef. This is an immense profit, and guarantees the company in making its vast expenditures. The trade in Minneapolis and St. Paul alone amounts at present to more than seventy-five head a day, and this is only a drop in the bucket to the market to be opened. Medora, as the headquarters of this gigantic system and the terminus of the freight and stage line, has a future opened up to it that is sure to place it among the first of the Northern Pacific towns.
The Medora Forwarding and Stage Co.

Now that the matter has gone thus far we will say that by the time this paper reaches the public everything will probably have been bought for the stage line. Messrs. Deffenbach and and Barr, armed with the ready cash, are after the stock and stages, and "ye editor" has deserted his sanctum temporarily and gone to St. Paul to close the final contracts which will put the Medora Forwarding and Stage Company in running order. Not a moment will now be lost, and we can assure our readers thot there is no room for doubt that in three weeks at the outside a well-equipped tri-weekly stage line will be running between Medora and the Hills. For some time past Bob. Roberts has been putting up hay along the line, and a large force is now at work building stations, barns, corrals, etc. The freight house, capable of holding 225 carloads of freight, is all complete except the finishing touches, and nothing will be lacking to make our route the most perfect in the west.

This is no place to discuss the delay in putting on the stages. Suffice it to say that there were good and sufficient reasons for the delay, and that the present certainty is due solely to the liberality of the Marquis de Mores.

Of the great benefit this line will be we need not speak, as it is apparent to all. It will furnish the shortest, most comfortable and incomparably the best line into the Hills. It will speak for itself.

There are so many points of interest in the Black Hills that it seems we have entered upon a hopeless task in attempting to describe them all. Before we finish, however, we must speak of Bear Gulch's tin and gold mines.

Bear Gulch proper is almost west of Spearfish and almost touching the Wyoming line. It is about 5,000 feet higher than Spearfish, and the road is as far from being a boulevard as anything we can imagine. Granite and quartz formations are constantly cropping out in the road-bed., making it very rough. There is a constant ascent all the way, except an equally as bad descent on the opposite slope of the hills. All the way there is a dense forest of lofty pines, which furnished a delightfully cool shade. We pass Potato and Beaver creek camps, noted as the scenes of successful sluice mining, and finally arrive at Bear Gulch camp and the Nigger Hill mining property. Here we stopped for dinner, and were hospitably entertained by Mr. St. John. The leaders of our party, Messrs. Johnston and Grassfield, of Spearfish, were old miners here and were thoroughly competent to show us all the points of interest.

The best and most property belongs to the Nigger Hill mining company, and but for the difficulty and expense of shipping in machinery, would vie with the Homestake system in its bi-weekly output. At present the mines are unworked. Sand creek, just over the Wyoming line, may be seen from the summit of Nigger Hill, and has also furnished profitable sluice mining. One of the largest nuggets taken from Sand creek weighs about $300, and is now owned by Mrs. Chapman. The ledges of gold ore here present about the same external appearance as those of the Homestake system, and our description will be confined mainly to the tin mines recently discovered here.

These mines were discovered by accident, through sluice-mining. Everyone has heard of the notorious black sand, the curse of sluicers. It is a very coarse sand, or fine gravel, of great specific gravity, and would be caught by the riffles in the sluice boxes as readily as gold dust. This occasioned much difficulty to the miners, both in panning and retorting, and has probably caused more dubious language than any other one obstacle. No one knew or seemed to care what was the composition of this black sand until some genius had it analyzed, and the mining world was electrified by the discovery that it was about 80 per cent. pure tin. The discovery of tin ore running from 3 to 30 per cent. followed immediately upon this, the discovery creating intense excitement.

The value of this find can best be determined by analogy. All, or virtually all, the tin in the world now comes from the Cornwall mines in England. At present these mines are [being operated?] at great depth and three miles out under the English channel. The expense of mining is consequently very large. The ore in the Cornwall mines runs from ⅓ to 1 per cent., and gigantic fortunes have been made in these mines. They have at present a monopoly of the tin trade of the world.

A glance at the difference between the Cornwall and Bear Gulch mines will show how vastly superior are the latter. In Bear Gulch the ore crops out on the surface, and there are mountains of it. It is easily mined and reduced, the only difficulty, as hitherto mentioned, being that the roads are poor, making transportation high. This difficulty is far more than counterbalanced, however, by the high grade of the Bear Gulch ore in comparison with that of Cornwall. There is none here that assays less than 3 per cent., and from this up to 30 per cent. That these mines will soon be developed is beyond all question. Here is one of the best openings for capital that can be found in the United States.

All the claims have now been located, and we found Mr. Chapman busily at work on one. An assay of his dump averaged 6 per cent. tin, and much of it runs enough gold to pay all cost of reduction, leaving the tin clear profit. Mr. Chapman has several claims, and showed us over all of them. On one is a deep shaft, which we descended, and at the bottom found a large snow drift. Immediately the snow-balls began flying at short range, and it was a sport whose novelty we fully enjoyed. Standing in a temperature of 30 degrees we could easily throw snow-balls at some of the party sweltering under a July sun at a temperature of 115 degrees. Mr. Chapman took us to his different claims and finally to his house, where his wife displayed the $300 nugget to our wondering eyes. Mr. Chapman is a good mineralogist, and has all the appliances for assaying his own ore. He has had his experiments confirmed by other assayers, and there is no doubt of the genuineness of the tin find and that at no distant day the United States will draw its supply of tin from the Black Hills instead of Cornwall.

Only a few weeks remain ere the legislative convention of this district will have placed its candidates in nomination. The citizens of Billings county may indeed be proud of having decided upon such a man as L. N. Cary as their standard bearer. Unassuming, yet thoroughly in sympathy with the needs of our people, he will make a record for himself such as few others would achieve. And to elect Mr. Cary means not only to place the right man in the right place but a victory of common sense over political intrigue and wire-pulling. Mr. Cary is in no sense a politician, in the ordinary acceptance of the word, and never sought any office. Let the people send him where he will do the most good--to the halls of the legislature.
