Since July 18 over 250 carloads of fat cattle from Colorado ranges have been shipped into Chicago over the Burlington and Quincy road.
The wool growers of Texas are petitioning the legislature to require the railroads of that state to act with justice towards the shipment of mutton interests.--[Breeder's Gazette.

The Albany Land and Cattle Company, with a capital of $5,000,000, has just been incorporated at Laramie City. The stock of the company is understood to be largely taken in Europe.--[Col. Live Stock Record.

It is said that Big Timber station will ship 400,000 pounds of wool this year. Twenty-five carloads have already been shipped and as much more is to come. The wool is grown on the Sweet Grass, Big Timber and Musselshell pastures.--[Livingston Enterprise.

The demand for well-bred American young cattle was never so good as right now. A moderate bunch of yearling and two-year-old heifers were sold here on Tuesday for $30 and $33 per head. Mr. George Brockway was the purchaser.--[Denver (Col.) L. S. Record.

A cowboy, whose name we forget, tells us that a rattlesnake bite has little or no effect upon a horse. All that is necessary is to open the wound and rub in a little ammonia, or in the absence of ammonia plenty of common salt, and the poison will be neutralizd.--[Exchange.

Fifty head of grade Galloway four-year-old steers, raised by Jim Galloway, in the Paradox valley, in Montrose--animals that never ate grain or known a shelter--turn the scale beam at twelve hundred pounds each, and there is not a horn on their heads or white hair on their bodies.--[Col. L. S. Journal.

The governors of Wyoming, New Mexico and Montana have issued proclamations declaring a quarantine against cattle shipments from localities suspected to be infected with the cattle fever. The various railroad companies have agreed to co-operate with the state and territorial authorities in their efforts to arrest the spread of the disease.

The Northern Pacific cut down carload cattle rates a week or two ago, 5 per cent., to correspond with a like reduction made by the Union Pacific. On Friday, President Harris of the Northern Pacific and President Adams of the Union Pacific, met in Chicago, and after a conference agreed to restore the old rates, to take effect at once.--[Livingston Enterprise.

In the cities of Canada the price of mutton is always as high as that of beef. This because they grow a finer sheep over in the Dominion than we do in the western States. Their big Cotswolds and their Shropshire sheep are equal to the best of Europe. There is a vast difference between the flavor of the mutton obtained at Quebec and that of Chicago.--[Colo. L. S. Record.

Sheepmen of Tom Green county, Texas, in a general convention, have demanded the restoration of the wool tariff of 1867. Tom Green is the largest wool-producing county in the world, having an area of over twelve thousand square miles. Drought now prevails over the entire county, and all small streams have disappeared. Already thousands of sheep are reported to have perished.--[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

Men who are predicting that the price of stock cattle will continue to decline will find themselves mistaken. So long as there are millions of money in Europe and America that seeks investment in live stock the price will keep up. Investment in cattle under any and all circumstances is better than investment in railroad stocks.--[Col. L. S. Record.

At Raton last week an intoxicated cowboy shot one J. R. Smith in the knee, inflicting a serious wound and making amputation necessary. There was no quarrel. Again we say, the six-shooter must go. Our editorial correspondent writes us from Puerto de Luna the particulars of a shooting at Chisum's ranch. In this case the killer was justified, but the fact of the killing remains the same.--[N. M. Stock Grower.

The Chicago cattle market has been struck with a serious decline in prices. A drop of $1 per hundred pounds in the best range fed beef was experienced within twenty-four hours and in prices of the same shipment. Though the market rallied slightly thereafter it has not nearly regained the standard of the past twelve months, and the feeling among dealers is that its buoyancy is gone, not to return this season. This will have an important bearing on times in that it will have a tendency to hold many cattle from the market that would otherwise be converted into cash.--[Livingston Enterprise.

Another disease has made its appearance among cattle in Iowa which promises to become very serious. It attacks the eyes of stock of all ages, which first become watery, then rapidly inflame, and a white film spreads over the eye until the animal is totally blind. Stockmen say they have never seen anything like it, and the doctors are at a loss to know what to do for it. All medicines thus far tried have had no effect. Over fifty cattle in one herd are already affected, and the disease is pronounced contagious. Great alarm is felt among owners of stock in that vicinity.

Western range cattle shippers often do well by trying new commission men, but it has been the experience of some that if "split shipments" are to be made they should be made on alternate days. A large bunch of cattle cannot often be handled to as good advantage to owners when divided into two or more lots on the same day, as when handled in one lot, and as a rule the best way to test the relative merits of salesmen on that class of cattle is to try them on different days and make proper allowances for market fluctuations. This, of course, does not apply to native cattle, hogs and sheep.--[Drovers' Journal.

Hugh O'Kane, who arrived from Poplar Tuesday, informs us that seven men came down the Missouri river in three boats last week, and while passing Poplar Creek they were stopped by Joe Culbertson and a party of soldiers and Indians. Five of the seven were captured and put in the [guard house?]. The other two escaped and secreted themselves in the brush which skirts the shore. They are supposed to be Pat Rolles and "Dutch." There is a reward of $1500 offered for the capture of "Dutch," who killed Cherokee's partner on the Musselshell two years ago. A large force of soldiers and Indians surrounded the brush which is about a quarter of a mile square.--[Glendive Independent.

It is said that Texas fever has appeared among some range cattle near Spearfish, D. T., having been introduced by cattle received by rail from Texas at Ogallala, and afterward driven to Spearfish. The distance from Ogallala to Spearfish is 300 miles, which seems to demonstrate conclusively that it is necessary to trail Texas cattle for a great distance before the fever germ can be completely eliminated from their systems. The impression held by some prominent stockmen that Texas fever cannot be introduced by cattle trailed from Texas, as their nature is radically changed by the long drive, is not confirmed by this intelligence. Another blow seems to be struck, however, at the transportation of cattle from Texas by rail.--[Kansas City L. S. Journal.

Advices from Cottonwood, Meagher county, give a meagre account of the killing of another batch of horse-thieves on the Musselshell, some 40 miles from the town above named. A band of cowboys who were in pursuit of stolen horses discovered a cabin in the timber on a mountain side, and the fact of its being so situated and in an otherwise uninhabited region, their suspicions were at once aroused. They secreted themselves and kept watch. During the day and night small parties of men, in every case having horses in their possession, came and went. It becoming evident that the place was a horse-thief rendezvous, the cowboys set about wiping it off the face of the earth. Waiting till after night, they crept up close to the house and commenced firing on it. What the result would have been if the thieves had stood their ground it is hard to say, but the whole outfit, fourteen in number, rushed out of the house and tried to escape. Nine were shot down and killed outright, while five got away. The cowboys then set fire to the cabin and left. Although this occurred somewhere in the vicinity where Granville Stewart's cowboys were reported to have a band of thieves corralled a few days ago, we are assured that it is an entirely different affair. It seems fair to assume that Montana horse-thieves will some of these days get tired of this kind of business and reform.--[Helena Independent.
C. L. Brinker, station agent, spent last Sunday in Belfield.
Gill Kennedy was down to Belfield on a two days' visit last week.
Owing to the delay of trains the Cow Boy comes out one day late this week.
J. C. Fisher and A. T. Packard start for Deadwood to-morrow, Friday, morning.
T. A. Matthews, stock inspector for Dakota and eastern Montana, has been in the city for the last few days.
Six trains of stock past through here on last Sunday en route east. They were shipped from Mingusville.

Governor Pierce arrived in the capital city on last Saturday and was given a hearty welcome by the Bismarckians. Judge Francis delivered the address of welcome, which was listened to by over 2,000 people.

A large party from the east, en route to the National Park, remained over on last Friday to view the wonderful and wierd scenery of the Bad Lands. They expressed themselves as well pleased with the country.

As soon as Capt. Wrenshaw returns from the scene of the washout he will order a number of improvements in the freight house. The west end will be partitioned off into three rooms, and a platform will be built on the same end. A large derrick will also be erected to move heavy freight and movable skids built on which to run freight into the warehouse.

Much work has been done since our last issue, and of a decisive kind. Exclusive passenger and express rates have been made to Medora, and there will be no such uncertainty as there has been in the freight business. Messrs. Fee and Footner especially have been very obliging, and they willingly signed the contracts giving Medora exclusive control of the business of their departments.

Word has ceen received from Messrs. Barr and Deffebach that all the coaches and a number of the horses have been bought at Helena, and by the time this article reaches the eye of the public it is probable that all the stock will have been purchased. There is a large amount of preliminary work that takes considerable time, but much progress has been made and our readers may rest assured that every effort will be made to hasten matters. Messrs. Deffebach and Barr are expected back on almost every train with the stock, which will at once be strung along the line. Four stations have now been built and hay put up near these and several others. Wells have been dug and a number of springs close to the stations found. The boulders are being cleared from the trail on Rocky ridge, and the road-bed graded in many places.

As before announced, A. T. Packard will be general manager, Rassie Deffebach superintendent of stages, and J. C. Fisher will be local manager.

One of the most severe rain, wind and hail storms within the memory of the traditional "oldest inhabitant" visited Medora on the afternoon of August 18. The storm made up about five miles northwest of the town. When first noticed the cloud resembled an old-fashioned thunder shower, but rapidly assumed alarming proportions and took on a greenish tinge which betokened the presence of wind and hail. In about 30 minutes after the cloud was first noticed the rain began to fall, and before any movement could be made for protection the storm burst forth in all its fury. The rain fall was simply enormous, resembling more than anything else the bursting of a water-spout. The force of the wind was terriffic, taking the water up which had deluged the earth and tossed it about in all directions. The hail was very severe, some houses having every pane of of glass in the south windows broken. We have not as yet learned of any loss of life as the result of the storm. The billiard hall was put to a very severe test as to its ability to resist the force of the wind. It is quite high and narrow and almost wholly unprotected from a wind coming from the northwest. The building on the north side of the track known as "Cowboy saloon," but now unoccupied, was turned completely around, occasioning much consternation on the part of two gentlemen who had been out gathering wild plums (or oats), and returning after the storm saw the building facing differently than when they went out, came to the conclusion that they had lost their way, and, animated by the true hunter's instinct, they immediately went into camp. George still thinks there was something wrong about it.

The washouts on the railroad exceed anything known in the history of the road. Five bridges between Medora and Glendive were washed away and more than twenty-five miles of track badly damaged. Telegraph poles were strewn around promiscuously, cutting off all communication from the west. Monday's westbound passenger train was obliged to lay here three days before the damages were repaired.

The storm was about seven miles wide and forty-five miles in length. Beyond a few minor stampedes [but?] very little damage was done to stock.

Pursuant to a call issued by J. C. Fisher, chairman of the county central committee, a convention of the Republican voters of Billings county was held at Medora on Saturday evening, August 16, for the purpose of appointing two delegates to the territorial convention to be held at Pierre on September 17, to nominate a delegate to congress.

After calling the convention to order and reading the call as published Mr. J. C. Fisher was elected chairman and L. H. Palmer secretary.

On motion of John Warn a committee consisting of the chairman of the convention and four others named by the chair, viz., John Warn, G. D. Kennedy, T. J. Kerr and W. F. Houk, were appointed to choose delegates. The committee after a short consultation reported the names of F. H. Ertel, of Belfield, and A. T. Packard, of Medora, as the delegates to represent Billings county at the territorial convention.

After a neat and appropriate address by F. H. Ertel and one of John Warn's characteristic speeches the first political convention of Billings county adjourned amid general good feeling and entire unanimity.

The indorsement of Mr. L. N. Cary's candidacy by the Dickinson Press adds another important straw to show which way the wind blows. Mr. Cary, with the united support of Stark and Billings county is more than ever entitled to proper recognition at home, and the Cow Boy trusts that Morton county will heartily endorse the selection of her neighbors when the time comes. There should be unanimity of action in this matter west of the Missouri, and if there are others who had hoped to capture the legislative honors of 1884, let them gracefully bow to the combination which decrees otherwise.

The steam shovel has been set to work east of town, supplying three gravel trains which are kept running between there and the washout. Owing to the seemingly great and continuous efforts it is expected that the repairs will be nearly completed this week.
J. T. Odell, vice-president, and C. C. Renshall, chief engineer, who have been here looking after the welfare of their road, left Tuesday on No. 2 on their special coach.
T. Greene, superintendent of the Missouri division, is registered at the Hotel de Mores. He is superintending the repairs and looking to the interests of his division.

Mr. C. C. Renshall, chief engineer of the Northern Pacific, through Mr. Grantier, foreman carpenter, is constructing a very substantial platform 35x60 across the west end of the new warehouse and placing a derrick to facilitate the handling of machinery and other heavy freight destined to the Black Hills; and when lumber arrives will petition off a neat office to be occupied by the forwarders. Meanwhile the painters are decorating the outside. When all this is completed we can boast of the neatest and most commodious freight warehouse in Dakota.

The Spearfish Register has the following in regard to the stage line:

The opening of this line we regard as fraught with speedy and early advantages and benefits to the Hills, of large magnitude and incalculable importance. It will at once bring to the attention of the country one of the richest and most valuable sections of the public domain in the great northwest, that has been unknown and is unsettled, that offers to the agriculturist and stockman attractions and inducement for settlement and cultivation that are unsurpassed in the west. The tide has already started in that direction, and the result is assuring and promising. At Valley creek, some 50 miles north of Minnesela, during the past two or three months, some twenty families have settled; while on the Little Missouri, about eight miles further north, about as many more have made a settlement, and they are all contented and satisfied with the land and the surroundings. Others have been in to see the country, and they return to induce others to locate on the land. The same is the case from Medora; and next year, both from the Northern Pacific on the north and the Hills on the south, a steady flow of immigrants will enter upon this domain, so that, by the middle of next summer it is fair to estimate 500 families will have found homes on the line of this stage route.
Bob Montgomery returned from the east on Monday, and his best friends failed to know him again. He came disguised as a Wall street broker.
Mrs. F. H. Ertel and children bid adieu to Belfield on Sunday last, and will remain at St. Louis for the present.
Farmers Burke and Davis, from Dickinson, Sundayed here.

There is some just indignation here against Supt. Greene of the Northern Pacific railrood. A few months ago he ordered the agent at this point to engage ponies and men to pursue some stolen cattle, promising fair pay. The cattle were found, and upon their return the men were asked to sign receipts for their claims, but as yet have failed to receive a penny. Some of the men believe they are being humbugged, and the temperature of their blood goes up as the thermometer goes down.
Some Black Hills freight is moving, though the town, outside of the hotel, is not being benefitted by it.
Max Bass, who enjoys the monopoly of the hotel trade, is quietly getting rich and investing some of his spare cash in paints and oils, which gives his hostelry a highly distinguished appearance.
The new store of Martindale & Hanauer is doing a land office business, and the proprietors are pre-eminently popular.
Mr. Pettit's family has arrived from Crook City in one of Pettit's finest stages, which is the most metropolitan thing that ever honored the town of Belfield.

Scotty, or Henry Scott, was arrested at supper at Dixon's ranch last night by Deputy Sheriff Louis King. He was connected with Clay Layton, whose arrest was published in the Journal yesterday, in the theft of four horses from Archie Morton, of South Heart, Dak. The pair sold two of them here, another to Mr. Dixon and the fourth was traded for a rifle. They are hard characters and their arrest was well managed by the sheriff and his deputies.—[Yellowstone Journal.

There will be a meeting of Bad Lands stockmen at Medora on Tuesday, September 9, 1884, for the purpose of effecting a permanent organization and making the necessary preparations for the fall round-up. A captain for the round-up will also be selected. Let every stockman be present.
Last week thirty horses were stolen from John Smith's herd on Alkali creek Montana.
It is estimated that the drive out of the state of Texas for 1884 will foot up 450,000 head of cattle.
The cattle round-ups in northern Colorado have been ordered stopped until the fever epidemic has passed over.
For the past six days Colorado beef cattle have been selling in Kansas City at $4.20 to $4.25 for steers whose weight would overgo 1,100 pounds.—[Col. L. S. Record.
Ninety per cent. of the cattle attacked by the Texas fever have been of the she kind. Many cows have died while their calves have not been affected.—[Col. L. S. Record.
The largest ranch in the world is in the Province of Cordoba, Argentine Republic, South America, and is owned by an English syndicate. It comprises 10,400 square miles of land.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

General George B. McClelland is now a cow owner on the western plains. His bovines browse the grass in New Mexico, while Ben Butler and P. T. Barnum have their cows in southern Colorado.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The great cattle wealth of the Messrs. Swans, of Wyoming, has been accumulated in the past ten years. They to-day control more cattle than any other syndicate in America, if not in the world.—[Col. L. S. Record.

A cow in County Carlow, Ireland, has produced four heifer calves in ten months. The cow was calved April 4, 1881, had her two first calves on July 25, last year, and two more on the 25th of May, this year.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

Twenty horses disappeared on Friday night from Mr. Field's herd, which was grazing near town. They are supposed to have been stolen. They are branded M P combined, or half circle R A.—[Livingstone Enterprise.

An exchange says that cattle are perishing in Chihuahua, Mexico, by the drouth. Two thousand died at the hacienda of Agustin Cordero. The dead animals are burned to prevent disease emanating from the frightful mortality.

American cattle are steady at Liverpool at 14 to 15 cents per pound, which is a very good price considering the price on this side of the water. Sheep are going over there at 15 to 16 cents. These prices are for dead weight.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Three hundred young Texas cattle were tramped to death on the Bloomfield range in the Arkansas country during a hail storm one day last week. They stampeded and collided against a wire fence, when the stronger ones killed the weaker ones.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Latest reports from the British markets are a little more encouraging to exporters, best American cattle being quoted at 15 cents per pound, estimated dead weight. The sheep trade was quiet and steady at 15@16 cents for good to choice heavy Americans.

Nearly 700 head of the Continental Land and Cattle Company's cattle were on sale Monday. This company have already sent 4,000 cattle to the Chicago market this season, and they have from 8,000 to 10,000 yet to ship. They have extensive ranches in Texas, Montana and Dakota.—[Breeder's Gazette.

A report from the department of agriculture gives the number of live stock in the United States as follows: Horses, 11,169,682; mules, 1,914,126; milch cows, 13,501,206; oxen and other cattle, 29,045,101; sheep, 50,626,626; hogs, 44,200,893, with a total value of $2,467,868,924.

The finest cattle shipped from the ranges thus far this season reached the stock yards Monday last. They were from the pastures of Montana. There were two bunches, 108 head averaging 1,226 pounds, and 290 head averaging 1,211 pounds, and they sold at $5.75 and $6, respectively.—[Breeder's Gazette.

In the first six months of 1884 a total of 81,016 live cattle were exported from the United States to England, against [illegible] in the same part of 1883. The totals received from all sources in the English markets were respectively 154,060 and 152,369. Of fresh meats the United States furnished 416,638 cwt. in the first six months of 1884, against 376,755 in the same part of 1883.

A report came here last Friday, August 2d, that the Kiowa and Comanche Indians were burning the range in the southern part of their reservation, and would keep up the work until the cattle were forced to leave. These Indians have no idea whatever as to the size of their grass bonanza, and although they have been offered much more than the business can stand as a steady drain they persistently want "more." It is said they will drive all the cattle south of the river.—[Mobeetie (Tex.) Panhandle.

Never in the history of the cattle business in the west has the outlook been brighter at this season of the year than it now is. With scarcely an exception, the feed on the range is abundant, and the gradual curing of the grass has made it all that could be desired for winter use. Pilgrim cattle have generally reached their new range and will have time to take on flesh and prepare for the winter storms. There is nothing in the air to indicate any material decline in values and cattle owners are generally in a hopeful mood.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Guard against prairie fires. The season is now approaching when the greatest care should be exercised to prevent the destruction of grass. Grass is money, and a widespread prairie fire will mean heavy loss to cattle owners next spring. Impress upon your employes the necessity of being careful with camp fires. A strong breeze will scatter sparks to spread desolation over the plains. The railroads have, we believe, complied with the statute compelling the plowing of fire guards on each side of the track, which will reduce the risk of fire from one source. Now it remains for ranchmen themselves to look after the rest, and see that tons of valuable grass are not wasted by the flames.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

Several of the principal stockmen of the country south and southeast of San Antonio who came up last week wore sorrowful faces. They say the country has dried up more rapidly within the past month than they ever knew it to do in twice the time, and the grass is parched, and there are many places where hundreds of acres are almost barren. Those who have obligated themselves to pay money, find refusals to let them have it on every hand, and unless men determine to be lenient and carry one another there must come heavy reverses, and ruin in some instances. The sale of stock is very slow, and there is nothing like the demand of last spring at a discount even of twenty per cent. on the spring prices. We hope for better times, but that is all we can do.—[Texas Wool-Grower.

It is one thing to raise cattle for market and another to know when and how to get them there. When to ship and when to hold require as much judgment and, it may be added, experience as it does to make purchases and care for the cattle after they are bought.

Any one who has closely observed the course of events at any one of the leading markets of the country for a number of years cannot but have arrived at the above conclusion.

The raising of cattle, as a general thing, is a profitable thing when well managed, but like every other pursuit in life it requires experience and judgment. A few dollars a head lost on the number of cattle owned are not often missed, for there is a profit anyhow, but if those few dollars had been added to the sum total they would undoubtedly be appreciated.

It has been observed that some cattle raisers, year after year, manage so as to reach the markets at a time and with their cattle in such condition as to realize prices which, when compared with those realized by their neighbors, make a good profit on the larger amount obtained, to say nothing of the satisfactory manner in which their business appears to be managed.

There are parties engaged in feeding cattle, who exercise poor judgment in their purchases, the handling of the cattle after making the purchase and then again in selling them for beef, whereas there are others who move along quietly, manage their affairs smoothly and who invariably come out ahead.

There are thousands of dollars lost annually by cattle raisers, who do not pay sufficient attention to the details of the business, and who, instead of watching the markets and the course of events, move along as if every season was alike and values were the same from year to year.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

The two horsethieves, Henry Scott and Clay Layton, who were arrested near Miles City for stealing four horses from Archie Morton of South Heart, passed through on No. 2 this morning in charge of Sheriff Cuskelly, of Dickinson.

Dr. F. Harck, of Germany, who has been visiting here as the guest of Marquis de Mores, left for the Yellowstone Park Sunday evening. From there he goes to San Francisco via Portland, from which point he sails for Japan and China.

During the recent storm that portion of the roof of the depot covering the telegraph and ticket office was badly demolished. The ceiling is good enough to keep out the dew, but our station agent, Mr. Brinker, not being webfooted finds it quite unpleasant when it rains.

O. F. Lindquist, an artist in the line of stone, enameled brick and terra-cotta, is here and will test some of our clay, which, from a test of a small sample sent him last season, he is satisfied is of excellent quality. If the requsite inducement is held out he will locate a manufactory of his wares here.

In another column we publish a call for a meeting of Bad Lands stockmen. The object of this meeting is for the purpose of establishing a permanent organization of Bad Lands stockmen. The necessity of such an organization is very apparent, and is a movement in which every stockman should personally interest himself.

Last evening Henry, who drives the team of gray horses belonging to A. T. Packard, drove to the store and went in after a sack of oats. The horses becoming frightened at the train started for home at a lively gait, but brought up on the river bank astride a stump, causing a dislocated reach, broken single-tree and harness somewhat demoralized.

The surveyors who are making the official plat of this and adjacent townships were here Tuesday, enabling us to locate ourselves, so to speak. The town of Medora is in the northeast one-quarter of section 27 and northwest one-quarter of section 26, township 140, north of range 102, west. The section line runs a little to the west of the freight house, between Medora hall and the hotel, on and nearly parallel to Third street, thus cutting the town nearly in the middle. The section corner is at the foot of the bluff north of town.

The storm of a week ago Monday seems to have been widespread, at lesat the rain, as nearly all our Dakota exchanges have accounts of a heavy rain-fall. At Deadwood the signal office records show a fall of 1¼ inches in about 36 hours, which is a very heavy fall of water for any country. In this locality its freaks were peculiar. Coming from the west, where it did most damage, it broke all the glass on the south side of buildings at Medora, while at Belfield the glass was broken on the west side, and the storm was accompanied by terrific thunder and lightning. Fields of grain and gardens were entirely destroyed, cherry and plum bushes stripped of their fruit and rabbits killed.

Preparations for the stage line are fast nearing completion, and another week of good weather will see the stations completed and hay put up on this end of the line. A. T. Packard, general manager, and J. C. Fisher, local manager, who started for the Hills on Friday last, have no doubt ere this effected arrangements at that end. Four eleven-passenger Concord coaches and the harness arrived here on Tuesday, and Mr. Barr writes from Helena that the horses would be shipped on the 27th, yesterday, so that by Saturday at the farthest the horses and the balance of the coaches will be here. Supt. Deffebach will at once distribute the stock, and by the first of the following week we may reasonably expect to see the coaches running.

Mr. James Vance, a ranchman, who served his apprenticeship as cowboy and "rounder-up," was yesterday corralled and induced to deliver up some interesting matter about round-ups.

"The round-up is the great event of the stockman's year. It's his Fourth of July, and generally lasts a month and a half. The territorial paper publishes such a notice as this," said Mr. Vance, taking a slip of paper from his wallet: "Round-up No. 5,—Laramie Plains Round-up will meet at the Lower Bridge, near McGillis ranch, on the big Laramie river on June 1, and proceed to work the country between the river and the Black Hills Divide as far south as Red Buttes; from thence it will work in two divisions as far south as Twin Mountains; thence back to Diamond Peak, working up Boulder and intermediate creeks up to the source of the Big Laramie river."

"That," proceeded the gentleman, "is an official announcement to all the stockmen, and they combine and join in together. The ranges are generally about ten miles in extent, though some of them are thirty."

"What's a round-up party?"

"That's an expression we have, and means about ten wagons and as many cowboys, a cook going with each wagon, and every cowboy has a string of about six or ten ponies. The 'out' comes off at 3 o'clock in the morning, under the charge of an experienced foreman. Everybody is on horseback, and the foreman operates something in this manner: He sends one party out on the divide as out pickets, and other parties along the canons and gulches with orders to drive the cattle up to the round-up center—a point previously agreed upon."

"The boys will be gone several days?"

"Oh, no. A good cowboy will ride from thirty to forty miles in the morning, coming up to his pony herd and taking out another one of his ponies just as he needs them. Sometimes a cowboy will ride down three or four ponies in a day. When the foreman 'covers his dog,' as it's called, the cattle are gathered on the prairie in small herds, and then comes the fun. On the wiry, little, fleet-footed Indians ponies, who'll dodge and back, and stop in a twinkling, the cowboy rush into the herds, and shouting, yelling, and swearing, separate the herds, and drive out those having the different owners."

"Then every man has his own brand?"

"Most assuredly. There are no two brands alike. Some are slits, some letters, some holes, and some figures. In fact, there is every conceivable form of mark. When a man wants a brand, he gets it up and has it recorded in the office of the county clerk, in a book that is especially kept for the purpose. All the cowboys are not engaged in 'cutting-out'—that is, getting the cattle that have the same brand all together. Others are busy in holding the herd to prevent a stampede. Thus all the heard are picked out."

"What's done with those that are left?"

"Those where the owner is not known are called estrays, and calves that are away from their mothers are called 'mavericks.'"

"What do you do with these?"

"These mavericks are branded with the mark belonging to the largest female herd in the neighborhood."

"Always at the wind-up of the round-up. The cattle are all driven into a corral, where a fire is burning and the branding irons heated. A cowboy rides in and swinging a lariat over the head of a calf or around his hind legs, secures the hand end of the lariat to his saddle pummel. The calf is quickly thrown, and lies wallowing on the ground. The brand is either burned into his side, or his shoulder or rump, or perhaps the ear is slit, and its done in a second, quicker than I'm telling you. There's a great noise made, but very little confusion. They have the business now systematized so that everything goes like clockwork.—[Cincinnati Sun.

A confidence chap picked up a New Mexico cowboy on the depot platform a day or two since, and after a chat of a few seconds decided he had struck something soft, and proceeded to work the claim. In a few minutes the sum of ten dollars had been transferred from the cow-puncher's pocket to that of the confidence chap. Just as the transfer was completed, the cowboy noticed the railway policeman approaching, drew his "45," and putting it uncomfortably close to the confidence chap's ear, yelled, "You d—d thief, hand back my twenty-five dollars!" The officer seconded the motion, and although the confidence chap insisted that he only received ten dollars the speaker decided the point against him, and he gave up the amount and disappeared as soon as the caucus adjourned. We don't think that sharp gentlemen will care to tackle one of our prairie dudes again.—[Deming Tribune.

Northern New Mexico cattlemen will make a test case of the sheep protection law and will carry it to the highest court if necessary.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
Driscoll & Son last week shipped from Dickinson fifty-eight carloads of fat cattle to Chicago. Their shipments from there this season will amount to about 12,000 head.

Texas "bronchos" are being introduced in Asia. A short time ago a train of sixteen cars of Texas horses, mares and stallions, left New Orleans, the destination of which was Constantinople.

Col. Gile, of Ellsworth county, Kansas, says she has thirty-six head of half-breed Short-horn cattle, the product of one cow within the last twelve years besides 20 head sold or slaughtered.—[Kan. L. S. Indicator.

The Arab compels his horse to feed from the ground, in order to maintain the curve of the backbone. Come to think of it this is the natural way of feeding, and is an agrument for low mangers.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

Four carloads of unbroken Colorado bred horses will in a few days be shipped to Europe. They are all half-breed Normans, of good size and style, and will be landed in London and placed upon the market.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The cattle shipments from here this season have already amounted to 295 carloads, or 6,000 head, and it is stated by the railroad officials that a great many more carloads will be shipped before the season is over.—[Dickinson Press.

A gentleman who held the watch on the boys tells us that John Farington and his outfit, at the Quistaque ranch, lately branded 400 calves in just 100 minutes, which is tolerably quick work.—[Mobeetie, (Tex.) Panhandle.

For five years I have had a horse with hoofs shelly and brittle, so that it was difficult to keep shoes on him during the dry weather of July and August. In may last I dressed his feet with pine tar, and now repeat it every week, and the hoofs are perfectly sound even in mid-summer.—[H. W. Dunning in the N. Y. Tribune.

Young men of England have been advised to come to America to engage in raising mutton for the English market. It is predicted that the supply cannot keep pace with the demand. Perhaps the young men of America will do well to consider such advice as being worthy their attention.—[Exchange.

If the cattle owners carry out their resolution made early in the season, every bull will be removed from the range in northern Colorado by the first of November. Had this been done last year, two or three hundred thousand dollars would have been saved in the death looses, and the bulls, after being fed through the winter, would have been worth one-third more in the spring.—[Denver (Col.) L. S. Record.

A man named Brown, one of the trail hands with a Texas herd, was shot and killed on the head of the Frenchman a few days ago by a fellow-herder. The man rode up to the wagon and found Brown asleep under it, went up to him and took his six-shooter, then woke him up and shot him; he then mounted a horse and skipped. The cause was an old grudge. Brown was buried where he was killed.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The Ute Indians continue their depredations in Utah and Colorado. They are making times very troublesome for the settlers and stockmen there. The latter had quite a skirmish with them on the Dolores a few days since, in which one Indian and a number of horses on both sides were killed. Cattle are being gathered with cavalry escort and a serious outbreak from the Utes and Navajos is expected to occur at any time.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The Cherokee nation think of holding a convention soon, to consider the wire fence monopoly of the land and kindred questions. It is sad to see the dying struggles of the Indian, in his foolish endeavor to keep a separate national life from the great American national life around him. Let him become an American citizen, instead of a government ward, and there will be some chance of his holding his property. The Indian Territory must be opened to the farmer and the cattleman.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Reports from all over the country are most flattering for the stockmen. The calf crop while not so large as hoped for, shows an increase over that of last year. The grass everywhere is luxuriant, and during the coming winter the stock on all the ranges will have ample feed. Should the winter be as severe as predicted by would-be weather prophets, the abundance of feed will carry the stock through. It is stated that never within the history of stock raising in this country has the outlook been so hopeful, and we hope all that is expected by owners of herds may be realized.—[Helena Independent.

Cattle receipts on the Chicago market were larger during the week than for the week previous. The prices have been generally fair, but not high. The prices of range stock have remained at $4.00@5.00. There was a somewhat better demand for good stock, and the market was more frequently "higher," "brisk" or "steady" than at any previous time during the present season. Some shippers are sanguine that the market will soon assume a better aspect, that prices will advance a trifle, and that the demand for their shipments will be a little more spirited.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Pat Ryan, one of the pioneer stockmen of this section, who is located on the Mulberry, a small stream emptying into the Arkansas river, eighteen miles southeast of Dodge, has what may truly be termed a living curiosity, in the shape of a calf that was born about two weeks ago which has not a single hair on its head or body, and but a few scattering ones on its legs. The skin of the young animal seems to be considerably bronzed and hardened. It is fully developed and appears as strong and vigorous as any calf in the herd. It is virtually a curiosity to behold. Mr. Ryan proposes to take the best of care of the young animal and see what it will make.—[Globe Live Stock Journal.

The New York butchers have endeavored to boycott Chicago beef. Inspector Myers was sent, in consequence of their protests, to Chicago to investigate the condition and circumstances of the beef. He says in his report: "In every instance I found, from the time the bullock is slaughtered until it is ready for shipment, the closest attention is given to cleanly and healthful methods. Scrupulous care was observed in excluding animals where any suspicions of disease existed, and I could not suggest a single improvement. In my opinion the board of health will have to look elsewhere than Chicago to find violations of the law, and I shall so report to that body.—[Col. L. S. Record.

John A. Blair returned from his northwestern trip last week, after having viewed the beauties of nature from the peaks around the Yellowstone Park and the fair daughters of the northwest from the car windows as he passed villages that have sprung into existence in the past year or so. He is perfectly fascinated with that region as a stock-growing country. The winters are severely cold, of course, but the temperature is so even and the atmosphere so dry and rains so seldom that the stock go through with but little suffering. His company located another ranch of about six miles square adjoining their old ranch, some 35 miles northwest of Glendive. Yearling steers from the States are selling there at $20 to $23, according to class.—[Caldwell (Kan.) Journal.

The all-important question now for stockmen is how to ship their beef to market. It is not probable that there will be any more buyers in the markets this season, and owners will be compelled to ship. The most economical way to do this is for a number of herd-owners to club together and contract for the transportation. The Northern Pacific railroad company has shown a disposition to be very fair in its arrangement for the shipment of cattle, and we have no doubt that by clubbing together very satisfactory rates may be made. A gentleman representing a herd of 11,000 head, whose range is near Fort McKinney, contracted last week with the Northern Pacific railroad company for 200 cars at $112 per car. The beeves have to be driven 200 miles before shipment. Forty cars have already been side-tracked for the purpose of loading. It would also be well to rent pastures near Chicago and turn the stock on them. Then go into the city and have the cattle brought in at such times as the market is best. It may be easily arranged to ship in from one to three carloads of beeves any day there is demand for them and good prices. This will be found much better than to unload large herds at the yards and take the chances of the market being overstocked.—[Rocky Mountain Husbandman.

Theodore Roosevelt, in a letter to the New York Tribune, declares that Gov. Cleveland's reasons for vetoing the tenure of office bill are "frivolous;" that it is difficult for him to believe "that they were offered in good faith;" and that "it is sheer nonsense to say that the amendment (the Dayton amendment) hurt the bill; on the contrary, it improved it."

The painters will finish painting the warehouse to-day.
Mr. Duncan, of Mandan, was in town a few days during the past week.
C. E. Dow, of the Pioneer furniture store, Mandan, was in town to-day.
Carpenters are repairing the damage done by the recent storm to the depot.
Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, was here Tuesday, and held mass at the Pyramid Park hotel.
J. D. Sears, boot and shoe merchant of Glendive, is in town looking up a location for a branch store.
Mr. Miles, a representative of the Armour Bros., was in town this week. He accompanied the Marquis west.
Harry A. Ahl, correspondent of the New York Mercury, came up from Deadwood this week. He is visiting Eaton's ranch.
Mr. A. Boyd has suceeded Frank Moore to the management of the Pyramid Park hotel, who is repairing and otherwise improving the house.
K. C. Meecher, an English gentleman who has been staying at Lang's ranch for some time on a hunt, went west last night en route to the Canadian Pacific country on a bear hunt.
Mr. Grantier, Northern Pacific carpenter foreman, has completed at the warehouse a very neat and commodious office and baggage room, which will be occupied by the Medora Stage and Forwarding company.

A number of Northern Pacific and St. Paul notables, including Passenger Agent Fee, Vice-President Oakes (possibly), representatives of St. Paul papers and others will visit the Hills by the first coach.—Deadwood Times.

Marquis de Mores arrived from the east on his special car Monday evening, departing again the following day for Miles City, where he attends the meeting of the Northwestern Live Stock Association. From there he goes to Billings and Helena.

Mr. T. J. Kerr, traveling auditor of the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car company, returned from the west yesterday morning. He reports both the wholesale and retail business of the company's various houses along the line in a flourishing condition.

Wm. Tinfrock and Sam Tary came down from Helena with Mr. Deffenbach and will be employed by the Medora Stage and Forwarding company. The former as blacksmith and the latter as conductor, head breakman and switchman. Both are men of experience, Sam having manipulated the ribbons for eighteen years.

Mr. Chas. Turner has made a general clean-up around the abattoir this week, and the nauseating oder which prevailed around the establishment has been thoroughly remediated. Next week they will commence slaughtering on a large scale. Mr. Turner is an expert in everything pertaining to the beef trade, and the business hereafter will be under his personal supervision.

The lands of the Northern Pacific railroad company will hereafter be sold, in quantities not exceeding 320 acres, to parties who agree to become actual settlers within one year from date of purchase on ten years's time. Terms, one-tenth cash down, and at the end of the first year seven per cent. on balance, one-tenth principal and interest at the end of each succeeding year.

A herd of buffalo, numbering between two to three hundred, made its appearance seven miles south of here one day last week. Lloyd Roberts and two others who sighted the herd succeeded in killing three of them, and undoubtedly would have slaughtered more had they not run out of ammunition. Wm. Vandriesche purchased one of the heads, which was a very fine one, and shipped it to Mandan for mounting.

Supt. Deffebach and Mr. Barr arrived Sunday evening from Helena, where they had been to purchase stock for the stage line. They evidently found a good market, as they brought an excellent lot of horses, which were purchased way below eastern prices. The horses arrived here without any very serious accident, except that two were somewhat disabled, but all were more or less bruised by being knocked around in the cars. A few days of feeding grain and grazing will fit them for work.
F. H. Ertel has accepted a position on the Bismarck Journal as business manager and assistant editor.

L. D. Pettit is erecting a fine residence, which will be ready for occupancy in about two weeks. We are pleased to note this fact, as he is one of the live men of our town, and indicates that he will reside here permanently.
[E.?] A. Henderson, of Bismarck, was in town a few days this week, initiating himself to the noble cayuse.
D. T. Bramble is putting a stock of groceries in the new store north of the depot.
Mr. Myers, who has been in the employ of Hanauer & Martindale, has departed for Glendive.

About the first of July three horses were stolen from Robert Milligan, of Sully Springs, and no trace of them could be found until a short time ago when information was received that they were in the hands of an Indian at Standing Rock agency, the Indian having traded for them on the prairie. Sheriff Cuskelly and Milligan started for the agency, and after arriving there and satisfying Agent McLaughlin that the horses belonged to Milligan they were turned over, but not without a vigorous protest from the Indian. A good description of the parties who traded with the Indian was obtained, and they are undoubtedly men who were around here all last spring and well known to all our citizens. The sheriff and Milligan stopped at the camp of "Crow Joe" and learned from him that while Sitting Bull and one of his band were taking a meal at his camp one of the same parties rode up and attempted to steal the old chief's horses, but was discovered and the Indians mounted two of "Crow Joe's" ponies and started in pursuit, overtaking him in a short time when shots were exchanged and the thief captured. After recovering their horses the Indians had no further use for the thief, and instead of taking his scalp, as they should have done, allowed him to go. The sheriff and Milligan arrived here Monday with the horses.—[Dickinson Press.

A special telegram from Pierre states that nothing has been done as yet except to organize.

An associated Press dispatch says: All the old leaders are on the ground and in active service for their man. Nearly all the Black Hills delegation are here and persistent for McMaster, of the Homestake mine, for delegate. McMaster has chartered the entire Grand Pacific hotel, three stories, for his delegation and friends. It is reported a combination has been entered into between Raymond and McMaster that if Raymond cannot get a sufficient vote to throw his support to McMaster.

Delegates from the following North Dakota counties stand about as follows, according to last report: Those refusing to go into the Raymond caucus: Barnes 2, Burleigh 7, Billings 2, Benson 2, Cavalier 2, Emmons 2, Grand Forks 9, Griggs 3, Logan 2, McLean 2, Mercer 2, Morton 5, Nelson 2, Ransom 3, Richland 2, Stutsman 3, Walsh 2, a total of 52 North Dakota delegates refusing to caucus.

The Republican territorial convention met yesterday at Pierre to nominate a delegate to congress. It is quite likely that one or two days will be occupied in effecting an organization, and that we will not learn the result before next Saturday and perhaps not until later. Indications are that a very stubborn fight will be made against the present incumbent, John B. Raymond, and the chances are that some man from South Dakota will receive the nomination. Mr. Samuel McMaster, of Deadwood, is spoken of, and may be properly termed a very prominent dark horse. The selection of Mr. McMaster as the standard bearer of the party would give very general satisfaction to the people of the territory, and particularly to the residents of the Black Hills, where he is recognized as a shrewd, active and energetic business man.
The Baron and Baroness von Hoffman are expected to return from their western trip in a few days.
Supt. Deffebach, of the Medora Stage and Forwarding company, returned from Helena this morning with eleven head of horses for the stage line.
Mr. J. C. Fisher, local manager of the Medora Stage and Forwarding company, is nicely ensconced in a cozy office which has been partitioned off from the large warehouse.

H. M. Jorgens and Vic Smith returned yesterday from a tour of inspection over the stage route. Vic is the pathfinder, and last week discovored a route from the first station on Davis creek to the second on Rocky Ridge, which to the right follows a divide and has a natural gravel road-bed the whole distance. This route will avoid nearly one-half of the bad road on this end. Lumber for two more stations is being sent out, and stoves and other utensils have been distributed to stations already built.

The cow boys take to the new style of locomotion as naturally as a Democrat takes to Stonewall or Valley Tan. Toll Caldwell was telling me of the fun he had last night. He said: "I am more used to riding on horseback, but last night I thought I'd try them little wagons. I got one with a double cinch, and another one to match it, and as soon as I straddled the layout I could feel them begin to bow their backs, and I was wishing I had buckrein, because I was expectin' 'em to stiffen their knees and go to buckin' every minit, but they didn't. I walked them over to the other end of the corral to gentle 'em a little, and directly they started off at an easy canter, and were coming around back right through the herd, and there was a dude there with a stiff hat that was trying to cut out a Polled Angus heifer with a blue dress, and I fouled and roped both my hind legs with a hoop skirt and it had me stretched out for branding, quicker'n a spring calf could brawl with its mouth open and its lungs stretched. But I got up and got on again and you oughter see me exercise those vehicles. Of course they wasn't bridle wise and of course tried to buck when I hurried 'em, and they'd rear up and fall back when I tried to stop 'em too quick, but I'll leave it to the boss herder of the whole round-up if I didn't gallop 'em round there for three or four hours, and had 'em roll over with me and they didn't get me of."
—[Muldoon.

A couple of enterprising young men of San Antonia, Tex., have undertaken to get up a car-load of heavy beeves to put on display at New Orleans during the exposition. Already several have been secured which will weigh from 1,400 to 1,700 pounds.

We notice that the Standard Cattle Company, of Wyoming, have ordered fifty cars at Mingusville, Sept. 20, to accommodate their herd now on the drive for shipment. Harris & Clevinger wanted twenty cars at the same place on the 25th.—[Glendive Times.

The Kansas City Drovers' News says: The Texas fever is no worse this year than it has been every summer for the past ten years, but the scare is greater because there are so many more commissioners than usual to write reports and publish articles on the subject.

The stockmen of western and southwestern Colorado, who have been having trouble with the Utes lately, now give notice that they will shoot on sight any of the red devils caught on their ranges. The only way to get rid of them—as the government seems unable or unwilling to afford any relief.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

A Denver gentleman is experimenting with chemicals, for the purpose of trying to discover some more convenient and cheap method of branding than is at present used. It is claimed that more than $1,000,000 are annually lost to the cattle owners of the county by the burning of hides in branding cattle.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

The sheep raiser must go on with his business, trying to improve his stock, to obtain more and better wool and more and better sheep, must stick close to his business, study economy, work hard, and then wait for the prosperity surely following one of the greatest periods of depression now happily passing away.—[Col. L. S. Record.

It costs more to ship wool from Denver to the Missouri river—a distance of 550 miles—than from Melborne to Liverpool, a distance of 11,000 miles. It also costs more to ship a car load of wool from Denver to Chicago than it does to ship the same bulk and weight from San Francisco to New York and thence to London.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Ed. Marron says he will introduce into this country the finest lot of Texas cowboys that have ever been seen around this section of the country. T. F. Burton, alias Texas, is the leader of the gang, and he is considered one of the best lariat throwers, besides being a dead shot, that the state of Texas can produce.—[Glendive Indpendent.

The cattle trade with Europe is said to be declining under the influence of the Australian and Canadian competition, and if it be argued that Canada buys in the United States a good many of the cattle she sells to Great Britain, the fact remains, nevertheless, indisputable, that she ships her cargoes by her own railroads and vessels, and not by ours.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Dorr Clark was in the city yesterday from the range. He says there are many sick cattle among some of the late through herds, but they are so effectually quarantined by the cattle men, that the disease will not be allowed to spread, if it could, to the range cattle. There has been many deaths among the afflicted herd, but it is thought the worst is now over.—[Black Hills Pioneer.

The French government has decided to place an increased duty upon the importation of cattle, but gives such a good season for doing so that the sensible American will find more to approve than condemn in the charge. A great depression exists in the live stock interests over there, and the government regards it as "sacred duty" to assist the farmers in this way to get on their feet again.—[National Stockman.

Old Mexico has both a herd and a lease law. An exchange says when one man's stock depredates on another's land, whether it be grass or grain, the owner is notified, if known, to take away his stock, which if not done, the animals are driven to the pound and advertised and sold. If an individual leases land in that country he knows he will get to use it, and not be compelled to pay for pasturing other people's stock.—[Exchange.

Official statistics of the loss of cattle in the Jonactepec district, Morelos through the excessively dry weather, are terribly suggestive of what the mortality must be for all the republic. In this district alone the figures show that 3,323 cattle and 423 horses have died this season for the lack of pasturage. The same report states that the grain crop has suffered from the ravages of a worm and from the dry weather, but no statistics are at hand to estimate the loss in grain.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

Every farmer knows that his cattle can be bred up to any attainable standard which he may choose to aim at, whether for breeding or dairying purposes; but few know how plastic their stock are in their hands. This is strictly exemplified by experiments made in breeding off the horns. If a heifer loses its horns by artificial means, and afterwards put to a horned bull, the offspring will sometimes have horns and sometimes not. By selecting the hornless ones the horns can be bred out altogether in a few generations.—[Exchange.

The contagious diseases among cattle appear to be finally subsiding. The American people are equal to almost any emergency and while they are frequently caught napping, and notwithstanding the laws in many cases are yet crude and defective, they have controlled these diseases remarkably well. That such diseases actually exist no reasonable man can doubt, and once the cattlemen know that diseases actually exist they are not slow to devise ways to eradicate the same, or to at least keep them under control.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The cattle brands as represented by the hundreds of oxen that freight into this city are a source of infinite amusement to the tenderfeet who study them. There are hundreds of different kinds of brands, and sometimes an individual steer will exhibit scars all over his body, from his shoulder blades to the root of his tail, to say nothing of the ear, horn and dewlap marks. A large ox stood in a team yesterday, that was as rangy and poor as they ever get, yet on his right side the expressive letters "F A T" stood out in bold relief. His mate is probably the oldest living animal in the world, that is if brands are evidence and Judge Church admits them in his court, as on his right side we saw the old time abbreviation, "B. C."—Before Christ.—[Black Hills Pioneer.

The profit and wealth of the cattle business may be realized in figuring up the value of the Texas drive of this year, estimated at from 500,000 to 700,000 head. At the smaller estimate $20 per head. There are $10,000,000 as the income of Texas stock owners for one year from one branch of their business only. Farmers need very much to realize this fact, which has more than usual force when the wheat crop now harvesting promises more than 500,000,000 bushels, and 75 cents a bushel seem to be a possible price. The most money made on farms henceforth will be made by the stock farmers.—[Exchange.

There is a good deal of complaint in cattlemen's circles about the disposition to crowd the ranges already stocked. New men who turn cattle on the range that is occupied are the greatest sufferers, because the cattle not located are most apt to die. The located herd will live where the strangers will all pass in their checks. But this is no excuse for taking another's range. We have the reputation of sending good beef to market, but if the range crowding business goes on much longer, we can only turn off steers. The farmers of Nebraska and other Mississippi valley states will have to make the beef with their corn crop. It may prove profitable to sell steers, but beef is likely to be in greater demand, and yield to the seller a handsome profit. Don't crowd the range.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Sir John Macdonald has authoritatively announced that the Canadian goverment has resolved to refuse the request of the Wyoming Stock-Growers' Association to have their stock conveyed through the dominion from the American border by the Canadian Pacific railway to Montreal for shipment to Great Britain. The premier supports his decision by charging that the scheme, if allowed, would be prejudicial to Canadian interests. The demand, he says, for cattle in England is limited, and it would be against the interest of Canadian farmers to give the stock-raisers of another country facilities to compete with them abroad. He expressed confidence from the progress already made that in a short time Canadian farmers would be amply able to supply the whole British market with beef and mutton. "Why, then," the premier urged, "should we let Wyoming ranchmen cross Canadian territory to do trade that we are prepared to do ourselves?" The first duty of the government, he held, was to encourage its own stock-raisers. The granting of the application would be adverse to their future progress. Sir John opposed any concession, lest disease break out in American cattle during transit, when the British goverment would schedule the whole continent, Canada included. These are the reasons adduced for adhering to the prohibition of American cattle coming into the Dominion.—[Breeder's Gazette.

The fall round-up commenced last Monday.
E. W. Crane, of Emigrant Gulch, Mont., was in town this week.
Mr. Duryea, of the government surveying party, was in town yesterday.
C. D. Edick, cigar manufacturer of Bismarck, was in town last week.
The stage horses are being shod as rapidly as possible and distributed along the line.
J. L. Crooks, of Spearfish, drove in this week 126 head of horses for H. R. Tarbell & Co.
T. M. Wright, formerly of the Bismarck Tribune, was in town a few days this week.
Supt. Green, of the Missouri division, passed through on last evening's west bound passenger.
The new church is to be built by the Marchioness instead of the Marquis, as stated in last week's paper.
J. A. Ferris, one of our enterprising merchants, has added a complete stock of groceries to his general store.
Gill Kennedy is decorating the stage coaches with a coat of paint, which improves their appearance wonderfully.
The firm of Coleman & Brown, proprietors of the Medora hotel, have dissolved partnership, M. M. Coleman continuing the business.
One of the railroad carpenters went to Dickinson Sunday, and while under the influence of tanglefoot was rolled for his watch and pocket-book.
Dr. H. M. Jorgens is daily expecting the arrival of his drug stock. The building which he is to occupy temporarily has been moved next to the company's store.
Frank Turner is overhauling the machinery in the abattoir and will put it in first-class order. Frank is availing himself of every interval in killing to get things in shape.
We were misinformed last week in regard to the new brick cottage the Baroness von Hoffmann is building. Mr. Grymes is the happy recipient of the Baroness' valuable present.
John Norton returned from St. Paul Tuesday evening, whither he had gone with several carloads of the company's dressed beef. He reports that they arrived in excellent condition.
Pat. O'Hara came in from the stage route last Monday. He has the coal mine running in full blast again and is prepared to fill all orders on short notice. Leave your orders at this office.

Remember the Republican county convention to be held at Medora hall on next monday evening, September 22, for the purpose of electing two delegates to represent Billings county in the legislative convention.

Bill Luse, an experienced stage driver of Montana, arrived in town this week. The stage company can congratulate themselves upon having secured the best and most efficient corps of stage drivers in the country.

A new refrigerator car, the "Antartic," was loaded with beef by the company, as an experiment, and shipped in care of the builder. If this car is a success, as it promises to be, several cars will be built and put on the road.

New and attractive buildings are going up in every part of town, and the building boom will undoubtedly continue for the next two or the months. This is an evidence of prosperity that few towns west of the Missouri can boast of.

The cool mornings of the past week indicates for a certainty the near approach of grim winter. A few weeks more and our verdant hills and vales will be covered by a blanket of "pure and spotless"—snow. Let her come. We have plenty of coal and a boy to shove it into the silver-mounted heater that graces our sanctum.

The railroad company is making a crossing over the track, which is a much needed improvement, but it is located two blocks from the stage office and freight depot and entirely out of the business part of the town, on an alley leading to the rear of the lumber yard and the company's stable. If a crossing is to be made it should be near the warehouse.

The editors of the Independent and Times at Glendive are complimenting one another by calling each other "liars," "thieves" and other choice names. It is rumored that the Times man carries a small arsenal in his hip pocket, and the residents of that enterprising city seem impressed with the belief that "bullud" will be shed.

A. T. Packard, editor of the Cow Boy, and the rustling general manager of the new stage line from Medora to Deadwood, left Sunday morning for Pierre to attend the Republican territorial convention as a delegate. A. T. grows eloquent at times and will doubtless do some effective mouth-work while attempting to paralyze the political aspirations of ——— ———. Mr. Packard will return by way of Deadwood and will reach Medora about the 30 inst.

The active and energetic managers of the Medora stage and forwarding company are indefatigable in their efforts to improve as far as possible the really natural road between this place and Deadwood, and in a short time freight will begin to roll steadily over the new route. Already trains are being loaded here with freight. The large and elegant coaches are models of beauty and and convey passengers to and fro with but little more discomfort than is encountered by the Pullman car tourist.

Pursuant to a call issued by the chairman of the county central committee a republican convention was held in Robert's hall at Medora on last Monday evening, September 22, 1884, for the purpose of electing two delegates to represent Billings county at the legislative convention to be held at Bismarck on October 15.

The convention was called to order by J. C. Fisher, chairman of the county central committee.

Moved that L. H. Palmer act as secretary.

Here a point of order was raised that the call should be first read and a permanent chairman elected. The chair overruled the point, maintaining that he held the office by virtue of former election. L. H. Palmer was then made secretary.

The secretary read the call as published.

A motion was then made and seconded that Robt. Roberts be elected by acclamation as one of the delegates.

F. H. Ertel offered as an amendment that they proceed to ballot for delegates and the two receiving the highest number of votes be declared elected, and urged it in the interest of fairness to all, but finally withdrew the amendment. The original motion prevailed and Mr. Roberts was duly elected without a dissenting vote.

J. C. Fisher and L. C. Hay were then put in nomination.

Mr. Hay declined the honor, and stated that he had not come to the convention to seek the delegateship, and explained his position in reference to the Belfield convention.

J. C. Fisher was then elected delegate without dissent.

F. H. Ertel offered the following resolution, which was unanimously adopted and the convention adjourned sine die:

Whereas, The Mandan Pioneer upon various occasions has presumed upon the good sense and competent judgement of the Republicans of Billings county, in trying to dictate to them through the columns of the paper, be it

Resolved, That grateful as the Republicans feel to the editors of said journal, for the deep interest taken in Billings county, the voters of Billings county feel sufficient confidence in themselves to manage their own affairs and assume all responsibility for their actions.

L. H. Palmer, Secretary.

The supreme court of Dakota has rendered a decision in the case of the territory against the capital commission, declaring that body a legal one and capable of exercising the powers given it by the legislature creating it. This finally settles the capital question and makes Bismarck legally what in fact it has been for some time, the seat of goverment for the territorry of Dakota.
