It is claimed that there are $10,000,000 worth of Jersey cattle in this country.
Hog cholera continues emptying the pens in the western part of Sarpy county, Nebraska.
A mare mule recently gave birth to a colt in the State of Oaxaca. The colt died shortly after birth.
The highest valuation of cattle in Colorado per head for taxation is $19.77; the average for the state is less than $15.00.
It is estimated that there is one sheep in the United States to every thirty-four acres of territory. In England the rate is one to one and a half acres.

The shipment of cattle from here to Chicago has commenced again in good earnest, and between now and the 5th of October no less than 500 carloads of prime beeves will be loaded at this point.—[Dickinson Press.

Twelve hundred head of cattle bearing the S D brand of S. Doyle arrived here yesterday in charge of about a dozen cow boys, who have brought the herd from the west and are taking the stock to a range fifty miles east of Glendive.—[Yellowstone Journal.

A Northern Pacific official denies that stockmen seek the rival roads for their shipments. He claims that the Northern Pacific is ahead of the others in offering inducements to shippers, and that this will be abundantly shown when at the end of the season the figures are published—[Mandan Pioneer.

It is often claimed and supposed by many that stockmen frame and influence legislation to suit them. The fact is, stockmen prosper in spite of adverse legislation. The stockman did best when lands were governed by no laws. They would as soon influence Indians as legislators.—[Tex. L. S. Journal.

Cocoanut oil cake is used in Java quite largely for live-stock food. It is made by crushing the kernel and extracting from it the oil by means of hydraulic pressure. The refuse left after the extraction of the oil is then pressed into cakes, and is eagerly devoured by cattle, who are said to fatten very rapidly on it.

Denver, Colorado, is fixing for a refrigerator establishment on a grand scale. The preliminary steps include securing a large pasture for grazing and feeding beeves purchased, so as not to be purchasing from hand to mouth, so to speak. They seem to recognize that capital is required. It should be a success.—[Tex. L. S. Journal.

A manager of a New Mexico cattle company who uses the Shorthorn as a cross, on account of their hardihood, is about to use the Spanish as another cross, on account of their gentleness. There is reason in all things and the hardy Shorthorn and gentle Texan are entitled to their honors—even if not exactly fitting them.—[Tex. L. S. Journal.

For mutton, Professor Brown, of the Guelph Agricultural College, Canada, says in his experience Leicester sheep are ahead of all others in putting on flesh in the shortest time. In early maturing he gives the following as the result of personal observations: Leicesters, Southdown cross, Leicester cross, Oxford Down cross, Cotswold being the slowest.—[Kan. City L. S. Indicator.

A disease has appeared among the cattle in the northwestern part of Osage county, Kan., and several fatal cases are reported. The owners of the cattle do not know what the disease is, but a quarantine has been established to prevent its spread. After being affected, the cattle only live a day or two. Drowsiness, costiveness and bloody discharges are its main symptoms.—[Kan. City L. S. Indicator.

The amount of wool shipped from Fort Benton and vicinity during the past season aggregates 795,722 pounds. Of this amount 689,558 pounds were shipped from Fort Benton; 4,681 pounds from the coal banks; 86,136 pounds from Judith; 15,346 pounds from Rocky Point. These shipments were all made by the Power line of steamers, the Benton on two trips carrying 997 bales, the Batchelor on three trips 1,427 and the Helena on one trip, 428.—[Exchange.

The Continental Land and Cattle Company, one of the wealthiest concerns of the kind in the country, shipped a train load of cattle from this place yesterday that were all black and averaged in weight about eleven hundred pounds each. It was a novelty, being the first train of black cattle ever shipped from Montana or Dakota territories. They were the selection of John N. Simpson and A. B. Combes. The company shipped from here this week over sixty carloads of fine fat cattle.—[Dickinson Press.

The day has gone by when size is considered before quality in cattle. The big, rough hulks of enormous weights are passed by in the sale pens for smaller, but smoother and neater cattle. These compactly built, smooth-bodied beeves are subject to less shrinkage both in shipping and turning into beef, require less feed, and give evidence of possessing a greater hardiness of constitution, and are by all means the most profitable for the farmer to handle. If farmers, in selecting cattle either for breeding or feeding purposes, would be assured that they are obtaining stock that will be profitable, they must bear these points in mind, and select more for quality than for size.—[Exchange.

A telegram from Cheyenne, Wyoming Territory, under date of Sept. 16, says: In accordance with the governor's proclamation and the law of Wyoming, the territorial veterinarian and the executive committee of the stock association to-day issued a circular to railroads and the public generally, stating that no cattle brought from the States here will be admitted without passing a quarantine of ninety days or longer, as may be judged necessary. This action is taken in view of the recognized fact that a contagious disease of a dangerous character exists in eastern localities, and is made thus public to save loss and detention to shippers and the possibility of unintentional violation by railroads or individuals.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

The Union Mutual Live Stock association have filed articles of incorporation with the register of deeds. The object of the association is stated to be "one of charity, benevolence and mutual assistance among its members, and to indemnify each other by mutual assessments for the loss by death or disablement of horses, mules and cattle." The corporation is to commence Sept. 24, and continue fifty years. The requirements of membership are: First, the payment of one dollar annual dues on each animal; second, an admission fee of 1 per cent. of the affixed value of each animal; third, the payment of one-half per cent. of the value of the animal on joining the association; fourth, one-half the value of each animal insured upon the death of any animal belonging to a member. The articles are signed by William Uril, J. H. Hasty, Charles H. Penrith and J. W. Molyneaux.—[Pioneer Press.

The following is a distressing picture drawn in a dispatch with reference to the suffering of cattle that were shipped to New York city recently, during the hot spell, and clearly demonstrates the advantage of western slaughtered beef against these fever-heated animals: "Since Tuesday of last week 20 per cent. of the western cattle have died on the cars or immediately after being transferred to the stock yards. The soap factories are over-stocked with carcasses of steers, hogs and sheep bought at prices ranging from ten cents to fifty cents a head. Saturday night an Erie train load of cattle arrived at Hoboken too late for transfer by boat, and they remained in closely packed cars until Monday morning without food or drink, suffering terrible agony. When unloaded 20 per cent. were dead or dying while the living were in such a state of fever as to render them unfit for beef until cold weather. Two cars of the train were closely packed with calves, hogs and sheep. The sight was an atrocious one, while the cries of distress from the tortured creatures made spectators turn away. From the mouths of calves and sheep hung tongues swollen and blackened, while hogs were gnawing their own fat. All day long the sun beat down on the wretched animals, and the neighborhood heard little save the fearful wail. Only nineteen animals out of two car loads lived to be unloaded Monday morning."

"Say Revenue, I tell you what it is; the Drag ain't no good after he's got a dose of horse thief fever. He don't represent worth a nickle. He'd better take a change of venue and make application for a sheep herder. He's coon-tailed and shows up nothing." Guess the Drag's about right and up near the line they give the rustlers, the fellows that get away with the horses, awful powerful medicine. Lariat rope and cottonwood tree, with tight cinch under the ear is a sure cure. An injection of cold lead from a Smith & Wesson syringe is a dandy where cottonwoods are scarce, and a lariat rope fast to a saddle horn with the loop around the patient's neck and the horse on a full gallop was frequently used by the Mexicans and Apaches. Yes, the remedy is severe, but recollect, you herders, the disease is powerful bad.—[Yellowetone Journal.

Lieut. Fred Schwatka, of the United States army, who is for a few days stopping at the Leland Hotel, is enthusiastic over a scheme of his to form a company for growing cattle on the Aleutian Islands, in the North Pacific Ocean. Having had ample opportunity to study the advantages offered by these Islands he speaks in glowing terms of what might come of a large company properly managed. The islands contain about 3,000 square miles of excellent grazing lands, mostly low, but most of it 2,000 to 3,000 feet above the sea. The islands are small, and most of them are naturally divided in several places by bold mountain headlands that extend from the "backbone" range to the sea, forming natural fences. This would do away with the necessity of fencing bulls or branding cattle; two very important considerations. There is enough rich grass to form abundant feed all winter and hay can be cut anywhere on the low lands. The climate is mild on account of the warm Japan current. In more than 50 years the mercury has not gone lower than 1 degree above zero. The prevailing winter winds are southwesterly and summer winds are northwesterly, thus favoring boats that would transport beeves to the Pacific coast market. It is claimed that the cost of transportation to market would be within $5@10 per head; the latter price being ample to take beeves to San Francisco. The Lieutenant has no lack of faith in the scheme being a real bonanza, and the facts and figures he presents to back his faith are certainly very attractive.—[Drovers' Journal.

The political campaign is growing more brisk but will not get "red hot" until all the local candidates are in the field. These are relied upon to stir the pot and bring out a full vote.

It is said the "oldest inhabitant" does not recollect a more prolonged season of verdure in the northwest than the present. The season began somewhat later than usual, but has been uninterrupted by drouths or frost, and seems likely to last at least a month later.

The brick cottages are rapidly nearing completion.
C. W. Sleeper returned from St. Paul last evening.
Alex. Metzger, of Bismarck, was in town Tuesday.
From thirty to thirty-five beeves a day are now being slaughtered at the abattoir.
On the second page of this paper will be found a full report of the Pierre convention.
T. J. Sharkey, traveling auditor of the Northern Pacific railroad, was in town yesterday.
The Baron and Baroness von Hoffmann returned from their western trip this morning in their special car.
F. H. Ertel, of the Bismarck Journal, and L. C. Hay, of Belfield, came up Monday evening to attend the convention.
J. H. Kelly, of Duluth, now manipulates the electric-telegraph apparatus at the telegraph office, Mr. Smith having departed for Illinois.
Mr. A. E. Grymes, of New York, arrived in town Monday evening, and is visiting at the Marquis' residence. He is the father of J. F. Grimes, who is employed in the company's office.
The Northern Pacific railroad surveyers, who have been in the vicinity some time for the purpose of locating the river, have completed their work and returned east last Sunday morning.
The dance at the Pyramid Park hotel last Friday evening proved to be one of the most enjoyable affairs of the season. The attendance was good and the music up to its usual standard of excellency.

D. O. Sweet and wife, of Forsythe, Mont., are among the new arrival in Medora. Mr. Sweet is looking for a location to engage in some business. He thinks the prospects are very bright, and it is safe to assert that he will remain with us.

John Sullivan, the world's champion, is beautifying his tonsorial establishment with a coat of paint. John fell from a step-ladder the other day, causing injuries which will necessitate his withdrawing from the pugilistic arena temporarily.

The museum in the Cow Boy office received two valuable additions this week. One was from Vic. Smith, which was a petrified knee joint of a mastodon. The other was donated by J. A. McGregor, and is the finest specimen of petrified wood we have ever seen.

Dr. Fletcher, who has been here on a hunt for some time, left for his home in Indianapolis Monday, and from the amount of baggage and boxes he had we infer he has made a large and valuable collection of curiosities during his stay in the Bad Lands.

Two cowboys attempted to paint the usual quiet town of Dickinson red last Thursday. They knocked down an old man, drove women off the street at the point of the revolver, shot one horse dead and badly injured another. One of them enjoyed the extreme pleasure of paying $268 for his amusement.

The Land Agent is the name of a new paper published at Deadwood. Jas. C. Moody is the editor and proprietor. It is circulated gratuitously, as it is issued in connection with the business of the publisher as a real estate dealer, and its aim is to inform capitalists and investors of the resources and advantages of the Hills.

The corner-stone of the new church was laid last Saturday afternoon, and was witnessed by quite a number of people, including the Marquise, who is building the church. On one side of the stone is inscribed "Athenais," and on the other, "Medora, Marquise de Mores, Sept. 15, 1884." The church is being completed as rapidly as possible and in a short time will be ready for services.

A new mode of communication is being introduced by William Vandriesche, who has sixteen carrier pigeons which he is training to carry messages between this point and the Black Hills. William has made several experiments with them, taking them out to the stage stations, and they have invariably returned in a remarkable short time. It is estimated that they can fly to the Hills in about two or three hours, which is very good time indeed.

Clay Leighton and Henry Scott, the two notorious horse-thieves who were incarcerated in the Dickinson jail upon the charge of stealing horses from Archibald Morton, of South Heart, made their escape Thursday evening. Their absence was not discovered until an hour afterwards, when a posse started in pursuit of the criminals, but up to this writing they have succeeded in evading their pursuers. They made their exit with the assistance of a chisel and a bar of iron eighteen inches long, which was undoubtedly provided them by outside parties.

Supt. Deffebach returned Tuesday from a trip over the stage route, and informed us that the stages would positively commence running on the morning of October 6. A coach from Deadwood will leave at the same time. The preliminary work has taken up much more time than was anticipated. The proprietors have exercised great care and skillful judgement in equiping the route with the best of everything. The stock is in splendid condition, the stations are nearly all completed and placed in charge of good and responsible parties, and the hungry tourist will not want for a first-class meal when he travels over this route.

A portion of the east wall of the church was blown down during the heavy wind storm Tuesday night.
The Marquis came up from St. Paul Monday evening in his special car. He will remain a few days.
Bob. Roberts' outfit will load with Black Hills freight to-morrow, consigned to Deadwood, Spearfish and Lead City merchants.
The plans of the new abattoir have arrived. Some alterations will be necessary, and we will not be able to publish a full description of the building until next week.
A. T. Packard, of the BAD LANDS COW BOY, General Manager of the Medora Stage Company, paid his devoirs to the Register yesterday, and to the G. A. R. ball last evening.—[Spearfish Register.

Bob Roberts was compelled to shoot one of his bears this morning in order to relieve it from suffering, it having been wounded a few months ago by some unknown person who was indulging in promiscuous shooting.

According to the time table which we publish this week the arrival and departure of stages will be as follows: The coaches will arrive Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, at 6 p. m., connecting with westbound passenger train, and depart Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, at 8:30 a. m., connecting with eastbound train.

There will be five eating stations on the route, the outfits for which are on the ground ready for business. The stations as located are as follows: Medora, Davis creek, Rocky Ridge, Springdale, Buffalo creek, North Grand river, Cave Hills, Gallup's, Middle Grand river, South Grand, Macy's, Indian creek, DeMores, Spearfish, Deadwood.

Under the head "Center of Stockdom" a St. Paul paper states that the center of the cattle trade has moved north from Colorado, Nebraska and Wyoming to Montana and Dakota. Three cattle firms have 88,000 head on the Cheyenne, Belle Fourche and Little Missouri rivers. Altogether the Northern Pacific road has shipped this season over 2,000 cars of beeves, or 40,000 head from Montana to Chicago, and expects to ship 75,000 head before the close of the season. To the ranges in Montana and Western Dakota it has shipped 100,000 head of yearlings and two-year-olds this season from further east. The Powder River Cattle Co. has 60,000 head of cattle on its range, valued at $3,000,000, and has purchased lands at South Duluth on which cattle pens and yards will be built, where cattle may be kept until ready for shipment by boat to the east.

Several cases of pleuro-pneumonia has been discovered in Illinois.
The Swan Land & Cattle Co., is now shipping from 1,000 to 1,200 beef steers per week to the Chicago market.
A Jersey cow at Hamilton, Ont, shows the unprecedented yield of thirty pounds and two ounces of butter in seven days.
W. J. Pitney, of Augusta, Ill., has a grade Short-horn cow that gave birth to three healthy bull calves that are doing well.
At a recent sale of Hamilton Short-horns at Flat Creek, Ky, fifty animals, several of them young calves, sold for $35,980, averaging $719,60.
A Cattle train was wrecked on the Rock Island road Sept. 27. The fireman of the engine and a stockman were killed. A car of cattle were consumed by fire.
We hear of no new cases of Texas fever. The epidemic has probably disappeared for the present season. With proper precaution there need be no danger of its reappearance another year.
The cattle shipments from Dickinson last week were as follows: Continental Land and Cattle company, 140 cars; Clark & Plum, 16 cars; Dickey Bros., 105 cars. They were all consigned to Chicago.

It is stated from all parts of the country that the cattle which a short time since were afflicted with sore eyes have recovered, and there is no new cases reported. The first frost removed the cause.

The Swan Land & Cattle Co. have 130,000 head of cattle in the Platte country and a capital of $3,375,000. They branded 20,000 calves this season and are shipping about twelve hundred head of beef steers per week.—[Yellowstone Journal.

At the great combination sale of Hereford cattle at Kansas City recently, Mr. Wm. Morgan, of Cheyenne, purchased "Primrose," the venerable mother of the Wyoming Hereford Association's famous bull "Rudolph," paying for the cow and her calf $1,500.

Colorado last year had but 14,000 swine. The present year it will have 25,000. Ere two years more it will have 100,000. Prior to the present time the playful hog has cut but light caper in this country. In the future he will command respect.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Those who give time, money and care to the breeding and feeding of scrub stock are, says an experienced breeder, beaten from the start. The same feed and care bestowed upon fine stock would yield a profit. Grade up by using full-blooded sires.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

A fine herd of cattle were poisoned on John Watson's stock farm, twenty miles southwest of Morris, Minn., last Saturday, by drinking in an arm of the Pomme Deterre river, upon which a heavy green scum had collected. Twenty-six of the cattle are dead and others are expected to die.

Miss Maud Reed, the cattle queen of the mountains, was drowned in the Grand river, a little below Grand Junction, a few days since. She was on her way to her cattle ranch on East creek, and while fording the river, in company with Coghill and Harry Taylor—two cattle men—were all swept down by the rushing waters and drowned.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The stockmen about Tombstone are excited, it seems. John Chisholm, a cattle king from Texas, is about to drive a large herd of cattle into Arizona. The stockmen of that section are aroused to the danger of being overshadowed by this cattle king, and if Chisholm moves in, they think they will have to move out, and they don't propose to do that without a struggle.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

The sheep market is assuming a more cheerful look. In addition to an improved demand for shipment alive, one of our dressed meat concerns is now shipping an average of 400 carcasses per day. Prices have been discouragingly low all the season, and while there is no likelihood of any immediate decided advance, it is safe to conclude that the period of greatest depression has been passed.—[Breeder's Gazette

Wyoming has 800,000 head of cattle, valued at $30,000,000. Seven companies own one-third of all the cattle in the territory. Of the vast herds of cattle in Texas it is claimed that 1,000,000 head are owned by parties living outside of the state, and that a revenue of $10 per head is annually received by outsiders on these investments. Canadian exporters of beef have been heavy losers this season on their shipments to England. Many extensive shippers have gone out of the business.—[Chicago Commercial.

Monday's run of range cattle was in the neighborhood of 7,500 head—a considerably larger number than reported for any previous day of the season. This was followed Tuesday by 6,000 head, making nearly 14,000 head for the two days. The indications are that shipments from the plains have now begun in good earnest, and from this time on to the end of October average receipts of from 5,000 to 7,000 head per day may safely be counted on. Since Friday last there has been a decline in prices of 40@50c, and the market is still weak, with the chances in favor of a further shrinkage.—[Breeder's Gazette.

A Montreal paper says: "Shippers of beef cattle from this point have been extraordinarily heavy losers this season. One firm shows a deficiency up to the present of $250,000. Another firm lost $150,000, and several from $50,000 to $150,000 each. The principal loss arises from purchasing before navigation, when prices were very high; and also in making contracts for freight throughout the season at increased rates over last year. The fall in prices in Great Britain made every consignment unprofitable. Over $3,000,000 worth of cattle have been shipped from here this season so far, the increase being great over last year.

It is said that there are 15,000,000 horses in the United States, the average size of which has been in some way contributed to by the importations of Clydesdales and Normans. As, to keep up the supply, 1,000,000 must be bred annually, those who have made horse breeding for a foreign market their object, need not yet despair, though the demand may have fallen off. They have the best of Clydesdales, the best of Normans and a few Shires, but they need more of all; and the Cleveland blood much, as the best of the studs of the old Yorkshire breed out there has not been heavily touched. The Soffolks they do not seem inclined to recognize.—[English L. S. Journal.

Sidney Dillon, of world-wide fame as one of the Union Pacific potentates, is one of the heaviest cattle-owners in the Union. The firm of which he is the principal is known as Dillon & Co. Isaac Dillon constitutes the Co. He is the manager of the business, and lives on a ranch near North Platte. Their cattle are numbered by the thousand on a thousand hills. Some are in this valley and others up in the Snake River country. The headquarters cattle ranch, known as the "Stone ranch," is in the valley near O'Fallon's station and is surrounded by a splendid range, extending for many miles on the north and south. The able assistant to Mr. Dillon is Frank Alexander, than whom there is no better in the state.—[Col. L. S. Record.

For the last sixty days our receipts of cattle have been declining at the rate of fully one thousand head per day, as compared with the corresponding period last year. For this heavy loss it is not easy to fully account. A part of it may be ascribed to the late stringency in the money market, which made it difficult for intending shippers to get the usual bank accommodation, and a part may be charged to the cutting of rail freights by roads leading eastward from St. Louis and Kansas City, by which means a good deal of stock was diverted from this market; but the principal cause of the shortage is no doubt found in the almost certainty of a tremendous crop, all over the west, of corn and fodder. This led farmers to keep back thousands of young and unfinished cattle which with a less encouraging outlook would have been sent to market.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Probably never before have the cattle raisers of the west been in better spirits than during the present season. Prices in some cases may not be quite so high at present, nor the profits be anything in excess of other years, but still there seems to prevail a good healthy feeling of satisfaction, all things considered. True the fall trade is attended with some drawbacks, as will always be the case in this or any other line of business, but up to date the receipts of cattle at Chicago and other points have been moderate, and this has had a tendency to keep the market steady. In no case have shippers been compelled to sell at losing figures on account of the market being glutted or over supplied, and if receipts at the market centres continue in the same moderate figures that have characterized them thus far, there can indeed be no cause for complaint.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Stock Inspector Matthews was in town to-day.
T. S. Houk, of Detroit, Mich., is visiting here.
Edward Rany, of Bismarck, was in town this week.
Otto Fisher and Chas. Williams, of Bismarck, were in town last Friday.
The N. P. Ref. Car Co. will ship two carloads of sheep to Duluth this week.
Dr. D. M. McIntosh came down from Glendive yesterday on professional business.
J. R. Widmyer, of the Glendive Independent, made us a pleasant visit last Sunday.
Mr. C. L. Brinker, station agent at this place, is contemplating a visit to his home in Pennsylvania.
J. A. Ferris' store not being adequate to hold his immense stock he has been compelled to build a large warehouse.
Mr. A. T. Packard, editor of the COW BOY, is expected to return from the Hills on the first coach, which will arrive Tuesday evening.
Passenger train No. 2 was thirteen hours late Tuesday. The delay was occasioned by a collision with a freight train on the Yellowstone division.
L. D. Pettit, of Belfield, stopped at Medora a short time this week en reute to Billings and other points in connection with his fast increasing bone business.
From five to ten trains of stock a day have been passing through Medora within the last few days. They are shipped from Miles City, Glendive and Mingusville.
J. Alden Eaton, manager of the Custer Trail Cattle company, and Mr. Stevenson, of Pittsburgh, Pa., who is visiting here, made the COW BOY office a pleasant call this morning.
Bismarck will send two or three carloads of products of Burleigh county to the New Orleans exposition. It is expected that a total of twenty carloads will go from Dakota.

D. H. Hostetter, of Pittsburgh, Pa., who has been visiting at Eaton' ranch for the past few weeks, started for home last Friday. Mr. Hostetter is the son of the celebrated Dr. Hostetter of bitters fame. Howard Eaton accompanied him east as far as Mandan.

The Minnesela Boomer says "considerable freight now passes through Minnesela on its way from the Northern Pacific to the Hills, and it is only a question of a short time until nearly all the freight comes this way, as the road is being put in good shape.

Bob. Roberts, who is one of the deputy commissioners of Dakota for the New Orleans expositon, returned from Bismarck this week, where he had been in connection with his office. He has engaged Vic Smith to collect petrifactions and other curiosities for the exposition.

Monday evening's westbound passenger train was delayed here about an hour and twenty minutes owing to one of the coaches running off the track while in the act of side-tracking the Marquis' special car. It seems that the track is in very poor condition, which alone caused the accident, no blame being attached to the train men.

The following gentlemen have been invited to accompany the first stage to Deadwood, which leaves here next Monday morning, October 6: C. S. Fee, general passenger agent; J. M. Hanniford, general freight agent, and M. J. Hall, assistant superintendent N. P. express company, of St. Paul; Governor Pierce, Alex. McKenzie and F. B. Allen, of Bismarck.

Mr Julius Lemoyne, of the Lemoyne Cattle company, who have their ranch on Tepee Bottom, arrived in Medora last Sunday evening. Mr Lemoyne's home is in Washington county, Pa., which is noted for its thoroughbred stock breeders, and is himself a breeder of thoroughbred Short-horn cattle and Berkshire swine. He is accompanied by Harry Kelly, of West Virginia, who is also interested in the breeding business.

The immigrant train last Tuesday had three carloads of Crow Indians aboard, who were in box cars and huddled together like so many cattle. They caused considerable amusement, as they were evidently hungry and commenced prying around the culinary departments of every hotel in town. They were gorgeously attired in various costumes and decorated with ornaments, paint, etc. They came from Fort Berthold, via Dickinson, and were en route to Fort Custer.

The Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, was in town this week, and held mass Tuesday morning. He informed us that they were building a hospital at Mandan, called the Sisters' Hospital, which is 80x50 feet in dimension. It is to be a three-story brick building with Mansard roof. It is estimated that the cost of the building will be $25,000. In view of this fact he says all contributions will be gratefully received, and that he will soon give our citizens an opportunity to subscribe for this good cause as liberally as they wish. As this will be the only hospital between here and Brainerd it certainly is a much needed institution.

If the scheme of the Marquis de Mores proves successful, it will in a great measure destroy, in the large markets of the east, the attempts to boycot western beef. The intense spirit of boycotting, which has recently manifested itself toward Chicago dressed beef is attributed solely to the disreputable methods of certain Chicago dealers in attempting to palm off stale beef for prime beef in the east. The eastern butchers with a keen eye to business, have taken advantage of the feeling engendered by this trick of the Chicagoans, and have worked up a formidable feeling of opposition to western beef. The Marquis de Mores, however, has the advantage over Chicago dealers in this, that all his beef is necessarily prime beef. His cattle are slaughtered at the abattoirs, fresh from the healthy herds on his ranches. The beeves are not transported several hundred or a thousand miles by rail to reach his slaughter houses. Hence they are fresh and healthy, and make only prime beef. His system of cold storage houses from Portland to Duluth enables him to store his meat until ready for shipment so as to bring it to the best possible point of fresh meat curing before it reaches the market. His meats are carefully graded and sold in accordance with well established rules, so that eastern dealers are always fairly treated and know exactly what they are purchasing and handling. This immense system of providing the world with fresh prime beef originated with the ingenious and clever Frenchman who now controls it. There is every reason to believe that his enterprise will not only prove a great blessing to beef eating mankind in general, and places within the reach of every man better and wholesomer foot. The man who lowers the price of every mouthful of food for humanity does the world infinitely more good than the hero of Austerlitz, who conquers armies and overturns empires. The Marquis de Mores may be called the pioneer in a business which promises to revolutionize the food supply of the civilized world. He has recently increased the capital stock of his company, and is now in a fair position to enrich his already large estates, and immortalize his much respected name.—[Mandan Pioneer.

TO THE FRONT

The First Coach Makes a Flying Trip and Comes Into Medora Half an Hour Ahead of Time.

The Company Guarantee to Reduce the Time to 30 Hours Between Medora and Deadwood.

Arrival of First Coach at Deadwood Greeted by a Large and Enthusiastic Crowd.

Deadwood, Oct. [3?].—Special.—Probably no event in the history of Deadwood outside of the gold fever has created the enthusiasm and excitement caused by the arrival of the first coach of the Medora and Black Hills Stage line. The well known liberality of the originator of the line is a sufficient guarantee to the Hills people that no pains will be spared to give every comfort possible to the patrons of this line, and the fact that the first trip was made in less time than that ever made by any other line running to the Hills, augurs well for the future of this new line. Deadwood extends a hearty greeting to her near neighbor Medora.

Spearfish, Oct 6.—The arrival of the first coach of the new line this morning was greeted by a large crowd of enthusiastic citizens, and was the occasion of general hand shaking and congratulations. The new 11-seated Concord coach, drawn by six powerful horses wearing bright new harnesses shows that the company means business. Spearfish sends greeting to Medora.

Medora, Oct. 8.—The first coach of the Medora and Black Hills Stage line arrived at 8 p. m., leaving Deadwood at 8:30 p. m. October 6, making the trip in 35½ hours, or two days and one night, being the only line into the Hills with less than two night rides. We are assured by the company that the time can very easily be shortened to 30 hours between Medora and Deadwood, making Medora the nearest railroad point to the Hills by at least 12 to 14 hours.

Denver will have a slaughtering and beef packing establishment on an extensive scale.

The total number of hogs slaughtered annually in the United States is estimated at 30,000,000, the average dressed weight being 175 pounds.

Holsteins mature early. It is a rule in Holland to have heifers come in at twenty to thirty months old. At this age they usually make a growth of from 1,100 to 1,350 pounds, and at maturity range from 1,400 to 1,800 pounds.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The receipts of live stock for the last month amounted to 167,700 cattle, 10,000 calves, 253,000 hogs and 56,500 sheep, which is a decrease as compared with September, 1883, of 4,700 cattle, 85,000 hogs and 4,900 sheep, and an increase of 4,800 calves.—[Breeder's Gazette.

The Union Pacific company are doing a fine thing by the cattle shippers along the line of the K. P. division of their road. Cattle loaded at Kit Carson and other points no farther west than that, are run through to Kansas City in 22 hours without unloading. The rolling stock and tracks are in the best condition, and their cattle trains run at thunderbolt speed.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Accompanied by a full force of employes, Mr. S. A. Marney, the proprietor of the Stock Grower' Journal, arrived in the city yesterday. He has purchased an extensive printing establishment in the east, and it is his intention to issue his paper early in the coming month. He'll be assisted in the editorial work by R. M. Hathway, Esq. Extensive encouragement has been extended to the new enterprise.—[Yellowstone Journal.

Cattle breeders cannot exercise too great care in selecting their stock bulls. By the selection of an extra stock-getter a large herd can soon be bred up to a good grade standard. In fact all our hopes and fears should be concentrated in him. He should be the best and most perfect animal in the herd—far better, if possible, than the best cow. The progeny of the bull may number fifty or more in one year, while the cow produces but one calf.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

In raising mules for profit says an exchange, the great aim should be to raise that kind that will sell readily and to the best advantage. Size and good build seem to be the principal requisites sought for by the best buyers. It pays to try to meet the demand. To do this the selection of the jack is of the first importance. He should be at least 14 hands tall, have a good length of body, a deep chest, with upright ears, a good temper and sprightly appearance, and above all a good, sound constitution.

W. J. Wilson and C. Pearson, two large cattle owners from Durango, Col., are at the Armijo. Both Mr. Wilson and Mr. Pearson are delighted with Albuquerque, and have purchased a ranch out on the Atlantic & Pacific road. Mr Wilson says he is leaving Colorado because of the trouble with southern Utes. He says that recently his two little sons, aged eight and ten years, and himself, were kept in the saddle for twenty-nine hours by the troublesome redskins. The boys stood it nobly and never whimpered.—[Albuquerque Journal.

Dick Havilock was arrested on the range near Miles City a few days ago on the charge of stealing cattle near La Junta, Colorado. He did not wait for a requisition but started with the officer for Colorado. Havilock is a noted character in the southwest, where he figured for years as a cattle thief, stage robber and gambler. He is a man of fine presence and polished manners. The cattle association of Colorado spent about $2,000 in tracing him to where he was arrested in Custer county.—[Livingston Enterprise.

Imported cattle have been distributed through all portions of the country. So far the short-horns lead any other breed as to numbers, but the Herefords and Polled-Angus are now moving strong. These leading breeds are now found scattered all over the country, from Texas to Montana, and they are fast making their impress on the quality of cattle all over that long stretch of country. Grades of these breeds—quarter, half and three-quarter bloods—are all the time making their appearance at all the leading cattle markets, and they are rapidly increasing.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

The hunt for rustlers in the southwestern portion of the territory still goes on, and the officers and stockmen of that section are now giving their attention to a gang who have been operating in Grant county, in the neighborhood of Silver City and Central City. We hope soon to be able to chronicle an item to the effect that the gang has been broken up, and the leaders sent to join the two horse thieves recently captured near El Paso, and "came to their death at the hands of unknown parties," in the language of the coroner's jury. To deal out summary justice is the only way in which this class of cattle can be taught that they must leave the property of stockmen alone.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

The whole of Northern Wyoming, particularly that part of the country east of the Big Horn mountains, is infested by coyotes and the gray wolf. Starvation, doubtless has driven them into a country where they can feed on calves and sometime full grown cattle. The loss from this source is greater than many suppose. The Conrad-Hurlbut Land and Cattle company alone estimate that they have lost three hundred head. There is only one effective method of decimating wolves, and that is by poisoning them. All the cattle companies will furnish the necessary article—strychnine—to those who wish to employ their time in the pursuit of wolf pelts and the reward per head offered by the territory for each wolf slain.—[Buffalo Echo.

A floating item says that the best horse doctor is a sensible horse. Give him liberty and he will take care of himself. Who ever saw a horse running wild that was troubled with the "heaves?" A nibble of a poplar pole, or a bite of "rose weed" and a full supply of grass is all he wants to put himself in a sleek, plump, happy condition; but if kept up and fed dusty hay and made subject to the unnatural demand of a thoughtless owner, it is no wonder he suffers. Father Clarkson says "rosin weed" is a sovereign cure for heaves, or a prevention, and any one who has seen the intelligent horse stretch his nose away over to brouse it in the uncut grass when hitched to the mower, has eviddnce in support. A good horse is his own doctor if you give him a chance.—[Kan. City L. S. Indicator.

Information comes from northern Wyoming that the cattle herds in that section are suffering severely from the ravages of wolves and coyotes. It will be remembered that at the cowmen's convention it was suggested by Mr. Heller, of the Conrad-Hurlbut company, that the shortage in the calf crop was due as much to these pests as to marauding Indians, and he urged a systematic and compulsory poisoning of the brutes by all the outfits in the infested country. This is the only true relief from the plague and it should be pursued without cessation until the nuisance is abated. Aside from the protection afforded to the herds, the bounty on wolf skins will amply repay the nominal expense of the war of extermination and afford a handsome largess for the cowboys or others who engage in it.

In transporting cattle by cars humanity and economy alike dictate that the best methods attainable for the care of stock ought to be adopted. A recent invention noticed by the scientific press is intended to furnish improved means of supplying cars with adequate water troughs. These are constructed of rubber cloth, or other waterproof material, and have slides, rods and bars arranged to fold the trough while being raised and open it while being lowered. The trough-operating slides have straps or chains connecting them with wheels and shafts, so the slides can be readily operated to raise and lower the troughs. The water tanks are placed in the upper part of the cars, from which pipes lead down to such position as to discharge water into the ends of the troughs when they are lowered and opened, the tanks themselves being supplied with water in the same manner as the locomotives are watered, through spout projections in the roof of the car. It is to be hoped that this or some similar method may be extensively adopted, as ultimately it will prove to be money in the pockets of those who thus care for their cattle while being transported to eastern markets.—[Journal.

Mrs. Eaton and daughter started for Chicago yesterday morning on a visit to friends.
The dances at Roberts' Hall and Hotel de Mores Tuesday night were both well attended.
A. T. Packard, editor of the Cow Boy, will arrive on this evening's coach from Deadwood.
Mr. Will Houk left last evening for Glendive to accept a position on the Independent.
Mr. A. E. Grimes, who has been visiting here for a week or two, returned home Monday.
G. F. Porter and wife returned from Chicago this week, where Mr. Porter has been buying goods for the company store.
Dr. Julius Lemoyne and Harry Kell[y?] who have been visiting here for a short time, returned to their home in Pennsylvania Tuesday.
The arrivals on the first coach from the Hills Tuesday evening were: H. H. Chandler, Lieutenant W. D. Wright, P. H. Wilson, P. D. O'Brien and S. B. Segen.
The work of getting out 150 cords of stone for the new refrigerator commenced yesterday. The Marquis telegraphed ordering 50 cords additional, making 200 cords.
C. S. Brinker, our station agent, has obtained a month's leave of absence, and has gone on a visit to his home in Pennsylvania. Mr. J. R. Fegan will act as agent until his return.
The Marquis de Mores and Baron Von Hoffman left for St. Paul Sunday morning in the special car Livingston. Miss Thomas, who has been visiting at the Marquis', accompanied them.

A band of Indians, consisting of four bucks and six squaws, have been camping here during the past week. Since their arrival they have been living "way up," so to speak, on the refuse of the slaughter house.

A. C. Huidekoper, of Meadeville, Pa., who is heavily interested in the Custer Trail Cattle Company, and also in H. R. Tarbell & Co.'s horse ranch arrived last evening on business connected with his interests here.

P. D. O'Brien, mining broker of Deadwood, came through on the first coach and took the train this morning for Chicago and the east. He says that if capitalists have enough gold and silver, he will give them tin.

Two more brick cottages have gone up during the past week. Pete Book has a large force of men at work who will make the brick and timber fly in a lively manner. Medora is enjoying a building boom no other town on the line can boast of.

Since the reopening of the Pyramid Park hotel, Little Missouri, by Boyd & Alexander, they are enjoying the large patronage, which they deserve, as the house from parlor to kitchen is first class. Their advertisement appears in another column.

C. L. Nothing, N. D. Carrin and J. D. Gilmor, of New York city; H. S. Shaffer, of Pittsburg, Pa., and B. F. Lamb, of Boston, are registered at the Hotel de Mores. They arrived on Tuesday evening for the purpose of viewing the wierd scenery and having a hunt in the famous Bad Lands.

E. J. Cattell, private secretary of W. J. Footner, superintendent of the Northern Pacific Express company, was one of the first passengers to Deadwood, where he goes to establish offices of the Northern Pacific Express company, as the express business will be under the management of that company.

A leading citizen and well known politican, resident of the county seat of Billings County, was a few evenings since invited to crack a bottle of champagne and interview "the governor" on the political situation. Probably no one at the county seat is more enthusiastic over the success of his adopted city than John, beg pardon, we mean the l. c. before mentioned, and he saw in this interview a rare opportunity to give the governor a few pointers. This same l. c. well knows that the surest and quickest way to reach a man's heart is via the stomach. Accordingly, with the air of one who is two-thirds owner of Alaska, he orders half a dozen of Mum's extra dry and proceeds to discuss the political situation with all the plausibility of an old timer. Meantime, Mum's extra had the desired effect on the governor, and he opened his heart to our l. c. and promised him all that he requested, even to the half of his kingdom and part of Alaska. Up to this point the most solemn silence had been observed by the select few who were permitted to be present at the interview, but here the admirable fortitude and calm self-possession of Gary gave way, and he snorted, so to speak, and gave away the whole business. Our l. c. says he tumbled to their racket the first thing, but—"Drop that oyster," John.

Altogether the Northern Pacific road will have shipped (including cars ordered for the balance of the week) this season, over 2,000 cars of beeves, or 40,000 head from Montana to Chicago. The road expects to ship 75,000 head before the close of the season. To the ranges in western Dakota and Montana the Northern Pacific has shipped 100,000 head of yearlings and two-year-olds this season from Iowa, Wisconsin and Minnesota. These will come back to the east as beeves the second or third season out, according to their grades. The Powder River Cattle company has 60,000 head of cattle on its range valued at $3,000,000, and has purchased lands at Superior City on which cattle pens and yards will be built, where cattle may be kept until ready for shipment, by boat to Toledo, Detroit and Buffalo. This method will be pursued by this company until direct shipment can be made to Europe. They will ship from Superior City this season 1,000 head, and 5,000 next year. A very significant fact in connection with the growth of stock empire in Montana is that the official Live Stock Journal, hitherto always published at Cheyenne, which was considered the center of stockdom has been removed wholy to Miles City.

The demand for good stock ranges in southern Arizono has been very great during the past month. The dry summer has shown many sources of water supply to be unreliable, and living streams are sought after. We venture the remark that by digging wells and putting in steam pumps good cattle ranches may be made at almost any point in the southern country.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The latest returns from Ohio indicate a majority of at least 12,000 for the Republicans. This result is especially discouraging to the Democrats, as they were basing great hopes on the moral effect of a victory in Ohio. The Republicans are correspondingly elated and everything now looks propitious for a Republican victory in November. Our next issue will contain the full report. West Virginia, as was expected, went Democratic.

Nineteen passengers the first week is a very creditable showing for the new stage line, as it has not been advertised as yet. The start was made a little too late to catch the bulk of the fall trade, but we learned in the Hills that we are sure to get the most of the out-going travel at least. Everyone wishes to try the new line, and this is all the proprietors wish. No one is going to undergo the tedious and uncomfortable stage journey on the other lines, which take two nights or more, when by our line only one night is spent in the stage. Our road-bed is already far superior to that of the other lines and from fifteen to eighty miles shorter.

The N. P. Express Co. has already made arrangements to carry and deliver express matter to all points in the Hills. This is an advantage possessed by no other stage line terminating in the Hills country. Through rates to all points can be quoted, and we are assured that the bulk of the express matter will come our way. The same rates as by the other roads are also made for passengers. The Northern Pacific being the road which broke the monopoly held by the Pierre lines, has a warm place in the hearts of the Hillers, and as freight will be carried at the same rates, there is no question that a large quantity will continue to arrive at this point for the Hills.

The line is now in good working order, but improvements will constantly be made. Everything that conduces to the comfort of passengers will especially oe added and the line must be pronounced the best going into the Hills.

If the present rate of travel is any criterion of what will be required when it is thoroughly advertised, a daily will be put on in the spring at least. At any rate one will be put on as soon as it is required.

We have never seen such perfect unanimity as is that of the Black Hills people in wishing our line every success. It opens a new country that can be easily reached, instead of travelling several more days by stage and railroad. For instance, it brings Bismarck a thousand miles nearer than via Pierre and St. Paul, and to points west the distance is lessened still more.

The M. S. & F. Co. has come here to stay, and we wish to prophesy right now is only the advance guard of a railroad from here to the Hills.

A subject of which we have never written editorially, and concerning which all argument is wasted, was brought to our notice by seeing in the Mandan Pioneer a notice of the "Billings county convention." This convention was held at Belfield, October 11, and elected Messrs. Blankenberg and Harbison as delegates. In the minutes of the convention there were only three names mentioned, and from one of the participants we learn that those attending did not greatly exceed this number. In any event their meeting was unauthorized, and they capped the climax by advocating the very plan that would be a death-blow to the future of Billings county—its still further division at some point a few miles west of Fryburg. In the event of such an impossibility taking place as this division, we would like to have the citizens of Belfield who attended the meeting rise up and explain where the property is to pay taxes for a a county organization for the eastern half. This is a subject that we have not before mentioned, but it is a fact that when the county is organized, the western half will for a long time have to support the eastern half. There is fifty dollars west of Fryburg to one east of it. In the light of this statement it looks a good deal like an exaggerated case of the tail wagging the dog for the eastern part of the county to try and dictate terms to the western part. For no other reason than that of blind jealousy, a few embryonic politicians in Belfield who should still be wearing swaddling clothes, have posed as marplots until patience has ceased to be a virtue. These few remind one of the tailors of Tuley street, who issued a manifesto beginning, "We, the citizens of Great Britain." They do not represent the citizens of Belfield, as we know from actual conversations. They do not represent the people of Billings county, as men and not babies must do that. All they represent is their own pitiably insignificent selves. It is time the people of Belfield stopped following such leaders and chose for themselves such captains as would come to the front and, even after one disastrous defeat, lead on instead of putting up cats' paws to be burned getting their chestnuts out of the fire. In all the conventions held at Medora, Belfield has received its share and more than its share. In the so-called Belfield conventions, Medora has never even been mentioned, except as to means for her defeat. Like the dog going across the stream with the huge chunk of meat in its mouth, and seeing its reflection below, dropped his original piece in grasping after the shadow, Belfield will get "heap nothing" if it pursues its present porcine policy.

Prices on the Chicago markets have been a little less encouraging this week.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

During Thursday and Friday last cattle shipments aggregated 12,656 head. This is the largest total for any two consecutive days in the history of the trade.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Range cattle continue to arrive at the rate of from 5,000 to 7,000 head per day, but all are promptly taken, local canners and dressed-beef shippers being the principal buyers.—[Breeder's Gazette.

We can supply the world with the best of meat. A second order for 50,000 pounds of compressed beef for the British expedition to Kartoum has been given to a Chicago firm.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Imported cattle haue been distributed through all portions of the country. So far the Short-horns lead any other breed as to numbers, but the Herefords and Polled-Angus are now moving strong. These leading breeds are now found scattered all over the country from Texas to Montana.

The cattle thieves and six-shooter ex-deputy sheriffs, who have so long held sway here, terrorizing quiet citizens and depredating upon the herds of legitimate stockmen, now appear as very ordinary individuals, and are actually seen in court playing the humiliating role of defendant in cases of theft of cattle. How the mighty have fallen.—[Henriette (Tex.) Shield.

The stock interests in Colorado and Wyoming are growing, and great difficulty is found in getting range. In talking with a number of the leading ranchmen, we were surprised to find the loss from last winter so small, many of them expressing great wonder at it themselves; but the round-up has shown a very healthy condition of stock, as well as small loss.—[Nebraska Farmer.

An exchange says that if the stockmen in the pastoral region of the United States, from New Mexico to the British possessions, desire to have the homestead law enlarged to four sections, they can accomplish this result simply by acting in unison and making the request. A general request accompanied by a complete exhibit of the situation to congress, will accomplish the desired end.

The treatment of all injuries of the foot must be conducted on the same general principles. We must remember that the hoof, its horny covering, is of the nature of a closed box, which will not expand and accommodate itself correspondingly with the swollen and inflamed structures that it incloses and protects. Any person who may have suffered from a "whitlow" beneath the finger-nail can only form a slight idea of the agony experienced by the poor horse suffering from inflammation and suppuration within the hoof. The elasticity of the insensible horn of the sole or frog usually closes the opening through which the injury has been inflicted, and there is no outlet for the pus or matter formed, the result of the inflammation, except at the coronet or above the horn at the heels. The original opening must, therefore, be searched for, the sole or frog well thinned around it, and a good and free orifice made, so that the matter can be freely discharged as it is formed, and the foot then placed in a warm bran poultice, till the inflammation has subsided and the discharge ceased.—[National Live-Stock Journal, Chicago.

Reports say that the Utes are still playing their cuteness in the northwest, and are making times very troublesome for the stockmen holding on those ranges. The cattlemen had quite a skirmish with them not long since, in which one Indian and a number of horses on both sides were killed. It is said that cattle are being gathered with cavalry escort, and further outbreaks from the Utes and Navajos are feared by cattlemen.—[Cheyenne (I. T.) Transporter.

Of all the seasons of the year, from now on and for sixty days the cattle upon the range wil put on the most substantial flesh. The nights are cool, and the quality of the grass is exactly what it should be. The frost has checked its growth, and what the animal now takes of it into its stomach has the substance to produce fat and marbled meat. Those who hurry the bullock away to market now lose the two most valuable months in the year.—[Col. L. S. Record.

In regard to the number of cattle driven out of Texas, a correspondent writing from Doan's Store, at Red river crossing of the Dodge City trail, says that up to a recent date there have crossed at that place 153 herds, containing 394,227 head, not counting horses. He has kept a record since '72, and says the smallest drive over this trail was in ['70?], when only 110,000 head crossed, and the largest in '82, when 415,000 crossed. This alludes to the drive over the Dodge trail alone.—[Col. L. S. Record.

T. J. McMinn, formerly attached to the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, spent last Tuesday in our city. Mr. McMinn is making the tour of the western range country to see how many cattlemen are likely to visit St. Louis at the time of the National convention, Nov. 17th next. He reports the boys all along the line in earnest as to the imporance of the meeting and thinks "our folks" will go down to the city by the river, in vast numbers. We are satisfied that he is correct in his views, for we know of hundreds who have expressed a full determination to go. The good people of St. Louis are making great efforts to render the visit of the stock-growers a pleasant and memorable one and they certainly will succeed in so doing. Wyoming will go a hundred strong and Colorado will do as well. Utah, Idaho, Nevada, Dakota, and Moatana will send large numbers, and we are going prepared to do good to ourselves and try to do good to our neighbors.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Among the important matters which will be likely to come before the Convention of cattle-growers to be held in this city November 13th will be a proposition for the federal goverment to open a national "trail" from the northwestern boundry of Texas through western Kansas, Colorado, Wyoming and Montana to the British possessions on the north. Such a trail it is proposed to make five miles in width, and as it will involve the donation of an immense amount of the public domain, and a large appropriation of public money to purchase private lands within its proposed lines, it is a matter of great importance to the whole country, which we are satisfied will not be conceded unless the necessity for it is shown to be great. Its object is to afford the breeders of Texas an outlet for their cattle towards the northwest of which they can at no time in the future be deprived. But we understand it is not desired by the Texas people alone, also by the people residing in the territories through which the proposed trail will be laid. These people, it is said, desire convenient opportunity for the purchase of the surplus cattle of Texas, not being so situated as to be able to breed cattle in sufficient numbers to keep their ranges as well stocked as they desire.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Already the prairie fires are beginning to appear, and it will not be many weeks until they can be seen raging on every hand. Every caution should be taken to prevent as far as possible the burning off of the ranges. At this season of the year the grass, parched by the hot sun during the late dry spell, is ready to blaze in a moment if ignited by the least spark, which is often borne on the wind from some camp fire. As a rule, freighters are more careless than anyone else, and, as much as they have been cautioned by the Indians and cattlemen, it is from their camps that the majority of our prairie fires originate. Of course it would not be reasonable to suppose that anyone could maliciously set fire to the grass; but some people, not being interested, are simply careless, who go about without sufficient presence of mind to be careful with their camp fires and to see that every spark is extinguished when leaving a camp. Last fall, a little later than this, a considerable portion of our best ranges were burned, consequently stock of all kinds died from starvation in large numbers, stock-owners suffering heavy losses. Whom shall we blame? Some laid it to the hands of Indians, but it is not reasonable to think that Indians, while directly interested in behalf of their own stock, would be guilty of such work; yet others say that it is a difficult task to "break an old dog of old tricks." Let it be as it may have been, this fall everyone should take the matter in hand and burn fire-guards around his range, making himself safe from the sweeping fires, from whatsoever source they may originate. Only a few fires so far this season have broken out, and it is to be hoped that the ranges will be saved.—[Cheyenne (I. T.) Transporter.

The church is rapidly nearing completion.
Rassie Deffebach will return from the Hills in a few days.
The Marquis returned last evening in his car, Livingston.
Peter Book returned from a short visit to Mandan last evening.
Mr. B. Barr returned from the Big Horn region this morning.
Rev. R. H. Dolliver and W. E. Adams were passengers on yesterday's coach going to Deadwood.
Howard Eaton received a number of high grade short horn bulls last Sunday from Pennsylvania.
Bob Roberts has completed a large beer cellar which he will fill immediately with his winter's stock.
Notice is hereby given that the new church will be blessed the first Sunday in November by Rev. Father Martin.
The brick dwelling that is building for J. R. Grymes will afford a very comfortable bachelor home for the residents.
There is a well-authenticated rumor that two horse-thieves were hung last night near Glendive. Let the good work go on.
J. C. Fisher, local manager of the M. S. & F. Co., is in Bismarck attending the legislative convention to which he is a delegate.
Cortez Fessenden, of Huron, surveyor general of Dakota, was a passenger on Saturday's stage from Deadwood, and is on his way to Portland.
Johnny Keifer and wife started for St. Paul the first of the week, where they will remain for some time for the benefit of Mrs. Keifer's health.
Again we can breathe freely for the safety of our property. The band of Gros Ventres Indians have left us, it is to be hoped, never to return.
W. J. Hornbeck, of Lead City, came up on the coach Tuesday evening and went to Billings Wednesday. He expects to pass the winter in Butte City.
Miss Josie Smith, sister-in-law of Rassie Deffebach, came from the Hills on last Saturday evening. She will stay all winter visiting Mrs. Deffebach.
F. E. Bowen, one of Mandan's rising attorney's, was in Medora a few days ago on business. He will be an early passenger to the Hills via the stage line.
We have been running off so much job work lately that our press finally got disgusted and "busted" on us. We will be ready for another rush in a day or two.
Miss H. R. Mead arrived from Dickinson this morning and will tomorrow open for business at the Pyramid Prrk hotel, for everything in the millinery line.
From the rustling ability of Messrs. Field, Roberts, Smith and Paddock we can rest assured that the Bad Lands will be well represented at the New Orleans exposition.
Vic Smith has been killing game to be stuffed for the New Orleans exposition, and some of his victims are beauties, especially some mountain sheep that he brought in yesterday.
Work has already begun on the new slaughter house, but there has been a change in the plans and work was stopped. To-morrow or next day work will be again resumed.
Owing to the absence of Mr. Fisher we cannot give the amount of freight forwarded last week. It amounts to 30,000 pounds, and is destined to Spearfish, Deadwood and Lead City.

William is mourning in sackcloth and ashes for the loss of all but one of his carrier pigeons. It is to be hoped that they will return, as they bid fair to afford ready and swift connection with the Hills.

Proofs of the hangers for the Medora S. & F. Co. have arrived, and they are truly works of art. They were made under the supervision of Mr. J. W. Hornick, of the Pioneer Press, and are as fine pieces of work as the P. P. has ever turned out.

The burning coal mine in the butte east of Medora is already a dangerous rival to the famous burning mine south-west of here. In the night the flames light up the whole butte, and it is a sight well worth seeing. After a look at it one is forced to admit that the description of the Bad Lands "looking like h—l with the fire put out," is rather inadequate.

The coal mine tunnel is now about ninety feet in, and the quality of the coal is constantly improving. It is undoubtedly the best coal yet discovered in northern Dakota. Provided low enough rates can be secured, a side track will be built and the coal shipped down the road. Orders for local consumption will be immediately filled by leaving directions at this office.

Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, was in town Tuesday. He reports that the foundation work has begun on his hospital building and that he has every confidence the money will be easily raised for its completion. He made arrangements for a dance to be held here soon at George Fitzgerald's, the proceeds of which will go to the hospital. It is a worthy object and should receive every encouragement.

The new drug store is fairly under way, and when the stock is all in we can boast of the best drug store between Mandan and Glendive. Dr. Jorgens, the proprietor, is still in Spearfish, but will be here in less than a week. Mr. Martin, the doctor's father-in-law, attends to to the business now, and is an experienced druggist as well as the doctor. We bespeak for the new store the hearty patronage it deserves.

Miss H. R. Mead, of H. R. Mead & Co., of Bismarck, dealers in dry goods, cloaks, notions, trimmings, fine millinery and hair goods, will open up a full line of notions, trimmings, corsets, gloves, ladies' underwear, wraps, children's and infants' goods, millinery and hair goods, etc., Friday, October 17, at Pyramid Park hotel parlors. The ladies of Medora and and Little Missouri are cordially invited to inspect these goods.

Mr. Field, sub-commisssioner of Dakota to the New Orleans worlds fair, is here rustling specimens and curiosities. It nearly broke our heart to part with the magnificent petrifaction Mr. McGregor gave us, but we could not resist Bob's persuasive eloquence. Our avowed object in getting up this collection was for just such an exhibition as this, but we find that each specimen is coupled with such pleasant recollections of its donor that it is hard to give even one of them up.
The Short Line to the Hills.

The Medora Stage and Forwarding company is doing a rushing business, both passenger and express. The coaches both ways have been heavily loaded, and if business continues to increase a daily will be put on in the near future. Manager Packard started over the line on Monday on a tour of inspection, and reports from the first home station that everything is in good shape. He intends to have the route in first class condition for the winter, and no pains or expense will be spared to have the "Short Line" the best stage line entering the Hills. Buffalo robes have arrived, and each stage will be supplied with three robes. The country traversed by this favorite route is far superior for agricultural purposes than that travelled by any other line. The scenic displays are also very fine, especially through the Bad Lands.

The drivers report plenty of game, and it is a common thing to see herds of antelope numbering from 50 to 100 head grazing within easy shot of the stage. Buffalos are also reported as working down from the reservation towards the line of the stage route. Some elk have also been seen. These reports are not surprising, as this country has long been known as the hunter's paradise.

When Manager Packard returns, the public can rest assured that the Medora Stage and Forwarding Company will be in a first class condition for all kinds of traffic. Parties going to the Hills will do well to give this line a trial.

The young man who resides in town and attempts to make money at farming usually comes to grief. The idea that a young man can run a store or a newspaper as his regular business and run a farm between times is a mistake.—Mandaan Pioneer. One thing is certain, and that is that a young man cannot work at the newspaper business in Mandan and make money, as the proprietors prefer hiring girls instead of paying men fair wages. That is a good way to boom the country.

It seems strange that there are no schools in this vicinity. We think there is a good opening for some enterprising individual. It is not the proper thing to let our young people grow up in ignorance, when by a little exertion a good school could be established. There are a number of our citizens who are anxious to have one started, and are willing to go down into their pockets to aid in sustaining a good school. Let us have a school by all means.

Vanderbilt has lost about $60,000,000 by shrinkage in stocks. He will not go to the poor house for some time, as he still possesses one hundred and thirty million flat dollars to help him out in his old days.

BISMARCK, October 20.—We noticed the conspicuous silence in your last issue in regard to the republican convention at Bismarck, and the inference we drew was that either your candidate got "scooped," or else your correspondent got "too full for utterance."

The convention was called to order by Chairman Wallace, of the district central committee, who read the call for the convention.

Hon. Johnson Nickeus of Jamestown and Mr. Charles Richardson, of Valley City were nominatee for councilmen, and Dr. Henry W. Coe, of Mandan; Julius Stevens, of Griggs county; W. F. Steele, of Kidder county, and Hon. E. A. Williams, of Bismarck, for members of the house.

A legislative central committee was appointed for the ensuing two years, and Charles W. Sleeper was chosen as a member of this committee from Billings county.

The convention then adjourned.
Mr. John McGregor returned to his ranch Thursday.
The Marquis presented Vic Smith a valuable rifle Wednesday. Mr. Smith is very proud of his new acquisition.

Mr. J. A. Ferris, of Little Missouri, reports things booming on his side of the river. Although Joe's stove requires a stove pipe, it is self-acting. All he has to do is to start the coal from his mine in the side of the bluff and it rolls into the stove. Joe says it is as handy as a pocket in a shirt.

The Marquis de Mores and Vic Smith returned from a three days' hunt on Wednesday. A number of black-tailed deer and several mountain sheep was the result of their trip. The Marquis succeeded in killing the finest specimen of mountain sheep ever seen around here. Vic says the Marquis is "away up" on the shoot.
