There is to be over 50,000,000, sheep in the United States.
Johnson, the pacer, made a mile in 2:06¼ in Chicago last Friday.
A large land and cattle company has been organized in Warren County, Iowa.
It is claimed that there are ten million dollars' worth of Jersey cattle in this country.
The number of cattle shipped from Chicago to the seaboard ports for the past week was 7,380, against 6,350 the previous week.
Information comes from northern Wyoming that the cattle herds in that section are suffering severely from the ravages of wolves and coyotes.
During the past week about one hundred head of cattle have been killed in railroad wrecks within five miles of Medora. It seems as though the riot act ought to be read to some one.
It is said that Hereford cows, more frequently than any other breed, produce twins calves. We have noticed six pairs of these little white faced beauties the present season.—[Col. L. S. Record.
From stockmen in different parts of the country we learn that the rains have been general throughout the northwest and south, and that cattle are doing remarkably well.—[Colorado Clipper

Said Mr. Henry Wendling the other day: "It took me twenty years to discover that a calf could milk a cow cheaper than I could, and since I have quit the competition, I have prospered and so has the calf.

A call has been issued for a meeting of the National Cattle Breeders' Association to be held in Chicago on the 13th and 14th of November. There will also be a convention of stockmen in St. Louis on the 17th of November.

Forty head of Colorado and Wyoming bred horses were sold in London a few days since for prices ranging from $210 to $250 each. The animals were large half-bred Percheron-Normans, and unbroken except to lead.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The mammoth cattle campany, of which Ben Butler was the head, has not purchased cattle this season as it was advertised to do. It was reported early in the season that they would place fifty thousand head on the country south of the Arkansas. They have not done it.—[Col. L. S. Record.

In an interview with Mr. Oakes, of the Northern Pacific railroad, he stated that the eastern stock shipments of the company this fall will amount to 75,000 head. One hundred thousand head have been shipped into Montana this fall, and about 150,000 head have come over the the trail into Northern Montana.

It is too bad that stockholders, as a rule, are short sighted. Dividens of the largest kind are what they want and expect the first year or two after freshly stocking a range. A little patience would be of great value to them. Range cattle should never be sent to market under three or four years of age.—[Texas L. S. Record.

Killing off rough, ungainly bulls and spaying the undesirable cows is the way keep down the surplus of poor animals. Texas rangemen will be overcrowded until they pay more attention to quality than to quantity. It would not be a bad idea to adopt the Colorado rule of castrating on sight every unimproved Texas bull.—[Texas L. S. Record.

The St. Louis Fair Association will exclude all cattle from their fair. It is a late decision, and it is to be feared it will cause some inconvenience to intending exhibitors. It may, howver, be wise.

It is stated from all parts of the country that the cattle which a short time since were afflicted with sore eyes have recovered, and there is no new cases reported. The first frost removed the cause.—[Kan. Cow Boy.

The cattle in the vicinity of Mexico, Missouri, are said to be dying in great numbers with mad itch. Hogs in the same section of country are said to be dying by thousands of hog cholera. No remedy has been found to check the disease.—[Kan. Cow Boy.

Twenty thousand sheep have already gone from Colorado down to the cornfields of Nebraska, to fatten the coming winter. Possibly as many more have gone to Kansas. Sheep are a blessing to the small farmers in Kansas who have grain to feed, since it takes so much less money to buy sheep than it does to buy steers.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The late rains, which are almost without precedent in the Black Hills, coming at this time of year, have started the grass afresh, and have created some little anxiety among stockmen, who fear the forage may not cure in as good a state as heretofore when the autumn months have been dry. Farmers, however, are benefitted, as the ground has been kept in good conditon for fall plowing. Early seeding seems to generally produce the best crops here, and it is only by having the fields plowed in the fall that early seeding is made possible. It is stated by stockmen that the rains of the past month have not extended out to the Cheyenne, so that the damage to forage—if damage there be—is not widespread.—[B. H. World.

The Fort Worth, Texas, Live Stock Journal gives the following account of the workings of a branding machine in some sections of the southern range country: "About ten thousand head of cattle have been branded this season at the Crawford corral, on the south side of the river, in the Parker machine. The capacity of this machine is about four thousand daily. The prices of branding is from seven to ten cents a head. This week one thousand head of Mathers cattle have been branded there. The machine is about twenty feet long and will hold from four to six head at a time. It is just wide enough for the passage of a full grown animal. When the cattle enter the machine they find on the bottom a wooden frame crossed by iron rods about six inches apart. When the machine is full the frame is elevated by pulleys operated by a horse. The legs of the animals are between the rods and presently the rods strike their adbomens and left them from the ground, their bodies resting on the rods, with their legs swinging underneath. While in this helpless condition the branding iron is applied. It requires five men to work the machine."

Prominent among the topics that will claim the attention of the convention at St. Louis next month, will be the great national highway—the trail up from the breeding grounds of Texas, to the grazing fields of Colorado, Kansas, Wyoming, Montana and the British Possessions. To most stock growers in this plains country, the necessity for this highway is apparent. But we are aware that there will be opposition to it. There will be men who think there will be an embargo laid as against the coming of more Texas cattle. Others would like to see the railroads carry the cattle, and still another class claim this north country can breed all the animals the grasses will sustain without further importation. We believe, on the other hand, that nine-tenths of the men in Colorado who represent three-fifts of the cattle wealth will be found in favor of this national trail. They have learned by experience that the better feeding ground is in Texas. That the calf crop there will go eighty-five per cent. of all the cows yearly, while at this high latitude it will not go sixty. They have also learned by practical demonstration that a steer coming up from the Lone Star State will mature, and put on one, two and even three hundred pounds more flesh here than the same steer would have done if kept on his native health. These facts alone will array the heavy cattle handlers of Colorado on the side of the National Trail. Without this trail, the cattle traffic as between the north and the south will be carried on with much difficulty. The Cherokee Nation are already kicking against the passage across there lands, and the settlers are fencing up the streams, and there will soon be no alternative but the trail. Then will the states and the territories into which they may come quarantine against the unloading of animals that are so fresh from their feeding ground, and liable to bring with them the germs of disease. It is our opinion that the interests of the northwest, as well as that of Texas, demand this national trail. It is of as vital importance to this grazing country as is the Mississippi to the valley through which it runs. Railroads may go parallel with it, but when the rates do not suit the shippers, the bovine can take the highway and by slow marches leave the contagious fevers of the southern clime ere he reaches the green hills of Colorado and Wyoming.—[Col. L. S. Record.

C. L. BRINKER, Agent.
Dr. Jorgens will not arrive here for a week or so.
A cold wave struck us this week and coal dealers are happy.
L. H. Palmer left for the Hills on Monday. He will winter there.
It is rumored around town that a marriage will take place shortly.
Mr. J. O'Sullivan, our gentlemanly barber, intends going to Miles City next week.
Mr. Bob Roberts has completed a cellar for the storage of his stock of liquors, etc.
Quite a number of Medora people contemplate going to the New Orleans exposition.
Mr. McGrecor brought in a load of petrifactions, which are to be sent to the New Orleans exposition.
Six passengers came in on the stage Tuesday evening. The new line is doing a good passenger business.
A wrestling match between two well known characters created considerable merriment on Tuesday night.
The increase in the earnings of the Northern Pacific for the first eight months of this year is $2,593,456.
The drug store is doing a good business, and as soon as all the stock arrives Medora will have a first class drug store.
Parties wishing to purchase their winter's supply of coal will have their orders promptly filled by leaving them at this office.
Dr. Jorgens has been unavoidably detained in Spearfish. His range has been burned, and he is looking for a suitable place to winter his cattle.
Bob Roberts shot an antelope within sight of town Wednesday morning. This is is one of the many evidences that game is very plentiful in this vicinity.
Manager Packard left on Monday's stage for Deadwood on a tour of inspection. He intends to have the "Short Line" in first class condition for the winter.
The slaughter house of Dietrich Bros. near Bismarck, was burned Monday night together with its contents. Loss, $1,400. It is supposed to be the work of an incendiary.
"Buckskin Joe," on Sunday, brought to town one of the largest deer seen around here for some time. Bob Roberts purchased it and will send it down the line to be stuffed.
The plastering of the church was completed Thursday, and the building is now ready for the finishing touches. Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, will bless the new sanctuary.
Mr. B. F. Charlton, of Deadwood, who has been stopping in Medora since May last, left on Monday for Butte City, Mont. He has been in the employ of the M. S. & F. Co. as head carpenter.

It is rumored that there will be a change in the arrival and departure of trains on the 2d of November. We have had a few changes during the past week. Trains from either direction have been from three to eight hours late.

Several of our business men complain of the slowness with which freight is brought here. They claim to have received the bills for their fall stocks some time ago, but no goods have arrived. It would be a good idea for some one to slip around a little.

Two wrecks within a week is doing pretty good. The first occurred last Friday morning, in which seventy head of cattle were killed and five cars and an engine completely wrecked. The second took place on Tuesday, and killed fifteen head of cattle and demolished five cars.

Sam Townsend, who left Medora on the 11th of October with 50,000 pounds of freight for the Hills, arrived in Deadwood on the 18th, the fastest time ever made from the Northern Pacific to Deadwood. He will be here again in a few days, and will load for the Hills. Sam is a rusher.

An almost successful attempt was made to burn Hotel de Mores early this morning. About half-past 1 o'clock Mr. McClellan, a guest of the hotel, was awakened by smoke coming through his window. He arose quickly and discovered that the building was on fire. The alarm was immediately given, and by strenuous efforts the fire was put out. A can of kerosene and a bag of shavings were found near where the fire started, indicating clearly that the parties meant business. Anyone who is so unprincipled as to set fire to a hotel full of sleeping guests, should be skinned alive, and if the parties are discovered the citizens will make it warm for them. Had the flames been discovered a little later, the result would have been very disastrous, both to life and property, as the hotel was full of sleeping guests and and our water supply is wholly inadequate. The damage will amount to about [$50?].
Jim Hannigan reports large flocks of chickens within a mile and a half of town.
The Pyramid Park hotel, Boyd & Alexander proprietors, is doing a rushing business.
Mr. Gill Kennedy is a fine artist on the banjo. Gill won't take a back seat from anybody.
About 150 head of cattle and 200 head of sheep are being slaughtered by the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car company every week.
Dr. Huber Roberts, of Dickinson, a Northern Pacific Beneficiary Association physician and surgeon, was a caller at the COW BOY office this week.
Coupon tickets for all the principal cities in the United States were forwarded this week to the Deadwood agent of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Company.

The new cooler of the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car company will be 40x120 feet. The company is also building a new slaughter and engine house. These buildings will be built as rapidly as possible, as the present quarters are entirely too small.

Soldiers are as bad as Indians when they get too much good elegant "booze" aboard. Several of them attempted to paint this town a bright vermillion on Saturday last. One of them became so boisterous as to necessitate his being tied up. He broke several windows of a N. P. coach.

Each week shows an increase of business transacted by the Medora Stage and Forwarding company, and when the improvements now being made are completed, the new line can carry passengers, freight and express matters in less time and better shape than any other route entering the Hills. Manager Packard reports everything progressing finely and is confident that when the public learns the manner in which this route handles everything entrusted to its care, they will not be slow in taking the many advantages it affords.

Already large shipments of freight have been made, and the freighters will leave for the Hills to-day heavily loaded. The last trip was the fastest ever made from the line of Northern Pacific railroad, and those who know say they can beat the time a day or so.

A mail route is to be established between Spearfish and Carbonate Camp, a distance of seven miles.

Bad weather has interrupted the business of some of the stage lines, but the Medora line seems to be especially favored in this respect. Very little snow falls in this region, and no trouble is anticipated from snow storms.

Taking everything into consideration, the Medora Stage and Forwarding Company is a success in every particular, and there are no good reasons why it should continue to be so.

A report that the Montana "stranglers" were on their way to Medora caused considerable talk, and all kinds of rumors were afloat. Last week they captured an innocent cow boy and held him in custody for two days. He says he could not convince them that he was honest, nor would they listen to anything he said, but knew everything. It seems strange that men from other territories should come to Dakota to hunt for cattle thieves, when it would keep an army of men very busy for a long time to eliminate that element from their own borders. Medora is able to take care of her own stock, and can dispense with the aid of the "stranglers," as they style themselves. A horse thief stands no show, nor does he deserve any, but to take men who are looking for estrayed stock and string them up a couple of times in order to get information, is going a little too far, and there is likely to be trouble should they attempt anything like that around here. If a man is caught stealing stock, give him the benefit of the noose; but unless a clear case is against him he should have a chance to prove his innocence. It is hoped that they exercise a little more precaution in the future.

The cow boy's cure for snoring is unique and effectual if not soothing. On the Utah & Northern railroad last Sunday a 200-pound man lay snoring on two facing seats. His roar had been heard to the discomfort of a carfull all afternoon. At about 4 p. m a cow boy got on at one of the canyon stations. He heard the foghorn with evident impatience for a half hour or so, when he stepped up to the sleeper and said: "Say, stranger, stop that 'ar snort or you'll get fired." The cow boy was not large, but he was full of guns and there was business in his eye. The big man said nothing but lay still, and his sleep, if he slept, was as quiet as the slumber of infancy.—[Dallas, Ore., Letter.

A large train of the smallest bulls that was ever seen in the world came in yesterday with freight from Belfield. The diminutiveness of many of them attracted the attention of the crowd. Charley Shanklin inquired of one of the teamsters where the mothers of those calves were, supposing they had been brought along to furnish milk for them. He was answered with a — stare.—[Black Hill Pioneer.

A colony of fifty settlers from Connecticut, under the patronage of P. T. Barnum, have bought a tract of land in Barnes county, Dakota, and will settle there in the spring. Nothing seems to effect permanently the Dakota boom. The growth of the great territory, soon to be a state, is something [phenomenal?].—[St. Paul day.

From present appearances it will not be long before we have telegraphic communication with Medora. A contract has been let to a Spearfish party to furnish the poles on the ground for the entire distance, and they are now being cut and peeled.—]Black Hills Pioneer.

The weather in this vicinity continues very fine. We have had a couple of cloudy days, but no cold has been experienced, and cattle men are taking advantage of it and are getting things in good shape for their stock.

Considerable interest is manifested here as to the result of next Tuesday's election. The republicans are very confident, and claim that the victory in Ohio virtually settles all chances of the democrats.
W. F. Storey, proprietor of the Chicago Times, died on Tuesday last. He had been in poor health for some time.
The silver bullion shipments from Carbonate Camp are expected to amount to 360,000 pounds per month.
President Arthur, it is said, is an aspirant for senator from a New York district.

Jay-Eye-See's new sulky weighs forty-one pounds, and is painted purple, to match Bither's suit.
In Western Montana, a contagious disease called catarrhal is causing considerable trouble among horses.
The British authorites, report the almost total eradication of foot and mouth disease in that country.
Parties desiring rules and regulations governing the coming Fat Stock show at Chicago should address the secretary of the state board of agriculture, Springfield, Ill.
The corn crop for the present year is placed by the national department of agriculture at the enormous figures of 1,800,000,000 bushels. This should fatten a great many steers.

The cattle shipments over the Northern Pacific from July 20th to October 25th amounts to 2,896 cars. The number of cattle carried is 74,920. It is expected that 3,500 cars will be shipped by November 15.

The country up around Spearfish and near Jennie's stockade is fast settling up. A party of land prospectors from this place have just returned, and are very much pleased with the country.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

W. H. Robinson of cleveland Ohio, obtained a verdict of $5,000 and costs against Amos Rank, Joel Sharp, et. al., for infringing on his patent of an appliance for feeding and watering cattle in railroads cars. Others suits will follow.

While Colorado will require, ere another harvest, a million bushels of oats for feed, it has not produced to exceed 25,000 bushels. The farmer who has raised wheat that is so far in excess of the demand should give this a thought.—[Col. L. S. Record.

There has been less of scab this year among the flocks of Colorado than in any prior year. The flock owners are paying better attention than heretofore, knowing that it will not do to be so careless of an animal that requires the best of attention to prosper.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The Chicago stock yards were constructed about twenty years ago, and are the largest in the world. They are capable of accommodating 20,000 cattle, 150,000 hogs, 10,000 sheep, and 1,500 horses. Seventeen different railroads center in the yards. It is estimated that the number of car loads received and shipped last year would make about 9,000 trains of thirty-one cars each. If placed in one train they would reach from New York to St. Louis and back, a distance of about 2,146 miles.

Experiments have been made in England as to the comparative value of good hay and stock, with the result that it is estimated that 100 pounds of hay are equal to 275 pounds of green Indian corn, 400 pounds of green clover, 442 pounds of rye straw, 360 pounds of wheat straw, 160 pounds of oat straw, 180 pounds of barley straw, 153 pounds of pea straw, 200 pounds of buckwheat straw, 400 pounds of dried corn stalks, 175 pounds of raw potatoes, 504 pounds of turnips, 300 pounds of carrots, 54 pounds of rye, 46 pounds of wheat, 59 pounds of oats, 45 pounds of mixed peas and beans, 64 pounds of buckwheat, 57 pounds of Indian corn, 68 pounds of acorns, 105 pounds of wheat bran, 167 pounds of wheat, pea, and oat chaff, 179 pounds of mixed rye and barley, 59 pounds of linseed, and 330 pounds of mangel-wurzel.—[Scientific American.

About thirty-five per cent. of cattle of Illinois are classed as high grade by the department of agriculture. By high grade is meant those having more than half blood of some of the recognized pure breeds. The increase of value from this source alone is $20,000,000.

Gov. Cleveland is about to start on an exhibition tour to advertise the advantages of New York as a stock-raising state. He expects to take the first prize at Newark. A special stock car is provided. He is the first Jersey product ever nomitated for the presidential office.

Any cow can be milked dry in a few weeks by irregular milking, sometimes at intervals of twenty-four hours and sometimes of six. Separation from her usual company, a change to new location, a strange milker and scolding voice, are sources of irritation that more or less impair the milking qualities of a cow.

A cane made entirely of the horns of cattle has been presented to Major Rainwater, of St. Louis, chairman of the executive committe of the national convention of cattle men that meets in St. Louis next month. He is also to be given a chair, the frame of which will be composed of the horns of Texas cattle, and will occupy it on the platform.

A citizen of Tarrant county, Colorado, whose wife was sick, wishing to go for his daughter, who was sixty miles distant on a visit, in the absence of a horse, rode a two-year-old bull, making the round trip—120 miles—in forty-eight hours. He said the bovine was rather too poor to ride without a saddle, and as he expressed it, "putty bad gittin on agin after the wind strikes me awhile."

The calf crop is surprising the cattlemen in northern New Mexico, and is likely to make up for the discouraging shortage last spring. From as reliable an informant as Col. Dwyer, of Colfax we learn that the calf branding of the last round-up in this neighborhood was much larger than was ever known in the fall season here before, and that the shortage of the first round-up will be more than made up.—[Col. L. S. Record.

It is the opinion of many of the larger cattle holders upon the plains that the death losses in winters will not exceed two per cent., if a term of ten years be taken into account. The winters of 1880 and '81 were severe and the loss was not less than four per cent. of all the cattle upon the open plains, but in '82 it did not exceed one and a half. In '83 it went to three. For several winters prior to 1880 it did not exceed one and a half per cent.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The Garden City Irrigator says a man south of us was approached lately by a "granger" who wished to buy a cow. It so happened that the c. m. had an old cow that had seen her best days, and being in sight of the ranch they rode out to look at her. She was pretty well covered with brands of various descriptions, and most awful poor. The granger walked around her a time or two and then remarked, "She isn't much of a cow." "No," said the c. m. "but [she's?] got lots of good reading on her."

The wintering of sheep depends much on the condition of the flock at the beginning of winter, remarks the Michigan Farmer. Sheep that are low in flesh in the fall hardly ever improve, but keep going down hill all along, until before the spring time draws around their pelts are hanging in the shade. See, then, that your flocks are in good condition, and if there are any thin ones among them, separate them from the rest and give them a little grain each day until they have gained their wonted vigor.

If there is one class of men in this world more noted than another for honesty, we believe it is the editors. The habit of appropriating cattle belonging to another when favorable opportunity offers is entirely too popular, but this is a crime of which an editor would not be guilty, at least this appears to be the case with Brother Hays, of the Avalanche published a Silver City, Idaho. He thus cries out: "Somebody's calf, with somebody's brand on it is sucking our cow. Take the calf away, for it is not ours."—[N. W. L. Journal.

The American race horse Foxhall that created such a sensation in Europe three years ago by winning the grand prize of Paris, the Cambrigeshire and the Czarewhitch, has been sold by Mr. J. R. Keene to Lord Rosebery, the price being $20,000. The purchaser recently returned from a trip around the world, and in the course of his journey witnessed the performances of American and Australian horses, and therefore the selection, on returning home, of an American-bred one to place at the head of his stud farm is a decided compliment to this country.

To a hard-working horse, repose is almost as much as good food; but tired though he may be, he is often very shy to lie down, even when a clean bed has been provided for him. Unless a horse lies down regularly, his rest is never complete, and his joints and sinews stiffen; and while it is true that some horses that sleep in a standing position continue to work for many years, it is equally true that they would wear much longer, and perform their work much better, if they rested naturally. Young, nervous horses not infrequently refuse to lie down when first made to occupy a stall, and, when introduced into a town stable, the habit may become confirmed, unless inducements are offered to overcome the disinclination.—[Reynolds on Draught Horses.

Will Kidd left on Wednesday for the east.
A roller rink will be opened in Roberts' hall.
Dr. Jorgens will arrive the first of next week.
Bob Roberts had the south side of his building raised.
Tilden R. Selmes and wife, of Mandan, were in town on Monday.
The Marquis received an order for 500 cattle from a Chicago firm.
The erection of the N. P. R. C. Co.'s slaughter house will be commenced shortly.
A large number of geese passed over Medora during the past week on their way south.
J. A. Ferris must do a rushing business, judging from the amount of printing he has done.
Dan McKenzie, the blacksmith, has been quite busy of late. He says work is picking up again.
The damage caused by fire to Hotel de Mores has been repaired, and everything is running smoothly.
Mr. Lloyd Roberts brought two cars of cattle for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car company on Wednesday.
Vic Smith brought in another lot of antelope, coyotes and mountain deer. Vic never comes home empty-handed.
A herd of buffalo was seen about twenty-five miles southwest of here on Tuesday. Several of our hunters went out after them.
Sam Townsend returned from the Hills Sunday making the round trip in 21 days. A broken wheel caused a delay of two days.
Baron Von Steiger brought in some very fine potatoes for the company's store. Billings county is not slow in raising potatoes.
The report that a cow boy well known around here was drawn up three times by the Montana "stranglers" seems to be without foundation.
Lee Eisenberg, representing the house of Dan Eisenberg, Bismarck, transacted considerable business in Medora on Saturday. Lee is a rustler.
Mr. E. Elmer's family arrived from Jamestown on Wednesday. Mr. Elmer will open up a place of business on the other side of the river.
Next Sunday morning at 9:30 the new Catholic church will be blessed, and mass celebrated. The Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan will officiate.
Work on the foundation of the new cooler has been temporarily delayed by the non-arrival of cement. It was to have been finished this week.
Hotel de Mores is having a good run of business. Mr. Fitzgerald tries to please everybody, and his efforts are appreciated by all who stop with him.
Mr. T. Smith is out looking for an estrayed horse. The animal belongs to the stage line and is a valuable one. See notice of reward in another column.
The drug store is being put in first class shape. A large supply of new goods have been received. The public is invited to call and examine them.
The Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car company received a large order for beef from Chicago. It will only be a short while before the company will work up a large business there.
The time of the passenger trains will probably be changed on the 1st of November. The east bound train will arrive in the evening and the west bound train in the early morning.

The town well is almost completed, and the quality of the water is very good. It is just the thing for lemonade, to say nothing about washing windows, etc. Some say it is even good to drink, but we never saw them tackle water, and do not consider them the best of authority.

Mr. Malloy, of the Western House, Little Missouri, has been very busy getting his hotel in first class shape for the winter. His cellars are filled with all kinds of eatables, and he is prepared to feed an army of hungry people. Mr. Malloy knows how to please his guests, and he never tires of doing so.

Quite a number of our young people attended the dance given in honor of Mr. N. A. Thayer, at the Pyramid Park hotel, Little Missouri, Tuesday night. All kinds of refreshments were served, and the affair was one which will not be soon forgotten. Excellent music was furnished by Gill Kennedy and Joe Dulgyee.

A man named Michael Strang, about 40 years of age, was brought to town on Sunday, charged with setting fire to the grass on the range about four miles southeast of here. He was taken to Mandan, where he was bound over to await the action of the district court. It is about time that someone should be punished for this offense.
Rassie Deffenbach, of the Medora stage line, went to Belfield Wednesday.
The switches in this vicinity are being repaired. N. A. Thayer it superintending the work.
As to-day's emigrant train was pulling out, the track spread and two cars were derailed. The damage was slight, and little delay was accasioned.
Mr. J. A. Field was here on Saturday collecting petrifactions for the New Orleans exposition. Billings county will show up well in that line, also in game and agricultural products.
When the roller rink opens there will be some great feats performed. There will be a contest between such artists as John Warn, Pat O'Hare and other well known local celebrities.

General Manager Packard, of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Company, is still in the Hills in the interest of the stage company. He reports everything in good shape. He is [expected?] back [the?] latter part of this week.

Last Tuesday night one of our young men got too much corn juice aboard and, while in this condition, attempted to gain an entrance into the house opposite his, thinking it was his own, when two shots were fired at him, the bullets whizzing by his head. He says it was a close shave, and that he will be more careful in the future.

ALBANY, N. Y., Nov. 7.—The evening Journal, republican, concedes the election of Cleveland. There seems no longer any douot that Cleveland has been elected president.

NEW YORK, Nov. 7.—Cleveland now has a plurality of about 1,000 in this state. The vote will not be 200 on either side of these figures.

More Tears.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., Nov. 7.—Reports coming in slowly, and the result still in doubt. Both parties claim the state, the chances seeming to be in favor of Cleveland.

A Discourager.

MADISON, Wis., Nov. 7.—Returns not all in for Wisconsin, but there have been large democratic gains, perhaps enough to carry the state for Cleveland.

The Latest.

NEW YORK, Nov. 7.—Latest reports and estimate of four counties not heard faom give Clevelane the state by a plurality of 831.

Dakota to the Front.

BISMARCK, Nov. 7.—Returns from all over Dakota indicate a clean-up for the republican party. Montana is also republican, judging from the meager returns.

Since our last report, a large amount of work has been done on and for the line. The work on the route consists of improving the stations, fencing hay stacks, plowing fire guards around stations, digging wells and improving the road-bed. An additional station is being built between South Moreau and Indian Creek, dividing the long drive of twenty-two miles in half. In the way of passengers and express, many merchants have decided to ship everything via Medora, enough, in fact, to almost guarantee expenses. The road is well advertised in the Hills, and all outgoing passengers are anxious to try the new route. The matter of getting a mail contract is only a question of time, but even without this, and contrary to all expectation the road is now paying expenses. Arrangements have been made with all roads so that through tickets are being sold in Deadwood to all points in the world. The proprietors of the line have in all things consulted the comfort of passengers and have now the best coaches, the best stage stock, the best and shortest road-bed and the best system of connecting railroads of any stage line running into the Hills.
Peter Book has gone to Mandan as a witness on a claim-jumping case.
Bob Roberts will load to-morrow for the Hills with freight for Gib Stone.
The two brick cottages are now finished and accepted by the company.
The church is receiving its finishing touches and will be entirely completed in a few days.

Charles Stevenson, of Pittsburg, has been here for some time visiting his friends, the Eatons. He came to recuperate, but finds it rather expensive as he had to invest in several suits of more voluminous clothes.

The coach coming in last evening from Deadwood made the best time that has ever been made by a stage on any line to or from the Hills. The time was thirty-four hours and thirty minutes. No endeavor was made toward fast time, and it is now proven beyond a doubt that thirty hours and less can easily be made. Tally another for Medora.

"The great grazing country of the west" is a section whose area is scarcply appreciated by most readers. It may be said to embrace a district 2,400 miles in length from north to south by about 1,000 miles from east to west.

The Northwestern Cattle Raisers association, of Texas, now offers $500 for the conviction of cattle thieves. Such sums as this will prove a great help in bringing the thieves and brand burners to their just deserts.—Ex.

A private note to this office from Fort Maginnis, reports the steer crop rather short, on account of the depredations of thieves, half-breed Indians and wild animals, but says the stock at hand are of excellent quality.—[Miles City S. G. Journal.

The market is not overstocked with wool yet, despite all that may be said to that effect, as we paid over $40,000,000 for foreign wool last year. There is a demand for wool, and as long as we do not produce enough for our own use sheep-raising will result in profit.—Western Rural.

For the week ending with Saturday last fifty-two diseased hogs, nine cattle, nineteen quarters of beef, and five sheep, amounting in all to 15,000 lbs., were condemned. It takes constant and careful watching in and around the Chicago Stock Yards to prevent certain unscrupulous dealers from putting the meat of diseased animals on the market.

An old farmer tells us that there is no feed so good to keep animals in flesh during winter as scalded oats. For mares, cows and sheep that are to raise young ones it is superior to almost any other feed, as it not only puts the animal in good condition to furnish milk abundantly, but the young at birth are strong and active. Wheat bran is also an excellent feed for breeding animals given in the form of a mess.—[Western Rural.

Northern Pacific cattle shipments this year have been the greatest since the road opened. The revenue from east-bound shipments already equals the earnings made last spring from west-bound shipments. So far, 50,000 head of beef cattle have been shipped east, and contracts already made call for the shipment of 25,000 more. Last spring 100,000 one and two-year-old cattle were shipped east.

Thursday a secret service detective from Montana arrived from up the river with Jack Wilson, better known as Club Foot Jack, in charge. Jack was wanted here for stealing a team of ponies from Long Wood about six weeks ago, and also for breaking into several shacks and stealing their contents. The prisoner was brought before Justice Stanton to-day and committed for trial at the next term of the district court. He takes a philosophic view of the situation and expects to "go over the road."—[Mandan Pioneer.

Some Tennessee breeders of throughbred horses have arranged a race for yearlings to be run at Gallatin during the middle of November, the distance being a quarter of a mile. Several years ago an attempt was made in England to institute a race for yearlings, but the Jockey Club promptly took the matter in hand and forbade anything of the kind being done. As a matter of fact there is little doubt that both English and American thoroughbreds have deteriorated considerably in point of stamina by reason of so many races at short distances, and for two and three-year-olds, being run.
A lot of horse stock was recently shipped from San Antonio, Texas, to Alaska.
The Leona pasture of 37,000 acres in Noalde county, Texas, was sold recently at $3 per acre.
The United States is the greatest sheep raising country in the world, except Australia.
Mr. John Splan, who drove Johnson during this season says that the pacer will make a mile in 2:02 some day.
Five hundred dogs, valued at $500,000 are now on exhibition in a New York garden. Among them are the Esquimaux dogs brought by the Greeley relief expedition.

Why should there be thought any more indelicacy in using the name of a male than in speaking of a female animal? What possible objection is there to the words stallion, bull, ram, boar? We say man, woman, boy, girl, without a thought of need of any evasion of the question of sex. Yet many, especially in the presence of ladies, seen to think it indelicate to call our domestic animals by their correct name. In this connection it may be said that buck is not properly applied to a male sheep. Ram is the proper word in such case.—[Breeders' Gazette.

We do not understand why Governor Glick, of Kansas, should have quarantined against Iowa cattle. There has never been a case of contagious pleuro-pneumonia discovered in that State, and her laws are quite as well adapted to her protection as are those of Illinois, and they are faithfully and efficiently executed. When we first saw Governor Glick's proclamation, as transmitted by telegraph, we supposed the mention of Iowa to have been an error. We are informed, however, that it was correct, but are utterly at a loss to know why it should be so.—[Breeder's Gazette.

The attitude of the Northwest towards Texas cattle interests has been severely criticised by this and other papers, and the action of the representatives of the cattle interests of the Northwestern states and territories, in the St. Louis convention, will probably go to show whether or not those criticism are just. If they show a disposition to aid us in securing a national trail we shall feel that their quarantine may have been, after all, against Texas fever instead of against Texas cattle, and we shall straightway do them the justice to take back some of the unkind things we have said about them.—[San Antonio Stockman.

The Rev. John Biggs, a Baptist preacher from Sadorus, Ill., who stole several horses, a buggy, and $130 in money a few weeks ago, has just been sentenced by Judge Wilkin in the Douglas county circuit court to sixteen years in the penitentiary. Biggs had formerly been a hard character and had served a term in the penitentiary for horse stealing, but he kept his record from the people there, and, obtained a license from the Baptists to preach a year or more ago. Most of the stolen property was found in his possession when he was captured at Flora, Ill., and he was almost killed by jumping from the cars while being brought to Tuscola by Sheriff Wyatt.—Breeders' Gazette.

Most persons feed their horses oats by measure, instead of weight, forgetting there is quite a difference in the weight of oats when different lots are measured. Some lots of oats are very heavy, and some quite light. Horses that are fed twelve quarts per day of heavy oats will fall off when changed to twelve quarts of light oats—there being from five to ten cent. loss of nutritious matter in them. It is always best to feed the best oats and hay to horses, but judgment is needed to regulate the quantity so as not to feed too much or too little. Many owners of horses trust the feeding entirely to their farm hands, who have little judgment and no care for the results. Owners of horses should determine the quantity required for their horses, and give strict instructions to have just the required amount fed. In this way horses can be kept in proper condition.—[Miles City S. G. Journal.

John Splan's dictum, that continual trial of horses from which a great performance is expected are in nearly every instance injurious, seems to be founded on fact. During the past week there were several trials against time by the best of our trotters, and in no instance were they successful. Maud S. started over the fast track at Hartford to beat her record of 2:09¾, made at Cleveland early in the season when her vitality had not been severely tried by continued training and when an absolute rest of a year had put her in good spirits and fettle to do her best. The Hartford trial was made only after weeks of careful preparation, and yet the best mile she could show was 2:12½, and after this exhibition Bair gave up the job in disgust. She has been hammered away at ever since last June, and evidently does not feel like making a great effort. At Lexington Elvira tried to beat her record of 2:18½, made at Cleveland a few weeks ago, and failed, 2:20 being her best mile. Nutbreaker, the fastest yearling ever bred east of the Rocky Mountains, was started to lower his mark of 2:43, and he failed. Splan is right. Once a year is often enough to give a very fast horse the best mile that can be got out of him. Continual trying only results in failure and disappointment.—[Breeder's Gazette.

The other day our newsboy sold an elderly gentleman a copy of the Cow Boy. When he opened the paper and saw the brand advertisements, he exclaimed: "Oh, what pretty cows; but they are all the same breed."

"Go away from home to learn the news." A Medora gentlemen while in Mandan heard that three men had been caught, supposed to have set fire to Hotel de Mores, and that one of them had been found guilty and hanged. We have heard nothing about a hanging bee.

Charles Cook, of Milbank, arrived last week, and will be a permanent resident of Medora. He is an energetic rustler and has come to stay. Mr. Cook will open a confectionery and tobacco store and dish up oysters in the highest style of the art. We welcome him and his family to Medora.

Considerable work is being done in the Medora coal mine preparatory to the winter trade. The tunnel is in about ninety feet, and a chamber fourteen feet square has been taken out. The coal is steadily improving in quality, and is now undoubtedly the best lignite that has been found in the west.

By mutual consent the firm of Boyd & Alexander, of the Pyramid Park Hotel, Little Missouri, dissolved partnership on the 1st of November, Mr. Boyd continuing the business, paying and collecting all bills. He will keep up the reputation of the hotel, and will spare no pains to make everything agreeable to those who are under his care. We wish him success.

The Catholic church erected by the Marquise de Mores was blessed by Father Martin on Sunday last. A large congregation gathered to participate in the ceremonies, which were very impressive. Father Martin took his text from the temple of Solomon, and delivered an eloquent and instructive sermon. He urged that the Catholic people use every means to maintain the church in a manner creditable to a christian community, and that a school be established for the enlightenment of our young people. It is expected that the bishop will be here to dedicate the church early next spring. Father Martin intends to hold services in Medora at least once a month, and if he succeeds in procuring an assistant priest in Mandan, will be able to give us more frequent visits. Now that we have a place of worship, the community at large should not fail to appreciate the efforts of the Marquise in erecting the holy edifice.

Bob Roberts' bear creates no little amusement for the boys. She is as active and nimble as a cat, and never seems to tire in her funny capers. The other day some one gave bruin a bottle of beer, which seemed to please her very much. It made her tipsy, and her efforts to draw beer from the bottle were very ludicrous. She finally stood on her head and held the bottle between her paws and sucked it dry. It got the best of her, and she was compelled to lie down and sober up.

It is hard to catch Jay Gould napping. The Union Pacific railroad owes the government a large amount for which it has not been pressed under republican rule. Under democratic rule Thurman will probably be secretary of the treasury, and as he has already shown his hostility to the Union Pacific, as a subsidized road, the wily Jay, as soon as Cleveland's election seemed probable, sold all his Union Pacific stock. This will cause trouble about the control of the Oregon Railway & Navigation lines, but it is very probable that they will again be operated in connection with the Northern Pacific.

It is singular what vaporings fill the [editorial?] mind of some newspaper correspondents, and what a mass of trash newspapers will use as "filling." We allude particularly to the discussion now going on relative to the division of this tier of counties in such a way that the eastern part of Billings county shall be merged into Stark county, and enough of Morton county set off so that Glenullin can be a county seat. The plan contemplating the still farther division of Billings county is one originated by a few disgruntled politicians without influence, money or common sense who hope to put a streak of county official fat over their impoverished skeletons. The original limits of Billings county have twice been contracted to make room for Dunn and Villard counties, and the only change that will be made is to restore to us our originall boundaries. As long as the Cow Boy is in its present hands, a county office in Billings county will be no place for a rascal who expects to fatten on his fellow citizens, and this very class that is now agitating division will find it very warm work to hold office here with their present lax ideas of morality. We have given more space than we ought to these political sharks, and have done with them until they "shtep on the tail o' me coat" to a little more purpose.

Executive Office, Bismarck, Dak., Nov. 8, 1884.

In accordance with the proclamation of the president, I do hereby designate Thursday, the 27th day of November, as a special day of thanksgiving unto God for the blessings and mercies of the past year, and do recommend that the people of Dakota observe that day. For health, abundant crops, the preservation of life, freedom from great calamities; for progress in material things, for intellectual advancement, for a peaceful land and a prosperous nation, let the people meet at the altar and fireside and reverently give thanks unto the power that has blessed and preserved us.

And let us pray that war and pestilence, famine and flood may still pass this people by; that righteous judgments and prudent counsels may prevail in all our borders, to the end that law and order may reign, and public tranquility continue throughout the land.

Gilbert A. Pierce, Governor.

In saddle or in camp at home,
I fear not fortune's change;
My wealth the branded herds that roam
The green wastes of my range!
Oh, who more independent, free,
And care exempt than I?
Not he that sails upon the sea
Or scales the mountain high.
I laugh and sing, give fancy wing,
And let the world go by.

The bustle of the run, the count,
The round-up and the drive,
Is pastime keen, if but the mount
Be mettled and alive.
Belted and spurred, devoid of fear,
To every risk resigned,
My cowboys [illegible] [reck?] career
As [headlong?] [as?] the [wind?];
Nor robber greed nor mad stampede
Can them unguarded find.

At work or play, with care to cause
No honest heart a pang,
And governed but by honor's laws,
On broncho or mustang,
Oh, who with more undaunted brow
Doth fell adventure bide?
Not he that speeds the pen or plough
Or stems broad traffic's tide!
In manhood's flower the plains I scour,
A ranchman true and tried!

Firm ward the mountain sentries keep
O'er my domain for me;
Far as the coursing gaze can sweep,
And rolling as the sea,
That cattle dotting realm expands,
Whence far abroad is strewed,
Rich nourishment for peopled lands,
The boon of wholesome food,
To mine the choice to here rejoice
Amid the solitude.

The saddle is my throne, the vast
Wild herds my vassals tried.
The lariat's swift, unerring cast
My mandate undefied.
My spurs were won by stubborn deeds
That ne'er a blush can bring,
Nor other, right or sanction needs
The care-free cattle king!
And joy brims up his stirrup-cup
In this the song I sing.

A leaf of suet and kidney taken from a beef steer one day last week weighed 33 pounds. The butcher who dressed the animal states that in all his experience in butchering, which has been large, he has never seen this equalled, not even in corn-fed beeves in the states. The animal was a four-year-old steer raised on Smith river, and weighed 1,200 pounds when dressed.—[Miles City S. G. Journal.

An exchange thinks that western stockmen who buy young eastern stock cattle must be prepared to shelter them the first winter from the severe storms. No greater mistake can be made than to compel unacclimated calves and ill-conditioned yearlings to rustle for themselves and have no shelter from the wintry storms.

M. W. Angle, living twenty-five miles south of Mingusville, sustained a serious loss Monday. His flock of sheep was stampeded over a bluff by a herd of cattle, and about 300 were killed. The coolie was filled with the bodies of the sheep, and the cattle used them as a bridge in crossing the coolie.

A reliable British authority has it that sheep will consume about fifteen pounds of dry and mixed food per week for each 100 pounds live weight. This, of course, when fattening for the shambles. The same authority says they should yield about one pound increase for every nine pounds dry food consumed. "Moderately fat sheep should yield 58 per cent. carcass in fatted live weight, and excessively fat sheep 64 per cent. or more."

The receipts of fat cattle and hogs at Chicago have been large of late and may be expected to continue large for some weeks to come. The percentage of fair to good quality arriving will naturally increase, as large numbers are now being fed feed freely. The range cattle may be expected to come forward freely. We see no room to expect an advance in prices, and possibly there may be a decline. The better grades of cattle will doubtless continue in the best request, but it may be questioned whether it will be wise to hold those already well ripened, and while there has been a somewhat discouraging fall in the price of hogs we certainly should not hold those already fully fat in hopes of any considerable advance in prices.—[Breeder's Gazette.

A floating item says that the best horse doctor is a sensible horse. Give him liberty and he will take care of himself. Whoever saw a horse running wild troubled with the "heaves." A nibble at a poplar pole, or a bite of rosin weed and a full supply of grass is all he wants to put himself in a sleek, plump, happy condition. But if kept up and fed musty hay and made subject to the unnatural demands of a thoughtless owner, it is no wonder he suffers. Father Clarkson says "rosin weed" is a sovereign remedy for heaves, and any one who has seen the intelligent horse stretch his nose over to brouse it in the uncut grass when hitched to the mower, has evidence in support. A good horse is his own doctor if you give him a chance.

Frequently of late we have heard the cow boys complain that the work on the range now is not what it used to be; and this reminds us that down in Tenos and out in New Mexico and Arizona, the same complaint is made, and the Sidney (Tex.) Independent, speaking of this, says: "Cow boys don't have as soft a thing as they did eight or ten years ago," remarked one of the fraternity. "I remember when we sat around the fire the winter through, and didn't do a lick of work for five or six months of the year, except to chop a little wood to build a fire to keep warm by. Now we go on the general round-up, then the calf round-up, then comes haying—something that the old-time cow boy never dreamed of—then the beef round-up and fall calf round-up, and gathering bulls and weak cows, and after all this a winter of feeding hay. I tell you times have changed. You didn't hear the sound of a mowing machine in this country ten years ago. We didn't have any hay, and the man who thinks he is going to strike a soft job now in a cow camp is woefully left."—[Barber Co. (Kan.) Index.

A very observing cattle breeder is Mr. Tuttle, of the Powder river country in Wyoming. Meeting the gentleman on the rotunda of the St. James the other evening, the Record engaged him in conversation on the bovine subject and the national trail, said he: "Up as far north as I am the people will have no use for this trail that you are advocating. I believe we have got all the Texas cattle that we need. The day is now on when a better breed of cattle will take their place. If there is no Texas cattle then there will be no fever, and if there is no fever then our northern cattle will be permitted to go down through Canada to the sea shore and out to Europe. And if there were no more broadhorns there would be more shorthorns and Herefords, and more beef, and more value in our herds. The four-year-old ox that comes over from Oregon will weigh an average three hundred pounds more than one of the same age up from Texas, and when fatted will put on a far greater per cent. of flesh. This is from the fact that the people of Oregon have been breeding up, while the Texans have been breeding down. No sir, we need no more Texas blood on our Wyoming heath. We need a race of cattle that should belong to the northwest. And I believe they will be produced by a cross with the shorthorns and the Herefords. Let them be called 'the North Cattle,' every steer of which at five years of age should weigh fifteen hundred pounds. These cattle will answer for export feeders, and will do credit to an English stall. A Texas steer with his broad horns would fright the yeomanry of their senses, and would only do to put on exhibition as a wild beast from the pampas of America."—Colorado L. S. Record.

Misses Mary and Annie Brophy return this evening to their home in Mingusville. We hope to see them here often.
Orrin Kinley returned Tuesday from work on the stage route, and reports the line as being nearly ready for winter. He starts back to-day to complete the work.
One of J. C. Fisher's buildings is nearly completed, and will be occupied in a few days by Mr. Cook. J. D. Garver will occupy the other as soon as completed.
[illegible] track is being raised and improved. Considerable difficulty has been experienced in getting cars up the grade, which this change will obviate.
John Kelly and wife, who have won a reputation on the Pacific slope as accomplished musicians, will give an entertainment here a week from to-morrow evening. Full particulars in our next issue.

Johnny Goodall has brought up five hundred stock cattle of the N. P. R. C. Co., and is holding them four miles below on the river. They are to be sold, as the company intends dealing exclusively in beef cattle.

Bob Roberts expects to start in two weeks for New Orleans, to stay until spring. After that he will go to Wales to receive a legacy left him there by his father, and during the summer he will return to Medora.

Hereafter receipts will be given to purchasers of coal from the Medora coal mine. The receipts can be obtained at the Cow Boy office, and cash in advance will be charged. Customers will please remember this rule.

Dr. H. M. Jorgens arrived Tuesday from Spearfish. He will make a most valuable citizen, and has come to stay. He intends immediately increasing his drug stock, and will carry everything necessary for a first-class drug store.

A new station has been built on the stage line between South Moreau and Indian Creek, and will be called Antelope. The stock is steadily improving, and schedule time must be lowered as the coaches are constantly beating it.

There are still twenty-one cattle strayed from the car loads that were wrecked west of here. Five dollars reward for each head is offered by the railroad company, but they are not by any means meek-eyed states cattle, and it probably will be some time before they are all rounded up.

Changes are coming thick and fast in the railroad employes here. Kelly has gone to Dickinson, and his place has been taken by L. W. Anderson. Ives is in Sentinel Butte, and S. P. Elverson has his place as night operator, and Mr. Maxwell, formerly in the car accountant's office in Mandan, exchanges places to-day with agent Fegan.

Great sport was had at the opening night of roller skating in Robert's hall. One gallant swain, while skating with a lady companion, observed that a nail was not driven home in the floor and proceeded to amend the defect with the end of his back bone. He afterward acknowledged that he would have felt much better if his partner had also fallen.

Johnny Munro has a calf, given him by Howard Eaton, and thereby hangs a tale; not tail, as will be seen. Johnny asked some round-up boys to brand the calf, and they did so. They grubbed both ears and the tail, wattled the fore-head, dew-lapped the brisket, and branded JOHN on one side and MUNRO on the other. No tenderfoot will pick up that calf for a maverick.
The dance last Thursday evening in Robert's hall was largely attended, and all enjoyed themselves thoroughly.
E. E. Ball, of Mandan, a first-class dentist, will be here the last three days of next week to do any work in his line that may be required by our citizens.

The stage arrivals from the Hills so far this week have been as follows: K. W. Kinneer, Mrs. N. P. Rodebank, Harry Rodebank, Jos. Browning, John S. Allen, G. A. Eleson, George Wager and Jacob Rodenhaus.

There is no better opening in the country for a shoe and harness maker than at Medora. Work in these lines has been accumulating for a long time and there is enough at all times to keep two men busy. Who will be the first to take advantage of the opportunity?

One of the Texas steers that escaped from the wreck, wandered upon the coal mine butte and out on the roof of the dug-out barn located on the east side. The roof caved in and the steer was effectually corralled, and only discovered yesterday. Sam English found him and intends roping him, tying the rope to the hind axle of a wagon and towing him into town. Medora has not yet been blessed with a circus, and we advise our readers to turn out immediately and see this one. It will probably last as long as the wagon does.

If solid comfort you would find,
Don't forget to bear in mind,
The way to travel in or out
Is by the new Medora route.

For the coaches are the best
To recline and take your rest.
And the agents, you will find,
Are the best of human kind.

The coaches come and go on time,
Bringing in from every clime,
The honest mining sons of toil,
And the tillers of the soil.

Likewise maidens brave and fair,
Also babes with curly hair;
And Chinaman with silken queues,
And honest Cornishman and Jews.

And if you're going in or out,
Don't forget to take this route
And if your purse is flush or lank,
Call next door to Merchants bank.

We can handle by express
All the wealth that you possess,
Either packages or cash,
Gin, wine, rum or sour mash.

We will feed you at home stations
On the very best of rations;
Serve it up on nice clean plates
At the very lowest rates.

The natural beauties of this route,
You can bet, without a doubt,
Is only equaled night or day
By the vale of Yosemite.

If information you would seek
Do not fear to come and speak,
For we love to answer questions
And charge nothing for suggestions.

For dealing fair by patrons,
Be they misses maids or matrons,
We will get our share no doubt
O'er this grand Medora route.
—[Deadwood Pioneer.
Northern Pacific bonds sold yesterday as follows: Common, 18½; preferred 43¾.
The capitol building at Bismarck was turned over to the territory by the capital commission, and the governor notified, as the capital commission act requires, on Tuesday.
A fire at Milbank, Dak., caused a loss of $150,000. Two blocks were entirely destroyed. The Continental hotel at Fargo was also destroyed by fire Tuesday. Loss, $70,000; insurance, $40,000.
Mr. Cook expects new stock in a few days.
Go to H. M. Jorgens for stationery and notions.

An Englishman, who has just returned from a hunt in the upper country, says he ate so much pork—'orrible stuff when a man's beastly 'ungry—that he can't look a hog straight in the face. This is rough on the hog.
Mr. J. L. White returned from a two weeks' hunting expedition on Monday. He succeeded in killing sixteen deer, and is much pleased with the result. Vic. Smith accompanied Mr. White.

Messrs. Platt Bristol and David Howe, of Mandan, came in on Saturday's train. They were here on business. Both of these gentlemen are highly pleased with Medora, and predict a brilliant future for us.

Mr. John Kelly, the celebrated California vocalist, has arrived with his wife, and was about to pass by, as no piano or organ was to be had. He was, however, persuaded to stop and give an entertainment to-morrow night in the dining-room of Hotel de Mores, kindly tendered him by Mr. Fitzgerald. The price of admission has been reduced to 50 cents. Doors open at 7:30, performance to commence at 8 sharp.

George Grinnell, well known throughout this region, was reported to have been hanged by the Montana Stranglers recently. He is spoken of here as a man who would not steal cattle, and it seems to be a case of personal enmity. The leader of the stranglers and Grinnell had some difficulty in dividing buffalo robes a few years ago, and it is supposed that the hanging was the result of this misunderstanding.

A passenger on last Saturday's east bound train saw a herd of buffalo grazing about four miles from here. He became terrible excited, and could hardly wait for the train to reach Belfield, so anxious was he to take a shot at the buffalo. Before leaving Belfield, he telegraphed the information to several of our ambitious hunters, and they also became worked up. There was a sudden demand for horses, and the way they flew around we supposed a large herd was near here. Finally a cloud of dust was seen in the eastern part of town, but it was hard to tell whether the Marquis de Mores or William VanDriesche would get the first shot. In about an hour they returned, and seemed surprised to hear that a buffalo hunt had been organized, but it was afterwards learned that Howard Eaton's tame buffalo had a narrow escape. Howard says he will have them whitewashed and a lantern with a red light attached to them, and hopes that this will be sufficient to save the lives of his pets.

On Thanksgiving Eve, Wednesday, November 26th, a social dance will be given in Robert's hall under the management of Mr. James Hannigan. The public is invited to participate in the festivities, and a good time is assured to all. The floor will be in good condition, and nothing will be lacking to make this the most enjoyable dance of the season.

The Crowe reservation is a harbor for horse thieves, Indians and whites alike. There are said to be from 300 to 400 head of stolen herses cached in the vicinity of Black canyon at the present time.—[Glendive Times.

Horses are not injured by labor any more than men, and it is only by exposure, overexertion and neglect that they become jaded out at a time when they should be in their best condition for usefulness.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Western stockmen who buy young eastern stock cattle must be prepared to shelter them the first winter from the severe storms. No greater mistake can be made than to compel unacclimated calves and ill conditioned yearlings to rustle for themselves and have no shelter from the winter storms.—[Kansas Cowboy.

Advices from the vicinity of Chanpaign, Ill., say that hog cholera is raging to an alarming extent along the Sangamon river. In Sangamon township, in Piatt, county, John Madden has lost 100 head, and many others each from 40 to 100. In Goose Creek township, H. F. Dillon has lost 200 head, H. S. McFadden, 150 and others have lost heavily.

Stallions on exhibition in Scotland are not awarded premiums as in this country. The awards are decided there by their get, which circumstance actually excludes the uncertain foal getter from successful competition. This is certainly a much more thorough test of merit than the American system, and that far at least is a decided improvement upon it.—[Col. L. S. Record.

And now comes Benjamin F. Butler in his new role of cattle king. If Ben cannot be President of the United States he can get up the boss cattle company. We are glad to welcome Ben as a cattle man. The New York and Boston Cattle company was incorporated the other day with a capital stock of $6,000,000, and Benjamin F. Butler, of Boston, heading the directory of the company. The company will operate in Kansas, Colorado, Texas, Arozona, New Mexico and Wyoming.—[Drovers' News.

The warden of the Manitoba penitentiary, at Stony Mountain, near Winnipeg, has a fine herd of hybrid cattle, crossed between the male buffalo and the domestic cow. They are very tame, taking no more notice of human being than ordinary cattle do. They are very hardy, and seem pre-eminently adapted to ranging our plains. They readily mate and nature seems to provide their offspring with a constitution adapted to all climatic charges of the northwest.—[Drovers' Journal.

A few day ago a Mr. Blasing, of Riley county, Kan., missed his cattle, 22 in number, and the next day heard of them being driven towards Manhattan. He found that two strangers, with more enterprise than good judgment had butchered 3 head of them, selling one carcass to local butchers and shipping 2 of them to Kansas City. A telegram with a sheriff at the end of it caught up with the exporters, in Topeka, and they are now, temporarily, gusts of the county. When the returns are all in it will doubtless be found that they are unanimously elected to State positions, with permanent headquarters at Lansing. The minions of the laws seem determined to crush out every attempt to establish what, if undisturbed would develop into a great traffic in dressed meat.—[Kan. City L. S. Indicator.
The slaughter house is fast nearing completion.

The following is a distressing picture drawn in a dispatch with reference to the suffering of cattle that were shipped to New York recently, during the hot spells, and clearly demonstrates the advantage of western slaughtered beef against these fever heated animals: "Since Tuesday of last week 20 per cent. of the western cattle have died on the cars or immediately after being transferred to the stock yards. The soap factories are overstocked with carcasses of steers, hogs, and sheep, bought at prices ranging from ten to fifty cents a [head?].—[Col. L. S. Record.

The first national convention of cattlemen ever held in this country opened its session in St. Louis, Tuesday at the exposition building, which was handsomely fitted up and decorated for the occasion. Delegates were present representing nearly all the western states, territories, several eastern states, Mexico, England and Scotlond. Col. R. S. Hunter, of St. Louis, originator of the project, called the convention to order and announced as the object of the gathering the formation of a national league of cattle intersts for mutual good. Addresses were made by Mayor Ewing, of St. Louis, Gov. Crittenden, Gen. W. T. Sherman and others. A very pleasant and amusing features of the convention is the cow boy band of Fort Dodge, Kan., twenty strong, in full frontier costume. They played several selections during the morning's session, exciting great applause. The leader wields in place of a baton his silver mounted Derringer, nearly a foot long.

One of the most startling and romantic features of border life occurred recently on the Wild Horse praire, thirty miles north of Los Angeles, when a band of wild horses, under the lead of a noble sorrel stallion, came galloping over the plain to reconnoiter a company of surveyors engaged in making a survey of the tract. The band dashed towards Capt. Keller and his party of surveyors till within about 500 feet, when the leader halted in a grandly proud and defiant manner, with neck curved, nostrils distended, erect, and tail on dress parade, and all the band ranged themselves on each side of him like a squad of cavalry in a battle charge. After surveying the scene for a moment the leader galloped proudly away, followed by the band in the most graceful and dignified manner. The scene was most romantic, and the picture of the lordly leader, with his most obedient subjects in their fleet and graceful motions, was worthy of an artist's pencil. There was another band of wild horses on the same prairie, under the leadership of a dark mahogany bay stallion, with black mane, tail and knees. In this band there are two white horses, while the rest are bay and sorrel mainly. Few people are aware that at the base of the Sierra Madre, only thirty miles from this city, wild horses roam in their native beauty and crop the rich grasses that grow on Wild Horse prairie. Yet such is the fact, and their slick appearance and graceful motions are the admiration of all beholders.—[Los Angeles (Cal.) Express.

A Des Moins, Iowa, corespondent of the St. Paul Pioneer Press writes as follows concerning the mysterious deaths of cattle in Iowa and Minnesota: Two months ago there was great fatality among horses in a western county. The cause was traced to a plant known as wild pea, which grows on bottom lands along rivers all over the state. A recent extended mortality among cattle in the northern part of the state has been traced to another plant, known to botanists as Limnactis minutulia. It is found extensively in Minnesota lakes, in Okoboji and nearly all lakes in Iowa. It appears in July in the shallow water about the shore. It is round, nearly the size of a pinhead, and is suspended in the water in masses. In the latter part of the month it undergoes several changes of color, from a greenish hue to that of frost-bitten grass. It floats in masses on the shore, undergoes decomposition, giving out a peculiar sickening odor, which will be recognizable by every person who has frequented the shores of these lakes in the months of July and August. For several years farmers around Lakes Tetonka and Sakatah, in Minnesota, north of Albert Lea, and around Okoboji, have lost cattle in July in a very sudden and mysterious manner. Apparently well, they would be dead in two hours. So, also, of horses and hogs. The cause was a mystery. It was discovered that the deaths occurred among animals that that had drunk at the lakes, by the fact that of a gang of men at work on a railroad in 1883, one evening several got water from Lake Sakatah; the remainder from a brook. Those that drank at the lake died. This year there was a repetition of the mortality, and it was noticed that this peculiar odor was present around the lake when the animals died. At other seasons animals drank the lake water without injury. A post mortem was made of some of the cattle, and the lining membrane of the stomach showed distinctly the line reached by the water drank. The membrane was sloughing off scalded cuticle. Prof. Stalker, state veterinarian, was called, who has traced the trouble to this plant. He is now investigating the plant to ascertain its poisonous properties.

Tuesday's stage from Deadwood made the trip in 36 hours and 5 minutes. If you want to go to the Hills in a hurry, take the M. S. & F. Co.'s route.
A couple of railroad men fired several shots at a hogshead, distance 100 yards, and no bullet marks were found on it. A local hunter says they could not hit a flock of balloons 50 yards away.
Mr. Thomas Matthews, cattle inspector for the Montana Stock Growers' Association, was in town Tuesday. He reports cattle shipments about over for the season.
If some of the young men who skate, or try to skate, keep on performing such wonderful acrobatic feats as they have been doing, the will be able to join some circus next summer.
Mr. Pat O'Hara gives it out loud and strong that no more coal will be delivered on Sunday. If you want good elegant shin heat, leave your orders for coal at the Cow Boy office.
Mr. Fisher's houses are completed. One of them is occupied by Mr. Charles Cook, the confectioner, and the other will be taken by Mr. Garver, the tinsmith, the first of next week.
It is reported that the time of the trains will be changed on the 23d inst. The morning train will arrive here half an hour later than at present, and the evening train an hour earlier.

Last Thursday evening a shooting affray took place between George Heywood and Bob Roberts, Mr. Heywood receiving a painful but not fatal wound. From information gleaned it seems that ill feeling has existed between these two gentlemen for some time, and on the night mentioned they met in a saloon on the other side of the river. Both had been drinking a little, and in the course of the evening some words passed between them, but as far as the shooting is concerned, it is hard to say exactly how it happened. Mr. Heywood had emptied his revolver, and was standing outside the door when a bullet was fired through it and came very near him. He entered the saloon and made some remark, when hot words were indulged in, Mr. Roberts leaving the saloon, telling Heywood not to follow him. Mr. Roberts went to another saloon, and in a short time Heywood put in an appearance, when Roberts fired three shots. Eye-witnesses think the shooting of Heywood was accidental, as Mr. Roberts is an excellent shot and could have killed Heywood had he any intention of doing so. He sent two balls through the ceiling, and it is thought the third was intended to be high, but the revolver went off half-cocked, the ball striking Heywood in the left breast, tearing the flesh and passing through his left arm. Roberts and Heywood are good citizens, and it is to be hoped that nothing serious will be the result of this little misunderstanding.
Be sure and take your watch to the King jeweler, Spearfish or Deadwood for repairs.

Peter Book has discovered a new streak of clay that makes the best kind of cement, and intends working it this winter. He will also make a large number of pressed brick.
The report so generally circulated that Half-breed Jack and Jack-ass Bob were hung in Montana for horse stealing seems to have been incorrect. They are both now in jail in Miles City.

The pleasantest dance that has ever been held in Medora took place last evening in Roberts & Co.'s hall. There was an unusually large attendance, and nothing occurred to mar the pleasure of the occasion.

J. C. O'Brien, a prominent broker of Deadwood, was in Medora Sunday, on his way home from the east. He was in New York during the campaign, and gave a vivid description of many of its prominent features.

Deer are more numerous than usual this year, and large numbers are being killed in the vicinity of Medora. The evening train last Monday ran into a band of about a hundred a few miles west of here and killed two.

The man arrested and taken to Mandan by Bill Jones, for setting fire to the prairie, was given his liberty last week. He started for Glendive, and west of here was caught in the cold snap and badly frozen. He is supposed to have been crazy.

M. G. Hall, assistant superintendent of the N. P. Express Co., was here Monday, arranging rates, etc., with the stage company. Mr. Hall is a thorough business man, and to him in a large measure is due the good working of the express line.

A meeting to organize a school board and arrange preliminaries for a first-class school will, by request of those actively interested, be held in Roberts' hall to-morrow, Saturday evening, at 7 o'clock. All who wish to have a good school should turn out.

A. Young came near having a serious accident last week, owing to a cartridge sticking in his Winchester. In ramming it out, the cap came in contrct with the firing pin and the cartridge exploded, breaking the breech of the gun, but not harming Mr. Young.

Of all trite subjects in this country, weather is the tritest. But we venture to say that no other country under the sun has been blessed with as beautiful fall weather as we have had up to a week ago. Then came snow, and last Saturday night it was twenty-four degrees below zero, and no one walking about town needed an overcoat. Wednesday a delightful chinook breeze struck us, sending the thermometer to fifty degrees above zero. In spite of this great change there has been no discomfort.

Again has the Medora stage smashed all records. The coach arrived here last Tuesday night just thirty-two hours and five minutes out of Deadwood. This is time never before dreamed of, and beats the best time in or out of Deadwood by any stage over any line nearly four hours. There was no attempt whatever to make extra time, and not a horse was over-driven. There is no possibility of any other stage line beating this time, and it will stand as a record, until on a race against time it is almost certain that the time of the Medora stage will go considerably under thirty hours.
