All the writers of the day
Put the cunning things they say
Into rhyme:
But the poets seem to think
That their dainty high-flown ink,
And their time,
Is better spent upon a dream,
Or some such other airy theme,
Than on beef;
But in this they are mistaken,
And for once I'll try to waken
The belief—
Indeed, the knowledge—that for so long
Has not broken into song;
That to meat
And it's heat,
Or caloric, I should say,
We're indebted for the play
And the very wit
That would ignore it.
All the men that move the world
Round their necks have always curled
Number sixteen collars.
Now it's meat that makes these necks,
Meat that's eaten down in pecks,
With an appetite that recks
Not of dollars.
David was a live stock man
And a greater race he ran
Than any since;
He did't mince
Matters much upon a lark,
And this fiery, kingly spark
Wrought sad ruin to Uriah,
He'd remorse enough to buy a
Place in the kindom come.
But beef
Was chief
Topic when I began,
And not the live stock man.
Now pork, and beef and mutton
Are not coarse, and gross, but on
The contrary quite the reverse.
Every silken line and terse
Woven into poet's theme,
Every flash and every gleam
Fresh from genius' richest dream,
All the lovely airy things
Born of brain on singing wings,
All conceits and sweetest thought,
Out of meat are deftly wrought,
Gastric juice and teeth between,
By man's physical machine.
—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

November 20, 1884.
Andy Williams was recently convicted of cattle stealing at Miles City. He has not yet been sentenced.
A meeting of the Shonkin and Highwood horse association, is announced to be held at Fort Benton, Mont., on the 29th.
The average weight of cattle now slaughtered is a third more than it was half a century ago.—[Stock Growers' Journal.
Probably the last shipment of range cattle for the season left Miles City Sunday. They were prime beef, and belonged to T. J. Bryan.
From present indications there seems to be no doubt that inside of two years all the stock ranges on the Little Missouri will be taken up.

During the past few months the value of American live stock exported has aggregated a sum in excess of a million and a half dollars per month.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The market east is still overstocked with wool and has been this entire year, and notwithstanding this the country has paid more than $20,000,000 for foreign wools in the past twelve months.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Mr. W. J. Marsh, of Sheridan Navada, writes the National Live Stock Journal, of Chicago, that the blackleg is making fearful ravages in Nevada. He says that it will probly sweep the entire Pacific coast, and that it is liable to last for two years.

Of the 450,000 head of cattle shipped north by rail this year from Texas, 300,000 steers were under two years. There were few of the mammoth cattle of former years among them, which show shippers are beginning to realize that steers weighing from 1,000 to 1,200 pounds, market better in lots than the larger ones.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Before this last contagious disease boomers of Government officials "appointed because of supposed competency," etc; we admitted that pleuro-pneumonia did exist in isolated cow stables in the east. This admission was based on the reports of veterinarians who had "axes to grind," and now we defy any man to prove that there is a single case of contagious pleuro-pneumonia in the United States.—[Drovers' Journal.

The Breeders' Journal says that the demand for Herefords in America was never so urgent as it is to-day. There is scarcely a thoroughbred bull that is old enough for service in the hands of the breeders. The grade bull breeders are in the same position. The supply of both is exhausted and there is a probability that cattlemen on the plains will be contracting in advance for the next year.—[Stock Growers' Journal.

A recent dispatch sent out from Kansas City says that the committee appointed by the National Bureau of Animal Industry, to gather statistics of the cattle interests in the west, has nearly concluded its work. It is said that the report will show that there are about 25,000,000 head of cattle in the states west of the Mississippi river, being a gain of 30 per cent, since 1880. Texas leads with a gain of nearly 70 per cent.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The demand for thoroughbred bulls in western Colorado and by our farmers along the foothills will be greater this next season than it has ever been before. But they must come with well-authenticated pedigrees, when they will command good prices. Every known family of cattle have their admirers here, and every variety will here sell. A hundred-dollar bull will not bring five hundred, but he will command his full value and sell quick in the coming spring.—[Col. L. S. Record.

According to the National Stockman, the following is the receipt for the "government" harness dressing: "One gallon neat's foot oil, two pounds bay berry tallow, two pounds beeswax, two pounds beef tallow. Put the above in a pan over a moderate fire. When thoroughly dissolved, add two quarts of castor oil; then while on the fire, stir in one ounce of lampblack. Mix well, and strain through a fine cloth, to remove sediment, let it cool, and you have as fine a dressing for harness or leather of any kind as can be had."

It seems to us that cattle growers might increase their herds very materially by arranging to wean the calves in the fall. The usual custom is to mark, brand and turn them with the herd. Some cows will wean their calves, while others will not. Heifers are most apt not to wean their first calves. They seem to become attached to them and allow them to suck as long as they choose. Often we have seen yearlings on the range with their mothers, taking the milk of a younger calf. In early spring before the green grass comes, new-born calves who have to divide with yearlings generally get a small allowance, and are therefore stunted in their growth. Cattle owners should secure lands and inclose pastures in which to wean calves. They will find that by so doing their cattle will grow larger, and it is large steers that make the best beeves and bring top prices in the market. We heretofore suggested the advisability of keeping the range bulls in pastures at certain seasons of the year, and the same pastures would answer for weaning calves. Herd owners will have to do this, and the sooner they begin the better it will be for the improvement and increase of their cattle.—[Rocky Mountain Husbandman.

George Heywood's wound is healing kindly.
Bob Roberts returned Monday night from Bismarck.
C. W. Sleeper started for the Hills Monday morning on a business trip for the stage line.
Our list has been increased this week by twenty-three new subscribers. "It's on account of our winning way."
Dr. Jorgens reports business as far better than he expected, and is greatly pleased at his choice of Medora as a home.
Oats along the N. P. R. R. are and for some time will be steady at 72 to 75 cents. In the Hills they are $2.50 and rising.
Pat O'Hara has a gun for sale that he will guarantee, as he is acquainted with its pedigree. He says he has known it ever since it was a pistol.
The N. P. R. R. Co., through B. Barr, has exchanged a number of stock calves and cows to the Custer Trail Cattle Company and Thompson & Co. for fine beeves.
Bob Roberts, while in Bismarck, gave away the town pet, Nellie, the cinnamon bear. There is liable to be an uprising of the citizens when the time comes for her shipment.
Frank Howard, of Spearfish, was here Sunday, having come in from work on the stage line. Frank is one of the best and [fastest?] carpenters in the Hills, and is kept constantly busy.

"Mike" is again officiating at John Warn's suburban retreat, alias the "oyster grotto." His recent political experience was disastrous, although it is currently reported that he beat Mr. S. for the postoffice.

Sam English is getting to be a great psalm-singer. Since Wednesday night he has been singing "Unto us a child is born," but sticks on the next line, "Unto us a son is given" for it's a girl. Great is the thanksgiving in the house of English.

Dr. H. M. Jorgens has gone to Cav[e?] Hill, on the stage road, to spend Thanksgiving at John Arrington's ranch. He will probably bring his family with him on his return. Mr. Martin will continue to hold down the drug store during the doctor's absence.

A petition for the establishment of a school was circulated yesterday by Messrs. Coleman and Riley, and enough money subscribed to guarantee its opening. Dan Williams will be teacher, and the school will open next Monday morning at the Cantonment.

Trips to all points up and down the road and to the Hills have thoroughly convinced us that "there's no place like home." There is not a place on the N. P. R. R. or in the Hills that in proportion to its size is anywhere near as prosperous as Medora. "We're little, but oh, my!"

The work on J. D. Garver's store is nearly finished, and he will soon move in. Mr. Fisher is so well pleased with his building plans that he contemplates the building of other store rooms and possibly a roller rink. From the present popularity of this sport the rink would be a success.

Dan Friedman has gone to Cold Springs, Minn., to spend the winter and engage cattle for next season's contracts. We alluded some time ago to his having a superfluity of side-saddles, and as he left the extra one behind, it is a very supposable case that on his return the boys will all "smile."

It has been found that no petition for the organization of the county is on file, and no further move towards organizing can be made until this preliminary is arranged. The governor is anxious to have the matter settled, and will appoint the third commissioner on the arrival of the petition. To this end we have drawn up the petition, and have it in the COW BOY office. All residents of the county, tributary to Medora, are requested to sign it, and it will then be forwarded to [Belfield?], or a second one will be gotten up there. Those desiring a speedy organization will come in and sign.

George Fitzgerald began Tuesday to excavate foundations for a large hotel on the corner of Third avenue and Third street. The dimensions of the building are to be [32?]x80, with the front on Third avenue looking south. The plan of the building is an exact model of the Merrill house at Glendive, and will be built in the most substantial manner. It will first be built of wood and then veneered with brick. J. C. Williamson has the contract for the carpenter work, and Peter Book for the brick work. The contractors are guarantees of the substantial nature of the work. When completed it will be the finest hotel between Miles City and Mandan.

Cigars and tobacco at Cooks.

The Marquis returned last night from St. Paul.
Operator Ives, of Sentinel Butte, came up last evening to attend the Thanksgiving ball.
Mrs. John Kiefer is still in Minnesota and not much improved in health. It is to be hoped that she will soon recover and return to Medora.

Mike Coleman rounded up his family Tuesday, and found an unbranded member that had put in an appearance. It is not a maverick, however, and Mike now has its name on the tally sheet when the family is corralled for the night.

The plan for the brick work on George Fitzgerald's new hotel is a work of art, and would be no discredit to a railroad draughtsman. It was drawn by Peter Book and Henry Brick, who, as will be seen in the change in the brick yard advertisement, are prepared to do any work of this kind.

The article in the last Cow Boy and the petition relative to the organization of the county seems to have stirred up considerable feeling among the cattle men. A review of the whole case may explain matters. Two or three years ago a petition was circulated by the cattle men for the organization of the county. In answer to this petition, commissioners were appointed, Messrs. Fisher, of Medora; Hay, of Belfield, and Doyle of Bismarck. This was under the Ordway regime, and as Doyle never had, as near as we can learn, been inside of Billings county, there was another hitch in the proceedings. During a recent visit to Bismarck, the governor, whose every act since coming to Dakota has been for the best interest of Dakotains, spoke to us relative to the organization of the county. We explained that the cattle men desired more than anything else, the repeal of the herd law, and that they had already petitioned for the organization of the county as the first step toward that end. The governor then said that he had examined all the papers left by his predecessor in office, and that there was no petition on file for the organization of the county, and that there was nowhere a record of it. That he had no official knowledge of any such petition, and, as he would like to have the matter settled, asked us to take it in hand to circulate one. To this we readily acceded, and in last week's Cow Boy published a notice to the effect that such a petition was here awaiting signatures. Several came to the office and signed it, and upon its presentation to some cattle men, they absolutely refused. As the petition was directly in the interests of the cattle men, we confess this rather put a damper to it, and as it was a matter of little moment to us, except indirectly toward the development of the county, we dropped the matter. The cattle men at some time will realize their mistake, as the herd law cannot be repealed unless the county is organized, and the expenses this law entails upon the stock grower are far greater than those of a county organization.

As per announcement in the Cow Boy, a meeting was held in Roberts' hall last Saturday evening for the purpose of organizing a school board. The meeting was called to order by M. M. Coleman, who nominated J. C. Fisher for chairman. Carried.

John S. Warn nominated L. C. Luke for secretary. Carried.

Comments were then made by several as to the object of the meeting. The chair decided that the election of a school board was in order.

On motion of M. M. Coleman, J. C. Fisher was elected secretary of the board to serve also as director. Carried.

Howard Eaton moved that E. G. Paddock be elected a member of the board. Carried.

M. M. Coleman moved that James Hannigan be elected as president of the board. Carried.

A. T. Packard moved that Wm. Van Driesche be elected treasurer of the board. Carried.

A. T. Packard moved that the school board have complete authority in the premises and be empowered to transact all school business that shall arise. Carried.

The Marquise offered the church for a school house. Referred to school board. Adjourned.

C. W. Sleeper returned last night from his trip to the Hills. Like every one else he was astonished with the progress made by the Hillers, and is a firm believer in their future.

Father Martin held mass here Tuesday morning, and during the rest of the day circulated a petition for establishing a library. The books will be here in about a week, and John O'Sullivan will act as librarian.

The new slaughter and cold storage houses of the N. P. R. C. Co., being so near completion call for a more extended mention. The main refrigerator building is 40x120 feet, and 28 feet high. The slaughter house proper is 60x105 feet. Besides these there will be a corridor 25x120 feet, and a passage way 15x80 feet. All these buildings except the ice house will have gravel roofs. This will be shingled. The foreman of the carpenter crew is John McGee, and L. Ayers is superintending in the interest of the N. P. R. R. The buildings are said to be the strongest ever built in the territory, and a glance at the immense timbers that have gone into the work will easily convince any one of this fact. Mr. McGee is pushing the work rapidly, and it will be completed in a few weeks. The N. P. R. C. Co. will be in a position to handle almost any number of cattle when the killing season again opens. It is the present expectation that three hundred will be a small day's killing. Enough workmen will be employed to make a small town of themselves, and when the spring season begins, this, in addition to other interests, will cause Medora to have an even greater proportional growth than we have had this year.

NOTICE. Of a Proposed Meeting of the Stockmen of the Little Missouri.

At the request of Messrs. Huidekooper, Wadsworth, Eaton, Truscott, the N. P. R. C. Co. and of several other stockmen having ranges on the Little Missouri and Beaver Creek, a meeting of the stockmen of this river and its tributaries is hereby called to be held in Roberts Hall, Medora at 11 a. m. Friday December 19th. The object is to bring together the cattlemen of this vicinity in order that they may discuss certain questions of immediate and pressing interest to them, and in order that they may take measures to provide for a more efficient organization of the stockmen of this vicinity in the future, both so that they may be able to act more as a unit than has been the case in the past, and so that they can combine to protect their interests against unjust interference from the outside.

All gentlemen interested in stock raising both those on the Little Missouri, and those on the neighboring waters, are urgently requested to attend.

[By request.]

Theodore Roosevelt.

The recent stock meeting at St. Louis probably destined to have great weight on the future of stock growing in the west. Not much real business was transacted, but the foundations were laid for years of it. The subject of a national trail was the principal topic discussed, and a committee was appointed to memorialize congress in its favor. Colorado and Texas combined against the other states and territories, and finally downed them on the chairmanship, J. L. Routt[?] being elected. An association was organized under the name of the National Live Stock Association of America, and a constitution was adopted. The subject of cattle contagion caused extended remarks, and considerable feeling was aroused at the efforts of specialists to magnify the disease and thus place themselves prominently before the public. The subject of the dreadful scourge made by the drouth in Virginia and West Virginia, came to the attention of the meeting and in a few moments $1,200 was raised and telegraphed to the sufferers. The question of leasing public lands to cattle growers so that they might have a certainty of a possessory right for a time at least called for the greatest display of oratory during the convention. It was finally voted that it would be better to lease the lands, as at present no cattle man feels like making any improvements when he is liable at any time to be dispossessed by a homesteader. The president for the ensuing year is Col. R. D. Hunter of St. Louis. The next place for holding the annual meeting was decided by the executive committee to be St. Louis.

Of all the finer cattle imported into Colorado the present season, the Shorthorns had the majority. The importations consisted of high grade bulls under two years of age. In Wyoming the Herefords were slightly in the lead. But be it said that those taken in there had a mixture of the Shorthorn with the Hereford blood. The popular cross in that grazing country is a whiteface mixed on a Durham. The largest number of imported cattle that came into Colorado, were Galloways and Polled-Angus.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The Oregon Horse and Land company, whose ranch is on Snake river, in Oregon, has the largest horse outfit in the United States, 7,200 head running on the range. The company has shipped this season 500 head of geldings to the eastern markets, one firm in New York taking 200 head, and the street car company of Chicago took five car loads at an average price of $127 per head, unbroken. The manager says the difference in price between broken and unbroken horses is too small to pay for the trouble of training.—[Stock Growers' Journal.

It is claimed by some of the Texas drovers that the day for big herds on the trail is over, and that cattle from that state will mostly come to market by rail. If such should be the case, much of western life would be done away with. What would the annual shipment be to the cowboy without life on the trail? Going up the trail in the spring has long been a looked for job by the cowboy, and one which has afforded him a change from every day life on the ranch, which combined pleasure with their business. Viewing it other than from a business stand point we would miss the annual visit of the great herds and their drivers.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The sporting season of 1884 is over, and the records now made are not liable to be changed before the return of the warm months. Maud S., though unsuccessful in beating her own 2.09¾, remains Queen of the trotting turf, with the little gelding Jay-Eye-See a close second for first honors. Johnston (2.06¼), the fastest living horse outside of the thoroughbreds, leads both and so widens the gap between pacing and trotting as to render it somewhat doubtful as to whether it will ever be closed. Over this problem, and the other which the past season has furnished, horsemen can ponder without interruption in the succeeding six months.—[Pittsburgh Stockman.

Texas has produced three hundred thousand calves the present year that will be looking for a market as yearlings early next spring. "What we are to do with them yearlings is what immediately concerns us," remarks the Stockman, of San Antonio. That there will be as great a demand for them in this north country as there was the present year is quite uncertain. The men who bought young cattle this year paid too high a price for them, and if a hard winter should follow, will surely lose money. It will be somewhat doubtful, too, if many are brought by rail next season, as the territories and some of the States will quarantine against their coming in that way on account of the fever scare charged to that mode of transportation; and the driving across the Indian country and through a corner of Kansas will be attended with much trouble from the Indians and the white settlers. And if the Government refuses to open a national trail up from that country to the northwest it will still be worse with the calf growers in the south in the years to come. We believe it is to the interest of Colorado that facilities be afforded and maintained for the moving of the young herds of bovines as they come along from that country to this. Here is the proper feeding ground, there the breeding. Ninety-five per cent. of the cows of Texas will drop calves and raise them, while in Colorado not more than sixty will do it.—[Col. L. S. Record.

M. Coleman has made a number of improvements on his hotel, and now says that with the assistance of the coal mine he is prepared for any weather that may turn up.

Lloyd Roberts sold his tame buffalo to Bob. Roberts, who shipped it to Bismarck Monday. It will there be killed, stuffed and sent to New Orleans. Bob. sent the pet bear in the same car to Bismarck as a present to George Reed.

S. Jacques, representing the Illustrated Northwest, was here yesterday in its interest. The Northwest has probably done more than any other publication toward developing our country, and Mr. Jacques is an able exponent of its virtues.

Count Rembielinski of Russia and Vic. Smith have been hunting down the river for about ten days, and during that time, the Count killed sixty-five deer and antelope. This is the best tenderfoot record to date. Vic. says he is a dandy.

[B. Rumsey?], who has been here for some time, recently bought twenty-eight Durham bulls of the N. P. R. C. Co. They were branded Tuesday in the stable corrall, and the boys showed wonderful agility in climbing fences when they were turned loose.

George Fitzgerald is going to work in earnest on his new hotel, and expects to have it finished, with the possible exception of the brick work, by January 15. We have seen the plans, and they show that it will be a first-class building. Peter Book has the whole contract.

Mr. Simpson of St. Paul arrived Sunday evening and began his duties immediately as traffic manager of the stage company. Such an office has been badly needed, both in seeing that shipping directions are complied with and in getting additional freight, express and passengers.

The secretary of the school board left before handing us the minutes of the board meeting. We learn, however, that the position of teacher was offered to Mrs. Barr, who was obliged to refuse on account of a trip east, and that it was decided to hold the school for a time, at least, at the cantonment.

Otto Fischer, of Bismarck, arrived yesterday morning, and proceeded to make it lively for the boys. As may be seen by the advertisement, he is manager of the Bismarck branch of the Franz Falk Brewing Co., of which Roberts & Co. are local agents. Where Otto can't drum up trade, others had better not try.

The weather report handed us by T. Martin is a sufficient evidence of the superiority of our climate. Mr. Martin has kept the weather record for years in the Hills, and says he has never seen anywhere near as good weather for this season. His reports will be published monthly hereafter, and will be eagerly awaited.

F. B. Allen, of Bismarck, came down Saturday night. As Luke would say, "He had the veneered gall to wear a plug." The boys seemed to think that the plug had a tendency to make Allen's head bald or something, and their intention was the best in the world to give it plenty of ventilation. F. B. was too cute, however, as the plug didn't show up until he was starting away.

A correspondent writes that: "Hunters should always carry a watch or clock. That is what Tom Caruthers says and believes. L. Austin Paddock and Amos Stowe of Wadena, Minn., came here a short time ago to paint the buttes with gore. They went down the river with Tom Caruthers. Austin, who was panting too hard for game to sleep, roused up the boys at 2 a. m. They laid in some grub and then took a sleep. Austin meantime aimed his gun at the fire, and thought he could just knock the eye out of a fawn every time at one hundred yards. After fondling his gun for a few hours, Austin roused the boys a a second time and cooked a second breakfast. This suited the boys pretty well, and they took another sleep. Austin was just getting breakfast for the third time, when Tom made a break for the bullberry bushes and hid till Austin left camp. Tom says he is not stuck on night hunting, and will take a rest while Austin is here."

Great preparations are being made at Bismarck for the meeting of the legislature, which will convene at the new capitol building January 1. The session will be short, sharp and decisive, as much work must be done. Several parts of the territory need special legislation, and will [doubtless?] get it. E. W. Martin, recently elected legislator, is urged especially by the Black Hills papers for speaker. Although Mr. Martin is a young man he could fill the position with credit. He seems to be the unanimous choice of the Black Hills delegation.

The notice for a meeting of the cattle men of this district, which we publish for the second time should attract the attention of every man on and in the neighborhood of the river who is interested in stock. The reasons are so manifest that an organization should be formed, that there is no need of enlarging on them. It is imperative above all things that the cattle men should be united to be successful in movements for their good. A number of points will come up for action at the meeting of December 19, and it is important that every cattle man in this district attend, as each should have a voice in the decisions. Should there be only a partial attendance or should the interest be half-hearted the effort to organize will be useless. Unanimous and united action will be of incalculable benefit to our stock men.

We have nothing but the kindliest feelings toward the N. P. Ex. Co., but we are nevertheless heartily glad that the Wells, Fargo Ex. Co. are making a beginning toward destroying a monopoly which is keeping this country down. The rates on everything are far higher than they are in the east. For this there is some reason, inasmuch as railroads, etc., cost much more to build. We are, however, laboring under the disadvantage, all over Dakota, of being a new country and paying higher prices for articles we use than almost any other part of the country.

Take the items of freight, express, passenger and telegraph rates that have come under our personal notice. A car load of freight from Milwaukee to St. Paul was thirty-four dollars. From St. Paul to Medora it was three hundred and sixty-four dollars. This was an unclassified lot of goods. Classified carloads have come nearer five hundred dollars. That these rates are extremely profitable is abundantly shown by the fac[t] that the N. P. is very well satisfied to ship goods to Medora for the Black Hills at fifty cents a hundred, unclassified, or one hundred and fifty dollars a car load. It is an actual fact, coming constantly under our notice since shipments began from Medora to the Hills, that freight from St. Paul, Chicago, and in fact all eastern points, is landed in Deadwood cheaper than the same freight can be landed in Medora for local consumption. It is also a fact, demonstrated by personal experience, that owing to this state of affairs, goods of almost every description are actually sold in the Hills cheaper than they can be sold in Medora. When we take into consideration the fact that the rail journey is equal, and that in addition the Hills goods must be loaded on wagons and freighted across country two hundred miles, it shows that there is "something rotten in Denmark." It shows that merely because it has the power, the Northern Pacific railroad is charging exhorbitant rates, and rates way above those it could adopt at a profit.

Almost exactly the same points can be brought against the express rates that have been mentioned in reference to freight. The Wells, Fargo Express Co., as is well known, do not by any means "stand in" as well as the N. P. Ex. Co., but they are, metaphorically, "knocking the eye out" of the N. P. on rates.

The passenger rates are also unreasonably high. Five, six, seven, eight, and in some cases we think ten cents a mile are charged. This is beyond all reason, and should be regulated immediately by the legislatures of the territories passed through. To show conclusively that these rates are not essential to the existence or profit of the road, we will mention the fact that it was, and probably is possible to buy a ticket from New York city to Portland, Oregon, cheaper than one from St. Paul to Missoula.

While we are about it, an illustration of telegraphic charges may not be inapt. Ten words from Medora to St. Paul, night rate, is sixty cents. Ten words to Grand Rapids, Michigan, is seventp-five cents. In this case the whole line is under the management of one concern, and the injustice of the discrimination is more apparent. It does not cost a particle more to conduct a telegraph line in this country than it does in the east, yet the same telegram costs only one-fourth more in going twice the distance, and has to be repeated twice. Oh, consistency, thy name is not a railroad or a telegraph monopoly.

The above illustrations show the difference between monopoly and competition. The time is probably far distant when just rates will be established and maintained, unless the Northern Pacific wakes up to the fact that their short-sighted policy of extortionate rates is the surest way in the world to cut their own throats.

The cattle owners in the Little Missouri country have wisely declined to have anything to do with a petition from that country to repeal the herd law for that section of the country. Such a repeal would work great injury to the settlement of the country, and it is good sense on the part of the stock owners to not interfere on this particular point, and it is further for their own interest to protect the settler from their herds, instead of the settler protecting himself. Fencing farm property belongs to a past age. Wise cattle owners will heed this, and as the advancing homesteader comes, they must and will protect him, that is men that have sense. A country that naturally feeds cattle, will when cultivated, raise all the cereals, roots, flax and vegetables. Cattlemen, be wise on this subject.—[Dakota Blade.

Uncle Jimmy Emmons often "flies open," but did it very effectually in the above article. There has never been started a petition for a repeal of the herd law here. Should there be one, it would receive the signature of every cattleman on the river. Such a repeal would not work injury to the settlement of this country, but help it, as the herd law is at present our greatest drawback. It is not for the interest of the cattle men to protect the settler as there is now, and from the nature of the Bad Lands always will be a thousand dollars invested in stock to one in agriculture. This country naturally feeds cattle, but except on the tops of high buttes and in places along the river is not at all adapted to agriculture. Jimmy, inform yourself on this subject.

Pale, sedentary reader, who sittest in the calm seclusion of thy home and propoundest questions to the omniscient opinion-moulder, we will enlighten thy childish mind, and give you some pointers which we have been at great pains to gather. We use the word pains advisedly, and in its fullest sense. A bronco is a horse. He has four legs, like the saw-horse, but he is decidedly more skittish. The bronco is of gentle deportment and modest mien, but there isn't a real safe place about him. There is nothing mean about the bronco though, he is perfectly reasonable and acts on principle. All he asks is to be let alone, but he does ask this and even insists on it. He is firm in this matter and no kind of argument can shake his determination. There is a bronco that lives out some miles from this city. We know him right well. One day a man roped him and tried to put a saddle on him. The bronco looked sadly at him, shook his head and begged the fellow, as plain as could be, to go away and not try to interfere with a bronco who was simply engaged in the pursuit of his own happiness, but the man came on with the saddle and continued to aggress. Then the bronco reached out with his right hind foot and expostulated with him, so that he died. When thoroughly roused, the bronco is quite fatal, and if you can get close enough to him to examine his cranial structure, will find a cavity just above the eye where the bump of remorse should be. The bronco is what the cowboys call "high strung." If you want to know just how high he is strung, climb up on his apex. We didn't travel far, but the ride was mighty exhilarating while at lasted. We got on with great pomp and a derrick but we didn't put on any unnecessary style when we went to get off. The beast evinced considerable surprise when we took up our location upon his dorsal fin. He seemed to think a moment and then he gathered up his loins and delivered a volley of heels and hardware, a straight out from the shoulder. The recoil was fearful. We saw that our seat was going to be contested, and we began to make motions to dismount, but the beast had got under way by this time so we breathed a silent hymn and tightened our grip. He now went off into a spasm of tall stifflegged bucks. He pitched us up so high that, every time we started down, we would meet him coming up on another trip. Finally he gave us one grand, farewell boost and we clove the firmament and split up through the hushed ethereal until our toes ached from the lowness of the temperature, and we could distinctly hear the music of the spheres. Then we came down and fell, in a little heap about a hundred yards from the starting point. A kind Samaritan gathered up our remains in a cigar box and carried us to the hospital. As they looked pityingly at us, the attendent surgeons marveled as to the nature of our mishap. One said it was a cyclone, another that it was a railroad mash-up, but we thought of the calico-hide pony that was grazing peacefully in the dewy mead, and held our place.—[Santa Fe Democrat.

With the extinction of buffalo comes an increase in the depredations of wolves. This is accounted for by the fact that buffalo calves and carcasses killed by hunters furnished the wolves plenty of food. Now, that the buffalo are all gone, the wolves have turned their attention to cattle, and the loss from this source is constantly increasing. It has not reached any alarming proportions as yet, but it is enough to show that unless active measures are immediately taken, the loss is liable to be considerable. Some of the cattle men and hunters are poisoning carcasses, and have good success in killing wolves, but the movement is not universal enough to produce the desired result. This is a point that should come up for attention at the cattle meeting to-morrow, and every man should pledge himself to do his utmost toward exterminating the growing pest. It would be a good plan to pay a bounty for all pelts brought in.

At the recent national stock meeting in St. Louis, the subject of damage to hides by branding was brought up, but nothing definite was done. From a practical tanner, who is also a stock grower, we gather the fact that the average hide is damaged three or four dollars by branding. He regretted the loss, but acknowledged that there seemed to be no cure. The tanners buy hides of wholesale slaughter houses which have already bought the cattle from stock growers. To the latter, the value of the hide does not enter into account, but the fact of his having a brand plain enough to be recognized by any one is a matter of the utmost importance. Hence the indifference with which stock men regard any attempt to change the present system of branding. It is even doubtful if any invention that will remove the hair and not damage the hide would be profitable, as there would still remain the question as to whether the price of live cattle would raise, and if it did not the stock growers would quickly return to the present system.

The sad duty devolves upon us this week of chronicling the death of Peter Malloy. Early last week he started down the river for a hunt, and was taken sick soon after his arrival at Young's ranch. He grew rapidly worse, but on Friday, seeming to be a little better, Mr. Young brought him to town, where he might secure medical attendance. His condition seemed hopeless, however, and Friday night he died.

Mr. Malloy was well known and liked all through this country, and had a warm place in the the hearts of his sriends as being a good husband, kind father and upright man. He was one of the pioneers of the west, and the first constable of Bismarck. While here he was proprietor of the Western house, and kept it in a high standard of excellence.

His remains were taken to Bismarck Sunday for burial by his relatives. He leaves a wife and three children and a host of friends to mourn his loss.

Who is it has no fixed abode
Who seeks adventures by the load—
An errant knight without a code?
The cowboy.

Who is it when the drive is done,
Will on a howling bender run,
And bring to town his little gun?
The cowboy.

Who is it paints the town so red
And in the morning has a head
Upon him like a feather bed?
The cowboy.

Who is it with unbounded skill
Will shoot big bullets with a will
That generally have the effect to kill?
The cowboy.

Who is it, after all, who makes
Town trade good, and uniformly takes
For big hearts what is called "the cake?"
The cowboy.

—N. M. Stockgrower.

Messrs. Miller and Lux, two cattle kings of the Pacific Coast, were poor men twenty years ago, and are now rated as worth $8,000,000 to $10,000,000. They have about 90,000 head of cattle and 115,000 head of sheep, of which latter they kill about 6,000 per month. They own an irrigating canal worth $1,000,000, fences 300 miles in length (a fortune in itself), in California 600,000 acres of land, in Nebraska 10,000 acres, and 15,000 acres of alfalfa grass.—[Montana Stock and Mining Journal.

Fifty years ago the average weight of beef cattle was 800 pounds, now it is 1,400 pounds. The increase is due to the introduction of pure-bred stock and more careful breeding, as well as the much better feeding of the product. It is now as common to have a animal of 1,800 pounds, as it was then to have them of 1,200 pounds, and the increase in weight is fully one-third. The improvement of the far western stock is still greater, and more, nearly double, since the large introduction of shorthorn blood into the herds.—[Kansas City Drovers' News.

We have no more use for thoroughbred bulls on the range, is the way a good many cattle men now put it. What we want is graded stock. We have tried the thoroughbred bull and find there is no money in him. He can't rustle even when there is good grass. It is not his kind. He knows nothing about it, and soon begins to look drooping where range cattle are fat and sleek. It's different with graded bulls, even if they are not range stock. They soon learn to rustle and keep in good order. To make hardy range stock, calves must be dropped on the range. The get of thoroughbred bulls are all right, and there are now enough of them on the ranches to bring up the class to a beef animal. You will find, says the posted ranchman, that the majority of bulls sold for the range in the future will be graded.—[Transporter.

The London Live Stock Journal, in an article relating to the selection of a horse for the work he is expected to perform, after stating the results of many observations on horses, remarks that it is the arch of a bridge, which, from its structure, can bear weight placed upon it, whereas, an inverted arch would fall to pieces, or would withstand a far less pressure. It has been observed that low-backed, or rather hollow-backed horses, working in harness, kept their condition, while those with high back lost flesh. Persons of not very inquiring or observing dispositions would probably attribute this to the fact that the former were of more hardly constitution than the latter, but this would be a false conclusion. It is owing entirely to the curvature of the back, for a horse which can draw a weight was least able to bear a weight upon its back, while the horses unable to bear the strain of draft could beat the other any day in carrying a weight. The line of the vertebræ indicates the sort of work for which the horse is fitted. If it is high the weight must be on the top to press it together; if low, the pressure must be from below for the same reason. A downward curvature is, therefore, the best form of spine for a draft horse.

An exchange says the foal is born with twelve grinders. When four front teeth have made their appearance the colt is twelve days old, and when the next four assert themselves its age will be about twenty-eight days. The corner teeth make their appearance when the foal is eight months, and these latter attain the height of the front teeth at the end of a year. The two-year-old has the kernel, the dark substance in the middle of the tooth's crown, ground out of all the front teeth. In the third year the middle front teeth are being shifted, and and when three years old those are substituted by the permanent or horse teeth which are larger and more yellow than their predecessors. The next four teeth are shifted in the fourth year and the corner teeth in the fifth, giving place to the permanent nipper. At five years of age a horse has forty teeth, of which twenty-four are grinders far back in the jaw, with which we have little to do. The buyer must be particularly on his guard against having palmed off on him as fully five years old a filly of less age, by calling your attention to the fact that "she has no colt's teeth left" when the truth is they have been cunningly extracted, and we have known the same said of a horse, when it was thought the customer was green enough. But, be it remembered, horses invariably have tushes, which mares very rarely have.

Five Indians were in town Monday, looking for a herd of twenty-six ponies which had been stolen from them. Their search here was unsuccessful, but there is a strong suspicion that the guilty parties are on the river. There has been considerable indifference in relation to the arrest of those who have stolen ponies from Indians, and it is time for this to cease. Indians are "not like men who won't play even," and some innocent white man is sure to suffer. Punishment should be as swift and sure on these criminals as on those who steal horses from white men.

A careful enumeration of our population reveals the fact that we number two hundred and fifty-one citizens. Of these a hundred and forty-six are men, thirty-nine women and sixty-six children, twenty-five or more being old enough to go to school. It will be seen in this estimate that only permanent residents in town are counted. There is a floating population of between fifty and a hundred working men who are not included, nor are any of the stock men on the river. Their vote inside the county would swell our number to nearly three hundred and fifty voters.

One might believe that wood was the principal fuel of Newcastle, that the Esquimaux ate no fish, that the farmers of Dakota had to ship in grain, but it would be hard to believe that, living as we do in the midst of a cattle country, we are entirely without milk, except what is shipped in from outside. Out of our plenty there arises a scarcity. And this very scarcity shows one of the best openings for business that can be found on the line of the road. A good dairy, conducted on business principles, will pay largely here. Cows can be bought or rented at a low rate, and the demand for dairy products will be practically unlimited. A fortune in this line awaits a practical man who will go into the dairy business here.

A freighter pulled out from Belfield recently loaded with giant powder and bug juice. It was "six and six" for awhile which would down the other, as the freighter imagined that he was driving a six-horse coach, and had his teams going so that the wagons only hit the high places. Minutes of the meeting of the stockmen of the Little Missouri, held at Medora, Dakota, December 19, 1884:

The following companies and individuals were represented:

SOHO Cattle Company.
Badger Cattle Company.
Custer Trail Cattle Company.
Le Moyne Cattle Company.
Maltese Cross Cattle Company.
Elkhorn Cattle Company.
Thompson & Co.
L. D. & B. Rumsey.
H. B. Wadsworth & Co.
N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.
Casey & Co.

The meeting was called to order by Theodore Roosevelt.

The following resolution was read and adopted;

RESOLVED, That it is the sense of the stockmen present, representing the companies and individuals named above, that an association of the stockmen of the Little Missouri and its tributaries be forthwith formed, and that this association shall be known as The Little Missouri Stockmen's Association.

Also the following:

The officers of the association shall consist of a chairman and vice-chairman, elected annually, at the first meeting held after the fall round-up, and a secretary elected at each meeting, whose work is to be superintended by the chairman.

Theodore Roosevelt was elected chair-main, and Henry S. Boice vice-chairman.

The Marquis de Mores was nominated as a committee of one to work with the committee appointed by the Eastern Montana Live Stock Association in the endeavor to procure legislation from the territorial legislature of Dakota favorable to the interest of cattle men.

A resolution was passed that if any of the members of the association had cattle run over by the railroad, for which cattle the railroad refused to pay full value, it should be at once brought to the notice of the chairman, who shall report it to the next meeting of the association, in order that it might be brought before the courts as a test case.

The following resolutions were also passed:

RESOLVED, That at the request, in writing, of any three members of the association, a meeting shall be called by the chairman, who shall, however, give at least one weeks notice thereof.

RESOLVED, That the representation in this association be by firm, each firm being entitled to but one vote.

RESOLVED, That the next meeting of the association be held on or about April 1, 1885, at the call of the convention.

RESOLVED, That if any of the cattle companies or stockmen along the river refuse to conform to the rules and by-laws of this association, that it will refuse to act with them or allow them to take part in the round-up; and the captain of the round-up shall see that no stockman debarred by action of this association from participating in the round-up is allowed to take part in it and he shall further see that no third party, acting in the interest of said stockman is permitted to take part in or derive benefit from the round-up.

RESOLVED, That no member shall gather cattle or brand calves between December 1 and the date of the general spring round-up, without giving due notice a reasonable time beforehand to the other ranchmen of the neighborhood.

RESOLVED, That each member shall hereafter have not less than 10 bulls to every 100 head of stock on his range.

RESOLVED, That the chairman draw up a series of by-laws for the association, or embodying the foregoing resolutions and in other respects following, so far as they are practicable, the laws of the Eastern Montana Live Stock Association.

At 1:10 p. m. the meeting adjourned.

The stockmen's meeting last Friday morning bids fair to be the beginning of a very efficient organization. The utmost harmony and unanimity prevailed, and under the able chairmanship of Theodore Roosevelt, a large amount of business was transacted in a short time. It is of especial interest to every stockman on the river to carefully read the minutes of the meeting and act accordingly. Every motion that was passed was carefully discussed, and when it was seen to be for the greatest good of the greatest number, was unanimously declared the sense of the meeting. Especial provision was made for the fact that the large companies would be apt to have things too much their way, by allowing each company to have but one vote. The intention of the organization is not to be an independent concern, run on an expensive scale. It is more on the mutual benefit plan, and will probably be made subordinate to the Eastern Montana Association. A first-rate start was made, and we can now look forward to an efficient organization ruling all stock matters on the river. May success attend "The Little Missouri Stockmen's Association."

Basing conclusions upon the fact that buffalo are almost extinct, many papers are foretelling the fact that deer in this part of the country will all soon be killed, and are calling for a law restricting the time of killing. It is an understood fact that their numbers will diminish, but our children's children will still be killing them. There is scarcely a state in the Union in which deer are not found, and long after their extinction elsewhere, the natural hiding places of the Bad Lands will give them shelter. There are a large number of persons who make their living killing deer, and it is doubted by those who should know if the total number of deer in the Bad Lands has materially decreased. We are no advocate of the wholesale slaughter of venison, but we will never see the deer exterminated from this country, and as the few that are killed are used for food and not for the sole pleasure of killing, we even think the game law should be extended another month instead of being decreased.

An item has been going the rounds of newspapers as follows: "There is too much money invested in cattle in the United States for our friends to allow temporary differences of opinion to last. Two and a half billions of dollars is the size of that investment. There has been much good work accomplished, and there remains much to be done. With everybody in the harness and all the collars pressing evenly on the shoulders the work will be easily done." The report of the commissioner of agriculture for January, 1883, gives the total number of cattle in the United States as 41,172,762, valued at $1,008,124, 516. The paragrapher who originated the item only missed the valuation $1,491,875,484; but a billion, several million, and a few hundred thousand dollars cut no figure in an average editor's calculations. However, this bull writer ought to put the "collars" on his head until it could be reduced to commonplace consideration.

A stock owner went out the other day over the divide to see how his cattle were standing the vigorous weather, and found a large fine steer in his last long sleep. The stockmen had to roll him over to see the brand, and he has regretted his curiosity ever since. He told me that the brand looked to him like a Roman candle making about a thousand revolutions per minute, and with 187 more prismatic colors than he thought were in existence. Sometimes a steer is not dead, but is in a cold stupor which precedes death, and when stirred up a little and irritated because he cannot die without turning over and showing his brand, he musters his remaining strength and kicks the inquisitive stockman so high that he can see and recognize the features of departed friends. That was the way it happened on this occasion. The stockmen fell in the branches of a pine on Jack creek, not dead, but very thoughtful.—[Laramie Boomerang.

Joe McCool had a streak of luck last week that is rarely duplicated. A bronco was put up for raffle with ten chances. Joe won. The next day he won a Remington rifle under the same conditions. The next day he put up his bronco, kept a chance, and won again. Total outlay, $10; total receipts, a bronco, a rifle and $45 cash. The chances were one in ten, which he accepted and won three times in succession.

A great excitement has been raised in eastern and southern Dakota over the fact that coal has been discovered there. The St. Paul Globe speaks about the report of a three-foot vein being found, but says it lacks confirmation. From the coal veins in the Bad Lands, there seems to be little doubt that the whole of Dakota, or the greater part of it, is underlaid with vast beds of coal. In the Bad Lands themselves five veins are sometimes seen in one butte, the veins running from three to nine and twelve feet. There is a vein between Ferris Bros. & Merrifield's and Lloyd Roberts' ranches which is twenty feet thick in sight. It runs down to the surface of the river, and may extend twenty feet more from that point as far as any one knows. Forty-five miles south of here, at Mattox' ranch, on the old tie trail, there is a vein forty feet thick in plain sight on apparently the same level as the one spoken of above. At Buffalo creek, fifty miles from here on the stage road, in the midst of the prairie, a good vein has been found on the surface and another at a depth of forty-two feet. Between South Moreau and Indian Creek, a hundred and forty miles south of here, a vein was discovered at a depth of seventy-eight feet. It seems almost impossible to sink a well any distance anywhere in Dakota without passing through one or more veins of coal. There is enough coal in the Bad Lands to supply the universe for ages, but we might casually remark that as far as it is concerned, the universe will remain unsupplied as long as the prohibitive charges of the Northern Pacific remain in force.

C. F. Ellison is fast filling the ice houses with a first rate quality of ice. He has built a long track from the dam to the houses, and the ice is drawn upon these, thus making much faster time than by loading on wagons. About thirty men are employed putting up ice. In addition to the ice to be put in the houses, Mr. Ellison will put up a large quality to be stored in the cooling rooms of the company as soon as completed.

Work at the coal mine has been brisk lately, and it is an undisputed fact that the quality is superior to anything yet found along the line. When mined the coal is almost as glossy as anthracite. It burns freely and gives out an intense heat. The great weight of the butte is doubtless the cause of its superior quality, shown by the fact that until the tunnel had pierced to a depth of eighty feet, well under the butte, the coal was only of ordinary quality, except for a twelve to thirty-six-inch strip at the bottom of the vein.

We are glad to see the name of E. A. Henderson mentioned prominently for the position of clerk of the senate. Leaving the consideration aside that Mr. Henderson has occupied similar positions both in Minnesota and Dakota, which gives him abundant experience, his many good qualities and the service he has done the Republican party entitles him to the position. No other candidate has been mentioned prominently, and we earnestly hope that he will be the unanimous choice to the position for which he is so well fitted.

The benefits of advertising are so apparent that it seems almost unnecessary to call attention to them. An illustration coming to our notice, however, deserves comment. William Miller, of Minnesela, lost some horses on Grand river, and as our readers know, advertised them in the COW BOY. Mr. Miller, after inserting the advertisement, went up and down the railroad and stage road and finally returned to Minnesela. He had hardly reached home before he received word from Mr. Becket, of Dickinson, to the effect that his horses were there, having been recognized from the description in the COW BOY. The end was not as pleasant, however. Mr. Miller return to Dickinson, and in company with Henry Turner, John H. Stevens and son Horace, started for the Hills. They reached the Cannon Ball late at night, and in attempting to cross, tipped over. They were so exhausted that they could not right the wagon and were forced to remain there till daylight. They then started for Springdale station, on the stage line, and arrived there in a badly frozen condition.

The northern country is full of prospectors from the east and south looking for range locations and stock. There will not be much changing of ownership until spring, when a general stock boom is looked for. Quite a number are talking of stock contracts for spring delivery, and with all western and Texas cattle are the favorites, as they take to the range readily and commence rustling as soon as turned loose. Old-time Montana cattlemen think Idaho, Washington territory and Utah cattle cheaper at $35 per head than Texas stock at $20. Being natives of the country, they do well where imported animals die. They are also said to be better breeders, and the cows takes better care of their calves—[Stock Growers' Journal.

"Ex-Representative Upson, of Texas, is here as the legal representative of cattle raisers in the Southwest, for the purpose of securing the passage of a bill through Congress requiring the cattle trails of the West and South to be kept open. Within a few days he will be joined by others interested in this matter, and a strong effort will be made to procure the legislation. The complaint made is that the fencing in of enormous tracts of country in the West for grazing purposes has blocked the trail over which cattle are driven to eastern markets. In Indian Territory particularly, it is alleged, lately erected fences, inclosing the grazing lands leased from the Indians, extend across the cattle trails in different places. This will entail heavy loss upon the southwestern cattle raisers, unless Congress grants the relief asked, and compels the trails to be kept open.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.

Reports from up and down the Little Missouri river shows that the cattle are suffering somewhat from the protracted cold snap, but, the cattle owners do not anticipate anything serious, as there is plenty of grass and the cold snap will not continue much longer.

A thoroughbred Kentucky heifer named Lillie Dale ate a leaf of tobacco and then lay down and gasped away $700 worth of blooded stock into the invisible beyond. By-and-by fine bred cattle will learn to leave the food of god-like man alone. Next thing you know, the race horse will get to drinking whiskey with the jockeys and a nice set of brutes we will have.—[The Review.

At a meeting of the Utah and Idaho Stock Growers' association, held at Ogden, on the 2d inst., among others the following resolutions were adopted, concerning the foolish habit of constantly carrying pistols where no necessity could possibly be shown for their use: Whereas, the custom of carrying fire-arms by those engaged in the round-up and in working in the cattle ranges is productive of great evil and frequently results in the damage of persons and property; be it therefore resolved, that the custom of carrying firearms, except in the immediate vicinity of Indian reservations, should be discountenanced, and it is hereby made the duty of members of this association, foremen of round-ups, and foremen of ranges, to use every effort in their power to prevent the carrying of firearms by cattlemen at times and places, except when absolutely necessary, and that the members of this association pledge themselves so far as in their power to carry out the spirit of this resolution.—[New Mexico Stock Grower.

One scarcely ever turns to an American paper, says a foreign cotemporary, but he comes on a discussion on the natural gait of the horse, the writers contending according to their opinions for pacing, trotting and galloping. Into this hop, step and jump of horse movements we do not care to enter, but we know that we have bred gallopers in the line of galloping for years, being determined that their ancestors could gallop, or, which is all the same, had a predisposition for galloping. The Americans have arrived at equally successful results. All of the paces are, however, natural, and there can be as much improvement made in either as in the formation of the animal when looked at from a stand-still showyard point of view. The old horse that could walk a mile and gallop a mile, is no more wanted now than the old groom who would advertise for a situation guaranteeing his ability to weed a garden, milk a cow, wait at table or drive a gig. We may have developed natural gaits, but we cannot say that any particular breed of horses, or horse as a whole, had one natural gait.

A Washington dispatch says: The investigation of Indian land leases will be given over to a committee of senators with authority to visit all the reservations where the cattlemen have gained a foothold. This will make a summer's work, which will not be unpleasant and it may be beneficial to the health of the senators and the exchequers of the Indians. The senate committee on Indian affairs have held one meeting on the subject, and there was a disposition on the part of some members to defer the investigation until next summer, on the ground that the present session is so short and there is so much to attend to the senators could not give time to the inquiry without neglecting other duties. Others of the committee insisted on prosecuting the inquiry without delay. Senator Vest appeared before the committee and submitted the basis of his charges and a list of witnesses by whom the fraud in procuring the leases, he said, could be proved. A resolution calling upon the secretary of the interior for a detailed statement of the leases, the acreage so occupied, prices paid, etc., was adopted. Secretary Teller will not reply to this for a fortnight or more.—[River Press.

The live stock quarters at the New Orleans exposition are unusually ample, and are situated in the northwestern portion of the park, towards St. Charles avenue. There are six distinct buildings for horses and two for cattle, with stall room for 1,000 horses and 500 cattle. The buildings for horses will be the two parallel rows indicated on the plan of the grounds. Each will be 368 feet long by 60 feet wide and 24 feet high, and have stalls on either side, permitting the heads of the animals to face outward, thereby leaving a broad passage way through the middle of the building. The buildings for the cattle stand at either end of the buildings mentioned and at right angles with them. They are 378 feet long by 72 feet wide and 21 feet high. In addition to the structures for live stock, a regulation half-mile track is laid out adjoining the line of buildings. The track and space enclosed will also be used as an area for the display of live stock. These areas combined contain 2,080x780 feet, the stock exhibition covering 37 acres of ground. Over $125,000 has been appropriated by the management for premiums and the necessary expenses of making the live stock display. This is by far a larger sum than has ever before been devoted to a similar enterprise. The object of the management in making this princely grant of money is to secure the presence of the best examples of all classes of live stock to be found on this continent.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

Mrs. Malloy's sister, from Mankato, Minnesota, returned home Saturday after a short visit here.

Mr. Ellison, a civil engineer of Mandan, was here last week assisting Mr. Ayres in finding new levels for the side tracks.
The pleasures of Christmas were not by any means forgotten in Medora, and our turkey engagement on that day at Rassie Deffebach's will be a long time sinking into forgetfulness.

The dance at Roberts & Co.'s. hall Christmas eve was all that heart could wish. These dances are fast increasing in popularity, and well they may, as the management is strict in not allowing anything objectionable to mar their pleasure.

Some despicable villain put a bundle of lighted hay between the buildings occupied by Gill Kennedy and E. Elmer, Christmas morning. It may have been done as a joke, but it would have been a choke if the perpetrator had been discovered.

The Gladstone Express is the newest aspirant for journalistic honors and comes to us neatly printed and well edited. It is a rather forbidding time of the year to begin such an enterprise, but there is understood to be good backing behind the Express, and we hope it will succeed.

"Ole" Anderson has left us. As a lightning jerker and jolly good fellow he has not a superior on the line. His change, taking Mr. Kelly's place as operator, at Dickinson, is a promotion, but it was as distasteful to him as to the many friends he left behind. Come again, Ole.

The invincible didn't exactly meet the immovable, but the N. P. and Wells, Fargo express companies did in the persons of their respective route agents on this division, Messrs. DeForce and Heath Scripturally, "Great was the meet thereof." The last seen of them they were arm in arm, steering for the depot and conversing in confidential whispers that could have been heard at Sentinel Butte. The air in the Bad Lands is exceedingly bracing.

We do not think there is a person in Medora but that regretted to see C. W. Sleeper depart Sunday morning. He has made a host of friends while in the employment of the N. P. R. C. Co. Mr. Sleeper's plans are as yet undecided, but it is his intention, if possible, to get hold of a bunch of cattle and start a ranch in the Bad Lands. William Van Driesche takes Mr. Sleeper's place as vice president, a choice that if the change had to be made, is more popular than that of any other man.

Mrs. L. A. Anderson, now of Glendive, writes the COW BOY regarding her domestic troubles. She claims Mr. Anderson abused her in a shameful manner, and that he is indebted to her and her son for work. She also states that he has women on the brain, and that two or more wives are not sufficient for him. According to her statement Mr. Anderson is on the verge of insanity. We hope this difficulty will be amicably settled before long, and that the parties interested will carry on their warfare in a less public manner. Newspaper airing of domestic troubles does not help either party, and causes any amount of gossip.

George Roderick returned yesterday from Jamestown, whence he had driven overland. He made the trip in fifteen days, being delayed by blizzards and cold weather. The report reached here ahead of him that his feet were badly frozen crossing the Missouri, but it was false, only his nose and chin being tapped by Jack Frost. The man George was working for failed, and his time is a dead loss. He is too much of a rustler, however, to be discouraged, and is already on the alert for work. He left McNeave Nally in Jamestown, and brought back Jack Cameron in charge of his outfit.

About every so often, papers in the outside towns contain articles to the effect that Bob Roberts is shot. Papers are now stating this as a fact concerning our Bob Roberts, when he is as alive and hearty as ever. The Bob Roberts shot is a cow boy living near Miles City. A man named Sullivan shot him at a dance and then skipped. He was followed by the sheriff and a posse and trailed to a house a short distance from Miles. The sheriff ordered the family to come out, and as they were complying Sullivan shot the man and an infant child, and again got away from his pursuers. He was again followed and toward morning was found in a clump of bushes, without ammunition and nearly frozen.

Dr. Jorgens and family, and John Arrington and wife, of Cave Hills, were expected on the last coach, but failed to arrive. They will doubtless be here in a few days, Dr. Jorgens to reside permanently and Mr. Arrington at least for the winter.

The heaviest timbers have been used, and the floor room is almost large enough for a base ball ground. The N. P. R. C. Co. is making preparations for a large business next season.

Senators Vest and Cockrell are blatant hypocrites. They are both opposing the admission of Dakota bitterly, and can advance no other reason for their opposition than that it will give two or four more republican senators if Dakota is admitted in whole or part to the union. They are now ranting against the lease of the Indian reservations to cattle men when it has been proven that their opposition comes solely from the fact that they wanted the land for some friends and could not get it. We would suggest to these two honorable gentlemen that Dakota is a splendid summer resort, and that if they should conclude to visit us they will be accorded a warm reception. We will also guarantee that they will make their stay permanent, as they will be "stuck" on the country so that they will never leave.

The Pierre coach on which Mr. J. C. Ryan was a passenger, upset on Cheyenne hill Wednesday. Mr. Ryan sustained a severe injury in the shoulder, and was otherwise badly bruised up. Arriving home Christmas evening it was found that the cap of the left shoulder was fractured. While the injury is painful, Dr. Louthan pronounces it not necessarily very serious.—[Dakota Register.

The above points a moral and adorns the following tale: Mr. Ryan went east via Medora, and while here made rates for the shipment of a large lot of groceries. He, in company with every other business man of Spearfish, had agreed to ship every pound of their freight and express via Medora, conditioned upon the stages running through Spearfish. He was given the very lowest rates—and shipped via Belfield. In going east, Mr. Ryan claimed to have been too frequently smashed up on the other lines to try them again and, as he had signed the contract to ship via Medora, and had repeatedly promised to help the line in every way he could, it was considered a matter of course that he would both ship and travel our way. He could not, by any possibility, have received a rate five cents lower than the one offered here without loss to the forwarder. Notwithstanding the fact that the Medora line has at any and all times said that any opposition rate would be met, he learned the lowest straight rate and then accepted a lower rate without giving the company here a chance even to meet it. He either had other business or a pass via the Pierre route on his return and took that way. The Medora line does not go begging for business, but like other business institutions, believes in living up to its contracts. It then sees no reason why Mr. Ryan or any other man should not live up to the terms of the one he signed.

BISMARCK, Dak., Dec. 31, 1884.

EDITOR COW BOY—Dear Sir:—Will you kindly allow a few facts in your valuable paper, regarding the vast amount of good and general benefit that the Marquis de Mores (N. P. R. C. Co.) has done for the general public, the working people especially. Heretofore prices of meat were very high in this section of the country, and are still at the retail markets, simply because a few retail dealers in each town combined to make them so. In the opinion of many thinking men, beef should be as cheap here as in Chicago, if not cheaper, whereas cattle are raised in thousands and shipped in hundreds of cars to eastern markets, paying high freightage, etc., and slaughtered and sold there cheaper than people here at home could buy. Now that the N. P. R. C. Co. has established storage and sale rooms in many prominent towns and accommodate the people with low prices, the enmity of the retail dealers is roused against them, and they will not buy of them except where necessity compels it.

The consumers in many districts should in my opinion, request of the company to establish retail markets and give the company all their patronage, and show these few combined dealers that they must keep pace with the progression of civilization and come to the standard of the times. The people here should cherish warm feelings toward the said company from the fact that they have spent, and are spending, thousands upon thousands of dollars here helping to build up the country, and filling one of the greatest necessities of the country.

Let thinking people stop and consider the number of men that this company gives employment to, not only in the summer season, but in the dull winter, filling their ice houses and getting prepared for the spring trade. The company will, at some near future day, reap the benefits of its good work by a liberal patronage of the people.
