The famous Staked Plains of Texas, as everybody who has looked at the maps of the country knows, are in the northern part of the State and lap over into New Mexico. Since they were first staked, nearly fifty years ago, they have been considered as mostly worthless; with plenty of grass but nary drop to drink. But of late wells affording splendid water are being dug, and the welcome fluid springs up at any time after twenty feet has been reached. This water not only supplies stock, but enough is expected to be obtained to use successfully for irrigating purposes.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The reports from the cattle region all along the Northern Pacific and through Montana, are to the effect that the weather out there in all respects is just as good as could be asked for by the cattle men, and the cattle are all in excellent condition. In Colorado, all through those ranges of mountains there is great cause for complaint. That country has been heavily visited with snow and the cattle are suffering very seriously in consequence. A letter received in St. Paul yesterday from a gentleman who has been out all through Colorado says that it has been very cold in western Kansas and eastern Colorado, and that stock has suffered very seriously indeed in consequence. It seems that the territory of Montana is proving to be the best country in the world to raise cattle in. It does not seem to be so seriously afflicted with snow as are the territories that are further south. The Montana and Bad Lands cattle stand very high in the eastern markets, and seem to be quite able to maintain the position they now occupy.—[Exchange.

Mrs. C. L. Russell, of South Bend, Ind., would like to learn the whereabouts of Isaac Stewart Russell, a boy of eighteen, who is supposed to be herding cattle somewhere in the west. Western papers will confer a favor on the lady by giving the above notice wide publicity.—[Stock Growers' Journal.

Assistant Secretary of the Interior Joslyn is "away up" on Indians, and the estimation in which their abilities are held by cattle men. He advances as a reason for leasing the reservations that the "Indians being employed as herders learn how to care for and raise cattle." We have had some cold weather lately, but it was tropical in comparison to the day in which stockmen will employ Indians as herders.

There are many brood mares in the country whose owners are so careless in regard to the kind of horses they raise that the true value of them is not known. Were such animals in proper hands they would soon make their mark as breeders. The man who is judge enough to select such mares as would produce a good colt each year could find but few better ways to invest his money, should he handle them properly and breed them with judgment.—[Stock Growers' Journal.

Farmer Hartzell, of the South Park, who raises from two to three hundred high-grade calves each year, takes the youngsters from the cows as early as December, and after keeping them in a close corral until they are gentle and become accustomed to the presence of men, turns them into a field and feeds them hay until spring. "This," says he, "puts my yearlings six months ahead of my neighbors, and at two years of age they are equal to ordinary three-year-olds."—[Col. L. S. Record.

Mr. T. W. Longley, manager of the Green Mountain Stock Ranching company, whose range is on Emmels creek, made the Stock Growers' a call New Year's morning. He says all the old range cattle are doing better than was expected, none of them dying, and not drifting to any extent, as feed is good and abundant. The through cattle that were poor in the fall are not doing so well. North of the Yellowstone cattle are drifting badly, and line riders are kept busy driving them back from the river. A few are crossing at the mouth of Rosebud. His company are wintering some stallions up Pumpkin creek, and Mr. Longley is on his way to this ranch. He says they have some native range stallions running with their cattle which are as fat as they can roll and don't seem to mind the cold weather.—[Stock Growers' Journal.

At a recent dinner of a farmers' club in England, some speeches were made which are of interest to the American cattle men. Mr. Marston Frewen, of Wyoming, said that there were immense herds of cattle in that territory perfectly healthy and free from epidemic, and that pleuro pneumonia was absolutely unknown there. The far west could supply England with dairy cows at $60 a head, and grazing beasts at low prices, with which it would be profitable to stock their present unoccupied lands. That the present low prices were due to low freight charges, and the English farmers would be very foolish to neglect the present opportunity to replenish their declining agriculture. If the farmers of Great Britain adopt this advice it will open another market for ranchmen of this continent.—[St. Paul Globe.

C. W. Sleeper was interviewed by a Pioneer Press reporter recently and we can't help but belive that either the reporter on the types misquoted him. He is credited with saying that 50 por cent. of the pilgrim cattle will succumb to the recent cold snap. It may have been that he said 5 per cent. or even 10 per cent. but either estimate is too high. We have recently spoken with nearly every stockmen on the Little Missouri, especially these who shipped in pilgrims last fall and the highest estimate is 3 per cent. Down the river there seems no doubt that the loss will be scarcely 2 per cent. Up the river there are several bunches of states yearlings that were driven in late and the loss may be as high as 3 per cent., certainly not higher. The interview alluded to has caused much comment and we have received many telegrams and letters relative to it. To all we have answered substantially as above. The old cattle, or these who have passed a winter here, are doing as well as the most sanguine could wish. The loss among this class is almost nothing. From the most authentic sources we think we are about the figure in quoting the per cent. of loss on all the Bad Lands cattle at one and a half per cent.

The Northwestern Live Stock Journal lets its vials of wrath descend upon our devoted head in a way calculated to make it ache. It states that we quoted an article from the Journal without credit, attempted to give it some advice and then make a mistake in our figures. The above is all right with the exception that we never republished an article without credit and consider that an editor who will do so is as low as any other thief; that we have never under any circumstances ever made a comment on such an article republished from the Journal, as we considered it good authority on all stock matters; and finally could have made no mistake in figures if we made no comment on them. The Journal is a little too soon. It can be sure that when we attempt to disprove any of its assertions we will be well fortified with figures. We would also like to have the Journal editor look over our files and we will allow its "bad man" to take a shot at us for every clipping that we have published without credit. We have too many times expressed our opinion of editors whose paucity of brains compels them to write original editorials with their shears to be caught napping.

There has been considerable discussion relative to the abolishing of the herd law in West Missouri papers, and there is much less opposition to it than was expected. This year's experience has clearly shown the farmers that success lies in diversified farming and not in the exclusive culture of oats and wheat. Hence more stock must be raised, and then will come the necessity of a fence law.

Harry Gregg, of Spearfish, formerly superintendent of the Homestake mine, and now member of the legislature for Lawrence county, came in on the coach yesterday, and this morning left for Bismarck. He was "held up" by the COW BOY, and we are happy to state that he will be one of the strongest workers for the repeal of the herd law here, or at least the adoption of a fence law. Mr. Gregg is both a ranchman and a stockman in the Hills, and says that in Lawrence county, where the fence law prevails, there is no difficulty whatever between the ranchers and cattlemen. During the past twelve or fifteen years there has been a great change in the demand for horses west of the Mississippi river. Formerly breeding was carried on with a view to speed and endurance. Now a large proportion of the breeders throughout the West, recognizing the demand, breed so as to increase size and strength. There has for several years been a steady increasing demand for heavy horses and a corresponding falling off in the call for small ones. The The heavy draft horse stands in about the same relation to work animals that the short horn does to the native Texas steer. Present appearances indicate that it will be many years before the supply of heavy horses will equal the demand. Small work horses are low and a drug upon the market, unless they have some special points of excellence to commend them, more especially perhaps as saddles animals. Our vast ranges covered with untritious grasses afford a good opportunity for investment in this most profitable industry, and we wonder that it is not utilized to a greater extent.—[Stock and Mining Journal.

A correspondent, writing to The Texas Stockmen from Gillespie county, communicates the information that a young gentleman residing in Western Texas, to recruit his health, being a fine chemist, turned his attention to devising a chemical substitute for branding. The goat is the animal for the ranch and the boundless west, says the Midland Farmer. There will yet spring up a large and profitable business in the
carcasses of the young and the concentrated milk and cheese sent east to the large cities. This will one day find profitable employment to thousands and healthful food to the chronic invalids of city life. The Angora goat possesses all the merits of the common goat, and furnishes a valuable fleece, the use of which is only limited by its scarcness as its beauty is unquestioned. About 5:30 this morning the peaceful slumbererers of Little Missouri and Medora were awakened by the prolonged whistle of an engine, the cause of which was the discovery of a fire between Bob Roberts and E. G. Paddock's buildings. The whole population turned out, and by strenuous efforts saved most of the stock in the buildings. Mr. Paddock's building was occupied by Gill Kennedy. There was little wind blowing, which was fortunate, as a disastrous conflagration would probably have happened. With considerable difficulty Mr. Roderick's house was saved. Bob Roberts had about two hundred bushels of potatoes stored in his cellar, which were baked in a first-class manner. He estimates his loss at about $1,700. Mr. Paddock's loss is about the same. Both buildings were insured in the Springfield Fre and Marine Insurance Co., of Springfield, Mass. The origin of the fire is a mystery, but it is supposed to be the work of an incendiary. An attempt was made two or three weeks ago to burn these two buildings, but was discovered before any serious damage occurred. The buildings will probably be replaced as soon as the weather will permit. Gill Kennedy's loss will be trifling, as most of his stock was saved. Gill is in Adrian, Mich., but will probably return as soon as he learns of his misfortune.

Reports from the Black Hil's are to the effect that cattle there are not doing well. Several herds have already lost ten per cent., and the rest of the cattle are not in as good condition as they should be at this time of the year. The above loss is the largest we have yet learned. As will be seen in another article the E 6 outfit are paying bounties on all wolves killed, besides other inducements to hunters. This move cannot be commended too highly, and should be followed by every outfit in the country. By making it worth while, men can easily be found who will exterminate the wolves in a short time. Viewing the matter in its broadest sense, the action of the E 6 is an economical one. Their per cent. of loss from wolves is probably greater than the bounty they will pay, and in the future it will certainly pay largely by a decrease of this loss. The E 6 is benefitting the whole cattle community by this move, and should receive their hearty co-operation.

The subject of enlarging Billings county should receive the attention of every citizen of our county and then of the legislature. At the very least, Dunn county on the north and Villard on the south should be added to Billings. Our limits formerly took in more than these two counties, and they should never have been detached. From the very nature of the occupation, a cattle country cannot be thickly settled, and there will never be too many inhabitants within the enlarged limits. It cannot be long before our county is organized, and when it is, the present counties of Dunn and Villard will probably be attached to us for all purposes. This will make them an expense instead of a source of revenue, and as it is doubtful if either of these counties will be organized inside of fifty years, Billings will be a long time getting her money back.

The future actions of the legislature are rather hard to bank on, but of one think there is a certainty. The writer of this article has personally interviewed a large number of the legislators, and to a man, so far as interviewed, they were in favor of a repeal of the herd law and the establishment of a fence law. Especially are the Hills members in favor of this and, as being the only place in Dakota where the herd law is abolished and a fence law established, it will be well to examine its operation. The whole country surrounding the Hills and up into the foot-hills is a first class agricultural country. It is also a good stock country, and the conflict between agricultural and stock interests now liable to happen at any time here, was there solved long ago. The herd law was made inoperative, and the fence law established. Under this law each farmer must enclose his ranch with a fence consisting of four boards, or wires, securely nailed to posts not over eight feet apart. The law works perfectly, and from many conversations in the Hills we believe that there is not a man there who would vote for the repeal of the fence law. Of course, it brings more expense on the farmer at the outset, but all agree that the fences far more than pay for themselves. They are an almost certain protection against the depredations of stock, they immediately enhance the value of the property enclosed more than the first cost of the fence, in many ways they encourage the farmer in traits of economy and neatness, and, especially to the one accustomed to the unbounded wheat fields of the rest of Dakota, they lend an indescribable charm to the country that can only be explained by the presence of fences.

If this law is applicable to the Hills country, how much more should it apply to the Bad Lands? This is pre-eminently a stock country, and not an agricultural country. The Hills country is far better for farming than it is for stock.

Then, under the present herd law, it is a perfectly simple thing for any evil disposed person to start an 8x10 garden patch, get cattle to run over it and cinch the owner of the stock many times the amount of the damage. This is a serious drawback to the growth of the stock industry, and something that concerns every citizen of Dakota, who is looking toward Dakota's advancement. The stock interests in her borders are already large, but under proper laws they will be vastly larger.

As far as we are concerned, we think it would be altogether better in the end to establish a fence law for the whole west Missouri country. This, however, would entail hardship on many poor settlers, although among those who can afafford it, and view the matter from an unbiased standpoint, admit that a fence law is better than a herd law.

There is certainly serious opposition in many agricultural quarters against the fence law, but this opposition in no way affects us, as the Bad Lands is a unit in desiring it. We in the Bad Lands could as well be exempt as the people of the Hills.

It is a matter that concerns us alone, will benefit the Bad Lands largely, can harm no one, and best of all, we think will be in operation here before this legislature adjourns.

The move to establish a fence law for the whole west Missouri countre is the cause of the only opposition to its adoption here. It should be adopted here without reference to the agricultural part of the country, and the problem will solve itself in time.

Come all ye sons of freedom,
In the old "Green Mountain" state,
While I sling my pen a little,
It will not keep you late.

I'll speak of joys and griefs I've had
While ranging on the plain;
Of my many dark and sunny days,
And my many hours of pain.

'Twas in the spring of '84
I left my quiet home,
And turned my back to father's door,
With the cow boys I would roam.

I got a bucking broncho,
And a leather banded hat;
A great big Colt's six-shooter,
You bet I togged out "pat."

I rode the darndest little cuss
I've seen for many a day;
He could beat all else at bucking,
And eat his weight in hay.

I've been amongst coyotes,
The deer and grizzly bear,
And many a time a quiet meal
With Indians I did share.

But now I'm fully satisfied
With rough and tumble life;
I'm going back down east again
To catch a little wife.

And when my children flock around

The following is an estimate of the number of cattle in Idaho, as given by Secretary Allen at the recent Stock Grower's convention. Shoshone, Owyhee, Alturas, Cassia, and Oneida counties, each 50,000 head; Bear Lake county, 20,000; Ada county, 2,000; Washington, 15,000; Boise county, 10,000; Custer county, 25,000, Lemhi county, 16,000. Other counties, 50,000. Total, 360,000.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

A lightning cattle express is a new feature on the L. S. & M. S. R. R. It is designed to run between New York and Chicago, and is expected to make the run in twenty-four hours, thus escaping the provision of the law which requires that stock shall not be kept on the cars longer than twenty-four hours without unloading. The new cars are fitted out with air-brakes, patent trucks, etc.—[Canadian Breeder.

The E6 outfit is offering to furnish provisions and poisons to all persons who will go out and poison wolves. In addition to this they will pay one dollar for each coyote and five dollors for each big wolf killed, and the hunters keep the pelts. They have been suffering from their depredations, and propose a war of extirmination. If others companies wold join them there would soon be no more trouble with wolves.—Deadwood Pioneer.

An old-time cattleman from the vicinity of Fort Maginnis says that wild animals of all kinds are very plentiful on their ranges, bears and mountain lions being the worst, and something must be done to rid the country of these pests, as cattlemen lose thousands of dollars yearly by them.—[Stock Grower's Journal.

The Colorado Farmer sensibly remarks that once in a while a partisan of one of the various breeds of cattle has something to say about the poor "rustling" qualities of the others, and the latest victim of such spleen seem to be the Polled Angus. The actual truth of the matter is as every stockmen well knows, that animals that are not raised on the range, and are stall fed, rarely, if ever, make good rustlers. Good range animals must be raised on the range and accustomed from birth to endure that kind of life, and no one who has knowledge in the premises can truthfully claim otherwise.—[Stock Grower's Journal.

The bill which is to be introduced in congress for the establishing of a cattle trail from Texas to the British possessions provides that: The secretary of the interior shall appoint three commissioners to lay out and mark by meter and bounds a quarantined national trail and grazing grounds, the trail not to exceed six miles in width and to be narrowed at places to a mere roadway, the grazing grounds to be established at intervals along the trail, and not to exceed twelve miles square; both trail and grazing grounds to be strictly quarantined, and no cattle allowed to leave it so long as they have any signs of Texas fever among them. When the commissioners make their report, the secretary of the interior is to file a map of the trail as laid out, and then to give public notice of its establishment and the withdrawal of public land occupied by it from either sale, location or settlement for a term of ten years. Ten thousand dollars is appropriated for the work. When this publication is made, the trail will be open at all times of the years for the driving upon it of any live stock by any person, firm or corporation.—[Chicago Times.

On Monday last Senator Van Wyck submitted a report from the senate committee on public lands, to accompany the bill also reported by him relating to the fencing of public lands. In the report the committee say that without the least authority, and in open and bold defiance of the [rights?] of the government, large and often foreign corporations deliberately enclose hundreds of thousands of acres of land, thus closing the avenues of travel and preventing its occupancy by those seeking homes. They all allege that the lands within their enclosures still remain open for settlement. Yet no humble settler, with scant means, would persume to enter any such enclosure to seek homes. The government has sufficient authortiy to drive those seeking homes from the Indian Territory and to burn the ranches of those inavding the Yellowstone Park, while those appropriating these vast areas hope the only remedy to be used against them will be the laws, with the usual delay in the courts. Therefore the committee has added a new section to the house bill, authorizing the President to summarily remove all obstructions, and if necessary use the military power.—[Livingstone Enterprise.

A Congressional committee sitting in Washington, has been investigating the leasing of Indian lands to stockmen, principally with a view to eliciting information as to the character of the negotiations, and whether any fraud has been practiced in connection with the leases. So far, no fraud seems to have been unearthed. It has been found that a number of these leases exist, covering, in most cases, millions of acres, and lasting ten years—the rate of lease-rental is in most cases nominal. The bill introduced, making all leases null unless approved by the Secretary of the Interior, should certainly be passed, the Indian wards affording altogether too easy a prey for parties who may see in this method of business an opportunity for securing large and valuable sections of land at a nominal annual renal for a long term, and then sub-renting to stockmen who want to use the land themselves for grazing purposes, at an advanced price, which however trifling, when calculated per acre, would mount up to a very large sum when estimated upon millions of acres. One such case is already reported, namely, that of the Cherokee Strip Live Stock Association, which holds some six million acres leased from the Cherokees at two cents an acre, and subrented to two Kansas parties for two and a half cents. The reply of Commissioner Price to a deputation of the Kiowa and Comanche Indians, who called upon him on Friday last to protest against the lease of their lands to cattlemen, showed that the department was prepared to act as though the bill referred to was already in operation with a retroactive effect. He informed them that if they would return home, call a council, and make it evident to the department that a majority were unfavorable to the continuation of leases the department would cause the lessees to surrender the land. The only proper course to pursue in regard to these Indian lands, in view of the relations now held by the Government towards the Indians, is to treat their property strictly as though held by minors, for whom the government acted as trustee. The leases should be made by the government, with the consent of the Indians, and the price set and the rent collected by the government, and applied to a diminution of the already too burdensome Indian Budget.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.

About six thousand tons of ice will be put up by the company here before work is finished. There are now five thousand tons in the houses.
The recent loss by fire seems to have called every one's attention to the subject of insurance. We have issued a number of policies lately.
Johnny Munro has taken a contract to supply the stage line with one hundred cords of wood. The most of it will be cut in the Cave Hills country.
Charlie Bronson, now tending stock at Indian Creek station on the stage line, sent in a box of petrified eels to the COW BOY office. Some of the specimens are very fine.
The following is a list of the arrivals and departures since our last publication. From the Hills: J. Davis, F. Gayler, Dan Futers, J. A. Hustin. To the Hills: Clark Tingley.
John McGee took advantage of the severe weather of last week to make a business trip to Jamestown. He is thinking of taking up his residence here and engaging in building.
There are from three to seven thicknesses of boards and paper in the floor, sides and ceiling of tue new cold storage rooms. This will preserve an equal temperature at all times.
George Wilkes left for Chicago last Friday on his annual visit home. Before returning, the Marquis and he will select the boilers and machinery to be used in the new slaughter house.
A. E. Pinkney, special agent for the Springfield F. & M. Insurance company, came in Tuesday night and left yesterday. He came up to adjust the loss on the two buildings burned last Thursday morning.

Although the cry of hard times is heard all over the country, there is little of its effect observable in Medora. There has been plenty of work here all winter so far, and the only difficulty has been to find laborers.

William Van Gundy came up with his outfit from the Hills last Friday, and has loaded and pulled out with oats for the stage line. He will return and take a load of freight to the Hills. He is well fixed to stand the weather of the last few weeks, having a stove set up in one of his wagons, which his better half keeps constantly roaring. A new 3½ inch Studebaker wagon bought from us is a good addition to his outfit.

Lloyd Roberts and Charlie Eaton returned from Jimtown Tuesday evening. They took two car loads of SOHO cattle with them. Upon their arrival the butchers formed a combination to lower the price. They had too good rustlers to deal with, however, for Lloyd and Charlie immediately began butchering, and before the local butchers saw the point had every one supplied. This brought them to time, and the remaining cattle were sold at good prices.

A large number of COW BOY subscriptions run out next month, and it behooves every one to renew as soon as possible. We realize that this is not the best time in the year to collect bills, but there is no one that cannot rustle two dollars. Due notice will be sent to each person whose subscription has or is about to expire, and as this is a cash business every one should pay prompt attention to it. Many of our subscribers have made successful efforts to increase our list, and we hope that such action will be continued in the future. There is not a subscriber but that can induce some one else to subscribe, and each should bear this in mind.
No. 2's mail car caught fire east of Dickinson, yesterday, and the interior was badly burned. Some of the paper mail was burned, but none of the letters.

The motion of Legislator Pickler for the relocating of the capitol from Bismarck to Pierre will be called up this afternoon, and we predict will not become a law. The southern delegation is not a unit in the desire for removal, and it is very improbable that a two-thirds vote can be obtained to pass it over the governor's veto, even though it pass both houses. The governor will veto the measure if it passes, not from any desire to favor the north more than the south, but because he has recognized the action of the capital commission, and should he sign the bill, it would show a vacillating spirit in our executive that we know he does not possess.
W. D. Simpson returned to St. Paul this morning.
Travel is not very brisk over the stage line but we are getting more than one third.
John O'Sullivan has been in Miles City for several days. His return is anxiously awaited by our beard growing populace.
The tanking is now all finished at the slaughter house and it is hoped that the season's slaughtering in the new house will begin about the middle of May.

The lathing is nearly completed in Geo. Fitzgerald's new hotel and plastering will soon begin. When finished, the hotel will be an ornament to Medora. On the first floor are the bar room, office, dining-room, besides small rooms for wash-room and baggage. All these are well-lighted and pleasant. Above are sixteen sleeping rooms and a parlor. As soon as the weather permits the building will be veneered and a long porch for the front added.

The wind of yesterday and last night, although it was of little consequence in the Bad Lands, was very severe on the prairies east and west. No. 1 passenger train that came through here last night an hour late, stuck in a cut just west of Sentinel Butte. Snow plows had to be sent down from Glendive, and the train reached there about seven this morning. No. 15 freight train was also blockaded near Richardson for several hours. There was no sign of a blizzard in the Bad Lands, but on the divide it was one of the worst of the season.
Be sure and take your watch to the King jeweler, Spearfish or Deadwood for repairs.
You can buy all kinds of chewing tobacco, plug and fine cut, at reduced rates, and a full assortment of wooden pipes at cost, to make room for new stock, at Cook's confectionery store.

A reporter of the New York Mail cornered Hon. Theodore Roosevelt in New York the past week, and among other things, elicited the following in regard to his Dakota experiences;

"I am president of the Western Dakota Cattleman's association, and it is imperatively necessary that I be in western Dakota during the months of April and May next. I am besides very fond indeed of the life of a ranchman. I like riding and shooting and the open air—vigorous, active camp life! I like the western men too, and get along capitally with them—a great deal better than I do with some of the New York politicians," he laughingly added: "Cow boys are a very much maligned order of human beings. I have always found them a very hospitable, generous sort of men with a certain rude chivalry about them. It seems to me, by the way, curious that eastern people should seem to pay so little attention to the really great outrage that is being perpetrated upon Dakota by refusing to allow it to be divided and admitted as two states. At the last election Dakota polled 80,000 votes, a vote larger than that of either New Hampshire, Vermont, Rhode Island, Delaware, Florida, Nevada or Oregon. Her people possess two or three times the number of savings banks, newspapers and schools that are possessed by any one of half a dozen such states as Arkansas, Mississippi, or Alabama. The growth of the territory is proceeding with a rapidity that is fairly startling, and in spite of an occasional disturbance such as invariably attends frontier life, the population can on the whole be said to be composed of most moral, orderly and intelligent people. Such being the case, there is absolutely no excuse for the refusal to admit those people to an equality with their fellow citizens in those portions of the United States that are now organized into states."

"Senator Vest, of Missouri, for one, has a different opinion," suggested the reporter.

"Yes! It would have been irritating if it had not been ludicrous to read his tirade against Dakota. The charge of being a disorderly state, coming as it did from a senator hailing from a state which could only get rid of the James brothers by hiring another set of ruffians to assassinate them is certainly rich, extremely rich."

"You recently had an unpleasant interview with a bear."

"Ha, ha! You've heard that story too, have you? Well let me give you the correct version. Be very careful and take what I say verbatim please. Are you ready? The report published stated that the bear got within nine feet of me before I saw it and that I killed it at such close quarters. Now while I must admit that I am rather near-sighted, still I think my eyes are sufficiently good to enable me to see a bear a good distance further off than nine feet. The one referred to was much further away."

"You have had pretty good luck at hunting during your absence, have you not?"

"I did have pretty good [luck?] this summer, killing about every kind of large game to be found on the plains, including three grizzlies. Yes, I own a great many cattle in western Dakota, and will have to be out there, as I said before, a great deal of my time during next year. Indeed, if I had no ties in the east I do not know but what I would be tempted to take up my residence there."

"And be a cow boy?"

"Yes, and in a measure be a cow boy. The life has a certain half adventurous side to it which is very fascinating, especially to a man fond of the horse and rifle, as I am."
Newspapers are rejoicing over the almost certain reduction of second class postage from two cents to one per pound.
To-day, the Cow Boy is one year old. It is a pretty healthy infant and we hope will grow rapidly with its increasing years.

The bills for the removal of the capitol in both the house and council have been "gently but firmly squashed." South as well as north, Dakotains realize that nothing is to be gained by opening the question. Bismarck is and well be the capitol.

We wish to say a word to every reader of the Cow Boy. A spirit of criticism never has and never can advance any business interest. When a man sees that another is wrong, how much better it would be to go to him and explain his mistake, than to go to another man and criticise him for his unintentional error. Many illustrations of this point have come under our notice, and we hope in the future that our citizens will advise rather than criticise, look on the bright side and not on the dark.

All over the country, there is a determined cutting of rates by railroads and and transportation lines. Rates from St. Paul to Portland will be greatly reduced and rates, especially to emigrants, will be brought so low by the Northern Pacific that northern Dakota can compete with southern Dokota in giving cheap homes to settlers. The "war is carried into Africa" by trans-Atlantic lines and through tickets can now be bought from Liverpool to Chicago for eleven dollars. The result will be that vast numbers of settlers will settle in the northwest this summer.

On and after the next issue of the Cow Boy the price of cattle brands will be reduced to $15 per year. This includes the whole cost, no extras whatever being charged. By reference to the rates of other cattle papers, it will be seen that the new rates are lower than any other. Our cuts are also larger and better than those of any other cattle paper published in the United States. We make this change in rates to meet outside competion alone, as we do not consider that our brand columns at present any more than pay for the space they occupy. Of course, every cattle man in the Bad Lands realizes that his brand in the Cow Boy is more valuable than in an outside paper, but we intend that the rates shall be no higher in the Cow Boy. The time of those who have paid in advance for next year will be extended in proportion to the reduction. By this move we expect to get every brand on the river and we can then, more than formerly, merit the patronage of the cattle men of the Bad Lands especially.

A check will be put upon shipping Texas cattle east and north by the railroads refusing to carry them until the responsibility for the spread of Texas fever has been placed. For instance, if a bunch of Texans are shipped east, and the same cars used afterward for domestic cattle, and the latter catch the fever, who is responsible? The railroads, or the owners of the Texans? During frosty weather there is no danger of the fever, but in warm weather it would seem that the only safe way would lie in a strict quarantine. For Texans shipped into Dakota, it might be a good plan to set off a portion of the Sioux reservation as a quarantine ground. Something of the kind must certainly be done, as a single herd of cattle infected with the disease might scatter its seeds through every herd on the river. For this reason it might be better for our association to call an earlier meeting than the annual one in April, as before then the frost will have disappeared and serious damage may be done. It is a good point for our cattle men to ponder.

We think there is scarcely a paper in the United States that has not expressed its views on the admission and division of Dakota. All, so far as we have seen, favor admission, but there is justly a difference of opinion on division. And well there may be, for we do not believe there is a private citizen of Dakota that way down in his heart wants our territory divided. The cry was first raised and is now kept alive by a set of pot-house politicians, whose only hope of making a living is in feeling on public pap, and a press bribed and bullied into obeying their masters, the politicians. The reasons for division all group into one, that the people of north and south Dakota cannot live together in harmony. This is as baseless a slander and as unmitigated a lie as could be perpetrated upon Dakota's citizens. The politicians of north and south Dakota, of course, cannot live together in harmony, because their future bread and butter depends on their present wrangling. Undivided, we can in time become one of the greatest states in the Union. Divided, we will ever occupy a middle plane. As every one knows, Dakota's politics have been and are now run by a close corporations of rascals who should, nearly every one, be behind the bars repenting of their sins, or more likely breeding new schemes of iniquity to hatch out on their release. It is time for the press of Dakota to come forth from bondage and pro[claim?] the voice of the people and not that of the politicians.

The Colorado stock Grower's association has a record of thenty-two horse and cattle thieves convicted at an average cost of $70 each. Cheap riddance.

The Helena and Miles City stock organizations have merged into one, to be known as the "Montana Stock Growing Association." The spring meetings are to be held in Miles City and the fall meetings in Helena. The success of the Cheyenne association has conclusively proven that it is better to merge all smaller associations into a larger or at least have them subordiate to larger. More concerted and far more energetic action is possible under this system and we wish every success to the new association.

Although Medora has never been the scene, in spite of all reports to the contrary, of a six-shooter row among cow boys, we cannot help but join with other cattle papers in urging the necessity of discarding the six-shooters while in town, On the range, one sometimes is needed, but in town there is never any use for them. To carry a six-shooter should be "a custom more honored in the breach than the observance." A determined and united movement is being made among southern cattle men to stop the custom, and northern men are falling into line. The six-shooter is the one thing that gives cow boys a bad name, and we hope its days are numbered.

From the oldest settlers and from weather reports we gather the fact that this winter so far has been the coldest that was ever experienced in the west. Notwithstanding this fact, cattle have never done better and were never in better condition at this season of the year. These facts are not stated as guess work but are the substanse of a large number of conversations. We must conclude then, that cold, especially where there is as good protection as there is in the Bad Lands has but little effect on the cattle. The snow is also deeper than for many years and in many places has crusted, but from all reliable sources we glean the fact that not over three per cent. of cattle will have died in the Bad Lands by spring and not over five per cent. in Montana.

From several reliable sources, comes the information that polled or hornless cattle are surely pushing themselves into favor as range cattle. Mr. L. C. Le Moyne, of the Le Moyne cattle Co. although an ardent admirer and extensive breeder of short-horn cattle, while here last summer expressed his firm belief that Polled-Angus bulls would be the future favorites and that polled cattle would be the most profitable for the range. Now comes the evidence of T. C. Power & Bro., who, according to the Stock Growers' Journal, have made careful tests as between Durham and Polled-Angus bulls and the result is that the latter are invariably the best rustlers, that they stay on the range longer, that they stand the cold better and that they are getting fat on the range while the Durhams are shivering about the corralls and finally that the Polled-Angus is "boss of the range." There are many good reasons for the superiority of Polled-Angus, the most important probably bring that all nourishment that goes to the horn in others cattle, goes to bone and meat in polled cattle and that the numerous diseases and accidents happening to horns are absent.

The evidence now seems to be good that the foot and mouth disease has been thoroughly eradicated in England. If so, it is owing entirely to the action of the English government in appointing commissioners with full power to do any and all things toward destroying the disease. With such an example before us, it seems that before the periodical scares in reference to pleuro-pneumonia and Texas fever again arise, our government should appoint commissioners whose sole duty it shall be to attend to such diseases and prevent their spread. This is another good point for discussion by cattle organizations.

A beautiful cow girl lives near Murkel County, Neb. She owns some stock, which she personally looks after. At a late round-up, her dazzling beauty and graceful horsemanship were wonderful to behold. A yearling broke from the herd which three cowboys failed to confine, when the beautiful girl dashed out after it, roping it on the second circle and pulled it by the horn of her saddle into the herd. The boys shouted, wept and never ceased to love. John Sergeant, of Montrose County, it may be added to this, has a 15-year old daughter, Miss Nellie, who has been bred in the saddle, and is accustomed to ride with her father all over his range. In addition to the young lady's graceful horsemanship, she can handle a lariat and branding-iron, and can ride a bucking horse with as much skill and grace as any cow boy that has been on the range since boyhood. Nellie Sergeant is dowered by her father with one-third of the increase of his herd, and when she chooses to marry, her husband will be a cattle king.—[Omaha Bee.

What is the matter with the Pittsburg Stockman? In the issue of January 8, appears an editorial very disparaging to refrigerator beef and to those butchers who deal in it. It concludes: "Those butchers who give it a wide berth are evidently the wisest and most prosperous of their class." One of the editors and proprietors of our esteemed contemporary is a dealer in and a shipper of cattle on the hoof, but that fact should not bias the judgment of such a paper. Perhaps the view taken is from the standpoint of the near-by Pennsylvania feeders, and is in no sense a view as broad as the name of the paper, "National," would seem to suggest as being proper. The idea that western dressed beef is in any sense inferior in quality to that slaughtered on the spot is absurd. Some of the best cattle arriving at Chicago are killed and dressed here and sent east in refrigerator cars. Would the beef be better if the animals were shipped in uncomfortable stock cars 500 to 1,000 miles farther and slaughtered within a few blocks of where they are to be consumed?—[Drovers' Journal.

Abe Goodkind, of Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, scattered a few of his mellifluous smiles among the boys Monday.
D. O. Sweet and wife, of Buffalo Creek station, on the stage line, came up on last Friday's coach to visit the metropolis and lay in supplies.

Tom Jones has been in New York for some time and it is supposed that Joe. Pennell is now there. The mule outfit, with which the contract work on the Canadian Pacific was done, is at Port Arthur.
Judge Bennett, of Deadwood, went down on Monday's coach. Ex-Sheriff Belding, who came up with him, still lingers in Bismarck, where he has been unanimously elected president of the third house.

W. B. Milne, who is doing a good business in Medora for his house, Wyman, Mullin & Van Dyke, of Minneapolis, was here Monday. He is always welcome and is one of the most popular travelling men on the road.

George T. Reynolds, of Albany, Texas, intends putting in about eight thousand head of Texas steers a few miles down the river this summer. He is already making preparations, and will ship the cattle to Cheyenne or Valentine and drive the rest of the way.

J. P. Elverson resigned some time ago as night operator at the depot and W. H. Minty of Minneapolis now takes his place. A. D. Green has been transferred to New Rockford and G. G. Cooper takes his place. Mr. Elverson will remain with us for some time.

The storm of Sunday and Monday was the deepest of the season, about four inches on a level. Considerable fear was expressed that cattle would suffer, but on the ranges, plenty of grass is showing above the snow and four more inches would not do much harm,

The report that four of the Hash Knife cow boys have been frozen to death has been corroborated. They became bewildered in a storm, shot two of their ponies, went into camp and were frozen. There is also a report that three of the VVV boys were frozen, but it lacks confirmation.

Howard Eaton reports that while in St. Paul, the N. P., through an agent, definitely agreed to put in shipping yards here. This will be a great advantage to our Bad Lands cattle men as much difficulty has been experienced heretofore, owing to a lack of loading and unloading facilities.

Bob Roberts started for Wales yesterday morning. He will stop off at Bismarck, St. Paul and Chicago several days, and in New York about a week. He will then go to Wales to settle his father's estate, and return to Medora in April. During his absence, Sam Townsend will have charge of his mule train.

A postal from Levi Deffebach to Rassie, written just before the former's departure from New York to Germany, contains the welcome news that all necessary papers had been found, and that there was no difficulty feared in settling the estate very soon. Our readers will remember that a large fortune in Germany is awaiting the Deffebach heirs.

Gregor Lang was in town Saturday and reports cattle at the Neimmela ranch as doing spledidly. The 7 7 7 and OX outfits are near him and loss is almost nothing. Mr. Lang only knows of three of his cattle dying, two killed by wolves and one by accident. There are probably other dead cattle but they are few and Mr. Lang estimates the loss in his neighborhood at less than one per cent.

"'Twas ever thus." There was an attempt to organize an operatic troupe here, but it broke up on the first rehearsal. The affecting ditty, "Dem Golden Slippers" was being sung. The basso-profundo attempted to ring in the tune to the doxology, the tenor was singing—well it must have been the tune the old cow died of, and the chorus consisted of "Oh, cheese it," "Hit 'em with a club," and the Alaskan echo of "The psalm-singin' [sackers?] must be abated, dead or alive."
Thomas Brydon, who has been clerking for Arch. Boyd, left this morning for Mandan.
As soon as Joe O'Brien returns, Dan. McKenzie will take a vacation and visit relatives in the east.
Windy Bill and Dutch Bill were in town this week, enlightening the pilgrims as to how to run a "stage wagon."
All stockmen should bear in mind the annual meeting of the Little Missouri Association in April, and be prepared to make it a profitable one.
The last ice house is about two-thirds full and a week more will probably see the ice crop harvested. There will be a total of six thousand tons, put up here.
Wallace Lozier, of New York, a friend of J. R. Grymes, is here visiting the latter. He will take up his residence in Medora, and doubtless make a good citizen.
Johnny Goodall is in St. Paul and will return in a few days. Joe O'Brien will come with him. It's ten to one that Johnny don't wear the same head-gear here that he did in St. Paul.

George Fitzgerald's new hotel is nearly completed, and it will probably be ready for occupancy next week. When completed, and the brick work finished in the spring, it will compare favorably with any hotel on the line.

"Jim" Cook, whom our readers will remember as Studebaker's northwestern agent, has secured a far preferable position with the Walter A. Wood's firm, and writes that he is enjoying life as much as he always did while here.

Work on the slaughter house is progressing rapidly and only a part of the inside work remains to be done. It is built on the latest and most scientific principles and will do the work intended as well as any in the United States.

Mr. Edick, of Bismarck, made our cigar dealers a call Tuesday. His appearance everywhere is an "Emblem" of success. He, as well as all other traveling men, says that collections are better at Medora than at any point on the road.

Business is brisk on the stage line Eleven passengers came in last night, and several others who wanted to come were forced to remain over until the next coach. It will be hard work to accommodate all who want to come when the spring rush for Butte City and Coeur D'Alene begins.

Howard Eaton returned from his eastern trip Sunday night. His leg has inproved considerably, but no operation was performed on it, as it might get well without and in any event it could as well be performed five years hence as now. Howard started for his Beaver creek ranch yesterday.

Lloyd Roberts, than whom there is no one better prepared to speak on the subject, says that there are more yearlings and two-year-olds for sale in Minnesota and Iowa than ever before, and that they are also cheaper than ever. Mixed lots can easily be landed in Medora for less than twenty dollars a head.

Alaska John broke out in a fresh place yesterday and the following sign now adorns the front of the "Oyster Grotto:"

FRESH OYSTERS, BLOOD RAW, DEAD OR ALIVE.

"Toosh."

A mistaken idea seems to be prevalent that we are not to have the freight shipped to the Hills via Medora this season, or that we will have to divide, as heretofore, with Dickinson and Belfield. We wish to make the statement right here that after July 22, 1885, every pound of freight shipped from the Northern Pacific into the the Hills will be shipped via Medora. A cast iron contract was drawn up some time ago between the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co. and the Northern Pacific, the terms of which are substantially as follows: That Dickinson, nor any other town on the Northern Pacific, shall have any other than regular local rates granted on shipments to the Hills, except Belfield. That as soon as the Belfield contract ran out, which will be July 22, 1885, Medora is to be the only town on the Northern Pacific that shall receive rates on Black Hills shipments. This contract is definite, and there is no question that Medora, after July, will receive all the benefit from the Black Hills trade. As every one knows, this alone will be enough to make a good town. Before this time, also, the Refrigerator company will be working on full time, all other industries tributary to Medora will be under full headway, and we are certain of having the liveliest, as we have heretofore had the best town for its size on the road.

A woman named Dudley came near doing the Irish cause more good yesterday than anything that has happened to it. She shot at O'Donovan Rossa five times, only one shot taking effect, however. We learn with regret that he is liable to get well. He has done nothing but harm to the Irish, and his death is "a consummation devoutly to be wished."

With this issue we enter upon Vol. 2, No. 1, of the Cow Boy. We have seen and now see many ways in which the Cow Boy could be improved, and our patrons can be sure that the improvements will occur as soon as our receipts warrant it. We are thankful for all patronage of the last year, and have every confidence that it will be increased in the year to come.

Still another illustration of the advantage of advertising for strayed stock in the Cow Boy has come to our notice. The two ponies taken up and advertised by Frank Walker have found an owner in Red Water, Montana. This makes a total of fourteen horses recovered by advertising in the Cow Boy and these owners at least are thorough converts to the benifits thus derived.

A lesson that our stockmen have been slow to learn has been taught them very conclusively this winter. This lesson is to leave yearlings alone. Were it not for the loss on these, especially on Texas yearlings, the loss this winter would have to be measured by fractions. The B X B and V V V outfits seem to have been the heaviest losers and their loss is almost entirely among this class of cattle.

Taking into consideration the rumors of losses from starvation and cold that have been industriously circulated in the east, it may seem almost beyond belief to state the facts. The real facts are that three out of five of all cattle in the Bad Lands, pilgrims included, are now in prime condition for slaughtering. It would be well for any one who doubts this statement to get a horse and ride among the cattle to see for himself. E. G. Paddock, who is certainly a good judge of stock, came in from a ride Saturday and made the statement that he had seen a thousand head of cattle and not a poor one in the lot. Also that he had not seen a dead one. This statement only confirms many others of the same kind that we have repeatedly heard.

The lease of the Crow Indian reservation is liable to be nipped in the bud. The investigating committee will report to congress that the Indians who did sign it, about one hundred and forty in all, were frightened into it by threats of agent Armstrong that unless they consented, rations would be stopped April 1. None of the Crows want their reservation used for pasture, and say they will kill all cattle and men found on it. This was a gigantic swindle from beginning to end in the interest of Colorado cattle men, and it is a matter for rejoicing that the plan has been exposed. Dawes, of Massachusetts, the fast friend of the Indian, is on the congressional committee before which the case will come, and it is a certainty that it will not pass congress. Monster petitions are now being signed in Montana against the opening of the reservation.

We are glad to see that nearly every paper on the line is agreeing with the Cow Boy in our opposition to the herd law. The opinion is unanimous that we in the Bad Lands, are entitled to a repeal of the herd law and an establishment of a fence law. The most of the papers also agree that it might be better to let the question of applying the fence law to the west Missouri slope outside of the Bad Lands "work out its own salvation." In the present condition of affairs it might be a hardship to compel small farmers in agricultural territory to fence, but as the absolute necessity of diversified farming forces itself on settlers, the herd law will be repealed almost unanimously. It will be no hardship to establish the fence law in the Bad Lands and will keep stockmen from being cinched by evil-minded ranchmen, a danger to which they are now constantly exposed.

A bill has been introduced into the house to establish a fence law for several counties on the western boundary of Dakota and a consequent repeal of the herd law. The bill includes Villard and Billings counties. It was yesterday referred to the committee on agriculture, where it is liable to lie for some time unless energetic action is taken to have it passed. It will be well to call a special meeting immediately of our cattle association to see that proper arguments are brought to bear for the passage of the bill. During our recent visit in Bismarck a number of legislature's promised their active co-operation in getting a fence law passed for the Bad Lands and we have no doubt of its passing should it receive the unbiased attention of the Legislature. We do not know that the bill has any enemies and certainly did not meet any in Bismarck. The most of the work is done in committees, however, and it may readily happen that evidence against a fence law on general principles may be introduced and our side be wholly unrepresented. "Now is the accepted time" for the stockmen's side to be heard.

To thee, sweet harbinger of spring days;
To thee, fit thought for poets' lays;
To thee, warmed by Sol's tropic rays;
To thee I lift my voice in praise,
Chinook!

Freed from us now the grip of frost;
The snow and ice are river-tossed
Since thou the hills of the Bad Lands cross'd,
Chinook!

Full many a wind has long been waited,
By ships upon the sea belated,
But thou the wish of stockmen sated,
Chinook!

And as the stockman counts his gold,
And figures cattle bought and sold,
He should to thee his praise unfold,
Chinook!

The price of mixed herds, one's and two's from Minnesota and Iowa is now but little if any more than $16 per head landed in Medora. The hard times has especially had its effect on small farmers and as almost all of these have a few head of stock, they are anxious to sell for almost any price.

The condition of cattle in the Bad Lands is almost beyond the belief of an eastern cattle raiser. They are mostly states' cattle, brought in here, turned loose and never received a grain of any kind. Their entire food is the rich grass and to-day, after enduring the hardest winter and deepest snows on record, a large majority of them are fit for slaughter.

We see and hear considerable about the letter sent from Fort Keogh to the Pioneer Press, stating that the loss on pilgrims in Montana and Dakota would be fifty to seventy-five per cent. In several instances we have heard that Lieut. J. M. T. Partello was the writer of the letter. We are in a position to know that the Lieutenant's estimate was in no case higher than fifteen per cent. and he averaged it at five to ten. Some other person must have been the author of the canard

The following is an illustration of making money easily and rapidly. Last June, Lloyd Roberts delivered a bunch of pilgrim one's and two's to Howard Eaton. These were all branded and the most of them taken to Howard's Beaver Creek ranch. There were several strays however, that Howard had never seen after branding and were consequently of no expense whatever. One of these Lloyd bought back last Saturday for $40, butchered at the Co's. slaughter house and made a satisfactory profit on the carcase. The animal dressed nearly six hundred pounds and was literally covered with fat and in perfect condition for butchering, although it would have increased proportionalety in value had it been allowed to live till it was a three or four year old. As this steer was brought in the latter part of last June and sold the last of January, it will be seen that Howard's profit was 313 per cent. This profit was net, as there was not a solitary cent spent on this steer after branding. Of course this is an exceptional case but it is one that can be almost duplicated wholesale by any one driving in a large herd of cattle here and being ready at any time to sell fat cattle. The local trade here and up and down the line would alone make it profitable, and by this means the refrigerator company could be kept running eight or nine months in the year and they would doubtless purchase all fat cattle that could be brought in.

Dr J. J. Clemmer, of Cresco, Iowa, and partner in the Cave Hills cattle ranch of Clemmer & Dell, is another convert to our Polled-Angus list. He intends materially increasing his herd and will use Polled-Angus bulls exclusively. The merits of polled cattle have been a long time forcing themselves on the attention of the public, but it is only a matter of time when all will become converts.

Buyers are said by a correspondent to be in Texas in large numbers and there will be no difficulty in selling, provided the sellers will take all risk of contagion. This they are not willing to do and we doubt if any cattle have been sold except to be received at the option of the buyer. This is the animus of Texas favoring a national trail. In other words, they want original or second buyers to shoulder the responsibility that belongs to them.

A point that we have before alluded to and one that must at some times occupy the attention of congress, seems now more worthy of consideration than ever. It is the German method of dealing with contagious diseases. A proper number of inspectors is appointed, before one of whom every case of contagious disease must be brought. If the disease is incurable, the animal is immediately killed and two-thirds of its value returned by the government to the owner. It will be seen that this plan is just, as the spread of the disease might be a national calamity, and thus the people at large would bear part of the burden. The amount returned to the owner is no more than two-thirds, so that there can be no gain to him by having the animal killed. This system, with a few modifications, would work to a charm in the United States. It would be a little difficult in the case of large herds, but as prompt action would be the most important in these cases, means could be found to bring the attention of the authorities to them and stamp out almost any disease in its infancy. Until some such action as this is taken, it will be utterly impossible to deal with the periodical scares of foot-and-mouth disease, pleuro-pneumonia, Texas fever, etc.

Dr. J. H. Detmer, of the agricultural department at Washington, has submitted his report on Texas fever to commissioner Loring The doctor certainly advances some original views on the subject, which in substance are as follows: The half-dead grass of Texas pastures becomes infected with a kind of bacteria, which cause all the symptoms of Texas fever. The disease is spread by the Texans already infected by eating the grass, being driven north and grazing over lands which are afterwards used by northern cattle. The bacteria are swarming in the blood, meat and secretions of the Texans, and the saliva makes the bacteria cling to the blades of grass, ready to spread the disease to any northern cattle which may graze over the same ground. When lodged on the grass, the bacteria germinate and are then more deadly than ever. It is well known that northern cattle grazing after a Texas herd, are not immediately smitten with the disease, while those grazing after a lapse of several weeks are almost immediately stricken. Dr. Detmer's germination theory explains this exactly. The reason that Texas cattle do not themselves suffer with the disease, is that they are from their birth inoculated against it by being born with bacteria in their systems. The doctor's theory altogether is very interesting, explains fully all the phenomena of the disease, and is the most satisfactory explanation yet given.

The discussion on the Texas cattle trail is becoming warmer, and from reliable sources we learn that there is imminent danger of bloodshed between its defenders and opponents. As some may not know the extent of territory asked for, we will state that Texas cattlemen want a trail six miles wide from some point in Texas to Canada, and that at convenient points the trail shall be widened sufficiently to allow for pasturage, and if found necessary, quarantine grounds. To say the least, the request is not conspicuous for its modesty. As "Griff," of Bismarck says, "They want the whole world—and some of the outside." In return for this trail, the Texas cattlemen are willing to allow the rich grasses of Montana and Dakota to fatten their stock, and use the profits thus gained to build up some other portion of the country. To begin with, there is no likelihood of congress granting the trail asked for, but if it should, it could easily be made inoperative by the different states through which it runs, passing rigid quarantine laws for their own protection. The fact of the matter is that the trail would scarcely be in operation before Texas fever would fasten its deadly grip on a large majority of all cattle here and between here and Texas.

There will be no hardship to Texas cattle owners by a refusal to establish a trail that they have not brought on themselves. Of course, it is harder to sell cattle from Texas than it is from Dakota or Montana, but is that any reason why our stockmen should suffer that outside men may reap a profit? Would it not be as just that the gold mines of of Butte should suffer because the Black Hills gold product is harder to get to a market?

If the Texas cattle men are so hard up for a market or for pasturage, they should sell out in Texas and go to places where both are handy, and not attempt to bring loss to our cattlemen. We prophesy that the Texas cattle trail as proposed will never be in operation.

At no distant day there will be a shooting match here for a friendly trial of skill. The contest is open to all, each to use any gun he pleases. Preliminaries can be arranged on the ground. Each contestant will put a dollar in a general purse, to be taken by the winner. A six-shooter contest may also be arranged.

One of our aspiring Nimrods thought he would make a mash on a dining car steward and give him a doe's head, that he explained he would not part with to any one else, as it was not only the first deer he had ever killed, but one of the prettiest heads he had ever seen. As the steward was receiving it, Dan walked up and said: "Hello, Max, what are you doing with my deer head?" Explanations.

As we enter upon the second volume of the Cow Boy, we hope that all our subscribers, especially our local ones, will make an effort toward extending our circulation. There is not a solitary one of our subscribers that cannot induce one or more other persons to subscribe. It is well worth the trial, and our friends will be surprised at the good they can accomplish by a little effort. Try it and see.

We are in receipt of a letter from Vic. Smith, written from Chicago, in which he gives a vivid description of his travels so far. Happening into a shooting gallery in Milwaukee he "gave a specimen of western marksmanship," and was immediately offered a salary of $40 per week. He says "Medora is good enough" for him, and will return. He had with him Bob Robert's buckskin suit, and took first prize at a masquerade. As he stepped off the cars in Chicago, one man was engaging in the festive operation of shooting another. He did a good job, and as Vic says, "as clean as I ever saw it done in the west." Vic's father and brother are very sick, and this, coupled with bad reports of the New Orleans exposition he heard from friends, has decided him to give up his trip there. He intends returning about February 25.

O when the maiden plays me false,
And loves the other fellow,
For maiden's scorn, and the heart forlorn
My solace is tobacco.

Philosophy doth comfort me
With counsel sage and mellow,
When that I stifle dreams of wife
And all that, in tobacco.

For when I whiff the ringlets up,
And watch them, hazy, yellow,
Her features there, with the wavy hair,
Repent me of tobacco.

But when the ringlets fade in air
And the vision fair dispel,—O,
No falser shade than the living maid,
I reason, in tobacco.

And so I whiff and smoke in peace,
A well contented fellow,
The heart forlorn and the maiden's scorn
Forgotten in tobacco.

—[Amherst Student.

The St. Paul Pioneer Press advertised for a boy at two dollars a week, and received 250 answers. To the young the future has a roseate hue. The roseate hue comes high, but we have to use it in this place. To the young there spread out a glorious range of possibilities. After the youth has indorsed for an intimate friend a few times, and purchased the paper at the bank later on, the horizon won't seem to horizon so tumultuously as it did aforetime. I remember at one time of purchasing such a piece of accommodation paper at a bank, and I still have it. I didn't need it any more than a cat needs 11 tails at one and the same time. Still the bank made it an object to me, and I secured it. Such things as these harshly knock the fluff and bloom off the cheek of youth, and prompt us to turn the strawberry-box bottom side up before we purchase it. Youth is gay and hopeful, age is covered with experience and scars where the skin has been knocked off and had to grow on again. To the young a dollar looks large and strong, but to the middle-aged and the old it is weak and inefficient. When we are in the heyday and fizz of existence, we believe everything, but after awhile we murmur, "What's that you're givin' us," or words of a like character. Age brings caution and a lot of shop-worn experience purchased at the highest market price. Time brings vain regrets and wisdom teeth that can be left in a glass of water over night.[—Bill Nye.

It looks now as though women would be granted the right of suffrage in Dakota. There is but little opposition to the bill and it seems as though the majority of the legislature are in favor of it. On account of the crankiness of the leaders of the womans' rights movement the subject has always been a matter of mirth rather than a serious one. Practical experience has shown, however, that women are as well qualified to vote as men and we hope to see the measure pass.

The Union News, of Union, N. Y. is the last tenderfoot sheet that has come to the front. The last issue contains the notice that snow is twenty to twenty-five feet deep in Montana. We do not think there is a place in Montana or Dakota where there has been even two feet on a level and only in exceptional cases has it reached a depth of eighteen inches. We merely make these remarks to show the animos of the eastern press toward the northwest. On every occasion they will publish articles such as the one referred to, knowing, if the editors have any sense, that they are entirely devoid of truth.

We have seen a letter srom Mr. McCall, who introduced a bill for the repeal of the herd law, stating that no one has petitioned for the repeal from here, and that it might be as well not to exempt the Bad Lands here, as no one seems to wish it. This is enough to call for immediate action on the part of cattlemen here, and a man should be sent at once to Bismarck to present our side of the case. While in Bismarck recently we were convinced from conversations with legislators that the herd law could be repealed and we have so expressed ourselves in the Cow Boy. Now the matter may go by default unless immediate action is taken.

The Dakota Blade, Jimmy Emmon's paper, is on the war path after corruption, but Jimmy has bitten off more than he can chew in attempting to show that the herd law should not be repealed for the Bad Lands, because farmers could not then come in. The truth of the matter is, that although Jimmy is well acquainted with the east Missouri country, he has never been in the Bad Lands, and does not realize that perpendicular farming does not pay. From the nature of the ground, farming to any extent is impossible in the Bad Lands, and as long as so much better farming land can be had farther east for the taking, there will be no hardship in a repeal of the herd law here.

Experience although a dear teacher, seems to be about the only successful one, especially in cattle raising. From its teachings, however, two thing have, or ought to have been learned thoroughly. Never buy yearlings and never drive in cattle later than August. An exception might be made in favor of yearlings, in case they are brought in before June or July, but even in that case there is a far greater percentage of risk than it is necessary to take. There is scarcely a cattle man in the Bad Lands with whom we have not spoken on these two points and we think we are above the mark in estimating a loss of one per cent. on all two-year-olds and over on cattle landed here early, whether they are pilgrims or not. Two-thirds of the total loss will be on yearlings and cattle landed here late. A good illustration of this point are the V V V and B X B outfits, on the Belle Fouche. The V V V has lost but little on old cattle, the most of their loss coming on yearlings and late dogies. The B X B, with a corresponding location and a mixed herd which was driven in late in the fall, have been heavy losers on all classes of cattle. Of course any estimate of loss is pure guess-work, but there is no question that it would be nerely nominal had it not been for yearlings and late cattle.

An organization known as the International Arbeiter, or workingmen's association, has been holding secret meetings in Philadelphia for some time. A reporter of one of the papers joined the body, and exposed the workings of the organization. Johann Most and Justus Schwab are the leading spirits. At first there was difficulty in securing members, but of late the ranks have been swelled considerably. The object of this association seems to be to overthrow all law and build up a government of its own. It seems strange that any workingman, who has the slightest respect for himself or anyone else would join an organization of this kind. There are rights which workingmen have, and the best thing they can do is to exercise them in the best and most honorable ways. By joining such an order as the International Arbeiter he does not advance his interests one whit, but on the contrary, tends to lessen his chances for a fair deal. The leaders, Most and Schwab, are cranks on this subject, and are men whom every true workingmen should combine against. If a man joins a workingmen's protective association, let him join one he is not afraid to own publicly, in which all the members are on an equal footing, and not one lead by such men as are at the head of this body—who want everything their own way, though thousands of dollars worth of property are destroyed, or even at the price of blood. A workingman has the right to say he will work for so much and no less, but he cannot stop others from taking his place; nor has he the right to destroy his employer's property. Such proceedings cause bitter feelings between capital and labor, and it is to be hoped that the "men of toil" will learn this and prevent the spread of the International Arbeiter's association.

It took just 22,437 cars to bring in Chicago January supplies of live stock. The eastward shipments were 6,084 cars.—[Breeders' Gazette.

Out of 12,000 sheep belonging to the Montana sheep company, on Flat Willow, Meagher county, only forty-one have died since the first of November.—[Stock and Mining Journal.

One of the largest and most experienced breeders and raisers of horses in Illinois says that if you will give one or two mouthfuls of hay to the horse before you water him, there will never be any danger of the horse being water-founded. After all the fuss about cattle losses, it turns out that about the only loss amounting to much was in two or three counties south of San Antonio, where there is no grass and the cattle are very poor. And even in these counties the loss is greatly exagerated. Thanks to the prickly pear, the loss of cattle even there is much lighter than expected.—[Texas Stockman.

Our reports from the different ranges of the territory are veay much alike. All agree that up to the present time there has not been much loss of stock, if any; but also all agree that unless we have fairly good weather from this out the loss is likely to make one feel uncomfortable. There is no use denying the fact that during the past 50 days stock has suffered much.—[Stock and Mining Journal.

The building of wind breaks on the range has been suggested by a cattlemen who thinks that the expense would not be very great and that it would keep cattle from drifting. The breaks could be built of sod, stone or lumber, in a straight line, so that cattle could seek shelter on either side. Where the herds are not too large the plan would work very well.—[Globe L. S. Journal.

Cross-breds are coming to the front as prize winners. Everyone has become so accustomed to thinking some particular breed is the best, that the fact of every one coming from the same parent stock has been lost sight of. A new breed might be obtained by judicious crossing, or even a single cross might bring an animal superior to either of its parents. These remarks are called forth by the fact that a cross-bred four-year-old, from a Hereford sire out of a Short-horn at the Smithfield, England, show, took the $150 cup as the best cross-bred, the $250 cup as the best steer, and the $500 cup as the best animal in the show. It is a well-established law of breeding that offspring take the good rather than the poor points of their parents, and right here lies the difference between Texas and northern cattle. By comparison, the Texans have but few points as good as the cattle of the north. Blooded bulls are seldom or never used in Texas. The consequence is that the Texans are now a distinct breed, never improving in quality, and according to the best judges, are deteriorating. On the other hand, northern stockgrowers have, as a rule, used full-blood or graded bulls. The consequence is that but for the one point of the Texans making better mothers, and even this is disputed, the northern cattle are far superior.

Last Sunday morning the little Missouri began to rise rapidly. A gorge was formed above the bridge, and it seemed as if we were going to have a flood. The weather here was very cold, which probably was the cause of no damage being done, as the river was frozen over Sunday night. The present cold snap came in good time, as the refrigerator company still requires 600 tons to fill its houses.

It is to be hoped that all will take an interest in the shooting club, and practice for the contests. The winning score of last Friday's shoot should be the lowest average. The cold weather accounted for much of the poor shooting, but lack of practice accounted for much more. There are enough good shots on the river so that a formidable team could be organized and matches made with other teams up and down the line.
