Vic Smith was showing the tenderfoot how to shoot, in a back yard in Milwaukee, when a policeman put in an appearance and Vic had to pay $5 and costs in court. Vic can make lots more money shooting here than in Milwaukee. He is already pining for the Bad Lands, and will return soon.

Joe O'Brien returned Friday night from a visit to relatives in Missouri and Iowa. He reports a complicated state of affairs in Iowa. A prohibition law was passed by a popular vote and, as it cannot be enforced, the saloon keepers are holding high carnival. They of course, can pay no license, and cannot be held responsible for selling to minors, etc., as the law does not recognize the right to sell liquor, and of course cannot punish any harm done from its effects.

The Little Missouri river resembles the peace of God, "in that it passeth all understanding." The break-ups of course all come from the south as the river runs north. Perhaps for several days previous to our coldest days, there has been a chinook blowing near the head of the river. The water immediately begins running, and it depends upon the length of the thaw how far the water flows on the ice. If it meets cold weather it is liable to freeze up at any time. Thus there are formed several thicknesses of ice. South of the railroad crossing there are four thicknesses, north there are three, and twenty miles down the river there are but two. A curious circumstance was also noted yesterday. At McGregor's ranch down the river, the water was at least six inches deep on the top of the ice and flowing rapidly. Coming up the river to Wadsworth's ranch there was no sign of a thaw, the top ice being about two inches thick. Farther up the river solid ice was found in some places and in others only a thin crust. Some top crusts had no water under them and some had two feet and over.

The transfer of the capital from Yankton to Bismarck, throws a large portion of of the more important mail matter passing between the Hills and the seat of government, over the northern route. At present such runs via Miles, and the service thereon is simply and utterly abominable. For instance matter mailed at Medora Jan. 15 reached us yesterday—twelve days after. Bismarck papers reach us four and five at a time, many days after publication and it is reasonable to suppose that letters are equally as long in transit. No regularly equipped stage line runs between the Hills and Miles, but in lieu thereforo a small buckboard outfit is operated between Spearfish and the railroad. A movement is on foot to secure a transfer of the mail service from the Miles City to the Medora route. A splendidly equipped stage line occupies the latter, making regular and quick trips, and if the change is made service will be expedited from two to five days. Petitions are circulating throughout the country and are extensively signed. It is hoped that the department will grant our reasonable request.—[Black Hills Times.

The same trouble is experinced in Medora. Papers and letters arrive here two or three weeks after the time of their leaving the Deadwood postoffice. All this delay would be dispensed with, had the Medora route the mail contract, and the desire of the people should be granted.

Several weeks ago a bill was introduced in the Legislature by Mr. McCall, of the Hills, to repeal the herd law and establish a fence law in several of the western counties of Dakota, including Billings and Villard as the only counties north of Harding. This bill was referred to the committee on agriculture and soon afterward word was received by one of our citizens from the framer of the bill that as no expression of opinion had been received from Villard and Billings counties, he thought of striking those names from his bill. Immediately on receipt of this word, it was manifest that something must be done immediately and at the wish of a number of cattlemen, Messrs. J. L. Truscott and A. T. Packard went to Bismarck last Sunday, to look after the interests of the bill. Upon arrival, it was found that another bill had been introduced, dividing Billings, Villard and Bowman counties on a line running north and south near Sully Springs and repealing the herd law in both the proposed new counties of Villard and Billings.

This bill made no provision for the establishment of a fence law and if passed would have put the cattlemen in a worse position than ever, as they would then be subject to the common law of trespass and damages, where, under the herd law, they are subject only to damages. It is very doubtful if this bill will pass the legislature and if it does, will be vetoed by the governor, as he will sign no bill for county division, without first leaving it to a vote of the people.

The McCall bill, on the other hand, is exactly what the stockmen want. Owing to the efforts of the two delegates from here, the whole western tier of counties, consisting of Fall River, Custer, Pennington, Lawrence, Butte, Harding, Burdick, Ewing, Bowman, Villard, Billings, Dunn and McKenzie will be included in the bill, with every chance of its passing both houses and becoming a law. The law, as amended will, if passed, repeal the herd law and establish a fence law in this whole western tier of counties.

In conclusion it will be well to say that the sentiment of the legislature was well sounded by the committee from here and as far as they could learn, the bill, should there be no outside interference, will pass almost unanimously.

There was no hint of bribery throughout. Not a cent, was expended beyond [the legitimate?] expenses of the committee and more than that, it would have been next to impossible to have bought the passage of the bill. It is a matter of justice that Dakota owes to the cattle interests and as it hardly conflicts at all with agricultural interests, it has every chance of passing on its merits.
There are strong probabilites that an extra session of congress will be called after March 4th.
The southern cattle papers are booming the Staked Plains as a cattle country. The difficulty heretofore has been a lack of water, but wells are now being dug, and are said to furnish an abundance.

Nothing definite has yet been done in reference to the Texas trail, and it is doubtful if the matter will be pushed farther. The bill has encountered very serious opposition, and its friends think better to let it be awhile.

A letter received from J. R. Wilson foreman of E 6 Ranch says: If snow and cold weather do not soon let up there will be little need of a "round-up" in the spring except for hides. The winter thus far in that section has been unusually severe on stock. Especially on pilgrims and yearlings.

It seems strange that nine out of ten editors in spite of plain facts will "strain at a gnat and swallow a camel" when they can just as well, consistently with the facts, reverse the order. There have been more snow blockades in each of the states of Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Minnesota and Wisconsin than there have been in either Dakota or Montana this winter. And still the eastern papers howl about "snow-blocked Dakota."

Swift wrote, "There never appear more than five or six men of genius in an age." This age has given us Talmage, Rossa, John L. Sullivan and Ben Butler, but where is other one?

He is a member of the legislature.--[Exchange.

This must be the man who has no county to divide or county seat to locate and died several years ago before any of the counties were organized.

The Black Hills papers seem to be but little interested in the proceedings of the legislature. The Pioneer does not published a line in reference to the action of that body, which leads the Tribune to believe that it is not well informed on the question of the division of Lawrence county.--Bismarck Tribune.

Give the boys a chance Bro. Plummer They have no telegraph communication with Bismarck and get their mail only once in two weeks. When the Medora stage line gets their mail contract the Black Hills papers will get the capital news at least three times a week, regularly, then if they dont come to the front with the news it will be their fault and you can take a shot at them without any injustice being done.

Held an adjourned meeting at Robert's hall last evening and the following officers were elected: Wm. VanDriesche President and Treasurer; John C. Fisher, Secretary, Executive committee: E. G. Paddock, A. T. Packard, J. N. Maxwell.

A move to "empower the committee to transact all business for the club, subject to the approval of the club at its next regular meeting," was carried.

Moved and seconded that a series of five contests be arranged. Contestants to be allowed five shots at each target ranging from one to three hundred yards.

Each member of the club taking part in the contest to pay into the treasury fifty cents at each contest. At the end of the series the member having the best score to receive a new Winchester not to cost over $25. Motion was carried.

A motion was also carried that each contestant is to use the same gun with open sights for each range.

The committee were also instruted to include glass ball and six shooter contests in their future programmes, when the weather would permit.

A very interesting and instructive letter from Lieut. J. W. T. Partello of Fort Keogh, to A. T. Packard was read before the club. The letter contained, the Creedmore rules and various valuable suggestions and offers of assistance. The club extended a hearty vote of thanks to Lieut. Partello and A. T. Packard for favors extended.

The next meeting of the club will be held at the same place on next Wednesday evening and all wishing to become members of the club are respectfully urged to be present, as the meeting will be of importance to all.

More and more are Polled-Angus cattle coming into favor. There seems to be a general awakening as to their good points, and a prominent stock authority has recently classed them as the highest in quality. We hope to see some one put in polled-Angus bulls with their herd in the spring and prove here their superiority, as has been done in many other places.

The following is said to be a sure cure for cribbing. Will some of our readers try it and report? Take a strip of sheep skin wide and long enough to cover all parts of the manger that the horse cribs. Nail it securely to the manger with the wool side out and sprinkle with cayenne pepper, renewing when necessary. The above is certainly simple enough, and we hope to be assured of its truth or falsity as a cure before long.

We learn from the Colorado Springs Gazette that a very novel arrangement to do away with round-ups has lately materialized in the shipment from the east of a ponderous forty-two inch telescope, to be mounted on Pike's peak for the purpose of keeping track of cattle. The scheme is to sweep the country with the telescope and telegraph the result to the cattle manager's office. When the instrument is in place, dispatches similar to the following will be flashed across the wires:

Manager of the Long Horn cattle Company, Denver, Colorado:

Your old bug-horn Texas cow is down below Walsenburg, eating loco and wishing she was a thoroughbred on clover. Just saw your bob-tailed roan steer cross New Mexico line with a fresh brand on his left shoulder--party of horsemen in pursuit. Cattle inspector is asleep under a tree this side of Dodge City. Two bears are doing the assessment work on a pale-faced yearling--your brand--in the woods, near Colver's, in Park county. One of your hides is hanging on a fence at Santa Fe--hide buyer on the premises and inspector 300 miles away. Vast herds of Texas cattle are drifting southward. They have evidently dropped on the repeal of the loco and mountain-lion bounty bill, and are leaving the country. Polled-Angus, the stockman, has just branded another maverick at Las Vegas. Eternal vigilance is the price of beef. Yours, Hereford Shorthorn,

In charge of Pike's Peak Stock Observatory.--[N. M. Stock Grower.
In 1870 there were 130,887,880 horses, mules and sheep in the United States.

About the highest price for steers we have yet heard of, is that paid by Phil Armour to J. W. Simpson, of Onslow, Iowa. There were thirty-four head, and they averaged $116.72 each. The most surprising part of the matter is that the whole herd were two-year-olds. They were grade Shorthorns.

Two cattle kings of the coast, Messrs. Miller and Lux, are rated at $8,000,000 to $10,000,000, and were poor men twenty years ago. They have about 90,000 head of cattle and 115,000 head of sheep, of which latter they kill 6,000 per month. They own an irrigating canal worth $1,000,000, fences 200 miles in length, (a fortune in itself), in California 600,000 acres of land, in Nebraska 10,000 acres, and 15,000 acres of alfalfa grass.--[Chicago Tribune.

G. G. Bond of the Little Missouri Horse Co., was in town this week and reports their horses in splendid condition. He says the weather can't get too cold or the snow too deep for them. Some of the foals dropped this winter have already hair on them like a buffalo. The valley of the Little Missouri river is without a doubt a "boss" horse country and we predict that within the next ten years the cattle men will find the horse men following them up close in size and value of their herds.

Nothing will so quickly reduce the weight of a ripened animal as to subject it to a long ride in a stock car with the thermometer below zero, says the stockman. Animal life is sustained by combustion, and the bullock or pig in transit through an icy atomsphere is being slowly burned up in flesh and tissue. To transport stock economically and safely then, as well as for humane consideration, the highest practicable degree of comfort, in the matter of protection from the severity of weather, as well as plenty of good and close personal attention, are necessary. Market platforms all over the country are covered with dead hogs after the close of a manitoba blizzard, and not a small number of cattle perish in the same way, while surviving stock is often so cut down in weight that the shipper is almost ready to dispute the story of the scales. Those who handle any kind of stock, whether breeding, or fat animals, can not afford to neglect their comfort while en route to their destination.--[Stock Growers' Journal.

From every range comes up the cry, "more bulls." We doubt if there is a cattle section in the United States in which every ranchman has a sufficient number. Invariably there are found a few that depend entirely on their neighbor's bulls. There is no need in commenting on the injustice of this practice, and the only thing to do is to consider methods to compel each ranchman to put in his proportion of bulls. In New Mexico the names of stockmen who have not a sufficient number are published over the signatures of responsible cattle owners. It is doubtful, however, if even this will shame them into providing the required number. Perhaps as good a plan as any is that adopted by our association, to debar from the privileges of the round-up any stock owner who fails in living up to the constitution and by-laws, which provide that ten bulls for every hundred she cattle shall be put on the range. There in no economy in skimping on the number of bulls, as low percentages of calves in such cases always shows. Hitherto the highest per cent. of calves on the Little Missouri has fallen short of sixty per cent., owing entirely to lack of bulls. The increase under the new rules will be a matter of interest.

Black polled cattle are fulfilling my predictions made in 18[72?], when I wrote repeated articles for the agricultural papers and used my best exertions privately to prevail on western ranchmen to introduce them among their herds, which was soon done. Now, after some years of experience with them on the great plains and in the Rocky Mountain valleys, they are found the hardiest of all the improved breeds of cattle tried there. This may be said more especially of the Galloways, for their extra-long, thick coats of hair protect them as well from fierce winter winds and stormes as similar coats have ever done the buffalo. In addition to this superior hardiness, is the great advantage of being without horns. The benefit of this absence of the worse than useless excrescence is bestowed almost universally on the stock got by these polled bulls out of the long-horned Texas cow. The form of this half-breed stock proves also much superior to that of their dams, for they mature a year or two earlier, turn out a finer quality of beef and are reared and fattened and transported to market more economically. Then there is the superior safety in handling them--their milder and quieter disposition, and the inability of goring and hurting each other when herded together, however closely. In rearing this sort of cattle on the great plains, in preference to horned stock, a larger profit is realized. Indeed, this advantage has been caculated at 5 to 25 per cent., dependent on the breeds of the horned animals being more or less improved, against which they are pitted in such trials.--[A. B. Allen in N. Y. Tribune.

Ed Staples has returned from his home in Wisconsin, and will again make his headquarters here.
Perfecto Fernandez, whom every one will remember for his ability as a rider, was in from Beaver creek Saturday.
Pennell & Roberts' mules with which the contract work was done on the Canadian Pacific, were brought back last Friday.
C. S. Grindall of the E S G ranch on Beaver creek, made us a pleasant call this week and reports cattle in that section as looking fine.
Johney Goodall says he is "going to follow suit," and hearts are trumps. When John says a thing "you can bet your high ocean wave it goes."
The lumber for the new roller rink has been ordered and we are assured by the proprietors that the rink will be in running order about march 1st.
Word has been received from Jones & Pennell. They have secured a contract for a tunnell on the New York water works that involves five years of labor. Every one here wishes them success.

On account of the high wind of last Saturday, it was deemed best not to have the shooting match. It would have been impossible to make even a fair score, and it is better in any event to wait until we could get the army regulations.

The Sullivan--Ryan wave has struck the Bad Lands. Quite a number of our boys are practicing and will be in shape to challenge John L, Paddy Ryan or any of the rest of the hard hitters. But you ought to practice with the gloves on boys, or some of you will get hurt.

A severe snow storm coming from the south-east struck us about six o'clock yesterday morning continueing all day. Passenger train No 1 was delayed about six hours by heavy drifts. This is the first snow of any consiquence that has been seen in the Bad Lands this season.

It seems strange that no one has started a dairy here. Ready sale could be found for a large quantity of milk here, and the dining cars would take enough to support a small dairy. Good butter and cheese must all be shipped in, where it could as well be made here. It would require but little capital to start, as almost any number of cows could be obtained from ranchmen free of charge for their keeping. Who will start into the business?

Vic. Smith returned last night from a six weeks trip in the east. He says he wouldn't have regreted the trip had it cost him $10,000.

Side walks are being talked of in places about town. Now is the time to attend to this matter, and have them all ready for use before the spring mud begins to make the walking disagreeable Gravel or scoria make very good walks for this country.

The work of refitting the hotel de Mores has been begun in good earnest and it will soon be in shape for occupancy. We have not yet learned who will be proprietor. Several names have been mentioned, among the most prominent are H. M. Jorgins, S. G. Smith and Arch. Boyd.

There is some talk of using the rubber wheels skates in the new roller rink. They are noiseless and avoid the necessity of using chalk on the floor. We think this would be a great improvement, as the use of chalk makes a fellow look like an animated black board if he happens to sit down on the floor a few minutes to rest himself.

"Fitz" says that the Metropolitan is "just booming." The weary traveler can now find a place to rest and no one (or half a dozen) to molest or make him afraid. A new combination billard table will soon grace the saloon. Pete still presides over the culinary department with his usual grace and urbanity and says he is bound to "fill up de boys" if he has to go dry to do it. Johnny Chute dishes up the lemonade to the boys and "Fitz" teaches them how to play a straight game of high low.

SMILES.

GOSSIP'S EXAGGERATION.

There was an old lady in Danbury
Made a meal on the half of a cranberry.
But the story it grew,
And the first thing she knew,
From a half to a few
It was started as true--
Then a gallon--then two,
Till old Mrs. McKew
Told the news as if true,
That a Mrs. Bellew
Ate a wonderful stew
Of a ton of cranberries in Danbury.
Herald-Chronicle.

"OWED" TO MY BOARDING HOUSE.

How dear to my purse is the boarding house racket,
Its sour-mash potato, its roast beef so dry;
Its dough-nut so hard that a hammer won't crack it;
Its fire-proof, back-number, dried-apple pie;
Oh, the piecrust so clammy, so greasy, so flammy!
No pen can do justice to boarding house pie!

The "tea dust" Bohea and chiccory Mocha;
The fraudulent bread made of papier mache;
The grocery cracker so freckled and smoky;
The burglar-proof butter, so brindled and gray,
Oh, the strong, long-haired butter--so utterly utter,
Please call in the barber--or take it away!

I am taking French leave of my present location;
But ere I depart--for my dear landlady's sake--
As a souvenir precious, of lasting duration,
I'll have my boots soled with boarding house steak.
Oh, the highway is rough; and the steak sure is tough;
It shall dance while I live, and then dance at my wake.
--[Texas Siftings.

New Jersey girls amuse themselves by playing leap frog, and the interest the old bald-headed veterans of the State have begun to take in youthful sport is remarkable.--[New Orleans City Item.

One blessing, they're never troubled with dyspepsia and never have colds. Young doctors don't go around gorging themselves like editors.--[Burdette.

One of the interesting characters at the St. Paul depot was a grizzly looking fellow, perhaps 40 years of age, who said he was on his way east from Idaho, where he had been engaged in the cattle business.

"I threw it up this year," he continued, "because its overdone."

"I thought that was a business that could't be overdone," said a bystander.

"You don't understand it, then," was the rejoinder. "You see, there's two kinds of cattle business. I was in the kind that gets men hung."--[Chicago Herald.

On Washington avenue, near First avenue south, a lot of home-made, warranted fresh, candy and taffy was exposed for sail on a small stand yesterday. A group of hungry, sharp-eyed boys clustered near it, and noticed with satisfaction that the boy who presided was completely enclosed by the three sides of the stand. A whispered consultation ensued, and presently one of the urchins seized a piece of taffy and started off. The boy owner made a sudden movement, the loop of a lariat flew out and settled over the head of the running boy, who was incontinently roped back and made to disgorge. The group moved sadly away, and one muttered: "Didn't know dey got cowboys to sell candy in dis town."--[St. Paul Globe.

Mrs. J. B. Raymond, wife of Dakota's delegate to Congress, was buried Feb. 22. Mrs. Raymond has been an invalid for over six years. Many expressions of condolence were received by Mr. Raymond and the funeral was attended generally by both houses of Congress. The interment took place at Rock Creek cemetery.

In spite of severe losses, the BXB outfit on the South Moreau is not at all discouraged. They have recently bought a large outfit in Nebraska and this season will drive up 10,000 beef cattle on their Moreau range. We wish them every success.

The warm weather which began yesterday is hailed with joy by every one as the first harbinger of approaching spring. The cattlemen especially are rejoicing as it will put a stop to losses already larger than usual unless some entirely unexpected weather ensues. A regular chinook wind set in early this morning and two more days will completely clear the ground of snow.

It may be a little inappropriate at this time to "lock the stable door after the horse is stolen" by drawing a moral from the accident to Frank Walker yesterday morning, but it seems necessessary to say something. The thoughtlessness of some people in handling fire-arms is simply criminal carelessness and should be punished the same as any other crime. There is no excuse for leaving a load in the barrel of a Winchester at any time as the cartridge can be thrown into the barrel from the magazine and the gun cocked with as quick a motion as the single one of raising the hammer.

Mr. O. H. Holt of Bismarck, private secretary to Gov. Pierce, has published a pamphlet on Dakota, which is full of valuable information to any one desiring to learn our resources. One of the extracts written by the editor of the Cow Boy in his tenderfoot days contains the information that cattle paw away the snow to get at the grass in winter. A settled conviction has come over our minds that this should be taken with a grain of allowance, perhaps two grains wouldn't do any harm. In all other respects the pamphlet is a model of compact information and should be in the possession of everyone who wishes to learn or give information about Dakota.

As a sort of addenda to our remarks on the river, may be mentioned the fact that last Saturday, when the weather was below zero here, word came that there was a raise of three or four feet of water coming, and at that time was about twenty-five miles up the river. The flood is travelling at the rate of four or five miles a day and will probably be here to-night or to-morrow. It may seem strange that although there is a pitch of over two thousand feet to the river, the flood does not come faster. This is accounted for by the fact that the channel is very crooked and that the ice is covered with snow which must all be melted thus reducing the water to a kind of thin slush.

From M. S. & F. Co., October 5, one sorrel horse; four white feet, white stripe in face, branded -Y- on left shoulder and [box brand] on left thigh. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery.

From my ranch on Little Missouri, ten miles south of Medora, the night of November 19, a dark sorrel mare, weighing about nine hundred pounds, left front knee stiff, white and red scar on left side, far back, brand M bar on left hip. Mare about nine years old. The finder will be paid for his trouble by leaving information leading to her recovery with me.

From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.

The cattle and horse business in the Bad Lands has passed the experimental stage and there is no doubt that they are unsurpassed for both purposes. As a horse country especially, it has many advantages not present in other sections. The soil is of such a nature that the quality of the hoofs constantly improves and no better quality can be found anywhere than on horses reared here. The winters are just cold enough to make the horses hardy and still not so cold as to hinder the largest growth of blooded stock. For wind, however, this climate is superior to any other. It is dry, light and considerably rarer than at the sea level. This latter fact will at some time be of great value if our horsemen raise racing stock. If in a comparatively rare atmosphere a horse's wind is good, it stands to reason that it will be better in a denser atmosphere.

Lloyd Roberts has already made a contract to deliver four hundred head of cattle to Glendive. The contract is made with the same firm to which he delivered cattle there last year and which was so well satisfied that they voluntarily paid yearling prices for some calves born on the road.

We are in receipt of a letter from Dan Friedman, who is now at Cold Spring Minn. He don't enlarge much on the use of side-saddles but mentions that he is having a first-rate time. He is a partner of Lloyd Roberts in buying cattle and states that cattle there are at the lowest notch, nine to ten dollars for yearlings and fourteen to sixteen for two-year-olds.

Beef is selling now from Helena to St. Paul at 10½ cents by the side and exceedingly hard to get, even at those figures. Why do not some of our enterprising stock men cut out a herd of their heavy beef cattle in the fall, and hold them for these high winter markets? Good hay can be secured during the summer and the cattle can be held on a pasture, reserved for that purpose, when the grass gives out, the cattle can be made to keep their flesh on hay, at least until the first of March. The hay of this country cut in season and properly cured is nearly as fattening as grain. Who will try the expirement next year?

The breeders of Aberdeen-Angus cattle in this country have so far done but little showing at our fat-stock shows, having necessarily but very few pure-bred animals to show. As it is, they point with just pride to the record they have made in proportion to their numbers. In 1883, Black Prince worthily upheld, almost unassisted, the honor of the breed. This year some younger animals came to his assistance. In spite, however, of the slimness of their exhibits, they have well sustained their reputation as prize winners, especially in the carcass classes—the block test, that feature of our fat stock shows which our English friends commend so highly. In 1883, with two of this breed slaughtered out of nineteen, Aberdeen-Angus took first prize in the two-year-old class, at Chicago. At the Chicago show of 1884, there were thirty animals slaughtered, of which four were Aberdeed-Angus grades, two of which took firsts in the two-year-old and yearling classes respectively. At Kansas City, last fall, the Angus men, as will be remembered by most of our readers, were justly jubilant over the record of Pride 3d of Blairshinnock, Burleigh's Pride and Abernethy, the latter, the same which, at Chicago, stood first in the two-year-old carcass class. In proportion then to the numbers exhibited both in live and carcass classes, but especially in the latter, the Aberdeen-Angus cattle have a record to be proud of.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.

This amusement has become the most popular indoor amusement of the day and doubtless many will be interested in knowing of its origin and subsequent history.

Roller skating is no new thing. Roller skates were patented and used in France in 1819. A few years later an Englishman by name of Syers invented and manufactured them in England. The Syers skate was a sandal placed on fi[ve?] wheels in a single row and arranged s[o?] that only two wheels touched the floor at one time.

The Plympton skate was the first patented in the United States, about the close of the civil war, and the first public rink was opened in Newport R. I. in 1866. It is still in existence. The "skating craze" sprung from this city rapidly all over the country. In '73-'74 it died down again in the United States but was was fully sustained in European countries, and in the East Indies and Australia raged more fiercely than in more northern countries.

In 1880 the interest in roller skating revived in the New England states and has since been rapidly spreading toward the Pacific slope, until nearly every town of eight hundred inhabitants or more in the eastern states has a roller rink and very many of the southern and western towns and cities are also supplied with this rapidly increasing popular amusement. The chief advantage of roller over ice skating is that the amusement in roller rinks may be indulged in during any season of the year, in well lighted and heated halls. In ice skating, it can only be indulged in during a very small portion of the year and at considerable risk to life and health.

There is an essential difference of motion between ice and roller skating. On ice it is a glide, and on rollers it is the motion of walking.

The first lesson on rollers, is to walk without allowing the skates to roll.

A beginner must become firmly impressed with the idea that "haste makes waste." Confidence is the first element of success and a few falls at the out-set are quite apt to make people more or less timid.

To attain grace and perfection in skating a careful study of the first movements and positions are very essential, in fact the more difficult movements cannot be gracefully performed without a thorough mastery of the rudiments. As there is soon to be a new roller rink built at Medora, we would suggest to our young people, and old ones to for that matter, that they provide themselves with "Spalding's manual" and if they will follow its instructions closely we will guarantee that they will not regret it in the future.

The following story, coming home to all readers of the Cow Boy as concerning a well-known character formerly living here, will be found full of interest.

Seven years ago, the subject of our sketch was living in a small eastern village, supporting by his labor an invalid father and mother. In this, he was assisted by a sister and between them they barely succeeded in gaining enough to supply food for the family. The boy, then fourteen years old, was eager to learn a trade and [get?] an education, but poverty compelled him to put them off.

An old friend of the family had come out to this country and engaged extensively in cattle raising. He was very successful and going back east on a visit, called on our hero's family. Seeing their poverty stricken condition, he immediately offered the boy whose name was Stephen, a position on his ranch at a salary more than he could possibly make at home. The offer was gladly accepted and Stephen, although immediately nicknamed the "Kid" became a valuable hand, as he was quick to learn and eager to please. Round-ups followed each other in rapid succession and last year Stephen was acknowleddyed to be one of the best cow-boys that rode the range. He grew in favor with his employer and and was then appointed foreman of his outfit.

Comfort at last came to the "old folks' at home" for the "Kid" regularly sent the most of his salary to supply their wants. The future looked bright and everything went along peacefully until late last fall, when the "Kid" and a bosom friend were driving in a bunch of cow-horses from a distant round-up. They were sleeping near the bunch and were awakened in the night by a band of rustlers who had stampeded the herd except two horses which were kept hobbled near camp. The "Kid" and his pard rushed to saddle up and start in pursuit. As it happened, two of the best horses had been kept up and as dawn was just breaking it was an easy matter to follow rapidly on the trail. An hour or two's hard riding brought them in view of the band and although there were five of the horse thieves, neither of the cow-boys thought of the odds but spurred their horses harder than ever to catch up. The thieves saw the boys at almost the same time and riding around a butte, two of them cached themselves and the others drove on with the herd. Just as they rounded the butte they were saluted by a discharge from the rifles of the rustlers. One of the balls struck the Kid in the breast knocking him from his horse and the other killed his pard's horse. The robbers, thinking both men were killed rode after the herd. The Kid's partner extricated himself from under his horse and hastening to his chum's side had only time to receive his dying words: "Take large envelope from—pocket and send to father."

The chum did as requested and accompanied his friend's body to the east. It was a mournful mission, as he had to inform the grief stricken family that their only support was taken from them. The loss of their dearly beloved son, poverty without hope and the poor-house as a sole refuge was a sickening prospect. The chum could offer no consolation and forgot the envelope entirely until after the funeral. Thinking of it then, he gave it to the father and imagine the flood of joy that overcame him at the thoughtfulness of his son when he found that it contained a policy for $5,000 in the safety fund department of the Hartford Life and Annuity insurance company. Sabe?

Dr. H. M. Jorgens, wife and sons came in on yesterday morning's coach from Cave Hills. The Dr. has already begun house-keeping. We are pleased to welcome this family to Medora and we know that the members will become prime favorites. The Dr. is thinking seriously of putting in a herd of cattle.

The snow is over a foot deep on the level, a heavier fall than there has been within the memory of the oldest inhabitant. All things considered, the cattle are doing well but from recent reports, the loss may be heavier than was expected. It is of course, impossible to state the loss accurately but our estimate of five per cent. as an outside loss may be realized.

M. M. and Mrs. Coleman celebrated their eighteenth wedding anniversary, the evening of the twenty-second. There was a large attendance of friends and many were the expressions of good will to the host and hostess. A thoroughly enjoyable time was had by all, the only disappointment being that eighteenth wedding anniversaries do not come eighteen times a year instead of once in eighteen years.

Geo. Wilkes returned from Chicago last Friday where he purchased all the machinery for the new slaughter house. The boilers are of the Buckeye pattern and George says the whole plant was just what he wanted. No expense was spared in getting the best, the total cost in Chicago amounting to nearly $8,000. Gorge also brought with him a superior Claybrough gun which we know by experience is a fine shooter.

It will be remembered that last fall Bill Jones arrested a man near Scoria cut for setting the grass on fire. Jones took the man to Mandan, made out the complaint and left the criminal in jail. Soon afterward the report came that he had been released and was found nearly frozen to death between here and Glendive. This report is now changed, and by good authority the man is said to be still in the Mandan jail. Something should be done in this case immediately. Jones is entitled to the reward offered for the arrest of anyone setting fire to the grass, when up to the present time he has not even had his expenses paid. The board of the prisoner is a constant expense that Billings county will at some time have to pay. The total costs now amount to about $20[illegible] and it is time this useless expense was stopped.
Geo. Wilkes wants it distinctly understood that no one shall take anything from the slaughter-house without his permission. Several tools are missing that he needs badly.

E. G. Paddock will immediately begin the erection of a first-class livery stable, 38x50 feet. The building will have drop siding, battlement front, two-inch ground floor, matched flooring to the hay loft and will be located on third street between Third avenue and Broadway.

Frank Walker was the victim of an extremely painful accident yesterday morning. He accidentally shoved his leg against a loaded rifle which was lying on a chair, in such a way that the hammer was pushed against a round of the chair and the rifle was discharged. The ball entered the leg just below the knee and shattered both bones. A very ugly wound was made and it is doubtful if the leg can be saved, although the attending physician, Dr. Robart will try to do so. Frank has the sympathy of the entire community and they all join in wishing him a speedy recovery.

By Jennie Wilkes.

Oh, how sad to see the red lips quiver,
The bright eyes filled with tears,
When two young hearts are parting
Forever or for many years.
The hands are clasped so tightly,
Tears on the white cheek lie,
When the last, last words are spoken:
Remember me—good bye.

I look in vain for the sweet blue eyes,
I breathe on the wind her name;
Oh, would that the echo might bring
That form to me again.
But the echo is all that I hear;
In vain for her I sigh;
I have watched that light form out of sight;
Oh, sad is the word, good-bye.

And memory calls forth another one
So haughty and so fair;
Her eyes like diamonds flash,
And jet black is her hair.
But I love the blue eyes better,
For gold her heart did buy;
She is linked by a golden fetter,
And we have said good-bye.

And oh! so many are gone
Where the sun shall never set;
Their eyes are closed forever
With tears to be never wet.
I have felt the clasp of many a hand,
Which cold in the grave now lie;
The lips are closed which uttered:
God bless you, Jennie, good-bye

So it is with all on earth—
We all must laugh and cry;
We never know how dear one is
Till we have said good-bye.
[illegible] as others live,
[illegible] [cal?]led to die,
[illegible] [pa?]ss to another world,
[illegible] said good-bye.

The following is the constitution of the Gun club as adopted last evening. All who wish to shoot must be on hand promptly at 1:30 Saturday afternoon as the contest will begin on time:

Constitution and By-laws of the Bad Lands Gun Club.

Sec. I. The name of this association shall be "The Bad Lands Gun Club."

Sec. II. The object of this association shall be to further the interests of rifle, shot-gun and revolver practice.

Sec. III. Membership in this association shall be obtained by receiving a majority of votes in any meeting containing a quorum of the association and by signing the constitution and paying the treasurer the sum of one dollar.

Sec. IV. Provided the weather will permit, weekly contests will be held on every Saturday afternoon, beginning at 1:30. The preliminaries and the kind of contest or contests to be decided by the executive committee.

Sec. V, Art 1. Rifle contests to be at ranges decided upon by the executive committee, provided they do not exceed one thousand yards, and to be subject to military rules. Each contestant to use the same gun at the several ranges, globe and peep sights barred except as permitted by military rules. Each contestant to have five shots at each range. Each contestant to pay the treasurer the sum of fifty cents before each contest or he is not entitled to shoot. The contestant having the highest average in any series of five contests to be awarded a new rifle not to exceed $25 in price. Each contestant when in town and able to shoot to be obliged to enter every contest in the series. Any contestant when unable to attend any contest may, at the option of the executive committee, shoot before them under the same rules as govern other contests to take place of the omitted contest.

Art. 2. Shot gun contests to be under the rules of Bogardus clubs.

Art. 3. Revolver contests to be at ranges not to exceed one hundred yards. Targets and ranges to be decided upon by the excutive committee governed by the same general rules as rifle contests, the prize to be a revolver not exceeding $15 in price.

Sec. VI. All disputes to be decided first by the executive committee and then by the next meeting of the association.

Sec. VII. This constitution to be amended by a three-quarters vote of any regular meeting having a quorum of the association, provided: the amendment is presented in writing and read at a previous meeting.

Sec. VIII. Membership fees to be used only for running expense of the club.

Executive committee:
A. T. Packard,
E. G. Paddock,
J. N. Maxwell.

We find that it is not as well-known as it should be, that the next meeting of the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association is to be held April 1.

It is absolutely necessary that every one interested should attend, as very important business will be brought up that all stockmen on the river are interested in and in the decision of which each stock owner should have a voice.

All round-up rules and arrangements will be discussed and these points especially need discussion. As all know, the Bad Lands are difficult to round-up thoroughly and it is absoutely necessary that there be a greater force on the round-up than there was last year. Each firm must not only be represented but well represented with good cow-boys and good horses. There will unquestionably be legislation on this subject.

There seems to be a growing sentiment that the rule passed at the last meeting naming ten as the number of bulls to the hundred cows is too high, a number favoring eight and a few six. It would seem best to keep the number of ten until the experiment can be tried thoroughly. It is a fact not to be denied that the calf crop is away below what it should be. It is also a fact beyond doubt that not one-third of the outfits on the river have even six bulls to the hundred cows. To this lack can be directly traced the small percentage in calf crop. There is but little doubt that every cattle firm on the Little Missouri intends increasing their herd. The matter then can be very easily decided. Try ten bulls for this year and have a committee decide as carefully as possible, the increase in the calf crop. If the increase pays a good per cent. on the cost of the bulls keep the number ten. If not, the number can be changed. At any rate, the experiment is well worth trying.

Another problem is now confronting our cattlemen. It is the question of buying yearling bulls. There is no question that these are the best to buy, provided they can weather the first winter all right. But right here comes the chief objection to them. No better herd of bulls has been driven into this country than the herd of yearling shorthorns driven to the E 6 ranch last summer. Many of them, in spite of the best of care, have died and the usefulness of the remainder could be seriously questioned. In such points as this comes in one of the great advantages of an association. They can all be discussed and from different experiences, many will learn valuable lessons. A list of these points should be made and brought up at different meetings.

The Kansas legislature has probably by this time passed a law which will effectually do away with the proposed Texas trail, at least so far as it relates to Kansas. The proposed law provides that no cattle capable of communicating Texas, splenic or Spanish fever shall be driven in or through Kansas between the first day of March and the first day of December. For every offense it provides a penalty of one hundred to two thousand dollars fine or from thirty days to one year in prison or both fine and imprisonment. The enactment of this law seems to be almost certain and as a prevention to the spread of Texas fever until its cause, origin and cure can be arrived at will receive the endorsement of every fair-minded man. That there is danger in the so-called Texas fever, there is no doubt. That the danger has been exaggerated there is also but little doubt. Both sides have a strong partisan following and both sides bring up extreme views. We hope the matter will be settled this year as prohibitory laws such as Kansas proposes passing are a great blow to cattle interests both north and south. The fact remains however that justice demands a strict investigation before allowing Texas cattle to be driven north indiscriminately.

Since the beginning of our crusade in favor of polled or muley cattle and Aberdeen Angus especially, a number of new converts have been made and old ones have come to light. The last one heard from is Dr. J. J. Clemmer, of Clemmer & Dell, of Cave Hills. Dr. Clemmer writes from his home in Cresco, Iowa, that he is pleased to see our advocacy of Aberdeen-Angus and that he is himself a strong believer in the fact that they make the best range cattle. Dr. Clemmer recently purchased six head of imported Aberdeen-Angus at a cost of four hundred dollars a head. They are registered in the Scotch and American Aberdeen-Angus herd books. A $600 Angus bull is at the head of the Cave Hills herd and is by long odds the best bull they have. He is now and has been in perfect condition and although a dogy is a better rustler than any of their old cattle. Dr. Clemmer is especially enthusiastic over his grades. They possess all the prominent characteristics of the thoroughbreds and for beef especially are better than any other grades. We are glad that at least one herd in our vicinity can soon show the practical effect of Polled-Angus blood and we will keep track of them in our columns.

Considerable trouble and bloodshed in Texas is being created by the stagnation of business in Mexico. Roving bands of Mexicans have repeatedly crossed the Rio Grande and driven off hundreds of Texas cattle. This has led to many encounters in which a number of Mexicans were killed. A truce has now been patched up although there is little hope of its continuance.

"Say what you mind," remarked Mayor Routt the other day; "but if you say anything of me, say I am a Polled-Angus enthusiast. That is just what I am. I tell you, sir, those Polled-Angus cattle, as rustlers and stayers these cold winter days and nights, beat anything I have ever seen. Why, they do not care anything more for cold than does a Polar bear. During one of the severest days we had in Jaunary, a Polled-Angus heifer dropped a calf out in the field and then came to the barn. My men, thinking the youngster was dead somewhere, placed the cow under cover and took care of her. The next day the boys going across the field discovered her black calf hid in some big grass and as lively as a cricket. It was brought to the house, fed some warm milk, and to-day it drinks from a bucket whatever we give it and is worth a hunderd dollars, as surely as one dollar is worth another. I can't see but these black calves dropped, in the winter time—and we have several of them—do just as well as other breeds dropped in the middle of summer. The fact is, they like cold weather, and seems to disdain a warm shed.—[Col. L. S. Record.

The St. Paul papers had better stop commenting on cattle interests or get some one to give them pointers that knows the difference between a Texas steer and a cayuse.

The Pioneer Press and Globe have both laid themselves open to ridicule by their outrageous misstatements as to the cattle business. The Pioneer Press is alone responsible for the statement widely published in the east, that the losses in cattle would be from fifty to seventy-five per cent. It has never made a decent attempt to deny the charge and even if it had, it could never excuse the gross ignorance which allowed the publication of such a libel.

As if the action of the Pioneer Press were not enough, the Globe must also air its ignorance. A short time ago it published an article that certainly is news. Among other rubbish, it states that stock detectives in the spring are employed to gather small herds of cattle that may have wandered a hundred miles from their range and "get stray cattle back to their proper place." The writer of that article couldn't for the life of him tell the difference between a round-up and a maverick and still he has the nerve to write about subjects of which he knows as little.

The article goes on to state that: "Cattle never freeze to death, but die quite often of starvation on account of the grass being covered with snow. The best way to winter cattle is to get them into the territory in the summer, for after a long tramp they are tired in their limbs and require much rest during which time they lose considerable flesh." Ye gods, another Daniel come to judgment!

The issue of the Globe of Feb. 28 contains other valuable lessons in stock raising—to pilgrims.

It states that: "It is not an infrequent occurrence on the western plains to have enough cattle stolen from a herd at one time to stock a Pennsylvania grazier's farm." And again that: "Our bold western robber will drive off enough big cattle to fill two large stock cars, and in broad daylight will ship them into the Chicago stock yards, butcher them, sell the meat, and then ship the hides to an eastern tanner, buy the leather back, and trade it to the rightful owner of the cattle for a Texas bull."

And finally the article winds up with the statement that "eastern folks have a good deal yet to learn from our wild western ways."

We know the experience exactly, for "we have been there." Not more than a life-time ago, we came to this country and two months after arrival had learned that a hackamore was not an article of diet and that "chapps" also could not be taken internally. We also had several seances with bucking broncos and consequently thought that about all we lacked was a quirt and sombrero to be a full-fledged cowboy. Cold experience soon taught us, however, that as much study and knowledge is required to conduct the stock business as almost any other. The writer in the Globe has just come from the east and if endowed with ordinary common sense will first be a scholar before he attempts the role of teacher. Meantime an inspector should be appointed to put all his stock notes in the "Smiles" column, where they belong.

There is a genuine cattle queen in the person of Mrs. Rogers, who lives between the King ranch and Corpus Christi, about fifteen miles from the latter place. Her first husband was a cow-man named Rabb. Right here I should explain that a decided distinction and difference exists between a "cow-boy" and a "cow-man." The former is a hired man who rides after the herd; the latter is his employer who owns the cattle. Well, after Rabb, from a small beginning and by good management and thrift, had accumulated a herd of 40,000 cattle, he died and left all to his better half, who had been a helpmeet in every sense of the word, and not only understood the cattle business, but had managed it successfully during her husband's long illness. Widow Rabb was not only thrifty, but she was pious and belonged to the Methodist persuasion. A young preacher by the name of Rogers came along, under whose ministration she grew in grace, and the result was a matrimonial one, although the odds in age were in favor of the parson by something like twenty-three years. She had no children and he had seven, but she took the motherless babes under her wings and the alliance turned out in every way successfully. Rogers had not long been married to the widow and her cattle when he acquired a bad case of bronchitis and was compelled to give up preaching. Such cases are frequent. But the widow gave him notice that she was competent to run the ranch and has kept the cattle in her own name, Rogers knowing no more about them than any of the neighbors. He took to politics when he found his services were not needed at the ranch and is now the democratic member of the legislature from Nueces county. Mrs. Rogers, although worth a round million, lives in quite an humble home and appears to have no ambition further than to carry on the business her husband left her and accumulate money and cattle. She goes to Corpus Christi every week or so to sell stock or purchase supplies, but has no taste for dress or society. She is fifty-three years old, but rides a horse like a cow-boy and does not even own a carriage. She never entertains any one except the few people who visit her place on business and lives in the plainest possible manner.—[Inter-Ocean.

"The history of red polled cattle can be carried back far into the last century. Suffolk had from time immemorial its breed of polled cattle, producing butter which, 150 years ago, was asserted to be 'justly esteemed the pleasantest and best in England. Arthur Young, in his 'Survey,' (A. D. 1794), defines the area—'a tract of country twenty miles by twelve, the seat of the dairies of Suffolk'—which, he said, must be peculiarly considered the headquarters of the Suffolk polled stock, though he found the breed spread over the whole country. In this 'Survey' we get the first accurate description of the breed. Though Young makes no note of Norfolk polled cattle, yet advertisement of sales held in and from the year 1778 prove that dairies of such animals were numerous in the country, and that they extended from the northern boundary of the Suffolk 'headquarters' well into the center of Norfolk. "Many of the old Suffolk polled cattle were much more massive beasts than the Norfolk; and this characteristic is still in evidence. They could easily be picked out from a collection by the comparative coarseness of the head—a difference which is now but seldom manifest. In other points there were but few divergencies in character between the two varieties. "There has been great improvement in the spring of the rib and in the outline of the carcass since that time, but otherwise the characteristics of the breed remain as they were. Clean, thin, short legs, a clean throat with little dewlap, a springing rib with large carcass, a large udder, loose and creased when empty milk veins very large and rising in knotted puffs to the eye, are points in a good red polled cow now as they were in Arther Young's days. The deep red harmonizes well with the landscape, and the docility of the cows recommend them as park cattle. "As graceful as the Devon, the red polled has the additional advantage of hornlessness—in itself no little gain where horses also run in the pastures, or where the stock sent to market have to make a long railway journey. Red polled cattle are found to lay on flesh rapidly on pasture of the poorest character, where other breeds need to have an additional supply of richer food.—[H. F. Euren.

Mandan Pioneer: It is stated, on what may be regarded as pretty good authority, that the grand jury will be called upon, at its forthcoming meeting, to investigate the charge against the Marquis de Mores of shooting the hunter Luffsey. It will be remembered that Luffsey met with his death about a year and nine months ago at Little Missouri. The case was brought before Justices Bateman and Collins at Mandan, both of whom acquitted the marquis. They did not think the marquis had committed any crime, but held that if he was the one who shot Luffsey he did it in self-defense.

Vic. Smith has again gone off on one of his "neck or nothing" expeditions. He started last night for a point several hundred miles above Fort Buford and will there buy a skiff and float down the big Missouri shooting beaver as soon as the spring break-up commences. If the trip is a success it will probably net a large amount, but it seems to be about ten to one that Vic's. skiff will be ground to pieces by the ice before he is fairly started. The best wishes of every one follow Vic. on his perilous trip.

The raffle last night for Frank Walker's rifle, belt and knife was the largest that has yet been held in the country. Every man who was in town was seen by Johnny Munro and all put their names down with one or two exceptions. A hundred and twenty-four chances were sold and the outfit was finally won by Frank Katela. The proceeds will be a great help toward paying Walker's bills while convalescing. He wishes to express his thanks to all his friends who have thus come to the rescue in time of need.

The cow-boys who delayed the train at Mingusville will find that they have a pretty large contract on their hands when they buck against the government by obstructing the mail, even though it was but for a moment. A number of them have already been arrested and taken to Helena. This outbreak was, of course, the result of a drunken spree, but that is no excuse in law or common sense. It is just such foolishness as this that has given cowboys the hard name that some tenderfoot recruits take pride in trying to keep alive. There is no more excuse in a man wearing a gun in town than there is in carrying a mountain howitzer and the very men who make the greatest display of going loaded are the only ones who could at any time be suspected of cowardice.

Mr. M. Wadsworth was in town yesterday and from him we have learned the most definite and the most favorable stock news we have learned this winter. There are over three thousand cattle in the Bad Lands Cattle Co's. outfit, of which Mr. Wadsworth is manager, and line riders have ridden over thirty miles every day this winter, going and returning through the herds. Mr. Wadsworth himself has done considerable riding and the most diligent search of all concerned has resulted in the finding of less dead cattle of his brands than can be counted on one's fingers. In addition to Mr. Wadsworth's men, four hunters have been on his range all winter and the number of dead animals found, after having thoroughly examined almost every clump of bushes, is included in the above number. Of course there are other dead animals that have not been discovered but few enough have been found to show that the loss will be very light. One or two other brands have not been so lucky but the loss on all cattle will undoubtedly be far less than was feared. Cattle are now in splendid condition for this time of the year and no further losses need be feared unless the weather changes very materially.
School closes this week. Arrangements will probably be made for another term.
Chas. Cook has received a large supply of oranges and lemons and we know from experience that they are excellent.
If any one thinks Peter Book hasn't a good command of the English language, he ought to have heard his remarks when he found he had up his three hundred yard sight at the two hundred yard range.

As spring opens up and our people begin again to plan their summer's work, we can see that Medora will more than keep up her reputation of being the best town on the road, in proportion to her size. Many buildings will be erected and new businesses will be established.

A prominent characteristic of western life was exemplified in the raffle last night. Although the rifle and outfit were not worth a quarter of the amount realized for it, everyone, and especially the working men were eager to help out the unfortunate man lying on a bed of suffering and all did their share and stood ready and willing to do as much more. In this connection it may be well to notice the generous donation of $50, given by W. B. Wright, before any other attempt to raise funds was made.

Frank Walker, an account of whose accident we published last week, is today resting easily. It was found necessary yesterday morning to amputate the leg, the amputation being preformed by the attending physician, Dr. Robart. The patient stood the operation well and is improving since. After the operation it was found that the bones had been so shattered that it would have been impossible to save the leg in any event. The operation was a complete success and if septic poisoning does not set in there is every chance of recovery. Provided everything is favorable, the patient will be out on crutches in three or four weeks.

Gen. Grant's condition is very serious and although there has been no definite report to that effect, there seems to be little doubt that that he is suffering from a cancer or some malignant affection of almost as serious a nature. Not till after his death will the true nobility of his grand character be appreciated.

Probably the sickest lot of sore-head political tricksters that were ever congregated together, can now be found in Bismarck. The capital removal bill passed both houses of the legislature, but there was "one wide ribber to cross" before it became a law. The Governor had to affix his signature, and right here is where the combination was broken. He vetoed the bill and gave as a reason for his veto such legal reasons as are absolutely unanswerable. Wisely passing by the manifest facts that the removal bill was originated by Pierre town-site boomers and supported only by this mercenary spirit and one of revenge, the Governor confined his reasons to the legal side of the question and conclusively proved that the seat of government could never be legally changed as long as Dakota remains a territory. Governor Pierce seems to have a happy faculty of doing exactly as he pleases and always doing right. Not a trace of political corruption has fastened to him, and although he has had to decide many vexed questions, over which there had been bitter wrangling, the unanimous verdict of the people has been that he has decided them all in a perfectly unprejudiced manner,

Reports from all sections of the country both east and west show that this has been an exceptionally hard winter on stock. Cattle and horses, especially the former, are looking very hard. Feed has been plenty but the unusual fall of snow has made it hard to get at. It is not expected that there will be any overwhelming losses, but a larger percentage than for several years past will be the result of the hard winter. The Bad Lands will suffer with the rest, but not as severely, as the fall of snow has been less here than in less favored localities. Chinooks have only visited us two or three times this winter and but once have been of sufficient duration to entirely uncover the grass. Some of the beginners in stock business are feeling a little blue over the prospects, but old timers say that "lightning seldom strikes twice in the same place" and are confident that next year will fully recover the losses of this year. There must be some exceptions to the general rule, therefore a hard winter must be looked for occasionally.

It is doubtful if any cattle will be driven from Texas this season. The railroads will not run the risk of damages from contagion, and Kansas and Nebraska have both adopted quarantine laws that are prohibitary as far as Texans are concerned. It is to be hoped that Texas fever will be investigated immediately and a cure discovered, if found to be as represented. The virtual loss of a market will be borne with difficulty by Texas cattle growers and it may be that this market is lost without reasonable cause. The best thing for the Texans to do is to have a thorough and expert examination of the source and effect of the disease and published the facts to the world. Their simple statement that there is no danger in Texas fever will now go for nothing until they prove it.

"Many are watching with great interest the steady onward march of those noble bovines of color. I believe the Missouri gentleman was correct when he said, 'The black cattle will take the country as the black hogs have.' Fifteen years ago black hogs were being introduced into Kansas and now no other kind has hardly been seen for more than five years. The progress of the cattle must necessarily be much slower, they not being so prolific as the hog. Let us stop with cattle. I rejoice to see the black muleys adorned with the many blue ribbons which they have been receiving of late and which they so well deserve. The sweeptakes prize won at the Kansas City fat stock shows last November by the Aberdeen-Angus heifer (Bride) for best dressed carcass, and the sweepstakes prizes won recenty at the World,s Fair at New Orleans by the three-year-old Golloway steer, when we consider their competitors, was a grand victory for the muleys. Happier, more contented, independent, devil-may-care sort of beings never lived. Twenty degrees below zero don't freeze them. They take on fat as readily as the slow and easy fat and greasy happy-go-lucky sort of people who laugh and grow fat. No one ever saw a black muley look sad; not even when he was being separated from his kin folks to be taken miles away never to see them again. Being without weapons, nothing fears him. Judging others as harmless as himself, he fears nothing. Further I would say that the black muley is the most cheerful, substantial, good-natured, contented, companionable bovine that your correspondent has ever had the fortune to form an acquaintance with, and i would rather feed one of them than a thousand long-horns.

The following is an account of the adventures of Jones & Pennell's outfit, written by Uncle John Seaton, whom all will remember as the one who always put up the jobs on the boys for which Bob and Joe always had to stand the blame:


Sec. 8, Croton Aqueduct, Yonkers N. Y.

A. T. Packard.

Dear Sir.

Permit me to give you a short history of our wanderings and doings since leaving Medora, the queen city of the Bad Lands. Leaving about the 16th of July last in company with your well-known friend Joe Pennell Esq. to join his partner who had taken a contract on the Canadian Pacific on the north shore of Lake Superior. This we completed on the 21st day of Dec. last, giving entire satisfaction to the company and gaining considerable notoriety as rail road builders. After remaining in camp some weeks to settle our business affairs we on January 13, received a telegram from Mr. T. G. Jones to move our forces immediately to this point where he had taken a contract of three miles of tunnel work. On leaving our camp in Ontario we fitted up six sleds to haul our baggage, blankets some rations for ourselves and forage for our mules, making comparatively a very light load, particularly our baggage which consisted of what wearing apparel we had on our persons. We anticipated rather a tedious though pleasant trip. However after encountering the snow a few hours, which measured four feet in depth, the thermometer ranging from forty to sixty below zero, atmosphere damp and heavy, we were induced to change our notions of pleasantness and felt somewhat disappointed. Anxious however to return to a "land of milk and honey" we pressed forward and accomplished our undertaking without a murmur from one of the fourteen persons composing our company. Three pairs of heavy wool mitts, four pairs of stockings of like character with Arctic overshoes, moccasins or shoepads. Even with that protection, our hands and feet suffered some from cold. Our sojourn in Ontario hardened our cheeks to such an extent that I am happy to say none were touched the slightest with frost. A few days out convinced us of the impossibility of proceeding further with our sleds, which we were reluctantly compelled to abandon at Pic River, one of the tributaries of Lake Superior, having yet one hundred miles to go before reaching rail road transportion. We had but a limited time to perform the journey, the train making only weekly trips and in the event of our missing it would compel us to remain over a week. We lighted up and packed our mules with our blankets, a small amount of rations for ourselves and some forage for the animals. Mounted on the hurricane deck of a hungry mule, we set out to cross a portion of the lake a distance of about forty miles, with quite a depth of snow on the ice and a very imperfect trail. In the afternoon we missed a certain point steered for, losing our way. We continued travelling until some time after dark, when we discovered the outlines of timbers, which proved to be a small island and afforded us good shelter. Here we made rather a comfortable camp for the night the mercury indicating about 46 below. At daylight the next morning we were again on the trail, fighting snow on an M. T. stomach arriving at our point of shipment about 1 o'clock P. M. We made an attack on the dinner table at the hotel groaning under the luxuries of Ontario, i. e. dried apples, condensed milk and oat meal porrage, which we devoured in a ravenous manner, much to the chagrin of the host and hostess. Shipping our stock to Medora and ourselves to this point, we arrived on the 14th inst., where we found Mr Jones busily engaged with a large force of men and first-class machinery, boring into the bowels of the earth to reach the top of the intended tunnel below, a distance of about fifty-seven feet through a solid rock, classed by engineers as gneiss, about like the ordinary lime stone in the west. The tunnel in length is twenty-eight miles, with twenty-six shafts, in depth of from forty to four hundred and seventy feet to top of tunnel, excavation sixteen by sixteen feet, to be bricked and cemented, for the purpose of conveying fresh water from Croton river to N. Y. city. Forty million dollars have been appropriated for the work, but it is thought a much larger amount will be requested before completion. Near our work is located one of the largest carpet factories in the country, turning out daily three miles or five thousand two hundred and eighty yards of carpet, and employing twenty-two hundred young ladies, in age from fifteen to thirty years. They are now on a strike for higher wages. As many of your ranch men and cow boys are leading bachelor lives in the far west it is suggested by Mr. T. G. Jones to follow the example of Gov. Andrews of Massachusetts, who, many years ago shipped a cargo of young ladies to California, and they were successfully married off to good husbands, many who in after years became wealthy and distinguished men. Should this experiment be carried out Mr. Joe Pennell who is so well and favorably known in the west, will be appointed Gen'l. Superintendant for the east and will be ably assisted by Mr. Howard Eaton with headquarters at Medora, who will receive them on their arrival and see that they are well cared for and properly distributed. No better appointments could be made and we feel assured that they have few superiors in handling a "calico brigade". We will watch the movements of things here, and report progress.

Yours & c.

J. P. S.

Bismarck, Dak., Special Telegram, March 3.—That the threats uttered occasionally during the past six weeks, by southern members in the heat of debate, that the north had not yet heard the last of the capital removal were intended to be carried out, was proven to-day by the resurrection from the special house committee of the bill relocating the capital at Pierre. The committee who have had charge of the bill for several weeks, last consisted of Messrs. Southwick, Huntington, Miller, Mark Ward and Williams. The first three gentlemen reported the bill back, recommending that it pass with the amendment that the capital should not be removed from Bismarck to Pierre until the 1st of May, 1885. Messrs. Ward and Williams submitted a minority report unfavorable to the bill. A motion was at once made to adopt the report, this being followed by another to indefinitely postpone further consideration of the bill, and this in turn by a motion to lay the motion to indefinitely postpone on the table. A call of the house was then ordered, and the last motion carried by a vote of 25 to 23. Of the southern members, Messrs. Clark, Huntington, Johnson, Huston, Langen, Dewoody and Mark Ward, voted in the negative. No sooner had the vote been announced than a bombshell was fired into the ranks of the South Dakotians in the form of a resolution offered by Mark Ward, charging W. S. Wells and V. P. Prentice of Pierre with

The committee appointed by the house today to investigate the charges of bribery, met in the parlors of the Sheridan House this evening and organized for work. Some preliminary evidence was taken. Prentice was called before the committee and denied the charges, claiming ability to prove his innocence. Prentice and Wells will appear before the committee to-morrow, at 10 o'clock, with an attorney to conduct their cases. The names of Dewoody and Pierce, members of the house, have been mentioned in connection with the case. Rich developments may be looked for to-morrow.

As an offset to Mark Ward's bribery resolution introduced recently into the house, the opposite party introduced another in the council, through Westover, which reads as follows:

Resolved, That a committee of five be appointed by the chair to investigate charges of corruption and attempted corruption of members of this legislative assembly, and the offer of bribes by Alex McKenzie, A. W. Edwards, L. G. Johnson and W. F. Steele, for the purpose of influencing votes upon the question of the removal of the capitol, now pending before the legislature, and that said committee be instructed to proceed at the earliest possible moment to take action in regard to such charges and to procure witnesses and take testimony.

and that they report their action and findings with all convenient speed.

After presenting the resolution Westover spoke excitedly for some ten minutes, claiming that definite knowledge had come to him that the gentlemen named had made corrupt offers to certain members, and that the same could be proved. Nickeus objected to the insertion of Steele's name, as that gentleman is a member of the house, and that one house had no right to investigate the action of a member of the other. Pettigrew spoke for several minutes in support of the motion, taking the ground that the council had a perfect right to call Steele as a private citizen before its committee. The motion passed, and Westover, Gamble, Lamoure, Twomey and Farmer were appointed a committee of investigation.

IN THE HOUSE

this morning the northern members made an attempt at delay on capital removal by moving that the clerk be ordered not to transmit the bill passed yesterday until ordered by a majority vote of the house. This called out hot words from the friends of the bill, and for nearly an hour the usual wrangle occurred, but the motion was finally lost, by a vote 25 to 23, the same as that of yesterday on final passage; consequently the bill was transmitted to the council this afternoon, where it was given a second and third reading and referred to the special committee who have had charge of a similar council bill for the past six weeks.

After disposing of the capital removal bill, the house settled down to business and passed a large number of bills, among which were Smedley's railroad bill, Gamble's bill providing for the organization of new counties, and Washabaugh's bill calling a constitutional convention at Sioux Falls in September.

These bills will doubtless receive the governor's approval. The railroad bill calls for the appointment of three commissioners, one each from North, Central and South Dakota. It is generally conceded that the Central Dakota appointment will be tendered Col. Smeadly, who is the father of the bill and well informed on the subject of transportation. The name of Alex Griggs of Grand Forks has been prominently mentioned as the candidate of North Dakota, while in the south there are several candidates for the office. The council committee on election reported Pickler's woman suffrage bill back to-day, with an amendment submitting the question to a vote of the people at a general election next November, recommending the bill to pass as amended.
