THE CAPITAL BILL

was next put upon its third reading. It has been conceded by the north for some time past that the bill would pass the council, the only question being by what majority. Nickeus, determined to furnish some amusement and perhaps worry the south a little, moved to amend by striking out the words "Pierre, Hughes county," and inserting "Stone Falls, Minnehaha county." This caused laughter at Pettigrew's expense. After the amendment was voted down Nickeus moved to insert Brookings in place of Pierre. This motion at once brought Natwick to his feet, who, taking the matter in earnest, stoutly protested that Brookings did not want the capital. This amendment was also voted down. The south then began to suspect that Nickeus meant to amend by moving to insert the name of the town of each southern member in turn, and the spectators were also of the same opinion. To preclude the possibility of any such procedure, Pettigrew jumped to his feet and moved the previous question which was carried. The bill was then put on its final passage and carried by a vote of 14 to 10.

Affirmative—Cameron, Dray, Duncan, Farmer, Gamble, Huetson, Jones, Kennedy, Natwick, Pettigrew, Smedley, Washabough, Wells, Westover.

Against—Austin, Bowdle, Flittie, La Moure, McLaughlin, Nickeus, Richardson, Twomey, Wagner, Walsh.

The fact that but forty-one of the seventy-two members of the legislature voted for its passage is strong argument in favor of the supposition that an executive veto will be attached. Gov. Pierce has also put himself upon record by depreciating any further agitation of the former troubles on the ground that such action would be inimical

to the best interests of the territory. The south places great emphasis on the fact that, as amended, the bill provides the removal shall not take place until May 18, 1886, claiming that removal at that late date will do much to secure division, an object dear to every South Dakotian's heart. On the other hand, the northern men claim, and with apparent good reason, that the territory cannot break the contract entered into with Bismarck, whose citizens have proceeded in good faith throughout. Great excitement prevails, but citizens of Bismarck do not feel greatly alarmed as yet at the prospect of losing the capital. After the disposal of the capital question, the council took up Pickler's woman suffrage bill, recently passed by the house and reported back from the committee yesterday with an amendment that the question be submitted to a vote of the people at the general election in November. Some discussion occurred on the bill, and an amendment inserting November 1886 instead of 1885 was lost by a vote of 13 to 11; Pickler meantime rushing hither and thither on the floor in the endeavor to secure support for his measure. It soon became evident, however, that the friends of the bill were

IN THE MINORITY.

Nickeus was their chief champion, while Gamble led the opposing forces, most of the other members remaining silent. On the roll call the bill was carried by a vote of 19 to 5, the only members voting in the nega-

tive being Gamble, La Moure, McLaughlin, Washabaugh and Walsh. Several who voted in the affirmative did so in the belief that woman suffrage would be snowed under by a large majority if submitted to a vote of the people. There are but ten members of the council really in favor of extending the ballot to woman. This vote practically kills the bill, as when sent to the house the amendment will not be concurred in. There are several principles to be observed in new towns which must be followed out if the town is to be a success. Chief among these principles is the one of "help your neighbor." It is a very easy thing and a very short-sighted thing to say, "we are not here for our health," and then send out of town for what you want instead of patronizing home industries, or perhaps start an opposition to one already established because there seems to be a little money in it and the idea never occurs to these men that where there is a living for one there will be starvation for two. But, some one will say, we can get our own goods cheaper in this way. Let us see if you can. A successful town is one where plenty of money is in free circulation. The mere fact that it passes rapidly from hand to hand is enough to guarantee the success of the town. Every one is satisfied because every one has money. On the other hand, take the extreme case of a town where every one buys where he can buy the cheapest. Nine times out of ten, especially in a small frontier town, this must be at some large town in the east. In this case then, all the circulating medium that we spoke of in the former illustration as going to make a successful town is sent away and the consequence is inevitable. The town is as dead as a horse-thief at a Montana neck-tie social. This illustration of all the money being sent out of town is, of course an extreme one, but it serves to establish the principle which serves to make a successful place. Looking at the matter in this light, is it not perfectly manifest that it is more profitable to spend your money at home? Of course you pay more for the articles you buy, but you get correspondingly higher wages if you are a laboring man or more for your goods if you are a merchant. This principle we have illustrated is scarcely a greater factor in the success of a town than the principles of avoiding over-production and ruinous competition. Because one man makes money out of manufacturing an article it is no sign that two will. It is a very easy thing to glut the market in a small town and then the dealers are sure to lose. In any event, competition in a small town so divides the trade that neither of the competitors make any money. Take our own town as an illustration. There is not a business man in it who is not satisfied and making money. But there is not an established business here that can stand the division of trade that will inevitably follow competition. We have made these remarks, not because our people as a class are guilty of them, but because a few are and others may be mis-led into being guilty. "Let him, whom the shoe fits, wear it."
PASSED!! THE FENCE LAW ESTABLISHED AND THE HERD LAW REPEALED!!

The news was received last Friday that the Legislature had done a good action and earned the lasting gratitude of the stock industry by a repeal of the herd law and the establishment of a fence law.

To the energy of Mr. McCall, of Lawrence county and the active co-operation of all the other Hills members, Messrs. Wells, Washabaugh, Martin, Gregg and Sprague is due the establishment of this law. To them, more than to anyone else we looked for support of the measure, as there is a strict fence law in the Hills, and nobly did they do their work.

As first introduced by Mr. McCall, the bill called for a repeal of the herd law and the establishment of a fence law in the counties of Fall River, Custer, Pennington, Lawrence, Butte, Harding, Villard and Billings. Owing to the seeming lack of interest in his bill from Villard and Billings, Mr. McCall was on the point of striking out these two counties, when the committee from here went to Bismarck and induced him by a plain statement of facts to add the counties of Burdick, Ewing, Bowman, Dunn and McKenzie to the list already mentioned, in short, the whole western tier of counties from the Nebraska line on the south, to about sixty-five miles north of the rail-road on the north, embracing an extent of country about three hundred and twenty-five by fifty miles. In comparison to the whole of Dakota this is a very small part, but it contains the most of the valuable grazing territory.

Right here we wish to correct what we find to be a very prevalent opinion and one that was brought forward as a prominent reason why the bill should not pass. The establishment of the fence law by no means prohibits agriculture, but rather protects it, as it puts the industry exclusively into the hands of those who intend to follow it legitimately and not to see to what extent they could cinch the stockmen in blackmailing damages. To the former class, the stockmen never had any objection except to regard them with a kind of pity and to the latter class they can now bid defiance.

There was considerable opposition to this bill and it may be well to show the justice of its passage. There is but very little agriculture in the western tier of counties, the whole tier being practically given up to grazing. In a great part the whole country is unfit for agriculture, and with the exception of the Hills counties, the stock interests outnumber all others combined over a hundred to one. From the very nature of the country, this is not only so now but will be for all time. Except in a very few cases it is impossible to find a large enough tract to farm profitably and it almost invariably happens that such tracts are perfectly devoid of water. Where was the justice, then, in laying an onerous burden on stock interests and putting it in the power of the few to legally rob the many. Especially where was the justice, when there are so many other portions of Dakota for better fitted for agriculture and none others at all comparable to the Bad Lands for grazing. The Legislature has simply righted a wrong by passing the bill.

At the same time with this bill there was passed another, which we spoke of in a previous issue. It was the bill in reference to the changing of the boundary lines of Billings, Villard and Dunn counties. Before the passage of this bill, the counties ran east and west, with Dunn on the north, Billings in the middle and Villard on the south. The present boundaries of Billings county run on a north line which used to be the north line of Dunn county and if the latest maps are right, runs about ten miles south of the mouth of Beaver. The west line is the Montana line, the south line nearly cuts Chalk Buttes forty miles south of the railroad and the east line is about six miles east of Sully Springs. This bill, dividing the county, was not a popular one, and if it had been brought to a vote of the people, would have been defeated about seven to one. However, it was known that the fate of one bill depended in a measure on the other, and as the county was not organized, no direct opposition could be made. For the information of those who may wish to know, we will state here that Billings county as it was is responsible for all debts taxed up against the county and not Billings county as it is. In other words the territory making the debt is responsible for it, no matter whether its name is changed or not. Consequently the Villard county that is will have a good share of Billings county's debt to pay upon organization, a contingency not at all calculated upon by the framers of the bill.

It might be well also to state that the present eastern line of Billings county is the western line of Villard, that eastern extensions of Billings' north and south lines form the north and south lines of Villard.

After diligent search only two more dead cattle have been found on the Bad Lands cattle Co's range, in addition to the nine already reported. There must certainly be others but the scarcity of carcasses indicates that the loss is hardly more than it would be from natural causes.

There is very little danger to fear for the stock interests now, in the Bad Lands. Spring is well advanced and except for the usual shrinkage in flesh consequent upon the appearance of new grass, cattle will constantly improve in condition until the beef round-up.

Harry Tarbell, of the Little Missouri Horse Co., is decidedly in favor of using large mares as breeders. The maverick question should come up for consideration at the next meeting of our association. We suggest that it would be an excellent plan to apply the proceeds to the school fund. In a moment of temporary aberration we once indited a sonnet to "Chinook." We did hope to be forgiven for it but our contemporaries are ruthless in their revenge. They lighten the burden very materially, however, by crediting it to any other cattle paper in the country except the Cow Boy. The article also brings forcibly mind the old saw: "Great minds run in the same channel," for at least seven others editors wrote exactly the same article a week or two after it appeared in the Cow Boy. It may seem strange, but it must have been original with all of them, as it was not even credited to some other paper.

Experiments will be made by the Co. this seasan to secure a profitable feed for the cattle that are to held here for winter markets. It would be a good plan if others would also try experiments, as it is liable to be a profitable undertaking for those who will have weak cattle to feed. There is not much doubt that alfalfa will grow well, although its cultivation has never been tried here. There are several other kinds of grasses which are claimed to be equal or superior to alfalfa. There is no telling but that a year may come when it will be impossible to put up hay and a supply of alfalfa would be a god-send.

The result of several experiences has taught that it is not a good plan to keep water holes open during the winter. Animals that are supplied from these holes seem to totally lose their rustling instincts. They will fill themselves with water and stand around the hole until they are completely exhausted from cold and hunger. There is scarcely any feed on the river bottom and cattle must drift back to get grass. When forced to it cattle seem to do as well on snow as they do on water and as it is impossible to find water and feed together it is far better to keep cattle off the river in winter and compel them to develop rustling instincts. Each stockmen should in the fall make a determined effort to run cattle off the river and keep them off. It means a sure loss in condition and probable death to all cattle that stay on the river bottom, especially if they can find a water hole to stand around. Experience is the best teacher and it has certainly taught the above facts.

The difference in opinion concerning the price of running a herd per head is remarkable. It varies from ninety cents to three dollars per year. Of course, much of this difference is due to the difference in the size of the herds, the larger ones being run proportionately, much cheaper. There is also a vast difference in the ranch expenses, with the profitable side, we believe, in favor of a liberal, rather than an economical policy. This will increase the cost of keeping, per head, but it will more than be made up by a decrease in loss. For instance, line-riding is an expensive thing to keep up and the outfits that practice it are liable to have larger expenses per head than those that do not. We will guarantee, however, that these outfits will not stop line-riding on this account for the cost is far more than made up in rescuing poor cattle and calves from death. Thus it is manifest that the outfit which spends the least money may in reality, be the most expensively conducted and vice versa. These remarks are occasioned by the fact that several exchanges quote the proportionate price for running different outfits as illustrating good or bad management.

The editorial harp is hung on the willow as far as the prize gun is concerned.

No one as yet has a sure thing on the gun and in any event all should be promptly on hand to shoot. If all should stop shooting who do not expect to win, the Gun club would soon be a thing of the past. The next shoot will begin promptly at 1:30, Saturday afternoon.
Joe Ferris has already entered the potato race.
John Warn is still holding it down in Bozeman, waiting for court to sit.
A pair of nickle-plated club skates will be given to the best lady skater, the contest to come off in about six weeks.

The Bismarck steam laundry deserves to "get there" if any firm does. Promptly on the day the amount of their bill for advertising comes without word from us. Such a manner of conducting business is rare enough to call for special commendation.

Robert I. Sloan came up from the Hills Sunday on his way to New York. He is chief engineer of the New York elevated railroad and was in the Hills looking up the feasibilty of a Hay creek coal road into Deadwood. He thinks it would be a paying speculation but is far more in favor of a road from Medora to to the Hills. He thinks it would be the best paying branch of the N. P. Mr. Sloan is one of the first engineers in the country and his word carries great weight.
Miss Annie Brophy came down from Mingusville to the dance Tuesday evening.
The Chimney Butte ranch brand, the Maltese cross, is the latest addition to our brand columns.
Mike Sexton and Andy Corcoran came in out of the wilds Tuesday evening to celebrate with St. Patrick.
A. Young recently found the mare that he had advertised for some time. It had fallen into a sink hole about a hundred yards from his shack and smothered.
The skiventeenth of Ireland was duly celebrated last night at the rink and the light fantastic and one other toe were "shook." A most enjoyable time was had.

Messrs. McCall, Gregg, Martin, Wells and Sprague of the Legislature, came down from Bismarck Sunday night and the three latter left in company with seven others for the Hills Monday morning. Messrs. McCall, Gregg and Geo. Bell of Spearfish, stayed over and went yesterday morning.

Little Tommy, our Tommy, Tommy Kerr "bobbed up serenely from below," Tuesday evening. He leaves to-night for the west and again will the mantle of gloom descend upon us even as the peregrinating hen descends upon the June bug. Ke-good bye, Tommy, pe-come again.

The slaughter-house will be ready for business several weeks before cattle can be supplied. Work will begin as soon as there is a certainty of five hundred head a week, the capacity of the house being nine hundred head. Work will go on night and day and it is hoped that steam will not be completely shut off until next spring.

We are in receipt of a letter from Vic Smith, dated at Prplar Creek, March 10. He states that loss among the Wolf Point agency cattle is very heavy and that the Indians are living high on "frozen-to-death" beef. He also writes that times are booming in Medora in comparison to any other place he has found. He says nothing about his trip but we suppose he has started by this time. He gladdened the editorial heart by sending in some new subscriptions.

At first sight it seems like a gigantic and profitless undertaking, but the Co. will soon begin the erection of a barn capable of holding 10,000 cattle. They will be fed on hay enough to keep them in prime condition and slaughtered as they are needed. This can scarcely be called an experiment as it turned out a complete success in Duluth, where feed is much higher than it is here. The complete output for this year of the Continental cattle Co. has already been contracted. Last year it was 12,000 head. These cattle will all be killed here.
The sporting world has again come forth from its winter quarters and from time to time a column of "Sporting Notes" may be expected by our readers.

Wednesday the 15th of April, has been selected by Governor Pierce as Arbor day. It is especially requested that everyone should observe this day and plant as many trees as possible. For the purpose of doing more effectual work in this direction we will in our next issue call a meeting to be held in the Cow Boy office, to see what our citizens are willing to do in this direction.

The latest report states that Gen. Grant's condition is much improved. It is very doubtful if he can live long but the hearts of a whole nation quicken at the joyful news. At every opportunity he works on his history of the war and it is sincerly hoped that he will live long enough to complete it. His financial troubles and present sickness have buried in oblivon all the factional enmity toward him and now in his weak old age he is again gaining the place in the hearts of his countrymen that he held after the war.

The Mandan Pioneer makes us tired. It is raising a constant howl against ready-prints and then fills up three-fourths of its space with "snakes." The ready-prints contain the latest news in condensed form, besides much other interesting and live reading matter. The "snakes" are mostly old, mil-dewed stories and are at best but poor "filling," and scarcely ever make a good impression on the paper, a point which the Pioneer never wastes its valuable time in getting in any event. Cork up on ready-prints or be consistent and discard "snakes,' Mr. Pioneer.

The Dominion government is reaping the result of its tyrannical policy toward settlers and now has a good-sized rebellion on its hands in the Saskatchewan country. The uprising is headed by Louis Riel, of Red River fame and is raised because of the non-settlement of land claims. Riel was sent for from Montana to direct the settlers and for a long time counseled law-abiding measures. These utterly failed in their object and rebellion is the result. The rebels are well-armed and will make a desperate struggle for their rights. The Dominion troops and artillery are being sent forward and probably by this time an encounter has taken place.

A great deal of newspaper talk has been wasted over the prospective removal of Governor Pierce and as to who his successor will probably be. If the prospect worried the newspapers as little as it does the governor much less space would be occupied in its consideration and much less reason could be given by the president for his removal if all the governor's would-be friends would stop showing the likelihood of his removal and trying the hit-or-miss style of hewing out gubernatorial timber for the purpose of standing in with a new administration. President Cleveland has been nearly consistent in his practice of civil service reform rules, which he interprets about as follows: Office-holders should be removed for inefficiency, for mal-feasance of office or for taking an active part in politics, or for having retained office on account of the votes he controlled. Not a solitary one of these reasons can be brought to the governor's door and the president will have to find new reasons for the appointment of a Democrat as governor of Dakota. We believe the president is in earnest about civil service reform and consequently that Gilbert A Pierce will be governor for the next three years.

"In the wild, unfettered west, beware of the man who never carries arms, never gets drunk, and always minds his own business. He don't go around shooting out the gas, or intimidating a kindergarten school; but when a brave frontiersman, with a revolver in each hand and a bowie down the back of his neck, insults a modest young lady, and needs to be thrown through a plate-glass window and then walked over by the populace, call in the silent man, who dares to wear a clean shirt and human clothes."—[Bill Nye.

With all his humor and fiction, the above article shows that Bill Nye occasionally uses a good deal of sound common sense in his articles. It can be put down as a fact that four-fifths of the reckless shooting done in the west, is the work of some sap-headed tender-foot who wants to pose as a bad man. As long as these characters tackle other pilgrims, their true charactsr is not exposed and the police papers of the east will come out with another account of the way a bad man held up a guileless tender-foot, and the goal of another would-be bad man's happiness is reached by this publication. At some time, each one of these Police Gazette bad men will meet the quiet, unarmed man spoken of in the above article and each one will get his head everlastingly swelled externally to balance the internal swelling. This is the most accommodating country in the world to the man who is looking for a fight and the only reason these men are not exposed sooner is that they are careful to pick upon men whom they know will not resist.

From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
There will be a meeting of stockmen at the Merrill house, in Glendive, March 31.
The Musselshell and Yellowstone cattlemen hold a round-up meeting April 5th at Billings.
S. A. Marney, of the Stockgrowers' Journal passed through Medora last week on his way to Miles City.
The Mingusville cow-boys who made conductor Clark "trip the light, fantastic" are out on bail of $500 each.
Cattle rates in car load lots to Medora from St. Paul, are $75 for this season, with a reduction of $5 on ten or more cars.
Mr. Stotts, of Spearfish, started home Monday morning. He has been in Iowa buying cattle, all thoroughbreds or high grades, for his Redwater ranch in the Hills.

The Stockgrowers' Journal reports that 100,000 head of Texas cattle will be ready for a northern movement within the next sixty days. It is doubtful, however, if a solitary head will be forwarded, as the quarantine laws of Colorado, Kansas and New Mexico are prohibitary.

It seems strange that some of our stockmen do not drive in a good herd of cow-horses and keep them for sale. There is right now a large demand for them and over two hundred could have been sold on the river since last fall. Our stockmen are waking up to the fact that there is no economy in buying cheap cow-horses and there is now a ready sale for first-class animals.

We are in receipt of a letter from Julius LeMoyne, expressing regret that he could not attend the meeting of stockmen here on April 1. He is in favor of seven or eight good bulls rather than ten to the hundred of she cattle. He is also very favorably impressed with the merits of polled cattle for the range. He intends being in Medora some time in May.

Action should be taken at the coming meeting of the Little Missouri association toward getting a territorial veterinary surgeon. It will be two years before the legislature meets again but something can be done now toward the making of such an office. Such action is necessary because in all probobility a territorial veterinary surgeon will be appointed at the next session of the legislature and it is important that a competent man be appointed and not some ignoramus whose chief qualification is his political record.

We are in receipt of a letter from Theodore Roosevelt and the printed by-laws of the Little Missouri river Stockmen's Association. In the by-laws we notice that the number of bulls to the hundred cows has been changed from ten to seven. The letter contains the following official call:

"A meeting of the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association is hereby called for 11 A. M., Wednesday, April 1, 1885, to be held in Pennell Hall, Medora, Dak. Matters connected with the spring round-up will come up for discussion.".

THEODORE ROOSEVELT.
Chairman.

By the sale of Billy Paddock's ranch to [B. S.?] Lamb and with the stocking of this range the Little Missouri river front will be pretty well occupied for fifty miles up the river and fifty miles down. To our mind, however, there are other ranges off the river, tributary to Medora that are as good as, if not superior to anything on the river. One can scarcely go amiss in locating a range six or eight miles back from the river provided water can be obtained in good quantity. From the nature of the country, there is little danger of enough cattlemen coming in on the river to overstock the ranges.

The Montana legislature at the recent session passed a bill relating to stock inspection that, from all we can see, will be a great advantage. The territory is divided into two districts; Custer, Yellowstone and Dawson counties forming the first, and Choteau, Meagher and Lewis and Clark counties, forming the second. For each of these counties a cattle commissioner is appointed by the governor, each commissioner to be an owner of cattle, and all to form a territorial board of stock commissioners who shall have general control of stock interests and be authorized to punish any unlawful act against such interests. The board is authorized to appoint as many detectives as it sees proper who are empowered to make arrests as they may be necessary. One and one-half mills on the valuation of all stock is taxed against owners to pay expenses as incurred by these detectives. The commissioners are to receive no salary but the detectives will be salaried.

We presume the by-laws of our association are pretty generally known as they were published at the time of the December meeting. For the benefit of those who were not there we republish them:

1.—This Association shall be known as The Little Missouri river Stockmen's Association.

2.—The object of this Association is to advance the interests of stockgrowers and dealers in live stock of all kinds in western Dakota, and for the purpose of the protection of the same against frauds and swindlers, and to prevent the stealing, taking, and driving away of horned cattle, sheep, horses, and other stock from the rightful owners thereof, and to enforce the stock laws of the Territory of Dakota.

3.—The officers of the Association shall consist of a Chairman and Vice-Chairman, elected annually at the first meeting held after the fall round-up, and a Secretary, elected at each meeting, whose work is to be superintended by the Chairman.

4.—The representation in the Association is to be by firms, each firm being entitled to but one vote.

5.—There shall be at least two meetings of the Association annually; to be held at the time and place appointed by the Association; and at the request in writing of any three members of the Association a special meeting shall be called by the Chairman, who shall, however, give at least one week's notice thereof. Seven members shall constitute a quorum for transaction of business.

ORDER OF BUSINESS.

I. Calling the roll.
II. Reading minutes of last meeting.
III. Election of new members.
IV. Unfinished business.
V. Reports of officers and committees.
VI. Election of officers.
VII. General business.

7.—No member shall gather cattle on any range not his own during the months between December 1st and the date of general spring round-up, without giving due notice a reasonable time beforehand to the other ranchmen of the neighborhood.

8.—In order to attain greater efficiency in round-ups, we hereby agree to place our men under the orders of the foreman of the round-up, so long as they remain with it, and in case of refusal by any man to do faithfully and well the duty assigned to him, or to obey the orders given to him by the foreman, in driving, cutting out, and other work, we hereby authorize the foreman of any round-up to prohibit any man so offending from any further participation in said work.

9.—It is the sense of this Association, and is hereby made binding on its members, that any man who shall hereafter turn out any female neat cattle upon the range shall place with them, at the time of turning loose, not less than seven (7) serviceable bulls for every one hundred (100) head of female cattle which are two years old and upward at that time; and that on or before July 1st, of each year thereafter, every member shall supply the same proportion of bulls of the same usefulness and quality to all female cattle of the above age of which he may then be the owner. Proved violation of the above rule shall be deemed a proper subject for complaint, the penalty to be decided by a majority of the Association present at the next meeting.

10.—If any of the cattle companies or stockmen along the river refuse to obey the rules and by-laws of this Association, it will refuse to act with or allow them to take part in the round-up; and the captain of the round-up shall see that no stockmen debarred by action of this Association from participating in the round-up is allowed to take part in it, and he shall further see that no third party, acting in the interest of said stockman, is permitted to take part in or derive benefit from the round-up.

We have repeatedly stated that the estimate of the cattle loss was all guess work and we are now more than ever convinced of it. We will now make the broad statement that there is not a stockman on the river who can be certain within one or two per cent., of what his loss actually is. It is utterly impossible to tell, even after the round-up. More than ever are we certain however that the loss in the Bad Lands is less than three per cent.

Notice has been sent to all outside subscribers who are delinquent and if their subscription is not received by the next issue, their names will be taken from the list. It makes no difference who they are. One man's money is no better than another's and cash in advance is the only way to get the Cow Boy.

Local subscribers have not yet been notified, but the same rule applies to them.
Peter Book returned Monday from a trip to Mandan.
That umbrella won't be worth insuring if Levi flashes it up here.
Let all our readers remember that the best and consequently the cheapest wagon is the Studebaker.
Fisher's wood-pile scattered on him last night. Two or three loaded sticks will adorn the pile in future.
M. Wadsworth has gone west to buy a band of cow horses. He intends returning in time for the stockmen's meeting.
Both the new tanks have been put in position and the old one is now in the new slaughter-house ready to be set up.
Peter Book has secured contracts for the addition to the hotel, for the slaughter-house smoke-stack and for a cellar in the Marquis' house to contain heating apparatus.
The prize in the potato race at the rink, last Saturday evening, was won by Johnny Chute. It was a good race, anyone being winner until the last potato was corralled.

The Rev. Schaffner, of Dickinson, will preach at the roller rink, next Sunday evening at half-past seven. Everyone is cordially invited to attend and if we mistake not, a very interesting sermon will be preached.

About the time Billy Jones breaks his neck running his horse across the railroad bridge he will quit it. Pat O'Hara says: "Its gettin to be a notorious job minden the holes where his cayuse's fut wint tru."

Levi Deffebach returnd from his trip to Germany, Saturday evening. He is now stopping with his brother Rassie. His trip was not a success, neither is it as yet, a failure. A good lawyer has taken the matter in charge and is confident that he can yet get the fortune.

We are much pleased to state that Mr. Foster will be retained here as superintendent of the slaughter-house. No better selection could possibly have been made and it is beyond question that he thoroughly understands his business and will make a success.

W. B. Pryor, of Dickinson, will be here in about a week and open up a boot and shoe store. He will also be prepared for all kinds of work in the above line. He has bought a lot near the church and will build a shop.

A grand carnival and masquerade will be held in the roller rink, the evening of April 15. Admission and skates, fifty cents. No objectionable characters allowed. A prize will be given to the person wearing the best costume.

Next Wednesday evening, April 1, there will be a Stockmen's ball at the Pyramid Park hotel. There is no doubt that it will be a complete success as J. B. Walker has already established a reputation as a genial host, as have Misses Morrison and Guardient as entertainers. Everyone is invited.

The cattlemen up and down the river are much encouraged over the prospect and are all coming to the conclusion that the loss is even less than the most sanguine had hoped. There is now very little danger of the weather being poor enough to cause any serious loss. With the exception of a flurry or two of snew, there will doubtless be good weather until the spring rains.

John Warn, Jr., is dead. We doubt if the death of any animate being here, outside of a human, could have called forth the expressions of sorrow that were uttered at the death of this faithful dog. He was as loving and gentle as possible to canine nature. He was a friend to everyone and everyone was a friend to him. No cause can be assigned for his death except poisoning and if there lives a wretch here low-lived enough to have committed this crime; we hope he will be discovered and summarily dealt with.

The shoot was postponed last Saturday, owing to non-attendance of a quorum of the members. Weather permitting, the contest will begin promptly at 1:30, Saturday afternoon. This will be the fourth contest in the series, taking the place of the omitted one. The final contest will take place a week from Saturday. Persons who have missed a contest will be given an opportunity to shoot off their back scores.

Up the River.

Editor Cow Boy

Items are scarce as goose dollars up this way. Everybody is lying on their oars, waiting for the bull round-up, though some ranch work is being done.

Deacon Wade has finished a 200 acre pasture. Ferris and Merrifield are building a corral to hold the day-herd.

Sylvane Ferris has returned from a visit to New Brunswick a little used up by dissipation we suppose, but will be around all right soon.

Will Eaton has not got done telling about the good time he had in Pittsburg and by his improved appearance, it is evident he had. Pittsburg is not noted for its temperance proclivities.

Tarbell and Bond are at their Deep Creek ranch and pushing the world ahead of them. The improvements on this ranch are very fine. Bond, the irrepressible, has renounced all evil associations and is leading a virtuous life. Nitch, Billy Jones and others would do well to follow his example.

There was a musical and dramatical entertainment at Will Dantz's ranch the other evening. Jimmy Stevenson was the Prima Donna. It is astonishing, the amount of musical talent there is lying around in the Bad Lands. The frying-pan symphony by Alden Eaton was especially fine.

Rheumatism has brought a kink in Pete Pilausie's back, which is painful to see. It is to be hoped the warm weather will soon draw it out.

Cattle are daily improving and the prospects are of a good calf crop. A few have come already, some in the late cold weather which are curiousities in their way; minus tail, ears etc.

Big horn.

Mouth of Cherry creek.
Little Missouri Dak., March 17, 1885.

Editor of Bad Lands Cow Boy:

A man by the name of Thomas Gibson was killed by a bear on the 16th. inst, at a point in the Bad Lands about ten miles above Cherry creek. The circumstances as near as ascertained are as follows: He in company with one William Dixon, started from Medora to come down the Little Missouri on a raft. They met with an accident, losing one rifle and all of their camp outfit and provisions. They then came to my place where they remained two days. Making another raft they went on. The next night, Dixon came back and reported his partner killed by a bear, stating that they had discovered a den while looking for deer in a clump of cedar, that Gibson, rifle in hand, had crept up to the den and when in the act of looking in had been seized and killed without having fired a shot, that having no weapon of any kind himself, he stood helplessly by and waited until the animal, finishing Gibson turned on him when he fled. The following morning we returned with Dixon and found Gibson's remains about 30 feet from the mouth of the den. From all appearances he was instantly killed. The rifle was found within six feet of the den loaded and the hammer up. No papers could be found upon the person of the dead man to indicate the whereabouts of his friends or relatives but from conversation held with him while at my place I believe him to have come to Dakota from either Wisconsin or Michegan. Dixon took charge of his effects, which consist of nothing as far as we know, but some old clothing and a val'se. We buried him on the top of a high bluff in the Bad Lands near where we found him. Further particulars, should they be wanted by his friends or relatives, can be obtained by addressing William Keldch or Chas. Tracy, Cherry creek, Little Missouri.

Yours
H. F. Pullen.

Notice is hereby given that any contracts or bills made by any of the employes of the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co., will not be paid or recognized unless approved by W. F. Van Driesche, Treasurer.

Marquis de Mores, Pres't.
The robins will soon be here.
"Big-horn" makes a good correspondent and we hope to hear from him again.
John Warn writes from Bozeman that he hopes to settle the estate there and return soon.
The Marquis intends staying till after the stock meeting and will also attend the meeting at Miles City.

The hotel is rapidly progressing but will hardly be completed under a month. It will be first class in every particular. Arch Boyd has leased it and will run it to the best of his ability, which as already demonstrated, is of a high order.

Ed. Drury, of Mandan, deputy-sheriff of Morton Co., came Saturday night and left for home this morning. When he came he had a Derby hat but the atmosphere seemed to be too rare to have it last. At any rate Jim O'Hannigan don't know how it lost its symmetry.

The roof of the slaughterhouse has been raised five feet to admit of easy access to the ice boxes and now Mr. Foster says it is the most complete establishment for its size in the country. Everything is on the most approved and thoroughly tested plan and is complete in every respect.

The reported gold discoveries near Bismarck, still create intense excitement. As a speculation we wouldn't give a hundred dollars for all the genuine gold, native to the territory fifty miles around Bismarck. As far as we know or have heard from good sources there is no formation short of the Hills which has ever been found to be gold-bearing.

If there is a war with England, the United States and especially the northwest is on the eve of the most prosperous times it has ever seen. We have no great love for England especially since her Egyptian policy was adopted, which, however, is in a line with many of her former wars. Now Russia, Germany and France may singly or together make an attempt to curb the grasping spirit of the English. It is impossible to fully know the status of Europeans affairs but to a man up a tree it looks vastly as though there was going to be a war between England and some other European power or powers. An order received by Swift's and Armour's packing houses in Chicago for 9,500,000 pounds of canned beef to be shipped to Woolwich seems to mean business.

It is a matter of regret that the laws intended to preserve the game animals of this territory are not more closely observed. It is only a few weeks since three big-horn sheep, all ewes, were brought into town and sold. The man who killed them stated that each ewe carried two lambs. Here was a total of nine lives lost and all for the sum of ten or twelve dollars. Some of our readers are not aware of the stringency of the Dakota game laws. The settler is not allowed to kill game out of season even for his own use. For each sheep, deer, antelope or Buffalo, killed between Jan. 1st. and Sep. 1st. there is a fine of $100 and costs. Elk are cheap as the fine for killing them out of season is only ten dollars and costs. We feel sure that no objections will be made by the people against any man who kills a deer for his own use, but the selling of game out of season, must be stopped. Our large game animals are disappearing very rapidly and it will be but a short time until they are virtually extinct. Only a few years since there were repeatedly seen from fifty to a hundred deer in a day and 300 to 600 antelope but now they are few and far between.

The railroad from the Hay creek coal mines into the Hills is now almost an assured fact. This of itself, will not help Medora much, as its general direction will be eastward. In this connection, however we may say that had the Hills merchants stuck to their contract to ship via the N. P., over seventy miles of railroad would already have been built from here south and this year would have seen the other end in the Hills. This was the settled policy of the N. P. and the Hills merchants have only themselves to blame if they are without railroad facilities after this year.

The Little Missouri River Stockmen's Association.

In the absence of the chairman Theodore Roosevelt, the convention was called to order by H. S. Boice, vice-chairman.

The following new members were unanimously elected: Griffin Bros. & Ward, J. A. VanEeghan, Pierre Wibaux, E. G. Paddock and John Sawyer.

Willis Eaton moved that J. L. Truscott be elected secretary. Carried.

Howard Eaton moved that a committee of three be selected by the chair to appoint the time, programme and foreman of the spring round-up of this district after first conferring with a similar committee from Glendive and with the round-up committee of the Territorial convention at Miles City. As such committee the chair appointed J. L. Truscott, John Goodall and Wal. Osterhaut.

It was moved by M. A. Griffin that a stock inspector be appointed for Medora and that in case the convention at Miles City refuse to appoint one, that one should be appointed by this association and the expenses be borne pro rata by the members. Carried.

On motion of J. L. Truscott a committee was appointed to see that the above inspector be appointed. The committee consisted of J. M. Simpson, Geo. Towers and Howard Eaton.

The committee appointed to confer with similar committees relative to our round-up were to act in conjunction with the chairman of the meeting and he reported that it was their opinion, having already conferred with the Yellowstone committee, that Wal. T. Osterhaut be appointed foreman and that our round-up begin at the mouth of Box Elder, the point where the upper Little Missouri round-up ends, thence down the river to the motuh of Big Beaver, thence up Big Beaver until the southern Yellowstone round-up is met. The time of the round-up to be decided by the Miles City convention.

It was decided that stockmen on the river should round up the country for about forty miles east of the river and drive the bulk of the cattle back to the river before the general round-up. Adjourned.

A meeting was held Tuesday afternoon at Glendive by the stockmen holding cattle north of the Yellowstone. It was well attened.

The meeting was called to order by Col. Hodgson who nominated W. W. Newlon for chairman. Carried. W. W. Mabee was then elected sectreary and S. A. Marney and A. T. Packard, vice-presidents.

On motion of Col. Hodgson, Frank Gibson, foreman for Tussler & Co., was elected as foreman of the North Yellowstone round-up.

After considerable discussion as to the most feasible plans it was decided to keep all cattle back from the Yellowstone valley, ten to fifteen miles. Frank Gibson and C. R. A. Scobey, foreman of the Fayette Live Stock Co., were appointed to see that line riders were appointed and did their duty in this respect.

B. Esterbrook moved that the chair select a committee to select another committee to go to Miles and look after the interests of Yellowstone stockmen.

L. P. Williamson moved that bulls be kept off the range between Nov. 1 and July 1, and that a committee be appointed to see that this rule be stricly enforced. During the discussion of this question, which was all favorable, it was brought out that one or two outfits would not comply with the resolution. It was decided to see these firms and if possible, gain unanimous consent to the resolution.
The cowmen took Medora by storm.
The bull round-up north of the track will begin a week from Tuesday.
The stockmen north and south of the railroad will divide into two round-ups to gather the cattle east of the river.
John N. Simpson, of the Continental Land and Cattle Co., is here making a contract with the Marqnis for the delivery of cattle here this summer. He expects to personally superintend the delivery.
Politicions could learn a good lesson from the stockmen in running conventions. They all come primed as to what they want, talk it up before the meeting and then rush it through in a hurry.
Texas stockmen are seeking relief on all sides from the quarantine laws and will doubtless find it in establishing slaughter-houses and canneries and shipping the beef to Europe

Young grass has already started on the slopes of the buttes and the warm rains of April will bring it forth everywhere. There is a well-founded belief that the hay crop this year will be much better than last.

The citizens of Miles City are making great preparations to receive the visiting stockmen tomorrow and it will doubtless be the largest meeting ever held in the northwest outside of Cheyenne. A number of our stockmen will leave tonight for Miles and our interests will be well looked after.

M. Wadsworth returned from the west last evening where he bought a bunch of horses. They are being driven to the ranch by a cowpuncher whom Mr. Wadsworth wants to back against anyone in the Bad Lands at riding or roping. Get out your buckers and reatas, boys.

A number of cowmen from the west and south were in attendance at the meeting yesterday. Among them we noticed H. S. Boice, Geo. Towers, Pierre Wibaux, Griffin & Ward, Mr. Rowe, J. N. Simpson and all the stockmen tributary to Medora.

Whatever can be said against the methods adopted by the "stranglers" who came through here last fall, it cannot but be acknowledged that the result of their work has been very wholesome. Not a definite case of horse stealing from a cowman has been reported since and it seems as though a very thorough cleanup had been made.

Last Friday the Humane Society of Pittsburg entered suit in the United States Court against the Pennsylvania railroad company, alleging that the recent act of Congress, which provides for heavy penalties on all public carriers of live stock for failure to properly care for animals during transportation has been shamelessly disregarded, the defendant company having allowed live stock shipped from Chicago to be on the road sixty-two hours without food, water, or rest. The suit is a test one, and is brought at the suggestion of the agent of the National Humane Society. Should the plaintiffs win the case an attempt will be made to enforce the act in all parts of the United States.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.
Cow horses are in active demand, not only here but through the entire northwest, first class cow horses are bringing from $75 to $80 per head.

It is reported that the new stock yards for this station are to be built near the old "Y" and will be large enough to hold 5000 cattle. This begins to look as if Medora was to be a shipping point of importance. There are thousands of cattle landed here every spring and this would have been a prominent shipping point last year if there had been any accommodations for that kind of business.

H. R. Tarbell, Manager of the Little Missouri Horse Co., was in town this week and reports his stock as looking fine. Mr. Tarbell is "pulling the right string" to establish a reputation for fine stock and fair dealing. He wishes it distinctly understood that he is no "jockey" or "horse trader" but solely a breeder and will deal in nothing but the best stock. Stick to it Harry, and you will win not only reputation but in the long run a large and paying business.

A Galveston news Wichita Falls special says: Arrangements have been consummated whereby Texas cattle destined for the northern market will be shipped to Harold, the new terminus of the Fort Worth & Denver railroad, thence driven north to Caldwell and Hunnewell, on the south line of Kansas; thence shipped by rail to the destination. Those for Colorado, Wyoming and other northern territories will go from Harold, by way of a new trail, the strip through the north of the Panhandle, and thence north to their respective destinations. This settles the question of an outlet for the cattle drive this year, and saves the Texas stock interests from being seriously crippled though the quarantine laws of Kansas and other states. Whether this scheme will work is hard to tell, but we think the opposition which will come from the ranchmen of the Panhandle, over whose ranges the proposed trail will have to pass, will be so great that it will be found that it is not practicable.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

The Northern Pacific has given virtual half-fare rates to all stockmen attending the Miles City meeting. Full fair is to be paid one way and a pass given the other. This applies between, Dickinson, Dakota and Helena, Montana. We are glad to see this evidence of liberality of the Northern Pacific especially as it is in line with a new policy that they have so far been in earnest about adopting. Hitherto, there has been much just cause of complaint and the plain facts have been freely exposed in the columns of the Cow Boy. We are as ready to praise as to condemn and will give the N. P. the credit of now looking to the future for their custom as much as to the present. On all sides can be heard expressions of approval at their un-looked-for liberality and the N. P. seems destined to attain the great praise which it so richly deserves but which it came so near forfeiting.

There is a point concerning the detection of stock thieves which we think has escaped the notice of editors. It is in relation to the capture of the thieves. Of course it is necessary to advertise the loss immediately and as widely as possible, as this alone very often leads to detection. Where the thief has gotten away with his booty, however, nothing should be said as to the means being employed to bring the culprit to justice as this is one of the most certain means toward making escape easier. An instance was brought to our mind by the Atchison Champion. It seems that a man named Griffith, an ex-sheriff, had sold a lot of cattle and then skipped to parts unknown. Thus far the article is all right and by the right kind of advertising the thief would almost surely have been cought. The article further says, however, that the losers by this steal had selected one of their number to catch Griffith and that he proposed going to his old home and see if he did not turn up there. If is manifest that a man in Griffith's position will keep well posted and the agent could as well look for Griffith to show up at his old home as he could for him to appear in the moon. It is a very easy thing for a paper to say too much as has doubtless been done in this case.

Smiles.

He Was Sorry.

The other morning a tramp walked up to one of our prominent citizens on the street and, shivering with cold, begged him for a quarter with which to buy something to eat. The prominent citizen stopped and looked at his trampship pityingly, then replied:

"My good man, how long is it since you had a meal?"

"Two days," said the tramp, as his kneees shook and his teeth chattered.

"I am very sorry, my friend, but I have not had a dinner for two weeks." The tramp opened his eyes and looked wild, and his teeth ceased chattering and his knees no longer quaked as he drew breath with difficulty and sadly said:

"Here is a quarter, poor fellow. Take it and go and get some grub."

"But I am not a beggar!" cried the prominent citizen.

"I know, I know," the tramp replied, "but you are the champion liar of the country. You were picking your teeth when I met you."—[Bloomington Through Mail.

The stockmen's ball last night at the Pyramid Park hotel was all that was expected and the expectations of all for having a good time were high. The dancing was kept up till a late hour and another social success has been recorded.

Our respected and versatile hardware merchant has just received an extensive consignment of papers through the mail. It is presumed that they were delayed by the recent eclipse of the sun, as some of them are of rather ancient date.

E. G. Paddock's new livery and sale stable is nearly completed and will be a great convenience as well as an ornament to the town. He will no doubt reap a liberal harvest from the tourists trade this summer as well as from the local trade.

The managers of the rink have decided to make the price for admision and skates as follows: Gentlemen, admission twenty-five cents, skates 10 cents; ladies, admission free, skates twenty-five cents. Gentlemen will be charged admission on regular nights whether they take skates or not.

Rev. W. B. Schaffner, of Dic[kin?]son, preached an eloquent serm[on?] in [th?]e rink last Sunday evening. There was a good audience, which listened attentively to the minister's words. Mr. Schaffner will preach here again a week from Sunday evening at half-past seven in the rink. There is no doubt that a large audience will turn out.

All those intending to take part in the skating masquerade and carnival April 15, should be practicing as much as possible beforehand so that they won't fall down and break their masks that evening. If you cannot afford a special costume for the evening, don't let that keep you from taking part in the festivities. Our worthy "six eyed" gentleman will have masks for sale at the confectionery and news depot. The masks will cost about twenty-five cents each. An old cotton umbrella and a plug hat makes a very good masquerade costume. That is, in connection with other necessary wearing apparel. However, to avoid monotony, we would suggest that this costume be not universally adopted.

The shoot last Saturday was a disappointment as far as scores were concerned. It was the worst shooting we have yet had, the only redeeming feature being Peter Book's hundred yard score.

The day was almost perfect for shooting, the weather fine and hardly a breath of air stirring. Almost all the contestants claimed to be in good trim for shooting and then would step up and miss the target. There is something about shooting which cannot be explained and still it will make a whole team shoot poorly. We cannot imagine what it is, but below is seen the result. It might be added that the target is the regulation army one of an eight-inch bulls eye at the three ranges.

Since the above was put in type, it was found to be impossible to give the score in full this issue. The next shoot will decide the winner of the gun, when the complete scores will be published.

As before announced, next Wednesday, April 15 has been set apart by the Governor, as Arbor day. Those wishing to help along the good work by planting trees are requested to come to the Cow Boy office before Sunday to talk the matter up and make preparations for a meeting.

We do not know for what good deeds we are being rewarded by this perfect weather. From exchanges all over the United States we judge that we are having about the only good weather prevalent anywhere. For the last four weeks it has been simply perfect. There is no rose without its thorn, though, and we are now wishing for rain.

The bull round-up south of the track begins next Monday. The one north of the track began last Tuesday and has already worked Knutson creek and the adjacent country. South of the track, Ferris & Merrifield's ranch will be a head-quarters until that vicinity has been worked, when the camps will be moved farther up the river, gradually working the whole country.

It may be blowing our own horn, but we wish to assert that Medora is and has been for some time the best town on the road for its size. It is almost impossible to find an idle man and those who are idle from choice are soon asked to seek a more congenial clime. We havn't had a boom and don't one. No business has been overdone, there have been no failures and everyone is presperous.

Although it is almost impossible to get accurate information from the seat of war in the Saskatchewan country, all reports seem to indicate that Riel has a large body of troops who are liable to give the Dominion soldiers much trouble on account of their superior arms marksmanship and bushwhacking mode of fighting. The man Riel has left a reputation wherever he has gone of being a two-faced rascal but he is now at the head of a good cause and it is to be hoped that it will be successful.

The latest news from the bedside of Gen. Grant is that he may linger for several months or he may die in a few days. Universal sympathy is felt for the dying hero and papers which formerly villified him in every possible way on account of partizan feeling are now [illegible] of his good qualities. He is now living simply on account of his immense will power and the determination not to give up.

We are in receipt of the report of the department of Agriculture in reference to numbers and values of farm animals which contains many valuable statistics. From it, we learn that the January returns on horses and mules show an increase of four per cent. Especially in the territories, where much attention has been given to horse breeding, is this increase manifest.

For the United States the increase for the year has been 391,889 on horses, the present number being 11,564,572.

In cattle there has been an increase of 820,472 the present number being 29,866,573. The average value of horses for 1885 is $93.70 being a decrease of ninety-four cents. The average price of cattle is $23.02, being a decrease of fifty cents. The total value of the horses in the United States is $852,282,927 and the total value of cattle is $694,382,913. The total value of all domestic animals is $2,456,425,933.

The pamphlet also contains many valuable tables, showing numbers and values of animals in different states and territories. By these, it appears that in cattle, Texas heads the list with 66,784,736, Montana comes thirteenth, with 17,324,550 and Dakota fifteenth with 11,001,649.

The price of beef in Chicago was highest in 1882, when extra beeves sold at $9.15 to $9.40 and choice were $8.65 to $8.90. On Jan. 1, 1884, extra beeves sold at $7.00 to $7.25, choice for $6.30 to $6.40 and medium for $4.50 to $5.00. On Jan. 1, 1885, the prices were $6.65 to $6.85 for extra, $6.25 to $6.60 for choice and $5.00 to $5.50 for medium.

It appears that sheep have increased in Dakota less than one per cent., "accounted for by the low price of wool and that so many tag-end and scrub flocks were shipped in from the east two years ago and did so poorly for their masters. It has also been proved that the ordinary breed of sheep need more care than flock-masters thought necessary to give them."

Animals in the northern part of the territory are valued higher than those in the southern part, horses and mules being of a better class.

Texas and Dakota have more cattle than all of Europe combined.

In the last pages of the pan[ph]let are freight rates, rail and water, to and from all the prominent shipping points, containing valuable information to all those intending to ship cattle in any direction.

Meeting of the Montana Stock-grower's Association.

FRIDAY MORNING SESSION.

The annual spring meeting of the Eastern Montana Live Stock association was called to order by chairman Bryan at 11:10 last Friday morning. The chairman made a few remarks to the effect that two years ago the association consisted of seven members and met in a little back room but now the largest hall in the city was scarcely able to seat the association and its friends who had come to the meeting.

Fifty-seven new names were read for membership and with one exception were unanimously elected by the secretary's ballot.

A conference committee on consolidation was appointed to meet one from the other association already appointed. Adjourned.

FRIDAY AFTERNOON SESSION.

At three o'clock, chairmam Bryan called the convention to order and appointed a districting committee which together with the north side members, should form round-up districts. Among the rest, John Goodall was appointed for the Little Missouri, Henry Boice for Beaver and A. Cole for Glendive.

Messrs. Green and Burleigh were appointed a committee to draft a memorial to the secretary of war to allow the erection of stock-yards on the Ft. Keogh reservation.

After a few remarks on the Indian question by which nothing definite was reached the meeting adjourned.

FRIDAY EVENING'S SESSION.

About eight o'clock the meeting was called to order by chairman Bryan who stated that the conference committees on consolidation were ready to report.

In brief the report was entirely in favor of consolidation. That the name be changed to the Montana Stockgrower's association, that the executive committe[e] [consist?] of twenty-five members [illegible] Dakota shall have two, that the annual dues shall be $10, that the association meet semi-annually and that the spring meeting be in Miles City and the fall meeting in Helena. The report was unanimously adopted.

The by-laws of the new association were then read and in brief are as follows: That the name of this association be the Montana Stockgrower's Association, that its object is in every way to advance stock interests in Mantana and adjoining territories, that the officers shall be a President, 1st. Vice-President 2nd. Vice-President, Secretary and Treasure combined and an Executive committee, all these officers to be elected on the first day of the semi-annual meeting in April. No person can become a member, except he be a stockgrower, defined as follows: A person owning or controlling cattle, horses, mules or asses and engaged in the business of herding, growing and raising the same for profit. By a very forcible speech of Gov. Potts and the hearty concurrence of the association, the bad custom of electing honorary members was done away with. Membership shall also be personal and not by firms. The entrance fee shall be fifteen dollars, the annual dues ten dollars, and and all members are subject to an assessment, not oftener than annual, of one cent a head on not over seventy per cent. of all his stock.

The round-up committee then reported, the Little Missouri, being district six. Our cowmen are well pleased at the incorporation of the western part of Dakota in the Montana territorial association. For some time we will be too weak to stand alone and by joining the Montana association we become a prominent part of what two years hence will be the strongest stock organization in the world.

The following was sent us by W. A. VanBrunt, president of the Badger cattle Co.: "A Paulding farmer having cattle trespassing upon his grain fields, posted up the following: 'Notis—If any man's or woman's cows or oxen gits in these here otes his or her tale will be off as the cass may be. I am a Christian and pay mi taxes, darn a man who lets his critter run luse, say i.'"

The Texas cattlemen are in really desperate straits on account of the quarantine laws. It is impossible for all of them to find a market for their cattle and sales at low figures are made wherever opportunity offers. Many of the Texas cowmen are working on borrowed money and pay-day will find them entirely unprepared to square up. It is thought that more cattlemen will be closed out there this year than ever before.

While in Miles City we spoke with a large number in reference to Texas fever and all agreed, even though some had [large interests in Texas, that the fever?] was by no means a scare. Several illustrations were cited where a Texas trail had been crossed by states cattle and every animal in the latter herd had died. Our best authority seemed to think that the name Texas fever was a mis-nomer for the same deadly disease arises when cattle are driven continually from one point to another. This rule he claimed to be nearly or quite without exception, the disease with the same symptoms having arisen on every well used trail the world over.

More and more are the cowmen beginning to realize that talk will do no good and that if they expect to have the proper per cent. of calves, each member of the different associations must be forced to put in the requisite number of bulls. This is a question that admits of no farther delay and one that must be immediately and strictly enforced. Where is the business man in the world but would add five per cent. to his capital stock if by so doing it were conclusively proved that he would gain fifteen per cent? The case is exactly as plain in the matter of a full supply of bulls and still a large number of cowmen havn't their proper proportion. We may as well come out flat-footed and state what is a notorious fact, that these men expect to gain the fifteen per cent. profit without the five per cent addition to the capital stock. Our association was very decided in this matter and it was fully decided to make every man on the river put in his required number. Some may still try to sponge off their neighbors and a close watch should be kept to see that the letter of the law is strictly enforced.

Some one has been writing to the Kansas City Live Stock Indicator objecting to polled cattle on the ground that the muley cow and calf on the plains will fall easy prey to the wolves on account of the absence of the pointed weapons worn by the Texas cow. Another correspondent and friend of the blacks says: "We respectfully refer J. P. S. W. to Prof. E. M. Shelton, whose testimony should quiet his apprehension in this matter. Says the observant and experienced professor, in speaking of muleys—'moreover they strike viciously with their mallet-shaped heads.' Those of us who have handled hornless beasts know that the sight of a dog will arouse warlike demonstrations on the part of the muley quicker than anything else, and it is an acknowleged fact that, although peaceable by nature, when it does come to the tug of war a muley will thump the everlasting daylights out of anything that wears hoofs and horns. Taking these two facts into consideration, it is reasonable to suppose that the howling wolf and the screeching coyote of the wild west will quickly learn to respect the butting bump on the mallet-shaped muley head."—[Stockgrower's Journal.
