Father Martin has made arrangements with Jim Butler, by which new pews will soon adorn the Catholic church.
Again must the Gun club express its thanks to Lieut. Partello for his kindness in furnishing a bountiful supply of targets, pasters, etc.
Marquis de Mores, John Goodall, Howard Eaton, J. L. Truscott, Wal. Osterhaut, Joe McCoul and A. T. Packard attended the Miles City meeting from Medora.
Howard Eaton and Joe McCoul bought a number of cow-horses in Miles City. The most of them were bought for J. A. VanEeghan and will be kept here for sale.
And now there is rejoicing in the house of Paddock. Tuesday afternoon there was born to Mrs. Paddock, a fourteen pound girl baby. The mother and child are both doing well.
Mr. Anderson, of the Drover's Journal, stopped off here Sunday on his way to Chicago, from the Miles City convention. Among stock dealers, he is probably the widest known man in the country.

Dr. Jorgens is putting up a new building for his drug store as his present quarters are too small. He will probably branch out into the crockery business. In a few days he will start for the Hills to attend to business matters there.

It will be noticed that the new time table of the Northern Pacific is now in force. No. 1, going west, arrives at 6:47 p. m. and No. 2, going east, at 8:43 a. m. The emigrant train is again running, being freight No. 17, and arrives at 11:40.

We have not the score of last Saturday's shoot and will now publish only the total scores when all the contestants have shot their full series. Nothing preventing, this will be done Saturday and the successful contestant will then be known.

J. C. Fisher offers two prizes for the best scores made before May 1st. in his shooting gallery at the rink. A box of cigars will be given to the member of the Little Missouri Gun club making the best score in a hundred shots and a like prize to any person not a member. All shots to count. Ten shots for a quarter. All shooting to be off-hand.

Again has the decapitator been at work and the heads of Gen'l. M'n'g'r. Simpson and Superintendent Smith fall into the basket. We are sorry to see Mr. Smith go as he was a good stage man and agreeable gentleman. It would have been a sin, however, to keep Simpson, as the Dakota atmosphere fairly ruined the bloom of his ashes-of-roses or dregs-of-wine complexion.

The brick work on the hotel will be almost completed this week and with the exception of the roof, will be as neat a looking building as could be wished. There will be two brick additions, one for the bar-room and the other for the kitchen. We understand that the porches have been taken from the plan. If so, it will take far more from the looks than the additional expense would have added. Peter Book is displaying his pressed brick to advantage and no better brick or brick-work can be found on the road.

Several persons from here learned from what was considered a reliable source in Miles City that John Warn had been sentenced at Bozeman to a year in the penitentiary. The reasons given, corresponded with those already known and as they were trivial and manifestly the work of enemies, a petition for his pardon to the governor of Montana was circulated here and numerously signed. It now turns out that John was only sentenced to thirty days through the efforts of his enemies and that he intends to "fight 'em, blood raw" at the end of his imprisonment.
Geo. Porter and wife are still absent in Chicago.
B. F. Lamb returned from Bismarck last evening.
A tasty gilt cross now adorns the steeple of the Catholic church.
Mike Knott should be appointed to the position of "foreman of the stiff-firing gang."
Mrs. J. D. Garver is quite ill in Bismarck and Mr. Garver went down this morning to attend her.
Dr. Robarts is kept busy, vibrating between Dickinson and Medora. He has number of patients in both places.
The grass is coming up in good shape and all that is needed now is two or thee days rain to give it a first-class start.
Marquis de Mores and Wm. Van-[Driesche?] started east Tuesday morning William will return in a few days and the Marquis about the 23rd.
W. B. Pryor is now started in good shape and prepared to do any work in the boot and shoe line. His advertisement will appear in the next Cow Boy.

Owing to the thoughtfulness of S. A. [illegible]arney, of the Stockgrower's, our editorial frame reclined on a downy bed while in Miles, where we might otherwise have had to rustle for a chair even so great was the crowd.

The masquerade to take place at the rink the evening of April 15, bids fair to be even above the usual order of parties in pleasure. The doors will be open at 7:30, the grand march will begin at 9:30. No person not masked will be allowed on the floor until ten o'clock, when all will unmask. Dancing will then begin and continue until twelve. Tickets one dollar, children fifty cents. No improper characters admitted.

For the first time in the history of the stage line, a coach tipped over. It occurred this side of Davis creek and ginned up the passengers pretty briskly. One, the Ft. Meade post trader, seemed to be hurt in the back, while Charlie Jolly, had a rib fractured and some of the muscles torn loose on his side. This was aggravated by the jolting of the coach and the hurt looked quite serious by the time he arrived here Charlie is now at Geo. Roderick's and resting easily.

Up and down the line the warning cry will soon be passed from mouth to mouth by all the bums, "Steer clear of Medora." This is a subject we have not hitherto mentioned, as we could not see that any good would be derived therefrom and the occasional process of "firing a stiff," was not altogether unenjoyable. Lately, however, what at times might be considered as a mild species of enjoyment under other circumstances, has now come to be a positive bore. The last stiff was fired Monday, being escorted out of town by two citizens. He was afterward pursued and brought back on a hand-car and acknowledged to stealing a lot of stage meal tickets. After several persons had used moral or other suasion on him, he was again escorted out of town. The treatment this man received was not altogether lamb-like, but by comparison with what others will receive, it certainly was. We want it distinctly understood that Medora is the unhealthiest place on the road for tramps and bums. There is scarcely an idle man in our busy little burg, loafing being an unknown art. We do not by any means intimate that honest working men are not wanted here. They are as welcome as spring showers and we doubt if a capable workman has ever yet sought here in vain for a job. But we do not want tramps and they will be fired out of town with an ever-increasing momentum liable to jar some of their finer sensibilities.
Bismarck's recent election was, on the whole, a Democratic victory. John A. Carland was elected mayor and the majority of the city council is also Democratic.

General Grant still hangs on to life, although death cannot be very far away. It is now hoped by the physicians that they can keep him alive until death comes from the cancer, which may be a month yet.

That bulls are scarce in the round-up is simply because they are scarce on the range. We doubt if to-day there is an average on the river of four bulls to the hundred cows. Our cowmen will remedy this difficulty soon by the addition of three or four more to the hundred.

The farce of trying to elect a U. S. senator for Illinois is still going on in the legislature of that state. In the whole history of our government we do not know of a more useless session of the legislature or more uncalled-for waste of the peoples' money.

There remains scarcely any doubt that England and Russia will soon have a war. Taking into consideration the many advantages such a war will confer on the United States, we can scarcely say we are sorry at the prospect. Already is the effect manifest both in the beef and shipping trades.

Some of the large factories in the east are having serious times with their employes. The workmen in the McCormick reaper works in Chicago are on a strike. There has been considerable shooting but only one man was killed. Much enmity has been aroused toward Pinkerton's police and serious trouble is feared.

The Riel rebellion has now become a serious matter. Strong efforts are being made to induce the Dominion government to accede to the perfectly just and reasonable demands of the rebels, but with the bull-headed obstinacy characteristic of the English, they seem to prefer force to justice. The cause of the rebels is almost hopeless but they can be assured of the hearty good wishes of all on this side of the line.

Spread-eagle Harrison has about reached the end of his rope in Chicago politics. He was recently supposed to be elected mayor by a very small majority. It has turned out that there were numerous frauds committed and the result is liable to be reversed. At any event, it has been made plainly manifest that all kinds of frauds have been practiced by the Harrison-McDonald gang, even to the stealing of the ballot-boxes and a committee of public safety has been organized, consisting of Republicans and Democrats, with the avowed purpose of sifting the matter to the bottom. For the good of Chicago it is to be hoped that Harrison will be ousted.
Doc. Pennell loaded and pulled for the Hills last Saturday with a lot of tree sprouts and shrubs.
It is perfectly impossible to even imagine more perfect weather than that with which we have been blessed lately. We would be willing to exchange some of it, though, for rain.
The Willard Bros. will probably be here to-morrow with eighty head of cow-horses, which they hope to sell on the river. They will then get another bunch for the Hills.

Dr. Jorgens will move into his new building the first of next week. He will soon open up a full line of crockery in addition to his drug stock. The building is 24x32 and is to have a full glass front.

The slaughter house is nearly ready for business and it is hoped that fat cattle enough can be found to start up by May 1. We scarcely see where they are coming from however, until June 1, at the earliest.

The bull round-up south of the track began Tuesday. Davis, Sully, Andrews and Garner creeks have been worked and to-day the country around D. K. Wade's will be rounded-up. Not a half a dozen dead animals have been found and bulls also are scarce.

Some one is missing the opportunity of a life-time by not starting a butter and cheese factory here. All the fresh cows wanted could be had for the keeping and ready sale could be found here and on the road for all the product. Who possesses the capital and experience to start in?

Some tenderfoot has sent us an article on roller skating, copied almost entire from an article which has been floating around the newspaper world until it has become stale, and signed it "Cow-puncher." We don't really think the writer knows the difference between a hackamore and a round-up and that he does know a great deal more about rubbing stage stock. We like to hear from you, boys, but write original articles and send your names so that the editor may know whom to get action on, provided he happens to get stepped on for publishing some other man's ideas.

From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
The Little Missouri round-up begins May 25.
Six weeks from to-day the ranges will be covered with cattle, rolling in fat from this year's grass.
By a resolution proposed by Mr. Towers, horseracing or anything else detrimental to the morals of cow camps are prohibited on the ranches of members of the Wyoming association.
Even though we have not had much rain, the grass is coming up finely, much of it being already three inches long. For about a month the cattle will run down on it but will then pick up rapidly.

The meeting of the Wyoming Stock-growers' association, at Cheyenne brought out many interesting points. The secretary's report on contagious diseases had to handle the subject with gloved hands as many of the principal members of the Wyoming association are prominent cowmen of Texas. Nevertheless it put forth many facts that conclusively proved the great danger of driving cattle from Texas into the north, without a quarantine of at least sixty days. The Territorial veterinarian, Dr. Hopkins, has made thorough examination and it was conclusively proved that every herd that crossed the trail made by Texas cattle lost from three to one hundred per cent., the latter loss being an entire herd of valuable bulls. There was no herd that crossed the trail, which did not lose some of its members, even after cold weather set in. In every case the fatal disease was unquestionably Splenic, commonly called Texas fever, and it was equally as certain that the losses all came from crossing the trail made by Texas cattle. The secretary's report recommended that Texas cattle be allowed to come north after a quarantine of sixty days, as at the end of that time all danger was over. In reference to contagious pleuro-pneumonia, the report stated that the disease had appeared in four states further west than ever before, viz: Ohio, Illinois, Kentucky and Missouri. One infected herd had also been taken to Tennessee and one to Texas, but there are as yet no outside cases in either of these states. It was strongly recommended that all eastern cattle be quarantined until it is certain they are free from disease. "Speaking without heat or prejudice" the secretary then showed the difference between the two national meetings held at Chicago and St. Louis. He stated that the Chicago meeting held in April was of perfect fairness, that it desired above all things to harmonize all conflicting interests and enroll all cattlemen in one grand national association. To this end only a partial list of officers was elected the remaining to be elected by the St. Louis meeting. A committee on consolidation then went to the St. Louis meeting but the idea of consolidation and the holding of annual meetings in rotation in all principal cities west of the Alleghenies was treated with derision and they were informed that if they saw fit they could join the St. Louis association but no union or any plan by which meetings would be held elsewhere than in St. Louis would be considered. The St. Louis meeting was also given up to but one idea, that of the national trail from Texas to Canada. There seemed to be no other object for the meeting. Also in this meeting Texas was given twenty-two votes. New Mexico twelve and only one to Wyoming, Nebraska and Dakota combined. The delegates from Wyoming association did not see fit to join the St. Louis association and went back to Chicago and joined the National Cattlegrowers' association of America, in which Wyoming is entitled to about forty votes. It was also reported that the commissoner of animal industry has been empowered by congress to expend his fund of $100,000 at his own discretion. This can now be used toward buying infected animals and thus stop almost any disease in its infancy. On the subject of transportation it was reported that both the Union and Northern Pacific had made reductions of five per cent., thus effecting a saving of about six dollars a car or a total of $72,000 on cattle shipped by members of the association. In regard to mavericks it was found that $26,000 had been derived from their sale. In every case but one, good prices had been paid. In the matter of inspectors, it was estimated that over a million cattle have been looked after by them since April, 1884. 2,779 strays were picked up at the different shipping points making a total saving to the association of $108,000. Many disturbances and in fact the possibility of many members resigning and forming new associations were finally settled harmoniously. All the old officers were elected for the ensuing year, the member of the executive committee for Dakota being Dorr Clark, of the E 6 and V V V outfits.
With those elected at the last meeting the Wyoming association has 461 members. The Montana association is close on her heels and will catch up inside of two year.

The committee appointed by the Wyoming association to look up the bull question were unanimously in favor of taking up and feeding them from December to July. In one case this action increased the calf crop to 85 per cent. and the beeves when sold averaged fifty pounds heavier than others.

In the year 1884 Chicago received 1,817,697 cattle; 801,630 sheep; 5,351,967 hogs and 18,602 horses. In nineteen years she has received 103,333,532 head of live stock, valued at $2,074,127,503. The report of the Chamber of commerce reports that the fresh beef trade is steadily increasing, owing to the improved methods and facilities for carrying on the work. Owing to the foot-and-mouth disease scare last May the market was for a time very suggish but picked up later on and 1,118,154 cattle were killed for the dressed meat, canning and packing trade.

In the report of Dr. Hopkins veterinarian of the Wyoming association, a cause of the death of states bulls and cattle was brought out that has escaped the notice of our cowmen. It was supposed that states cattle die in larger numbers than others because the cold was more intense and the feed of a different kind. It appears that they do not die as much from this reason, however, as from the fact that these changes bring diseases, common to all pilgrims on the range. The fact has now been established beyond all doubt that bulls and especially pilgrims, cannot run with the herd the whole year without serious loss. They must be taken up and fed. If they are not, disease in some shape and death are sure to attack them. In view of this fact, we prophesy that the time is close at hand when the cowmen will see it is to their interest to not only take up their bulls for seven or eight months in the year, but also to feed them well and give them some kind of a shelter besides a wire fence.

The question of leasing public lands is getting to be one of great importance in Indian territory and one that we think should be decided in favor of leasing. At first sight it would seem that this would be entirely for the benefit of large capitalists and would creat a virtual monopoly in the leased districts. There are two sides to the question, however and the other side is that the lands in question are generally desert or virtually so on account of the lack of water. No one is going to put improvements on public lands when they are liable at any time to be driven off and the only way to make this land productive is to lease it for a term of years with the privilege of buying at the end of the lease. Plenty of water will then be obtained in wells and what are now deserts will become as good grazing land as any. Again the inevitable tendency of the cow business is toward monopoly. By the leasing of lands many smaller outfits will be given a good show, where now they will soon be crowded to the wall. For these and many other reasons the Cow Boy is in favor of leasing any and all public lands that can by any construction, come under the Desert land act.

In all cattle papers the question of hornless cattle is being discussed. Numbers and testimony are immensely in their favor and the question has now narrowed down to the point as to whether it is better or not to dehorn cattle. The evidence is strongly in favor of this, but in reference to range cattle we are still in the dark as to whether it would pay. There is scarcely any doubt, however, that it would pay in the case of calves. As to naturally hornless or polled cattle, it is past dispute that they make by far the best beef-producing and range cattle. Almost without exception Aberdeen-Angus took the first prize in the block contest in all fat stock shows, the most noticable victories of this year being the national contest at Smithfield, England and the international contest at New Orleans. Among the polls, however, there is quite a rivalry as to which is the better for the range, Galloways or Aberdeen-Angus. The Galloways have longer hair and may be able to stand greater cold, but the Aberdeen-Angus have repeatedly shown their ability to stand any kind of weather with perfect ease, so that on account of the superior record of the Angus for beef-producing qualities, we still hold them as the coming prime favorites for the range. They have been a long time gaining their present popularity but are certain of its being increased. A strong point in their favor is that any one who handles them is immediately an uncompromising partisan in their favor. In some late cattle sales we notice that T. C. Powers, of Ft. Benton, a pioneer in Angus cattle for the range, recently bought a number in Chicago and J. J. Hill, of St. Paul bought a small herd in Scotland. We are glad also to see that our stockmen are realizing the value of Aberdeen-Angus bulls. There are several now on the river and the LeMoyne cattle Co. will put in either Angus or Galloway bulls this season. Clemmer & Dell, of Cave Hills, have a number, their best bull costing $600. The name of their company is the Aberdeen-Angus cattle Co. Sam Wallace, formerly of Glendive is puting in cattle below Howard Eaton's ranch and the Co. will be called the Angus cattle Co.

No. 2 was about eleven hours late yesterday.
Just stop a minute and listen to the hammers.
Bob Roberts is on his way home, being now in New York.
John Warn expects to return from Bozeman in about ten days.
B. F. Lamb has decided that his new brand shall be BL connected.
A new barn for the accommodation of stage and other stock is nearly completed.
Nothing has been heard from J. D. Garver, since he went to Bismarck to see his wife and it is feared she may be seriously ill.
Sam. Whitney has decided to make Medora his home and has gone to housekeeping in Bob Roberts building. His eldest daughter arrived last evening.
It is perfectly wonderful, the change that even the little rain of last night effected. Everywhere now can be seen the tinge of the rapidly growing grass.
The LeMoyne cattle Co. will soon ship in one or two car loads of bulls. From letters of Mr. LeMoyne, we judge that they will be grade Galloways or Aberdeen-Angus.

E. G. Paddock's livery stable is completed and, as predicted, is by no means a detriment to the looks of the town. He has already opened up and in a few days will be able to meet nearly any demand made on him.

The whole of the plateau east of town burned over Monday evening, the fire spreading in all directions. We wish to remark that the reward of $250 for the arrest and conviction of anyone setting the grass on fire still holds good.

Several times we have heard the question asked as to whether the stage line would get a mail contract. Bids were advertised for last February and the first day of July will surely see a mail go out of Medora for the Hills.

None of the contestants have shot off their back scores in the shooting match. Two members of the executive committee are to make up back scores and as the president was out of town it had to be postponed last Saturday. Weather permitting, the scores will be shot next Saturday.

Much improvement work is being done at the coal mine. An air shaft is being tunnelled, a new chute built, tracks and coal buggy added and many more improvements. The expenses have already gone beyond the receipts, but it is hoped that a contract made for all the coal the Co. uses and next winter's trade will straighten matters.

G. G. Cooper, formerly day operator here, went to Billings Monday night to accept a corresponding position there. We are pleased at his promotion but sorry to lose him as he made many friends here, not particularly on account of his good looks, but more by reason of his "winning ways." W. H. Fortier, of Gladstone, relieves him here.

Tom Jones passed through Medora last night on his way to Tacoma. He will return as soon as possible. His trip probably has some connection with work on the extensions of the N. P. He reports that capitalists are become interested and mean business in reference to the Hay creek coal road. Joe Pennell is in charge of the aqueduct work in New York.

James W. Allen arrived from Deadwood yesterday morning and immediately entered upon the duties of superintendent to which office he was appointed by John A. Gaston, who is now General manager. This looks more like business than any move that has been made for some time. The way to secure patronage is to place authority in the hands of men who are well-known in the Hills and who know how to rustle. These requisites are both filled by Messrs. Gaston and Allen. We learn also, that in all minor affairs, full power is put in the hands of the manager and superintendent the only way in which the line can be run satisfactorily. We now will prophesy that our line will do a much better business than formerly

In spite of the rain the masquerade last night was a complete success. Nearly thirty were masked, some of them being strikingly original. That of Mrs. Elmer was perhaps the best, but as she did not skate, she was out of the contest. The first prize was won by Miss Maggie Guardient and second by Polly Fitzgerald. The first prize among the gentlemen was won by Martin Timlin. First prizes are three-week's skating tickets, second, a week's ticket. The calling and playing of F. Bernan were very satisfactory, he introducing several new and pleasing movements in the dancing, which began at ten o'clock, the maskers having about exhausted themselves on skates, trying to disguise their movements. The masquerade will be repeated shortly.
Arbor day has been postponed to April 25th by order of governor Pierce.
B. F. Lamb is making many improvements on his ranch and will soon be in shape to receive cattle.
W. B. Pryor's boot and shoe business has opened up in good shape and he is now on the lookout for a shoemaker.
Two wagon loads of leather goods for the Glendive branch of J. S. Collins' Cheyenne house, passed through Medora last Saturday.
Postmaster Gallup, of Cave Hills, came up last week on business. He reports the loss of cattle in Cave Hills at a little more than average, the Hash-Knife outfit being the heaviest losers.
A number of subscribers will miss the Cow Boy owing to our motto: "Cash or no Cow Boy." There are still a few delinquent local subscribers who are requested to call at their earliest convenience.

C. S. Grindall went east Sunday morning accompanied by his family. He intends buying between five hundred and a thousand States cattle for his Beaver creek ranch. He reported that there was an enjoyable dance at Mingusville Friday night.

If present indications hold out, Medora will soon have a gold mine craze. Messrs. Martin and Keeler recently panned out about twenty cents in one pan of dirt up the river. This is excellent pay and if it holds out will make first class diggings.

There is a good deal of uncertainty in reference to the stockyards to be built here. They were at first laid out on a liberal plan and afterwards the corrall was contracted to 50x50 feet. This was again changed to a hundred feet square and now again the dimensions are uncertain.

Rev. J. B. Schaffner preached again last Sunday night at the rink. His sermon was an eloquent one and well deserving of a larger audience. Probably the reason that so few attended was that it was doubtful if Mr. Schaffner would arrive. Hereafter there will be no doubt as he has made arrangements to come every Sunday evening. Hereafter also there will be better music as his organ will be in the rink. Let every one turn out Sunday evening.

One of the worst wrecks for a small one that it has ever been our lot to see, occurred Saturday afternoon, four-and-a-half miles west of here. A steer thought he was "as big a man as the engine" and came nearly proving it, the effect being disastrous on both sides. The engine and tender were completely disabled and ditched, four empty freight cars were badly demoralized and two more ran off the track. C. S. Grindall, of the E S G Beaver creek ranch, engineer White and the fireman were in the cab and all escaped unharmed, though how they did it after seeing the wreck, is a mystery. The loss will be about $4,000.

Levi Deffebach came in Monday from the bull round-up north of the track. The bulls were in splendid condition as were all the cattle. There will be a large calf crop, which may reach 75 per cent. The most encouraging thing about the round-up was the few dead cattle found. Only eight were found on ranges over which about 8,000 cattle graze. This again puts us all at sea in reference to loss but it makes us all the more certain that it will fall far below three per cent. There isn't another range in the United States that shows up like the Bad Lands.
The Dominion government is making concessions to Riel.

The order of President Arthur, opening the Winnebago reservation has been rescined by President Cleveland. There is great injustice in this to the settlers as many will be hopelessly bankrupted. Troops will be necessary to expel the settlers. Indignation meetings are being held and well they may be, as the Indians do not need or even want the land now occupied by settlers.

As will be seen in another article, a strong feeling seems to have grown up against stock interests among the numerous farming class. It is difficult to give a reason for this feeling except on the ground of envy. Almost invariably a stock country is in no sense an agricultural country and vice versa. Consequently their interests do not clash but on the other hand are in many ways dependent on and an aid to each other. We ask our brothers of the eastern press to examine the facts carefully before condemning unheard the principal industry of the west.

There seems to be scarcely a doubt that England and Russia will go to war. Both are defiant and neither cares in the least to explain any of its actions to the other. Both have repeatedly knocked chips off the other's shoulder and as Russia has stepped over England's line, England is now shedding her coat preparatory to "give a licking, take a licking, lick or be licked." As to which wins, makes little difference to the United States. If they will only stop their quarrelling and go to fighting, it will make our beef and wheat men the happiest set in existence. Sic 'em, Bull, sic 'em Bear.

Strange as it may seem, Gen. Grant is constantly improving. There is a very well defined suspicion that the physicians did not diagnose his case correctly and that the national patient is not really suffering from cancer. Be this as it may, Gen. Grant's sickness and near approach to death have shown conclusively the place he occupied in the hearts of his countrymen. There is no other citizen of the United States, whose health would have been so closely watched. No other citizen whose death would have been so sincerely mourned. Gen. Grant is to-day the foremost citizen of the United States.

As we stated once before, we are in a position to know whereof we speak, when we state that ere now a railroad would have been built from Medora to the Hills or a good share of the distance, had the Hills merchants stuck to their written and spoken pledges to ship via the Northern Pacific. The writen contracts were handed to capitalists who were ready to build as soon as it was proved that these merchants would ship as much as estimated. The estimate was low and if all the merchants had done as they agreed, twice the estimated amount of freight, would have been shipped and the Hills people would now have direct or easy railroad connections. As it was, not half nor a quarter of the merchants stood to their agreements and less than that proportion of the freight came by the way of the N. P. It did not make a particle of difference at what point the goods were forwarded, so long as they were sent over the Northern Pacific. This freight was the only guide the capitalists had to go by in figuring on the road and it will be only with the greatest difficulty that they can be induced to invest when the facts speak for themselves that the Hills do not have enough freight to pay for a railroad or that Hills merchants do not stick to their bargains. It is a choice of evils, the latter being the solution.

There are some sayings which are so common that people do not realize their force. Just as spring poets, St. Louis girls' feet and fifty other topics have become butts for the wit of paragraphers, so have cattle companies come to be objects of attack when granger papers want "filling." We are now sorry to see the Bismarck Tribune fall into line with the statement that: "There is one thing for which secretary Lamar ought to be commended by the people of the entire country, and that is the determination to keep cattle kings out of the Indian territory." A sufficient answer to this unsupported statement is, "Why?" We care not how prejudiced the man is, if he honestly attempts to thoroughly answer this question, he will as certainly take the side of the cattlemen as they will their own. The facts are simply these. The part of the Indian Territory in which stockmen now are was a practical desert, of no use to the Indians and not wanted by them. The government had given the Territory to the Indians, however, and only by their consent could cowmen move in. This consent was gained and offers were then immediately made to buy or lease from the government also, so as to get as good a title as possible. Repeatedly have the cowmen tried this but the government has invariably refused payment, although tacitly acknowledging the right of the Indians to lease by leaving the stockmen in undisturbed possession. Even as late as April 7th the cowmen tried earnestly to induce the government to lease to them and they stand willing at any time to pay a fair rental. No one is disturbed by the presence of cattle in the Indian territory, the Indians are satisfied and again we ask: "Why should secretary Lamar be commended."

From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
Large horses of all kinds are higher now than they have been for twenty years. There is no danger of the supply outgrowing the demand, as there is always a ready market for good large horses.

We are in receipt of a letter from Russ Wilson, foreman of the E 6 in which he states that the horses are looking first-rate, being fat and lively. The grass is well up and looks like the map of Ireland, the cattle are looking well and there is a prospect of a large calf-crop. Preparations are nearly completed for the round-up and everyone is busy.

The Wyoming association at their last meeting appointed a committee to see about getting passes for its members. The committee, with John N. Simpson at its head, met a committee representing the lines in question and the subject was put off until the official meeting of the lines.

We commend the New Mexico Stock Grower for the firm stand it has taken against the reckless shooting sometimes practiced by cowboys. It has utterly lost any power even of amusement to outsiders. The Stock Grower says: "This 'bad-man-with-a-gun' business is foolish, cowardly and unmanly and will be stopped in the near future, and some of the experts at 'shooting up things' will find themselves rustling for jobs with none in sight."

That contagious pleuro-pneumonia has really broken out near Fulton, Mo., there seems no reason to doubt. Gov. Marmaduke. all the stockmen of Missouri and commissionor Coleman are taking active measures to stamp out the disease and as everyone is working to that end it is believed that it will not spread at all. Only heroic measurs will be successful. It is absolutely necessary to kill every animal that has the disease and put those that have been exposed, under the strictest quarantine. Already about two hundred animals have been killed and others will be at the first symptom of the disease.

Norman J. Coleman, commissioner of Agriculture has asked the following open questions of the cowmen of fifty-nine Texas counties, with a view to securing a modification of the quarantine enactment and a relief to the present depressed state of the Texas cattle industry: "1. Have you purchased any bulls or other cattle, or do you know of any that have been bought from north of the south line of Kansas to your vicinity, or to any part of any of the counties named above? If so, state the number, the location as near as possible to which they were taken, and the number, if any, which died of acclimatization fever. 2. Do you know of any case in which cattle from the eastern counties of Texas have been taken to the counties above named in the spring or summer months, and allowed to pasture on the same ranges with the cattle native to these counties. If so, state if any disease occurred among the native cattle, and give symptoms and numbers afflicted as far as possible."

The Kansas City Journal tells of a game of poker played recently in that city between Major Drumm and a Texan. The Journal says the Texan had no money but plenty of cattle and an immense desire to play poker with the major. The latter is known around the stock-yards for his great natural resources, and he swept away the seemingly insurmountable difficulty by proposing a game of one steer ante, two steers to come and no limit. They played on this basis. Major Drumm dealt and the gentleman from Texas antied one steer. Both came in and the game opened with four steers on the table. Major Drumm drew two tens and caught an unexpected full, while the gentleman from Texas struck a bobtail snag and passed out. The third was a jack pot and it took three deals to open it. The gentleman from Texas finally drew two jacks and opened the pot with a fine breeding bull, which counted six. Major Drumm covered this with five steers and a two-year-old heifer, and went him twelve better. The gentleman from Texas who drew another jack saw the twelve cows and went fifty steers, twenty two-year-old heifers, four bulls and twenty-five heifers better. Major Drumm looked at his hand and placed upon the table six fine Alderney cows, five imported Durham bulls, one hundred grass fed two-year-olds, fifty prime to medium corn-fed Colorado half-breed steers, with a side bet of a Normandy gelding to cover the bar bill. The man from Texas made his bet good with an even two hundred and fifty straight Kansas wintered Texas half-breeds and ten Scotch polled cattle, fourteen mustangs and the ne 1/4 of the sw 1/4 of section 10 of the Panhandle of Texas, and called. Major Drumm held three aces, and put in his hip pocket 750 steers, heifers, etc, and a big stock ranch.
A number of sales of Texas cattle have lately been made at fair prices, in Texas. They are mostly stock cattle and will go to fill ranges depleted by last summer's sales and this winter's losses.

Some action should be taken by our cowmen to prevent round-ups after the beef round-up in the fall. This is the time when the cattle become attached to one range and, if not disturbed are liable to remain there all winter, only drifting back and forth a little way to avoid storms. If they are disturbed and driven off their range they are liable to drift hundreds of miles. If this subject is discussed in time it will save many dollars to our cowmen.

The cowboy seems to be losing the pristine gorgeousness of his character. Only a few years ago people knew him as a wild and terrible factor in the development of the west. He had things his own way, took possession of towns, ran whole counties, and if he did not drink hot blood, shed it with a recklessness that painted all the streams that sloped away from the Rockies a delicious pinky red. He was the ideal b-a-a-d man from the head-waters of Bitter creek. He ate fire and spat snow. He was wild and wooly and hard to carry. When he ordered a drink it was rattle-snakes' stings with the bite in them. When he sat down to a restaurant table it was to demand a white man's liver and a dead nigger's toe-nales. He waded in gore, and was always in the business of starting graveyards in new towns where the locality was too healthy for any other kind of sudden death than that which comes with old age. This is only a feeble suggestion of what the old-time cowboy of fiction was. In his most peaceful moments he had his hand on his revolver and a big bowie knife between his teeth. His word was law. The statutes of the United States had no more weight than his simple say so. He carried his own court with him, and when the time came to pronounce sentence, whether he was right or wrong, this ancient cowpuncher seldom failed to administer justice with his six-shooter. Where is such a man?—[St. Louis Globe-Democrat.

Papa, who is that man?

My child, that is a cowboy.

Why is he standing there?

He is rolling a cigarette, my child.

What is that just over the hill?

That, my child, is a big herd of cattle.

Why is not the cowboy along with the rest?

My darling, his health requires that he must stop for ten minutes and roll a cigarette before leaving camp.

Is his health poor, papa?

Very poor, my child.

See papa, now he is going.

No, my dear; his saddle is not on straight and he has to put it on again.

Ah! look papa, now he is going.

Yes, my child, he is going—to roll another cigarette.

See, he is looking for something

Yes, he is looking for a match.

Will he find his match?

My child, there are no snails in the country.

Does he not see the cattle running.

No, darling.

Oh! but papa, see he has picked up a coal to light his cigarette and it has burned his hand. And look! his horse has ran away.

Yes, my child; when the foreman comes back to camp he will tell him that his horse ran away and in trying to stop him the rope burned his hand.

But papa, that will be a story.

Yes, my dear, two stories and a basement.

Will such a bad cowboy live in such a high house?

Yes, darling; there is a higher place for him.

Where?

In heaven, my child.

We should elongate our features.

—[Dum Colly Oddle.

Duck and geese are plentiful up and down the river.
Charlie Jolly is nearly recovered from his recent injury.
F. W. McKinney, of Bismarck, stopped over a train Tuesday.
McKenzie & O'Brien will soon move their blacksmith shop to this side of the track.
Dan McKenzie returned Monday evening from a three months' trip to Nova Scotia.
The stock-yards are completed but are scarcely large enough to receive three car-loads of cattle.
Dr. Hebar Robart, of Dickinson, came up last night to see Mrs. Draper who has been ill for some time.
Again were the remaining shoots of the delinquent contestants put off on account of the rain Saturday.
Tom Matthews stopped off a train Monday. He has been appointed inspector by the Montana board of stock commissioners.
Those who have been shooting in the rink for prizes must have their scores completed by May 1, as the prizes are given on that day.
Jack Bullion's brother, Robert, from Maryland Junction, Minn., has been here several days. He intends putting in some horses with Jack.
Large corralls have been built both here and on Sully creek, in addition to the others the Co. has, to accommodate the cattle here this summer.
"It almost breaks my heart to be the bearer of this sad news. Would that I could suffer for you." Ask the night teleg. to diagram this "goak."
It is entirely feasible to bore an artesian well here and the water will be entirely free from alkali. We will have something more to say about this matter soon.
Word has been received from the Willard Bros., that they will be here Saturday or Sunday, with several car-loads of horses. Several sales have been missed by their delay in coming.

W. H. McKanlass, the colored skater and musician will give an exhibition at the rink to-morrow evening, which promises to be a very interesting entertainment. His performance is highly spoken of by the papers along the line.

J. C. Fisher has already set a good example which we hope to see followed extensively, Arbor day, the 25th. Several have already made up their minds to set out trees, which will do much toward improving the looks of our town.

Miss Lou Eleson, of Glendive, will be here Tuesday and Wednesday the 28th and 29th., with a complete assortment of ladies' millinery and fancy goods. Anything desired in this line will be on sale and it will be an excellent opportunity to buy.

A meeting will be held next Monday evening at the rink to organize a bucket brigade. The movement is a commendable one and it behooves all our citizens to turn out to the meeting. We are liable at any time to have a fire and effectual work can be done with buckets.

To-night at the rink there will be a tournament, the person securing the greatest number of rings to be given a prize. Saturday evening May 2, there will be a masquerade, many of the participants in the last one desiring a repetition. Admission to both entertainments will be only the usual rates.

The post-office has been again moved to its old location in the Co's store. The change will not be popular, as lock and call boxes possess many advantages over the general delivery system. It is also rather severe on Mr. Fisher, "wich wuz P. M.," as he had gone to considerable expense in fitting up the office in the rink.

The round-up east of the river and north of the track and to include the whole Killdeer Mt. country will begin May 1. This round-up is for the purpose of driving all the cattle possible to the river so as to be caught in our general round-up. The date for a corresponding round-up south of the track has not been decided.

We notice in the St. Paul dispatches that day before yesterday a number of prominent cowmen were contracting with the N. P. for the delivery of 40,000 cattle to Medora from Washington territory. On account of the large number of cattle and the fact that several of the cowmen mentioned have all their herds in Montana, we are inclined to discredit the report.

The rainy, drizzly, snowy weather of Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, was a perfect godsend to western Dakota. The rain came scarcely faster than need be to have every drop soak into the ground and this, followed by the damp snow of Tuesday and melted by yesterday's genial weather will fill the ground as full as it can hold of water. One can almost see the grass grow now.
Lee Eisenberg, of Bismarck, was here Saturday with a line of dry goods.
Arthur Smith has almost recovered from his accident of two weeks ago.
Geo. Porter returned from Chicago last Friday night. His wife will return in about ten days.
Theodore Roosevelt came in last Friday night and started almost immediatily for his Elkhorn ranch down the river.
Wal. Osterhout went to Miles, Sunday evening to arrange for some horses for Howard Faton, who went up Monday night.
"Sadie" Houk, who will be remembered as a Cow Boy comp. last summer passed through Saturday night on his way to Glendive.
J. D. Garver returned from Bismarck last Friday, with his family. His wife's health is improved though she is far from well. His sister-in-law also accompanied him.
If by any chance a subscriber should not get his paper, it would be a favor if the fact were immediately reported to this office. We will rectify any mistake of this nature.
The body of Mrs. Hawkins, of Spearfish, President Garfield's niece, was brought up on the coach Saturday night from Spearfish and shipped to Mrs. Garfield at Cleveland, Ohio.
B. F. Matthias, formerly superintendent of this division of the N. P. is president of the Charlotte Harbor and Northern Central R. R. with headquarters at Tampa, Florida.
Mr. T. Martin will make a complete digest of his weather reports for the last six months, to be published in connection with his monthly reports. It will make a valuable paper for reference.
"Skinny" Wallace, who drives on the stage line from Buffalo creek to Middle Grand river, was in town Saturday. While here he laid in a good supply of paint and spread a thin coat over the suburbs.

Rev. H. B. Schaffner preached an eloquent sermon in the rink last Sunday evening to a small congregetion. The weather was very stormy which doubtless accounts for the few in attendance. Service will be held every Sunday evening hereafter, at half-past seven.

Lloyd Roberts returned from Glendive Monday morning and started for St. Cloud again Tuesday morning. He delivered several hundred cattle in Glendive in prime condition. He has also delivered mixed herds in Jamestown and Bismarck. He will return again about May 10.

Our thanks are due A. McCall of the Black Hills for a complete list of house and council bills passed at the last session of the legislature. Mr. McCall originated and with the able assistance of the other Hills members, had the bill passed repealing the herd law and establishing the fence law in the western tier of counties.

Mr. and Mrs. and Miss Hattie Eaton parents and sister of the Eaton boys, came in Monday evening and for the summer will make their headquarters at the logging camp. Mr. Eaton reported that while we were having splendid weather here, they were having the worst weather in the east, that he ever experienced. For a time it almost paralyzed business.

Last Friday evening, No. 1 was delayed seven or eight hours by the falling of a huge rock upon the track just east of Sully Springs. A serious accident nearly resulted, as the train could not be stopped until the engine had struck the rock and threw the two front drivers off the track. The rock should have been blasted off long ago as it has been threatening to fall for two or three years.

Our spirits are alternately raised and dampened by the conflicting reports of the war talk between England and Russia. There is no use denying the patent fact that this war will be of vast benefit to the United States. With hearty good-will do we see war-like measures inaugurated.

The latest news of the condition of Gen'l. Grant is very favorable as far as his present condition is concerned but as cheerless as ever in reference to the future. The latest examinations seem to have conclusively proved that the disease is a cancer and this must at no distant time end his life. Should he improve he will be taken to Saratoga and thence to the Catskills.

Medora will see better times this summer even than it has had up to the present. The slaughter-house will employ about a hundred men and several times that number will have steady work outside. It is altogether probable that this year and if not, then next, there will be built here a tannery, glue works and other factories to use up the parts of cattle not fit for beef. Not a particle of the animal will be wasted that can possibly be utilized. In fact the business will be conducted on the economical principles of the Chicago slaughter-houses. Several other industries are bound to arise here and altogether Medora can look forward not only to a continuation but to an increase in her prosperity.

We wish again to call attention to a matter that has heretofore gone without explanation. It is in reference to the man arrested by Wm. Jones for setting fire to the prairie.

The facts in the case are briefly these. Last fall a man was found near Scoria who had built a fire and allowed it to spread. When spoken to on the subject, he returned an insulting answer and refused to put out the fire. Jones was then asked to arrest the man and put out the fire which he did. The man was kept here a few days and Jones then took him to Mandan for trial. Just as they were getting on the train, the man unsuccessfully tried to bribe Jones to liberate him, showing that he had money. Arrived in Mandan, the man was tried, his guilt clearly proven and he was bound over to the circuit court and as he could not furnish the $200 bail he was put in jail. His crime, by the way, was punishable with a fine of $200 or six months in jail, so it will be seen that the bail was certainly small enough.

In the jail, the prisoner was put at all sorts of jobs and as near as we can make out, became tired of his surroundings and walked away one day.

There has been much comment on this case and no one as yet has been able to learn any particulars as to the man's release. Of course, all put the worst construction on the case and state with a good show of truth that the man put up all the money he had to parties in the ring and he was turned loose. We have no means of knowing whether this is so or not and we write this article with the intention of finding some sort of an explanation.

Somehow and by some legal officer a crime was committed in allowing the criminal to escape. At some time also, Billings county will be called on to pay a large bill in this farce. We propose to know before that bill is paid whether it is a just one or not. If not, it will as surely not be paid as that the COW BOY is published in Medora.

The history of county government in Dakota is blackened all over with crimes committed by legalized robbers in the garb of county officers and as far as Billings county is concerned we propose it shall stop before it has fairly begun.

This remark may not apply to the case in hand, but it looks mightily like it. Under no circumstances except the death or insanity of the criminal could he have been liberated legally. He must have stood trial at the circuit court, which has not yet set.

To stop all further comment on this question we would like to have an answer from the officers interested and will cheerfully make room for their communications.

A marked copy of the COW BOY will be sent to the justice who tried the case, to the prosecuting attorney and to the jailer. From these men we shall expect answers, to be published in our next issue.

We do not take this stand on this one case so much on account of itself, but on account of the principle involved. It has been altogether too customary for county officers to learn "what there was in it," receive their divvy and keep mum. Especially is this the case when one county is joined to another for judicial purposes as Billings is to Morton. All the officers of the older counties cared for was to run up as much costs as possible on the unorganized counties, get their share of the plunder and then like a squeezed lemon, throw the rind away.

We have had enough of this outside interference in our affairs and want to give notice that Billings county's affairs shall not be tampered with by any blood-suckers, legalized or not. A perfectly honest administration of our affairs by Morton county must and shall be had. Any other outside interference is liable to leave the meddler with badly burned fingers.

When we have received an answer as to how and by whose authority this criminal was released, we will have a few other questions to ask relative to other matters.

From every direction comes news of the pressing necessity for draft horses, especially those averaging over twelve hundred. The raising of these horses is an industry that has even less chance of being overdone than that of raising cattle.

The Shorthorns, formerly often called Durhams, came from northeastern England, and are the most numerous and mostly widely distributed breed in this country, or in the world. The size is of the largest; the color is either red, white, or a mixture of either of these in any proportion. The horn is short and comparatively light, but no more so than in some other breeds. Although valued chiefly as a beef-making animal, Shorthorns as a breed are good milkers, but less attention has been given of late years to their dairy qualities than formerly. No cattle are more attractive than the best Shorthorns. The body is long, the back straight and broad, the ribs well sprung, the rump straight and well filled out. As a rule Shorthorns are taller than cattle of most other breeds, and not infrequently they are subject to the criticisms of being too long in the leg. The head and neck are generally light and well formed. The beef is good and the milk is of full average richness. No other breed has had anything like the influence on the cattle in the chief beef-producing States as the Shorthorn.—[N. W. Farmer.

At the risk of hammering too often on one nail, we will say a word more on the subject of cheap bulls. We think that breeders generally will concur in the opinion that, as a rule, cheap bulls, in the sense in which we now use the term cheap, "dear at any price," would perhaps be the most correct expression of our meaning, have wrought more harm to the cause of pure breeding than aught else in the history of livestock development. It is to utter a mere truism to say that the bull is the most important part of the herd; that while an inferior cow stamps her impress upon but one calf in a season, the inferior bull will deteriorate the whole season's crop of calves. These things are so plain that to emphasize them is to be tedious, and yet of all things worth remembering none seem so easily forgotten. We have seen inferior bulls sold at less money than could have been obtained for them as steers at the same age, and they brought too high a price then. It is the great mistake which so many make, to imagine that the registry makes the bull. Registry is the certificate upon which we base our faith in the animal's pure breeding, and as far as that goes it is not only desirable but essential, but when it comes to merit we must look to the animal itself, and to its record as a calf-getter. The difference in the quality of a bull will readily make a difference of $200 to $400, or $500 in the value of the first crop of calves, and the greatest mistake a man can make is to deceive himself on the importance of getting a good bull, and equally great, and still more culpable is the mistake of the breeder who permits himself to sell inferior bulls that he knows are not fit to breed from. It is a suicidal policy, and unfortunately one that affects all breeders as well as himself.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.

"Experience is a dear teacher," but from some remarks we have heard, the losses on late states' yearlings has not had its full weight on some of our stockmen. From points gathered from all sources we will state it as a fact that outside of late one's and two's the loss in the Bad Lands has not been two per cent. This includes all cattle brought in early last spring and old cattle. At least three per cent., if not more, of the late one's and two's succumbed to their ignorance of the ranges and of how to rustle. In view of these facts it certainly seems foolish to hear stockmen say that there is plenty of time to put in cattle later in the season and that they will contract for some after a while. "Now is the accepted time" to contract and inside of a month every head of cattle should be on the range, that is expected to winter here in safety.

The arrival of a shipment of cattle at the Union Stock Yards, Chicago, last Friday, from Walla Walla, Washington Territory, marked something like an epoch in western cattle trade, this being the first shipment of cattle ever made to the Chicago market from the Pacific coast. The drove in question numbered 330, and averaged 1,294 lbs.; they brought $4.40 per 100 lbs., a price which was declared satisfactory to their owners. The cattle were range cattle, and had left Walla Walla by train March 30th, and arrived in Chicago April 10th, having been eleven days on the way. They, of course, made the whole distance, nearly 2,300 miles, by rail, and were unloaded but five times; they traveled over four great railways, and through three of the largest territories and three of the largest states. While there was no great profit, taken altogether, as an experimental shipment, it was a success. Only one animal was lost, its horns being caught between the slats of the car, and in trying to free itself it was strangled. The cattle were bought for the dressed beef trade, and if they should be destined to make up some of the orders for the supply of British troops, it is more than likely that they may reach, before fulfilling their ultimate destiny, the mountains of Afghanistan, after traveling more than half way around the world.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.

When the Polled-Angus and Hereford association met in Chicago, last fall, the call was made on the members at both meetings to agree to steer some pure-bred bull calves for the purpose of preparing them for future exhibits. The call resulted in members of the last named, although it was a very full meeting, agreeing to steer thirteen bull calves, and the members of the Angus association agreeing to steer sixteen. Members present expressed themselves as encouraged by this readiness (?) of members to sacrifice males for the benefit of the breed. One would certainly be justified from this in supposing that the great majority of those present regarded every male calf dropped as fit to breed from. Yet there is not one of the gentlemen present who does not cordially concur in the advice so frequently given to breeders, to "use the knife unsparingly." It is, then, as in so many other things, simply a question of temporary profit. It is true pure-bred bulls are better than scrubs any day in the year, and that the number of pure-bred bulls is comparatively insignificant in proportion to the whole number of cattle in the country. It is also doubtless true that our pure-bred cattle probably average higher than they do in other countries, owing to the fact that so many of them have been imported, and it is presumable that importers, if they have not always secured the best, have rarely, if ever, undertaken to bring over inferior animals. At the same time, it is useless to deny that breeders are setting but a poor example to the numerous farmers who are using, or offering for service, grade bulls, when they decline to use the knife on any of their pure-bred animals, and every year send out some which they well know themselves will do little or no credit to the breed itself or to themselves, as breeders. As nothing does the breeder so much good as the get of the bulls he sells in the neighborhoods where they go, if they are a credit to him and his bulls, so nothing permanently injures his reputation more surely than to send out an inferior bull, sold exclusively on the strength of his being registered. We hope, during the next few months, to hear of many pure-bred bull calves put in the way of being converted into prime beef.—[National L. S. Journal.

Kittleman is again raking in the shekals in California on his hundred yard time.

Dan Mace, probably the best trainer and driver of trotting horses this country has ever produced, died April 19. Among other horses he brought out and gave records to Lady Thorne, American Girl, G. M. Patchen, Pocahontas, Ethan Allen, Judge Fullerton, Medoc, George Wilkes and Fearnaught.

Sullivan has kept up his hippodroming and deceitfulness so long that all his backers are losing confidence in him. He and Ryan have signed articles to fight at Butte City, Montana, but it is money to marbles that the fight never takes place. Sullivan will have few sympathizers should he lose the championship.

J. N. Maxwell has gone to Mandan on a short visit.
Tom Matthews was here yesterday on official business.
E. Elmer is building a dwelling house on Williamson & Copeland's lot.
To-day is the last chance for contestants in the shooting match in the rink.
The historical shack just vacated by Dr. Jorgens is already rented for a dry-goods and clothing store.
L. Ayers again loomed up on us yesterday. He is always welcome to Medora, where he has a host of friends.
It is estimated that 150,000 cattle will be shipped into Montana and the Bad Lands of Dakota this summer.
About one hundred men will be employed constantly at the slaughter-house as soon as the season's work begins.
Peter Book is building a fine dwelling house near his brick kiln. He will veneer it as soon as he can make the brick.
F. D. Foster started for Chicago this morning after his wife, and a lot of men to work in the slaughter-house. He will return in about three weeks.
What we want to know is whether Johnny Munro has been and gone and done it or not. Any information will be cheerfully received at this office.
Remember that the masquerade at the rink will take place Saturday night. Those who attended the last one will need no invitation to come again.
Mr. Paddock finds that his livery barn is altogether too small for his business, although it is of good size, and intends immediately to about double its size.
Mr. Jordan's wife and daughter arrived from the east last week and the family will go to keeping house as soon as a dwelling, already begun, is completed.
T. L. Skinner, attorney for the Caledonia mine in the Hills, went out on this morning's coach. He has been in New Orleans in charge of the Black Hills exhibit.

A large number of cattle have been contracted for by the Marquis, the principal firms contracted with being the Hashknife and Niobrara companies. About 20,000 will be delivered here this summer and fall.

"Oh, its nice to be a daddy," sings Frank Keeler. In confidence, he admits that it is the prettiest little ten-pound male cherub in the country and was born April 11. Mrs. Keeler will come to Medora to live in about two weeks.

The stock-yards across the river are of very little use, being entirely too small. They should be four times as large and have a good branding chute. Should the railroad company not improve the yards, it would pay our stockmen to do so.

Foot-ball and base-ball are becoming popular sports among the boys. If a nine were organized anywhere between Dickinson and Glendive, or even at a further distance where expenses were guaranteed, we could make it very warm for them.

Our readers will notice the new advertisment of the Fargo Ins. Co., appearing in this issue. This is a perfectly safe and reliable company having a paid-up capital of $100,000. It should be patronized extensively as it is a home institution.

Dr. Jorgens and Mr. Martin have been busy moving the drug-store for a day or two and are now nearly settled in the best store room in town. It is of good size, painted in light colors and has a full glass front. We hope to see other stores as good go up speedily.

And it came to pass that William the bronco-buster bet Johnny he could ride a bucking cayuse. But William was afflicted sore and he did pound a hole in the ground which in the wet season will fill up and become like unto a lake. And a glittering shekal did pass from the hand of William to that of Johnny and after a season of barter gurgled down the throats of those who had come forth to see. And all grinned gleefully.

T. W. Ives is still shooting lightning at Sentinel Butte.
Jack Robinson, partner of the Willard Bros., came Monday morning and will go to the Hills by stage.
The Heinze Bros., of Bismarck, came Tuesday night and are now engaged locating lines for the Co.
The plans for the hotel have again been changed and the veranda will be added as at first intended.
A letter from A. M. Sinnott, dated at Butte City seems to indicate that he is doing well in his new home.
The stages have not been making as good time as usual, owing to the poor roads. Business is very good, however, for this season.
Scarcely a day passes but that from one to five trains of cattle from Minnesota and Iowa pass through Medora on their way west.
Denny Friedman expects to return with Lloyd Roberts about May 10, and will remain at the Sloping bottom ranch the most of the summer.
A bank building will soon be put up on the vacant hotel square. It is understood that it will be a branch of Stebbins, Mund & Co. It will be certain of success.
Wm. Jones, an old-time college mate of the editor's, is now private secretary to the Marquis. There is no one of our friends whom we wish or who deserves greater success.
It is now the intention of the Co. to put up a large lodging house, capable of accommodating all the slaughter-house men. It will be put up as soon as the brick can be made.

Two duck hunters from Medora were badly disappointed in getting ducks at Beach last Saturday, but their disappointment was greatly lessened by the pleasure of a very enjoyable dance held at the section house under the auspices of Mrs. Gustin and Miss.

The Willard Bros. arrived Monday evening with one of the best herds of horses that has ever been driven in here. They were a long time in the cars and many had their manes and tails eaten off, but as a whole they showed up well. Several head were sold here but they were too late to strike the market. They [start?] to-day or to-marrow for the Hills and will reach there in about sixteen days.

T. K. Long prosecuting attorney of Morton county and Ed. Drury, deputy sheriff came up Sunday night to enforce the law passed during the last legislature, compelling the liquor dealers of unorganized counties to pay a county license to the senior counties. Partial payments were made by the liquor men and the whole will probably be paid. We very much doubt the constitutionality of this law and by all means advise our liquor men to make a test case and fight it out. It is worth the trial in any event and this is undoubtly only an entering wedge to further taxation.

A meeting to organize a bucket brigade was held in the rink last Monday evening. It was called to order by J. C. Fisher and A. T. Packard was elected chairman. The necessity of such an organization was unanimously conceded. On motion, a committee of five was appointed, the names of J. C. Fisher, Jos. A. Ferris, Marquis de Mores, F. D. Foster and J. B. Walker being suggested and adopted. This committee was authorized to go ahead and perfect all arrangements. They met Tuesday evening and decided to purchase buckets, ladders, hooks, axes &c., the money to be raised by subscription. The force-pump and pipe at the Marquis' house may also be brought into requisition.
Night before last, in Miles City, the whole post-office block was destroyed by fire.
The improvement in General Grant's condition goes steadily on and now it is confidently expected that he will live long enough to finish his war history.

Sorrowfully do we chronicle the fact that the war feeling between England and Russia is subsiding and that the two nations are now resorting to arbitration, Emperor Wilhelm, of Germany, has been appointed arbitrator.

There is really no news of the Riel rebellion, except that the revolutionists seem to be strengthening constantly and the Dominion troops are either under command of an inefficient general or he is badly handicapped by the government officials. The only just and sensible way for the Dominion to settle this matter is to grant the half-breeds every one of their demands.

Butte City is determined to make herself notorious. A bill has been prepared and doubtless by this time passed by the city council providing that the law prohibiting prize-fighting in Montana, should be inoperative June 16, the date set for the Sullivan-Ryan fight. Butte could be in far better business than to encourage such an exhibition. The worst of the matter is that by this measure Butte will take all the odium and receive not a penny's worth of benefit. It is almost a foregone conclusion that the fight will never take place.

The Belfield Courier, Vol 1, No. 1, is lying on our table. Louis C. Hay and Geo. Auld are editors and it is published by the Mandan Times. This latter fact is not mentioned editorially, but the earmarks of Bro. Cates' skill as a printer are as plainly manifest as is the idiocy of trying to get up a boom for a town by the aid of a paper which advertises its own inability to live otherwise than as a boom issue. It is a wonderfully short-sighted piece of folly for the boomers not to see that all will soon learn that the Courier is not printed in Belfield and then indeed will it prove a boomerang. We have the utmost good wishes for the future of Belfield but we have often expressed our views of the utter foolishness of booming a town. In this intance, however, the reason is plainly manifest. It is the last dying effort to squeeze a little juice out of a lemon that was picked too soon to ever contain any juice. If carefully nourished, the Courier may last two months, but we doubt it.

From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.

Senators Dawes and Ingalls, sub-committee of the senate committee on Indian affairs, will visit the Indian Territory soon and will either make a report making the closing of the Oklahoma country legitimate or prohibiting it altogether.

State veterinarian Paraan, of Illinois, reports that it is extremely difficult to stamp out pleuro-pneumonia as the local authorities manifest the greatest indifference in aiding him. The rooting out of contagious cattle diseases is a matter that should be taken entirely out of the hands of local authorities and placed in that of state and national officials. In this way only can contagious diseases be kept from spreading.
