Four trotting horses have been recently purchased in this country by a gentleman from Vienna, Austria, and will be taken home by him for the purpose of starting a stable of this class of horses. A mile track has been established in that city, and racing will be instituted there during the coming summer upon the American plan.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

And now, to still further dispel the illusion that Texas fever is only a scare, gotten up by northwestern cattlemen to to keep their ranges from being overstocked, the stockgrowers north of the Texas Pacific in Texas have quarantined against all cattle south of the road. This is liable to lead to serious difficulty among Texans, but the fact of the quarantine goes a long way toward proving that there is such a thing as Texas fever. In any event, it more firmly establishes the positions of the many states and territories which have recently quarantined against Texas cattle.

Cattle on the range are said to be in tip-top condition for this season of the year, and a large calf crop is anticipated. However it is not to be understood that they are beef fat, for that day has past, or that there are not a great many that are quite thin; but what we mean by tip-top condition is that they are in good living fix and thriving. Calves dropped now will find their mothers strong, and the range being good, will supply them with plenty of milk and the loss will be nominal. True, calves dropped out of season had a tough time of it, but it is safe to calculate on raising 95 per cent of those dropped since March 1st is, of course too early for calves to come. May 1st would be early enough if cattle men could regulate this as handily as sheep growers do. But this being an exceptional year the March crop fared well. And if the branding does not turn out well, owners will know the reason why and may conclude that the day of big calf crops like many other good things has passed and will return no more until cattle men learn, like sheep men, to control the breeding season.—[Rocky Mountain Husbandman.

The secretary of the Interior, according to instructions of the Montana association, has been earnestly petitioned by the president and secretary of the association, to see that the Montana Indians are properly cared for. Almost all the difficulty ever had with the Indians was due to the fact that the government promised to provide for them and then, through Indians agents, almost starved them, forcing them in many instances to eat their horses and dogs. In other words, although the intention of the government was good, the Indians have experienced a perfectly unreliable policy, being promised things that were never fulfilled. It is easy then to see how so many difficulties have arisen with the Indians. Smarting under a sense of wrong, they have tried, in their own way, to right it. We are not over-friendly to the Indians but we are more an enemy to the policy the government has adopted toward them and still more an enemy to the miserably ineffectual way the government has of carrying out its policy. By all means let us have a change. Anything will be an improvement over the present system.
Duck and geese are becoming plentiful on the river.
The work of filling the new cold-storage rooms with ice is nearly completed.
A well, to be used for fire purposos has been built south of the Co's. offices.
A tight corrall for pigs is being built at the foot of the butte north-east of the slaughter-house.
There will be a mile race at the rink Saturday night between George Bicknell and Pete Campbell.
"Max" has again gone home for a visit of a week or two. J. M. Stickel takes his place temporarily.
Considerable grading has been done lately and much more will be done soon. It materially improves the appearance of our streets.
Many train-loads of gravel have been brought in to the slaughter-house side-track and the track will be raised several feet.
The Hash-knife outfit was to begin gathering fat cattle for the Co., April 15. The first bunch can be expected here before June 1.
Grass never received a better start here than it has this spring. It is now long and old enough so that cattle will begin to pick up rapidly.
Everyone should remember the meeting at the rink to-morrow night and attend it with the intention of doing his individual best for the points brought up.
"Otto von Bismarck" descended upon us yesterday and has now firmly convinced everyone that Franz Falk's beer is the elixir of life.
Hereafter, we will publish a weekly weather report by Mr. Martin and give the summary monthly. From many sources we have received complimentary notice of the faithful record kept by him.

Large lodging houses will soon be built on the vacant lots north of the hotel for the accommodation of the Co's, men. It is also to be hoped that the Co. will build more dwelling houses, as there is pressing need for them.

We have heard of several remarkable case of absent-mindedness, but the climax was capped Tuesday by Vic. Smith, who got so interested shooting flies off a log that he didn't notice that his bullets were going straight into the freight house, until his fire was returned.

There is every probability that the stage line will be pulled off this week. Had the Hills merchants lived up to their promises, there could have been no difficulty in paying expenses. As it is, there is no use in benefitting people who will not return the compliment.

As a result of the recent surveying work the lots on the south side of the track will be so arranged as to allow a side-track to be built near the bluff and extending to the brick-yard. The streets will also be changed so that the lots next the river will face that way. On this side the track, room will be made for a side-track next the butte and next to the right of way all the lots will be made to face the railroad. The Marquis will also try to secure the right of way from the railroad to turn it into a park.

There has been some talk of appointing a deputy sheriff for Billings Co., to be under the Morton county sheriff. To this we wish to put in a desided negative for two reasons. First, it will put us more than ever under the dominion of Morton county and second, will do us but little more good than formerly as there will be no justice here before whom to swear out complaints. Instead of deputy sheriff we should have a deputy U. S. marshal.

Howard Eaton came in from Belfield Tuesday evening, to which place he had ridden from Wadsworth's line camp at the head of Frank's creek and reported that a gun in the hands of Joe. Graham was accidentally discharged, shooting off his right middle finger and then the bullet went completely through the left thigh of Frank Wadsworth crushing the bone and making an ugly flesh wound in the right thigh. From what we could learn it will be necessary to amputate the leg, involving a serious operation. Dr. Roberts happened to be here and started immediately on horse-back for the scene of the accident.

[A later report brought in by Pierce Boland is that the leg was successfully amputated by Dr. Robarts and that the patient was doing as well as could be expected. At the time Pierce left the ball was still lodged in the right thigh.]
A Cowboy in a Sleeping Car.

"Where do I camp?" he inquired, and was shown a lower berth next to me.

"That's the pigeon hole, is it? All right, old son; just watch my motion while I file myself away."

At this juncture he was ordered to turn over his revolver to the porter, which he declined to do in a most prompt and spirited manner.

"Old Dad (his revolver) and me always sleep together, and we don't want no divorce," he explained.

The conductor remonstrated, but was advised not to try to "braid this mule's tail."

"This here's a sleepin' car, ain't it?" he at length inquired.

"Yes."

"Well, why in——don't you let people sleep, then, when they've paid and gone into your game? If you're aiming to keep people awake, and want company, just dance into the next car; there's lots of folks there that don't want to sleep, nohow, and 'll be glad to see you."

The conductor withdrew, and my friend pulled off his boots and stretched himself, with many comments, in an undertone, on the poverty of the surroundings.

In about ten minutes this erratic person had his head out in the aisle.

"Say! you boy,"—to the porter.

"Well, sah."

"Come a runnin'."

The porter drew near and was handed a pillow about as big as a pin cushion.

"Take that gooseha'r thing away," commanded the cowboy.

"Don't you want a pillow, sah?" asked the porter.

"That ain't no pillow, and I don't want it, nohow; I'm afraid it'll get in my ear."

After this, silence, and for a short time I slept. I roused up, however at an exclamation on the part of my neighbor.

"Hold on there, my son, jest drap them boots."

"I was only jest gwine to black 'em, boss."

"Drap 'em."

They drapped.

"Jest gwine to pull them spurs, I reckon. Now, don't monkey 'round my camp, takin' things, no more. If you want anythin' speak for it. If you can't speak make signs, and if you can't make signs, shake a bush. You hear me?"

"Yes, sah."

After this more silence. The wheels and rails again sang together, and the cars again kept approving time, and presently I slept without interruption.—[Northwest.

A dance was given at the residence of Mr. Graham in Mingusville by the Misses Graham, last Monday evening. A very pleasant time was had and Mingusville kept up her reputation as a getter-up of pleasant social gatherings.

Revs. Schaffner and Huntley came down Sunday evening and the largest congregation yet assembled here, listened to an interesting sermon from the latter who has charge of north Dakota missions. We hope to see as good a turnout next Sunday evening when Mr. Schaffner will again be here.

The N. P. R. C. Co. expect by next year to handle at least 500 cattle a day. About half of these will be shipped alive. From figures furnished us by the Marquis it appears that on this number of cattle, over $250,000 will be saved during the season by adopting the lake route via Duluth to Buffalo and thence to New York.

The St Paul Globe, with its usual correctness, states that Theodore Roosevelt passed through St. Paul lately on his way to his ranch on the Elkhorn. For the benefit of the Globe's thick-witted stock editor we would state that the name Elkhorn applies to the brand on the cattle and not to any river, creek, coulie, ravine or butte in the Bad Lands.

The rink shooting contests have been decided, A. T. Packard winning the one offered to members of the gun club and Mose Ryder the one offered to those not members. Packard's score averaged fifty-three and three-twentieths out of a possible sixty and Ryder's averaged fifty-one. The range was seventy-five feet, the bulls eye being an inch and a half. The best score was five straight bull's eyes, made by Packard.

The Marquis is enthusiastic over the fact that the streak of whitish clay found about twenty feet above the largest lignite veins near here has turned out to be kaoline. This is the finest kind of pottery clay, the most costly ware being made from it. If it turns out as expected the Marquis will put up large works, which will draw more money to Medora than the slaughtering business. We certainly hope there will be no disappointment in this new discovery.

The Medora branch of the Boston clothing, boot and shoe store opened up in good shape last Friday. Their goods are of first-class quality and prices are scarcely higher than those quoted in St. Paul. The Co. now has branches at Dayton, Ohio, Bismarck, Mandan and Medora, Dak., and Miles City, Billings and Glendive, Montana. They own a factory at 631 Broadway N. Y. and are thus able to undersell any firm in the west. The establishment of a branch here is gladly welcomed and will be liberally patronized. The resident manager T. W. Gordon has already made a good impression here and we see no reason why the store should not do a large business.

The Willard Bros., after selling a few horses here and allowing the bunch to recruit up started for the Hills, where the most of the band has been contracted. Cap., Fred and Ed. Turner made many friends here and if they will quit rustling we would be glad to see them again. We regret exceedingly, though, that Cap. should have wasted so much raw material as to have picked such places to pound holes in the ground off his bucking cayuse as can never be used even for post holes. Fred said that he never was so sorry for anything in his life as to see Cap. thrown but—well, we all know Fred. We might add that Fisher intends getting out a writ of habeas-corpus to recover the coat Cap. rustled.

Sylvane Ferris and W. A. Merrifield returned with the Elkhorn and Chimney Butte cattle.

All members of the order of A., F. & A. M., in good standing, are requested to meet at the rink on Friday evening this week, after the firemen's meeting, to consider the advisability of establishing a lodge at this place.

Fifteen hundred head of states yearlings and two's came in Tuesday morning for the Elkhorn and Chimney Butte ranches of Theodore Roosevelt. They were in fair condition after their long ride and except for the disadvantage of a large number being yearlings, give every evidence of growing into good beef. The larger majority are steers. A good lot of Short-horn bulls and one Polled-Angus were in the herd. A thousand of these cattle will be driven to the Elkhorn ranch and five hundred to the already well-stocked Chimney Butte ranch.

There will be a meeting to-morrow night at the rink which every man having a cents worth of interest in Medora or Little Missouri, should feel it his duty to attend. Several points of interest will be brought up, the first of which is fire protection. As good a bucket brigade as possible will be formed which will be able to do much good in case of fire. A movement will also be set on foot to organize a regular school, which will receive the consideration of the meeting. A third point will be to organize in such a way that in case of any lawlessness or the desirability of "firing stiffs" we can have men to depend on in doing the work. Another point to be brought up is that of grading and otherwise improving the streets. Bob Roberts has proved beyond doubt that scoria, when beaten down and mixed with the clay and sand makes a first-rate macadam. There is enough scoria here to pave a city and means will be found to utilize it. The meeting will be held at 7:30 and we hope to see every one interested present.

Having read the private diary kept by Vic Smith on his trip from Poplar river to Bismarck by boat in search of beaver, we are only sorry that we cannot publish it in full. He started from Medora March 4th and reached Glendive in time to see a "Democratic twenty-years' drunk." Starting from Glendive for Poplar creek in a buckboard stage(?) he had one drunken driver after another until the climax was capped by one jehu trying to pull to pieces a bedstead with a good Indian on it. As Vic had too great a respect for his scalp to meddle with dead Indians he induced the driver to go on. At Wolf Point about 200 government cattle had died and the Indians were having a glorious time. At Ft. Galpin, on the Missouri, he got a team to take him to Milk river, camping in the deserted shack of Tom Cambell, a man who kept forty-seven diffierent squaws. He became wringing wet from breaking into streams and for some time had to live on sage hens and prairie dogs. At Milk river he camped awaiting the spring break-up. One day shooting a goose, it fell on a gorge and just as he had secured it with the aid of a long pole, the gorge broke and he had a parrot and monkey time getting on shore. When he did return, he found that the Indians had stolen all his grub. Here in his diary he remarked that he observed the fourth commandment. The day was Sunday and we are left in a state of harrowing uncertainly as to whether he meant the fourth or fifth. Here he killed several beaver and on March 26th the river broke and he started down stream in his skiff. After a number of dangerous experiences he landed in Bismack with about $300 worth of beaver skins.

All the U. S. treasury money has been counted and the amount found correct to a cent. So much for Republican corruption. The Democrats can well be proud to show such a record.

The Illinois senatorial contest is coming to a focus. Morrison's name will be dropped by the Democrats if he cannot secure a full vote and some other name proposed. The Republicans are still loyal to Logan and have the best chances of success.

There has been fighting at Batoche, between Gen. Middleton and Riel's forces, the half-breeds getting rather the best of it. At any rate the dominion troops could not dislodge the enemy and Middleton has sent for more forces. Although the matter must end in Riel's defeat, we can hope that the Dominion will be taught the lesson that it cannot trample on the rights of citizens with impunity.

There have been stirring times in England lately, owing to the government's war policy. Gladstone recently was was voted a large credit, supposably with the intention of prosecuting war measures against Russia. As soon as he had this credit, measures were immediately taken to grant Russia everything she demanded and England was thus forced into a very humiliating situation. The war party, lead by Sir Stafford Northcote, has aroused intense feeling against Gladstone and it may end in his overthrow. Should this occur war will likely be declared.

The Deadwood Pioneer, in an article headed "What Arguments," attempts to answer our statements relative to a railroad being built from Medora to the Hills. As our readers will remember our article stated that a large number of the Hills merchants contracted to ship their freight and express via the Northern Pacific to the Hills. These contracts, with a low estimate of the amount of freight and express involved were handed to capitalists who agreed to build the road provided the estimate held good. We know that the actual amount shipped would have been twice as much as the estimate had the Hills merchants stuck to their bargains and in reality the the amount shipped was not half the amount of the estimate. The capitalists could only judge by the facts and as there was not enough business to guarantee a road, refused to build without additional income. These are the facts as we stated them and we might add that the stage line was merely a feeler as to the Hills trade. The Pioneer then talks about the folly of whipping the Hills people into subjection or suffering the vengeance of the Northern Pacific. There was no attempt to whip the Hills people into subjection. They voluntarily signed contracts to ship via the N. P. and as voluntarily broke their promises. No attempt was made to compel them to stick to their agreement and none will be made. As far as the Hills people suffering the vengeance of the N. P. is concerned we will state that the N. P. would have had nothing whatever to do with the road, except that it would get a haul out of the Hills freight. Outside capital entirely was interested in the matter. The Pioneer then states that other roads are building Hillwards, while the N. P. is dozing and grumbling over broken promises. As we have just stated, the N. P. has nothing to do with the contemplated road and the Pioneer should be in far higher business than blaming a corporation for refusing to deal with persons who have violated contracts and then itself finds no word of fault with the contracts breakers. The Pioneer can readily see, that it has in no way answered our article and we will reiterate our former statement that had half the Hills merchants stuck to their promises they would now have direct or convenient railroad connection with the N. P.

The Refrigerator Car Co. have nearly completed arrangements to handle cattle for the slaughter-house. The bottoms up the river from Pete Book's coal mine are being entirely cleared of trees and underbrush. The cattle from the Hashknife and the whole southern country will be driven down Sully creek from the divide and those from Montana will come down Garner creek. Two large corrals have been built on the bottom this side of the Custer Trail ranch. They are without doubt the best corrals in this part of the country, being made on the stockade plan and are capable of holding about a thousand cattle each. The animals will be driven into one corral in the evening and in the morning will be weighed on scales 40x14 connecting the two corrals. Thence they will be driven down the river to the slaughter-house. Inside of two years all the bottoms will be plowed and sowed to alfalfa or millet, the object being to get sufficient feed to keep cattle fit for slaughtering at all seasons of the year.

A bill of considerable interest to all stockgrowers in the northwest has been passed by the Illinois legislature. It is a measure to regulate the charges of the Chicago stock yards for yardage, freight grain, hay and other articles furnished and to prevent extortion and unjust discrimination. It provides among other things that the stockyards shall not receive for yardage more than fifteen cents per head for horses, cattle and mules, five cents for hogs and four cents for sheep, nor more than five per cent additional to the current market wholesale price for hay, corn or other articles supplied by them for the sustenance of such animals; and that sales shall be made by actual weight. The penalty for collecting higher rates or unjust discrimination is a fine not less than $300 for the first offense, and not less than $500 nor more than $1,000 for subsequent offense.—[Livingston Enterprise.

In answer to several inquiries from the east, we will state that it is very seldom any cattle are fed in this country. The bulk of the cattle have nothing and need nothing to eat but the range grasses. Only in exceptional cases where an animal is very weak and the weather severe is any feeding done. There is enough alkali in the water and grass to furnish cattle all the saline matter they need. Old range cattle almost invariably refuse to touch salt in its crystalline state.

A train load of cattle, nine hundred and fifty head, have been quarantined for several days at Sentinel Butte. They belong to F. W. Fry, of Arkansas. It is impossible to learn the cause of the quarantine but it must be on account of Montana's pleuro-pneumonia quarantine law. The owner maintains that the cattle are free from disease although they are very poor. The whole herd was turned loose at the Butte, orders coming from the railroad officials to that effect. There were no horses and only the men on the train to aid in holding the cattle. They are now widely scattered. In whatever light this affair is viewed it is a badly botched mess. If the cattle are free from disease, as the owner claims, and come from a healthy country, it is a great imposition on him. The railroad company had no right to ship the cattle in the first place if they were diseased and by their being scattered at Sentinel Butte endanger other herds. There seems to be no fear of contagion and we are forced into the belief that the owner has been treated unjustly.

Following close on the heels of the news of the accident to Frank Wadsworth, which happened a week ago Tuesday, came the sad news of his death, occuring Friday at noon. It is seldom that a death is so widely mourned as was this one. Frank was a very quiet, unobtrusive man, one who always attended strictly to his business and left the impression of having a reserve force of character that impelled him to do right at all times. It will be remembered that he was accidentally shot last Tuesday and that his leg was amputated Wednesday. He was a splendid patient, cheerfully enduring the agony incident to the operation. Even within a few minutes of his death he was talking pleasantly to the watchers. The bullet was probed for to a depth of eight inches but it could not be found. It undoubtedly entered his abdomen, thus making the fatal wound. The funeral services took place at Belfield last Sunday, a number of citizens from here, attending. Rev. H. B. Shaffner conducted the ceremonies and the body was laid to rest near the church, a beautiful site for the resting place of the dead.

The meeting last Friday evening was called to order by Marquis de Mores and A. T. Packard was elected chairman.

The chairman stated the objects of the meeting to be, to organize a fire department, to adopt measures to keep the town free of all rubbish, to perfect a school organization and to appoint a committee to see that order is kept.

In reference to the fire department the chairman of the old committee, J. C. Fisher, reported that a sum of money, probably sufficient for present need, had been subscribed but that no word had as yet been received from F. D. Foster relative to material. Further time was given the committee. Chief of the fire department were then elected as follows: J. A. Ferris and J. B. Walker on the west side of the river and A. T. Packard and Bob. Roberts on the east side.

A report of the old school board by J. C. Fisher was then given by which it appeared that about $40.00 was yet due on last term's expenses. Sufficient money had been guaranteed, however, and the old board was requested to collect the amount due and liquidate all indebtedness. It was decided to begin a new term of school as soon as practicable, a new board being appointed, consisting of H. M. Jorgens, Wm. Van Driesche and J. A. Ferris.

The cleanliness of the town was then considered and a committee consisting of J. C. Fisher, Wm. Van Driesche and C. F. Brown, was appointed to request all citizens to thoroughly clean their premises and to keep them clean.

As there is no county organization here means were discussed to preserve good order and it was decided that the fire committee, Messrs. Packard & Robberts should give their personal attention to the subject of good order.

No more business coming before the meeting, it was declared adjourned.

The Black Hills papers have come to the sensible conclusion that the Cow Boy was right in stating that it is entirely the fault of the Black Hills merchants that they have not had railroad connections ere this. But their way of acknowledging it, outside of the Spearfish Register, shows a want of backbone which is a lamentable characteristic of Black Hills journalism when speaking on public topics. It would be far better if the exact facts were spread before the attention of the Hills merchants and let them thoroughly understand that their treachery is known and give them a chance to do better in the future. Let them thoroughly understand that it is owing simply to them that the Hills is no better developed. Let them learn that they may make a better use of strangers than to play them for suckers. That their breaking faith with outside parties and making promises that they never intend to keep is a boomerang that has again and again reacted on the Hills merchants and should now knock a little sense into them. In fact, the Hills papers should read the riot act to their readers. Not cover up or palliate a thing, but show the facts in all their nakedness and teach the merchants how to do right instead of how to cover up their crookedness.

This article is prompted almost solely by the desire of the writer to see the Hills developed. We firmly believe that there is no extent of country of the same size in the world that has been so richly blessed with Nature's gifts as has the Black Hills.

This very development has, however, been thwarted and delayed, simply because of the back-capping of the Hills people.

It is time that all this was stopped. It is time that the Hills people should consider self less and the Hills at large more. This can be accomplished best by the Hills papers. Let them take for a text the fact that it is entirely owing to the treachery and broken promises of the Hills merchants that they have not now complete or convenient railroad connections.

Lest it may seem that we write this article because we did not have any more freight and express shipped via Medora, we will state that it made not a particle of difference from what point on the N. P. the goods were shipped. The amount forwarded from all point was to enter into the figures of the capitalists. The project of building the road is not yet given up but if it is brought to a successful conclusion it will be in spite of the treachery of the Hills merchant and not because of their aid and good-will.

We do dot mean to say that these remarks apply to all Hills merchants. There are a few bright exceptions to the rule but they are very few.

Now let us see if the Hills papers will have the courage to state the facts.

A point that seems to have attracted but little attention in the Bad Lands is the subject of the laws on branding. Whether there are any in Dakota seems to be entirely unknown by our stockmen, all seeming to depend on the association rules on the subject. It is unfortunate however, that the headquarters of the association are in Montana and that the territorial laws which apply to the Montana association do not by any means apply to Dakota cattle. Our cowmen should see to it that laws relative to branding be passed in Dakota similar to those in force in Montana. As it now is all the cattlemen are members of the Montana association and governed by its laws while legally none of those laws apply here. This is a topic for discussion at the next meeting of the Little Missouri association.

As one means of ascertaining the condition of cattle in the country through which I pass I drop into the meat markets, where at a single glance, a long story is made short. At this place I found some of the finest beef upon the hooks I have seen anywhere in the south-west. Upon inquiry I learned that this meat was the product of alfalfa hay fed to steers that were quite thin in the fall. I saw the farmer who fed this lot of cattle, and found him much elated with his experiment. He paid an average of $25 per head and sold at an average of $60. This result from hay alone surprised me. To all appearance this meat is equal to a first class grade of corn-fed beef. Other farmers are following his example and hereafter this country will be blessed with an abundance of choice fat beef.—[Kansas City Record.

R. G. Head, general manager of the Prairie cattle Co., has issued a circular containing the following, to his cowboys: "You can just as easily be a gentleman with leather leggings, snake hat band and big spurs on, as you could be were you dressed in broadcloth and linen. Politeness and gentlemanly manners cost less than most any cowboy's out fit. Yet you could come nearer estimating the value of an undeveloped quartz mine than you could these qualities; they are awful handy for even cowboys to have, especially when he goes to see his best girl. Do not deceive yourself by the delusion that if you can be connected with some six-shooter notoriety it will be a big thing for you. * * * * I will now call your attention to the most objectionable habit that is liable to find its way into cow camps—gambling—playing cards. * * * * You cannot play cards in camp during the working season and do your work properly at the same time. It will not be tolerated, and any employe knowingly violating this rule will be subject to discharge, and the strict attention of superintendents and foreman is called to this requirement. * * * * I am competent from experience to insert the suggestion that it will never hurt you to refuse a drink, neither will it stifle the good sense of the common community to fail to refuse to take a drink, provided you posess the manhood to refuse to repeat too often."

The above evinces the universal tendency of cowmen at the present time and the most of the rules apply to all cow camps. From this sentiment has also arisen a feeling among all cowboys to be gentlemen instead of toughs, and in our northern country it is scarcely necessary even to establish such laws.

Bad Lands Cow Boy, By A. T. Packard. Thursday, May 21, 1885.

Come to think of it, we don't see any reason why the recent marriage should cause surprise after such an evidence of affection as was displayed in Truscott's foot-gear at a recent dance.

The entire stage outfit rolled in Tuesday evening, horses, coaches, station furniture and all. It is altogether likely, however, that the line will be partially or wholly stocked again for carrying the mail.

E. V. Smalley, editor of the Northwest, with a party of four will be in Medora about June 1. A day's stop will be made and photographs taken of the places of interest and the points the country in general written up.

The case in Glendive against the Marquis fell flat. It seems that parties who expected to get sheep from him on commission sued him on two counts for $20,000 and $17,000 respectively. No case at all was made out, the judge dismissing it almost before it had begun.

T. Martin sent the weather report for the last six months to Gen. W. B. Hazen chief of the weather bureau at Washington and received an autograph letter in return complimenting Mr. Martin highly on the report and stating that blanks would be sent him and his name added to the volunteer contributors to the weather bureau.

The new contractor, H. N. Warren, who has secured the mail contract, between Medora and Deadwood should be made to either sub-let it, or put on the service needed. The route has become one of importance to the Hills and the northwest by the excellent stage accomodations given us by the Marquis DeMores, who would have kept it up had the contract for carrying the mail been given him. We learn that there are prominent stage men in this city who will at once revive the route and equip it with good horses and comfortable vehicles providing the contract for carrying the mail can be obtained at a reasonable compensation.—[B. MARRIED.—On the morning of the 16th., at Bismarck, by the Rev. Father ——, Miss Margaret, daughter of Joseph Gardient of New Richland, Minn. to J. L. Truscott, of Medora, D. T.

The above announcement is certainly a surprise to many here, but it would be hard to find a better mated couple or a couple who are so universally liked. After the first surprise was over, every one began congratulating and the best wishes of all follow Mr. and Mrs. Truscott. The former has returned to his ranch to prepare for the coming round-up work, while the latter has gone to her home in New Richland, Minn., to improve her health, which was rather poor here.

Again we repeat that if the saloon men would club together, we think it is possible to prevent Morton county from collecting license and the money can be left in our own county for school purposes. In any event several queer things have been done, showing that there may be some doubt as to the legality of the licence. If our informant is correct, fifteen dollars was demanded from the saloon-keepers of Belfield for license to apply before May 1. Three persons paid this, Max Bass refusing payment. That this fifteen dollars applied before May 1, seems evident from the fact that at least two of the saloon-keepers have not sold since May 1, and their money has not been returned. Here, the fifteen dollars paid was the first installment of the license money from May 1. In Belfield, Max Bass has not been compelled to pay, nor have those here who quit selling May 1. There are inconsistencies in these facts which go to show that there is some doubt as to the application of the law. Then again, why is it necessary and by what authority do the prosecuting attorney and deputy-sheriff of Morton county come here to collect the taxes? Why is it not the treasurer's duty to try and collect the license money first? Then in case of failure it is time for the prosecuting attorney to have warrants issued and send the deputy-sheriff to collect them. Then again, why is it that the checks for this money should be personal checks to T. K. Long? They were not issued to him as prosecuting attorney and even if they were, what other authority could receipt for this money outside of the treasurer of Morton county? These are a few points for our saloon men to decide immediately and before they pay another cent to Morton county. Then on top of all these, we think the law itself is unconstitutional. According to Mr. Long's statement Billings county does not owe Morton county a cent. All expenses incurred by unorganized counties are paid first by the senior county, in our case this is Morton county, and then by the territory levying a tax on the organized counties for the benefit of those that are unorganized. Then what earthly claim can Morton county have against Billings county? We do not cost her a cent and still are compelled to pay her enough yearly to keep a good school running here. This is a simple outrage and one that cannot be sanctioned by a constitutional law. By all means, we say to the saloon-keepers, have a test-case, show the unconstitutionality of the law and stop paying Morton county's expenses with money that should stay in our own county.

Kaolin was discovered by John Fredrick Bottgher in the year 1707. He had for years experimenting with different kinds of clay to make white porcelain and finally stumbled on to the right thing by accident. One day he found his perruque unusually heavy, and upon investigation found the cause to be the unusual quantity of white clay used in the hair powder, and which he found upon experiment to be kaolin, from which he produced the first piece of porcelain in October 1707.

It is undoubtedly a fact that a government capable of prosecuting such a war on its own subjects, is perfectly competent to rob its soldiers' widows, and orphans. Next.

In our next issue, will begin the true history of the Lost Cabin mining claim. The location of which, it has been generally thought, was in the Big Horn mountains, but this history will prove that blief to have been erroneous. The account is by an old miner, now living in Medora, and who is a nephew of the original discoverer of the mine. It is not improbable that a prospecting party will outfit here this summer and make an attempt to find the Lost Cabin, where untold wealth is waiting the lucky finder. If a party is organized it will be for a two years trip.

The Deadwood Times of the 18th., says, work will begin on the Deadwood & Redwater R. R. about June 1st. Grade and slope stakes have been set for 25 miles on the northern terminus. The road will have a total length of 50 miles, reaching Centennial through False Bottom, traversing Centennial to the mouth of Whitewood Canyon, thence to Deadwood. It will be narrow gauge and constructed in the most substantial manner at an estimated cost of $500,000. Representatives of the syndicate who are furnishing the capital are on the road to the Hills for the purpose of letting contracts for grading, ties, bridge-building, &c.

The Butcher and Drover, a Philadelphia paper and the Drovers Journal, of Chicago are having a "set-to" over the condition of cattle that are slaughtered at the abbatoirs in their respective cities. The Philadelphia paper says, "the board of health should appoint a committee to investigate the quality of the western dressed beeves that are sold in this city, as well as all the maimed and sick cattle that are brought from the far west and killed at Chicago, embalmed and sent here for our people to eat." The Chicago paper in reply says, "our health agent says this is an insulting lie." "Go it old man, go it bear," and Medora will kill beef on the range, where it does not get sick or crippled, and supply both your cities.

W. J. Tompkins is the pioneer in a new branch of industry in the Little Missouri valley. He outfitted here Monday morning with the necessary implements to start a hay ranch which will be located about 15 miles from town. About one hundred acres will be broken and seeded this year. Experiments will be made with alfalfa, red clover, timothy, millet, &c. This new enterprise will without doubt be successful and will be of great advantage to our stockmen. It is a well known fact that the native grasses will yield a crop of hay only once in about every two or three years, and in addition to this, the country is filling up so rapidly with stock that even this supply will be entirely cut off within the next two or three years. The Refrigerator company expects to feed cattle here through the winter and must look for their supplies, to some other source than the native meadows. It is claimed that cattle fed on alfalfa will not only retain their flesh, but will take on more. This hay business is a matter that should be looked into by stockmen, as there is a possibility that they will need hay when there is none to be obtained.

Annoncement.

Cattle-men of the Little Missouri river are advised that the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, will give them during June for the beef and dry cows that they wish to sell, Chicago prices less seventy cents per hundred to cover freight and shrinkage. The cattle to be delivered in the evening at the Sully Creek corrals and weighed in the morning.

Marquis de Mores,
President.

Good horses are bringing better prices in all parts of the country than they have commanded since the war, and poor horses were never so unsalable as compared with the best as they are to-day. A farmer who breeds a good mare to a good horse will have a sure and profitable market for his colt. There can be no profit in breeding to common stock. Select the best stallions, those that are surest, and having size, form and action. It will cost a little more for the service, but it will pay to breed to the best.—[R. M. Husbandman.

The Continental and Hash Knife cattle companies have recently made an important sale of 35,000 head of stock cattle at $17.50 around to the Aztec Land & cattle Co. This purchase includes all stock cattle belonging to these companies below the New Mexico line on Pecos river excluding beeves and twos. The Aztec company is composed of heavy New York capitalists and is the largest in the southwest. Their investment including one million acres of railroad land on the Atlantic and Pacific road in Apache county, Arizona, already aggregates over $1.500.000 in land and cattle. The cattle purchased are of a high grade and make an excellent foundation for such a largo outfit.

The St Paul Globe says, "no cattle have been quarantined on the Montana border. The Frye cattle were taken off the cars by their owner to be branded and grazed before being taken on their range near Billings." It is to be hoped that the Globe is not so much of a "tenderfoot" as it is trying to make itself out to be. The fact is well known that these cattle were turned loose on the prairie at Sentinel Butte, Mont., where there are no yards, much less a branding chute, and that the owner had neither horses or men at hand to hold the cattle after they were unloaded from the cars. It might be well for the Globe man to "go west" and try to learn a little about handling cattle before attempting to gloss over some body's sculldugery.

The adjutant-general of Texas, is in receipt of information that 6,000 heed of cattle, purchased in south Texas by Abner, Taylor & Co., and now enroute to their Daltam county ranch, have been stopped at Harrold, Wichita county, by the north Texas cattlemen and forbidden to proceed further. Those having the cattle in charge applied to a company of rangers, located near Harrold for protection, alleging that armed men would resist their passage through the country. The rangers telegraphed to the adjutant-general for instructions to-day, and were ordered to respond promptly to any call made upon them by the civil authorities, to whom the men in charge of the cattle were referred for aid and assistance. If they refused or failed, the government will invoke the military of the state. Bloodshed and trouble is anticipated when the drive is attempted.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

"The question of a public trail through the Texas Panhandle, which has been agitating the minds of the ranchmen for some time, has been solved to the satisfaction of southern cattlemen, if not to the Panhandle men. From H. W. Cresswell, of Ft. Elliott, Texas, The Indicator learns that while there is considerable dissatisfaction in regard to the location of the trail, it is generally conceded the route selected will work the least possible injury to the Panhandle cattlemen." * * * The new trail as projected is laid out as follows. "Leaving the old Ft. Griffin and Dodge trail, at 16-Mile creek, the trail runs westward 20 miles to Clear creek, thence 16 miles to Kiowa, thence 18 miles to Clear, thence 20 miles to Fulton, thence 15 miles to the rifle-pits on Palo Duro, thence 20 miles to Coldwater, thence 8 miles to second water on Coldwater, thence 35 miles to Buffalo Springs, thence in a northwest direction through the Neutral Strip to the mouth of the Carizzo, near the Colorado line." **

A meeting was held at Dallas, Texas last week which was attended by nearly a hundred representative ranchmen, including members of the executive committees of the various [local?] associations. At this meeting, Col. Simpson expressed the opinion that if an outlet through the northwestern part of Texas, was not given, the stockmen would without doubt make one for themselves. It was intimated by some one that Gov. Ireland had as much as said that he would call on the rangers to assist them.

"Continuing, Col. Simpson said that what they wanted was harmony, and if possible, a cattle trail. There was likely to be, if the matter was not satisfactorily adjusted, trouble, and the cow-boys did not mind a little loss of blood occasionally, but they were rather sensitive when it came to touching their pocket-books. They were good men, and looked after their own interest. The cattleman in the eyes of the law had a right to drive over the highway to effect an outlet, and the live stock interest of the State depended largely upon the action of the meeting they were holding. He closed by advising calm, dispassionate deliberation, with fair play as the watchword. President Simpson parenthetically remarked that one of the most important questions which would come up for consideration, was the stopping of the shipments of cattle of the cattle syndicate by the Panhandle association. These were en route to Dallam county, and had been stopped at Harrold." * * *

A conference committee of five members from northwest Texas was appointed to report on the proposed new trail. The committee all signed a report in favor of the trail, with the exception of W. A. Towers who explained his position to be due to instructions from his association. The following resolution was unanimously adopted as the final sense of the convention."

1. Believing that a trail should be established in some legal manner, it is the sense of this convention that the State should, in some way provide such a trail, and we pledge ourselves to use means in our power to bring about in some way such legislation as may be necessary to secure such a State trail.

2. That a committee of three be appointed by the chair to present the matter to the governor.

Messrs. O. H. Nelson, H. W. Cresswell, and J. R. Hamilton were appointed as such committee."

Fannie Field says in the Prairie Farmer as to roosters: "Do not overdo the rooster business. Too many roosters in one flock are as bad as not enough; in fact, too much rooster is worse than not enough, for in the latter case more of the eggs will be fertile, but in the former, the hens are so worried by the everlasting attention of the males of the flock that they become disgusted and dodge them altogether." * * *

Well Fannie, we agree with you in this matter. What we need, is more hens. We are not overstocked with roosters in this country but are terribly short of hens.

We rather look to see the Medora line running again before long but hope it will not be done by an outfit who will be tenderfoot enough to place any reliance on the statements of Deadwood merchants.

Marquis de Mores Residence in Medora the Victim.

A severe thunder storm visited this section last Wednesday afternoon. The lightning struck a chimney on the residence ofthe Marquis and ran down to the water pipe leading to the well. The rooms through which the electric fluid passed, were pretty badly demoralized. Plastering torn off, mirrors broken and a large hole knocked in the outer wall. Several people were standing near the chimney when the lightning struck and were all more or less shocked. As the colored lady remarked, "da was all knocked clar sensible." Mr. Day who was doing some painting in the room where the chimney was, endeavored to capture some of the festive fluid, but succeeded only in leaving the marks of his fingers on the wall. He also assumed a recumbent position and gazed upon the azure sky above him, through the hole in the roof. Happily, no one was injured, aud on extensive damage done.

"What benefit is the Montana Stockmens association to us"? This is the question which the Dakota stockmen are asking, and no one seems to be able to answer. They say, "we have paid our money whenever it has been asked for, and in return supposed we would be entitled to some of the benefits of the association. Late developments would seem to indicate that such are not the views of the association. We think it important and that not only Dakota interests but those of eastern Montana, demand that we should have a stock inspector located at Medora. We are told by the association that they 'can not furnish one because all the inspectors are employed and paid by the Board of stock commissioners and are Territorial officers, and the funds to pay them are raised by taxation, which is paid to the county Treasurers, who in turn pay the inspectors.' It seems a little strange that no arrangement has been made for emergencies of this kind." It will be remembered that the BAD LANDS COW BOY, from the start advocated that it would be better to have an association of our own here in Dakota, but it was thought at the time by the stockmen that the expenses of a separate association would be greater than the benefits we were likely to receive. It now looks as if we were likely to pay two expenses for one benefit, as the Montana association says that if there is an inspector here the stockmen must pay for it themselves. It is to be hoped that the Montana association will reconsider the matter and do the fair thing by us.

The Miles City Stock Grower commenting on the difference of opinion prevailing among cattlemen in regard to some of the more important questions of the cattle business, says, "one man will tell you to stock your range with Short-horns, another will insist upon Herefords, and so on through all the different breeds of cattle. Some will tell you to let bulls run on the range all the time, and others will tell you to take up your bulls in the fall without fail, and still others will tell me that I am an idiot to think of putting anything on my range but steers." In replying to this we would say that without doubt there are a great many theoretical stockmen even in the same section of country, with widely different opinions, on such questions. The practical men are those who are constantly on the range and know from experience. It is also true that a class of cattle suitable to a range in Montana, might be entirely unsuitable to a range in Texas, and in southern countries it might be more profitable to let the bulls run the year round, while in northern countries the bulls should be rounded up in the fall. There can be no invariable rule established, by which the stock business can be run. Common sense, with a "right smart" stock of practical experience, together with a knowledge of the climate and seasons of the country in which the location is to be made, are the principal requisites of succesful investment in the cattle business. If the capitalist is not personally in posession of these essentials, and is not willing to pay an exorbitant price for experience, our advice would be to first engage a man who has, and then leave the management of affairs to him. Men do this in other classes of business, and why should they not in this. If the capitalist will put himself under the tuition of a good competent foreman on his own range, he can learn the business at his leisure, and to much better effect than to go about asking opinions of theoretical cranks.

EDITORS BAD LANDS COW BOY:—As the quarantine subject has become a question of grave importance I would like to express my views through the columns of your valuable paper. I have tried to keep myself posted, and from the different stock Journals I obtain my information. It appears that pleuro-pneumonia is dying out and now the veterinarians are more seriously affected than the cattle have been. Stock Journals disclaim the existence of pleuro-pneumonia and veterinarians insist on strict quarantine, if not for one reason, for another, as will be seen in the case of T. Corwin Anderson a breeder of blooded stock in Kentucky. After his public sale of bulls he was approached by the state veterinarian for the state of Illinois who tried to impress upon Mr. Anderson's mind that it was absolutely necessary for him to secure his (Dr. Paaren's) certificate of health before shipping his bulls to the purchasers, and intimated that his services were worth $5,00 per head of cattle inspected, but subsequently reduced the price to $20,00 for the lot, stating that if they were all together the inspection would not take long. If I have been rightly informed it is undoubtedly his duty to inspect those cattle and is paid for his services by the state at the rate of $8,00 per diem. It is simply a scheme gotten up to employ a few men who are willing to resort to such means to extort money from the cattleman. According to the statement made by the National Live Stock Journal, Mr. Anderson had paid all expenses in his own state, of strict compliance with all that the laws of any other state requires, and it should not be required of him to pay extra. What is needed on the ranges of the west is more bulls, and if cattlemen can not get their bulls from the east without havinS them held and inspected at an additional expense of about $5,00 per head for every health certificate issued by the different veterinarians of states through which they have to pass, they will have to resort to some other source for their blooded stock.—[Cow-Puncher.

The first 500 H S cattle received by the Ref. Car Co. June 1st for slaughtering at this point averaged 1006 pounds per head live weight. This is considered pretty good weight for Texans at this season of the year and is another evidence of the fattening qualities of the grass in this country.

The horse industry of this Territory is yet in its infancy, but is rapidly coming to the front and in a few years at most Montana horseflesh will prove a formidable rival to America's favorite Kentucky horses. An exchange says: "It requires three or four years to convince the cattle-growers of Montana that their beef products could be marketed in the east, but the horsemen will not be slow in being brought to realize this fact. It has now been scarcely twelve months since the first carload of horses went forward, but we find that there has already been more horses forwarded this way east than there were cattle for the first two years. Already it may be said, the industry is fully established and that there need in the future be no more surplus of horses in Montana. It is, indeed, remarkable how soon the tables turn. Only a few years ago a few expert drovers were just coining money shipping in state,s horses (geldings), which found a ready sale. Now our territory has not only become self-supporting, but has horses to sell. It is true we are still receiving large consignments of stallions and mares for breeding purposes and will continue to for some time yet to come, but we are in a position to grow work horses cheaper than any other portion of America and the superiority of the animals grown over that of other sctions is a sure guarantee of a steady and reliable market.—[Glendive Independnet.

THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES.

By J. S. WARN.

Many conjectures and newspaper reports have been scattered broadcast over the country from time to time, in regard to the Lost Cabin mines of the Big Horn mountains. My friends have many times requested me to write the history of the mines, as my uncle, Allen Hulburt, the original discoverer, told it to me. As will be seen later on, I went on the first expedition with my uncle after he was driven out by the Indians.

In the spring of 1849 Allen Hulburt of Jonesville, Wis., in company with others started overland for the gold mines of California. They arrived there in October of the same year, having endured many hardships and perils in their five months trip across the plains. Years passed, and his family and friends received no word from him, and after diligent inquiry, could not learn of his whereabouts and concluded that he must have perished on the plains. In this however they were mistaken, for all these years he was in the mountains prospecting and mining, always confident, as only miners can appreciate, that the next day might open a "rich find" and he would be able to return to his family and friends with untold wealth at his command. Thus time rolled on until the spring of 1863, when he in company with Wm. Jones and Jos. Cox, left California and went to Walla Walla, Washington Ter. Arriving there they bought an outfit of six horses and the other necessaries for prospecting east of the Rocky Mountains. Leaving Walla Walla, they took the old Mullen trail for the eastern side, prospecting as they went, whenever there were any signs of colors. The Indians were always on their trail and never failed to give them trouble when opportunity offered. Undaunted by the perils surrounding them they still moved on, sometimes by night and sometimes by day, until they finally reached the valley of the Yellowstone, which they struck below the mouth of the Big Horn river.

It has been generally believed that they had crossed the Big Horn river previous to this time, but I will endeavor to show that such was not the case, and also that they never got into the Big Horn mountains to prospect, as Mr. Hulburt supposed at the time. It was very easy to be mistaken in those days, when the geography of that country was so little known. He says that where the mines were, there was no snow until November, and it is a well known fact that there is snow in the Big Horn mountains the year round. I have been there at all seasons of the year and know whereof I speak.

When the party struck the Yellowstone they crossed a branch of it on to an island and went into camp to give themselves and their stock a chance to recruit up and to reconoitre and find where to get out of the valley and avoid the Indians. After resting two days they made up their minds as to the best route, and at dark struck out, crossing the other branch of the river and arrived safely on the southern bank. Proceeding southward they left the valley and travelled over a rolling prairie until daylight when they went into camp. Just ahead of them could be seen a range of mountains. That night they started again and at daylight were in sight of a stream that was undoubtedly the Rosebud.

"There is nothing in our stock Journals now days," is a remark made in our hearing a few days since by one of the most prominent stock-growers of the northwest. The worst feature about this remark is, that there is too much truth in it. Whose fault is it? Why yours Mr. Editor of course. You fill up your paper with clippings which if not always stale are often of more interest to yourself than your readers. You are not careful enough to find out what your reader wants to know. You also write articles from half a column to two columns long, when you ought to know, if you do not, that the average stockman will not read an article that is over a quarter of a column in length. Give us short articles and to the point. Why cannot stock papers have an associated press report of their own, and get stock news from one section of the country to another before it gets stale by being copied from one paper to another? There has probably never been a time in the history of thorough-bred cattle in the United States, when they could be purchased at such low figures as at the present time. There is no reason now why range cattle should not be bred to a higher standard. The objection may be advanced, that the higher bred stock will not stand privation because it is not invested with as much vitality as natives. This objection is undoubtedly to some extent well founded, as that is an end that has not been sought by breeders to any great extent up to the present time. The man who produces an animal especially adapted to the range, and popular in the eastern markets will have a fortune at his command. An animal possessing the instincts of the Texas cow, and the body of nearly any of the high bred cattle barring the Jersey, would very nearly meet the demand.

"JOSIAR."

I never kin forget the day
That we went out a-walkin',
And sot down on the river bank,
And kept on hours a-talkin';
He twisted up my apron strings
An' folded it together,
An' said he thought for harvest time
'Twas cur'us kind o' weather.

The sun went down as we sot there;
Josiah seemed uneasy,
And mother she began to call:
"Loweezy! O Loweezy!"
An' then Josiah spoke right up
As I was just a startin',
An' said, "Loweezy, what's the use
Of us two ever partin'?"

It kind o' took me by surprise,
An' yet I knew 'twas coming;
I'd heard it all the summer long
In every wild bee's hummin';
I'd studied out the way I'd act;
But law! I couldn't do it;
I meant to hide my love from him,
But seems as if he knew it;
In looking down into my eyes
He must a seen the fire;
An' ever since that hour I've loved
An' worshiped my Josiar.
—Exchange.

THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES. By J. S. WARN.

During the day they sent a man to explore the valley for signs of Indians. Finding the coast clear they struck camp and started for the head of the stream up in the mountains, prospecting as they went, wherever there was any signs of colors. When they arrived near the mountains they made a permanent camp, in order to give the numerous gulches a thorough prospecting, and if possible find the source of the colors which they had panned out on the sand bars along the river. They constructed breast works and dug trenches in order to protect themselves against attacks from the Indians. Every thing being in readiness they began digging and struck bed rock in about seven feet. They found gold from the grass roots down, from five cents to one dollar to the pan. The men were nearly fantic over their success, after so many long years of fruitless toils. Having fully satisfied themselves that they had at last realized their long cherished hopes, they at once began preparations for mining in good earnest. They whip-sawed lumber for sluice boxes and run a dam across the creek which was near at hand, dug a ditch and set their boxes, and then worked all the dirt from the top down, finding it very rich, realizing from fifty to one hundred dollars per day to the man. This was in the month of September. They worked for a month and took out large quantities of dust. Mr. Hulburt could not tell exactly how much but thought it would measure a good "half bushel."

As it was now getting rather late in the season, they set about preparing for winter quarters for themselves and their animals. They cut hay and built a stockade with their cabin in one corner and had everything in first class shape for cold weather. All kinds of game were plenty and the brooks were filled with speckled trout, and they looked forward to a comfortable winter. All went well for several months.

In the spring of '64 as the snow was melting off the ground and the hill-sides were getting bare, the water was running in the creeks, and every one was in good spirits and full of activity, setting sluice boxes and getting ready for the summers work. After they had been at work about a week, just before night Hulburt went to the cabin to get supper, and as he was busily engaged he heard the report of several rifles in the direction of the mine. Running to the door he saw his comrades weltering in their blood and the red-skins scalping them and stripping them of their buckskin clothing. The Indians then started for the cabin but the bold miner kept them at bay until dark, and thinking that they had him safely corralled, did not renew the attack until the next morning.

Come boys, if you are afraid to shoot against Seth's score, just say so and quit.

Marquis de Mores had a very narrow escape from drowning last Tuesday afternoon. As he was fording the river just above the bridge on horse-back, his horse got mired in the quick-sand. The horse finally got loose and made for the shore, leaving the Marquis standing on a sand bar in the middle of the river, and obliging him wade out.

There never was a time in the history of our country when there has been such a demand for horses, in the east as well as the west, as at present. In order to keep up the supply, especially for the eastern markets, the east and west will have to combine. The east to supply the stallions best adapted to the greatest demand, while the west can furnish mares sufficiently good, that when bred to a thoroughbred stallion, will produce horses, surpassed by none for beauty, size and endurance.

A correspondent of the Live Stock Journal, England, who has been looking up the history of the polled breeds of cattle, finds that hornless cattle have been known for many centuries. A Greek coin of Mytilene, of the fifth century, B. C. which he has seen, has on the obverse, the heads of two hornless cattle. As far back as 2700 B. C., the Egyptians had hornless cattle depicted on their monuments, which would give the breed a history more than 4,500 years old. Twenty-three centuries ago there were known to be polled breeds of cattle in Siberia, and it is believed now, that they were kept in that cold climate in preference to the horned breeds, because they could endure the cold far better than cattle with horns. Hippocrates makes mention of "chariots drawn by oxen which had no horns," and says that the "cold prevents them from having any." It is very evident that the polled cattle are in no sense of modern origin, but that they existed beyond the date of any written history.

The north, west and northwest has long been an outlet for Texas cattle, and trail drivers in the early days all started their herds as early in the season as grass would permit and foremen tried to see who could bring his herd through in the best condition. Those were days when cattle were driven by the purchaser. At present cattle are nearly all driven by contractors and not much regard is paid to the time of starting and herds are rushed through in far too short a time, as a late movement of stock is seldom profitable to the parties finally ranching the cattle, unless a very mild winter follows the drive, and for several years the drive has been getting later and later. This is a very serious error that many ranchmen make, and it is only dear-bought experience that impresses upon the minds of cattle should be on the range not later than the first of August, as it takes stock some time to locate on a new range. They should be well rested and located before winter. Now in order to do this purchaser should make it his interest to see that his cattle start early enough to get here in the right season and specify the time for passing certain points. We think losses would be much less on southern cattle were they properly handled.

The following is in reply to an inquiry sent Sec'y. Teller, a few days ago in regard to the taxes that have been levied on Billings county by Morton and Stark counties. "Chapter 81 of 1883 authorizes commissioners of organized counties to grant liquor licenses in unorganized counties which are attached to them for judicial purposes, though nothing is said as to which organized county shall grant such license. There has been no change in this law so far as I know. An act was passed by the last legislature, providing for the assessment of taxes in unorganized counties." From the above, it would seem that the assessments that have been made are both legal, and now it only remains to be decided whether the taxes we are to pay, together with the railroad tax, would be sufficient to run an organized county of our own, or whether it is better to pay for the support of other counties. The railroad tax of this county amounts to about $4,000. The saloon tax at the present time amounts to $1,400. The personal property tax levied by Stark county will possibly amount to $2,500, making a total of $7,900. On two sides of us are unorganized counties from which we would be entitled to collect taxes. The stockmen of this county should look into this matter thoroughly and find out if they are not "buttering some body else's bread," as they are the ones most interested. Will it be better for them to control the amount of their own taxes or let some other county with a large debt to pay, do it for them. We have no school, in a county twenty-five miles wide by eighty miles long. We would be glad to have some one present the other side of the question, as we have only touched one side of it. The "balance of power" in this county will always, it is to be hoped, be in the hands of the stockmen as it is now. The motive in qringing this matter to their attention is with the hope they will give the matter a careful investigation and if any steps are necessary for their own protection, take them in time.

THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES. By J. S. WARN.

In the mean time, Hulbert packed his knapsack, buried what gold dust he could not carry conveniently and fled for his life. He knew a trail east to the top of the mountains and by day light the next morning he was far away from the old camp. He could see to the east an open country and to the west of him a range of mountains covered with snow, which he thought at that time to be another spur of the Big Horn mountains. In this however he was mistaken, as he was without doubt, now standing on the Little Wolf mountains. He struck an easterly course and travelled nights, the snow capped mountains remaining in view a long time and finally on the eighteenth day struck the North Platte river [90?] miles above Fort Laramie at Reshaw's bridge, where he found the old trail that he went over in 1849 to California, and also found Reshaw and his family, the first white people he had seen except his two comrades, for many months. Here he heard of the great discovery of gold in the Alder gulch in Montana, and also of the big stampede from the east, coming up the Platte. He rested for a few days bought a horse and saddle and started down the Platte to meet the stampede.

I was among the first who arrived at Ft. Laramie. We had about a dozen wagon loads of pilgrims in our outfit and were waiting for more to come, as the Indians were very hostile and we did not dare to start out without a large crowd. Captain Hulbert came into our camp from the west and told us his story as it has been related in the foregoing account, and showed us the gold which he had. As might be expected it created a great stir in camp and everyone was crazy to start at once for the mines. Accordingly arrangements were made with him to pilot us, as there was no doubt in the mind of any one that his account was true. He was to take us there within twenty days. We waited until we had 140 wagons in the train and 550 men women and children.

The Indians learned that we were going through their country east of the Big Horn mountains and old chief Spotted Tail went to the commander at Ft. Laramie and made a protest. We were ordered not to go and the old chief made a speech, saying that he would fight us every step of the way. Hulbert told him in reply that there were not Indians or soldiers enough on the plains to stop us, and that we were going anyway. We started out and followed the old California trail until we arrived at Reshaw's bridge on the Platte, where we went into camp. It was here that I met Mr. Bozeman for the first time. He had come from Virginia City, Mont., on horse-back to pilot a train of Pilgrims on a short cut to the mines in Alder gulch and was now on his return. It was arranged that Bozeman should remain here and pick up another train of emigrants and follow us as soon as possible. We started on and went slowly, as we had a large train, and had to make roads and bridge streams to get the wagons across. We moved about fifteen miles a day. Captain Hulbert was with me a great deal of the time so that I had ample opportunity to question and talk with him, and had a good idea of where his mines were. He was looked-up to and respected, by the whole party and his word was law in everything. We finally arrived at the foot hills of the Big Horn mountains.

J. A. Ferris has set men to work digging a cellar twenty-five be sixty feet on his lots on main street, where he intends to erect a store building twenty-five by seventy-five feet, which he intends to occupy as soon as completed.

Jim. Asborne of Glendive Montana was arrested in Jamestown Dak. last week. He had eighty head of horses in his possession to which he could not prove his right of ownership. Jim's reputation for rustling has not been of the best for some time past.

A serious accident occurred at the E6 ranch that proved fatal to one of the boys in the employ of that outfit. Just before starting on the round-up one of the boys whose name we failed to learn, received a severe kick on the head, which caused his death not long after.

The stockmens ball last evening at the rink was a grand success. Everybody was there and nothing occurred to mar the enjoyment. The music was good and very much of the pleasure of the evening was due to the efficient services of the floor manager Mr. Frank Smith.

C. E. Marvin president of the crescent creamery, Rochester Minn., made us a call this week. He reports business as being very good in his line, having sold 100,000 pounds of butter and cheese on this trip. Their annual sales amount to 1,000,000 pounds of butter and 500,000 pounds of cheese.

A shooting affair took place in Little Mo., today in which Ed. Severson was shot through the thum and fore finger and side, the bullet entering the right side between the hip and last rib, not necessarily fatal. The person doing the shooting was foreman for Webo, and has left the town. He was known Perfect.

T. H. Van Voorhis of Beallsville Pa. arrived last Friday with a car load of bulls for the LeMoyne Cattle Co. There was one full blood Devon and eighteen grade Shorthorns. Mr. VanVoorhis expressed himself as well pleased with the country and talks of putting in some cattle or horses next spring. He is a promient cattle dealer in the east.

Wm. Higgins a young man who is well known in this country and who lived about six miles from Dickinson, committed suicide at his ranch last Tuesday morning at seven o'clock. He complained of feeling blue, went and set down beside the house, placed a pistol to his head and blowed his brains out. Love was supposed to be the cause of the act.
