Greatest rainfall at one time, seventy hundredths of an inch. Prevailing wind, northwest. Golden sunsets, 2. On the afternoon of the 12th., a heavy hail storm passed over, which lasted five minutes, hailstones the size of a quails egg. Two beautiful rainbows during hail-storm, no wind during the storm.
Al. Canter foreman of the Bad Lands Cattle Co., lost a rawhide lariat near mouth of Box Elder, it was on a VI horse, he will pay $10 on its return to this office by the finder.

On the evening of July 4th Prof. Wel Hung, a Jappanese juggler of great renown, will give an entertainment at the rink. The Professor is unequalled in his feats of legerdemain. The performance will close at 10 o'clock after which there will be dancing. Good music will be in attendance.
Lamps and lamp goods at the drug store.
The N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., received 500 head of beeves from the Continental Cattle company, on the 15th., and began slaughtering forty head per day on Tuesday.

The sagacity and affection of animals, especially the horse and dog, for young children and the weak in general, is well known, but has never been so thoroughly exemplified as it was last Sunday morning. Some cruel, blood thirsty cow boys inveigled a little, weak, emaciated boy, just fresh from the green pastures of Chicago, into attempting to ride a broncho, noted for its bucking proclivities. A large and sympathizing crowd collected, fully expecting to see the buttes around covered with the gore of the poor little boy, but the instinct, heretofore mentioned, was possessed by this broncho to a remarkable degree. The crowd cheered and patted "Fatty" on the back, (some of the blows falling a little short and hitting the broncho) but the broncho remained firm and carried Ed. as carefully as if he was a last years egg, and all went well, until the broncho made a misstep in a mud hole and Ed. glided gently into a soft place in the mud. Ed. says he did not have to pay for the drinks and that was the most he cared for. We will only give the initials of the small boy, which are Ed. Meyers as we do not wish to alarm his friends to whom marked copies have been sent.

At the examination into the case of Win. Roberts, charged with stealing six horses from the Hash Knife outfit, the testimony of the prosecution was nearly all in when Mr. Middleton, attorney for the defendant, addressed his honor, Judge Staehle, stating that the defense was willing to waive examination. The Judge accordingly fixed the amount of Robert's bail at $2,500 to appear before the district court, and recognized the witnesses to appear also, fixing the bond in the case of one witness for the prosecution at $1,000. Judge Strevell and A. H. O'Conner appeared for the prosecution. The horses in question are part of a lot of nine horses that were stolen from Hughes & Simpson in the spring of '84 and were run north to the Moosomin. The horses were traced to the Moosomin and the principal testimony against the prisoner details his operations there. The story of his arrest has already been told in these columns. It was a notable search and capture by Stock Detective W. D. Smith, who got his man at Rapid City, Dak. Win. Roberts is an old timer in eastern Montana and is well known by many who were here in the early days of freghting and steamboating.—[Yellowstone Journal.
General Grant is much better. He is now resting quietly at Mt. McGregor and in every way his condition is improving.
Beginning with July 1, the reduced rate on postage will go into effect. Instead of being two cents per half ounce it will be two cents per ounce.

Poor Keily, he of anti-Catholic fame is having a parrot and monkey time getting a government appointment. He was first given a ministerial position to Italy, the poorest place in the world to send him and on account of his pronounced anti-Catholic sentiments the Italian government very properly refused to receive him. Lately he was appointed minister to Austria and now the Austrian government refuses to receive him.

President Cleveland is in earnest about enforcing the executive order for the vacation of the Winnebago and Crow Creek reservations. We have already expressed our opinion of the injustice of this last order as it will bankrupt many bona fide settlers who were induced to settle there when the reservation was opened by the order of President Arthur. We have seen no reason to change our opinion and now as before consider the order for the settlers to move as a mere catch-penny devise of the administration to obtain the support of th maudlin Indian sympathizers of the east.

From late and authentic sources we learn that a New York company has been organized, the capital subscribed and nearly all preliminary arrangements made toward building the railroad from the Hay Creek coal mines along the Belle Fourche and into Lead City. All the iron will be shipped to Medora and freighted from here. This will bring Deadwood within a hundred and sixty miles wagon road from Medora. The project of building a railroad from Medora to intersect this road at De Mores, on the Belle Fourche, is by no means a dead one and in fact depends in a great measure upon the completion of the Hay Creek coal road.

Stark Co's. assessor has completed his work of assessing Billings county and now the question is whether it will be cheaper to pay all the taxes to another county which does not possess as much taxable property as Billings or to run our own county organization. The rate will tell the story. If we are taxed over $2,000 it will pay pecuniarily to organize, not taking into consideration the dependent position we are now in and the fact of having to transact all our legal business in Mandan and Dickinson. It will cost about $6,000 or $7,000 a year to organize and the railroad will yield about $4,000 in taxes. Whether under these circumstances it will pay to organize is a business proposition to be settled by our citizens.

The government has sent a special agent to the Crow reservation to enquire into their condition. The Dawes party will also come up through Wyoming and probably go as far north as the southern limit of the Crow reservation. These visits are doubtless due to the petition of the Montana stockgrowers, association requesting the government to examine into the condition of the Indians. We hope that some definite action will be taken at the next session of Congress and that in all justice to both intending settlers and Indians, the government will throw open a part at least of the reservation, now entirely unused by the Indians and see that they are properly compensated, most desirable things to all concerned.

Politics in England are in an extremely muddled state. It is very possible that Gladstone voluntarily had himself and party defeated so as to put the burden of running the government upon the Conservatives. Lord Salisbury, as leader of this party is placed in the unenviable situation of occupying the position of Premier and making almost a certain failure on account of the presant chaotic condition of England's foreign and Irish policy or giving up the power again to Gladstone and the Liberals. This will show want of back bone on Salisbury's part and he is equally allured and repelled by his own chances of failure or success Meanwhile Victoria is coquetting with both parties and compelling the leaders to follow her all over the Highlands to obtain an interview.

Gen. Brisbin in a recent communication to the National cattle and horse growers' association gives a number of able reasons why the eradication of pleuro-pneumonia should be placed in the hands of the government. Among the reasons are the following: The government can make it uniform in all the states at the same time; it can best stand the expense; it can best determine the extent, location and prevalence of the disease; it will adopt one system of extirpation; it should take the matter in hand because the disease threatens to become a national calamity; the disease is now only prevalent in the fenced or eastern regions and prompt measures will guarantee that it will never appear in the unfenced regions of the west where its eradication will prove well-nigh impossible. The Cow Boy the more readily coincides with Gen. Brisbin, as his argument is directly in line with what we have so often advocated. We wish to go further, however, and put the eradication of every contagious diease in the hands of the general government. In this way only can contagious diseases be successfully stamped out. This will also put an end to the jealousy and hatred arising beween different states and territories on account of the quarantine laws. The placing of contagious diseases in the hands of the government is a question calling for the earnest consideration of all stock associations.

The splendid growth of grass has had the effect of making the round-ups this year shorter than ever before, in spite of the increased number of cattle.
From reliable sources we learn that the cattle loss in the Black Hills country was at least ten per cent. This is accounted for by the deep and lasting snow there.

Authentic reports from Montana seem to indicate that the calf crop will average higher in most districts there than in the Bad Lands districts of Dakota. That this is the case is owing to no other reason than of an insufficient supply of bulls. From all we can learn, however, this will be remedied in the future as an abundance of bulls will be put on the range.

An exchange says; "A correspondent wishes to know whether the Illinois State Board of Agriculture will, at their annual fair this year, permit the exhibition of cattle, and also if the St. Louis Fair Association will do the same or rule them out entirely, as they did last year?" We think that under the present quarantine regulations, no cattle will be admitted unless accompanied by a clean bill of health.

Messrs. Fisher and Deffebach, who have just returned from the E6 say that the report of the death of nearly all the short-horn bulls driven there last summer, is false. There are about five hundred bulls at the E6 bull-camp, and of these only about twenty have died, really a very light loss for bulls. The grass is so abundant in the neighborhood that the E6 outfit will put up about five hundred tons this summer.

The abundance of rain this spring has forced the grass wonderfully. In fact it has grown a little too fast and although twice as abundant, is not as strengthening as it was last year, judging by the condition of cattle. This will soon be remedied and quality and quantity will rule together. Old timers say that the only year they remember when grass was so abundant was that of 1882. Last year it was a matter of great difficulty to get hay in sufficient quantities. This year there is plenty everywhere.

The Las Animas, Col., stockgrowers, association met not long ago in Trinidad and passed resolutions which meant war to the knife against any man who attempted to cross the ranges of any members of the association, with southern cattle. The northern Colorado men are in favor of a trail but Las Animas and Bent counties are strongly opposed to the plan. Several large herds are now on the southern border of Colorado in one of Joe Pennell's "jack pots." At present they cannot cross Colorado and even if they could, would surely be stopped at Wyoming, as the authorities there are determined not to let any cattle in that have not passed the ninety days in quarantine.

The loss on cattle in the Hills country has been greatly exaggerated except on late through cattle. In this class the loss in several instances has gone above twenty-five per cent. The loss on wintered cattle has not reached five per cent. however, in any case and good judges estimate ten per cent. on all classes as high. Out of a bunch of two hundred and fifty in Cave Hills, John Arrington's herd, all but four have been rounded up. These four are as likely to be strayed as dead. The upper Little Missouri and Belle Fourche round-ups are finished and all the cowmen are greatly pleased at the smallness of the loss, contrary to their expectations, and the largeness of the calf crop.
A car of very fine short-horn bulls from Ontario was received by J. L. Truscott last Friday.
It has been found that in many diseases of horse and cattle, vaccination is a radical cure. It has been found so in black-leg and would doubtless prove equally effectual in other diseases.

Lieut. J. M. T. Partello, of Ft. Keogh, is one of the best and most entertaining writers on stock interests that there is now in the west. He is a very prolific writer and none of his articles contain the twaddle and highly colored accounts of profits so common to most writer on stock not directly interested in the cattle business.

At Medora of course the cowboy was in great force, and the ladies of the party one and all fell in love with him; not with any one individual cowboy, but with the general class. There were not enough cowboys to go round all the ladies, so each one stood the center of an admiring party (husbands being away in the background, to whom he distributed cartridges and tabs of fringe from his pantaloons as souvenirs. The conductor's lady-killing capacities are proverbial, but when he comes in competition with the untamed cowboy he finds himself side-tracked with some rapidity. The ticket-punch stands no show with a Smith & Wesson 44. When the slaughter-house inspection was over the cowboys gave an extempore exhibition of lariat practice, which was well worth seeing. They lariated cows and ponies, they lariated dogs, they lariated each other, they lariated the ladies' hearts and carried them away hanging from the "fraid straps" of their saddles. In fact the air of Medora was full of whirling lariats until the train moved out, and for every lariat in the air there were half a dozen handkerchiefs waving from the windows of the cars.—[Minneapolis Tribune.

THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES. By J. S. Warn.

I obtained permission of Captain Hulburt to take a party up in the mountains to prospect. Fourteen of us made preparations, took six days provisions and pulled out to the Big Horn mountains. The train was to travel on, making as much speed as possible and when we had finished prospecting we were to come down and overtake it. Instead of six days, our prospecting tour took twenty. Travelling up the west side of the snowy range we prospected along wherever there seemed any signs of gold. We found very little to reward our search and before the six days were up, we were ready to join the train. This we found a difficult task as it was impossible to get over the range of snow. After repeated failures we were forced to take the back track. Finally we found a pass through the range and came out on the east side all right. Here we found nothing except snow, rocks, creeks, lakes and an abundance of all kinds of game, but no gold, although if it had been a foot thick on the ground, we wouldn't have seen it. Getting down off the mountains we struck the wagon trail and pulled out for the train as fast as we could go and there might have been ten thousands cabins near us for all the attention we paid to anything but the trail. We froze to it like the gold fever to an old prospector. We finally came up to the train camped on the Little Big Horn river, waiting for us. Our reception was very cordial for after the threats made by the Indians and our lengthened absence, two weeks longer than we expected, the people in the train had about given up hope of ever seeing us again.

While the train was in camp, prospectors had been sent out everywhere on the east side of the mountains, but they had found no cabin or trace of one.

In the meantime, Bozeman's train had come on and passed us, intending to wait for us at the Big Horn river. When we reached Captain Hulbert's camp on the Little Big Horn, everything was in an uproar. There had been so many failures to find even a clue of the lost cabin, that it finally began to be believed that Hulbert had been misleading the train. These suspicions rapidly grew into complaints, these culminating in threats and when we arrived it seemed as though every man in camp could only be satisfied by Hulbert's death. Everyone was fairly crazy with disappointment and their rage was about to be expended on Captain Hulbert. From suspicions and complaints all were now saying that Hulbert had lied to them and led them off on a wild goose chase for some purpose of his own. Every preparation had been made to hang the Captain and it was altogether the worst crowd I ever saw. The Captain hadn't a friend in camp. He sat to one side, his head down in his hands, his elbows on his knees, staring vacantly at the ground. His heart was broken. I never saw a man in a more pitiable state and I made up my mind that I would be his friend at any rate. I went up to him and called him by name. He raised up, grabbed me by the hand and fairly cried for joy that we had arrived in time to save him. He said that he had found he was in the wrong range of mountains, a mistake easily made as he had travelled away from them during the night. It was impossible to make the crowd believe anything and I didn't try much. I jumped on a wagon tongue and talked about five minutes and finally dared the first man to come with a rope. No one came.

The telephone line is proving of great convenience.
There is not a cleaner town on the road than Medora.
The skating rink will only open Saturday evenings hereafter.
A Howe platform scales has been placed in front of the Co's. offices.
Ed. Severson has nearly recovered from his wound and is already out of bed.
Bert. Zigler is in St. Paul. He will return here some time during the summer.
The new refrigerator cars are of the Hamilton patent and are giving perfect satisfaction.
John O'Sullivan has located at Butte City, where his tonsorial shingle will fly in the breeze.
Don't forget the meeting to-morrow night to arrange for field-day sports on the fourth of July.
E. G. Paddock's new building, to be occupied by the Boston clothing house is nearing completion.
The cooler of the old slaughter-house is rapidly beieg transformed into one equal in all respects to the new coolers.
Dick Carr was kicked yesterday by one of his babies, commonly called mules, and is taking an enforced lay-off of a few days.
William Tolbert is conducting the Elk in first-class style and would be pleased to see his friends at all times. Give him a call.
M. W. McDonald has bought out John Warn's resturant and will run it up to the highest "Oyster Grotto" style of excellence.
Frank Axthelm, of Miles City, is taking Fred Banan's place as barber, while the latter completes his term of service at Ft. Keogh.
Joe Ferris expects to be established in business on this side the river inside of six weeks. Mr. Ellison is now assisting him in the store.
Almost every train from the east leaves one or more tourists at Medora, who are intent on looking at the beautiful scenery of the Bad Lands.
Miss Taylor, of Boston, a young friend of Mr. and Mrs. Wade came last Friday evening and will spend the summer at the Tepee bottom ranch.
Al. Gifford came down from Glendive yesterday. He has been thinking of going to South America but should this fail he intends to settle in Medora.
W. H. Holland, of Buffalo, Wyoming, sold fifty herd of fine steers on Monday to the Co. They averaged 1171 pounds and dressed out almost as well as fall cattle. The bunch sold for $4.40.
The next lot of cattle from the Hashknife will be delivered July 1. Full time at the slaughter-house may begin then. It is more likely to be a week later.
Mrs. M. M. Coleman was prostrated last Saturday by a kind of spasm that left her entirely unconscious for several days. She is now considered out of danger.
There are constant expressions of satisfaction and delight at the able manner in which Arch. Boyd and wife conduct the Northern Pacific hotel. It is a credit to Medora.
Medora has never looked prettier than at present. A walk to the top of the neighboring buttes will be well rewarded by the magnificent view at the feet of the spectator.
Our thanks are due in this public manner to the able and entirely satisfactory way in which J. C. Fisher and Levi Deffebach have conducted the Cow Boy during our absence.
T. J. Kerr, whom all in Medora know and like, has his summer home on the banks of White Bear lake. Never have we had a pleasanter time than when entertained there by Mr. Kerr and his charming wife.

The condition of the cattle is not at all satisfactory for killing and the Co. will shut down until July 1st. Between fifty and a hundred head a day will then be killed until the 15th, when work will begin on full time.

The Marquis, wife and friends and J. N. Simpson will make up a party for a pleasure excursion to the neighborhood of the Big Horn mountains. The party will start about July 15, and will be under the leadership of Vic Smith.

J. C. Fisher and Rassie Deffebach started last Friday for the E6 and returned last evening. They report the grass as knee-high all over the Cave Hills district, as good feed as there has ever been in the country. They stopped at Harry Tarbell's and are enthusiastic over his outfit. Everything is arranged in first-class shape and there is every probability of ninety per cent. of foals. Mr. Huidekoper is now visiting at the ranch. At the E6 they found one of the most systematically conducted ranches they ever visited. There are about thirty cow-boys here under the foremanship of Russ Wilson and each one has his duty as well defined as have the employes in a manufactory. Coming back they went to Arrington's ranch in Cave Hills, probably as pretty a location as there is in the country. Here they found Fred Willard and in company they came to Medora, striking the river at Eaton's logging camp and coming down the river road.

Carl Parks formerly of Mandan, is spending the summer here.
Prof. Wellung's entertainment at the rink on the evening of the 4th.
Fred Willard has been appointed stock inspector at Medora and arrived last evening to enter upon his duties. Fred made a host of friends while here and the appointment will give general satisfaction.
The queerest malformation in the shape of a deer horn we ever saw is now on exhibition at Bob Robert's saloon. One old horn was not shed and the new horn grew up around it in a very curious manner.

John Warn left Monday for Miles City where he intends organizing a party to go in search of the "Lost Cabin" gold mines. He has the good-will of all on his trip. His continued story will be concluded next week.

Mrs. A. Fox, of Minnoiska, Minn., and Mrs. E. Fox, of Ojata, Dak., made a call at the Cow Boy office Monday. Their husbands will be remembered as two of the party who went in a boat from here to Bismarck last May.

The base-ball craze has again struck Medora and an unexpected number of good players have already been developed. We understand that Glendive and Dickinson will have a match game on the 4th. If nines are organized at both these places it will be easy to arrange contests with them.

Much to the disappointment of our readers, who have noticed the literary improvement in the Cow Boy under the able leadership of Messrs. Fisher and Deffebach, the editor turned up on the late train Friday evening. The population of Medora is also increased by an editorial better half.

Baron A. von Steiger has had another horse-thief experience. He bought a horse in McLean county and the same night it was stolen from him. He followed the trail for about three weeks and finally got the horse. Taking it back home it was again taken from him by its rightful owner who lived near Ft. Stevenson. A horse is not worth much unless accompanied by a bill of sale signed by a responsible party.

There will be a great fourth of July entertainment and ball combined at the roller rink, the evening of the immortal fourth. The doors will be open at 7:30 and the misery will begin at 8:30. In connection with Prof. Wellung's magic entertainment there will be a variety consisting of double and single song and dance, negro sketches, laughable puns etc., lasting until 10 o'clock, after which dancing will commence and continue until everyone is dead.

And now we wish "to arise to remark" that the glorious 4th is almost upon us and no preparations have been made for any celebration during the day. The entertainment at the rink in the evening will doubtless be interesting but besides this, much enjoyment could be had by contests of various kinds during the day. To further this end we will issue a call for a meeting to elect a board to conduct the entertainment. The meeting will be held to-morrow, Friday evening at 8:00 o'clock at the rink. Let everyone turn out.

A meeting was held Monday evening to organize a church society, to see how many would take an active interest in paying the expenses of holding weekly service here. The officers elected were; J. C. Fisher, President; T. W. Gordon, Vice-president and W. B. Wright, Secretary. It was decided to find out how much could be raised weekly and for this purpose the secretary was instructed to prepare lists both of those who wish to become members of the association and of those who will contribute a stated sum weekly. The meeting then adjourned to meet early next week and hear the report of the secretary.
During June, the Northern Pacific has sold over 40,000 acres of land, the largest single sale being 4,000 acres to the Anaconda company.
The county commissioners of Stark Co. will meet as a board of equalization next Monday at Dickinson, to hear any complaints relative to the assessment of Billings county.

Washington Territory cattle are becoming a marked element in the cattle business. Over 28,000 head have so for been shipped into Montana this season and others will follow. They will be marketed this year principally.

The settlers on the Crow Creek reservation seem to be confident that they will not be disturbed for some time and that they can bring their case to the attention of Crongress before Cleveland enforces his order for the reservation to be vacated.

At the latest account, Gen. Crook had not made much headway in his war with the southern Indians and the settlers were beginning to organize for their own protection. When will the people at large and the general government learn the true definition of a good Indian?

Fred. Willard, our new stock inspector, returned Monday evening from Fargo, where he had gone to receive his commission as deputy U. S. Marshal. He says he hopes there will be no occasion for his services in the latter capacity. His wife will be here in a few weeks.

Russia is still continuing her warlike preparations and under the surface there is trouble in European politics. It has long been known that Lord Salisbury desired to form an offensive alliance with Germany against Russia and this, in connection with Russia's war preparations creates a very uneasy feeling. We still live in hopes of a European war.

The trial of Mrs. Yseult Dudley, for shooting O'Donovan Rossa, began yesterday in New York. She proved herself to be a regular vixen, constantly interrupting Rossa's testimony to cast slurs upon him and his evidence. She is doubtless trying the insanity dodge. Although public feeling is in her favor she will not help her case any by her present course.

It is a burning disgrace that even after the arrival of Bartholdi's statue of "Liberty enlightening the world," there has not been money enough raised to build the pedestal. France's generosity in presenting this gift is in striking contrast to the delay of the United States in finding it a resting place. As soon as Congress meets, it should solve the difficulty by appropriating a sufficient sum to cover the present shortage.

That General Grant is dying, seems now to admit of no doubt. The cancerous sore is now involving his jugular vein and he writes all communications to his physicians and attendants. Monday, he wrote on his writing tab: "Do as I do. I give myself not the least concern. If I knew that the end would be to-morrow, I would try and get rest in the meantime. As long as there's no no progress, there's hope." It seems that even to the end he will keep up the same stoical coolness that has been his marked characteristic.

The division idea is again being forced on the people by newspapers whose editors see some official pap in the dim future. It is needless to hope for a time when the press and political leaders of Dakota will unite for admission of Dakota as a whole, to make in the future one of the best of states. The animus of the whole division movement arises from the desire of Dakota's numerous political aspirants to double the number of state offices and thereby be more certain of an office for themselves. We have not; do not and never will uphold the action o these politicians in trying to increase the burden of taxation for their own benefit. Spot a divisionist as an axe-grinder every time.

We notice that it is the prevalent opinion that the recent assessment of Billings county by Stark county is for the purpose of levying a territorial tax. How this impression has gained ground is a mystery, as the assessment is strictly and solely a county tax and is entirely for the use and behoof of Stark county. It seems that the idea of this being a territorial tax has come from Stark county and if so, goes to prove what we thoroughly believe, that the law empowering senior counties to tax junior counties is unconstitutional. All debts contracted by senior counties to pay expenses of unorganized counties are finally paid by the territory. Where then is the justice of the senior counties being twice paid for those expenses? It would be a good plan to have this matter carefully considered by our citizens, and if deemed advisable, to make a test case and decide the constitutionality of the law. In any event, every one who pays taxes to Stark county should do so under protest so that in case a test case should be tried it will be easier to get our money returned.

It seems that we, in the Bad Lands, are far more blessed with rain and grass than farther west. It has been found nearly impossible to put up hay near Miles City and the supply for that point will probably come from the prairie east of here.

The Bad Lands Cattle Co are greatly pleased over their abundant calf crop. It will run about seventy-five per cent. and is the largest increase on the river. Next year, however, we look for this per cent. to be the average increase on the whole river.

Gen. Brisbin recently wrote an article for the Salt Lake Tribune, the substance of which should be deeply engraved in every cow-man's heart. It costs no more on the range to take care of or raise a hundred dollar animal than it does one worth forty dollars. Except for the original cost the profit is vastly on the side of the man who raises high-grade or full-blooded cattle.

The second annual round-up of this district came to a close at Mingusville Monday morning. The estimate of the calf crop at sixty per cent. is, if anything, too high. On the whole, the round-up was a success, although, on account of the difficulty of working the Bad Lands it is impossible to get the satisfactory results obtainable on more open ranges.

The Texas and New Mexico round-ups are strictly enforcing their rules forbidding the carrying of six-shooters. A cow-boy near Springer, N. M. recently had one taken from him and was fined $25 besides. If this rule can be made to work in old cattle countries it certainly can here. If it is necessary there, it is necessary here. Who of our western readers is there that does not know of one or more instances where serious or fatal accidents would not have happened if the six-shooter had been prohibited? Does the satisfaction of carrying six-shooters pay for the loss of life and suffering occasioned by them? We certainly think not and will hail the day when the habitual carrying of six-shooters is ended. There are occasions when it is necessary to carry revolvers but these do not come as often as every waking hour for three hundred and sixty-five days in the year.

There are Percherons, so-called, which are not Percherons, any more than Pennsylvanians are Virginians; but they are both French, as these are Americans. Perche is an ancient province of France, and lies south of Normandy, adjoining its southwestern border. Perche has long been known for its splendid breed of horses, which have been reared with much care and jealousy, and which date back in breeding to Arabian blood. Normandy has also its breed of horses, equally ancient but coarser and heavier; they were used a thousand years ago in war when an enormous weight of steel armour was borne, both by the rider and the horse. To bear the burden, and to ride down an opponent by mere force of shock, very heavy horses were required, rather than more active ones, and the Norman horses thus became, as they are still, they heaviest race known. The Percherons, on the other hand, were used for carriages, and are now the stage, omnibus and diligence horses of the country, able to trot with ease ten miles an hour, with a heavy vehicle behind them. These are consequently more finely built, have harder and finer bone, and while quite heavy, look lighter than they really are, because of their fine proportions, due to their Arabian ancestry.—[American Agriculturist.

THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES.

By J. S. WARN.

After a while things quieted down and by a good deal of talking the excited men were shown the folly of their suspicions and that Hulbert could not possibly have gained anything by lying to them. In the morning we made an early start and after two days' hard drive we found Bozeman camped on the Big Horn river below the canon. Hulbert thought when he first saw the Big Horn that it was the Yellowstone and he rode up and down the train excitedly declaring that now he was certain of the location of the mines. Again was he doomed to disappointment but he still insisted that he would reach the mines all right when we could find the Yellowstone. He knew the country there and could reach the mines without fail. But all except a few of the people in the train had entirely lost faith in Hulbert and could not be aroused from their discouragement. A discouraged tendefoot is the most miserable work of God. He is a worse failure than old Sitting Bull would be as a Prohibition candidate for the presidency.

Early in the morning we made a fresh start and crossed the river. What a hard job it was, only the old timers who have had to find their own roads, build their own bridges and work their way first in new countries can imagine. After an all days' job we finally crossed, with the loss of two wagons and their contents and went into camp.

The next day, all of the two trains pulled out for the Yellowstone. In time we reached it after very severe labor, we having to make roads all the way. When we finally reached the banks of the Yellowstone we found ourselves in a beautiful grove near some high bluffs. All that wanted to, went fishing and never was sport better rewardeds as the river was full of trout. From this point Capt. Hulbert could see down the river for a long way and he declared that this was the country he had been in. He said that he had been at this very spot and that he could easily find his way to the mines. We hunted up Bozeman and talked the matter over with him and all the leading men of both trains. We tried to stir up a friendly feeling and worked hard to get at least a part of the train to keep on in the search. Hulbert was positive in his statements that he could go to the mines. He said that a short distance down the river was the island on which he had camped, that there was a good crossing here and a good place to get out of the valley. However, it was impossible to interest enough now to even protect ourselves from the Indians. As they were on the war-path big at this time, it wouldn't have done for a small body of men to start out alone. After trying our best we had to give up our persuasions. For the present the chicken-hearted pilgrims were determined to go to Virginia City. They finally did and found every claim taken, clear up and down the gulch and a claim owner wouldn't look at a tenderfoot. For my part, I would have been glad to see every one of them starve.

Those who were willing to take chances of going in as soon as the Indians were again at peace, formed themselves into a company and took each others' addresses, both in the states and Montana, for the purpose of going to these mines, as we had the utmost confidence in the stories Capt. Hulbert told.

I saw Capt. Hulbert in Virginia City in the fall of '64. He was still engaged in trying to get men to go with him but he was always unsuccessful. I saw Bozeman in the fall of '66. I was going to the states in the winter in a mackinaw boat and took his wife with me to Omaha. That is the last I have seen of them. Bozeman was killed by the Indians down in the Yellowstone country and I have always thought he was going in search of the Hulbert mines.

For my part, I have by no means given up hope of finding the mines and expect soon to start in search of them. I am as certain they exist as decribed by Hulbert, as I am of any [uncertainty?]. The Lost Cabin mine will yet be found and richly repay the finder.

(Concluded.)

Joe McCoul had a serious accident Tuesday at Van Eeghan's Garner creek ranch. He was hauling a load of posts with a gentle horse and a broncho when the latter started to run away, throwing Joe off the load, breaking his leg and spraining his ankle. He was brought to town and is now at the Pyramid Park hotel. Dr. Duncan was called from Glendive and states that the fracture is not serious but the sprain is liable to cause trouble.

Again we weep. Our proud position as fighting editor will be occupied by us no more forever. Our heavy-weight assistant who at train time makes the air musical and the pilgrims' eyes bug out by his blood-curdling way of shouting: "B-a-d L-a-n-d-s C-o-w B-o-y" has usurped our prerogative, so to speak. A callow news-boy who objected to the aforesaid heavy-weight assistant's presence on the train is now mourning his rash objection. So, we might add, are his eyes. The above should be a warning both now and forever to all news-boys not to interfere with our b-a-d man.

A little breeze of excitement was created this morning by the barber shop catching afire. No damage of any amount was done but the cause of the fire deserves comment. It was owing to a stove-pipe being used in place of a brick chimney. There are a number of pipes in town used in the same way. Even with secure fastenings, this is an extremely dangerous expedient, certainly a false economy. Persons having such chimneys should immediately see to it that brick ones take their place. The cost is slight in comparison to the additional safety secured.

The meeting to get up a programme for the 4th. of July sports met according to call in the skating rink last Friday evening. J. C. Fisher was elected chairman and A. T. Packard stated that the object of the meeting was to informally discuss a programme of races and contests for the 4th. and moved that a committee of five be appointed to take charge of affairs. Bob. Roberts moved to amend by placing the name of the original mover at the head of the committee. The following committee was then elected: A. T. Packard, Bob. Roberts, E. Deffebach, John Goodall and Vic Smith. It was decided to make the principal event a six hundred yards' cow-horse race, with prizes of $25, $15 and $10. This race is open to cow-horses only or to those that are not considered or known to be fast horses. Besides this race, there are on the programme a free-for-all three hundred yards' horse race, with prizes of $15 and $10, a slow mule race, a hundred yards' dash foot race, a fat men's race, a rifle contest and other races contests which will be arranged on the ground. The base-ball will be in the forenoon, the rifle contest at one o'clock. The other contests will follow. Entries in any of the contests can be made with any of the committee.
Northern Pacific preferred stocks are selling at 39⅜; common at 16½.
The Indians near Lawndale, Pratt Co., Kansas are on the war-path and have killed several settlers.
The English cabinet has decided not to declare what its foreign policy will be. Lord Salisbury says that in reference to Russia, Gladstone's policy will be carried out.
Bradlaugh, the atheist who was returned by the electors of Northampton and has repeatedly tried to take his seat in the house of Commons, was again refused permission to take the oath of office.
Samuel T. Hauser, of Helena, has been appointed governor of Montana. The appointment has called forth many expressions of commendation, Mr. Hauser being a prominent business man of Helena.

The hotel Ryan, at St Paul, one of the largest in the United States, is now open and has created havoc among the other hotels and restaurants. The Metropolitan and Brevoort cafe have closed permanently.

All the West division street car employes in Chicago have been on a strike for the last week, causing great inconvenience to the traveling public. The matter is now being arbitrated and the men have gone back to work.

Gov. Pierce has given notice that the senate committee on Indian affairs, senator Harrison presiding, will visit the Crow creek and Winnebago reservations the 16th. and 17th., to try and adjust difficulties with the settlers.

Mr. Leo Welz, a nursery man in Ohio, has been authorized by the department of agriculture to purchase in Russia as many varieties of all kinds of fruit trees as in his opinion will grow in the northwest. We hope that this move will be successful as Dakota is not now blessed with a large variety of fruit trees.

The number of tramps on the road seems to be increasing year by year and their nerve increases with their numbers. Not more than half will do any work to pay for food. We call upon every citizen not to give a tramp a bite to eat until he has earned it. This is the best way of ridding ourselves of the pests.

A riot was narrowly averted on the 4th. at Salt Lake City. The Mormons, not content with living in open defiance of the law, placed all flags on public buildings at half-mast. After much trouble they were either lowered completely or run up to the masthead. Such an evidence of treason should receive cordign punishment.

The bids for territorial bonds were opened Tuesday at Bismarck. The total amount of bonds to be issued is $176,000 and are for the penal, charitable and educational institutions of Dakota. There were ten bidders Preston & Co., of Chicago, bidding 3 1-5 per cent. premium will probably get the award. The bonds are to draw six per cent. interest and the credit of the territory must be high to call for such large bids.

Ex-Gov. Mc Cook, of Colorado, comes out in a letter, declaring the Indian leases in Indian territory to be illegal. Under the law, the secretary of the Interior has full control of Indian affairs, subject to direction by the President. No purchase, grant. lease or other conveyance of land can be made except by treaty or convention, according to the constitution. The United States alone can make a contract with the Indians for their lands. Gen. McCook quotes the law to substantiate the above points. He also states that nearly 9,000,000 acres have been leased by different individuals and corporations from the Indians all of which leases are illegal. General McCook farther states that in many instances the present lessees of the land are foreigners who have no other interests in the United States. He also shows that only a few acres per capita are left to the Indians, not enough for each to have a respectable farm. It seems strange, if all Gen. McCook says is true, that such a state of things could exist. How the matter will end is problematical, but it seems now as though the leases in Indian territory must be given up. If so, it will greatly enhance the value of our northwestern grazing lands.

A popular amusement among cattlemen is guessing at the weight of animals. Some of the guesses are remarkably accurate. A case has recently been noted where two men guessed at the live weight of 1,075 cattle, each marking his guess on a slip of paper. On comparisons their guesses were found to be within a hundred and fifty pounds of each other and when the cattle were weighed the higher guess was found to be within five pounds of the true weight. Guessing how much cattle will dress out is a much harder task, the most authentic instance being the guess of John Deffebach. He guessed at the dressed weight of fifteen head of cattle and came within five pounds of the weight. This guess is authenticated by Rassie and Levi Deffebach and a large number of men in Central City.

It is safe to assume that a year or two more will see the Bad Lands as full of range cattle as will be profitable, taking into consideration the natural increase and the additions to the present herds. The question of quantity, or having as many cattle on the range as is safe, is, therefore, on the point of solving itself. The question of quality, however, has by no means had a sufficient share of the general attention. It has been proved so conclusively that it pays to raise grade cattle instead of scrubs that we will leave that point unnoticed and look for the cheapest and best way to raise a higher class of cattle. Of course this is done by using a better class of bulls but it seems to us that in the way of getting these bulls a large amount of money is spent that could be saved. Nine out of every ten ranchmen send east after bulls that could be raised to far better advantage here. It is not necessary for every cowman to have a full-blood herd but it would be an extremely profitable business for men of means to start such a herd in the range country. This would by no means be an experiment as it has been successfully tried in the south and to some extent in the west. By this means, there would be a large saving in three ways: transportation from the east here, an absence of the heavy loss occasioned by acclimatization and the comparative cheapness of raising cattle here to the cost in the east. These three reasons certainly make the cost of each animal $20 more. The range breeder therefore, could undersell the eastern breeder by this amount and make the same profit. Added to this would be readier sales owing to nearness to the market and the greater and acknowledged superiority of range-raised bulls. Who will be the man to accept this opportunity?

Mr. Van Brunt, president of the VI cattle Co., left for his home in Milwaukee after a six weeks' visit. He is greatly pleased with the condition of the cattle and has enjoyed the round-up hugely. He has also established a reputation as a host that will be long in fading away. Not a solitary VI bull died last winter, every animal having been rounded up.

It has passed the funny or amusing point when persons indulge in such promiscuous shooting as was done the night of July 4. Of course there is no objection to a reasonable amount of jollity on that day, but when anyone persists in shooting far into the night and in the immediate vicinity of hotels, where people desire to sleep, it is time that the foolishness was stopped. Not content with keeping would-be sleepers on this side the river awake, a gang went over the river Saturday night and shooting unexpectedly near the Pyramid Park hotel, where Joe McCoul is lying with a broken leg, gave him such a start that he labored under intense pain all night and until the doctor came in the morning. It was Joe's opinion and that of his watchers, that his leg was broken again. Happily, this did not prove to be the case. Acting under full authority, therefore, and with the full concurrence of all good citizens, Fred. Willard has published the notice in this issue that the law will be strictly enforced in reference to promiscuous shooting.

The sport on the 4th., although interrupted by the rain, which fell at frequent intervals, was much enjoyed.

In the morning a game of base-ball was begun which, on account of the rain only lasted three innings. The game served to develop the fact that we have a number of good players here. The nines were chosen, as near as possible, one from the slaughter-house and one from the town. At the finish the score was a tie, two to two.

The first race of the afternoon was the fat men's race, won in a canter by Ed Myers, the fairy sylph who officiates at the slaughter-house scales. Sam Whitney and MacDonald ran a close race for second, Sam finally winning, while Shorty, the gazelle-built manipulator of buffalo horns was distanced, he having tripped on a blade of grass or some other obstruction.

Putting Bob Roberts' mule outfit into requisition the hole Shorty made in the ground was soon filled up and the ground again smoothed for the 600 yard race, the event of the day. For this there were only four starters, the slippery track deterring many from the dangers of such a race. The starters were Blue Jay entered by Van Eeghan, Splinter and Lengthy by Goodall and Fox by Van Driesche. It looked like a clear walk-away for Blue Jay, who was freely backed against the field. The slippery track, however, upset the calculations of every one and the dark horse won, Splinter coming in a good two lengths ahead of Lengthy, who was closely followed by Blue Jay and Fox. Splinter ran a splendid race, carrying Mose Ryder and a heavy California saddle, the two weighing at least two hundred and sixty pounds. Contrary to expectations, Fox made a brilliant race. He is only four years old and is not fairly broken but he lapped Blue Jay at the finish.

The next event was a hundred yard foot race, arranged on the ground between Joe Houston and Walter Watterson. It was a close and exciting race, Joe coming in about a foot ahead. An animated discussion arising over the decision of this race it was decided to have a repetition in the regular hundred yard race.

For the hundred yards' race there were nine starters and for the number starting was a remarkably even race. It was won by Pat. Moore. Houston again beat Watterson, though neither secured a place in the race. The last race was the free-for-all three hundred yard horse race and it is seldom that a prettier finish is witnessed. There were only two entries: Gopher by Van Eeghan and Topsy by Goodall. Topsy lapped Gopher all through the race but could not get his nose ahead of the horse on whom every boy on the river will "go broke" if anything can beat him. Gopher was not struck a blow during the race, seeming to know that he was only required to keep ahead.

Johnny Goodall captured the bulk of the prizes, walking away with the remnants of $65, the remainder gracing the till of Bob. Roberts' wet goods hostelry.

The money for the purses was easily raised by subscription and had it not been for the rain, nothing would have marred the day's entertainment.

At the close of the racing, a boxing-match was held in Roberts' hall. Although the result was one-sided it showed that Medora certainly possesses her share of "talent."
Special agent Armstrong telegraphed Tuesday from Fort Reno, that there was no danger of trouble arising at the Arapahoe and Cheyenne agencies.

There are 96,596,480 acres of land in Dakota, 55,297,180 of which are unsurveyed. In total area, Montana comes next with 92,016,640 acres, then come New Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, Colorado and Wyoming in the order named, the latter having a total area of 62,645,120 acres.

There have been 42,667 timber-culture entries in Dakota, including 8,246,304 acres. Nebraska comes next with 25,031 entries and an acreage of 3,553,479. As this calls for the raising and growth of about 515,418 acres of trees in Dakota, future generations may well thank the foresight of our government in making the timber-culture law although its provisions are greatly abused.

The Pall Mall Ga[z]ette, of London, has been exposing the vices of the nobility in such a way that it is seriously arousing public opinion. It has long been an open secret in England that the common people have no rights that the nobility consider themselves bound to respect. The Gazette is the first champion the people have ever had that has done them any good. It is doing a good work and has the support of the large mass of the English people. Rev. Spurgeon, as well as many other ministers, are giving enthusiastic sanction to the Gazette.

In the course of time, a vast amount of land in Dakota which now is unproductive, can be made as valuable as any with artesian wells. Especially between Medora and the Black Hills there is a large extent of country that is valueless for agriculture and only moderately valuable for stock, owing to the scarcity or total lack of water. There is plenty of land at present nearer the railroad and better watered, but the time is coming when this land will all be readily salable and the ones who establish successful artesian wells will reap a rich profit.

We are indebted to a pamphlet entitled "Range and ranch cattle business of the United States" by Joseph Nimmo, Jr., Chief of the Bureau of Statistics, for many of the figures in this week's issue. The pamphlet covers a great deal of ground, giving many interesting facts relative to the cattle industry and dealing especially with the bearings of the cattle business upon the internal and foreign commerce of the United States. It gives a complete history of the range cattle and dressed beef industries of the United States and is in the main correct. The article on Dakota is however, not only misleading but almost entirely wrong. The facts(?) were furnished by a man who is personally entirely ignorant of the cattle business. With this and a few other exceptions the pamphlet is the most valuable one on range cattle ever published.

Trouble has at last begun between the trail men and the Kansas cattle men. J. R. Blocker, Pugsley Bros., N. Dowling, H. S. Holly, J. W. Driskill, J. T. Lytle, M. C. Campbell and others have been arrested by deputy U. S. Marshal Bell and taken to Dodge City, Kansas. These men have over 50,000 head of cattle on the trail, which are now stopped south of the Canadian river. Their preliminary trial has probably already occurred. It is likely that every means will be used to avoid the trial as, it being a test case, thousands and probably hundreds of thousands of dollars will be spent before its decision. At any rate the arrests show that the Kansans are thoroughly in earnest about the enforcement of the quarantine laws. The decision will materially affect cattle interests, especially those of the south and will be looked forward to with intense interest.

For the benefit of those of our readers who have not a personal knowledge of the history of stock raising in the northwest, a short account may be agreeable.

In 1864, or rather early in 1865 it was learned that cattle would fatten in the north better than in the south. A government trader was overtaken by a hard snow storm on the Laramie plains and turned his oxen out, as he supposed to die. Early in the spring, however, he found them in even better condition than when turned out. This, taken in connection with the fact that buffalo lived and grew exceedingly fat in Dakota, Montana and Wyoming, first drew the attention of cattlemen to the northwest as a beef coutry.

Capitalists soon took advantage of the opportunities offered and began driving cattle from the southern ranges to grow into beef. This has been kept up to the present time and it is fair to presume that within five years the northern ranges will be as full as is safe, taking into consideration the natural increase of the herds.

The range territory includes the principal part of the Indian territory, the western parts of Kansas, Nebraska and Dakota, nearly all of Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, Nevada and portions of California, Oregon and Washington. This area includes over 1,160,000 square miles.

A fair illustration of the marvelous growth of the cattle industry is shown by the growth of the Montana and Wyoming associations. Two years ago, according to President Bryan, the Montana association consisted of seven members. Now there are over a hundred and fifty members. In 1873 the Wyoming association consisted of ten members, owning about 20,000 cattle, valued at $350,000. In 1885 the Wyoming association has 435 members, owning 2,000,000 head of cattle and valued at $100,000,000.

The cattle business of the west and northwest differs somewhat from the way it is conducted in the south. In Texas, the most of the land is owned by the cattlemen themselves. In the Indian territory the land is for the most part leased, but in Wyoming, Montana and Dakota, the vast majority of the cattle are grazing on government land. In these territories, this will doubtless be the case for some time to come, as the cattle country is in the dry area and agriculture cannot be carried on except by irrigation. It will be many years before the land not requiring irrigation will be taken up and the time is especially far distant when it will pay to irrigate lands far from railroads in this western country. The grass receives an abundance of moisture from the snows and spring rains, the dry weather comes on early and cures the grass standing. It is then equal to cut timothy.

Only a few years ago the Indians held almost undisputed control of what is now the range cattle country of the west and northwest. After the Custer massacre the government adopted stringent measures with reference to compelling the Indians to stay on their reservations, thus practically opening the country to the stock interests. There is now no farther danger in the cattle country from Indian outbreaks as the cow-boys could easily quell any disturbance.

The cattle business is now as firmly established and the profits can be as easily calculated as in other pursuits, the results of which are not absolutely certain. There is always a market for beef and stock cattle. Prices vary a little but have steadily increased from the $3 to $4 Texas steer of twenty-five years ago, to the $50 to $60 Montana steer of to-day.

The work is now reduced to a system and everyone is compelled to act honestly by his neighbor. Ten years ago a man might draw to a branding iron and get a herd. Now he would as surely get a rope or states prison. From the thorough detective and inspection system of the stock associations, it is almost impossible to act dishonestly. A man's cattle when branded, are as safe a hundred miles from his ranch as they are at home. The unwritten law of the range is "treat your neighbor white and he'll treat you w[hit]e."

Of the slaughtering-houses in Chicago Swift Bros. & Co., did the largest business, killing 401,617 cattle. Armour & Co. came next with 306,374.
There were 98,000 cattle shipped west over the Northern Pacific last year according to the statement of General freight agent Hannaford. They were mostly she stock, one's and two's.

In Wyoming there are fifty-six varieties of natural grasses. As the soil, physical characteristics and climate of Dakota are about the same as Wyoming, there are probably the same number in this territory. In addition, alfalfa and several other artificial grasses have been tried and we have not yet heard of any failures in this direction.

The largest number of cattle received during any one month last year at the Chicago yards was 198,717 in October. The lowest number was in March, 122,633. The large receipts during the latter month as well as in the winter and early spring is probably due to the fact that farmers are making a general practice of raising feeders for a high market.

The total value of the live cattle and beef products exported from the United States during the year ending June 30, 1884 was $41,080,001. Of this total, Great Britain and Ireland took more than three-quarters. There has been a steady and rapid increase in this export business since 1875, the total value of shipments during that year being $11,728,358.

All live cattle shipped from the United States to England, must be killed at the port of entry within five days of their arrival and cannot be taken into the interior. This is a distinction made against our cattle by England, without any just cause. The dressed beef industry of the United States makes it far more profitable to ship beef in that way, but as a matter of principle, the government should have England's restriction on our cattle removed or give her a taste of how a similar restriction on our part would seem. Cattle shipped from Canada to England are subject to no restrictions whatever.

The Marquise, Wm. Van Driesche and hunting party consisting of Vic and Frank Smith, Tom Skinner and Sweet start this evening for Huntley, Mont. The horses have already been shipped there, this being the starting-point for the overland journey to the Big Horn. The party will be gone about a month.

A. R. Kelsey, manager of the Glendive branch of J. S. Collins & Co., called at the Cow Boy office this morning. He reports a first-rate trade for his house, but as the most of it is in and west of Miles City, the branch will be removed there on or about August 10. The firm is now building a brick store room for their accommodation in Miles.

Experience is the only teacher in regard to the way beef will dress out. There was every prospect that range cattle would be in condition fully two or three weeks earlier than last year. The grass was fully that much earlier and larger in proportion than last year. It is doubtful though, if the beef is any earlier. The grass has grown to quantity and not to quality. Considerable good beef has been slaughtered here, but it has not come up to the high standard expected of it. It is doubtful if any first-class beef will be killed before August 1.

Prairie fires are again forcing themselves into notice and it is time that stockmen took immediate steps to protect themselves. A large portion of the country south of Belfield has been burned over and yesterday one was burning in the Bad Lands near Sully Springs. No effort has yet been made to make fire guards either by individuals or the railroad company. This is a short-sighted policy. A week of such weather as Tuesday and Wednesday will put the whole country in condition to be completely swept by a fire. This is liable to do incalculable damage to the stock interests and is a matter that admits of no delay in remedying.

Bob. Roberts will soon move his saloon into the skating rink. The rink will be re-finished throughout, ceiled, papered, painted and fitted with a glass front.

John Munro and the Gifford Bros. are putting up a thousand tons of hay on the Big plateau. This will be the cleanest hay ever put up in this country, as the same ground has been cut over once or twice.

Geo. Eckhardt, treasurer of the Milwaukee Brewing Co., who are now operating the large brewery at Bismarck, was in Medora, Monday. He is on his way west and reports trade as opening up well for the new brewery.

The wa[y?] Norwegian Abe clawed leather, at the beef camp Monday night, would take the pie in any contest, but he couldn't stay with his name-sake "Crazy." This is the reason he has gone into mourning and not because his love's young dream was blighted.

We know of several cases where pilgrims have come to Dakota with little or no summer clothing, thinking that it would be useless here. The pores of our skin fairly wept at their delusion Tuesday, when we saw the thermometer register 104 in the shade and never crack a smile.

Warren Packard, of Warren, Ohio one of the most prominent iron and lumber men in that state and J. J. Fisher, a wealthy young business man of Allentown, Pa., spent the first of the week in Medora and vicinity. They expressed themselves as greatly pleased with their visit, especially at their treatment at the beef camp on Davis creek. As near as they could make out, everything was done according to Hoyle, except that they looked in vain for the piano to accompany the evening lullaby of the cowboys when they were singing the herd to sleep, after having been driven up to the corrall to be milked.

We neglected in our last issue to mention the Bad Lands minstrel entertainment, given by home talent at the rink, on the evening of the fourth of July. The variety part of the entertainment would have been a complete success if we had brought our guns along and killed all the performers at the beginning of the first act. The orchestra, led by Mose de Spicer, was simply indescribable. To escape a popular uprising, Mose fled the next morning for the Pacific coast. Two other members of the gang, for this or some other reason, skip to-night for the Big Horn country. One of the finest pieces of legerdemain ever witnessed was the invisible way in which the invisible Prof. Wellung deluded a confiding public into believing that there was a professor on the stage who knew the difference between a sleight of hand trick and four dollars a week.

DEAD! His Life Work Ended, The Old Hero Dies.

DEAD!

HIS LIFE WORK ENDED, THE OLD HERO DIES.

Special Telegram to the BAD LANDS COW BOY.

MT. MCGREGOR, July 23.—General Grant died at eight o'clock. He passed quietly away, in the full possession of his senses and surrounded by his family. SPIZA.

We have only room to state, in addition to the above telegram, that General Grant had been failing for the last few days and it was manifest to all that his end was near. He had the determination to keep death at bay until his historical work was ended, when, there being nothing more to fight for, he, for the first time in his life surrendered. Future poets will sing his praises, future warriors will take him as a model, future painters will delight in picturing him as the third of that triumvirate, dear to every American's heart, Washington-Lincoln-Grant.

Secretary Lamar has put his foot into it in bad shape in ordering the opening of the Texas trails. He puts his own power against the wishes of every state and territory on the line of the trail, besides that of every stock organization between here and Texas. Beyond that, he overrules laws made by the states and territories crossed by the Texas trail against this very invasion. More than all this, he takes the word of the few men driving cattle from Texas that the cattle are not infectious, against the combined statements of all others that they either are or are probably so. At present the trail advocates are decidedly on top.

At last visitors to Niagara Falls can be free from the extortionate charges that have coupled the name of that grandest work of nature with all manner of greed. The American side of the river near the Falls, Goat island and the small islands north and south of it, including Bath island have all been bought by the state of New York and the whole is now turned into a free public park. This movement is one that will go far toward redeeming New York from the load of shame that oppresses her legislation. New York virtually makes a national gift to the United States of Niagara Falls and should receive every credit therefor.

Great excitement has recently been caused in the east and especially in Chicago, from several cases of poisoning from dried beef said to come from the Chicago stock yards. At Momence, Ill., there were thirty-four cases and other isolated cases are being reported from other places. The poison is probably germinated from putrefaction and its action is very severe. The Chicago packers are unanimously of the opinion that the beef came from an irresponsible dealer and desire the strictest investigation and the blame laid to the proper source. In Adrian, Mich., a case has been reported where the poisoning came from canned beef, but in most instances it comes from dried beef.

John Roach, America's greatest shipbuilder, has been forced into bankruptcy by Secretaries Whitney and Garland. On the shallowest of pretences, they have refused to accept the Dolphin, a vessel built by Roach under government contract and under the personal supervision of a committee appointed by the government. Aside from the Dolphin, Roach had contracts for several other vessels which Attorney General Garland now declares illegal. The whole matter is a scheme on the part of Whitney and Garland, backed by enemies of Roach to ruin the latter. At present it looks like a success, but the law may step in and prove that it is mightier than Attorney General Garland.

The Mormons have begun showing their hand in such a way that it is impossible for the government longer to avoid taking cognizance of their actions. The laws passed respecting their marriage customs have no effect whatever and in other respects they are living in direct violation to the law. Their crowning act of treason was on the 4th. of July, when all national flags on public buildings were lowered to half-mast. This is an insult to our flag that no nation on the face of the earth dare put upon the United States. That such "scum de la scum" as the Mormons should not only live in open defiance of the law, but should go out of their way to insult the flag can not be endured. It calls for instant and condign punishment that a Republican administration would not be long in inflicting. Add to all this the fact that even now troops are being brought into Salt Lake City to quell a threatened disturbance on the Mormon's national holiday and we have a state of affairs only explained by the liberty of our institutions. This liberty has been trampled on and villified long enough. It is time for the government to take a hand and crush forever such a disgrace as Mormonism.

The Niobrara cattle Co. delivered a bunch of steers to the Ref. Car Co. Saturday that averaged 1295 pounds. This is the highest average yet and it is to be hoped that hereafter good cattle can readily be obtained.

Joseph Nimmo, Jr., chief of the bureau of statistics and author of the recent "Report in regard to the Range and Ranch cattle business of the United States" is already collecting the material for a popular work on the subject. The government edition of his work is exhausted and the call for it has been so large that it shows a good opening for the work Mr. Nimmo has in contemplation. It is a field entirely unoccupied except by newspapers and we wish the author every success in his undertaking. Mr. Nimmo informs us that he intends soon making a tour of inspection of the range country and will spend some time in the Bad Lands.

According to the latest reports there are very nearly, if not quite 50,000,000 cattle in the United States. Of these Texas stands at the head of the list with 9,000,000. Iowa comes next with over 3,500,000. Then comes Missouri, New York, Illinois and Kansas in the order named with over 2,000,000 each. Ohio, Nebraska, Pennsylvania, Indiana, Wisconsin, Wyoming and Indian Territory, following with numbers from a few over a million in the latter to nearly two million in the former. Montana has nearly 800,000 and Dakota has nearly 400,000. Little Rhody foots the list with 35,000.

The cattle raisers of Dakota have an advantage over those of Wyoming which is scarcely valued as it should be. This is in the matter of freight rates. Whatever can be said in reference to rates charged by the Northern Pacific in other matters, it must be acknowledged that their rates on cattle are extremely low. In car-load lots, according to Nimmo's report, the tariff is at the rate of fifty-three cents a hundred miles from Chicago to New York, the rate on the Union Pecific is sixty cents and that on the Northern Pacific is fifty-six cents. When we notice that there are many roads competing for the business from Chicago to New York and that there is no competition on the Northern Pacific, it is manifest that the latter is giving every encouragement to cattle raising. In Dakota especially, as we started to remark, do these rates benefit our cowmen. The average rate per head from Dakota shipping points to Chicago is $4.88. The rate from Wyoming points is $7.22. Thus the Dakota cattleman gains an additional profit of $2.34 per head over his Wyoming brother. In dealing with large herds this is a very neat figure to save.

Joe Ferris intends, before the counters are put into his new store room, to give an opening dance. It will be a well-attended party.
Drive care away by smoking the Republic de Gautemala cigars. They are the best and of course John Munro has got them.

The pay-car passed through yesterday and the boys are uncertain as to whether to buy out a controlling interest in the railroad or become cattle kings.
A round-up party consisting of outfits north of the track has gone to the Big Missouri and will round up the whole country from there to the Bad Lands.
The dance at Mrs. Malloy's last night was a complete success. The owners of several sleepy looking pairs of eyes declared this morning that they wouldn't have missed it for a ranch.
Joe McCoul went to Glendive last night, where he can have more constant medical attendance. His leg is doing well, but paining him more than will be the case at Glendive.
We have just received a large stock of paper of all kinds and can offer those wishing job work, of any sort, their choice of stock. Bring in your orders for anything in the job printing line.
Charlie Connelly, of the Hashknife outfit, has returned from the Hot Springs. He outfitted at Medora last week and started for the home ranch of the Hashknife Co., on Box Elder creek.
Medora is getting up an extended reputation as a watering place. The gentlemen of the dining car keep their heads inside though, lately, as they object to taking it from a syringe.

The Co. has recently shipped in a number of large kettles in which to render the tallow and make stock for butterine. The butterine itself will not be made here but the stock will be shipped to eastern markets.

There has been more rain this season than for any to which the oldest inhabitant's memory extends back. It is now getting to be rather a nuisance than otherwise to stockmen, as those wishing to put up hay find the grass too green.

W. H. Mintey, night operator here, started this morning for Augusta, Wis. We are in a state of painful uncertainty and will be until his return three weeks hence, as to whether he intends anything serious or not. E. W. Jordan relieves him.

Dr. H. M. Jorgens and family start this afternoon for Cave Hills. Messrs. Powers and Johnson, of Grand Rapids, Mich., came last night and start with E. G. Paddock, on their way to Spearfish. On his return trip, Mr. Paddock will bring back Mrs. Fred Willard.

A very pleasant social gathering took place at the Rowe, Parker & Easton cattle ranch, on the evening of the 12th of July. Music, singing and dancing were all on the evening's programme. At twelve o'clock supper was served. It was voted by all in attendance to be the most pleasant evening ever spent by the young people of the Little Beaver.

The Chimney Butte ranch was the place and Merrifield and Ferris Bros. were the hosts, that entertained a party last Saturday in a way to warm one's heart to Bad Lands hospitality. Riding, horse-racing, shooting, a runaway and a good exhibition of bucking, crowned by a bountiful ranch supper, completed an afternoon of pleasure long to be remembered by the participants.

Grasshoppers or seventeen-year locusts, authorities differ, are doing great damage in Montana and north-western Dakota. Many fields of grain north of the Yellowstone, in Montana and some of the ranges south of the Yellowstone have been nearly or quite destroyed. It is doubtful if they will get as far south as the railroad in time to do much damage. Their advance is slow and they are now at least seventy-five miles from the end of the wheat belt, which ends at Belfield. We advise our eastern neighbors to harvest their grain as soon as possible.
