In Justice Gordon's Court.

Territory vs R. Roberts. } Assault.

At the regular session of Justice Gordon's court yesterday afternoon, the only case on the docket was the assault case against Robert Roberts. Nate. Baker, a gentleman of elegant leisure, who rode into town on a tie and brake-beam pass, was the complaining witness.

Court was opened at three o'clock by sheriff Lincoln Lee. The first witness was the plaintiff, Mr. Nathaniel Baker. He testified that his home was the same as that of his satanic majesty and that he was a hunter, having spent all his life killing time. Occasionally, or about seven times a day, he branched into a profession he had down finer than a bug's bill, that of "bumming chuck." As a means of livelihood, outside of his business and profession, he was a scissors-grinder. To prove his statement he drew the implements of his trade from his vest pocket; a piece of scoria for a grindstone and a broken-bladed penknife for a screw-driver. He further stated that entering the doxology works of the prisoner at the bar he had been saluted by the discharge of a deadly weapon, aimed in his direction and held in the hands of the aforesaid prisoner. That he had then sworn out a complaint before Justice Gordon and had the prisoner arrested. On cross-examination he testified that his home was in Belfield. The court then very properly over-ruled the motion of defendant's counsel to quash the case, owing to the conflicting evidence concerning the plaintiff's residence by complaining witness, holding that there was no conflict in his statements.

Fred Willard was then sworn. He testified that he was a barber by trade and very nervous by temperament. That he had been extremely bothered in the practice of his tonsorial occupation by defendant playfully holding him up whenever he had a splinter or two. The prosecuting witness had come into his place of business, complaining that the defendant had held him up for a coin about as big as a dollar or a dollar and a half or two dollars. As witness had often suffered in the same way he willingly loaned the prosecuting witness a six-shooter and took pains to look carefully at the loads and see that the powder and ball were removed from the cartridges. The complaining witness then started for Mr. Roberts place of business and the next witness saw was the form of Mr. Baker fairly clawing the air in a race against time and bullets. He also remembered that Mr. Baker while jumping over a ten-foot corral fence casually remarked something about murder and things. He also saw Mr. Roberts in hot pursuit who playfully kept up his target practice at a variegated piece of cloth on the sag of Mr. Baker's pants, commenting meanwhile to the effect that, "Nobody but a rank tenderfoot would turn loose on him."

During the course of the trial the testimony had been several times interrupted by the defendant and it was found necessary to handcuff and gag him and then lay him in a corner where the court feather-weights Shorty and Sam Whitney placidly anchored him down by sitting on him.

Being released, the defendant testified that his name was Robert Roberts. That his home was in Landdasant Anglesay Bightyoughertougueough, Great Britain. That he was a foreign missionary sent out by his home congregation to spread the glad tidings of great joy among the buttes and coolies of the Bad Lands. Here the prisoner had a convulsion of the countenance which the court interpreter declared to be a wink. On suspicion, and because the boys were getting dry, the court immediately found the prisoner guilty of breach of promise, ordered the prosecuting witness to resume his tie pass and adjourned court to try and induce a little boy to buy a winter suit that would have looked baggy on Myers, the Fat.
The first shipment of tea direct from China, over the N. P. is now going on. One cargo will make two hundred car loads.
The question of opening the Oklahoma country to settlement has been seriously considered by the cabinet and the last report seemed to indicate that it will soon be done.

We willingly give Chicago every credit due her, but when the Inter Ocean cracks her up as a summer resort and talks about the pure air from the lake and prairies; fragrant memories of Bridgeport and Chicago river oblige us to put in an emphatic denial. As a summer resort Chicago is not a success.

The Montana stock association will assemble for its fall meeting at Helena, Aug. 26. The Little Missouri association should have a meeting before that time to report to the Helena meeting. There was no definite time set for our fall meeting but one should be set now. The constitution calls for two yearly meetings and it will undoubtedly be best to have ours before that of the Helena association. It is time for some of our officers to come to the front with a notice of the meeting.

The census report of northern Dakota will probably be finished to-morrow. Major Edwards has been hurrying the work as fast as was consistent with accuracy and our report is far in advance of that of southern Dakota. From reports, we judge that the enumeration will show a gratifying increase in all directions. In conjunction with that of southern Dakota, it will show that we are far better prepared to become a state in all that concerns material welfare than are at least a half dozen of the present states.

Our second and third pages give such a detailed account of the life and death of General Grant, that anything further is almost superfluous. We must, however, put in our mite to swell the volume of sentiment against the burial of the General in New York. Riverside park, an extension of Central park has now been selected as his last resting place. It is by no means appropriate that he should be buried in a pleasure ground. Washington is the only fit place to receive the remains of such a national character as was Grant.

The cattlemen of the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservation in Indian Territory have gathered in force at Kansas City and unite in petitioning the president to extend the date of removal from forty days to one year. Reports are coming in that the Indians are already beginning to slaughter the cattle on the reservation and the cattlemen are positively at a standstill as to what to do. Further developments are anxiously awaited. It is by no means probable that the Executive will grant an extension until he finds that an honest effort will not remove the cattle in forty days.
The Hashknife herd to be delivered the 1st. has been grazing on the divide for several weeks. They are said to be in good condition.
Mrs. J. L. Truscott, nee Miss Maggie Gardient, arrived Monday evening. She will live at the Northern Pacific until Mr. Truscott finishes his house on the ranch.
The fast freights on the N. P. will not start until next Sunday. They will make the run from St. Paul to Portland in 160 hours and take the places of freights 13 and 16.

The sad news was received last Sunday that Janie Fitzgerald was dead. It will be a surprise to many of her acquaintances even to know that she was seriously ill. It was but a short time ago that she seemed full of life and health and to be cut down in her young womanhood seems scarcely possible.

J. L. DeHart, of the DeHart Land and Cattle Co., whose range is on the Rosebud passed through on his way east this morning. He reports that the grasshoppers are doing a great deal of damage on the Rosebud and vicinity. The reports of seventeen-year locusts appearing, at least in his district, are unfounded. The dam recently built above the cut seemed to do little good Tuesday evening in turning the rush of water from the freight house. An immense quantity of rain seemed to have fallen several miles down the track and in its rush under the freight house it tore away the underpinning so that the building sagged over a foot in the middle. New propping has been put in, but the building will have to be raised.

We have noticed several articles in our exchanges relative to the attacks of the "heel fly." Although the existence of such a fly seems to be credited by a number of cattlemen, we very much doubt its existence. We have never yet seen a responsible cowman who asserted that he had seen a "heel fly" and that the peculiar antics cut by cows at times is due to the attacks of the fly. The true explanation in all probability, is that the peculiar actions are caused by the working out of grubs on the animal for the results are exactly similar from this cause in districts where "heel flies" are never mentioned.

B. F. Reynolds arrived from Texas Monday and will make his head-quarters at Medora for a time. He has forty-five hundred Texas cattle on the trail, now in the neighborhood of Rapid City. Thirteen hundred of these cattle will be sold and the rest will probably be grazed in this vicinity. Mr. Reynolds cattle being from northern Texas, he had no difficulty in driving, from the quarantine laws. He reports the feeling between northern and southern Texas cowmen as being far more bitter than that between the former and northwestern cattlemen. He does not consider that there ever will be a permanent stop put to driving by trail. The discovery of the causes and cure of Texas fever will again send thousands of cattle from Texas to the north.

The most interesting thing of late to cattlemen is the order of President Cleveland, warning cattlemen and "other intruders" to leave the Indian Territory within forty days. There are two very distinct sides to this question. On the one hand, the present residents and owners of cattle in the Indian Territory are for the most part innocent sub-lessees. The organized lessees are wealthy speculators who took the chances of their leases from the Indians being declared illegal, the Interior department merely giving them their tacit consent. Nevertheless, innocent parties will for the most part be sufferers unless they can make the original lessees responsible for all damage. On the other hand, if the government did not declare the leases illegal and compel cattlemen to remove, they would most certainly break faith with the Indians. Up to the present, no move has been made toward driving the cattle out and a policy of delay has been inaugurated which, in view of the present attitude of the administration, can only do harm to the cattle owners. But where in the world to drive between 400,000 and 500,000 head of cattle is what is bothering the Territory cowmen. Neither Kansas, Colorado or Nebraska can possibly find room for them and it is too late in the season to drive as far north as Dakota or Montana. If the cattlemen take immediate steps to try and carry out the executive order the limit of forty days can easily be extended. If the present dilatory policy is kept up, it can but result in immense loss to the cattlemen. The COW BOY has too often declared its sentiments on the reservation question to be misunderstood. We believe thoroughly that every Indian reservation should be thrown open to settlement except say 160 acres for each Indian and an honest manner of conducting the distribution of food to the Indians be inaugurated. This is the only way to settle the difficulty and the way it must finally be decided.

Prices on all classes of cattle dropped fifteen to twenty-five cents in the Chicago market during the last week, as will be seen by our market report.
Rattlesnakes are more abundant this year than for a long time in the Bad Lands. From the number now being killed it is to be hoped that we will soon be rid of them.

Never, since the first white man came here, has there been as much rain as we have had this season. There has even been more than is wanted as the grass should at this time be better cured than it is.

No service was held last Sunday evening, although Rev. Schaffner was here, owing to the improvements going on in the rink. Next Sunday evening service will be held in the depot waiting room, where all are invited.

Strange as it may seem, Medora has a larger freight, express and passenger business than any point on the division, Mandan and Glendive included. Fifteen to twenty thousand dollars is no uncommon freight business to do in a month.

Max Bass has "struck his gait" as agent for the Milwaukee Brewing Co. It must needs be a temperance town where his persuasive eloquence will not introduce the now famous Bismarck beer. The brewing company would have had a hard time finding a better man to compete with "Otto, the spotter." We live in hopes of seeing the two in town together. There will certainly be room for an argument then.

D. F. Barry, "Bismarck's best" in the photograph line, has placed us under many obligations for a number of large panels and photographs of noted Indians, Sitting Bull, Rain-in-the-Face, Slow White Buffalo, Crow Eagle, Iron Thunder, Fool Thunder, Standing Holy, Sitting Bull's daughter, Gaul and nephew and others all bedecked in Indian finery are among the number. Mr. Barry has made a specialty of Indian photographs, he having a gallery at Standing Rock. He is thinking of putting up a gallery here and taking a number of Bad Lands views.

The St. Paul jobbers came in like a cloud of seventeen-year locusts but apparently with no such greedy design. Their trip is one, more of pleasure than business, but a weather eye was always kept open for trade. The excursion train arrived at 4:30 and immediately the Northwestern band enlivened all with the first strains of brass-band music that have ever been heard in Medora. The whole party then fell in and headed by the band marched to the slaughter-house. Here the busy scene was viewed for a few minutes and the system displayed was warmly approved. On the return trip considerable amusement was aroused by Pete the cook, who was riding a kicking cayuse and passing as chief of police. The only real, live, wild, genuine, untamed cow-puncher, disporting on his native heath was Fred Willard. To look at his calm, untroubled lineaments while stating to an eager questioner that his revolver cost two hundred and sixty dollars and other answers of a like tenor, one would actually have believed what he said—if he didn't know him. The excursionists expressed themselves as especially sorry not to be able to stop and learn something of the cattle business, but this, of course was impossible. The trip will last ten days from the time of starting, the western limit being Butte. The trip will give the jobbers a good idea of the growth of the country along the line as well as its needs. The trip cannot but be mutually profitable as this whole country naturally claims St. Paul as a headquarters.

Jack Bullion came in yesterday from his ranch and reported that between his ranch on Bullion creek and Van Eeghan's on Garner creek a heavy hail storm occurred last Saturday. In some places the hail was piled up a foot deep. There was only a narrow strip in which the hail fell and no damage was done.

Tuesday, owing to the absence of wind was the most oppressive day the inhabitants of Medora have ever experienced. Until half past two the sun itself fairly sweltered. Then a rain storm accompanied by hail set in and in half an hour lowered the temperature to seventy-one, a decrease of twenty-nine degrees.

W. T. Ingersoll, the best photographer in St. Paul went through Medora with the St. Paul jobbers, on his way to the National Park. He will remain there about five weeks and on his return will stop off at Medora provided enough work is guaranteed him to pay expenses. He will then take a number of views of the Bad Lands which our citizens and others are anxious to secure.

Ed. Drury, deputy-sheriff of Morton Co., came up Monday evening and served an attachment on the Cantonment property. The attachment was issued at the instance of Bellows & Co., of Mandan. It is difficult to determine the effect of Commodore Gorringe's death on this property, especially as the original title to the property is in dispute. The matter will probably be straightened out at the coming term of court in Morton county.

"Do you want a horoscope, I don't know."

The above was addressed to William, he of cold turkey fame. William, seated behind his dry-goods counter and being in the midst of a calculation as to how many cold turkeys at steen bits a piece it would take to satisfy the yearnings of an empty stomach such as his; said "naw."

The mouth and head from which had emanated the opening sentence was slowly withdrawing when William had a sudden thought and yelled: "Say, is them hoorahscopes good to eat."

The head popped suddenly forward, followed by a body and a pair of bandy legs and the same voice said: "No, my christian friend, they are not fit for the feast unless viewed from an allegorical or intellectual standpoint. Viewed thus they beat the mental pabulum of the immortal gods. A horoscope, my dear friend is a fortune-telling instrument that tells your lucky star and through this, your subsequent fortunes and misfortunes. What was your birthday?"

On being informed that it was the thirtieth of February, the horoscope fiend said:

"You were born under a lucky star. You will become wealthy and fat. You delight in hard work and love good things to eat. You must never gamble with your face toward the east. Always think of something pleasant, to eat for instance, when throwing dice and you will always be lucky."

"Well" said William, let's test this thing. I will face the east and bet you $5 I beat you a game of seven up."

This the horoscopist declined as also several other invitations of like nature, besides hints to the effect that talking was dry work.

Some of the boys meantime had been rigging up a pail of water over the door which accidentally fell on him as he started out after tripping flat on an invisible wire that had carelessly been stretched at just the right distance to have such an effect.

Monday the boys were going to have him up on a charge of heresy before Judge Gordon, but he had left the winsome Bad Lands far behind and was probably by that time working the inhabitants of Glendive.

The Mandan Pioneer, to further its scheme of division on the Missouri river, states in a recent article that the cattlemen are anxious to have the Territory divided and want it divided on the river. We have been at considerable pains to learn the sentiment among stockmen and find that the opposite opinion is almost unanimous. As business men, they look at the proposition from a business point of view and can scarcely see the object of doubling expenses without a corresponding benefit. In this case, there is absolutely no benefit whatever to be gained, but in case the western part should be admitted, the expense of running a state government would be more than double what it would be if the Territory were admitted as a whole. This is not only the sentiment of the people here, but that of nine-tenths of the people of all Dakota, "Admission without division." It can be put down as an axiom that every man or paper crying for division has an axe to grind. Of course it is manifest that in case this division is made, the Pioneer expects Mandan to become the capital of western Dakota. In this, it is greatly mistaken. The capital location, as here-to-fore, will be a matter of bargain and sale. In that event, there will be other towns, for instance the terminus of a railroad in the Black Hills, which can easily put up ten dollars to Mandan's one. In any event, western Dakota is not and for many years will not be able to support a state government. And now, will the Pioneer or any other axe-grinding division paper tell us a few good reasons why Dakota should be divided at all? Why not make it one magnificent state that will stand among the first of her sister states, instead of two states, neither of which can expect to occupy higher than a middle position?

A revision of Webster's dictionary is now being made and will be published some time during the year. In looking through the pages of a late edition, we found scarcely one of the words referring to the cattle business and in common use here. We wrote to this effect to the revisers and received a pressing invitation to gather together a complete collection of cowboy and other western words to be published in the next issue of the dictionary. We do not claim perfection in any way for the following list. We publish it for the purpose of having additions and corrections made. A few words have been left out because their proper definition is already given, but it by no means indicates that if a word is lacking that we do not want it. The very commonest words are the ones most likely to be missed altogether. If a number of persons will send us in additions and corrections we can be moderately sure of a full list. Our list extends through the "O's" this issue and will be concluded in our next.

A

Aparejos, n. (Definition wanted.)

B

Brand, n. (cattle.) A mark burned or cut on an animal, signifying ownership.

Brand, v. t. (cattle.) To burn or cut a mark on an animal.

Brand-book, n. A book containing all recorded brands of an association or district.

Branding-chute, n. A narrow enclosure, wide enough for the passage of a single animal, where it may be held convenient for branding.

Branding-iron, n. A metal device usually made of iron, which, when heated and pressed against an animal forms the brand.

Break, v. t. To accustom to the saddle or harness. To break a horse. Syn. To train.

Brow-band, n. The part of a bridle passing over the brow of a horse and holding the throat-latch and cheek-straps in place.

Buck, v. i. A violent jumping by a horse, stiff-legged, forward or side-wise up and down. Confined to western horses.

Bucker, n. A horse that bucks.

Buck-strap, n. A strap secured to the saddle to enable the rider to keep his seat on a bucking horse.

Broncho, n. (Bronko.) [Derivation unknown.] An unbroken western horse.

Bed-ground, n. The place used to hold cattle at night.

Bridle-wise, adj. Referring to a quality of being guided by a bridle.

Buffalo-trail, n. A path worn by buffaloes.

Buffalo-wallow, n. A bowl shaped hole worn into the ground by buffaloes while rolling.

Buffalo-berry, n. A berry growing on bushes, something like the whortleberry, peculiar to the northwest.

Bull-berry, n. See buffalo-berry.

Bull-whacker, n. A man who drives oxen.

Bunch, n. A small herd of cattle.

Bunch-grass, n. A very nutritious kind of grass, about six inches high, growing on western prairies. It is the principal feed for stock in the west.

Buzzard-head, n. A lazy or useless horse.

C

Cabello (cavayard), n. The bunch of cattle following the round-up, or belonging to private persons.

Cache (cash), v. t. To hide.

Cache (cash), n. The place where a thing is hidden.

Camp-rustler, n. A ranch cook.

Cabalo (cavi-ya), n. A horse.

California-bit, n. A spade-bit having an iron curb.

Cavejo, (Definition wanted).

Cayuse (ki-use), n. 1. Indian pony. 2. Derogatory name for a horse.

Chapparal, n. Thick under-brush.

Chapparejo, (always contractedand pronounced "shaps"). Leathern pants used by cow-boys to protect their legs from wet, cold and under-brush.

Cheek-straps, n. Straps of a bridle passing over the head of a horse down his cheeks and holding the bit in the mouth.

Chute, n. See branding-chute.

Cincha (always pronounced "sinch"), n. A strap or web belt passing under the horse's belly holdihg the saddle in place. There may be one or two cinches. An expression of superiority. "I have the cinch on him."

Close-herd, v. t. To keep a bunch of cattle together and prevent them from wandering.

Concha, n. Silver or metal ornaments in the shape of buttons worn on the outside of a spur.

Corona, n. A fancy cover for a saddle-blanket.

Corrall, n. An enclosure made of logs, rails or boards in which to keep cattle or horses.

Coulie or coulee, n. A small ravine, usually having at the bottom, the bed of a dry creek, lined with under-brush.

Counter-brand, v. t. To repeat the original brand immediately under the original.

Counter-brand, n. A repetition of the original brand on an animal, signifying that the animal is sold to some one other than the owner of the original brand.

Couresta, n. A hempen rope.

Cource, n. Leather cover for half-breed saddle.

Cow-boy, n. A person hired to take care of range cattle.

Cow-camp, n. A cattle-ranch.

Cow-girl, n. Feminine of cow-boy.

Cow-man, n. An owner of cattle.

Cow-puncher, n. See cow-boy.

Crease, v. t. To shoot a wild animal especially a horse, in the neck, over the spinal column, stunning him temporarily, for the purpose of catching him.

Cricket-bit, n. A peculiar kind of cow-boy bridle-bit having a grooved wheel, which, rolling on the horse's tongue, gives rise to the name.

Cutting-horse, n. A horse used to cut out cattle from a herd.

Cut-out, v. t. To separate from a herd a [particular?] animal or animals wanted.

Crop, v. t. To cut off the end of an animals ear. An ear-mark signifying ownership.

Crop, n. An ear-mark on an animal made by cutting the end of the ear square off.

D

Doga, n. A motherless calf.

Dewlap, n. A cut on the lower part of the neck of an animal by which a piece of skin is detached, holding by the end. It has the same significance of ownership as a brand or ear-mark.

Day-herd, n. A herd of cattle held and grazed during the day.

Double-cinch, adj. Referring to a saddle having two cinchas.

Double-rig, adj. See double-cinch.

Drags, n. The footsore and weary cattle on a drive which fall to the rear.

Draw, n. See coulie.

Dug-out, n. A kind of house built by digging into the side of a hill.

E

Ear-mark, n. A cutting or slitting of ear or ears of cattle to signify ownership.

G

Gag-bit, n. General name for all bits except snaffle and straight bits. A bit that will force the horse to open his mouth.

Grade, adj. Referring to improved cattle, viz. those having any proportion of pure blood.

Grass-cattle, n. Those living and fattening on grass alone. In general, all range cattle.

Grass-rope, n. A hempen rope.

Greaser, n. A Mexican having negro, Indian and white blood in his veins.

Grub, n. An ear-mark made by cutting the ear square off at the roots.

H

Hackamore, n. A head-gear for horses used for the same purpose as a bridle. It is usually made of horse-hair.

Half-breed-bit, n. A peculiar kind of gag-bit used by cow-boys.

Half-breed-cow, n. A cross between a Texas cow and a blooded bull.

Half-breed-horse, n. A cross between a wild mare and thoroughbred stallion.

Half-breed-saddle, n. A saddle having a Texas tree and a California rig.

Hat-string, n. Strings, usually of leather, worn by cow-boys, to keep their sombreros on.

Head, v. To ride against or in front of an animal, turning it in the direction wanted.

Heel, v. To throw the lariat in such a way as to catch the hind leg or legs of an animal to throw it down.

Horn, n. The front part of a saddle. The pommel.

Horse-wrangler, n. The man who takes care of a bunch of cow-horses in the daytime.

J

Jinglebob, n. A slitting of the ear of an animal in such a way that the end of the ear lops down. It is a mark signifying ownership.

L

Latigo-straps, n. The straps connecting the cinchas with the saddle.

Legadero, (definition wanted).

Line-riding, v. The act of riding back and forth over certain territory to keep cattle within specified limits.

Loco, n. A weed poisonous to stock.

Loco, v. To poison animals with loco weed, making them crazy.

M

Maverick, n. Any unbranded neat animal not following its mother. Term originated from a man named Maverick who turned loose a lot of unbranded cattle in Texas and then began branding everything with no brand on.

McCarty, n. A hair rope fastened to a hackamore.

Milling, v. Cattle in act of running around in a close circle.

Mule-skinner, n. A man who drives a mule team in a freight outfit.

N

Night-herd, v. To take care of animals at night.

O

Outfit, n. In cattle parlance, usually meaning; the herd, ranch &c.

Over-bit, n. A v-shaped cut in the top of the ear. An ear-mark signifying ownership.

Over-hack, n. A straight cut in the top of the ear. An ear-mark signifying ownership.

Over-half-crop, n. An ear-mark, signifying ownership, by which the outer and upper half of the ear is cut away.

Over-slope, n. An ear-mark, signifying ownership, by which the top part of the ear is cut away from the middle to the point.

Sheriff Harmon, of Morton county, was in Medora this morning, impanelling jurors for the district court.
The bridges on Sully creek have all or nearly all been washed out. They should be repaired immediately.
B. F. Lamb has completed a fine ranch building four miles down the river and in the spring will stock his range with a good lot of cattle.

Geo. Wilkes severed his connection with the company last week and went to his home in Chicago. His resignation was due to a conflict of authority and reflects in no way upon his ability as an engineer, of which there is no question. His Chicago address is 190 Campbell avenue.
A very pleasant house-warming took place in Joe Ferris' store Tuesday night. All enjoyed themselves thoroughly tripping the "light fantastic."
The rink is being refurnished in good shape and its appearance is consequently much improved. Bob. Roberts will move in as soon as it is finished.
Between grass-hoppers and its being an off year, Montana will be short on hay this year. It is well that there is such an abudant crop in Dakota.
Word comes in a rather round-about way that Wilmot Dow, one of the managers of the Elkhorn ranch was married last week in Maine. We commiserate.
B. F. Reynolds and J. C. Fisher started Tuesday on a trip down the river, to or below the mouth of Beaver. Mr. Reynolds is looking up a range for his cattle.
The middle Grand stage station has been burned and others are likely to go. Mr. Paddock, on his recent trip extinguished the fire from one that was just catching.

A hard hail-storm visited Medora last evening. If it had been accompanied by wind doubtless much loss would have resulted. As it was, the gardens probably suffered severely and a number of window lights were broken.

Five hundred Hashknife cattle were weighed out to the Co. Aug. 1. They averaged 1064½ pounds. Three of them weighed 4980 pounds and one weighed 1950 pounds. The last only dressed 1116 pounds, showing he was not in good condition.

Last night No. 1 consisted of fourteen cars and two engines, probably the largest passenger train ever seen on the road. Several of the cars were filled with Boston excursionists and the air was positively oppressive from the vast amount of "culchah" lying around in chuncks.

We wish to call special attention of all to cur "cow-boy Dictionary." As stated, we do not claim perfection in any way for it. It is published principally to have corrections made to it. All should take pride in making it as complete as possible by sending or handing us corrections.

The two-year-old daughter of J. A. Freeze, died at about seven o'clock last evening. She will be buried at five o'clock this afternoon on the coal mine butte. Our citizens sympathize deeply with Mr. and Mrs. Freeze, as the child was a general favorite.

The two-year-old daughter of J. A. Freeze died at seven o'clock last evening of cholera infantum. The funeral services, led by T. W. Gordon, will take place at five o'clock, on the coal-mine butte. Our citizens sympathize deeply with Mr. and Mrs. Freeze in their loss, as the child was a general favorite.

A number of changes have been made in the running of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., chief of which are the renting of all the cold-storage houses to outside parties. The local business along the line is to be discontinued as it pays better to wholesale. The Marquis is still in the east making the necessary changes.

The two horse-thieves who have made Medora three visits and known as the "Two Jacks," have been captured at Mitchell. It will be remembered that about four months ago they were here and sold a team of horses to E. G. Paddock, which were afterwards reclaimed. The capture of these two ends the career of about all the horse-rustlers in this country.

To look at Fred Willard one would not think him such a guileless youth. Attempting to cross Sully creek lately he found it was swimming and then turned carefully up the bank so as not to discourage any future comers from attempting to cross by seeing where the horse had turned around. His Honor Cole coming along behind and thinking where man had crossed before, there he could cross, plunged boldly in. That is the reason Cole is wearing a clean shirt.

Mr. L. C. Magee and wife and F. M. Magee, all of Pittsburgh, arrived Monday night for a visit to the Eaton's. They have gone to the logging camp and before they leave will visit the VI ranch.

Frank Axthelm, who has been running Fred Banan's barber shop for the last two months will leave next Tuesday. Banan, having completed his service in the army, will return to take permanent possession of his shop.

Howard Eaton and a companion killed an elk last week on Magpie creek, the first one that has been killed near here for some time. It was a fine fat cow elk and the VI outfit have been picking fat from their teeth ever since.

Tommy Smith came in Monday from the E6 ranch. He reports that there will be about 4,000 steers shipped from this range during the next month or two. Messrs. Clark & Plum have between 50,000 and 75,000 cattle in the Indian Territory and will probably drive a large number of these to their E6 ranch next year.

Attention is called to the change in the N. P. time-table, which went into effect last Sunday. West bound express freight No. 13, has been changed to 8:59 p. m., instead of 5:00 a. m. Eastbound passenger No. 2, now arrives at 8:36 a. m., a change of seven minutes and east bound freight No. 16 arrives at 1:50 a. m. instead of 1:45 p. m.

The round-up which has been working the country between the bend of the Little Missouri and the railroad and the Big Missouri and the Bad Lands, finished its work last week. The outfits represented were the Hashknife, VI, 777, OX, SOHO, Maltese cross, Elkhorn and others. The whole country was thoroughly worked, but the only animals found were nine belonging to the OX outfit.

E. G. Paddock returned Monday night from his Black Hills trip, accompanied by Mrs. Fred Willard and baby and John Ryan, of Spearfish. All the creeks, especially at this end of the line were swimming and some of them were only crossed with great difficulty. The abundant rains had caused millions of mosquitos to appear, making the trip extremely disagreeable. Mrs. Willard and baby stood the trip remarkably well.

A cow-boy named James Boyd was killed about two weeks ago on O'Fallon creek. He was working for the "Capital B" outfit, whose ranch is on the Sandstone. When last seen alive, he had just turned over a bunch of cattle to a brother cow-boy. The horse he was on was not very bridle-wise and it is supposed that he fell over a bluff with Boyd into O'Fallon creek. The body was found about three days after the fatal accident. Boyd was a first-class cow-boy and all who knew him, deeply mourn his loss as he seemed to have no enemies whatever.
The President's foot is down and as he wears a No. 14 brogan, the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservation cattlemen must stand from under or get hurt.

As will be seen by our market report, the prices on Texas cattle have risen twenty-five cents and shipping and dressed beef cattle have risen ten to fifteen cents. Montana cattle sold at $4.75 and Oregon cattle at $4.85.

Several train-loads of cattle have gone east during the week. We wish we were in a position to protest to some purpose to the shipping of some of the cattle. The most of them were in fair to good condition, but every car-load was disfigured by scalawags that there was no profit whatever in shipping. They would certainly bring down the price of the bunch more than they are worth.

The only resource for the Indian lease cattlemen to get rid of their catile is to send them to market. This will have to be done with at least 200,000 head. It behooves our cowmen to watch this narrowly, as the putting on the market of this immense number of cattle inside of thirty days, will bring the price way down. Dakota and Montana cattle striking the market at that time will suffer seriously in the general depression.

The Colorado brand law is now in force. It possesses many good points that should be embodied in a statute that can easily be passed at the next session of the Dakota legislature. The Colorado law provides that the state brand-book shall be in the possession of the secretary of state. Every person or corporation owning live stock in the state by August 1, must have forwarded his or their brands to the secretary. After Aug. 1, any new brand must be forwarded to the secretary who will record the same provided it is not already recorded. The secretary will forward to the owner a certified copy of the record, when the brand shall also be recorded in the offices of the clerk or recorder of the county or counties in which the stock will range. It shall be unlawful for any county officer to record a brand not authorized by the secretary of state. The brand, properly recorded, becomes personal property and can be sold or traded as such. The secretary of state must publish the state brand-book ninety days after Aug. 1, for general distribution.

A number of persons have lately spoken to us and in fact the burden of the conversation seems to be the advisability of organizing the county. This is by no means confined to Medora alone, but at least half the stockmen in the county have voluntarily expressed their wish that the county be organized provided it does not cost an unreasonable amount.

In conversation with sheriff Harmon, of Morton Co., our eyes were opened on the subject of expenses. The actual running expenses of a county are about as follows: $300 each to the recorder and treasurer, $150 to the county attorney, $100 to the assesor, and $3 each per day to the commissioners while in actual session. The sheriff's fees will surely fall short of $1,000. This will make the running expenses of the county not over $2,000. In addition to this, a good set of county books will cost about $1,2[00?] and rent of buildings for county offices, say $600. This will make the expenses for the first year in the neighborhood of $4,000. Of this amount, at least $3,600 and perhaps more will be obtained from the railroad, leaving less than $400 to be raised from the county.

Is there a man in the county after this showing, who does not want to organize? More than this, if we organize before the tax is collected by Stark Co., we do not need to pay a cent to that county. Sheriff Harmon says that this fact is proved beyond a doubt.

Even if the organization cost the people of Billings Co., $4,000 instead of $400 we think there would be no unwillingness to organize.

With official power a hundred and fifty miles away, life and property are not safe. Who would object to paying his share of $400 or even $4,000 to secure protection?

An easy problem for each to solve is to figure the total assessable property at $500,000. Then say even $4,000 had to be raised. This would equal a tax of eight mills. Now figure yonr share and see if protection to life and property is not worth the price. After figuring your share of $4,000, consider that the tax is liable to be only one-tenth of that original amount and see if it is profitable to be at the mercy of any drunken ruffian who wants to paint the town red.

All the above figuring does not include the subject of licenses. Medora is now paying Morton Co. $1,200 per yeer for license tax. This amount will pay all the school and road expenses of the county.

To conclude, we think that there is scarcely anyone in the county opposed to organization. All it rednires is a little effort in getting the signatures and the thing is done. We have sworn off on plans for organization and propose to let others "run the masheen." We do not ask for nor want any office whatever but propose to be entirely free to criticize any move we see fit.

Stockmen should see that it is for their interest and themselves start the ball rolling.

Our first issue of the cow-boy dictionary attracted much attention and a large number took enough interest in it to offer additions and corrections. Our thanks in this direction are especially due to C. R. Kelsey, of Glendive and Rassie Deffebach. We hope that as much interest will be felt in this issue, and corrections and additions sent or handed us as before. Our next issue will contain an addenda, with all the corrections and additions handed us.

P

Paunch, v. t. To shoot through the paunch any cattle that are hard to drive. It sickens them temporarily and makes them docile.

Pen, v. t. To drive animals into a corrall or enclosure,

Picket-pin, n. An iron or wooden stake driven into the ground to hold a horse, tied to it with a rope.

Picket-rope, n. A rope used to tie up horses.

Pilgrim, n. Referring to cattle, means an animal new to a country. A tenderfoot.

Pinto, adj. An animal spotted with large white and bay spots. A calico-horse.

Pitch, v.t. See buck.

Q

Quarter-breed, n. A man or animal having one-fourth white or pure blood.

Quirt, n. A short cow-boy whip usually with loaded handle and two leather thongs for lashes.

R

Ranch, n. A cow-camp dwelling-house.

Ranch-brand, n. A brand used on animals after they are on the owner's range.

Range, n. The territory over which cattle graze.

Range-cattle, n. See grass-cattle.

Range-riding, v. t. To ride over the range, looking after the welfare of cattle.

Reata, n. A rawhide lasso.

Remoutha, n. A bunch of saddle horses.

Riding-circle, v. t. To ride on the out-skirts of a round-up party driving all cattle into the round-up bunch.

Rig, adj. Denoting the kind. Generally used with reference to saddles. Ex. Double-rigged saddle, meaning double-cinch saddle.

Ring-bit, n. A cow-boy bridle-bit with ring extending entirely around the lower jaw.

Rope, n. General word for lasso, reata, couresta, grass-rope &c.

Round-up, v. t. The act of driving all animals in a district into a bunch or bunches, for purposes of branding, reclaiming, or shipping.

Round-up, adj. Referring to the party or outfit on a cattle-gathering expedition.

Running-brand, n. A brand made with a running iron.

Running-iron, n. A branding-iron consisting of an iron rod with a bend in the end like a fish-hook.

Rustle, v. i. To be wide awake to opportunities of advancement.

Rustle, v. t. To steal.

Rustler, n. 1. A wide-awake energetic man. 2. A thief, usually a horse-thief.

S

Saddle-iron, n. Short branding-iron to be carried on the saddle.

Shack, n. 1. A horse's gait, between a walk and a trot. 2. A cheap western dwelling.

Single-foot, n. A horse's gait, resembling pacing or racking, except that one foot is placed on the ground at a time.

Slicker, n. A water-proof coat, made of strong porous cloth, saturated with oil.

Sombrero, n. A light-colored, broad-brimmed, cow-boy hat.

Spade-bit, n. A cow-boy bridle bit, with a spade-like extension of the bit toward the throat.

Split, n. An ear-mark signifying ownership, made by cutting the ear from the middle to the tip.

Squaw-trot, n. Slow run. Favorite gait of Indians and hunters.

Stock-inspector, n. An officer appointed by a cattlemen's association, to oversee all sales of cattle, with authority to rectify any illegal proceedings.

String, n. The bunch of horses ridden by one man.

String-team, n. Horses or mules hitched in pairs, one after another. Sometimes there are thirty or more animals hitched in this way.

Swallow-fork, n. An ear-mark signifying ownership, made by cutting a v-shaped piece from the ear, the apex being in the middle of the ear and the ends at the tip.

T

Tailing, v. t. Throwing down cattle by the tail, after being lassoed and heeled. Holding cattle down when thrown, by pulling on the tail passed between the animal's hind legs.

Tapideros, n. Leather coverings for stirrups, used by cow-boys for protection to the feet.

Tenderfoot, n. A stranger, ignorant of western ways.

Tepee, n. An Indian lodge, made of poles and skin or bark.

Texas-fever, n. A kind of disease, insufficiently diagnosed, which southern Texas cattle communicate to other cattle, usually terminating fatally. The disease is contagious but harmless to the southern Texas cattle themselves. The disease is often called splenetic fever.

Texas-trail, n. The trail made and used by Texas cattle being driven to the northern ranges.

Thorough-bred, adj. Referring to a horse descended from pure Arabian animals.

Throat-latch, n. The strap extending around the neck to keep the bridle in place.

Through-cattle, n. Cattle driven from one range to another a long distance away. Usually referring to Texas cattle driven to northern ranges.

Trail, v. t. To drive cattle over a trail, usually referring to the Texas trail.

Trail, n. A path worn by men or animals.

Trail-brand, n. A brand used on animals while on the trail.

Trail-cattle, n. Cattle driven over a trail, usually referring to the Texas trail.

Trail-cinch, n. The hind cincha on a saddle.

Trail-herd, n. See trail-cattle.

Travois, n. A kind of vehicle made by strapping the ends of two poles to the sides of a horse and allowing the ends to drag on the ground. Burdens of all kinds are strapped on the poles.

Tree, n. The frame-work of a saddle.

U

Under-bit, n. An ear-mark on cattle, signifying ownership, made by cutting out a v-shaped piece from the under side of the ear.

Under-hack, n. An ear-mark on cattle, signifying ownership, made by a slit from the middle to the bottom part of the ear.

Under-half-crop, n. An ear-mark on cattle, signifying ownership, made by cutting away the bottom outside half of the ear.

Under-slope, n. An ear-mark on cattle, signifying ownership, made by cutting away a portion of the ear from the under side to the tip.

V

Vaquero, n. (pronounced "boccario"). A California cow-boy.

Vint, n. A brand signifying that an animal has been sold.

W

War-bag, n. A cow-boy's Saratoga trunk. The bag in which he carries his extra clothes &c.

Wash-out, n. A gully worn in the ground by water from rains or melted snow.

Wrangle-footed, adj. A horse's gait. A mixture of several gaits.

Wrangler, n. See horse-wrangler.

Wm. Van Driesche returned Tuesday morning from the hunting trip in the Big Horn. The Marquise and party are coming more slowly and will be in Medora in a day or two. The party hunted on the west side of the Big Horn, on the Meteetse river, not going into the Big Horn range. The hunting was good but would have been much better had they gone into the mountains. A number of bear were killed, the Marquise getting an old bear and two cubs and William securing a fine silver-tip. Elk were not very numerous nor were mountain sheep. Antelope and small game were very plentiful. Mountain trout abounded in every stream, averaging from one to three pounds. Other parties that had gone into the mountains reported large numbers of bear, elk and mountain sheep. The Marquise delayed a day or two in hopes that she might get a mountain sheep. Vic and Frank Smith expect to start on another hunting expedition immediately, probably going into the Big Horn M't's. Tommy Skinner and Sweet will return to Medora with the stock. Altogether the trip according to William, was one extremely full of pleasure.

Monday morning our citizens were startled by the news that Peter Birch had been shot. As luck would have it Dr. Robarts happened to come in on the east-bound train and, taking charge of the case, found that the ball had gone through the biceps muscle, entered his side under his arm and going around under the skin to within an inch and a half of the backbone, where it emerged. The account as told by Peter, was as follows, the other participators in the affair having gone to Mandan as witnesses at court, only his side can be learned. Peter states that at about half past twelve o'clock Monday morning he was in Bob. Roberts' saloon, in company with Roberts and Wm. Jones. That Roberts suggested playing a joke on some one in MacDonald's restaurant by cutting down the hammock in which he was sleeping. Peter started with Bob to the restaurant and the hammock was cut down. Bob asked Peter to take the knife back to the saloon and Peter started back in company with Jones. The latter asked Peter who was running the restaurant now and Peter told him that he had been cooking there for about a week. This led to what Peter thought was playful banter when Jones struck him on the forehead with the but of his revolver. His eyes were blinded with blood but he attempted to ward off other blows, when Jones shot. Attempting then to run, he was struck several more times on the back of the head, there being eight gashes extending to the skull. Peter did not know he was shot until the morning when he found his arm covered with blood and examining it, found he was shot. He further added that he was perfectly sober, only having two drinks early in the evening. This is one side of the case and we will gladly publish the other. We have few comments to make, as there were no witnesses. Both men have reputations for peaceable dispositions. Jones is well liked and every one is anxious to hear his side of the story. Peter is as harmless a man as ever lived, he being his own worst enemy. The principal point we make is the one so often mentioned in the COW BOY, that of carrying revolvers in town. Every shooting affray we know of has been caused by whiskey, coupled with the senseless custom of "packing a gun." We have many times mentioned our opinion and cannot sufficiently condemn a practice that no one can say has ever resulted in good and many times results fatally.

[Since writing the above, Sheriff Harmon arrived in Medora with a warrant for the arrest of Peter Birch. Probably for assault and battery. Jones was arrested at Mandan and released on his own recognizance. Sheriff Harmon returned this morning to Mandan. Birch was unable to be moved.]

A mistake has certainly been made in not holding a meeting of the Little Missouri Stockgrowers' association before the semi-annual meeting of the Montana association at Helena, which begins Aug. 25. The stockmen of the Little Missouri are almost all members of the Montana association, paying just as much in proportion toward the expenses of that association as the cowmen of Montana. For this, the only return they have received is the appointment of an inspector at Medora, and this was secured only after considerable wrangling. Nothing whatever could have been secured and nothing will be secured for Dakota cowmen except by authorized representatives of the Little Missouri association. If any of our cattlemen now go to Helena they will go simply as members of the Montana association, not authorized in any way to speak for Dakota. A moment's thought will show that this is all wrong. We should have authorized representatives ready and willing to demand what we need from the Montana association. The great difficulty our cowmen have to contend with is that we are considered a mere side issue by the Montana association, a good point from which to raise money but a poor one on which to spend it. For this reason our stockmen must be on the alert to gain all the advantage possible from the Montana association, and a lack of authorized representation is not the way to do this. It cannot be urged against a meeting of the Little Missouri association that it is too early. To send delegates from our association is a sufficient cause for calling a meeting, the cowmen at this time are not unusually busy and all arrangements could have been made a month ago for the beef round-up.

Joe Ferris has received a full line of powder, shot and rifle cartridges, and is prepared to meet all demands in that direction. A stock of nails has also been added and prices will bear comparison with anyone's.

The train-load of tea that passed through Medora last Wednesday evening reached New York in eight days and four hours from Tacoma, making the run of 3,378 miles in the fastest time ever made by a freight train from ocean to ocean.

The two best saddles and outfits on the river arrived Tuesday. One was for Theodore Roosevelt's own use and the other was a present by him to George Myers, a Chimney Butte cowboy. Silver conchas adorn the bits and spurs and on the latter are raised Maltese Cross and Elkhorn brands in solid gold. The outfits cost about $300 in Cheyenne.

Earl, infant son of J. D. Garver, died Sunday night of cholera infantum, after a sickness of only five or six hours. The funeral took place Monday afternoon from the home of the bereaved parents. Appropriate remarks were made by J. C. Fisher and T. W. Gordon, at the house and on Cemetery butte, where the burial took place. The parents wish to express their sincere thanks to all for their kindness during and after the funeral.

John Munro and Anne Brophy were married yesterday morning at the Catholic church, by Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan. The couple made a fine appearance and both looked their best. John and Annie are both general favorites here and the only possible objection to the union is that it did not occur some time ago. John Goodall and Mary Brophy were groomsman and bridesmaid
and they bore up well under the honors of the occasion. A tasty wedding-lunch was served at the Northern Pacific to all who called on the happy couple. Mr. and Mrs. Munro left on the evening train for Miles City on a bridal tour. They will return next Tuesday or Wednesday. A wedding ball is an event of the near future. The best wishes of the whole community follow the newly married couple and here's an old shoe from the Cow Boy for their future prosperity and happiness.

A letter from Vic Smith, written at Billings, gives some further particulars relative to the hunting party. On the third day of the trip, Vic was prostrated with mountain fever and the same morning Mrs. DeMores and he killed four bear, she killing three, and Vic killing one near the camp-fire. Vic was sick five days and on the sixth, the Marquise and he went higher up into the mountains and killed a fine bear apiece, making six in all, besides which, William VanDriesche killed a handsome silver-tip. Elk, antelope and sheep were numerous. Brook trout was the staple food. The nights on the mountains were so cold that it was necessary to keep large log fires constantly burning. The Marquise was "loaded for bar" and would hunt nothing else. Seventeen were seen in all. Vic characterizes the Marquise as "an excellent shot and fearless as a cowboy." Miss Sophia, who accompanied the Marquise, comes in for a share of praise for her Tapley-like quality of being always pleasant under difficulties. The party finished their hunt by a 185-mile ride across the country in four days. Vic and Frank will be gone about a month longer, they having a good engagement meantime.

ADDENDA.

The following words were omitted from our dictionary. With these additions the list is about full. Should anyone know additional words we hope they will hand them in within a week, as by that time we wish to send the list to the revisors of Webster's Dictionary.

A

Aparajo, n. A pack-saddle, consisting of a leather pad stuffed with hay or hair, to which the load is strapped.

B

Bridle-trail, n. A trail used by horsemen. Usually too narrow or dangerous for a wagon.

Broncho-breaker, n. A man who makes a trade of breaking bronchos. Also called broncho-buster.

C

Cavia, n. A mare.

Cavio, n. A horse.

Chinook, n. A warm winter wind from the west. Originating from the Japan current and felt in the west and northwest, generally raising the temperature to forty or sixty degrees above zero.

F

Flying-brand, n. A brand made by flaring or curving the extremities of the letters or characters.

H

Hondou, n. The slip-knot to a lariat. Usually made with raw-hide or a mountain sheep's horn or it may be a knot in the rope itself.

Horn, n. The top part of the pommel.

J

Jerk-neck-team, n. A team hitched to the hind end of a lead wagon. The lead team has a driver but the jerk-neck does not.

L

Lazy-brand, n. A brand having the letter or character lying down.

Legaderos, n. The straps holding the stirrups.

M

Mess-wagon, n. The round-up wagon, carrying the food and cooking outfit.

A Specimen Oregon Girl.

The women, says a Portland, Oregon, correspondent, are very expert horsewoemn. The writer recently approached a mansion situated on Poverty Flat and observed the daughter of the house in the front yard cinching a man's saddle on an Oregon horse that objected to this proceeding. She was about the age where "standing with reluctant feet, womanhood and childhood meet." I offered my assistance as she was hopping around on her right foot, her left foot in the stirrup, while she firmly grasped the bridle-bit in the left hand.

The cayuse, meanwhile, was making mad bounds, bellowing as only an Oregon horse can bellow, and standing first on his hind feet and then on his head. "No, thanks;" "I can manage him!" she said, and vaulted into the saddle, [not?] sidewise, but otherwise.

The instant the girl gained the saddle and the horse felt that she was there, down went his head, an arch sprung in his back, and away he went, jumping stiff-legged, over sage brush six feet high, until horse and rider disappeared in the distance. After a while she came back at a thundering gallop, and reined up at the door a trifle excited, but smiling.

"You sit your horse like a Centaur. Where are you going, Miss Oregon?"

"Over to the Bully Creek Sunday School. You bet your life I can set him straight up, and don't you forget it."

Of course no corn fed girl in the State could hope to do so well as this product of the bunch hills. But character goes for more than trivial incident, and of the gentler sex it must be said that here, as elsewhere, they teach in the Sabbath schools and are the shining lights that point out the way onward and upward to the weary and faltering feet of the sons of men.
A Range Rider on the Calf Crop.

Having been over a great deal of the cow country of southern Colorado in the saddle, this spring and summer, and having had similar trips for the last twenty-five years in Colorado in connection with the live-stock interests of the country, I can notice a big difference in the cattle breeding interests to what there was ten or fifteen years ago, and even five years ago. I have seen in different papers reports of the big calf crop, whereas my observation in the different round-ups and the different ranges I have been over, and the counts I have made of calves and of cows that were in calf and those that ought to have calves or be in calf, I say, Mr. Editor, that the calf crop is sadly short of what it should be and what it would be if the proper efforts were put forth by the owners and stock associations to remedy the causes responsible for this deficiency. The stock associations put me in mind of the old time peace commissioners that used to be sent out here to treat with the Indians. They would get the Indians together and have a big talk, and that ended the matter. The same is true with the associations; they know there is a deficiency, they know why they talk the matter over and perhaps they think will go right to work and remedy the evil, but they part and cool off, and time flies on, and before they realize it another year is gone and the same old complaint is more visible at the round-ups. The cow business as managed to-day is on the wane. The profits are less and the efforts put forth are less than they were years ago. One will see very few owners now with the round-ups, whereas years ago, the round-ups were composed principally of owners. They have dropped into the habit of sending out hired men and as few of them as possible. They gather up a bunch of cattle and drive them half a day; the calves all get back to the back end of the herd and seem thick and plenty, when if they would count the cows and heifers that comprise the bunch they would see those that had calves, those that were in calf and those that ought to have or be in calf; then the deficiency would be apparent, and would greatly modify the report of the calf crop. It is astonishing, really, the money that is being lost annually in Colorado in this one item of calves that are actually bred and what should be and might be bred if the proper efforts were put forth and the attention and appliances given to the business that should be. Men will keep an office in town and be there from early morn till late at night, knowing that to spend their time punching billiards will not pan out well in the fall, and put these same men into the cow business and they will seldom ever be seen in the saddle, and most of them will run the cow business on the plan the old woman did her hennery. Her theory was that the hens had to lay eggs any way and couldn't help themselves, but when she came to set eggs to raise broilers, she found herself left. Now I expect if this is published it will raise the ire of some; but pitch in, men, this thing needs stirring up. It took the shock of an earthquake to arouse old Rip Van Winkle; the breeders of cattle are asleep to their interests, and if it has to be an earthquake, let her come. I am ready.—[Cor. Colorado Live-Stock Review.

Editor Cow Boy:—
I would like to ask through the columns of the Cow Boy, what has become of our Board of Health?

There are certain parties who would like to have the Board see that other people clean up their yards and remove all filth that would prove injurious, but not to trouble them about the filth in their own yards.

Last spring there was a man in town who kept hogs. The Marquis went to him and told him he must either kill or sell them. That man told me that he had to dispose of them at a sacrifice.

Now, Mr. Editor, I would like to ask if there were hogs kept all over town and around it, would the stench be one-half as bad as that which we get from the offal that is carried away from the slaughter-house and left uncovered to taint the air and breed a pestilence among our citizens? It certainly would not cost much to have that pile covered up and not compel us to breathe air that is rotten.

Something should also be done about draining off the water which has been standing so long between the hotel and saloon. It is breeding malaria that is felt by all in the vicinity.

A Citizen.

Mack. and Mack's. wife and Pack. and Pack's. wife have just returned from one and know all about it.

The start was to have been made at five o'clock in the morning and contrary to agreement but according to prophecy the Cantonment was left behind at just nine o'clock. The road leads past Joe Knutson's Spring creek ranch, across the Big Plateau, where Gifford Bros. and John Munro are putting up a thousand tons of hay. From here to Wadsworth's, the home ranch of the Bad Lands Cattle Co., the road leads over a country that no one but a Bad Lands pioneer would have thought of crossing except in a balloon. At Wadsworth's "the gang" stopped for dinner and the way the fresh milk and butter-milk was encircled would have astonished anyone not acquainted with Bad Lands apetites.

The gang upon starting, were warned that some of the river crossings were full of quicksand. One of them proved to be all the fondest fancy could paint it. Going down a steep pitch into the river, the double-tree began parting as soon as the quicksand was struck. "Pack." said Mack., "the measly pajimmicle's going to bust." Just then it did "bust," and Pack. who was driving, thought he would be jerked over the outer battlements of the Hence before he could get the team stopped. Then the team began sinking and Mack. sprang into the Little Muddy to lead them out. First the man was on top and then the horses. But Mack. "stayed with the leather" and got safe on shore with the horses, leaving the buck-board in the middle of the river. It must have been lots of fun but "the gang" have only just begun appreciating it. The muddy waters gurgled their enjoyment of the hilarity and the quicksand in its appreciation of the festivities opened its hospitable maw in a way that threatened a complete swallowing up of the outfit.

A double-tree was finally rigged with a couple of cottonwood saplings and some lariats, the horses were duly argued with and made to see the necessity of "getting a gait on 'em" and the bed of the Little Missouri began moving up with the buck-board. The shore was at last reached safely and a rest was made while "the gang" ate a quart each of choke-cherries, warranted to pucker boiler plate with one application.

About four o'clock Mack's ranch was reached, Pack. meantime stopping off and killing a supply of chickens. Then began the pleasure of a camping-out trip. The sensation of not having an earthly thing to do except to enjoy one's self was fully appreciated.

Mack. and Pack. arose at four the next morning and started after some chickens. A covey was soon flushed and bang! bang! bang! bang! Not a bird dropped. Mack. glared at Pack. and Pack. glowered at Mack. Another covey was flushed and another fusillade was started. Same result. More glaring. Again was a covey flushed and again did all the birds sail away unharmed.

"Guess you haven't lost any chickens" said Mack.

"Guess you haven't enough advantage over me to swear by" said Pack.

Then the latter got out a cartridge, lifted a wad and found a choice collection of rags and paper where the shot ought to have been.

"Mack, you're a gay deceiver" said Pack: "and I've got a mind to mow a ton of hay with you."

But Mack. was rolling on the ground fairly screaming with mirth. At last he held in long enough to say:

"Well I'll be jiggerdy jammed if I didn't put that job up on Fisher and when he [petered?] on the procession and didn't come, I forgot all about them."

Then ensued a great laying together of heads and the solemn promise of each to the other that they would never give the thing away. And neither ever will if the court knows herself.

Two shells loaded with shot were found and with one Pack. wounded a chicken and then ran it down and clubbed it to death, while Mack. crawled up so close to a cotton-tail rabbit, that when the other went off it blew the rabbit's head clear over the outer battlements of the New Jerusalem as Mack. graphically expressed it.

Several plausible lies were concocted to tell the waiting wives, to account for the large number of shots and the small size of the game bag. But they somehow failed to hold water under the caustic remarks of the "t'othermost halves."

The next day was devoted to hunting specimens and a splendid collection of leaf impressions in rock was obtained.

On the following day an early start was made down the river. On the way a wild goose was killed and it was immediately agreed that when the gang returned to Medora the number should be raised to thirteen. In a calmer moment, however, and in spite of Mack's. cogent reasoning that no one would believe it anyway, the number was lowered to three. This number now stands on record and is quoted with authority.

At the side of the road, on a high plateau was found Tompkin's hay camp. As Tompkins expressed it, the assent was "a leetle sidlin'." Further comment than that, Mack. who was driving, dropped his whip and it fell out over the hind seat in the buck-board is unnecessary. This is not stated as a fact but Mack. thought it would be a good scheme to say it was. It might be well to add, as giving force to the statement that Mack. is considered perfectly truthful in all his statements, by strangers.

On the top of the plateau were found Mr. and Mrs. Tompkins camped very snugly in a tent. The plateau was cool and airy, bringing appetites that did full justice to the bountiful dinner spread by Mrs. Tompkins.

The next objective point was the Elkhorn ranch where a warm welcome was received at the hands of Messrs. Sewall & Dow and their wives. This ranch is probably the best one on the river, being 20x60 and built very substantially. It is situated in a beautiful grove of cottonwoods and will be made a hunting head-quarters by Theodore Roosevelt, the owner. Mrs. Sewall and Mrs. Dow are strangers to the Bad Lands, only having arrived lately, but they and their husbands fully understand the art of hospitality and "the gang" was made to feel at home immediately.

A pleasant drive back to Mack's. ranch in the evening was followed in the morning by an early start for town. A road through the buttes avoided the bad river crossings. This road leads through the heart of the Bad Lands Cattle Co's. range and showed as fine a looking lot of cattle as one can see anywhere. The calves especially were numerous and in fine condition. Arrived at Wadsworth's, Miss Birdie was found keeping house. Rich milk was handed around until the bottom of a gallon pail was reached. A fresh start was made, the next stop being at Joe Knutson's, where an ice-cold drink from his spring and a raw turnip each, rustled from his garden refreshed the travellers. They arrived home rather tired but with enlarged ideas of Bad Lands hospitality.

The range between Miles City and Glendive and as we are credibly informed, for a radius of fifty miles about Miles City and other parts of eastern Montana, clearly show the reason for the low price of cattle on the Chicago market. The range is absolutely bare in the places alluded to, owing to drought and grasshoppers. There is scarcely a ton of hay in sight all the way from Glendive to Miles, not enough in a place to even picket a horse. The Bad Lands stockmen can well congratulate themselves on having escaped both grasshoppers and drought and having hay to sell.

A discovery has recently been made that, if verified, will be received with joy by residents of our county. The line dividing Dakota and Montana has recently been surveyed, the report sent in to Washington, and the official decision returned to the surveyor. If no mistake has been made, the boundary line, instead of running just the other side of Sentinel Butte, runs several miles the other side of Mingusville. There may be some mistake, however, but this will be decided soon. The people of Mingusville are as well pleased as our people will be over this change in boundary lines and it is certainly to be hoped that the survey will stand.

The census enumeration of northern Dakota discloses the fact that of the fifty-eight counties enumerated, all but four have had their boundaries changed since 1880 and all but two of these since 1883. In some of these cases it was proper that the boundaries should be changed, but the history of four changes out of five is one of corruption and was the result of a deal in which personal gain and not public good was the end sought. The changes in the boundaries of Billings county for instance, although in spite of the schemers it is now a far better county than it was before, was the result of a deal, in which outside parties thought to derive a benefit. There has been but little, if any objection to our new boundaries, but that such a move could have been originated and carried to a successful issue without the consent and almost without the knowledge of the citizens of our county, is a very unfavorable comment on Dakota legislation.

The census returns are all completed as far as concerns northern Dakota and have been forwarded to Washington. From the returns, it appears that Cass county heads the list with 21,085 inhabitants. Grand Forks comes next with 20,453, while Burleigh county is ninth with 5,354. There are fifty-eight counties enumerated in the northern Dakota census. Billings county stands twenty-eighth in the list as concerns inhabitants, we having 737. In material wealth, we are not lower than tenth. In the fifty-eight counties enumerated, there is a total of 152,199 inhabitants, 32,503 farms and 612 manufactories. The returns from southern Dakota have not yet been sent in, but the principal footings are as follows: inhabitants, 263,465; farms, 50,264; manufactories, 442. The totals for the Territory are as follows: inhabitants, 415,664; farms, 82,767, manufactories, 1,054. For the above figures, we are indebted to the Bismarck Tribune.

The most profitable cattle to put in are two-year-olds at $20 each. These will net $30 when sold as three's. The net profit, according to the figures is then $50,000 in eighteen months on an original outlay of $100,000, exclusive of running expenses and loss. We would increase the running expenses at least $2.500 for incidentals and a manager. Five per cent. of loss would be about right, making $5,000. All the cattle could not be found at the end of eighteen months, but as four-year-olds, they would yield enough additional profit to pay all expenses of gathering. Our figures would then increase the total outlay to $20,085. This in turn, would be decreased by at least $2,500 from the sale of horses, wagons, etc., leaving a total outlay of $17,585, the net profit on the whole transaction being $32,415. The above figures may be modified somewhat, but good judges would be more apt to figure a larger profit than a less one on the deal.
