Our Chicago market report shows a lowering of prices all around, especially in grass-fed Texans and western range cattle, both dropping about fifty cents. Heavily increased arrivals of all classes of cattle was the cause of the depression. The arrivals of Texas and western cattle was 26,000 of which 17,000 were from Texas and about 4,000 from Dakota and Montana. Extra prime beeves were the only class to escape the general depression, they advancing ten to fifteen cents. The present outlook would seem to indicate that prices will be low for some time, as many cattle are now being sent to market that should stay on the range another year. There is also every chance that a large number will be marketed from the Indian Territory and this will result in another drop.

It was late in the afternoon when we rode up the steep and rocky path that led into the green valley where round-up 34 was camped. On the rich hillsides the horses of the different outfits were being bunched up by the day herders, and the odor of fried bacon was being wafted from the camp-fire where Eli was officiating as cook. Sam. Basset had fed his hungry gang and was putting away the supper things, and in a little while the boys were rolling up their beds and seeking a shelter from the storm that was coming up. After everyone had finished his supper, the different camps put in order and the night herders sent out, all the rest of the boys gathered in the cabin to spend the evening. The two flickering candles stuck in empty beer bottles, shone over a motley looking crowd. There were twenty or twenty-five of them, ranging in age from the "kid" of fourteen to the old "broncho buster" of fifty. "Give us some music, cookey," called out one of the boys throwing a mouth organ to Fred. Reynolds. Clearing out his mouth and filling himself up with wind, Fred. blew the music out of the mouth organ with the skill of a born musician, and was greeted with great applause. Then an old fiddle belonging to a sleepy Dutchman was brought out and a grand quadrille improvised. It was an inspiring sight to see Watts promenade across the floor with Rocky Mountain Bob as a partner, jab his spur into the knee of a spectator and back Skinny Dick over a saddle. Probably John Cassius Templeton, the Colorado cowboy, was the most limber-legged of all the artists, and he would have attracted attention even in a Boston drawing room. "Jumbo" also waltzed with the tender grace of a young elephant, though the rest of the boys
had to climb up on the table and chairs to make room for his feet. The more intricate steps of the Newport and racquet were executed by that young but shining ornament of society, Charley Mellor.

A song from Lee was the unanimous demand when the fiddler was finally exhausted. "I can't sing," protested Walter with the modesty of true merit, but the excuse would not go down and he finally sang one song. A wild tempest of applause rose from the assembly at the conclusion of this song and there was scarcely a dry eye in the crowd as the last tender strain died away. A clog dance and a song by Fred the cook was the next demand, and was filled with neatness and dispatch. The dance was performed to the music of the harmonica in the agile mouth of the triple-tongued Englishman. The music was fine, the dance excellent, and the song that fluttered out doors, wandered up over the mountain and drove the coyotes back into their holes, was as follows:

I am cook of the cowboy's camp,
A dancing, roving, musical tramp.
I can fry a slice of bacon to the achme of perfection,
And my latest batch of duff will bear the closest of inspection.
I can boil a pot of 'taters 'till they are in the right condition,
And can handle the harmonica just like an old musician.
A break-down, clog or hornpipe I can dance with great agility,
And dish you out a plate of beans with even more facility.
I grind a mess of coffee every morning with dexterity,
And get the breakfast ready with unusual celerity.

"But no body will get up in time if you don't all go to bed pretty soon," broke in Charley Rader the foreman. The hint was sufficient. Beds were unrolled and spread out on the floor. The disrobing process was completed by taking off boots, spurs, coats and hats, and in a short time nothing was heard but the steady snore of the cowboys, the
whinney of a strayed horse, or the dismal howl of a lonesome coyote on the mountain.

Sunrise in the mountains! Can we find language to describe the scene that met our view after we had scrambled through the mountain cedars, and over the rocks to the top of the hill overlooking the camp. The rain of the night before had cleared the air, and earth and sky were resplendent with all the colors of sunrise. In the white cups of the mountain lillies hung the glistening tears into which the clouds had dissolved themselves, and a million raindrops were sparkling like diamonds from sage brush and cedar. A thin veil of mist rested lightly upon the rounded crest of the mountain across the valley. Far beyond—away to the southwest rose the Uinta mountains against the blue horizon; rugged, snow-crowned, and shining like polished marble in the morning sun. Nature is wide awake; the long eared jack-rabbit bounds lightly over the sage brush, the little birds call to each other from among the twisted cedars, and two old sage hens—looking as large as turkeys—come from behind a clump of grease wood.

In the camp below, the horses are being corralled; Jumbo is showing how many times he can throw his lasso at the white faced roan without catching her, and Albert the Kid, is untying himself from the fence where he has been fastened for safety. Isam Dart, the negro broncho buster, takes a tumble to himself as his horse stumbles into a badger hole, and George Scrivner is left to tackle the bucking bronchos that nobody else cares to handle. Soon we are all on the move; the 300 magnificent horses that are in the outfits are driven up the valley to the new camping place, the well mounted cowboys follow and the white covered wagons bring up the rear.—[Rock Springs (Wyo.) Independent.

Joe Hampson, one of the leading cattle men of southern New Mexico, has drifted into literature, and the following aphorisms are the latest efforts of his facile pen:

It's a cold day when you can freeze the horns off a Galloway bull.

A cow on the range is worth three steers in southern Texas.

It's a wise maverick that knows its own owner.

The green cowboy fears not the bucking broncho.

Rev. Schaffner has been tried for assault and battery at Mandan and by this time the jury have returned a verdict though we do not as yet know what it is.
Mr. and Mrs. John Goodall wish to return their sincere thanks to the numerous friends who so kindly remembered them on their marriage day. They hope at some time to "play even" with each one of them.

Chas. Cook has on hand a fine lot of peaches and will receive this week, ten boxes of choice eating apples from Oregon, besides four boxes of Muscat grapes and two each of plums and pears. Treat yourself and friends to something good.

Theodore Roosevelt arrived Tuesday night and will stay until after the beef round-up. As president of the Little Missouri association, he issues a call for a meeting Sep. 5. The call will be found on our first page.

The Bad Lands cattle company will start on a beef round-up next Tuesday, beginning at Sentinel Butte, working Big and Little Beaver to their mouths, thence up the Little Missouri to the mouth of Garner. All wishing to join this round-up, will be at Sentinel Butte early Tuesday morning.

It is rather a surprise party to learn that E. G. Paddock has been indicted for murder in connection with the Marquis, for the killing of Luffsey. There is certainly no evidence against him and the case must be dismissed for lack of evidence. The only reasonable explanation is that Mr. Paddock is one of the principal witnesses for the defense and the prosecution hope in this way to weaken his evidence.

The report was current here for some time and is still generally believed, that Half-breed Jack was hung for horse-stealing by vigilantes in Montana last summer. He is now in jail at Miles City, having been captured with Muley Bob. They both plead guilty to horse-stealing and were sentenced to a year each in the county jail. W[m.?] Roberas is in jail at the same place and professes perfect ignorance of the charge against him. It seems that he was first arrested on the charge of murder, but it has now been changed to that of horse-stealing.

The cattle disease at Sentinel Butte is still unchecked. Only nine or ten head have died, but A. Osborne, who has a small bunch of cattle on Andrews creek states that the disease is contagious. In any event, something should be done immediately, as prevention is far better than cure in a case of this kind. We can scarcely explain the reason, but Fred. Willard, in writing for instructions as to how to act in this case, learned that there was no Dakota law in reference to contagious diseases. In this event, the work must be done by individual cowmen, and not by and by, but now.
MARRIED:—Wednesday, Aug. 26, at the Catholic church, in Medora, Dak., by the Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, Mary, eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. M. M. Coleman, to John Goodall, both of Medora.

The above notice will be read with more interest and pleasure than that of
any we could publish in these columns. It is seldom that one can say as in this case, "They had no acquaintances. All were friends." The happy couple were well known in Medora and vicinity and we merely voice the sentiment of the entire community in wishing them a long life and every earthly enjoyment. The marriage at the church was followed by a reception and wedding lunch in the parlor of the Northern Pacific. The bride never looked prettier and the groom took a pardonable pride in the congratulations showered upon him. In the evening, Mr. and Mrs. Goodall joined with Mr. and Mrs. Munro, the bride and groom of a week ago, in giving a party at the Northern Pacific, in which all joined with the expectation of having a good time and none were disappointed. A bountiful supper was served at twelve o'clock. The dancing was kept up until about one, when the company dispersed, having registered in their minds another social success for Medora. Mr. and Mrs. Goodall were the recipients of several useful and valuable presents. An elegant walnut, marble-topped chamber set and full toilet set came from "the Gang," Marquise de Mores gave a handsome lamp, T. Martin presented some fine table cutlery and a silver butter-dish and castor-set were the gifts of Miss Alice Morrison and Martin Timlin. The bridal couple will board at the Northern Pacific for a time, at least.

S. W. Russel, book-keeper of the Niobrara cattle Co., delivered four hundred of that Co's. cattle to the N. P. Ref. Car Co. last Thursday. They averaged 1298½ pounds.

L. A. Huffman, Miles City's photographer, has "struck a new lead" that is and will be profitable. It is in the shape of a series of forty instantaneous photographic views of prominent stock ranches and the most interesting events of a round-up. The views were all taken from the saddle and are startlingly realistic in their illustrations of cowboy life. We are under many obligations to Mr. Huffman for a full set of these views and wish him abundant success in selling them. Single copies are twen-
ty-five cents; per dozen, two dollars; and the full set of forty for five dollars. They will be mailed to any address on receipt of price by L. A. Huffman, Miles City, Montana.

The policy of patronizing home industries has lately received another argument in its favor in the matter of insurance rates. All rates are established by the companies, no choice being left to the agent. Among all companies, the rate charged on all classes of risks is nearly, if not exactly the same. The details differ somewhat in some companies accepting and others rejecting a class of risks, some will take a three-years risk at double the rate of a one-year risk while others will not, etc. In general, the charges are exactly alike. It will thus be seen that the local agent has every advantage over a visiting agent who must pay travelling and other expenses. An illustration of this arose recently where a travelling agent for an insurance company came here and quoted a $3 rate of $18 for insuring a risk of $600. The most that is asked by any company is a $1.75 rate or $10.50 for $600 insurance. To prove the matter conclusively, both rates were quoted by agents of the same company. The above is only an illustration of the broad principle, proved over and over again, that it is altogether better to patronize home industries wherever it is possible, thus increasing your neighbor's prosperity and consequently your own.

As the Mandan Pioneer says, there will be much difficulty in finding an intelligent jury in this district, none of whom have expressed an opinion in the case of the Territory vs. Marquis de Mores, for murder. In other states and territories a person indicted for this offense is not allowed to furnish bail, but the law passed at the last session of the legislature makes the offense bailable. The Marquis started west from New York yesterday and will probably be in Mandan in a day or two. We have already expressed our opinion and that of the
entire community in reference to bringing up this case again. Everyone wanted the matter to drop, except a few blood-sucking lawyers. The whole matter was adjusted as well as could be and the additional expense of the trial is entirely unwarranted. Eastern papers have been publishing such highly colored accounts of the affair, that for the benefit of those of our readers living there, it may be best to publish an outline of the case. In the summer and fall of 1883, a few months after the Marquis came here, he began fencing some land he had bought. Before he had finished the fencing, several persons expressed decided opinions concerning it, unless gates were left in the places where the roads ran. From this arose Frank O'Donald's remark about shooting the Marquis on sight. That he was drunk when he made it, no one who knows him can doubt. When drunk, he recognizes neither friend nor enemy, but wants to pick a quarrel with everyone. When sober, he is as peaceable as he is quarrelsome when drunk. O'Donald's remark was carried to the Marquis, who considering his life in danger, telegraphed to Mandan for officers. O'Donald was in Little Missouri when the sheriff arrived. He was drunk and defied the officer. Riding out of town with Luffsey and Wonegan, the Marquis and party were met and Luffsey was killed. Eastern papers have been fond of referring to Luffsey and Wonegan as desperadoes when the fact is they were quiet, peaceable hunters, who only happened to be with O'Donald and whose innocence there was, of course, no time to establish when the shooting began. The whole affair arose in misunderstanding [the?] true sentiment on both sides. Wonegan is now in Mandan to release his bondsmen in the present case, while O'Donald has left the country. As we said before, no one here wanted the case brought up again, it is a useless expense to the county and will serve no purpose except as a benefit to the lawyers employed.

The latest addition to our exchange list will indeed be a good one if it "keeps up its lick" and we see no reason why it should not. It is named the, "Hoof and Horn" and is published in Prescott, Arizona. We wish it every success.

The day after to-morrow, Saturday, Sep. 5, is the regular fall meeting of the Little Missouri association. That a full attendance is desired and expected, it is unnecessary to state. There is much business of importance that should come before the association and each should consult his own interest by being present.

The editor of the Mandan Times can do us a great favor if he will, and we sincerely hope that in the bigness of his generous heart, he will oblige us. The favor is, to pronounce the word "Medora" and see if it gags him. If it does not, we humbly request that when a circumstance does come up in which the word must be used to be correct, he will cease keeping our name from the hundreds of thousands of weekly readers whose mental pabulum is his "literary luminary of the Northwest," and allow us to enjoy the notoriety that a mere mention of our name in his l. l. o. t. N., would give us.

DIED.—We know not when, where or how, the Belfield Courier.

Thus has passed away from our midst a little babe of which it can truly be said: "None knew it but to love it." Its lovers consequently, were the editor and an eastern tenderfoot, who, in a moment of temporary aberration, subscribed for it. It always was a weak child, but it lived out the measure of its usefulness in the few months, prophesied by the COW BOY as the period of its earthly existence. Perhaps it couldn't stand the prosperity incident to its obtaining a new subscriber, or perhaps the $2 obtained from its previous subscriber would no longer pay expenses. In the words of a Michigan tombstone, "Let her R. I. P."

Granville Stewart is and always has been the friend of the cowboy, and his resolution at Helena should be written in letters of gold on parchment and given to him by the grateful cowboys of Dakota and Montana. The resolution passed at the Miles City convention, prohibiting any owner from employing a cowboy who owned stock branded with a separate brand from his employer's was a virtual death-blow to a cowboy's saving his money and put a premium on spending it for whiskey and gambling. Owing to Mr. Stewart's influence, this resolution was unanimously repealed and now the cowboy is encouraged to save his money and invest it in cattle.

The resolution of E. S. Newman, adopted by the Montana association, at Helena, will be as good as an insurance on stock, if Congress can be induced to act on it. We have many times advocated this plan in the COW BOY, of having the government appoint officers, whose duty shall be to look after diseased cattle and if the disease is found to be contagious, to have the animal killed and the owner reimbursed at government expense. In Germany, this plan works to perfection, two-thirds the value of the animal being returned to the owner. It is the only true way to check the spread of disease and we certainly hope to see the plan adopted.

The Glendive Times takes us to task for the article in our last issue in which we described the country between Glendive and Miles City as being almost bare from drought and the attacks of grasshoppers, and asks us to do the handsome thing by apologizing. The Times states as a reason for this apology, that the grass was never better than it is now in the region referred to. We can scarcely see Bro. Mabee's object in making such a statement as the above. That he does not know better, would be to say that he keeps himself entirely aloof from his fellow-man and is entirely unacquainted with the commonest topic of conversation. It is so perfectly well-known that the ranges in many parts of eastern Montana are absolutely ruined for this year, that the veriest school-boy could have acquainted him with the fact. This leads us to remark that stock journals as a rule, make a constant habit of covering up the losses and extolling the profits in the cow business. This is all wrong. It harms everyone interested and makes the wise reader suspicious of the paper and leads the ignorant one astray. For instance, there is not a Montana reader of the last Glendive Times, but that knows the article referred to was pure buncombe, while it might induce outsiders to put in cattle where an Indian pony would starve.

The fall meeting of the Montana association was held in Helena, beginning last Wednesday.

The meeting was called to order by President T. J. Bryan. Fifty-three members, scarcely a third of those present at Miles City, answered to the roll-call read by Secretary Harrison.

The minutes of the Miles City meeting were read and approved and R. B. Harrison's report as treasurer was referred to the executive committee.

The Helena board of Trade invited all members of the association to attend the play "Only a Farmer's Daughter," which invitation was accepted.

The convention then took a recess until Thursday morning. The first business after the recess was the report of the executive committee on the treasurer's report. It showed a total on hand of $2,625.61.

A telegram was read from the secretary of the National cattle and horsegrowers' association of the United States, asking the Montana association to join its ranks. In response, the following resolution was adopted: "That this association acknowledge with gratification, the courtesy of the National cattle and horsegrowers' Association, as conveyed by the communication from its officers and will communicate to them any action it may take at a later date."

E. S. Newman introduced a resolution which was adopted, recognizing the benefits of the Bureau of Animal Industry and memorializing Congress to pass such additional legislation as will enable the Bureau to buy up all cattle suffering from infectious diseases within the United States and kill them at the government's expense.

Further time was granted the committee on incorporation.

Granville Stewart offered a resolution which passed with an amendment by Mr. Donnegan, calling for a committee of three to confer with the territorial Secretary in reference to conflicts in brands and a committee of five to report on the whole brand question, offering such changes and improvements as they may deem necessary. The committee of three consists of the following members: A. J. Seligman, J. P. Woolman and John Freezer. The committee of five is Dr. Azel Ames, Granville Stewart, M. E. Downs, R. B. Harrison and E. S. Newman.

The executive committee offered a resolution which was adopted, that the annual dues should be $10, payable at the April meeting and that dues should not be collected from new members during the first year of their membership.

A resolution by Granville Stewart was unanimously adopted that the different Indian agents should be communicated with in reference to their instructions allowing Indians to leave their reservations and that they use every means in their power to keep them on their reservations.

Votes of thanks were passed to the Helena board of Trade, to the N. P. R. R., the different hotels of Helena, the stock journals, the Colorado association for an invitation to meet with them, to president Bryan and secretary Harrison.

The resolution adopted at Miles City last spring, prohibiting any member from having in his employ any owner of stock running a different brand from his employer's, was, on motion of Granville Stewart, repealed.

Association adjourned to meet in Miles City next spring.

To the Members of the Little Missouri River Stockmens' Association.

Pursuant to the request of several members of the Association, and in accordance with the wish expressed at the last meeting thereof, I hereby call a meeting of the Little Missouri River Stockmens' Association, to be held in Pennell's hall, Medora, Saturday September 5, at 9 o'clock a. m.

THEODORE ROOSEVELT, Chairman.

I have the honor to submit herein an article for publication and sincerely trust that you will grant it space in the name of justice. I wish to say a few words in behalf of the much-abused cowboy; not that I feel called upon to champion their cause at all, but in justice to a noble, generous-hearted set of fellows. There is hardly a day passes, year in and year out, but what you can pick up a daily paper and read of some dastardly depredation accredited to cowboys, when if the occurrence ever did take place and the truth were known, it was committed by another class of citizens entirely—men as remote from the cowboy as day is from night—but men who are too often confounded with them through ignorance or pure cussedness. These so-called cowboys are the scum of western society, the evil of the West; low-down, dissipated loungers who hang around the low resorts of a western town. Tin-horn gamblers and dead-beats, who are often supported or "staked" by some unfortunate woman of the town; men who are too lazy to work, or are unfit to do so by reason of disease; men who came here from eastern cities either as fugitives from justice or in the hope of making a stake, but who found men before them who were not to be caught with their chaff; men who, either through their own boastfulness or cowardly assaults upon drunken men and women and cripples, have gained for themselves the name of "bad men," but who, in reality, will cringe to the earth in the presence of an equal, or in fact, a child, if he had the drop on them. Such are the men that are photographed, written about and served up to eastern readers as the "wild and wooly cowboy, so hard to please, that has never been curried below the knees." Yes, men who will draw their revolvers and shoot out the lights in a saloon; but who would not dare to draw a "gun" if slapped in the face by a boy half their size, if he was as quick as themselves with a "pop;" men who will follow and rob a drunken man, but who have not the courage to hold up a blind pack-mule.

These are the men who are classed as cowboys. Fine indeed. Who do not know the difference between a hackamore and a round-up, who could not throw a rope over a post, nor tell one brand from another except on a barrel of whiskey. These are the alleged cowboys. And why? And by whom? To the first, because ignorance dresses all western men alike. If a man wears spurs, he is a cowboy. If he wears a big white hat, a six-shooter and sports a 25-cent handkerchief, he is a cowboy also. At any rate he must be a cowboy or he would not be bad. Who are the writers of this trash? They are many. 1. The eastern dude who comes west a tenderfoot, who is one and always will be one. 2. The would-be tough, who writes home to the "b'hoys." 3. The ignoramus of a would-be correspondent. And last, but not least, the reporter who stumbles on an ant-hill and makes it a mountain. Those are the parties who are responsible for this nonsense and wanton malignity, and who, through ignorance or otherwise, defame the character of an honorable, whole-souled class of men.

Men who are stanch friends and brave foes. Honest men who earn their money in an arduous calling, but who are willing to share that money to the last farthing with their fellow-man if they find him in need, irrespective of age, color, persuasion, politics, or nation. Men whose duty keeps them in the mountain, on the range and far from the haunts of men often for a year at a time and then when granted a rest, in the brief interval they take a trip to town to supply their few wants and take a little diversion. This diversion sometimes winds up in a spree, by which they generally do more harm to themselves than to anyone else. Because cowboys are sometimes hilarious and sometimes rough of speech is no sign that they are devoid of honor and that they are incorrigible and also illiterate. On the contrary, the majority are intelligent young men, often-times collegians.

In this strain I might proceed for an indefinite period, but let it suffice that all that is said of them is not true. The cowboy and his calling are much abused, but he is human and when enjoying himself in his rough way, his whole-souled nature and big, generous heart oft-times lead him into excesses that can be over-looked. Yet the true type of cowboy is hard to duplicate in any other calling which has its black sheep, but not as black as they are painted. People should discriminate between the numerous classes that go to make up a western community. Don't cry "cowboy" in explanation of all crimes committed. Another bit of advice is: "Lay the blame where it belongs and keep your city hoosiers at home, for in my experience west, I have found that a boy who cannot get along well at home, cannot do so west and in many cases, a faro table, a dance hall or a big white hat and a pair of spurs have made a fool of a good boy. But there is yet room and help for good, energetic boys in the west. But remember that the ability to spit over his shoulder, give old guff, or otherwise be too fresh will not make a cowboy of him. He must be a man among men, or he will sooner or later find out the mistake of his eastern idea of a western cowboy.—[A Tenderfoot, in The Inter Ocean.

The case against Rev. H. B. Schaffner of assault with intent to do great bodily harm, was ended Tuesday with a verdict of guilty. The accused was sentenced to six months in the penitentiary. On account of many mitigating circumstances, Mr. Schaffner was released on $1,000 bail and given a month to file a notice of appeal. Many petitions are in circulation for his pardon and from the strong influence brought to bear, it is not thought that the sentence will be executed. There was really no evidence offered to convict him of anything besides assault and battery and we learn that public sentiment at Mandan is all in his favor.

The case for murder against Marquis de Mores and E. G. Paddock, for the killing of Luffsey, has been taken to Bismarck on a change of venue. Both are now under arrest, bail being refused. It is difficult to tell how the case will terminate, but notwithstanding the many attacks on Judge Francis, we are sure there will be a fair and impartial trial as far as he is concerned. Prosecuting attorney Long's definition of Bismarck however, as "the home of more dishonesty, skullduggery, rascality, scoundrelism, fraud, perjury, subornation of perjury, bribing of juries, corruption in public and private places than any other city of the same size on the face of the globe," would seem to indicate that justice pursues a dubious way there. We might add that attorney Long knows whereof he speaks. It seems to us rather a risky piece of business to transfer the case to Bismarck, as justice is far more likely to be obtained in Mandan. The meddlesome interference of blood-sucking lawyers has made this an important case where it would have been far better and probably better subserved the ends of justice to allow it to be buried in oblivion.

It would be a good scheme for the stockmen at their meeting, Saturday, to change the names of some of the numerous Beaver creeks in this vicinity. It could easily be done and would save a vast amount of misunderstanding.

G. W. Reynolds went east last week, his brother, B. F., taking charge of the cattle, which arrived at Mingusville in fine condition. Five hundred one's and two's were sold to the 777 outfit and the remaining four thousand head will be ranched on Cedar creek, about forty miles below Howard Eaton's ranch at the mouth of Beaver.

No definite news has as yet been learned concerning the relocation of the territorial line, except that it is really west of where it was supposed to run. It may or may not locate Mingusville in Dakota. The citizens there are as anxious to become citizens of Dakota and Billings county, as those here are that they should be.

In the robbery case against E. G. Paddock, tried at Mandan this week, the jury disagreed, standing seven to five for acquittal. The case was continued under $500 bail to the next term of court. We learn that a good deal of sentiment was manufactured against Mr. Paddock, but there is no one in Medora who believes him guilty of the charge.

As No. 2 was pulling out, Tuesday morning, a gentleman standing on a car platform, excitedly punched a lady in the ribs and exclaimed: "There's a cowboy," pointing to Van., who sat with his parenthetical legs wrapped around two or three barrels and a crate of crockery on the depot platform. The lady gave a perfect squeal of delight, and cried, "What, a real one?" The gentleman's reply was lost in the roar of the receding train, but the lady's head was only lost to view when the train disappeared in the cut. Meanwhile, a mellow smile dimpled Van's. classic features and as he uncoiled himself from around the barrels and things, he exclaimed, "Py sheeminy, poys, I made a mash. Vont effer-r-r-rybody take somedings?" And it cost him just six dollars and seven bits to treat the thirsty multitude.

The commonest and the greatest curse of a western country is the habit of borrowing. It arises from the whole-souled generosity that characterizes a western community and from the fact people get along here with as few as possible of the luxuries of life. When in need of any, the first impulse is to borrow. This trait makes a nuisance of those who would otherwise be good neighbors. Guns, horses, wagons and in fact everything but wives are borrowed with a total disregard to the fact that the owner thus, in many cases, does not get half the wear out of the articles he has bought, that he should. Fully half the time, the owner must look up the borrower and himself take back the article loaned. There is not a reader of this article who has lived in the west any length of time, who has not suffered from the chronic borrower. How often does it happen that a person borrows a horse of one man, a saddle and bridle of another, a gun of a third and ammunition of a fourth and goes hunting? It actually seems as if the person who has none of these articles uses them more than the person who has all of them. We fully realize the fact that borrowing is more of a necessity here than in the east but there is certainly no necessity of the wholesale system as practised here. Does it ever occur to the chronic borrower that there are horses for hire here, which he should rent and not impose on his friends? Does it ever occur to him that no man wants to lend his gun? Does it ever occur to him than an expression of sorrow is not a sufficient recompense for a broken or soiled borrowed article? And lastly, does it ever occur to him that he could easily deprive himself of the pleasure he gains through borrowed articles by not borrowing them? It would be a good idea if all our citizens would combine and refuse to loan a thing that could be bought or rented in town. It would almost double the circulating medium. We hope the chronic borrower will take this lesson to heart and also take a tumble to himself.
The Minnesota state fair opened Monday with a good attendance. It is said to be a complete success.

Gov. Ross, of New Mexico, is giving every encouregement to the Cheyenne and Arapahoe stockmen to locate in New Mexico. The stockmen there do not like his cordial invitation but can scarcely help themselves.

The cattlemen of the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations have been working hard to remove their cattle and now the President's order has been almost carried out. The number of cattle on the reservations was greatly overestimated. We doubt if there were any over 150,000 on the disputed ground. They have been driven in all directions, the bulk being driven into Texas.

A call for the annual meeting of the National Cattle growers' association at Chicago has been issued. It takes place in the Exposition building Nov. 17 and 18. This is the third annual meeting. Cattle raising in all its branches will be discussed by such men as Commissoner Norman, J. Coleman, Judge Carey, Gen. McPherson, Senator Cullum, A. A. Libby, Prof, Salmon, Abram, Hewitt, Col. Harris and others.

A gambling spirit seems to be second nature to all cattlemen. Not that they are gamblers in the common sense of the word, for probably not one in ten ever gambles literally. It is their willingness to take chances to which we allude. For instance, several times lately we have heard of offers being refused on cattle on the range, which would net a larger sum than the gross Chicago price. There is a chance, though, that the price will raise by the time the cattle strike a market and the cowman is willing to take chances. We think it is an actual fact that it would be impossible to buy any large number of prime range cattle at Chicago prices, deducting freight and commission expenses.

The editor of the Glendive Times comes back at us in his last issue by almost entirely begging the question and misconstruing an expression we used in our first article about the poor ranges in eastern Montana accounting for the low prices of cattle on the Chicago market. He makes us use the expression as applying to the low price all cattle are bringing there, when to the most careless reader, it is manifest that we meant it to apply only to the cattle from the poor ranges. As well exactly might he apply the expression to the price of cattle from Australia or Patagonia as to apply it to any cattle foreign to the very ranges in question. Our article has been widely commented on, but in no instance has such a far-fetched construction been placed on our words. We are glad however, to see that the editor of the Times is beginning to acknowledge the corn by admitting that the ranges have been damaged slightly, when in his former issue he claimed that they never were better. We did not in any way wish to speak ill of the eastern Montana ranges in our first article, to the advantage of our Bad Lands ranges. We wished simply to state facts and have done so. Montana ranges are too well and favorably known to be permanently let alone because of one season's attack of drought and grasshoppers combined. That very many of those ranges are ruined for this year remains as much a fact as ever. Neither do we wish to exalt our Bad Lands ranges. They are known by all to be the very best in the country, but it is equally well known that they are nearly stocked to their full capacity allowing for the increase of the present herds. In a year or two they will be full and no advantage can be gained by either praising or condemning them in comparison with other ranges.

Little Missouri River Stockgrowers Association Meeting.

The third semi-annual meeting of the Little Missouri river stockgrowers' association, met for the regular fall meeting in Roberts & Co's. old hall, last Saturday morning.

The meeting was called to order at ten o'clock by the president, Theodore Roosevelt.

Nearly all members were present or represented. The reading of the minutes of last meeting was omitted.

It being the regular meeting for the election of officers, the president advanced many cogent reasons for the election to the chair of some resident member and against his own re-election, whereupon he was immediately and unanimously re-elected president for the ensuing year.

On motion, Henry Boice was unanimously re-elected vice-president and J. L. Truscott, secretary.

On motion, it was resolved that in the absence of the president and vice-president, the secretary be empowered to call a meeting.

J. L. Truscott moved that a committee of three be appointed to consider questions relating to the fall round-up. Carried, with an amendment by Willis Eaton that the association adjourn for half an hour, pending the report of the committee. The chair appointed Chas. Rowe, Willis Eaton and H. B. Wadsworth as the round-up committee.

The meeting being again called to order by the president, the report of the round-up committee was read by Willis Eaton.

The report recommended that Jos. McCoul be appointed foreman and that the round-up date and route be as follows: Beginning at Medora, the last Tuesday, the 29th, of September, to work thence, to and one day below the mouth of Big Beaver. Thence up Big Beaver to its source, thence across to the mouth of Little Beaver, thence down the Little Missouri to Medora. The committee recommended also that the foreman receive five dollars per day salary. The report was unanimously adopted.

The chair and Willis Eaton nominated Benjamin F. Lamb as a member of the association. Mr. Lamb was unanimously elected.

The chair stated that at the spring round-up, nine mavericks were found and sold for $213.

The chair, speaking as a member of the association stated that in view of his excellent services as foreman of the spring round-up, he thought a present should be made by the association to Wal. Osterhaut.

On motion, $100 of the maverick money, was set apart, to be given to Mr. Osterhaut.

There having been reports on the river that Gregor Lang had illegally branded an animal, he explained to the satisfaction of all, that his action was entirely lawful.

Willis Eaton moved that the chair have authority to call the spring meeting a few days before the Montana association meeting at Miles City.

H. B. Wadsworth moved that the foreman be paid from any money in the treasurer's hands and that any deficit be made up at the next meeting. Carried.

Association adjourned on motion of Wm. Merrifield.

The association can congratulate itself on again electing Theodore Roosevelt as president. Under his administration, everything moves quickly forward and there is none of that time-consuming, fruitless talk that so invariably characterizes a deliberative assembly without a good presiding officer.
Chas. Rowe, of Mingusville, attended the meeting.
John W. Buster represented the Hashknife outfit.

One of the most commendable things about the convention was the granting of an opportunity to Gregor Lang, to clear himself of the charge of illegally branding an animal. As was explained, he acted only as he should. We think every such charge should invariably be brought to the attention of the association. If the charge is unfounded, as it will nine times out of ten prove to be, the accused should be given the opportunity every honest man covets, of proving himself innocent. If the charge is proved true, it is for the interest of the association to find it out and punish the offender to the full extent of the law. We have heard several reports, all probably as unfounded as the one against Mr. Lang, which it would be for the interest of all concerned to have explained.

The motion to pay the foreman of the round-up good wages from the association treasury, passed unanimously, as it should. Good wages will call for and inspire good and faithful work and the fact that the foreman is receiving his pay from the association and not from an individual, will infuse a fairness into his decisions, not as likely to be found otherwise.

The combined receipts of cattle at Chicago, New York, Kansas City and St. Louis last week were 72,646, against 79,916 for the previous week. Prices during last week were very unsettled; ruling from 15 @ 30 c. lower for Texan and Western cattle. The Liverpool, England market is steady at 14 c. ℔ lb dressed for best American steers. A year ago best native cattle sold in Chicago as high as $7.50 and Texas cattle at $4.50 @ 5. During last week in Chicago, 42,000 cattle were received, making 137,969 for the past three weeks. Of the 42,000 last week about 32,900 were Texas and western cattle. Dakota range cattle touched the highest notch, Towers & Gudgell receiving $5.25. Top price for Wyoming was $5.10; for Oregon $5 and for Montana $4.40. Lowest price for western cattle was $3.25 and for Texans $2.80. Day before yesterday the market advanced 10 @ 15 c.

The 12,000 or more stock brands now on file in the secretary of state's office, afford an interesting field of study. The display of ingenuity in the matter of forming combinations is remarkable. The number of combinations upon any one letter is surprising. There are, for instance, over 250 on the letter H; 150 or more on both C and D; no less than 100 each on B E, and so on through the alphabet. In making up the brand index book Mr. Edward Hanley, assistant secretary of state, says the Denver Times, has displayed excellent judgment. The brands are twice indexed; once by the names of the owners and again by brands. The latter index is the one which is to be printed and filed with the county clerks of the State. It is a very elaborate affair. The brands are arranged alphabetically or numerically, as far as practicable. There are, however, combinations on the letter, I. The letter O, the cipher, the circle, the half-circle and quarter-circle are also confusing. They are all indexed under the letter O. There will be of the 12,000 brands filed, more than 500 of each of these combinations. Those brands which cannot be classed either as letters or numerals are indexed as miscellaneous. There will probably be 1,000 of these. A large proportion of these are figures which have not been named and are as unnamable as the hieroglyphics on the pyramids of Egypt. But there are others that represent articles in common use, animals, birds, etc. The whole forms an exceedingly curious selection. The artists who have sent in these certificates have usually taken the precaution to label their representations of the various characters; a wise and thoughtful act on their part, as it would in many cases, have proven worse than a Chinese puzzle to attempt to classify them. Here are a few of the character brands: Moccasin track, turkey track, crow's feet, anchor, trowel, flags crossed, spear, table forks and pitch forks of all sorts and shapes, staples, compass, boot, shoe, cup, canteen, dipper, scissors, spades in endless variety, cow's head, jar, cannon, anvil, saddle bags, fish, hat, key, key-no, nippers, pick, hatchet boat, wineglass, horse, bull-ring, pistol, lamp, lamp chimney, arrow, swan, goose, etc., etc. The task of indexing the brands will prove an exceedingly long and tedious one. Owing to the nature of the work upon it at a time, and allowing that he works Sundays, holidays and every day, it will require nearly three months to complete the work.—[Pueblo Chieftain.

Frank Conly passed through Medora on the train Monday evening, with an alleged horse thief. He is accused of stealing thirteen head of horses but the man himself says that the horses were given to him to sell. That he sold them at public auction in Miles City but afterwards lost the money and started east. If his story does prove true, it should still go hard with him, for he was undoubtedly trying to get away from the country.

What a sermon could be preached on the sentence used by "A Tenderfoot" in the article in last week's COW BOY, republished from the Inter Ocean: "A big white hat and a pair of spurs have made a fool of many a good boy." Add to these two a six-shooter and you have the history of four-fifths of the "ba-a-ad men." There is no westerner but has seen this very transformation. Take an eastern boy of sixteen, who at home would grow up into a good citizen, and put him in a frontier town. It actually seems that in the majority of cases, he has scarcely had time to get off the cars before he begins "packing" a six-shooter. What in the world he does it for, the poor fool himself cannot answer. As a protection, it is trebly useless. In the first place, if he conducts himself as he should, there is far less danger of getting into trouble in the west than there is in the east. In the second place, the very fact of his wearing a six-shooter gives him a "ba-a-ad" kind of feeling that will surely get him into trouble at some time and then it usually means business, for no westerner will take any chances with a man who "packs a gun." This is the most accommodating country in the world for a man who is spoiling for a fight to have his wishes gratified. But the would-be bad man and most of all, the irresponsible "kid" who thinks he must make a "gun play" to gain any reputation, receive greetings that generally paralyze them for a time. In the third place the six-shooter is worse than useless as a protection for the chances are that if he attempts to draw on a man in this country, before he can get his revolver out of the scabbard, he will be filled so full of lead that "some tenderfoot will locate him for a mineral claim." And now boys, just stop and think of the matter a moment. Not only the tenderfoot but all who make a practice of wearing six-shooters. What occasion has any one of you ever had to use a revolver in town? While a cowboy is on the range, there is some excuse for it, but how has the wearing of a six-shooter in town benefitted any one of you? On the other hand, how many instances do each one of you know where the carrying of one has lead to serious results? A little reflection on this subject by the elder heads may be of incalculable benefit to the younger ones.

Seven Hashknife cowboys who have just come through from Texas with 3,000 cattle, under the foremanship of W. D. McFarlane, started home from here yesterday morning. The through cattle are in splendid condition and have been turned out on the Little Missouri Hashknife range.

Those who have not improved the opportunity of gathering plums for winter consumption, had better do so at once. No finer fruit grows than the common wild plums with which the Bad Lands abound this year. The slight frosts we have had are rapidly ripening them and they will soon be gone.

Wadsworth's cavayard was coming into town Tuesday morning when Heinze was surveying the scene of the killing of Luffsey and the cowboys took Heinze for a photographer. They all began posing, and when Heinze had tired them out pointing his transit at them, he turned them loose. In the words of the immortal poet: "he never touched 'em."

It would be a good idea for some people to receive exactly the kind of treatment they give their stock and see if it would sharpen their feelings any. We have seen one team especially driven into town early in the morning and allowed to stand all day long and sometimes far into the night, without a bite to eat or a drop to drink. If this had happened once only, it might be excusable, but happening time after time makes the matter not only a subject for public comment but for public action, if this shameful mal-treatment continues.

The article in our last issue about the chronic borrower has, we think, received more favorable comment from our readers here, than any article that has ever appeared in the COW BOY. Of course there are times when a person is compelled to borrow, but they are exceptional circumstances. The point of borrowing reducing the circulating medium in a town and thereby proving a detriment did not receive due attention. The borrower is a non-producer to just the extent of his borrowing and to the same extent damages the town, for if he had bought or rented what he borrowed, he would have put into circulation just that much money. By his borrowing also, he actually takes away from the circulating medium by keeping back value for value received. Even when a person realizes the true spirit of the chronic borrower it is very hard to refuse the loan of some article which is asked. One scarcely likes to tell him that he can hire or buy the same article right here and for this very reason the chronic borrower has a rich field to work and the man who provides himself with the articles he needs is thus a constant prey to the one who is either too stingy to buy what he needs or wants to indulge himself in luxuries beyond his means. We doubt even now if our article will cause any refusal of loans but we already know of several instances where it has kept people from borrowing articles. It is an unpopular plan with some to champion the anti-borrower cause, but we have enlisted for the war now and propose to keep hammering on this subject just as often as we see it will do any good.
THE LATEST. From Bismarck.--The Prosecution have rested. Sensational scene in Court.--Attorney Long to the Fore.

Bismarck, Dakota, Special To the Cow Boy, Sept. 17.

The prosecution rested yesterday, having only proved what is already known, that Luffsey was killed by the party, of which DeMores was a member.

This morning, witnesses McClung, Harmon and Walker testified that they heard Luffsey and O'Donald say the day before the shooting that they would shoot DeMores on sight. To-day's testimony is to the effect that they bore bad reputations, especially O'Donald.

A sensational scene was enacted in court this morning. Judge Francis and Prosecuting attorney T. K. Long became engaged in an unseemly wrangle, which ended in Long giving the Judge the lie direct. The Judge immediately committed Long to jail for contempt of court, where he now languishes. J. H.

The Sioux Falls constitutional convention is working away as hard as if their labor stood some chance of being recognized by Congress. They have about decided that the name of the new state shall be "Dacotah" with a "c" and a "haich," that the motto shall be "Under God the people rule" and that attendance at school shall be compulsory between the ages of six and twelve.

Bismarck is reaping a harvest in the case of the Territory vs. Marquis de Mores, E. G. Paddock et al. Everyone who knew anything of the case and about as many who knew nothing about it, have been subpœnæd as witnesses. They were also subpœnæd at least four days before they could by any possibility be needed. This gave all the witnesses time to go decently broke before their attention should be distracted by the trial, a state in which they were almost unanimously found last Saturday. If the Bismarck gang havn't the art of "blowing a man in," down fine, then indeed is it a lost art.

The question of county organization has been discussed on a plain business basis and it is the opinion of all with whom we have conversed, that taking into consideration the recent assessment, it would cost less than to remain unorganized, provided an honest board of county commissioners is appointed. That these will be honest men, there can scarcely be a doubt, as the large majority of citizens now in the county are and will be in favor of honest men for commissioners, plenty of whom can be found here. The new law respecting the organization of counties, passed at the last session of the legislature, gives the governor no option in the matter and completely does away with his appointing a non-resident for a commissioner. The law was passed at the request of the present governor and compels him to organize a county and to appoint as commissioners the three men recommended in a petition signed by one hundred and fifty qualified voters; residents of the county. This law gives us an opportunity of recommending good men as commissioners. There are many such in the county, possessing the entire confidence of their fellow-citizens. This matter of organization must be attended to immediately, as the Territorial board of equalization has met and apportioned the tax. Meantime, we advise that any taxes paid to Stark county be paid under protest and they can then be reclaimed, either by Billings county or the individual tax-payers, as there is but little doubt as to the unconstitutionality of the law.

There being a very hazy impression abroad as to the definitions and degrees of homicide as defined by Dakota's Penal code, we publish the following from the charge of Judge Francis to the jury in the Magill case: "Homicide is the killing of one human being by another. Homicide is either:
1. Murder.
2. Manslaughter.
3. Excusable homicide, or
4. Justifiable homicide.
Homicide is murder in the following cases:
1. When perpetrated without authority of law and with a premeditated design to effect the death of the person killed or of any other human being.
2. When perpetrated by any act imminently dangerous to others and evincing a depraved mind regardless of human life, although without any premeditated design to effect the death of any particular individual.
3. When perpetrated without any design to effect death by a person engaged in the commission of any felony.
Homicide is manslaughter in the first degree in the following cases, viz:
1. When perpetrated without a design to effect death, by a person while engaged in the commission of a misdemeanor.
2. When perpetrated without a design to effect death, and in a heat of passion, but in a cruel and unusual manner, or by means of a dangerous weapon, unless it is committed under such circumstances as constitute excusable or justifiable homicide.
3. When perpetrated unnecessarily, either while resisting an attempt by the person killed to commit a crime, or after such attempt shall have failed.
Every killing of one human being by the act, procurement, or culpable negligence of another, which under the provisions of this chapter (which I have read to you) is not murder, nor manslaughter in the first degree, nor excusable nor justifiable homicide, is manslaughter in the second degree."

The verdict in this, the Magill case, was "Manslaughter in the second degree." The greatest punishment under this verdict is four years in the penitentiary. The defendant can be let off with a fine however. Sentence will be pronounced in a day or two.

In looking over the daily market reports one must often be puzzled to understand why it is that side by side he will find scales of stock of similar or identical average weights showing a difference in price of fifty cents, seventy-five cents, and $1.00 per hundred, as the case may be. A farmer will also marvel that the car-load of big, fat, but rough cattle which he had flattered himself were equal to the best in the land and which he sent up to Chicago with confident expectation of getting "the top of the market," should sell fifty cents per 100 lbs. below the price obtained the same day by his neighbor who had what he derisively called "high fangled notions" on the subject of blooded stock. It had taken the farmer three years and more to make his cattle worth $5.50. while his wide-awake neighbor who, by observation and experience, had learned the value of good blood, had in a year's less time and by the expenditure of one-third less in food produced animals worth fifty cents per 100 lbs. more in any market in the land. Examples of this kind by the score may be seen any day at the Chicago stock yards. And the difference is as marked in horses and hogs and sheep as in cattle.--[Breeders Gazette.

We are glad to record that our eastern and northern publications are forming a more correct conception, and giving to their readers a truer portrait of the Texas and western cowboy. The National Stockman of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, says: "The typical ranchman is no swaggering desperado or animated arsenal; but is a business man and gentleman. If the national political convention to be held in Chicago in the next few months shows a better average of citizenship than was exhibited recently at Cheyenne, W. T., when four hundred and fifty ranchmen met in convention to deliberate on matters affecting their interests, they will reflect the highest credit on the nation they represent. A few years hence the standard of personal character and public demeanor will be as high on the plains of the trans-Missouri country as it now is in Pennsylvania. The ranch hands now employed for the work once performed wholly by the knights of the derringer are of a character which must in a few years rob the life of the herder of much of its risk and the blood-and-thunder press of most of its atrocious sensations. A great many farmers' sons, raised to habits of industry and trained in the usages of good society, are filling up vacancies which occur among herdsmen, and in many places they preponderate among the employes of the district. They take this method of learning the business from the very beginning, and are effecting a revolution in it as thorough as it is gratifying. We are personally acquainted with young men of character, intelligence, education, and even of moderate wealth, who are now, with the end referred to in view, voluntarily undertaking the hardships of the herder's lot. And we are in correspondence with others, of equal personal worth, whose applications are already filed, and who are only awaiting an opportuity to change the farm for the ranch. There can be but one outcome to all this, an outcome to which the whole country, and especially the west, must look forward to with satisfaction." Formerly he was unjustly classed as "wild and wooly," a dare devil, and outlaw. This character was given to the class simply because a few desperadoes occasionally were found in the ranks. They were the thieves and outlaws who were among, but not really of the cowboys. They gave the unsavory reputation to the ranches, and when stock associations were organized and the ranch business systematized this class were hounded out. Now there are no truer, better or more deserving men in the west than can be found among the managers and employes of cattle ranches.

The wild horse of America, although now native to the soil, is descended from the tribes of wild horses that still rove the plains of Central Asia. When the discoverers of this continent first landed, there were no horses anywhere in either North or South America. Centuries before, the horse had been introduced into European countries from Asia, and had become common all over that continent. When Columbus arrived here on his second voyage, in 1493, he was accompanied by one Cabæa de Vaca, who brought with him a number of horses, which were landed in Florida.

Cortez took horses with him to assist in the conquest of Mexico, as did Pizarro in his conquest of Peru. The natives were greatly affrighted when they beheld these strange animals. At first they supposed that the man and the horse were one complete creature, something like the centaur of which we read in ancient fable. And when they saw the rider dismount and disengage himself from his steed, their amazement knew no bounds.

In time, the savages learned that the horse was an animal that had been subdued by man, and that it was a separate creature; but they long dreaded the horse of the Spaniards as a beast of prey. And when the horses escaped from their masters and made their way into the forest, as they did after a space, the natives avoided them as something to be shunned. The quarreling Spaniards neglected their steeds, which soon found homes on the plains of Mexico, South America, and the unexplored regions of North America. From these escaped animals have sprung the wild horses of America. The mustang, as the native horse of the North American continent is usually called, is generally of a bright chestnut color. The horses marked with odd colors and patches are called "pinto" or "painted," by the Mexicans and "calico" by the Americans. The mustang is smaller than the domesticated American horse; for we must remember that the larger horses now found in our stables are the direct descendents of later importations from Europe.--[St. Nicholas.

Saturday and Monday were consumed by the court at Bismarck in obtaining a jury in the Marquis' case, resulting in the following being chosen: "W. S. Moorhouse, Frank Frisby, C. H. Edick, F. W. McKinney, C. R. Williams, Timothy Griffin, F. E. Young, C. W. Renard, George Wahl, Anson Northrup, W. B. Watson and B. F. Gage. The prosecution will try to prove that Wannegan, Luffsey and O'Donald were riding home when they were fired at by concealed parties. That twenty-five or thirty shots were fired. That Luffsey was then killed. That Marquis de Mores fired the fatal shot. That there was a feud between O'Donald and Paddock. That Paddock falsely represented to De Mores that his life was in danger and instigated him to join this attempt to put O'Donald out of the way. The first witness when the case was called Tuesday morning was James McShane. He testified that he was working on the railroad about two hundred yards from the scene of the shooting. That he saw the Marquis and others come out of the brush with guns in their hands. That he went to where Luffsey's body lay and also to the thicket where he found the brush cut away and tramped down. Paul Heinze exhibited a sketch of the scene, showing the relative positions of the parties. McNeave Nally testified that he was on the coroner's jury and described the wound which caused Luffsey's death.

We are glad to see that the Stockgrowers' Journal is also willing to state the exact facts in reference to the cow business. If there are any losses, or any unprofitable points come up, we believe that the plain facts should be given to the public. The cattle business is undoubtedly the most profitable legitimate business in the world and why some editors wish to "paint the lily" by magnifying its profits, is beyond our comprehension.

The cattle are by this time nearly out of the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations in Indian Territory. It is now finally decided that the boundary line between Montana and Dakota was located twelve miles too far east. It then behooves the advocates of an honest county organization to get out their pencils and figure some more. The additional twelve miles of railroad will bring the taxes from that source up to if not quite $5,500. This will pay the ordinary running expenses of a county organization. In addition, we are credibly informed that Stark county's assessment will be about $4,000. This makes over $9,000, to which must be added the $1,400 we are now paying Morton county for liquor licenses. The whole makes a total of far more than enough to pay the expenses of a county organization. In addition to all this is to be added over $200,000 of taxable property that the changing of the line brings into Billings Co., and we ask any friend of the law, of the common good, of his own pocket book, shall we organize? The answer, taking into consideration everything, must be an almost unanimous affirmative.

The prairie fires on the west extend from Beach to Sentinel Butte and thence south of the track for at least ten miles and it may go fifty before it stops. A movement ought certainly to be made to find the parties responsible for the fire and punish them to the full extent of the law.

The long waiting is finally over and Marquis de Mores is a free man. When the case was given to the jury it took them less than ten minutes to come to a verdict of acquittal. The Marquis is to be congratulated on the result and every true friend of the west will rejoice in his acquittal. There is no one man in Dakota who has done more to develop the west than he, and a conviction in his case would have been a calamity to western Dakota. The merits and demerits of the affair are now set at rest and it would do no good to bring them all to mind. To any who are disposed to cast blame on the Marquis for the killing of Luffsey, we would say, put yourself in his place. Virtually a stranger in a strange land, almost entirely unacquainted with the habits and entiely so with the people, is it strange that he should have adopted fatal measures to protect his life which no one will say he did not believe was in danger? The fact that his life was probably in no real danger has nothing to do with his belief. Any one, situated as he was, would come to the same conclusion. The expenses of the trial hsve been very heavy, but it is probably better that the matter is now finally set at rest.

The air has been full of smoke from prairie fires for the last week and from all sides, especially the east, come accounts of serious loss. We think at a moderate estimate, 100,000 bushels of wheat and oats have been burned, besides houses, agricultural implements, etc. It seems that in most cases, not even the most ordinary precautions have been taken to guard against fire. An ordinary double furrow, will stop a prairie fire nine times out of ten. Two double furrows, fifteen or twenty feet apart, with the grass burned between, will stop any prairie fire that ever existed. Such criminal carelessness as allowing a wheat or oat stack to remain in a stubble field or prairie, without such a simple and effective protection as a furrow or two, is hard to explain. The recent losses will prove a serious but instructive lesson to the grangers.

How to Take off a Hide.

The hides of farm-slaughtered animals have a poor reputation, because of the careless way in which they are stripped. Calf skins and sheep-pelts are reduced one-half in value by being cut and gashed, and improperly stretched. When a hide is stripped off, it should be stretched at once, and pegged out to dry, with the flesh side upward. If it is rolled up, or thrown into a heap and left to dry in that shape, it is so mean-looking that a buyer will offer only half its real value. A few hints in regard to taking off a hide, may be useful. The throat should never be slit cross-wise, either in killing or taking off a hide. The skin is slit from the chin down the brisket, in a straight line to the tail; it is then cut around each hoof; the hind legs are slit behind over the gambrel, but the fore legs are slit up in front, over the knees. This leaves the skin in good shape for finishing the leather. The head and legs are first carefully skinned, and all cutting of the skin is avoided. The skin is then easily drawn off by taking hold of it firmly, and pulling it steadily. It is then spread out evenly on a floor, and salted with fine salt. If there is but one, it is best to take it out as soon as the salt has taken, and dry at once in a cool, shaded place. If there are more than one, they are laid upon each other and salted quite freely, and afterward are thoroughly dried. If the skins are to be kept on hand, they should be closely watched for moths or grubs.--[Montana L. S. Journal.

A Lawyer Jailed by a Judge.

At the trial of the Marquis de Mores [at?] Bismarck, a remarkable incident occurred which illustrates the hostile feeling existing between Judge Francis and some of the members of the bar. A correspondent says: Several witnesses had been examined. Irvine Kinley and Frank Pecket testified to having heard Luffsey and companions threaten De Mores' life. Justice Mark Bateman testified concerning the examination in his court and his discharge of De Mores on the ground that Luffsey was killed in self-defense and when resisting arrest. Howard Eaton testified that he was sent by De Mores to meet Sheriff Harmon, warn him that the Luffsey party would resist arrest, and advise him that De Mores and party would prevent their leaving town. Thomas Carruthers, who was with De Mores' party but some distance away from the place where the firing began, testified that he saw smoke from the first shots, and they were fired by Luffsey and companions. Martin Wadsworth testified regarding O'Donnel's quarrel with De Mores. This witness had been dismissed, when Prosecuting Attorney Long of Mandan called him to his side, and privately asked him if he was the Wadsworth who had accompanied Wannegan to visit De Mores in jail. Being answered yes, Long then asked to be permitted to place Wadsworth again on the stand. Objection was made, and the court ruled that the witness could not be placed on the stand again unless he was called as a witness for the prosecution.

Long undertook to state what he intended to prove, and was called to order, and ordered to take his seat, but continued speaking, when the judge vigorously used his gavel, and threatened to commit him for contempt. In the course of his remarks Long advanced close to the judge, and gesturing with his right hand near to the judge's face, said:

He came here unwillingly to perform official duty. He had no feeling in the case. He only desired to see a fair and impartial trial. He appeared as a subordinate officer of the court, and was here to assist in the enforcement of substantial justice; that instead of the court extending to him the aid and support which he was entitled under the law to expect, the court had uniformly, during the whole trial, sought to tie the hands of the prosecution and openly aided the defense; that the court had shown by its action in this case that it had determined to aid in the acquittal of the defendant, and that the court would not leave a stone unturned in the accomplishment of such acquittal; that the court throughout had shown a most marked feeling in favor of the defendant and against the prosecution; that the court had sought at every point to embarrass the prosecution and to aid in the acquittal of the defendant.

During all this time and for some time after, while Long was still talking, Judge Francis endeavored to silence him by the use of the gavel and by threats to commit him for contempt, but Long dared the judge to commit him and talked himself out, when the judge ordered him in custody, and he was taken to the jail building. The court then took a recess to 2 p. m.

During the recess dinner was sent to Long from the Sheridan house with a message to the effect that an apology for his conduct would be accepted and it need not be abject, but he must expect the court to preserve its dignity at all hazards. In jail Long said to a correspondent:

I have done nothing to regret. I have only tried to perform an official duty, and in the performance of that Judge Francis has abused me personally and insulted me repeatedly professionally. I shall stay here until I am ordered out. I will ask no favors or concession, and will grant none. I have no apology to make, and will make none. I maintain that Judge Francis acted in a manner unbecoming the office of a judge, and provoked me to say all that was said.

When the court opened at 2 p. m., Long was brought in and refused to apologize.

We will have something to say in the future about this herd, as we believe that Polled Angus and Galloway grades are to be the northwestern range cattle of the future.

H. B. Wadsworth, while superintending the Bad Lands cattle Co's. shipment of beeves at Dickinson, last Saturday, slipped and fell from the top of a caboose, breaking his leg in the fall. Mrs. M. Wadsworth went to Dickinson, to attend him. The accident will disarrange Mr. Wadsworth's business plans and it is to be hoped that he will speedily recover.

One by one they join the Benedicts, and now it is Maxwell's turn to get ready to fight if anyone says he hasn't the best wife in the world. Mrs. Josie Maxwell, nee Smith, is the happy bride and all join in the hope that the newly married couple may experience none but the joys of life in their new relation of husband and wife. They return to-night and will go immediately to housekeeping in the cottage formerly occupied by Dr. Jorgens.
