Geo. Fitzgerald is making a number of improvements in his hotel.
Near New Salem a woman and child were burned to death while fighting prairie fires.
E. Elmer has veneered his cottage with brick and is now ready to go into winter quarters.
Last Sunday night a bridge between Sims and New Salem burning out and a freight train off the track at Sims delayed No. 1 about eight hours.
The club kept by Mrs. Fortier, has been dissolved on account of losses by marriage and otherwise. Mr. and Mrs. Fortier will keep house in one of the brick cottages.

Cornelis VanEeghan, brother of our "Van" left Tuesday for his home in Amsterdam, Holland. He is much pleased with the Bad Lands and seems to have learned much of its advantages during his brief visit. He is thinking of coming again for a longer stay next year.

Supt. Green will be here Friday or Saturday to locate new stock yards, capable of holding a large number of cattle. It will be a great convenience to our cattlemen as the present yards are but little better than a nuisance.

Word came in yesterday that E. G. Paddock was discharged on his trial for complicity in the Luffsey killing. Prosecuting attorney Long turned the case over to Judge Francis, who probably discharged him on the same evidence that acquitted the Marquis. This will probably set the whole matter at rest, as, even if Moore and Miller are tried they must be acquitted.

England never had a greater white elephant on her hands than Riel is proving to be. Canada has convicted him but dare not hang him and England is afraid to decide the question. Whether Riel is hung or allowed to go free a large faction of Canadians will become disaffected.

A late report issued by the Bureau of Statistics, at Washington, is strongly in favor of a National cattle trail and declares that it is a necessity. Northern ranchmen, who have had their ranges damaged or ruined by grasshoppers, drought or prairie fires hardly think this.

The labor troubles in Washington Territory and other places in the west have assumed serious proportions for the Chinese. It seems that in spite of the law restricting the immigration of Chinamen, large numbers have been landed in British America and thence come overland into the United States. Washington Territory especially is already overcrowded with whites and this influx of Chinese is added to the already large number of idle whites. The whole has culminated in a determination to rid the country of Chinamen and the initiative has already been taken by several trades-unions. Every effort will be made to drive them back to the land of birds' nest soup and rat porridge.

With all the attention to business details, which characterizes the cattle business, it seems strange that cattlemen should depend almost entirely on commission men to conduct their sales. Of course it is the simplest and easiest way to dispose of cattle but we doubt if it is the most profitable. The commission man sells at whatever price he chooses, deducts his commission and expenses and gives the balance to the cattleman. It is astonishing that the commission men are as honest as the lack of serious complaint shows them to be. It would be a very simple thing to have an understanding between the buyer and the commission man and make the seller lose the "cahoots." A remedy for this is hard to find but it seems strange that some move is not made toward limiting the absolute power of the commission men in making sales. We confess that these remarks arise from a well-founded ill-will the editor has for commission men in another line of business. Lately, however, we have seen two cattlemen who are seriously dissatisfied with the present way of making sales. It is a matter that should be considered by stock organizations.

Never, since this country was first settled, have there been such extensive and destructive prairie fires as have raged within the last three weeks. The general limits of the fires, as nearly as can be learned, are Jamestown on the east, between Mingusville and Glendive on the west, the Killdeer Mts., to the bend in the Little Missouri and north of the Yellowstone on the north and as far as Cave Hills on the south. Of course we do not mean that the whole country within these limits is burned clean, but that half of it is a blackened waste, is a moderate estimate. The damage done to the agriculturalists of Dakota, must be over $100,000, in the loss of grain, houses, stock, implements etc. To the cattle interests also, the danger is menacing. The Bad Lands form a pretty effectual fire-break on account of the numerous wash-outs and bare places, but many coulies and ravines leading in from the prairies both east and west have acted as regular flues to lead the fire into the Bad Lands and in some cases, clear to the river. Tongues of fire have fairly riddled the whole country. This makes the question of finding sufficient range for cattle, a serious one. It is a matter of doubt even now, if there is enough unburned range to pasture the cattle now in the Bad Lands and as we write these words the air is full of smoke from the still burning fires. There are still some ranges untouched, but they are liable to be pretty well crowded this winter by cattle from the burned ranges. We have heard that several new outfits intended driving into the Bad Lands this winter, but the fires must have caused a change of programme. No experienced cattleman would think of taking the risk involved by such a move.
T. R. Selmes of Mandan, was in town Monday attending the Cantonment sales, he being attorney for the estate.
Abe. Goodkind of Bismarck, was here this morning, making the buttes and coulies fairly ring with praises of the "Far West" and "Our Pet" cigars.
Judge Francis and clerk of the Supreme court Haight arrived Sunday night and started Tuesday for Deadwood, for the session of court there. While here they were guests of the Marquis.
A deer was killed by the cars at Sully Springs yesterday, being the only case of the kind on record, as far as our knowledge goes. The pilot of the engine was also badly demoralized.
One of Osborne Bros. Polled Angus heifers was killed by a train Monday. Such a loss is more serious than usual, as the railroad will probably pay no more for it than they would an ordinary animal.

The market report of this issue presents but little of interest to our readers. Northern wintered Texans are quoted the same as last week, while the lowest price on northern range cattle has raised and the highest price lowered, twenty-five cents. The combined receipts of cattle at Chicago, New York, Kansas City and St. Louis, were 70,840, of which Chicago received about 38,000. The cattle averaged poorer in quality than the week before and the reason the price kept up was that buyers were present from New York, Boston and Baltimore, who bought freely. Dressed-beef operators also furnished competition.
The Texas Live Stock Journal lays the great loss in cattle there last winter to the practice of allowing bulls to run with the herd the year round.
The Maltese cross, Quarter circle diamond and L C outfits will gather all their bulls this fall and feed them near the Big Plateau. Sufficient hay has already been provided.

It seems that the branding of all calves by the Bad Lands Co., as mentioned in our last issue, was not the first time it has been done in the Bad Lands. We can however, repeat our commendation of the act, as it is liable to save many dollars to neighboring outfits and is an act that will certainly be appreciated by any one. We hope to see it universally practised hereafter.

As we have before stated, there are a number of minor points about the cattle business in the Bad Lands, which are still in their experimental stage. The one of most importance is the value of keeping herds off the river bottoms in the winter. Several outfits have made preparations to keep all their cattle back from the river, and thoroughly test the matter. On account of the fires, however, it will be impossible to arrive at decisive results this winter, as the feed is decreased by at least one-third.

It is hard to believe that the bottom is so knocked out of the Chicago market that the Bad Lands cattle Co's cattle, only brought $3.85 and $4. We learn however, that they did not average 1200 lbs. which accounts in a measure for the low price. Their being in such fine condition at the start was deceptive. Perhaps Will. Dantz' experience may also explain the low price. His cattle refused food and water during the most or all of the trip to Chicago. After leaving St. Paul, a fog from Lake Michigan was encountered that made the floors of the cars so slippery as to keep the cattle constantly off their feet. Sometimes over half a car load would be down at once. Of course, when they were unloaded they looked gaunt and in poor condition, no matter how they looked when loaded. Such a series of mishaps would be fatal to a high price for any kind of stock.

Bill Jones tackled a broncho when the round-up started, Tuesday morning, that could have given points to Mark Twain's prize bucker. Bill says that he had Joe McCoul's coat on when he started up and Joe yelled to him to throw it down if he didn't get back in time to join the round-up. When he came down he spoiled a fine brand-new stump with the back of his head. That is, it posessed no further utility as a stump. As kindling it would have topped the market. It seemed "sorter" like tempting Providence for Bill to mount that mild-mannered looking brute again but he did and Bill says he couldn't hear the little birds sing until some time after on the way down. This time he lit in some buffalo berry bushes and the bronch., going in to see if he was hurt walked all over him, repeated and did it again. Bill led the brute into town, got spliced up, and yesterday morning was seen rounding the slaughter-house on the way to the round-up, holding on to leather with a life-preserver, blanket roll on the horn, and hobbled stirrups, while Uberman and Bemis were herding him out of town.

I hereby give you a bit of my experience in the way of sawing off horns. Mr. Haaff's last letter seemed to lay the matter down so simply that a neighbor offered to furnish the subject if I would wield the saw. Being desirous of seeing the experiment tried, I readily consented. The animal was a two-year-old shorthorn bull that had shown strong symptoms of viciousness, having backed the owner out of pasture two or three times. Our first attempt proved futile, failing to secure the brute properly. The head was tied around as Mr. Haaff directs, but the stanchions gave way, and out went Mr. Bull with a horn half off. We were obliged to abandon the job till next morning, when a suitable stanchion was fixed. This time the Hon. Gentleman left the stable a hornless muley, not having lost any more blood than would naturally flow from a cut on your finger. Not a groan did he give, but threw himself down, and there he lay till the horns dropped in the manger before him. About an hour afterward we made him a visit in the pasture, found him feeding as quietly as though nothing had happened, suffering no perceptible inconveniende, only that he could not gore us. There are several others in this vicinity who will soon share the same fate. Some very humane people denounce us as cruel and unfeeling, and are somewhat inclined to complain of us. But let them once get horned by a mad bull and I'll venture they will be willing to see the brute sawed in two in the middle. I now believe "dehorning" perfectly harmless, as well as a benefit to the herd. I intend to denude my cattle of horns at an early date. The operation was performed four weeks ago; bull all right yet.—[I. E. S., in Western Rural.

A few facts may be of some interest to your many readers if you will allow me to give them through the columns of your valuable paper. I have taken a trip this spring by the way of Abilene, Colorado, thence north in the Panhandle and back home again on a round trip. I noticed a great improvement in cattle; all seem to be trying to improve their stock, and to economize in every way to meet hard times. I find no improvement in the way of handling cattle. We see everything moved on the same jump. Here we go boys fifteen or twenty miles to a round-up, we ride at the rate of seven miles an hour, and often more. We cut our cattle and go back almost the same speed, reach camp with horses often ridden down, and I often noticed blood dripping from their sides and shoulders. The cattle are all so foot-sore, lame and driven so it will take a month to get over it. We often see yearlings that are a little hard to drive, roped, beaten, spurred, their eyes crammed full of sand, and very often killed with abuse. I cannot believe that owners of stock know altogether just how rough stock are handled. If they did, surely they would realize the damage done to them by the utter recklessness of every move in the handling of range cattle.

We notice the way of grazing herds. Yes, we see two or three hands down off their horses talking together, letting the cattle scatter over territory sufficient for three times the size of the herd, then they get on their horses, round them in on the jump, which is an injury to both horse and cow to some extent. Also when they drive on to the bed ground the movement is still too rapid, crowding them up and causing them to step on one another's feet. It accounts for 75 per cent. of the trail cattle being lame. There are other causes for the poor condition of driving cattle that could be prevented if the trail bosses would take more interest, stay about the herd and see what is going on, instead of being in camp so much of the time. There is as much in a boss knowing how to handle men as there is in knowing how to handle cattle. A man not knowing how to handle men, especially without showing partiality, is not a fit subject to be intrusted with the management of a trail herd. I claim to know of what I speak, having been on the trail almost yearly since 1871, and I am a man who ought to learn something in that time.—[Trail Driver in Texas Live Stock Journal.

The general offices of the Ref. Car Co. have been moved from St. Paul to Medora.
J. W. Buster superintended the delivery of five hundred Hashknife cattle to the Co. this morning averaging 1066.
You will never make a mistake in buying cigars, if you go to Roberts & Co's. and order a "Far West" or "Our Pet" cigar. They beat any cigar in town for the money.
We are indebted to Mr. John Carr of Delavan, Ill., for late papers from his home. He returned home from his visit to Dick, with a very much and favorably changed idea of Dakota.
Sheriff Harmon has made many friends in Medora and if it laid with Billings county to give him a life lease on the office of sheriff in Morton county he would easily get it.
Geo. Porter left last week for Chicago and the east, on his annual purchasing tour for the Co's. general store. Messrs. Keeler and Grymes will hold down the store during his absence.

P. S. Bemis, of New York, lately of Ransom county, Dakota, came to Medora last Saturday and has joined the round-up. He intends getting a practical insight into the cattle business and may go into it.
At his recent trial in Miles City, Wm. Roberts was found guilty of stealing six horses at the Hashknife camp last winter. We hear that he has been sentenced to sixteen years in the penitentiary.

The round-up started from Medora Tuesday morning and is now at Wadsworths and will camp four miles below him tonight. The smoke bothers the boys greatly and it is feared that some of the cattle will be missed and that there will be a consequent increase of mavericks found in the spring.

Supt. Green was in town Saturday looking over the ground preparatory to building new stock yards here. No particulars have as yet been learned but on account of the difficulty of finding feed both at Dickinson and Mingusville it is probable that large ones will be built immediately.

Postmaster Harbison, G. H. Zirngebel and Geo. E. Scales, of Belfield, attended the sale here Monday. The latter chartered a flat-car or something and brought along the prize potato of the season. It was raised near Belfield and except in size is said to be a fair sample of his crop. The West Missouri country ought to come to the front with such a vegetable to advertise it.

Julius LeMoyne of Washington, Penn., and president of the LeMoyne cattle Co., arrived last Saturday evening from his home. It has been decided to keep the LC herd on its present range for this winter at least. Mr. LeMoyne thinks of starting a blooded herd here, for the purpose of raising range bulls, an enterprise we have hitherto advocated as offering greater profits than any other branch of the cattle business. Mr. LeMoyne is president of the Washington county breeder's association, in Pennsylvania and possesses great facilities for starting such a herd.

Jos. W. Nimmo, Jr. ex-chief of the Bureau of Statistics and editor of "Range and Ranch Cattle Area of the United States," besides many other works was here Tuesday and yesterday and made us a very pleasant call. He is looking up facts soon to appear in a popular work on cattle raising. Mr. Nimmo goes east tomorrow morning but will return in a week and make his next stop west, at Miles city.

There is probably not a more successful mercantile institution on the line of the road than the Boston Clothing, Boot and Shoe store, in its various branches. Two causes have contributed to this success: an abundant use of printers ink to attract and hold custom and an honest and well-carried-out intention of giving value for value received. The first fact is illustrated by the large ad., appearing in this issue of the Cow Boy, and the second can easily be proven by a visit to the Medora branch of this institution, presided over by T. W. Gordon.

The sheriff's sale of the Cantonment property took place last Monday according to advertisement. There was a good turn-out and prices were bid up in almost all cases to a high figure. The stock was sold first, the mares bringing fair figures in nearly every case. The cows and calves sold low. Harness, saddles, wagons, furniture, carpets etc., brought first rate figures and in some instances more than they could be bought for new. Four yearling colts were about the best property. They were bid in by Ferris & Merrifield for $155 and sold for $200 before they even had a chance to pay for them. E. G. Paddock obtained the choicest of the mares, he securing three good animals and the Norman stallion. The rest were bid in by M. Wadsworth, Link Gates, Jim Harmon, T. R. Selmes and Messers. Zirngebel and Scales of Belfield. As stated the horses brought fair prices but they were good animals and we doubt if there is a purchaser who is dissatisfied with his bargain.
The supreme court of Dakota adjourned Tuesday, at Deadwood, to meet in Bismarck Nov. 14.

Captain Dan. Maratta has been appointed United States Marshal of Dakota to take the place of General Allen. All who know the new Marshal recommend him highly and look for a "clean-up" of some of the rottenness that has disgraced Dakota.

No progress seems to have been made by the men who are trying to "civil service" Governor Pierce out of office. For the sake of honest government, cleanness in politics and the good name of Dakota, it is to be hoped that in this instance at least, there will be no change.

Riel has again been repreived by the English government. We doubt if any one man has ever been a greater white elephant to Canada and even to England, than Riel is proving to be. Canada put her foot into it badly by not in the first place granting some or all of the half-breeds' requests and is now suffering the just retribution she deserves. Canada has too near a neighbor in the United States not to adopt a liberal policy with all her citizens.

The Republicans carried Ohio Tuesday by about 20,000 majority. This shows a Republican gain over 1883 of about 25,000. The Prohibitionists did not materially change the result. The next legislature will be Republican, which insures the re-election to the Senate of the old war-horse, John Sherman. A queer anomaly of the contest was that the Prohibitionists joined the liquor interest in an attempt to down the Republicans, by which party alone they can ever expect to have any of their cranky notions carried out. Politics makes queer bed fellows.

Chief Justice Edgerton sends his resignation to Washington and will enter the senatorial race against Judge Moody of Deadwood. To a man up a tree this looks as though Judge Edgerton had abandoned a very plump bird in the hahd for a very poor one in the bush. There is no state as yet and no real likelihood of there being one, of which he can become senator and the chances are few of his beating such an accomplished wire puller as Judge Moody in the senatorial or any other race. Bartlett Tripp is taking Judge Edgerton's resignation to Washington, with a good chance of being appointed in his stead.

It looks as though the Northern Pacific rail road and the Montana Improvement Co. would have to pay handsomely for the wood they have cut from government land. M. J. Haley, special timber agent, has made his reports to Washington, which include thirty-one separate indictments against the above companies for a gross amount of $613,402. Mr. Haley is especially denunciatory of the Montana Improvement Co., calling it an "unscrupulous organization that will leave nothing undone to gain its point." The Improvement Co. cut the most or all of the timber, but the rail road company is implicated as it held a controlling interest in its stock.

The mistakes of the eastern press in reference to the range cattle business would be amusing were it not for the fact that in many instances they are unjust and damaging. They are also gradually leading eastern public opinion into the belief that the "cattle kings" are in all cases interlopers and that in some way people in the east suffer a personal loss for the money made in the range cattle business.

The true facts in the case are so apparent that it seems strange eastern papers have not manhood enough to publish them. In a nut-shell, the country occupied by the range cattle business would be entirely uninhabited, were it not for this industry. We doubt if a case has ever occured where range cattle business has crowded out agriculture. On the other hand, in Texas, Colorado, Kansas and other states and territories, agriculture is constantly restricting the bounds of the cattle business. These facts are so apparent that they scarcely need mention. As fast as the range country is needed for agriculture, as much as is fit for that pursuit will be given over to it.

Thus far only is the cattleman an interloper. He makes profitable a country that without him would be a howling wilderness and as soon as he has established a market the farmer comes in, with no opposition from the stockman, chooses the best hundred and sixty acres he can find and goes to farming.

All this cry about there being need of laws to allow farmers to settle up range territory is the purest cant. There isn't a range in the United States, not absolutely owned by the ranchman, upon which the settler cannot come and establish a farm. The laws of the United States would uphold him in it and if the venom-slingers of the east knew as much about land laws as they do about penny-a-line mud throwing they would see that attempts to arouse public opinion against cattlemen for keeping out farmers were built on a foundation of sand.

Another howl the eastern press is raising is: "Why don't the cattlemen buy the land?" If these editors knew what they were talking about, they would see what a boomerang their question is. How can one man legally get posession of more land than a homestead, pre-emption and tree-claim will give him and how far will this go in pasturing even a small bunch of cattle.

Time and again, in the Chicago meeting of 1884, of the National Cattle growers' Association, in the Wyoming association meeting of 1885 and by many other associations, have attempts been made to get Congress to pass laws, leasing the land to cattlemen at a reasonable figure. These attempts are disregarded, however by eastern editors, who bid fair, either through ignorance or sheer spite-work, to arouse a sentiment in the east that may fall with crushing force on the way of legislation, on the range cattle business.

S. E. Grindall, of Beaver creek, has been appointed deputy sheriff by sheriff Tuttle of Glendive. We congratulate Mr. Grindall, and also Mr. Tuttle for securing such an efficient deputy, but it would turn out somewhat of a joke if Mr. Grindall was found to live in Billings Co., Dakota.

Mr. John H. Obery, the Superintendent of Indian schools, under Secretary Lamar, gave his idea of the Indian question at the Lake Mahonk, N. Y., Indian Civilization Conference last Friday. We might also add that he gave himself dead away on the same occasion. In speaking of the education of Indians, he says: "After educating the boys I would suggest teaching them cattle raising, allowing them to contract with white men to take herds on their reservations and return them when called for, all the work on the reservations to be done by Indians. I would also favor assisting them to raise cattle for themselves." Mr. Obery said in conclusion: "I hope to make some radical changes, for I believe that only through the school-house can the Indian be let into the light of civilization." We were going to make some comments on the above extract, but hope we have no such tenderfoot among our readers that it is needed. We wonder though, that it did not occur to Mr. Obery, that it would be a good plan to first educate the cattlemen into allowing the Indians to take care of their cattle. This is an avenue of wealth that the cowman has hitherto not seemed to grasp.

Our market report shows a great improvement in the price of northern range cattle, the highest quotation raising 40c., to $5.00. The receipts of cattle in Chicago, averaged 7,237 per day last week, against 7,523 per day for the preceding week. New York prices ruled 30@50c. higher and English prices were generally lower. Two cars each of VI and SOHO cattle were shipped from Mingusville last Friday. Charlie Eaton went with them to Chicago.

Speaking of their quality, Mr. Gray of Canada says: "Of all the ox-kings, I have found the Aberdeen-Angus to be the best feeders. They respond the quickest to rich, concentrated food, and when they are in the stalls they are the most contented cattle I have ever tried. When the Aberdeen's stomach is filled, he lies down and rests. Of them, says Mr. Leonard, of Bell Air, Mo., who has imported, bought and sold more of them than any other man: "I can load a Burton car with Angus cattle at New York, carry them across the continent and back again, and have them gain flesh every day on the journey."—[Montana Stock Gazette.

As there is often a mixing up of the use of terms used by breeders, the following, from a manual on cattle, may serve to give our readers a proper idea as to their meaning:

A breed is a race, class or kind of animals, having certain peculiarities of form, and other characteristics different from others of the some species.

Thoroughbred animals are those which have been bred in a direct line sufficiently long to establish a fixed type, which they have the power of transmitting with uniformity to their offspring.

Cross-bred animals are the offspring of a thoroughbred male of one breed out of a female of another breed.

Grades are the offspring of a thoroughbred male or female and what are known as common stock, which belongs to no particular breed, or any other thorough or cross-breed.

High grades are those having a preponderance of pure blood, such as the offspring of a thoroughbred bull out of a half-bred cow, which is three-fourths.

Low grades embrace half-breeds and all graduations below so long as the impress of the thoroughbred is visible.

Common stock, scrubs, or natives, are those which have been indiscriminately bred until there is no recognizable trace of any breed and no uniformity of type.—[Farm Journal.

The above will be found interesting but in the definition of "Thoroughbred" we believe misleading. Although considerable license is now used in this meaning, the word "Thoroughbred" refers only to horses that can be traced back to an Arabian origin. "Thoroughbred" as applied to cattle is strictly a mis-nomer, "full-blood" being the term to use. Consequently the word "thoroughbred" in the above definitions should be changed to "full-blood." We publish the article as it is being widely copied, in order that this distinction may be recognized. It might be admissable in conversation, to speak of a thoroughbred heifer as one's meaning can be easily understood, but in the printed definitions, it is necessary to be exact.

A close observing horseman gives the following rules and marks for determining a horse's age: "At one year the colt has a full set of temporary front teeth, which are short, round and very white. At the age of two the colt sheds two center front teeth, above and below, and the horse teeth make their appearance. At three four others are lost, one on each side of the first. At four the corner teeth drop out. At the age of five the new horse teeth at the corners are up even with the others, the mouth is full and the tusks appear. At five the cavities or cups in the center will be nearly worn away and the tusks are up full, white and sharp. At seven the cups disappear from the front middle teeth, being brown curved lines. At eight the cups are all out save the corner ones. At nine the teeth are all full, shut even, and present a fair appearance. At ten the teeth turn yellow or brown, the tusks are either blunt or very long, the gums shrink away, giving the teeth a very large appearance. At eleven the teeth are black and foul, the gums form points between them. At twelve the upper teeth begin to overhang the lower ones. At thirteen the front teeth thicken and assume a triangular shape. A horse has forty teeth; twenty-four grinders, four tusks and twelve incisors or nippers. The colt is born with eight double teeth; at about two months four more appear, one upon each jaw. At one four more come, and at the age of two four others, and at three four more, making the mouth full, twenty-four grinders.—[Ex.

Several persons are making preparations to hunt for the market during the coming season. We doubt if there will be anything more than a living in it for good hunters, as deer are scarcer than usual and owing to the immense territory tributary to the St. Paul market, prices will be as low as they were last season.

E. Kessler and Tommy McGregor, while hunting below the mouth of Beaver, came upon two bears feeding. The former carried a rifle, while Tommy had a shot-gun. Mr. Kessler hadn't lost any bear and refused either to shoot or allow Tommy to use his rifle. As trees were not very handy, it was, perhaps a wise move, though Tommy even yet regrets that he did not turn loose with No. 6 shot.

The most of the outfits north of the track dropped out of the round-up when it reached Mingusville. Their places were more than filled by the outfits south of the track. The round-up is making rapid headway and will probably be back at Medora inside of a week. The cattle are in good fix and unless something unforeseen turns up, will pass through the winter with even less loss than there was last winter.

We stated incidentally once that the coal-bank at Mattox' ranch, on the old tie road, was about forty feet thick in sight and extended an unknown distance below the bed of Deep creek, on which it is located. We couldn't at the time have imbibed enough Dakota ozone as Mrs. Mattox has measured the vein and declares it is sixty feet in height from the top of the vein to the water in the stream. Western Dakota ought not to suffer with cold as long as it its foundation consists of such strata of coal.

It is hard to tell where the poetical muse will sometimes strike, and we publish the following self-explanatory verse on account of its authorship. Every local reader of the Cow Boy can give a good guess as to its origin:

To J. H.—
I lushed up and went on a racket,
Billy Smith, he gave me a steer,
They brought me before Judge Coburn,
Who immediately gave me five year.
He saw that my health was fast failing,
And mentioned the same there and then,
But he told me to get ready for calling
And go visit the boys in the pen.
I was met at the gate by the warden,
Who told me to banish my gloom,
For although the hotel was quite crowded,
He could manage to find me a room.
So they washed me, they clipped me, they shaved me,
They gave me a suit to begin,
Two blankets, a pillow and bucket,
And I commenced to keep rooms in the pen.
We get breakfast at six in the morning,
At seven we go on parade,
Our style is so grand and imposing,
It would rival the Irish brigade.
Corporal Conly then gave his orders:
"Keep step there, and close up, my men!
Or I'll skull drag you bold seventh warders
And banish you all from the pen."
We walk out in line in the morning,
And immediately go to our work,
And I pity the fellow caught talking,
Or the poor devil who offers to shirk.
You can show this to all of the boys,
And if you have a dear friend,
Just tell him to keep clear of Montana,
If he wants to keep out of the pen.
W. R.

Of all the dismal failures in the history of American politics, civil-service reform is the dismallest. The true heart and soul of politics always has been, is and ever shall be, spoils. The Democratic party nor the Republican party could either live through an election, if party leaders could not promise a distribution of patronage. This is so evident that even a child can see it and the spectacle of one party trying to perpetuate itself in power and the other trying to regain power through the transparent cry of "civil-service reform" would be amusing if it were not disgusting.

One effect of the prairie fires may be exactly opposite to what was expected. As is known, almost the whole country for a number of miles east of the Bad Lands has been burned. This drove the antelope both east and west from the burned district and now it is doubtful if those driven eastward will cross the burned country into the Bad Lands. If they do not, there will be far less, instead of more than formerly. It is now thought that a large number will winter in the Knife river and Killdeer mountain country.

The Northern Pacific, probably incited by the opposition of the Canadian Pacific on the north, the Union Pacific on the south and the Northwestern to the east, is leaving but little to be desired by cattlemen in the way of shipping stock. Every other detail of the freight traffic is made subservient to the one end of getting cattle through as quickly and in as good condition as possible. Passenger trains have even been side-tracked to wait for stock trains and not a minute is lost from the time the cattle are loaded until they are turned over to a Chicago road at St. Paul. We suppose the principal share of the credit, in connection with Mr. Hannaford, for this expedition, is due to Stock agent Wilson, than whom there is no one to whom we would sooner give it.

A curious reversal of "the eternal fitness of things" is seen in the fact that there are in twenty-two states, 308,478 more women than men. The greatest excess is in Massachusetts, where there are 66,205 more women. In all the Territories, except the District of Columbia, there is a large excess of men. In Dakota there is the largest excess of men, 29,415. In the whole of the United States, there are, according to the census of 1880, 24,636,963 women and 25,518,820 men. Thus we see that "hope may yet spring eternal" in the female breast for, in the United States and Dakota there is somewhere a manly heart and true for every husbandless female who considers it her "spear to cling." Maidens of Massachusetts, or at least about half of you, come to our arms, that is, to Dakota's arms and help our sturdy pumpkin-rollers starve to death or our bashful cowboys to round up the lean kine.

The monthly bulletin for September, of Lauren Dunlap, Commissioner of Immigration for Dakota, is at hand and reflects great credit on our worthy commissioner. The following is a resume of the Bulletin: The weather during September was extremely good all over Dakota, pleasant days being followed by cool nights. Dakota has nine stations for observing the weather and from their reports it is learned that the mean temperature for September was 57.26 degrees, the highest mean being 62.4 at Yankton and the lowest, 53.1 at St. Vincent. The rain-fall averaged 1.67 inches, the highest being 4.80 at St. Vincent, the lowest, .14 of an inch at Bismarck. Dakota's wheat yield for this year averages 96, as against 78 for Minnesota, 88 for Iowa and 77 for Wisconsin. Dakota's wheat crop this year is about 25,000,000 bushels, out of a total yield for the United States of 351,000,000 bushels. The Sioux Falls convention, for framing a constitution for Southern Dakota, is highly praised, too highly in fact when it comes to a question of a supposed-to-be neutral territorial officer advocating a measure that he knows is strongly opposed by at least half the territory of which he is an officer. $30,000 has been set aside for surveying 104 townships, the work to done before July 1, 1886. The contracts are to be let by the Surveyor General of Dakota to the lowest responsible bidders. There were 4,547,750 acres of land disposed of in Dakota during the last year, out of 20,113,663 for the United States. The military encampment at Fargo is spoken of and our soldiers come in for a large share of praise. There are at present about 450 miles of railroad under construction, the principal ones being the branch of the Northwestern from Chadron toward the Black Hills and the James river Valley road, between Jamestown and LaMoure. Dakota's first territorial fair was held at Huron, beginning September 29, and was a pronounced success. The stock exhibit is especially praised for its splendid showing. The report intimates that about half the Sioux reservation will be opened for settlement during the coming session of Congress, a consummation devoutly to be wished. Although we could wish that Mr. Dunlap was not so partisan in his championship of South Dakota, we can yet congratulate the Territory at large on having secured such an able and tireless worker as Mr. Dunlap for his present position.

Cattle Raising in Uruguay.

The republic of Uruguay is devoting itself to cattle raising on an extraordinary wholesale scale. One of the leading raisers, recently interviewed, has given the statistics. Eight million horned cattle, 20,000,000 sheep, and 1,500,000 horses constitute the stock in trade of this model but extensive pastoral republic. The export returns show what a heavy customer England continues to be. She takes 5 per cent. of the total exports, Brazil being debited to 20, France to 17, the United States to 11, and all others to the remaining 27. The country is most prosperous and the tide of immigration [steady?]; 20,221 last year. Women are, however, in an alarming minority, and constitute less than a quarter of the arrivals. Four thousand vessels sailed in the same year from the port of Montevideo, with a registered tonnage of over 1,500,000. Next come statistics about the cattle. The average novillo, the steer most used for fattening, gives 150 pounds of jerked beef, 68 pounds of salted hide, and 40 pounds of grease, and besides that there are the bone ash, the hair and the horns. Business is done on such a wholesale scale that everything is utilized. All his constituent parts thus counted up, and allowed for, the novillo brings in $20 a head, while the commission for bringing to the packers, the cost of killing and preparing for market is about $4, leaving the net proceeds at $16. It will be seen that such a business as this is necessarily extremely profitable. In the slaughter houses, called "saladeros," 500 cattle a day are killed. A lasso, one end of which is attached to a steam winch, is thrown over the horns of the victim and the winch set working; the beast is summarily hauled up against a bridge upon which stands the slaughter man, "who with a stab back of and between the horns with a large dagger-knife cuts the spinal cord, and the animal drops dead without a struggle."—[Chicago Tribune.

We are in receipt of a letter from Vic. Smith, written at his camp on the Meeteetse river in Wyoming, in which he announces that the Smith family is flourishing. Elk, he says, run in herds about their camp and keep them awake nights by their bugling. Mountain sheep are as plentiful as antelope near Medora. The Smith brothers have two tons of smoked elk meat, which they have already contracted at fifteen cents a pound. They will bring down with them about thirty-five elk heads and as many sheep heads. Bear have also been very plentiful and they will bring some choice robes. Raspberries and strawberries are plentiful near their camp. They will start on their return to Medora in about a week. Vic winds up his letter by saying that he will send us a bear head from Billings. Woe be unto him if he doesn't!

It has been so often said that it was difficult to hold or drive cattle in the Bad Lands that it had tacitly come to be understood that none could be shipped from here. This summer's experience has, if not entirely done away with this idea, at least modified it to a great extent. We do not know the exact figures but there have been in the neighborhood of 8,000 cattle delivered to the Ref. Car Co. here this summer. Out of all these not a solitary animal has been lost owing to the Bad Lands. This, of itself, is enough to disprove the prevalent belief, but we have besides, the expressions of opinion of the men who have delivered cattle here, that they experienced no more difficulty driving in the Bad Lands than they would on the prairie, with the same number of cowboys to drive. This is further shown by the fact that the Hashknife outfit have contracted the rest of their shipments for this season at Medora. These were the reasons that lead the railroad company to build the yards here and to expect that all the beef on the river will be shipped at Medora.
Avoid delay and possible loss in obtaining your winter reading by subscribing for any paper you may want at the Cow Boy office.
The party at the Metropolitan hotel last Thursday evening, was a gratifying success. With dancing and refreshments, the time pleasantly and quickly passed away until an early hour in the morning.

Conductor Garlick made the run from Sentinel Butte to Medora yesterday, seventeen miles, with eighteen cars of stock, in twenty minutes. If we mistake not, this is the best time on record between these points, with such a train.

Geo. E. Cole left for St. Paul yesterday to superintend the closing up of the St. Paul branch of the N. P. R. C. Co. All books and papers will be brought here and in the future, the business of the company will be transacted from Medora. Mr. Cole will be absent about a month.

L. C. Hunt, a recent graduate of the Law Department of the University of Michigan, arrived in Medora last week and will spend some time in the Bad Lands getting an insight into the cattle business. He is a friend of Lieut. Casey's and is now at the KC ranch.

Superintendent Green made us a pleasant call Monday. He was here to overlook the erection of the stockyards. He stated that there are no yards on the road where cattle can be so easily penned as at the Medora yards. When they round the butte at the brick-kiln, the cattle are hemmed in by the river on the left, the buttes and the wing of the yards extending to them on the right and the railroad in front. The yards are so planned that they can easily be enlarged, the need of which we join with Mr. Green in hoping will soon come to pass.

Col. Lounsberry, being interviewed in St. Paul, says that "of course" Gov. Pierce will be removed. In the face of the fact that Cleveland has said that there will be no removal, it looks as though Col. Lounsberry did not have a very high opinion of our President's veracity.

A man named James Gray, living four miles north of Glenullen, was last week attacked by a couple of Indians, probably from the Fort Stevenson agency and nearly killed. He struggled desperately for his life in a hand to hand conflict with both of them and finally drove them off and it is thought killed one. There should be no delay in finding out who these Indians are and bringing them to justice. A case of this kind allowed to pass unpunished, may sow the seeds of many murders. Instant and condign punishment for misdeeds is the proper way, to discipline Indians as well as whites.

County Organization.

Again has this become a subject of paramount interest from the fact that the rate of taxation on the recent assessment of Billings county by Stark is now known and is either twelve or thirteen mills on the dollar. This is the rate on an assessed valuation in Billings county of over $500,000. It takes but little figuring to show that, should the amount of this assessment be paid to Stark county, it will be over $6,000, enough in itself almost to run a county organization in Billings county on a liberal scale.

We have before spoken of county organization as an economical plan for the county and it would be well to again bring it forward in that light.

First as to the officers. There will be needed a sheriff, justice of the peace, assessor, county attorney, three commissioners, treasurer and register of deeds. All county business can be transacted by this number of officers as well as by a greater number.

Besides officers, the running expenses of the county are included in buildings, school and a few other expenses which are trifling. The whole will amount to about $1,200 a year.

The shersff's office will cost more than any other but ought not to go over $600 or $800 a year. Sheriff Sebastian of Stark county, says that his office will cost this year about $2,000. This probably includes five times the mileage and fees that a sheriff here will have, as Mr. Sebastian has made numerous trips into counties attached to Stark Co. which our Sheriff will not need to do. $600 should be abundant for this office. A justice of the peace will not cost over $100 a year, the assessor $100, the county attorney $150; three commissioners each, $150. $450; register of deeds, $150. The treasurer gets a certain per cent. for handling the county money, but nothing as a salary. His per cent. will probably amount to about $300. This makes a total for salaries of about $1,850 per year. To be on the safe side, call it $2,500, add the $1,500 for sundries and we have as an outside, $4,000 for the ordinary running expenses of the county.

And now, what resources have we to meet these expenses? In the first place, there is the railroad tax. With a mileage of twenty-four miles, it was estimated by County Attorney Long of Mandan, that we would receive $3,400. Since then our limits have been stretched so that we have thirty-six miles of rail-road with a consequent tax of over $5,000.

In addition to the rail-road tax, we have the liquor license, which is now $1,200. This amount, Morton county now receives, but of course it will stay in Billings county after organization.

This makes a total of $6,200 to pay the ordinary running expenses and not a cent raised by taxation.

The first year there will be extra expenses, such as books, safes etc., but scarcely enough to make up the difference between the running expenses and the $6,200.

Suppose now, we add the $6,000 which must certainly be paid to Stark county unless we organize soon and which of itself would be enough to pay the running expenses of the county. It will be raised on an assessment of $500,000, which with our increased boundaries and former undervaluation could easily be raised to $750,000 or more. This will almost all be a surplus and will erect good county buildings, grade roads, build bridges and then leave a handsome sum in the treasury.

In view of the above facts, the matter of organization is being seriously considered by the stockmen, as it cannot but result in good to all.

No definite action has as yet been taken in respect to county officers. but the names most prominently mentioned are J. L. Truscott, Jos. A. Ferris and Mr. Rowe of Rowe, Parker & Easton for commissioners, Fred Willard for sheriff, Wm. VanDriesche for treausurer and "Judge" Gordon for justice of the peace. The choice for commissioners would of course have been different but that our county has been enlarged by the changing of the territorial lines and it is thought best to give Beaver creek a representation. Of course all the names mentioned are subject to approval and we merely voice the common sentiment in mentioning them. They are all good men however, in whose hands no one will fear to entrust the welfare of the county and are every man of them above any suspicion of dishonesty.

J. A. VanEeghen has been west looking up desirable horses with which he will stock his Garner creek range next spring.

The worst black eye the cattle market has had this season, was received last week in Chicago. Native shipping and dressed beef cattle dropped 40@70c. and most grades of western cattle, 50@75c. The highest price received for Montana rangers during the week, was $4.15 and some scalawag cows sold at $1.00. Texas cattle about held their own. The receipts in Chicago last week were 45,500 as against 48,000 the week before. Foreign markets were weak and lower and exporters did but little business. The prices were a little steadier at the close of the week.

A case will come off in Dickinson tomorrow, that will be extremely interesting as involving a test case which it is for the interest of every stockman on the river to have decided; although there are none but will regret to see the case assume such prominence. It seems that during the progress of the round-up, an animal was found that besides a blotched brand, had also one of the brands of the Bad Lands Cattle Co. This brand was vinted by the round-up and the animal sold as a maverick. For this reason, suit has been brought for grand larceny. The case has an unfortunate side, as no one can believe that there was any intention of stealing on the part of any members while no one can blame Mr. Wadsworth for wanting to clear himself of the suspicion of having branded some other man's animal. It would probably have been better to have settled the matter by arbitration; but the law must now take its course.

The round-up came in to Medora Saturday and ended the work by rounding-up Andrew's creek on Sunday. Taking everything into consideration, the work was done as thoroughly as possible. The principal cause of complaint is that cattle were missed and that there will be an undue amount of mavericks in the spring. How true these reports are, only time will tell. There is no one who says that anyone shirked his duty. On the other hand, as all concur that every man worked hard, we are brought to the facts in the case: there were not enough men on the round-up. The complaint of a year ago last spring, that the riders were not well enough mounted, has almost disappeared. The complaint of too few men is as serious as that of too few or too poor horses and should be remedied as quickly. Round-up work is no "soft snap" and twenty-five men cannot do forty men's work any more than the best kind of a cow-boy, with a string of four or five poor horses can do one man's work. This is a matter that should be attended to at the next meeting of the association. The round-up lasted twenty-seven days and worked the Little Missouri and tributaries from below the mouth of Big Beaver on the north to the mouth of Little Beaver on the south and also the Big Beaver and its tributaries.

Rev. Father Paul arrived last night from Bismarck. He announces that hereafter there will be service in the Catholic church on the first Sunday of every month, beginning next Sunday. Services will begin at 9:30. In the afternoons at three o'clock, there will be catechistical instruction.

Herbert D. Hostetter of Pittsburgh, who has been visiting Howard Eaton for some time, accidentally cut himself in the foot a few days ago and is now in Glendive, under the care of Dr. Duncan. The hurt is not serious but will lay up the patient for some days.

John Munro has decided to again embark in the sheep business, this time on his own account. His ranch will probably be in the neighborhood of Mingusville. We wish Johnny only the best of success, but are sorry that the history of the sheep business in this country doesn't hold forth very bright promises for the future.

As the shooting contests of the Gun club were still unfinished and Seth Wyland, who was at the head of those who had completed their scores, started for a winter's hunting trip Monday, it was deemed best to give him the first prize. There were two contestants who had not finished their scores and who stood good chances of winning but as there had been too long a delay it was deemed the fair thing to make the above decision.

The Marquise is especially interested in having a school started here and has renewed her proposal to pay the teacher. The room recently vacated by Roberts & Co. will make a first-rate school-room. Nothing but a little effort on the part of the school board is now required to set things going. Several persons have objected, thinking it was the intention to start a Catholic school. We are assured that no such intention exists.

It is a good time now to mention that the petty thieving which has been going on whenever occasion offered, must come to a stop at once. There are at least two persons here who are known to possess this rustling spirit and who will be cinched to the limit the first time after this fair warning that they are caught stealing the value of a pin. A word to the wise is sufficient and ought to work on rustlers.

It is time that the new school board took action on the subject of holding a school this winter. The Marquise has already offered to pay the teacher's salary, an offer that may be withdrawn if some steps are not taken soon by the school board. There is no reason why the children here should not have as good educational facilities as is needed. The remaining expenses, beside the teacher, are trifling and could readily be raised by subscription. Brace up, honorable members of the school board!

In Memoriam.

DIED—Sunday morning, Oct. 25, of concussion of the brain, J. Hayes Moore.

The above notice comes like a shock to everyone in the Bad Lands. Hayes Moore was well known and liked here as a quiet, unassuming man who would go far out of his way to help anyone and who never had an enemy.

He was born in Steubenville, Ohio, the eldest son of Geo. D. and Lydia A. Moore and at the time of his death was thirty-eight years old. He came to this place in 1879 as clerk for his brother Frank, who at that time was sutler at the Cantonment. For the last two years he has been at the KC ranch on Garner creek.

The accident which caused his death occurred last Thursday at the mouth of Garner creek. He had gone on horseback to watch the progress of the round-up and having to move a little to avoid a herd of cattle, his horse stumbled and fell and in rolling over, struck Hayes just above the temple, knocking him insensible. He remained constantly in this state up to the time of his death, which occurred at 4:30 Sunday morning. The funeral took place Tuesday at twelve o'clock at the KC ranch. D. K. Wade officiated by reading the burial service and the remains were borne to their last resting-place on the summit of the high butte back of the ranch by the pall-bearers Messrs. Merrifield, Ferris, Myers, Bennett, Willis Eaton, Truscott, Elliott and Rowe.
The Marquise and hunting party returned from their hunt Monday. They had good success.
T. W. Gordon has received a large consignment of quilts and blankets, which he will sell at very reasonable figures.
Jos. Ferris started for St. Paul yesterday morning to lay in his winter stock of goods. He will be gone about a week.
Johnny Sawyer sustained a painful accident Saturday night in the dislocation of his shoulder. It was set by Dr. Robarts.
Before the winter's snows have whitened the ground very long, there will be at least two more marriages to record, or the Cow Boy is greatly mistaken.
J. H. Gilmore of Minneapolis, one of the owners of the "square 47" outfit, was in Medora Saturday, and left his brand, which will appear in the next issue of the Cow Boy.

The new stock-yards were broken in Saturday, by the shipment of three cars of cattle, two of 76 (monogram) bar and one of quarter circle diamond. Alden Eaton and Will Dantz accompanied them and will sell them in St. Paul, where small lots can be sold to better advantage than in Chicago.

Sheriff Sebastian of Dickinson, dropped into the Cow Boy office Tuesday, while in Medora on business. He has just returned from Canada on a successful search after the stock stolen from the Gallien Bros., at Belfield last summer. They had been confiscated from Wm. Roberts and Tommy Hughes as smuggled property and sold by the Canadian government. Roberts and Hughes were convicted of smuggling and each served six months in prison. Territory of Dakota, Executive Office.

In accordance with a long established custom the president of the United States has set apart Thursday, the 26th day of November as a day of national Thanksgiving and gratitude to Almighty God for his manifold blessings during the year.

The citizens of the territory have more than ordinary cause for thankfulness. Though ill fortune has attended some, the masses have been abundantly blessed.

Peace and plenty are upon the land and prosperity in all its borders.

It is a season for gratitude, for benevolence, for charity. It is the day for the prodigal to be welcomed, for differences to be reconciled, for injuries to be forgiven.

I recommend therefore that the day designated by the president, be observed throughout the territory by ceasing from toil and by appropriate services in church and home. Let kindly deeds towards the suffering and destitnte, and tender sympathy for those who are in sickness and trouble distinguish our observance of this gracious time. Forgetting the strifes and enmities of life let us open wide the doors of charity and good will, remembering that "One touch of nature makes the whole world kin."

Given under my hand and the great seal of the territory, this sixth day of November, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and eighty five.

Gilbert A. Pierce.

There are 24,705 men and 2,154 officers in the United States army. It certaiuly speaks well for our country that order is maintained here at less cost than any country on the globe of any considerable importance.

Captain Lee, acting agent of the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations telegraphed Commissioner Atkins that all cattle have been removed from the reservations, that thousands of cattle have been turned loose in Oklahoma and that a hundred and twenty boomers have been arrested.

Louis Riel was executed at Regina, N. W. T. on Monday. At present, only associated press reports are at hand and as they have all along been inimical to Riel only a one-sided story is told. The greatest care has been taken to guard against the escape of the prisoner and the execution was not public. It is difficult as yet to tell what the effect will be on the half-breed population but if they do not glorify him into a martyr and at some time again strike for their rights with "Remember Riel" as a battle cry, many prophecies will be unfulfilled. Riel was perfectly calm to the last and his death was instantaneous. He left no property but bequeathes blessings and good will to men.
Rassie Deffebach was in town Monday from the Bad Lands cattle Co's. ranch.
The dance at the Northern Pacific last Monday euening was well attended and everyone enjoyed themselves thoroughly until a late hour.
Frank Filbert was thrown from his horse last Monday and had his collar-bone broken and his shoulder badly smashed. The accident will probably lay him up for some time.
Willard & Keeler have as neat a meat-market as one would wish to see. Their advertisement, appearing in this issue, is an indication of the kind of stock they will keep on hand.
A brand-new brick-maker has appeared at the house of Peter Book. It put in an appearance Tuesday and by the way Pete is walking on clouds, it appears to be a very welcome arrival.

T. W. Gordon has received a stock of men's, ladies' and children's boots and shoes that for variety will compare favorably with any stock on the line. A call is sure to result in finding what you want.
The last delivery of Hashknife cattle occurred last Sunday morning, completing their contract with the Ref. Car Co. Sunday's delivery was five hundred and the average was 1050.

Jos. Ferris and J. C. Fisher have opened up a feed stable back of Ferris' grocery, to which they invite the attention of all. The best of care will be taken of all horses entrusted to their care, and an abundance of feed guaranteed.

Too late for last issue, we learned of the marriage of Jos. Knutson to Miss Anderson of Belfield. The wedding took place in Belfield at the home of the bride's parents. The most cordial expressions of good-will follow the newly married couple from their many friends. They are now keeping house at the Knutson creek ranch.

There were three suspicious characters lurking about on the river lately, and it was thought that they were horse-thieves. No horses are known to be stolen and although there has been considerable talk on the subject, we doubt if the men took any. For a long time, no horses have been stolen in the Bad Lands and a horse-thief must be considerable of a tenderfoot to ply his vocation here.

The management of the Southern Pacific Railroad instructed the section hands to make note of the marks and brands of cattle killed along the line of that road. An Aberdeen-Angus steer, owned by J. J. Hill of St. Paul, took first prize at the Chicago Fat stock show over all competitors. There is no question that the Aberdeen-Angus are at least the equal of any cattle in beef-making qualities. When we add to this their shaggy coat impenetrable to cold, their gentle disposition, their inability to harm one another owing to lack of horns and their rustling disposition only equalled by Texas cattle, it requires no prophet to fore-tell that they are the range cattle of the future. They are making more rapid headway in public opinion than any breed has done heretofore and a very strong point in their favor is that every owner immediately becomes an enthusiast.

Last Tuesday we received a visit from M. Wadsworth, Manager of the Bad Lands cattle Co., who wished the following facts published, in answer to the communication in last week's Cow Boy: When this animal in question, together with a number of others was originally branded, the work was done hurriedly and as a consequence, many were branded too deeply. The brands on twenty or more suppurated badly and the animals were kept up for better care. The particular animal in question was kept for a long time at the home ranch corrall and on account of the care it required, became well-known to several persons. The brand not only suppurated freely, but worms got in under the skin, and necessited cutting it several times. Of course this, together with the suppuration, blotched the brand. The reason the animal was not claimed this spring was that Mr. Wadsworth's representatives who saw the animal when it was caught up were new men and unacquainted with the facts. Frank Filbert, who was with the round-up, knew the animal and all the circumstances of the branding, but did not happen to be present when the animal was caught up. This was the reason she was not claimed at the spring round-up. During his own beef round-up this summer, Mr. Wadsworth, seeing the animal, had her branded again, as he considered he had a perfect right to do, knowing the animal so well. With reference to his manner of settling the case, he says it is very manifest that some one is in the wrong and he wants the result of this wrong-doing to be finally settled, as no committee on arbitration would legally have the power to do. He is perfectly willing to suffer for any wrong he has done and wants the blame settled in a final manner.

Frank Moore returned from St. Paul last Thursday, where he sold the KC cattle for $3.65.
Charlie Bronson writes us from Chadron that he is doing well there and that the town is booming.
Jos. O'Brien is in Buffalo Gap, a new town on the Black Hills branch of the Northwestern. He has a black-smith shop, but the business there is over-done and he contemplates moving.
T. G. Jones, well known here is now in Spearfish with John Guild, the backer of the Hay creek coal road. It looks as though that project may develop eventually.

Charlie Eaton writes from Pittsburgh that he is enjoying himself hugely and will stay some time longer in the Smoky City. By the way, it changes the subject, but this name is likely to prove a mis-nomer to Pittsburgh, as the introduction of natural gas for fuel has already decreased the smoke fifty per cent.

Jack Matlock writes us from Lavina, Montana, where he is driving on the stage line between Billings and Fort Benton. He says that he has a forty-mile drive through a fine agricultural and stock country. There is plenty of water and as fine timber as one would want in the Bull mountains. Money is plenty there and Jack has his share.

As we have a constitutional objection to working on a National holiday, the Cow Boy, barring accidents, will appear next Wednesday instead of Thursday. The editor-in-chief, business manager, associate editors, reporters, foreman, printers and his Satanic Majesty will all take a holiday to eat Thanksgiving turkey.

Nothing has been heard of J. B. Walker and all his goods that he left have been seized by the sheriff to satisfy executions issued against them for unpaid labor bills. The sale is to come off on the 25th. of this month. Numerous other unpaid bills have come to light, making the amount of his indebtedness in the neighborhood of $2,000.

A letter received from A. C. Huidekoper expresses his strong opinion that the future of horse-raising in this country is a bright one, especially with high-priced horses. Next summer he intends putting up a barn at the Logging camp like the one at the Deep creek horse ranch. Such expressions of confidence, coming from a keen business man and practical stockgrower like Mr. Huidekoper mean much for the future of the Bad Lands.

Fred. Ertel, well-known on the line of the Northern Pacific is making a great success of his pictorial paper, "The St. Louis Whip." It is gotten up in "Puck" style and some of the hits are as good as any we have seen. Notably the cartoons on Cleveland ordering the cowmen off the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations and the appeal of the Territories for admission into the Union, which now adorn the walls of the Cow Boy office.

We have refrained from remarks on Rev. Mr. Schaffner of Dickinson, hoping that we could find some good to say. During his many visits here, he did not impress our people favorably. He was too much "on the make." A ministers ruling passion should by no means be a love of gain but Mr. Schaffner's certainly was. Lately he had another fight with a neighbor on account of which his bondsmen went back on him. Deputp Sheriff Drury arrested him, but gave him considerable freedom in searching for new bondsmen, on his solemn promise not to escape. His solemn promise seemed to have little effect for it looks now as if he had skipped the country. We suggest that the officers look for him in his old home in Canuckland.

S. G. Miller of New York and a representative of New York capitalists arrived Tuesday night and is awaiting the return of the Marquis from his hunting trip down the river. He is here to look up the feasibility of building a rail-road to the Belle Fourche, where the plan must be to connect with the prospective Hay creek coal road. The New York capitalists are in earnest about the road and a favorable report from Mr. Miller will probably set the project in motion. The Northern Pacific is actively interested in the plan and will give it every encouragement. For many reasons, we would not be at all surprised if we would inside of two years, have direct railroad connections with the Black Hills.

Two of the petitions for county organization are now in, containing more than enough names, according to law, for the organization of the county. The petition for down the river is not yet in, but is known to contain a goodly number of names. No names have as yet been secured from the Beaver creek country as it is not certain where the territorial line runs. The sentiment there is, however, entirely in favor of organization. The manner of organizing counties was changed last winter as follows: The number of signatures on the petition must be 150 instead of fifty. The Governor is then authorized to appoint two officers of the senior county, in our case this is Morton Co., who shall divide the county into voting precincts and appoint three judges of election who shall divide the county into commissioners districts and appoint a day for the general election of county officers. All this will take some time and the work cannot be delayed.
HENDRICKS DEAD. The Vice-President died at 1 o'clocd yesterday.

INDIANAPOLIS IND., Nov. 25.—Vice-President T. J. Hendricks died very suddenly at one o'clock this afternoon at his home, of paralysis of the heart.

The above telegram puts a curious phase on American politics. There being a Republican senate, a Republican Vice President will doubtless be elected. Should this man be Senator Logan, an anamoly would arise, unparallelled in American history. In case then President Cleveland should not survive his term of office, we would really have a Republican administration and in any event the fact of our having a Republican Vice President with a Democratic administration is a curious enough circumstance to set political prophets all guessing.

We are in receipt of the fourth monthly Bulletin, by Commissioner of Immigration Dunlap. Amongst other valuable information, it contains the following: The weather has been highly favorable all over the Territory. The mean temperature for the nine weather stations has been about forty-three degrees; eighty degrees during the day-time and a little over eighteen at night making very enjoyable weather. There have been slight falls of snow at all stations except Yankton. The average of wheat to the acre in Dakota is 14.5 bushels, being the highest of any state or territory, Minnesota coming next with 11.5 bushels. There were 1136 homestead and pre-emption entries during October, an increase of 224 over September. The Governor's annual report to the secretary of the Interior is complimented, especially the part in reference to admission and division. The bonded debt of the territory is $568,200. The last legislature authorized a loan of $176,000, and the bonds were sold at 103.2, a splendid showing for Dakota's credit. The question of opening the Sioux, Winnebago and Crow creeek Indian reservations is spoken of and commissioner Dunlap thinks it will not be long before they will be opened. With this number of the bulletin comes a map of Dakota, revised to date, and probably the most accurate map of our Territory ever published. There are the usual inaccuracies concerning land-marks in the unsurveyed portions of western Dakota, but the surveyed portions are correct. Any person wishing the Bulletin, the map and O. H. Holt's pamphlet on Dakota can get them by sending their names and three cents in postage to Lauren Dunlap, Huron, Dakota.

A sensational report has been telegraphed broad-cast by the Associated Press, that Wyoming cattlemen not only refuse to remove fences enclosing public lands but are building others, the President's order to the contrary notwithstanding. There can be little doubt that foundation is almost or wholly lacking for this report and that it is only one more of the many petty devices originated by eastern feeders whose profits are cut down by the range cattle industry, to turn public opinion against western cattlemen. The life and soul of the range cattle business is obedience to the law, both written and unwritten, and cattlemen too well understand this to disobey any law or executive order. The report on the face of it, is false. It may be that the charge is true in the case of one or two, and from this it has spread so as to involve all the Wyoming cowmen. Cattle associations should look to it that the originators of such criminal libels are punished to the full extent of the law.
