The bulls of the quarter-circle diamond, LC and Maltese cross outfits, to be fed this winter at the Big Plateau, are now in good fix and will probably go through the winter in the same condition.

Reports are already coming in from the Cave Hills country to the effect that cattle are being killed there by wolves. The E6 outfit last year offered liberal inducements to hunters for poisoning wolves and the offer probably still holds good. If the ranches would all combine in offering liberal terms for wolf scalps, the result would be a great saving.

The Nationl Cattlegrower's Association held their third annual meeting in Chicago last week Tuesday and Wednesday, too late for a report in the Cow Boy. Norman J. Coleman, Commissioner of Agriculture, read a long and interesting paper in which he mentioned some very interesting statistics relative to the cattle business. In 1850 there was an average of 776 cattbe to every thousand inhabitants. In 1860 there were 814 to the thousand and in 1880 there were 716 to the thousand. In the United States there is an average consumption of meat of 150 pounds per capita, in Great Britain 109 pounds [and?] in Italy only eighteen pounds. Upon report of the committee on organization, Maj. H. E. Alvord of Mountainville, N. Y. was elected president. The association adopted a resolution asking Congress to appropriate not less than $1,500,000 to pay for diseased cattle which were slaughtered and for the payment of experts who should settle the value of cattle thus slaughtered.

The following is the St. Louis Whip's version of Sitting Bull's application for membership in the National Cattlemen's Association:

SECRETARY ATWATER:—

I am thinking of joining the national cattlemen's association and write to ask if I am eligible I own a steer, a calf, three dogs and a buffalo skin. Next year I want to invest in a cat and a tame coon and make better provision for raising stock. It is proper to state, however, that I cannot undertake to attend the cattlemen's ball in full dress and will insist on fixing up my costume to suit my own taste. I always dress with severe simplicity. A buffalo round-about and a pair of raw-hide knee-breeches constitute my full dress suit, which I would use in attending the cattlemen's ball. I would likewise insist on taking my own grip in dancing with the girls; when I waltz, I seize my partner by the hair with both hands and whirl around. The steps which I adopt in dancing are entirely original and were invented by myself.

Yours truly,
SITTING BULL.

Westward bound, I entered the Bad Lands after dark. This was a fortunate circumstance, for it left the grandeur of the scenes to be a surprise when morning's light should reveal them. Stopping at Medora, I walked out quite early in the morning to see the town from the eminence behind it. Making a circuit of half a mile I was able to ascend the steep incline. A plateau as level as an Iowa hay-field, and quite like one in appearance, stretches before me, and the eye passes from this flat surface to another beyond, and the valley wherein the town lies is not revealed. A two minute's walk takes me across this plateau and brings me to the brink of the precipice and to a scene of surpassing lovliness. Down in the valley lies the town, a toy city, 300 feet below. The most conspicuous object is the group of buildings comprised in the slaughtering establishment of the Marquis de Mores. It is in reality a huge affair, but appears small indeed from so great a height. Some workmen were singing there, and up through the still morning air came faintly and intermittingly the strains of "Climbin' up de Golden Stair." Across the valley and upon a plateau about fifty feet above the town, was the residence of the marquis, with its green sides and red roof; the palace of the village. The riv-
er ran its tortuous course like a band of silver through the town and beyond the cliffs. At the foot of the bluff, upon the summit of which I stood, miners were boring through a nine-foot vein of lignite coal, with which the country abounds while but fifty feet above the tunnel, smoke was issuing from another vein, which was on fire and had been burning for no one knows how long. Soon the hills began to echo the rumbling of the passenger train from the west, and then the locomotive rounded the spur of a bluff and brought after it a long train that bended and twisted and turned as it moved slowly (it seemed slowly from so [great a?] distance) down the valley at the foot of the bluffs.

Six or eight miles from Medora are the burning mines, of which every one has heard so much. I determined to see them, and engaging a conveyance and a guide, we set out. We rode a "buckboard," and nothing but a "buckboard" would have remained upright. Our mustangs took us up hills and down declivities, our vehicle tipped first to one side and then to the other, until it seemed as though nothing could tip it over. My guide was "frum Californy," and didn't like this country, and so would soon return. He told me we might see some deer, and once when upon an eminence his trained eye discerned an animal on a distant plateau. I leveled my field glass and discovered a deer lying down, secure from intrusion, however, because of the gullies between us and him. Cedar Canon is well described by its name. A long series of gullies, whose depths are a tangle of bushes and cedar trees, whose sides are the sides of buttes that rise hundreds of feet and terminate in a point, buttes that are table lands and have little hay fields for their tops, buttes that take the shapes of beasts and men, buttes that rise in terraces, buttes that have been mixed with others and tossed about indiscriminately, buttes that behave themselves and stand as orderly as soldiers, buttes that rise in conscious majesty above the common herd, buttes that crouch with modesty in the shadow of the monarchs, buttes with their heads shaggy in their coverings of cedars, buttes as bald as billard balls, slender little buttes that tip their heads coquettishly, and try to flirt with the clumsy, corpulent buttes across the way, ambitious buttes that fail in their attempt to be dignified because they are so small, Indian buttes that take on all the colors they can find, the green of the cedars, the red of the [scoria?], the gray of the clay and the [yellow?] of the sand, buttes fantastic, grotesque, buttes plain, commonplace. These were the hills I saw in Cedar Canon. It was wildly beautiful, and an adequate description demands a more eloquent pen than mine.

The burning mines were the objective point of the trip, and after many ups and downs, twists and turns, we at last reached them. We smelled the sulphur of the burning coal from afar, and as we approached, the hot air rose from the place just as I have seen it often from the mouth of a furnace in which iron was being melted. There was little smoke, though I am told that at times great volumes ascend. On one side of the butte was a depression, in the center of which was the greatest heat, and with this spot as a center there were innumerable cracks in the lines of concentric rings, formed as the earth sank in the center. These cracks ranged from a few inches to a foot or more in breadth, and the center was an undefined opening. Placing one of my feet over one of the outer cracks it was quickly warmed and I thought how great an improvement this would be over the ordinary method of warming by hot air registers. Approaching cautiously nearer the center, I threw into one of the orifices a handful of grass, and it blazed and was consumed within eight feet of my hand. If such is the heat at the surface, what must it be at the center, in the heart of the burnihg hill!

This was a very easy lesson in geology, and I saw right there the process nature had adopted to form the Bad Lands. Along the streams that years and years ago flowed across the country, drift-wood accumulated in immense quantities. Then followed a long period in which sediment, sand, gravel and dirt, was deposited, and the wood was buried two or three hundred feet deep. This drift-wood in time became coal, which by spontaneous combustion or electricity was ignited. As it burned, the deposits above fell into the cavities where the coal had been, and the depressions were widened and deepened by rains and winds. This, at least, is the theory of scientists; and it is very reasonable. Where the coal veins remain unburned the buttes are lofty and often their tops are plateaus on a level with the country on both sides of the Bad Lands. Very many of the buttes show on their summits unmistakable signs of heat. They are as red as burned bricks and the scoria, or burned clay, has an appearance very similar to broken bricks. Many of the prominences are surmounted with great formations best described by the name "clinkers," almost exactly in appearance like the "clinkers" everybody has seen in the ashes of bituminous coal. These have assumed fantastic and sometimes startling shapes, one reminding me of a blanketed Indian, another of the human face and still another of a crouching animal. Fragments of these formations roll down the sides of the buttes and are encountered everywhere.

—[C. W. Wilcox in Minneapolis Tribune.

The pay car passed through Tuesday.
Bob. Roberts started Tuesday for the Black Hills. He will be absent several weeks.
Messrs. E. G. and Billy Paddock, Fisher and McGregor are down the river on a hunting trip.
C. A. Spurling formerly operator at Little Missouri, is now agent for the Northwestern at Bruce, Dak.
A grand ball is to be given at Dickinson this evening by the firemen of the Missouri Division.
Wm. VanDriesche has made another addition to his flock of pigeons, by the purchase of a pair of beautiful fan-tail doves.
Supt. Green passed through Medora yesterday morning in his new car, which is now one of the handiest on the road.
Route agent Stedman of the Wells-Fargo express Co., was here this week, looking after the interests of the company he so ably represents.
M. G. Hall, for a long time Ass't. Sup't. of the N. P. Express Co. has resigned his position to take the agency of the same company at St. Paul.
Henry Bennett recently killed a fine silver-tipped bear at the mouth of Magpie creek. The most of them are now hived up in winter quarters.
Norman G. Dakin, a boy-hood friend of the editor, made us a pleasant call Tuesday night. He is travelling for the Bissell plow Co. of South Bend, Ind.
The petitions for county organization have been pronounced sufficient by Governor Pierce and progress will be made as fast as the law allows.
W. G. Taylor left on yesterday's train to accept an agency on the Fremont, Elk Horn & Missouri Valley railroad. R. J. Curran of Miles City takes his place here as day operator.

Howard Eaton reports that the Indian band who were thought to have left for their reservation, are still down the river. They are back in the Bad Lands and since the party went down the river to remove them, have caused no trouble.

The Marquis returned Monday from his hunting trip down the river. He had good luck with deer and antelope, but did not succeed in getting a mountain-sheep or bear. He leaves in a couple of weeks for New York, to be gone until the last of February.

It is rumored that the new house now going up by the Catholic church, will soon be occupied by C. F. Ellison and wife. We hope the rumor will prove correct as Medora is in need of just such young business men as Mr. Ellison.

And now it is Fred Banan's turn to cast single blessedness behind him and enter upon married life. Miss Georgiana Jordan is the happy bride and together, the newly married couple are sure of the happiness so earnestly wished them by all their friends. The ceremony takes place at Dickinson to-day.

The sale of J. B. Walker's effects took place yesterday morning in the hall building. Everything sold at a high price and enough was realized to pay the labor bills. It was rumored that Walker had been seen in Helena, but as he had attractions in the east, he is probably there now.

There is scarcely any diminution in the number of people suffering from small pox in Canada and in several places the disease is spreading across the line. A few cases have been reported along the line of the N. P. in Dakota. In view of these facts it behooves every man, woman and child to be vaccinated and that immediately. A slight cost and a temporary inconvenience are liable to save many lives.

Considerable game is brougt in by hunters and shipped east. Owing to the low price in St. Paul, however, none of the hunters are making anything. The game is also getting scarce in contrast with former years and the hunters have to earn every cent they make. We learn that immense quantities are being shipped from Dickinson and other points along the line and this supply, together with that killed in Minnesota, keeps the St. Paul market flooded.

About the only instance on record in which mountain sheep have been herded, occurred recently on the Yellowstone divide. A flock were found on top of a high butte to which there was but one ascent, by the cook of a hunting party. He had no gun and there being no other person in camp, he jumped on a horse and by a little riding, kept the flock on the butte for several hours, until one of the hunting party returned when three of the sheep were killed. To those who know the nature of mountain sheep, the idea of herding as mentioned is about as unique as herding a flock of wild geese.

S. G. Miller, mentioned in our last issue as being here in the interests of a railroad project from Medora to the Hills, started east yesterday morning and will go into Deadwood via Chadron, he being afraid of the trip across country from here. Nothing was decided about the road before he left, but he is more firmly convinced than ever that the plan is not only feasible but will result in large profit to the builders. In the course of time there will surely be a branch of the Northern Pacific running into the Hills and we expect to see it start from Medora.
Monday, it looked as though winter was almost at hand, but now the prophets think we will have more good weather.

Mrs. James Wishart, wife of the well-known freighter, and who drove a string-team with the grace of a true mule-skinner, died a short time since in Deadwood. She was here several times last summer with her husband.

Before the next issue of the Cow Boy every person who is delinquent will receive a notice to that effect, except those getting their mail at this office. Prompt returns are hoped for as our rates are cash in advance. Those on the home list who are delinquent will call at the office and settle. We hope each delinquent will make a point of remitting as soon as he receives his bill.
Another revolution is in progress in Mexico, Manuel Rodriguez is the leader.
Jay Gould has decided to entirely abandon all stock speculation and except for his interests as an investor in many concerns, will turn over his whole business to his son.

A man named Hopkins has invented a telephone on an entirely new principle by which the sound of the voice can be transmitted as far as a telegram can be sent. It bids fair to run the Bell and other telephones out of the market.

Chicago reminds one constantly of Griffin's Irishman who "wanted the earth and some of the outside." She is now making preparations to hold a World's Fair there in 1892, the anniversary of the discovery of America, and will probably succeed in her endeavor.

Ada Sweet, the Chicago pension agent who created such a flutter some time since by refusing to resign and wrote a severe letter signing herself "Ada Sweet, Spinster," was married recently to a man named Carter. Remarks from Puck, to the effect that it was a Sweet thing to do to Cartor away off there, are now in order.

New York, for its size, is the stingiest city on the face of the globe. Bartholdi presented his immense statue to her and they have not succeeded in raising money to buy a pedestal. Not long ago they were going to build a $1,000,000 monument to Gen. Grant. They have succeeded, mostly through outside subscriptions, in raising the beggarly sum of $10,000 and there the project is likely to end. Chicago was scarcely a week in raising $50,000 for a monument fund.

The Black Hills Times is the only southern Dakota paper that dares tell the exact truth in reference to the true animus that actuates the prime movers in the statehood movement for South Dakota. Try to smooth over the matter as they will, the papers of southern Dakota must admit that the prominent leaders in their statehood movement and their present candidates for offices in their hoped-for state are in almost every case, chronic office-seekers and professional politicians. It is refreshing to see the Times nail the banner of truth to its mast-head and tell the truth about the whole matter. Show us a prominent mover in this statehood movement and we will show you a man who is preparing to warm his heels in some snug political berth. Show us a professional politician and we will instruct the house-wives of his neighborhood that it is unsafe for them to leave their washing out at night. To one who has seen anything of the all-absorbing selfishness and total lack of principle evinced by the average Dakota politician, the high-minded and patriotic stand those of the south take in attempting to form their new state, is so gauzy as to be ludicrous. The sole reason in their minds for wanting to make two states of Dakota, is to double the number of offices and consequently giving each politician twice as great a chance of securing one. Dakota admitted as a whole, will at once take a prominent position in the sisterhood of states. As two states, we would always be at the Rhode Island end. The recent election in the southern half of Dakota brought out only a fractional vote, showing the lack of interest there in the statehood movement and we fully believe that the whole vote would show a majority against division even in southern Dakota. The full vote of the Territory would show an enormous majority against division.

Granville Stewart represents Montana and D. T. Whiteside, Dakota as vice-presidents of the National cattle and horse-grower's association, until the new officers of the consolidated associations are elected in Chicago, next November.

The cattlemen of the two National associations, with headquarters respectively at Chicago and St. Louis, did a very sensible thing by consolidating. The new association is to be called the "Cattle Growers' Association of the United States" and the annual meetings will be held in Chicago.

The range business, it would seem, has another sin to answer for and it is one which affects everybody. It appears that by improper branding, thousands of hides are so injured that they are comparatively worthless. It is estimated that the loss from this source alone at Chicago is $2,000,000 a year and that throughout the entire country it will reach $5,000,000. But considerable leather that is damaged in this way gets into the leather articles that we use and of course is not so serviceable.. The cattlemen say that they cannot remedy the evil. They must brand and practically as they do now to protect their property. They cannot, they say, use smaller brands, for they could not be distinguished in rounding up. They cannot brand on a less valuable part of the hide, for the brand would not be prominent enough. That may all be true, but it does not help the tanners or the purchaser of an imperfect leather article. Five million dollars, too, is a pretty high cost for a method and to save that, ought to be sufficient motive to attempt to devise some less objectionable means to reach the desired end. But there is one fact that is plain enough to anyone who will examine these branded hides. Many of them are not properly done. They show that they have been done either by somebody who did not care how he did it or by somebody who was mad when he did it. The depth of the brand is often powerfully suggestive that the brute who did the work, became angry with the animal for some reason, and branded for punishment. In one conclusion all will agree and that is that there is no necessity of burning the animal clear through. A little sense and humane feeling would do much [to?] modify the evil complained of.

The above article, from the Western Rural, is in the main written in a fair spirit, but throughout, it shows the inaability common to all eastern writers, of putting themselves in the place of the cattlemen and looking at the matter from a range stand-point. The simple facts are as follows: A man's brand is his signification of ownership. According to range law, it is impossible for a man to claim an animal unless his brand is on it. As a natural consequence a man wants his brand to be as plain as possible. Another reason for wanting the brand plain, is that probably millions of dollars are saved yearly in word being sent concerning strays, as a ready means of identification when stolen, as a virtual insurance against theft if the brand is large and distinct, and in many other ways. The whole matter resolves itself to this: An unbranded animal can be claimed by no one, while the chances are that even should a well-branded animal stray a thousand miles from the home ranch, the owner will be as safe in finally getting full value for it as if he had kept it constantly in his barn. The Rural must remember that the range cattleman does not by any means see his cattle every day or every week or even every year. A plain brand, however, makes his ownership as secure as if they were constantly in sight. The Rural must also remember that tanners cut but a small figure in range profits; immeasurably less than the loss would be if animals were not branded. Then also, the question arises, will animals branded with a small brand or none at all, bring a higher price in the Chicago yards than those well branded? We have the answer from a man who is not only a practical tanner, owning one of the largest tanneries in New York state, but is also a large owner of range cattle, that the beef-producing qualities of an animal are alone taken into consideration by the buyer and proves his belief by branding with two large brands that about cover the side of the animal. Again, the cowmen are no more responsible for tanners using these damaged hides than they are for the grocer putting chicory in his coffee. He sells the carcass and the hide goes with it. Finally, let the Rural find some better plan than branding as a means of identification and we will guarantee that there will be a perfectly unanimous and willing change to it. No one appreciates the bad qualities of the present branding system more than the stockmen themselves.

Black polled cattle have been bred in Scotland for hundreds of years, but no effort was made to improve them before 1700. Since that time, they have gradually grown in popular favor. At the Paris exposition in 1878, they were awarded first premium for best cattle of any breed and also championship prize for best group of beef-producing breeds. The first polled Scot introduced into this country was imported in 1872 and the demand for them is now so great that their yearly importations exceed that of any other breed. Most of these importations have been distributed among the western states, Missouri at present, having the largest number. Black polled cattle are divided into two classes, Aberdeen Angus, bred in northern Scotland and Galloways in southern. There are no very distinct points of difference in the two breeds. They are a hardy, fine boned, early-maturing race of cattle. Their hornless condition has contributed much to make them popular, for it is a [noticeable?] fact that stockmen are com[ing?] to consider horns as useless appendages and [illegible] shipping and stabling cattle. As a beef-producing breed, they are unsurpassed. In London, England, they command two cents a pound more than other beef. As a dairy breed, they excel many of the prominent horned breeds. They give a fair yield of very rich milk.—[Rural and Stockman.

In some portions of the range country a mistaken notion has prevailed in regard to [illegible]ing cheap southern cattle. It was argued by some that if the price of young cattle in the south was depressed the margin to the drover or the purchaser from the north, who went south to buy would be increased to the amount of the depression in the south. Results have proven this a fallacy. The blockading of the drives the past season and the quarantine against Texas cattle from below the thirty-fourth parallel caused a shrinkage of over $5 per head on all classes of Texas cattle, but in sympathy with this decline values have gone off equally as much all along the line from Texas to Montana. And this will always be the rule. There is a sympathetic connection between values of any article of traffic which is as certain and true as the magnetic needle. Commerce is argus-eyed, and at once discovers the means for restoring any temporarily disturbed equilibrium in trade or values.

A very large per cent. of the cattle on the northern ranges have been graded up from Texas cows. In 1881 there was a large drive from Oregon and Washington territory, and since that time a good many young cattle and some cows have been shipped in from Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri and a few other states. These "pilgrim" cattle from the east have not shown as ready adaptation to range life as the western and Texas imports, and the tendency is rather to discourage the traffic in them. Raised on the pitchfork, so to speak, they know nothing of self-dependence, and when the winter storm strikes them they naturally look for man's help, and fail to "rustle" for themselves. On the contrary, the western and southern cattle for generations have had to make their own provision for winter, and are always found rustling for something to eat. But the southern cattle are of light weight, and as increased weight means increased profits, northern ranchmen have for years been buying high grade bulls from the east and grading up their herds. The native cattle today on all the northern ranges are as good or perhaps a little better than half-breeds. Shorthorns and Herefords are, as a rule, the improved breeds used, and our three and four-year-old steers weigh from 1,100 to 1,300 pounds in the Chicago market.

This makes a very profitable animal when the markets are not broken by too large receipts, and the question is being generally discussed among ranchmen as to whether the herds are not sufficiently graded up to be safe and profitable. A few herd owners claim that a thoroughbred animal will sustain as much hardship and do as much rustling for food as the scrub or grade, but the general opinion is that the rustling qualities belong to the scrub, and that grading up means a larger carcass at the expense of the ability to endure the necessary hardships of our northern winters. The practical point to determine is, how high can we grade without losing the self sustaining qualities? Large, well-shaped and weighty cattle are desirable, but if the mortality is increased beyond the gain in size, the improvement is a mistake. Sufficient experiment has not yet been made to definitely determine this point. Present information leads to the opinion that in time there will be established a fixed type of range cattle: something better than a half-breed Shorthorn or Hereford, but developed by a blending of beef breeds. The Swiss cattle have been produced in this way, and they are a very good "all purpose" animal. No particular strain of blood can be traced in them, yet they are uniform in characteristics. With a range animal built up after a good model, uniform in size, containing all the improved blood consistent with a retention of the "rustling" qualities would tend to create a more uniform market. At present the periodical breaks in the beef market are caused by the sending in of unripe animals, or those that are ill-shaped in undue proportion. Uniformity in size and appearance will do much to maintain evenness in market values. There is room for marked improvement in many ways touching range management, but perhaps the most important is the one above named, for securing the best animal, and then ascertaining how to hold on to the proper type.—[Texas Stockman.

Before tee next issue of the Cow Boy every person who is delinquent will receive a notice to that effect, except those getting their mail at this office. Prompt returns are hoped for as our rates are cash in advance. Those on the home list who are delinquent will call and settle. We hope each delinquent will make a point of remitting as soon as he receives his bill.
Go to the Drug Store for jewelry, silver plated ware, etc.
If you are in need of a good tea-set either in figured gold or china, H. M. Jorgens can fit you out.
H. M. Jorgens has just opened up a complete stock of crockery and glassware. Now is your time to purchase.
The Marquis started for New York Tuesday morning, to be gone until the latter part of February. He expects to visit France before his return.
The sale of Jack Bullion's ponies took place Monday forenoon. Sixteen were sold altogether, averaging about twenty dollars each. The price was lower than expected.

Congrtulations are in order and for the last week have been showered on James Butler and wife. Their Thanksgiving present was in the shape of a thirteen-and-a-half pound baby boy. Mother and son are doing finely.
Christmas is coming and you can get anything you want in the way of presents of H. M. Jorgens.

From all quarters come favorable reports as to the condition of stock. The cattle in the Bad Lands are all in good condition at present and for the most part, will winter well. Prairie fires and the over-crowding of ranges will in some cases make a scant supply of feed, but the cattle will drift enough to regulate this.

H. M. Jorgens wishes to announce to the public that he has connected with his business a gift enterprise. Buying three dollars' worth of fancy goods, notions or jewelry entitles you to a number in the gift enterprise. Every number draws a prize varying in price from ten cents to ten dollars.

The case of Geo. Fitzgerald against Gregor Lang was settled yesterday by the latter buying the former's brand. This was altogether better than going to law on the subject, as the matter throughout was a mistake, there being no suspicion of criminal intent.
The Drug store is the place to buy anything you want in the way of fancy goods or notions.
The hunting party we spoke of last week, consistsng of Messers Fisher, Paddock and McGregor, came back laden with thirteen deer and eighty-five prairie chickens.
Dr. Jorgens has received some fresh vaccine virus and everyone should make a point of being vaccinated immediately. A simple operation now may save your life.
Miss Jennie Macbeth left for her home in Mankato, Minn., yesterday morning. She is followed by the regards of a wide circle of friends and wishes for her return are numerous.

Remember that you can buy your fancy goods and notions as cheap at the Drug store in Medora as you can anywhere this side of St. Paul. Besides this you may draw a prize to exceed the value of the goods.

Although it is rather doubtful, there may be some one whose name has not been mentioned for an office. If so let him see to it that the ommission be corrected. We may as well be unanimous about the thing.
Politics are the all-absorbing topic apparently and we have heard a number of tickets proposed. We are still in favor of the one we published in the Cow Boy some time ago.

A letter from the Govenor seems to indicate that our county will be organized about the middle of January. He promises to take immediate steps in the matter and a call for an election will soon be issued.

The dance given Thanksgiving evening at the Maltese cross ranch is still a topic of conversation. Everyone who went had a splendid time and Merrifield & Ferris added fresh honor to themselves as accomplished hosts.

School began last Monday morning in Medora hall, with Edward Simmers as teacher. Twenty-two scholars are in attendance and others will soon join. Every thing will soon be in good running shape, unless we are mistaken in Mr. Simmers' capabilities. We suggest that parents and friends make a practice of visiting the school occasionally. It is a wonderful incentive to both teacher and scholars.

There has been so much discussion relative to the new law concerning the organization of counties that it seems best to publish the main points and a synopsis of the whole. Section 1, under "County Boundaries and Organization" reads: "Whenever the voters of any unorganized county in this territory shall be equal to one hundred and fifty or upward, and at least one hundred and fifty thereof shall desire to have said county organized, they may petition the governor, setting forth that they have the requisite number of legal voters to form a county organization, and request him to organize said county, as hereinafter provided.

The second section under this head reads: "Whenever the voters of any unorganized county in this territory shall petition the governor, as provided in the preceding section, and the said governor shall be satisfied that such county has one hundred and fifty legal voters, it shall be the duty of the governor, and he is hereby authorized, to call an election in said unorganized county, and fix one or more places in said county as the polling places therein, and shall fix the time for holding said election; and the governor shall thereupon issue a notice of election, which notice shall be substantially in the following form, to-wit: (then follows a form for election notice, not necessary to publish.)

The third section directs that at this election, all officers shall be elected to hold office until the next general election and until their successors are elected and qualified.

The fourth section provides that at this election the county seat shall be chosen, the place receiving the highest number of votes to be the county seat.

The fifth section requires that when the governor has made out the notice of election, he shall cause it to be delivered to the clerk of the district court of the judicial subdivision to which the unorganized county is attached for judicial purposes, (in our case this is Morton county,) at least fifty days prior to the date set for the election. At least forty days prior to the election, the said clerk shall, with the assistance of the chairman of the board of county commissioners and register of deeds of said county, divide the unorganized county into election precincts, in accordance with the notice, regard being had to the convenience of the voters. The clerk must then publish and circulate the notice of election, together with a further certificate, issued by him.

Section sixth provides that the said clerk, chairman and register of deeds shall, at the same meeting in which the above business is transacted, appoint three capable and discreet persons, possessing the qualifications of electors, to act as judges of election at each polling place in the county.

Section seventh provides that five notices of the election be posted in conspicuous places throughout the county, at least twenty days before the election.

Section eighth provides that in case there should be a vacancy in the office of judge of election, the vacancy shall be filled by the vote of the electors then present at the place of voting. This section also provides that the judges shall choose two persons possessing the qualifications of voters, to act as clerks of such election.

The eighth section provides that the previous laws in reference to elections shall be in force, except those conflicting with the provisions of this act.

The ninth section provides that the governor shall, at least thirty days before the election, appoint a supervisor of election to serve at each polling place in the county. Each supervisor shall make oath that he is neither directly or indirectly interested in the location of any county seat in said county and is not the owner of any land or interests therein.

The tenth section provides that the supervisors shall furnish ballot-boxes and poll-books, failing in which, they may be furnished by any qualified elector.

The eleventh section provides that the supervisor shall use every means in his power to prevent any fraud in the election.

The twelfth section provides that the supervisor can do almost anything he sees fit in his efforts to secure a fair election.

Section thirteen provides for the punishment of anyone who in any way interferes with the officers of election or the sanctity of the ballot.

Section fourteen provides that the ballot be folded by the elector and handed to one of the judges of election and if all or a majority of the judges and supervisors are satisfied that the person offering the vote is a legal voter, the clerks shall enter his name and number in the poll-books and the judges and supervisors shall immediately endorse on the back of the ballot the voter's number and immediately deposit the ticket in the ballot-box.

The fifteenth section provides that no adjournmen shall be taken from the time the first vote is polled until all the votes have been counted and the result publicly announced. The ballots, as counted, shall then be strung on a stout cord and the cord then knotted and the knot sealed. They are then to be enveloped and sealed by the judges in the presence of the supervisor. After this, they are to be replaced in the ballot-box, which is then to be sealed and delivered to the supervisor.

The sixteenth section provides that one of the poll-books shall be enclosed in the ballot-box and the whole deposited with the clerk of the district court having jurisdiction over the newly organized county. The other poll-book is to be deposited in the office of the register of deeds of the county having jurisdiction, to be kept as a public record.

Section seventeen provides that any election officer, who shall be guilty of, or connive at any fraud, shall, upon conviction be punished by a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars and by an imprisonment of from one to five years in the penitentiary.

Section eighteen provides that the register of deeds and a majority of the county commissioners of the senior county, shall canvass the returns and on separate sheets of paper count the votes for officers and the location of the county seat. The register shall then issue certificates of election to the person receiving the highest number of votes for each office and the place receiving the highest number of votes shall be declared the county seat.

Within twenty days after this canvass of votes the officers elected shall qualify. If any fail to qualify within thirty days his office shall be declared vacant and shall be filled according to law.

The concluding sections of the law specify that the commissioners newly elected shall divide the county into commissioners' districts, not to be changed oftener than once in three years. At the ensuing general election one commissioner shall be chosen for one year, one for two years and one for three years. After that, one is to be elected annually.
Robert Tombs, the "great unreconstructed" died Tuescay night at Washington, Ga.
Minneapolis has expended eight million and a half of dollars in building during the last year.
B. Gratz Brown, who ran for vice-president in 1872, on the Greely ticket, died last Saturday in St. Louis.
The Merrill House at Glendive, burned last Sunday morning. The loss is $41,000, insurance $26,000. E. C. Waters, the proprietor, expects to rebuild in the spring.
Slosson, Shaefer and Vignaux will begin next Monday a series of games to decide the billiard championship of the world. This time the games will be continued until one is victor.

A fire in Bismarck Monday, burned out Schonberg's, boot and shoe store, Edick Bros. cigar factory and did about $600 damage to the First Nat. Bank block. The total loss is about $15,000. Insurance about $7,000.
A fund is being raised for a monument over the tomb of Thomas A. Hendricks. It would seem that there are enough languishing monument funds in the country now, without adding another to the list.

Senator Harrison introduced into the Senate Tuesday, a bill for the admission of a part of Dakota. Southern Dakota is doing well to have its statehood bill introduced thus early in the session, for it will have a hard row to hoe before it becomes a state.

There seems to be good foundation for the rumor that the American Express Co's. proposition to the Northern Pacific to buy out their express line, will be accepted. To-day's meeting of the N. P. directors in New Yurk will probably decide the matter.

[Since the above was put in type, the American has bought out the Northern Pacific Expr[ess] C[o]. and after the first of January will have exclusive control of the express business on the Northern Pacific.

Through freight rates from St. Paul to Black Hills points have been made via the Fremont, Elkhorn & Missouri Valley R. R. They range from $2.30 on fifth class to $3.30 on first class merchandise. This is really no reduction of rates.

Great fear is expressed that there will be another out-break in Canada on account of the death of Riel and his Indian associates. The Indians especially are becoming hostile and it is thought that Gabriel Dumont is planning to head a rebellion.

The state legislature of southern Dakota met at Huron on Monday. Govenor Mellette sent in his message Tuesday and Judges Moody and Edgerton were elected senators. We wonder if anything will finally come of what all in the north think is a gigantic farce.

Representative Seney of Ohio, will, as soon as possible, introduce a bill in Congress to repeal the civil-service law. There is not one capable business man in a thousand who can pass an examination according to law and it should certainly be amended or repealed. We doubt however, if enough back-bone can be found in Congress to repeal it.

The president has asked that immediate relief be granted to the northern Cheyenne Indians on the Rosebud and Tongue rivers. There are reported to be 700 Indians on these rivers, without food.

The Apaches are giving serious trouble in Arizona. Every day brings new stories of murders, and the troops seem entirely unable to cope with the Indians. It would be a good scheme to raise a company of cow-boys to put down the marauders.

To-day and yesterday have been as beautiful days as any we have had during the fall. We just had a taste of winter, enough to get cattle used to it, when genuine fall weather has again set in. Cattlemen are enthusiastic over the prospect.

The Cheyennes and Arapahoes are again dissatisfied. They were anxious to have the cattlemen leave but now that they do not get money for leases they are becoming turbulent. It has been so long since Indians any where have received a good thrashing that it will probably be necessary to give them one soon.

From late British returns, it is found that for the year ending June 4, 1885, of 682,693 cattle born in England, 134,941 died of disease. In Wales, the number of cattle born was 147,702, of which 18,439 died. The total for Great Britain shows that 1,072,409 cattle were born and that 193,056 died. The above figures from the Drovers' Journal, furnish a fine comment on England's restrictions on our live stock importations. Such a terrible per cent. of loss would seemingly paralyze any stock interest. Such a showing of fatal diseases in England also calls for rigid quarantine measures on the part of our government. Nine-tenths of the disease among cattle in the United States came originally from English cattle and in view of the state of things now prevalent there, too strict measures cannot be adopted against them.

Two horses belonging to the SOHO cattle Co. were in Red Cloud's alias George Wood's posession when he was killed by Chris Gross. They will be brought back to the ranch soon.
Alden Eaton returned Monday evening from his eastrn trip. He was visiting in Pittsburgh and Meadville. He reports having a delightful time, but glad to get back to the Bad Lands.
Fred Willard's residence will be finished in about two weeks. It will be comfortably arranged, of good size and will present a neat appearance. Copeland & Williamson have the contract.

Remember that you can buy your fancy goods and notions as cheap at the Drug Store in Medora as you can anywhere this side of St. Paul. Besides this you may draw a prize to exceed the value of the goods.

Charlie Eaton returned from Pittsburgh last night. Between the enjoyment of his eastern trip, his pleasure at returning to the Bad Lands and his endeavors to again get used to a cow-boy hat after wearing a dude outfit so long, his sensations are as badly mixed as are the reports concerning the likelihood of there being a new Mrs. Eaton in the spring.

Win. Roberts and a number of other prisoners in the Miles City jail made an attempt to escape recently. They got through the floor of a cell but then ran across a plate of chilled steel that stopped further progress. The jail officials could not find the tools with which the work was done but a diet of bread and water for four days made Win. weaken and show up a case knife, with which the job was done.

H. M. Jorgens wishes to announce to the public that he has connected with his business a gift enterprise. Buying three dollars' worth of fancy goods, notions or jewelry entitles you to a number in the gift enterprise. Every number draws a prize varying in price from ten cents to ten dol[la]rs.

An extract from the marriage license notices in the Pittsburgh Penny Press, of Dec. 8, sent us by Charlie Eaton, makes rather interesting reading. It states that on that date a marriage license was issued to John B. Walker and Jennie Dolish, of Irwin station, Penn. Hereafter the Cow Boy will pose as a prophet. It will be remembered that in spite of the fact, that Walker was reported to be in Helena, the Cow Boy predicted that he could be found in Pennsylvania.

We refrained from mentioning anything concerning the proposed reduction in the depot force here in our last issue, hoping that the change would not be made in Mr. Maxwell's position. A large remonstrance was sent in by our citizens to the proposed change, and Auditor Sharkey and route-agent Stedman also sent in protests. It seems that the change is to be made, however, and Mr. Maxwell will probably accept a position in the Wells-Fargo company at Helena. He has been altogether the most popular agent we have ever had here and there is no one but that regrets seeing the change made.

[Since the above was put in type, Mr. Maxwell has decided to remain in Medora and will accept the agency of the Wells-Fargo.

An insurance agent was here last week soliciting trade in a way that showed either him or the company he represented, to be a fraud. He tried to do business on a sliding scale of rates that no responsible insurance company would authorize. He offered to insure a dwelling house with an adjacent exposure for one per cent. This is a fraud on the face of it, as no responsible company offers such a rate. All can easily see that it is to their interest to insure with a home agent, who will certainly look after the policy holders' interests better than a tramp agent of a snide company.

It now seems settled that Govenor Pierce will serve out his term of office. Ziebach has been appointed receiver of public monies at Yankton and as there is no other opposition to our present governor, his tenure of office will likely remain undisturbed.

We are in receipt of a letter from Lieut. J. M. T. Partello, dated at Anvers, Belgium, in which he states that he and his wife are having glorious times. They are "doing" Europe in good shape and we hope at some time to publish one of his interesting descriptions of travel. He is as fine a writer as he is a marksman.

Mandan is not the only place that is troubled with itinerant insurance men. Some of the snide fellows have been to Medora, trying to work the honest citizens at that place. Editor Packard, who is the agent doing business there with honest companies on honest basis, is justly indignant. He may tell his patrons and readers that the experience of Mandan people with these travelling agents is bad. They are a lot of dishonest scoundrels.—[Mandan Pioneer.

The government astronomers and surveyors operating on the line between Dakota and Montana have completed their labor. The length of the east line of Montana is 277 miles geographical survey. These officials chained it making it 276 miles 27 chains and 80 links, which is good chaining. The line crosses the railroad about 6½ miles east of Mingusville and leaves Ayott's ranch about four miles in Montana. The survey is now definitely settled and the line clearly defined.—[Glendive Times.

The COW BOY subscribers for this year and next year will get more than they bargained for. There will be fifty-three issues each year. An interesting case will soon be tried, in which the editor of an eastern weekly published on Thursday is sued by a subscriber, because the editor skipped an issue. The subscriber claims that he was to receive the paper every week and the editor claims that he was to furnish only as many copies of his paper as there are weeks in the year, fifty-two. Pending the decision of this suit and barring accidents, the COW BOY will appear every Thursday and throw in the extra issues to its subscribers.

Nothing definite has been learned concerning the organization of the county. No steps have been taken in Bismarck to carry out the plan of organization on account of the protest offered by F. B. Allen. It seems scarcely credible that the wishes of 174 citizens can be so long thwarted, but the end must soon come. The governor is perfectly right in taking time to consider the matter and he cannot but become satisfied soon that the people of Billings county want the county organized. Only two refusals of voters to sign and 174 legal signatures is an overwhlming majority that is rarely duplicated. The foundation principle of our Democratic form of government will be overthrown, if this or any other majority is not allowed to rule.

We are in receipt of Governor Pierce's annual message to the Secretary of the Interior. It is published in the form of a large, fifty-three-page pamphlet and contains information extremely valuable to anyone wishing to learn about Dakota. From this report, it appears that we had at the last census, 416,000 population and this number is increasing at the rate of sixty-six per cent. per annum. In 1880 there were 17,435 farms in the territory and in 1885 there were 82,017. Banks increased from twenty-four in 1880 to 195 in 1885, with capitals of $440,000 and $4,514,000 respectively. The total number of miles of rail-road now in operation in Dakota, is 2,701. Although Dakota is not rated at all as a manufacturisg territory she has $6,593,218 invested in manufacturing industries, exclusive of the mining industries of the Black Hills. The total bonded debt of the territory is $568,2000, which will be or has by this time been increased $176,000, authorized at the last session of the legislature and bringing 103.2. The report ends with a number of tables, from which we glean the fol- figures on Billings county: We have a population of 737, of whom 518 are males. It appears that we have about as small an area of land under cultivation as any county, the total acreage being 167. We have, however more cattle than any county in the territory except Fall River, the total value being $1,226,380.

The so-called government of the southern half of that territory is a mere make-believe. The so-called legislative assembly at Huron is a hollow and tasteless sham. The so-called senators that have been appointed by that hollow sham are a couple of private citizens that are not senators in any meaning or suggestion of that word. The so-called governor at Huron is a person who is playing governor. The so-called legislature is an assembly of persons that are playing legislature. Huron is a youthful and ambitious town that presents the novel attraction of a new kind of theater comique, where a company of Dakota politicians are performing an original farce for the edification of a more or less fashionable audience. The part that each represents is that of Bottom the Weaver enacting the lion. They are roaring the same as if they were real lions, instead of absurd Bottoms.

There is not a grain, a color, a shadow, a tint, or even a faint tinge of authority for the existence of the company of political comedians at Huron, or that casts a reflection of the faintest validity on anything they have done, are doing, or may do. The pair of pretended senators they have appointed will not occupy any seats in the senate; the pretended statutes they have enacted will not be laws nor have the slightest effect of law; the expenses they are incurring will create no form or likeness of any public obligation to pay, and will be paid honestly only by the individual performers that incur them. The southern half of Dakota will not be politically organized by the name of "[stuff?]." The scheme of cutting Dakota in twain to make more offices for the political immigrants and more taxation for the struggling pioneers that are not seeking offices, is a speculative scheme of wrong that ought not to be executed, and will not be executed. The company of political comedians that are playing government at Huron would do well, therefore, to close the dramatic season and retire to attend their own business, if they have any.—[Chicago Times.

Vol. 1, No. 1, of the North Dakota Farmer, published at Jamestown, is at hand. Typographically and editorially it is as near perfection as any agricultural paper we have seen. If it "keeps up its lick," it will be a credit to Dakota journalism and set a mark for agricultural papers of the east to copy after.

The article clipped from the Glendive Times, relative to the Dakota-Montana line is of especial interest to the people of our county. All persons living east of a line drawn north and south six and one-half miles east of Mingusville, are in Billings county, Dakota. It will be comparatively easy for all to decide where they are located. Probably, also, the line is marked in such a way that it will be an easy matter for those located near it to tell in which territory they are.

The total number of cattle received at Chicago last week was 40,569. Prices were generally lower, owing to a demoralized eastern market. The Liverpool market on American beef dropped 2½c. on Monday. The year 1885, owing to a number of unforeseen accidents, will be the banner year for demoralized prices in cattle.

In considering the beef market as a basis from which to figure on the future, do not forget that many thousands of cattle, especially from Texas and the Cherokee strip, have been thrown upon the market this year that were not fit for market and would never have been sold for beef but for circumstances well known and over which the owners had no control. While this heavy run of inferior cattle has to an extent paralyzed the market, it has at the same time diminished the supply.—[Texas Stockman.

The wild horses of Wyoming and Western Nebraska are compact little animals weighing from 800 to 1,100 pounds. The majority of them stand 14 hands high. In color they are usually brown, sorrel or bay. A gray is seldom seen, unless it has strayed away from civilization. Their tails grow long frequently dragging on the ground, but their manes are like those of other horses and not growing to the knees as are represented in some books. The eye, probably from being constantly on the watch, is larger than the eye of the domestic horse, and even when tamed the eye remains a distinctive mark of the horse's origin. Wild horses when captured or tamed are superior to other horses of the same size. Many of them are used by the cow boys and others are broken to harness and driven as carriage horses, being entirely trustworthy.—[Hoof & Horn.

Estrays can only be taken up by house holders, claim holders, under United States land laws, and then only when such estray is found in the immediate vicinity of his or her claim or place of residence in the county wherein he or she resides, except that any person may, when the estray is found ten miles from any habitation, in an uninhabited part of the territory.

Estrays cannot be taken up between the first day of October and March 1, inclusive, unless found trespassing upon the premises or within the enclosure of the person taking the same up.

Publishing notice—Whenever any person shall take up an estray, he or they must, within fifteen days thereafter, give notice of such taking up or finding three times in a weekly newspaper printed in the county wherein such estray is taken up.

If such estray be not claimed or called for within twenty-two days after the first insertion of such notice in a newspaper, such taker up or finder must go before a justice of the peace of the county wherein he resides and make oath to the facts in the case.

A warrant [must then be?] issued by the justice to three (3) householders of the county to appraise such estray, and report marks, brands, description valuation and name and place of residence of taker to such justice in writing, under oath.

Publication by justice—Whereupon the justice must immediately publish such report and appraisment according to law.

Register of deeds must keep a book entitled "Estray Register," and record such reports therein.

Upon claim being made to the ownership of such estray, both the taker up or finder and claimant shall go before the justice, and the claimant make oath to his name, place of residence, ownership and description of property, after which, upon payment of all fees advanced by him and reasonable charges, such estray must be delivered up.

At the expiration of one year after such taking up or finding, if the taker up or finder has caused the same to have been advertised and appraised, and is not to exceed in value fifty dollars, title shall rest in taker up or finder.

If over the value of fifty dollars, notice must be given to such justice of the peace or his successor; such justice shall then appoint a day of sale, and cause the same to be published three (3) times in a weekly newspaper published within the county, fixing a day of sale at the county seat, sale to be made by the justice; and after paying from the proceeds of the sale the cost of advertisements and all legal costs and charges, pay to the county treasurer the residue of the proceeds, and take his receipt therefor.

If the moneys so deposited be not claimed within six months therafter, and proper proof made, the same shall be by the county treasurer paid to the school fund.

The justice must also file with the treasurer a certificate setting forth a description of the estray, marks and brands and name of taker up.

The fees of the justice—advertising and appraising must be paid by the taker up or finder and be a first lien thereon.

Any person not authorized, taking up an estray, failing to advertise the same, imprudently working or failing to properly feed the same, shall forfeit to the owner the sum of $25, and be recovered by action for debt before any justice of the peace. The taker up may work the estray in a prudent manner.

Should any estray, after being taken up and advertised, be lost or injure without negligence on the part of the taker up, he is not liable to the owner.—[N. W. Farmer.

J. E. Cates of the Mandan Times, has issued an attractive annual that is a fine specimen of the printer's art, of which Mr. Cates is master.
A baby girl was born to Mr. and Mrs. J. L. Truscott last Saturday at the Spring creek ranch. Mother and daughter are reported to be doing well.
Wm. Tolbert went west with Chas. Jolly last week. They expect to secure positions on the Benton & Billings stage line for the winter.
Geo. Roderick, who has made his headquarters in Bismarck for several months, has sold his outfit and gone east with his wife, whose health is not good.
A social hop will be given at the Northern Pacific hotel Christmas night. All are invited to attend and all are sure of having a good time.
There are 13,958 newspapers in the United States and the COW BOY joins with the unanimous sentiment they all express, of a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year to all.

Oberne, Hosick & Co's. warehouse in Chicago, was burned last Sunday. The loss is $350,000, and the insurance is $250,310. Their agent, J. E. Hempl, is well known here, having several times bought the Co's. stock of hides.
The school is in flourishing condition, and praises of Mr. Simmers' instruction are numerous. There are now twenty-six scholars in attendance. A night school is conductec in addition.
James Hannigan returned from Bismarck Tuesday evening. The Tribune speaks of him as "a distinguished Frenchman from Medora." It won't do, Monsieur de Quinn, Jim. is no countryman of yours.

Even for Dakota, this weather is wonderful. So far this fall we have not had ten days of anything resembling winter weather. To-day is a perfect fall day. The sun is shining brightly, the thermometer registers 41 in the shade and in the sunshine it is if anything, too warm. We feel for the denizens of the frozen-up States.

A large variety of Holiday meats can be found at Willard & Keeler's meat market. Oysters, fish, turkeys, ducks and geese, not to speak of as good beef as was ever hung up, mutton, pork, all kinds of sausage, venison and bear meat, form an array that is not beaten on the line of the road for variety or quality.

Lee Bros. of Gladstone, have their mill in first-class running order and are grinding as good flour as can be made anywhere. They ought, and are now making preparations to supply this part of the country with their goods. A glance at their advertisement will be of benefit to our readers.

A remark, expressive of surprise was made last week, at our ability to turn out a certain kind of job work. Lest others should have the same idea, we "wish to remark" that we have abundant facilities for turning out almost any kind of job work and guarantee our work in every case, equal to the same class of work done anywhere.

We do not believe much in the practice some papers adopt, of offering premiums to gain subscribers, but as the COW BOY will be a three-year-old soon we wish to have a number of new subscribers to add to our already large and growing list. To this end, between now and March 1, we will send the paper for a year from next March for the regular rate of $2. In addition, we will give the person bringing us the greatest number of new subscribers, $10 in cash. In all cases, as heretofore, subscriptions must be accompanied with the cash. This offer ceases and the prize will be awarded on March 1. A little effort is likely to win the prize and the combined efforts of a number of our friends will make a gratifying increase in our list.

Mr. Ba-a-d Man Finnegan again put himself on exhibition last Sunday. After filling up with "valley-tan" he tried some of his "Bad man from Bitter creek" idiocy and came near doing some fatal work with his rifle, before Fred Willard relieved him of it. He was taken to Dickinson Monday morning by Sheriff Sebastian and pleading guilty to the charge of discharging fire-arms in a public place, was given a Christmas present of $5 and costs by Justice Starr, which will net him about twenty days in jail. We have heard several apologists for Finnegan say that he would not have done as he did if he had been sober. This is no argument, either in law or the commonest of common sense. He has repeatedly done the same thing previously and it is high time that he was made to feel that there can be some control over him. Mr. Willard did his duty both as a citizen and an officer in putting a quietus on Mr. B. M. Finnegan.
Monsieur Jules Grevy has been re-elected President of France after a most exciting election.
The Grand Junction News has issued a Year Book that is a credit to its editor and ought to do much toward building up the country, the News so ably represents.

There is scarcely a newspaper received at the Cow Boy office that does not ridicule the so-called state of Dakota. All over the United States the project is so laughed at that it bids fair to be jeered to death, even if it were not sure to die on its own merits or rather, lack of merit.

The rumored buying out of the Northern Pacific express Co. by the Wells-Fargo proves to be false. Word has now been received that there will be a reduction in rates after Jan 1. This may or may not be the precursor of another slashing of rates such as we had last winter, but it looks wonderfully like it.

Last nights' papers show that the government is waking up to the fact that the Apaches in Arizona must be crushed into submission. There are only about 200 Apaches and Gen. Crook has been chasing them for a long time with 3,000 or 4,000 men. Six companies of infantry and one of cavalry in addition have been ordered for duty against the Apaches and with these the government hopes to succeed. If 200 Texas and Arizona cowboys were well armed and equipped and sent against the Apaches the Indian war would not last two months.

The Indians are still giving great trouble in Arizona and murders by them are frequent. To a man up a tree it looks as though Congress had better stop quarrelling over the silver bill awhile and exterminate these red devils, if it takes every soldier in the United States army. To send a few companies of tenderfoot swaddies against the Indians on their chosen fighting ground is on a par with the idiocy which has all along characterized the government's treatment of the Indians. The Apaches, who are causing the present disturbances, are as barren of anything productive of sentiment as a possum's tail is of hair and it would be impossible for even Dawes' ultra-philanthropic constituents to find anything to love in them. They are the scum de la scum of the Indian nations in all that relates to deceit, treachery and blood-thirstiness and will only be improved mentally, morally or physically by being filled full enough of holes to let out their miserable lives. If necessary, let the government send 50,000 men against them and stop this shedding of innocent blood. Lives are worth more than money. Peace in the United States is more valuable than discussion as to whether we shall have greenbacks or silver dollars.

News came in yesterday afternoon that a Mr. Church, associated with Ben. Mason in the mercantile business, was shot and instantly killed Thursday night by some one of a number of cowboys who were enjoying themselves at Mason's bar. The shooting is said to be entirely accidental and all express deep sorrow at the occurrence. Church was said to be a favorite among the cowboys generally and a good man. The particulars of the unfortunate affair are meagre but it seems that Church was just entering the door when some one who was on the inside thoughtlessly or accidentally fired a pistol shot through the door and struck Church in the breast.—[Stockgrowers' Journal.

The above is the brief description of what is no better than a cold-blooded murder. We do not know any of the parties to the affair nor any particulars further than the above. We only know that one or more men were carrying six-shooters and that he or they had been drinking. The particular one who fired the fatal shot did not know, as the fact proves, that his shot would prove harmless. According to law, this is manslaughter in the second degree. According to the highest justice, a man who wears a revolver and then gets drunk, knowing that while under the influence of liquor he is liable to discharge it, and finally winds up by accidentally(?) shooting anyone, is no better than any other murderer. To know that at any time he may kill some one, and to still continue the drunken shooting, is equivalent to premeditation, which constitutes the distinction between murder and manslaughter. It is time that cow papers and cowmen everywhere should combine and crush out the worse than idiocy that so many times culminates fatally. A revolver in the hands of a drunken man is something altogether too dangerous to jest about. Whether it is owing to the efforts of the Cow Boy or not in this direction, the fact is certain that not one-quarter of the revolvers are now carried here, that there were two years ago. The consequence is that promiscuous shooting and the consequent accidents have decreased by more than three-fourths. We hope soon to see the time when everyone carrying a revolver will be compelled to lay it off while in town.

The Express advises southern Texas stockmen to abandon the trail, as they will be compelled to do it eventually and the sooner the better. The Express should not lose sight of the fact that to abandon the drive involves a revolution in our system of handling cattle, and which new departure cannot be brought about in a day or year, but must come gradually; the drive then, must be abandoned by degrees. That no time should be lost perfecting arrangements for maturing and transporting our beef, we not only admit, but emphasize. But meanwhile, a great many of our cattle owners have young cattle, for the maturing and fattening of which they have made no provision and they need the money for the cattle. Therefore, just at present, there is no question of such vital and immediate importance to southern Texas cattlemen as that of the spring drive to the northwest.—[Texas Stockman.

The above is the frankest article in relation to the Texas trail, that we have ever seen in a Texas paper. If the whole controversy had been carried on in the same open spirit that actuated the writer of the above, there would have been none of the ill-feeling that now exists between northern and southern cowmen. It was the bull-dozing, you-will-and-you-won't style of argument that has caused the most of the trouble. The cattle business of the past made the interests of the north and south dependent on each other. In the future, except for the competition they offer, they will soon be almost as separated as if the interests were in different countries.

Lloyd Roberts will probably start east next month to contract cattle for spring delivery. He reports that he can lay cattle down here as cheap or cheaper than he did last year.

The social hop given by Mr. and Mrs. Arch. Boyd at the Northern Pacific, was thoroughly enjoyed by all of the large number in attendance. Christmas evening could not have been spent in a pleasanter way.

Harry Tarbell has measured some of the distances up the river with an odometer and from Medora, they are as follows: To Ferris & Merrifield's, 7½ miles; to Dantz', 15 miles; to the Logging Camp, 29½ miles; to the HT horse camp, 37½ miles. These distances will be authority in the future.

J. N. Maxwell and wife intend leaving for St. Paul in two or three days. Mr. Maxwell has accepted a position as messenger for Wells-Fargo with a run between St. Paul and Fargo. He has only accepted the position for three months and will return in the spring and put in cattle. Mr. and Mrs. Maxwell are general favorites here and even a brief absence is regretted by all.

A year ago to-day the thermometer registered forty-four degrees below zero. This morning at ten o'clock, it was thirty two above, and the light snow which fell last night had already begun to melt from the roofs. New Year's day a year ago was the coldest day of the winter, the mercury crawling down into the bulb and trying to pull the tube in after it, while spirit thermometers registered from forty-six to fifty below. Unless there is a sudden and unexpected change in the temperature, we expect to make our New Year's calls to-morrow in a linen duster and straw hat.

Never before have cattlemen in this section felt so jubilant at this time of the year. We have had no real winter weather and there has not been a day since the round-up that cattle have not been taking on fat. A ride over the ranges shows sleek, well-contented cattle that will easily stand the two months at most of winter that we can have. In all the coolies and broken country, there is an abundance of the very best feed, at present entirely untouched, but which will be of use if we have any weather that will force the cattle back from the more open ravines into the sheltered nooks. The loss so far has been nothing as the cattle thrive far better in this weather than they do in summer and the grass also is more fattening.

Reports from Nebraska state that the recent storm will occasion severe loss on cattle. In places, the telegraph lines were down for several days, it being impossible for linemen to face the storm.

Specials from Montreal express great fear that there will soon be another uprising on the part of the half-breeds and Indians. They are now plentifully supplied with ammunition, the lack of which they think was the cause of their former failure.

Sections of Texas, notably Galveston, Austin, Laredo, Palestine and Corpus Christi report the coldest weather in forty years. There will be great loss on stock but as yet it is too early to estimate it.
The manufacturers of barbed wire have formed a combination for the purpose of raising prices. Within a few days the price has advanced sixty cents a hundred and a further advance is contemplated.

Vol. 1, No. 3, of the Buffalo Gap Advance comes to us with boom! BOOM!! BOOM!!! all over it. The Advance prophesies permanency for the town and with good reason for it is a natural supply point to a large country. The boom times will probably leave it in the spring, however.

The death of Hon. John B. Raymond of Fargo, was curiously foretold by a Norwegian woman who worked on his farm. A turkey was accidentally killed on Christmas day and she was greatly effected thereat, declaring that either Mr. Raymond or one of his family would soon die. It seems strange that coincidence should so often come to the aid of superstition.

It would be a blessing if some patriot would make a "physical wreck" of him.
