The meeting for the organization of a National range stockgrowers' association will be held in Denver on Jan. 27. Unless cool and cautious heads are allowed to rule, this convention may do more harm than anything from which the range industries have ever suffered. The eastern press will narrowly watch proceedings, and mole-hills will be magnified into mountains in adversely criticizing the "rapacity of the cattle kings." Properly conducted, it will be a means of the greatest good to rangemen, as there has never been any united action among them of a national character.

The list of victories of the "Bonnie Black Doddies," published in another column, is of especial interest to all range cattlemen. When we add to this list of victories over all other breeds for all purposes the fact that they are par excellence for range purposes, we have a combination of good traits that stamps the Aberdeen-Angus as beyond question the range animal of the future. Those that have been brought into the Bad Lands, notably those of the Maltese cross outfit, are now in the pink of condition and are apparently as contented with the thermometer forty degrees below as they are when it is forty degrees above zero.

The following letter, received by Bob Roberts, probably contains a plain, unvarnished account of Alaska and shows how magnified are the reports from that country. It would be well for those who contemplate going there to "look before they leap."

Juneau, Alaska.
Dec. 17, 1885.

Friend Bob:—

You were anxious to find out something about this country and I will try and inform you to the best of my ability. The biggest excitement here now is the Yakon country but so far there is nothing discovered there yet outside of some bar diggings on the rivers and they pay from $5 to $10 a day to the man. But that Yakon country is a big country and I am in hopes that in a couple of years more they will strike something worth going after but so far they have not got it and what little they have found is in British Columbia under the English government. There is more going on here than in any other part of Alaska. This summer they just completed the finest mill I suppose in the world at an expense of three hundred and fifty thousand for the mill alone, but it will not take them long to get out money at the [illegible] have been doing since they started, [illegible] yet there is nobody that knows for certain how much they are taking out. They have one hundred and twenty stamps running on the mill and use from 300 to 350 tons of ore every twenty-four hours, the ore averages about five dollars at the least. Their actual expenses when things are running in good shape will be about $1.25 a ton for mining and milling so that gives them a profit of $3.75 a ton that is as near as you can get to it and next summer they are almost sure to put up another mill like this. But this company with lots of money that they had and are making now, have the best of the country right here corralled to themselves and outside of what they have got there is nothing done or being done in this place at all. They are working about forty white men on the mine and mill all told, the rest are Chinamen and Indians. There is a little placer mining camp about three miles from here, and in the summer a few white men work there but now all is idle for the winter. There are about four or five hundred white men and women in and around this place and that is about one-half of the population of all Alaska. It is doubtful if there are a thousand in the whole country, still the governor in his report has put it a good deal higher. I beleive there are some doing pretty well in the fur business. But that big fur company has that pretty well to themselves the same as anything else. There are a few Indians here maybe two or three hundred and some of them are at work, the rest do nothing and live on dried salmon. That is pretty near all their support, the Indians here are different from those around where you are. These will work and some of them do work from one end of the year to the other. No whiskey is allowed to be brought into the country but yet there are about twenty saloons in Junean alone and all selling is as public as in New York city, the only trouble is in getting it in and a good deal is manufactured right here, and the Indians are the worst you ever saw. If a white man gives them any whiskey they are liable to go right straight to the first officer they can find and tell him who gave it to them, so you can judge there is not much of that done. There is civil law here now, and some one is hauled up every day or two. So on the whole I would not advise you to come here and invest anything in the country at the present time. Still there are men here that are going to make money, and others again after bringing considerable money into the country will leave it broke. But that is the way with mostly every mining camp and excitement. Undoubtedly there will be a good deal of money taken out of here for years to come, but the work will be done by Chinamen and Indians and that will not help the country any. This country has got the meanest weather you ever saw, raining or snowing all the time but it is not cold, the rain or snow does not stop any one from working outside. Sometimes it never stops raining for two weeks at a time.

Your dear friend,
Owen Jones.

The season of the fat-stock shows is over and the final contests of the year decided. Let us take a summary view of the whole and see what part the Aberdeen-Angus have taken in the fray, in competition with the other breeds.

We will commence at Riverview park, Kansas City, Mo., and wind up at Islington hall, London, England. At Kansas City, the doddies were only represented by six animals out of 108 of all other breeds that were represented. The first winnings the blacks could compete for, outside of their own class was, "Sweepstakes All Breeds," early maturity. In class for steer or spayed heifer, two years and under three, we find the Aberdeen-Anguns steers Blaine and Logan stand first and second. In the one-year-old class Messers. Gudgell & Simpson win with that marvelous steer Sandy, and in class under one year old the same gentlemen win first with their Angus steer calf Alex, while Messers Estill & Flliot take second place with their calf Felix. Here plain out, the Aberdeen-Angus make a clean sweep of all the early-maturity classes wherever they competed.

Let us visit Chicago, the American Smithfield; here the blacks appear even more microscopical in numbers, yet they fill a proud position. Mr. J. J. Hill's Aberdeen-Angus steer Benholm wins the consolation stakes as best two-year-old, and Messors. Gudgell & Simpson's Sandy is first in the yearling class, both in competition with a strong array of good ones of all breeds. Mr. Hill's black steer Turiff sustains the reputation of the Scots by winning the $75 prize as best three-year-old carcass of any breed. He too comes in first for carcass prize showing greatest amount of edible beef. Their honors do not rest here, as Mr. Hill's Angus steer Benholm makes the highest per cent of dressed to gross weight, 71.4 being the highest given by any beast of any age. Noble doddies! here again you sustain your last year's reputation, reflecting additional lustre upon the fame of the Aberdeen-Angus as prime butchers' [illegible] It will be interesting to compare weights of various cross-breeds at Chicago. Twelve grade Herefords, shown at an average age of three years, six months and five days, give an average weight of 2,070 lbs., an average gain per day from birth of less than 1.60 lbs. Thirteen grade Short-horns, at an average age of three ytars, six months and sixteen days, show an average weight of 2,037 lbs., an average gain per day from birth of less than 1.58 lbs. The three cross-bred Angus shown by Mr. Hill out-do either Short-horn or Heroford grades. At an average age of three years, four months and nineteen days, give an average weight of over 2,271 lbs., with an average gain per day from birth of 1.88 lbs. The Angus crosses are over 200 lbs. heavier than that of either the Short-horn or Herefoad, are two months younger, and make a greater gain per day, another invaluable triumph for Angus blood.

Let us visit Rutland show held at Oakham, one of England's best cattle districts. In the class of oxen other than Short-horn, three years old, we find the first and second winners are Aberdeen-Angus crosses; the third prize is a pure-bred polled ox. In class of steers of any breed, three years, the prize is won by Mr. Stephenson with his pure-bred ox, Sultan. The second and third prizes were won by polled crosses also. In the two-year-old class, open to all breeds, Mr. Stephenson again figures with his pure Aberdeen ox, Freedom. In class of best heifer of any breed, Mr. Stephenson is an easy winner with his charming Aberdeen-Angus heifer, Luxury, of ancient lineage. What a success the black blood proves to be! What of the Yorkshire society's fat-stock exhibition, held at Yorkshire? In class for cross-bred oxen not exceeding four years old, there is keen competition, yet all in favor of black blood. Mr. Curry wins first and Mr. Wallis second with two admirable Aberdeen-Angus crosses. The highest award on cross-bred cow or heifer class was allotted to a daughter of the [Erica?] bull, Escourt.

At Birmingham, we are told, there was a splendid show of Scotch cattle and as not infrequently happens, the highest honors of the day fell to them. We will merely notice their winnings in competition with other breeds. The champion ox again is a black polled cross, property of Mr. Robert Loder. He was placed champion at Norwich, but at Birmingham he wins a special prize of $250 as the best cross-bred animal in the show. This steer was by a Short-horn bull from a polled cow; let his sire have a share in the honor. Mr. Loder's ox weighed 2,624 bounds, a younger steer than the Chicago Regulus, yet weighing 334 pounds more, showing the decided superiority of the Aberdoon-Angus and Short-horn cross to that of the Hereford and Short-horn. In class of two-year-old cross-bred oxen, the Duchess of Sutherland is victorious, with a gray ox by an Angus sire and Mr. Stephenson ranks high with a black polled ox. In the yearling class, a cross by the polled bull Proud Knight is winner.

Thirteen were entered in the cross-bred cow or heifer class. Black blood comes to the front once more, Flora MacDonald is winner, she the produce of a renowned Aberdeen-Angus sire. The butchers of Birmingham present a prize for the best animal for butchers' purposes of not less than seventeen hundred weight. Guess who won it? Mr. Cridlan's pure Aberdeen-Angus ox did, weighing at three years, 2,215 pounds; a proud victory indeed. Now for that much-coveted trophy, the Elkington Challenge vase. Who wins it? A doddie, of course! Mr. Clement Stephenson's charming, sleek, black, Aberdeen-Angus heifer Luxury wins the great prize over 209 of England's choicest animals, her live weight 1,724 pounds.

Now ror the grand wind-up, Smithfield, a repetition of black victories. The blacks are all-conquering. We read that the blacks contain by far the grandest display. Flora MacDonald, a two-year-old polled cross was brought to the front and received the silver cup as the best cross-bred anemal in the yard. Finally the greatest prize is decided and Mr. Stephenson's Aberdeen-Angus heifer Luxury, amid the greatest excitement and enthusiasm is declared the champion; the bucolic queen of the day. For three years in succession Mr. Stephenson has won the Elkington vase, valued at $500. In every case it has been won by black polled two-year-old heifers.

Such victories are unprecedented in the annals of show-yard history. Never, during the eighty-eight years of the Smithfield club have such honors been approached by any other breed.—[Wm Watson in Breeder's Gazette.

The bulls at the Logging camp are in fine condition. They have comfortable stables and the best of care. Where an outfit takes care of its own bulls, it is undoubtedly the best plan to house them well, as the loss is reduced to a minimum and the feed that would otherwise go toward keeping up animal heat is consumed directly in making flesh.

Last Friday morning was a "screamer." The spirit thermometers nearly knocked the eye out of fifty below, while the mercury thermometers might as well have been in business in Patagonia as far as any good they did here was concerned. There was no wind and it was much more comfortable than the day before when it was twenty-five degrees warmer but windy.

The cold weather of Thursday night was too much for one Maltese cross and one LC bull at the Big plateau camp. They were the weaklings of the herd and it was scarcely expected they would live the winter out although they had gained encouragingly since being taken up. Continued severe weather may result in the loss of a few others, but it would not be surprising if there was not another loss.

Since last Thursday we have had occasion to revise our figures on the number of deer killed in the Bad Lands tributary to Medora. The number is certainly over 1,500 and probably will come nearer 2,000. It seems scarcely possible, but this is the smallest winter's killing in four years. The cream of the hunting is gone forever and as many weary hunters who have tramped all day and scarcely seen a track can testify, the man who kills a deer will earn it.

The following we clip from the Milwaukee Daily Journal. It alludes to Vic Smith and his brother Bill, under the names of Yellowstone Vic and Montana Bill. A letter from Vic states that they are having a jolly time at a big salary:

"The fancy rifle shooting of the two scouts, now at the Dime museum, is an exhibition of wonderful skill. 'Yellowstone Vic' is performing some wonderful feats. Last evening he snuffed a candle at seven or eight paces, held between the teeth of his companion, Montana Bill. The candle was only two inches long.—[Glendive Times.

The "Blonde butcher," Cranston, who will be remembered as working here last summer, bit off more than he could chew in Chicago recently. He was to have a hard glove contest with a man named Ware in the Stock yards theater. Elaborate preparations and announcements were made. According to the Inter Ocean: "Ware forced the fighting from the start with a stinging blow on Cranston's jaw. The latter fled to his corner, closely pressed by Ware and before the first round closed, jumped over the ropes and escaped."

Tomorrow is the time fixed by Judge Carpenter for a hearing in the matter of the Luffsey estate. Luffsey is the hunter who was killed in 1883 at Medora in a melee in which the Marquis de Mores was engaged. A. N. McGindley was appointed administrator. The question involved is as to how the estate should be distributed. There are two claims, one for burial expenses, and one of O'Donnell the hunter, companion of Luffsey, who claims to have been a partner of Luffsey's in the estate. The matter is now under consideration by Judge Carpenter and will doubtless be decided in a very few days.—[Mandan Pioneer.

On account of the Bismarck opposition to the organization of Billings county, we see no way of avoiding the payment of taxes to Stark county, which become delinquent on Feb 1. After this date a penalty of five per cent. is added. There is grave doubt as to the constitutionality of the law authorizing the levying of this tax and we earnestly advise that all taxes should be paid to Stark county under protest. Then a test case can decide the constitutionality of the law and should it be decided in our favor, there will be no difficulty in recovering our money. The expense of a test case will be very slight proportionately and upon the receipt of good legal opinion that the law can be declared unconstitutional we will issue a call for a meeting to take steps in the matter. Pending this, it will certainly be safer and may avoid a five per cent penalty to pay under protest before Feb. 1.

A motion was introduced into the Senate, Tuesday to allow G. C. Moody, senator-elect from the so-called state of Dakota, a seat in the Senate chamber, until the division and admission bill should be decided. The motion was held over until yesterday.

The yearly report of the Wells-Fargo express Co., on the amount of gold, silver, copper and lead mined west of the Missouri river, shows a grand total for 1885, in the four metals, of $90,181,260. Colorado is first with a total output of over $21,000,000, California is second, Montana is third, Nevada is fourth, Utah is fifth, Dakota is sixth and Washington is fourteenth and last. California is first, Colorado second, Dakota third and Utah last in gold production.

It is plain that the eastern breeders' and farm journals are watching the Denver convention of range cattlemen with Argus eyes. More strongly then than before do we repeat that unless level heads rule the convention, it will do more harm than good. Of course these papers are naturally inimical to range interests and will magnify any point against them. This, however, does not lessen their influence and if the convention is not careful, it will give them an opportunity to do lasting injnry to the range industry.

Nothing new has occurred in reference to the organization of the county. In other words, the Bismarck opposition to the organization of Billings county has so delayed matters that we are compelled to virtually throw away nearly enough money to pay the running expenses of the county for a year, unless the law authorizing the tax is declared unconstitutional. We are in receipt of a letter from a legal friend, however, that fully bears out all we have said on the subject. He advises that the taxes be paid promptly, but only to avoid the five per cent. penalty. He advises, however, that one tax-payer should not pay his taxes and that a test case should be the result, in the expenses of which the whole county should contribute. The reason given in the Cow Boy last spring is also used by our correspondent as an unanswerable objection to the constitutionality of the law: A law was already in force and is now unrepealed by which senior counties receive pay for all expenses incurred in the government of unorganized counties. Consequently, Stark county would receive pay twice for the same services. He also advises that the county should conduct the suits and to that end, should compel the opposition to the organization of the county to publicly state the cause of their opposition, so that their trifling reasons can be exposed and that on the organization of the county, the proper officials should conduct the suit. In case the law was declared unconstitutional, the tax-payers' money could be recovered. In case it was not, the money that would by the other law have gone to Stark county, will be paid direct to Billings county. In either event, our money would be returned to us.

There are some things that make us tired. Two of these are: civil service reform as at present practiced and the howl about the silver dollar. To go into a full discussion of the merits and demerits of each woutd require volumes, to judge by the voluminous way in which both points are treated by the daily press. In a word, Civil service reform is a mis-nomer, because except in minor points, there is nothing to reform. For the last twenty-five years our civil service has steadily improved, until now it is beyond the power of human beings to reform or improve it, except perhaps in the minor point of filling vacancies. The record made by the last administration is unequalled since the world began by any public or private corporation. In all tde thousands and hundreds of thousands of ways the government has of receiving and disbursing money the entire loss and total cost is included in three mills on the thousand dollars. And the civil service which performs such a totally unparalleled feat must needs be reformed. Bosh! The whole thing is a catch-penny device of politicians both Democratic and Republican, to catch votes.

The cry against the silver dollar because it is only worth in silver 79½ cents is equally as "stale, flat and unprofitable." What does any one care what it is worth, so long as it will buy a dollars worth of goods? Wall street does, because Wall street's nest would be nicely feathered if a change were made. And Wall street and its minions in Congress are doing all the howling. Senator Leland Stanford recently gave an unanswerable reply to a senator who was arguing to him that the present silver dollar was worth only 79½ cents: "You say this dollar is worth only 79½ cents. I will give you 99½ cents for 100,000 of them and you can make $20,000 by the operation." At last accounts the trade had not been consummated. It is the sheerest nonsense to meddle with something that is giving perfect satisfaction to the public at large and politicians will burn their fingers fooling with the "dollar of our daddies."

My first is first prattled by infantile tongue,
And has often been honored in story and song,
And when men are anxious in search of a wife,
They make friends with my first, to be first in the strife.

My second is two letters with only one sound,
On the clock-face, a figure, it often is found.
May your pocket-book never hold anything less,
And you never will lack a good dinner, I guess.

My last is a large stack of hay I am told,
Tho' the word is not used much, because it's so old.
Yet the man who can't find it with hints in a heap,
Should quit herding cattle and go and keep sheep.

My whole as to gender, is common, I trow,
Tho' 'tis masculine sometimes and feminine now;
It does not belong to a stockman by law,
Yet stockmen all claim it wherever they go.
—[Glendive Independent.

The receipts for last week at the Chicago stock yards included 46,918 cattle, a gain of about six thousand over the previous week. As a consequence, and because also there were no really prime cattle on the market, the price dropped on all classes. The highest price paid was $5.30 for some 1,450 ℔ steers.

There is a growing sentiment among cattlemen that the Chicago market was, at least during the last season, under the control of the great packing-house proprietors. With no actual cause whatever, and in the face of diminished receipts, the price would go down in the most mysterious and remarkable way. The heavy buyers may not have pooled and had one or two do all the buying, but they are not at all like men who wouldn't do such things.

It may not be generally known that there is a very simple and inexpensive remedy for cuts and bruises on horses and cattle at the command of almost everyone. Furthermore, the remedy is to be relied upon. In cases of fresh cuts or injuries from barbed wire, however severe, or running sores, apply to the wound lime, fresh slacked, of the consistency of thick cream, with a common paint brush. Cover the wound as thick as possible and repeat daily or oftener, if necessary. In a short time, new flesh will form and the wound will heal with hardly a scar. This remedy may seem too simple to do much, if any good. Others may think the lime, applied to a flesh wound, too harsh treatment. One trial, we are confident, will convince the most skeptical.—[Texas Stockman.

We do not know of a solitary instance of the above disease in the Bad Lands, nor is it at all liable to appear among range cattle. It generally attacks only calves and then only when they are in first-class condition, from being kept up and fed. Hitherto, the disease has been considered incurable, but the following treatment, published in the Kansas City Live Stock Indicator is claimed to be an infallible cure. It would be well to preserve it.

"I would take a knife and strike a hole through the dew-lap at the point of the brisket; take a strip of muslin, put some lard on it with as much black hellebore root as would make a pill about the size of a small pea. Fold the muslin so as to put it through like any other seton and tie the ends. It will make a sore that will act as a vaccination. Those who try this will never have any more black-leg."

Great care should be taken in selecting the broncho, the younger and gentler he is, the better. After you have made your selection, throw and tie him; Then bandage his hoofs in a heavy swathing of gunny sacks, for he may accidentally kick you, and when he is up and bucking, your liver is more apt to stay in its place. Then put on the saddle and bridle and blind; then let him up. Now draw the reins over the horn, hobble your stirrups, and put on a pair of buck-straps and a large, soft "roll."

If you have previously padded the seat of your pants and sewed two porous plasters together back to back, place the plasters in the seat of the saddle and yourself on top of them. If you have not made the last two preparations, do so before you attempt to ride.

Now, if you have followed the directions and are in the saddle, take a firm hold of each buck-strap and have the person holding the broncho pull the blinds from his eyes and turn him loose. It is presumed that you have previously taken a few fingers of sand-producer so all you have to do now is to keep cool—and your seat.—[Glendive Independent.

Fred Willard went to Jamestown Monday to inspect a lot of horses that were being taken east.
Much good scholarship is being aroused by teacher Simmers, in a competitive system of rank in classes.
Five cows were instantly killed near South Heart last Friday by No. 2, and five more were so badly injured that they had to be killed.
J. A. VanEeghen and "Tap" Bemis went to Miles last week. The latter has returned and "Van" is still in Montana's cow-town.
The Ref. Car Co. have still further reduced their working force and have turned out for the winter, six or eight teams that have been kept up.
Frank Foster has made a contract with the railroad company to car for them here, five hundred tons of ice. The ice will probably be taken to Dickinson.
We don't wish to seem un-neighborly but a remark to the effect that a hay-stack is not public property may not be amiss. We know one that will have a steel-trap attachment before long.
Quite a number of range cattle are making a winter resort of Medora. It would be a good plan for their owners to drive them back where they wouldn't have to rustle so hard for feed.
The Luffsey estate has been settled, though how much there was or who received it, was not stated. The only claims are the burial expenses and Frank O'Donald's claim as partner.

Although the thermometer is not lower than twenty degrees below, to-day is the hardest day on stock that we have had this winter. A keen wind is blowing that on the prairie, must be the worst if it is not the only blizzard of the season.

Jack Tisdale, the N. P. track rider reports that the cattle are giving but little trouble between here and Glendive, except at Mingusville. A large herd has gone in there and no effort to drive them out had been successful up to the time when he left.

The present cold snap has in several instances, made the most beautiful frost work it has ever been our lot to see. The frost figures on the window resemble the finest kind of embossed velvet work, raised at least a sixteenth of an inch.

The last ten days has furnished the only hard spell of weather we have had this winter. Rarely has the thermometer been above zero and double figures below has been the rule. Range cattle have drifted considerably, but with the exception of the herd south of Dickinson this drifting has carried them to better feed in more sheltered places.

Geo. Roderick came in from Jamestown Saturday night, but had scarcely arrived when he received a telegram to return immediately. Some time ago we mentioned that Mr. and Mrs. Roderick had started for the latter's home. On the way, she was taken suddenly ill and they were compelled to stop at Jamestown. Here she seemed to be recovering and George ventured on the trip to Medora, where he received the telegram that his wife was much worse. We join heartily with the many Medora friends of Mrs. Roderick in wishing her speedy recovery to the same good health she enjoyed in the Bad Lands.

The ice was all put up by Saturday night, making the total amount in the Co's houses here, about 10,000 tons. It is hard to conceive how it could have been put up more economically, except in the one fact of having the ice-houses nearer the dam. The cost, stored in the houses, was a little less than thirty cents per ton. In view of this, the statement of Hough & Dustin of Miles City, that they have been putting up ice at ten cents a ton and would still further reduce the cost to five cents, sounds slightly mythical.

A letter from a friend in Dickinson states that about fifteen hundred cattle have drifted down below Dickinson and are in bad shape there. The ground over which they are travelling was nearly or quite burned off during last fall and the cattle may be said to be without feed. The recent severe weather would make severe losses in this herd if the range is in as bad condition as our correspondent claims. No brands were mentioned and we have no means of knowing to whom the herd belonged. In all probability it is a mixed herd, representing a number of brands. In any event, a party should be made up immediately to look after them. A total lack of feed, on the exposed prairie, would soon so weaken them that they could not be driven to feed.

Notice is hereby given that on Jan. 16, 1886, the partnership heretofore existing between A. T. Packard and Patrick O'Hara in the coal-mining business, was dissolved by mutual consent. The business will be continued by A. T. Packard and W. F. [Vandriesche?].
Fire destroyed Galloway Bros. livery stable in Mandan, Tuesday evening. The loss is about $1,500. Insurance, $250.
The ice palace in St. Paul will be completed by Feb. 1. Grand preparations are being made for the opening carnival and reduced rates will be quoted on all roads.
All through the east, snow blockades have been the rule for the past week or two. The Northern Pacific has not had a serious blockade this winter, the greatest delay being only a few hours.

Judge Moody, senator elect from the would-be state of Dakota, has been accorded the privilege of admission to the floor of the Senate. Its dollars to doughnuts his state (?) will get no farther than this recognition.
Glowing reports of a new gold field in Honduras are published. Col. Pat. Donan is one of the syndicate who seem ta be advertising the matter, however, and the account is very liable to be flowery.

The statehood movement has made no progress except that advocates of all manners of division and admission as a whole have ventilated their opinions before the House commitee on Territories. We see no reason to change our opinion that either Dakota will be admitted as a whole or that nothing whatever will be accomplished.

There seems but little doubt that the county will soon be organized. It is utterly impossible that the wish of over 170 citizens can longer be thwarted, especially when there were only two citizens who refused to sign the petition for organization. It is high time the call was issued, so that immediate steps can be taken toward fighting the law under which Stark county is attempting to tax us. It will be well-nigh impossible for individuals to fight this law separately but as a county we can fight it well and we think successfully.

Reports from Missouri, Kansas and Nebraska show a terrible loss on cattle owing to the late blizzard. The universal tendency of reporters with reference to cattle losses and we might add, with reference to all cattle interests, is to grossly exaggerate the facts. The losses referred to are too well established to admit of doubt. While stockmen in Dakota and Montana are congratulating themselves the southern stockmen are counting losses. "Their gains are not."

A good deal of quiet work is being done toward opening up the Crow reservation in Montana. If we mistake not there are nearly 5,000,000 acres in the reservation occupied by about 500 families of Crows. As the game is practically gone, at least three-quarters of this valuable land is utterly useless to the Crows and they could make it much more profitable by getting Congress to increase their rations by relinquishing the greater part of the reservation. Exactly a parallel case is the great Sioux reservation of Dakota. We hope, and have good reason to believe, that this reservation will be opened this winter if Congress can stop quarrelling long enough to attend to it.

A number of persons to whom we have spoken, do not intend paying their taxes to Stark county. Except for the five per cent. penalty, in case the law authorizing the tax is declared constitutional, the more who refuse, the better. We believe the law can be declared unconstitutional, and in that event, those refusing to pay taxes will be gainers in the use of their money from the time they would have paid, to the time in which they recovered them. The only real and substantial reason for paying taxes under this law, is to avoid a possible five per cent. penalty. As far as we personally are concerned, we do not intend paying our taxes to Stark county until compelled to do so. Our reason for this is solely our belief in the unconstitutionality of the law. As we have said in this and former issues, the only reason for paying at all, is to avoid a possible five per cent penalty.

Although crowded ranges in the Bad Lands have in a few instances made the cattle scatter badly, in search of food, the vast majority of stock is and has been doing well. It is the general remark that this is the lightest winter we have yet had on stock in the Bad Lands.

There is a big scheme on foot to establish a grand system of dressed meat refrigerators at San Antonio, with a line of steamers to aid the Aransas Pass road in getting it to market. The Aransas Pass road has a finger in the scheme and it will sooner or later be a go. Get the beef and mutton ready.—[Texas Stockman.

All over the range country, from the Canadian Pacific to the Gulf of Mexico, come rumors of the establishment in the near future, of large slaughter-houses. Texas will be forced to adopt the plan and the increased profit in cattle sold as dressed beef, will draw many others into the plan. It requires no prophet to foretell that this will soon become the popular method of marketing range beef.

The Marquis de Mores, the Dakota cattle king, was among the passengers on the steamer Labrador, which arrived from Havre this morning. In answer to questions, the Marquis said he had a splendid trip and received a warm welcome in France. He thinks the prospects of the cattle business are very good, especially between France and America. He intends to make the experiment of exporting young cattle and taking them to France for feeding and breeding purposes and expresses himself as confident of success.—[Inter Ocean, Jan. 21.

A. Osborne of the Ætna ranch, was in town Tuesday. His "black doddies" are doing well and he is an enthusiastic champion of black blood. He advocates a plan that is novel enough to be striking and the more we think about it, the more its good points, at least in a modified form, impress themselves upon us. His plan is to have a mid-winter calf round-up and take the calves and if necessary, their mothers, to different ranches, to be cared for. It is an indisputable fact that although the most of the cattle are in fine condition, the winter calves and their mothers are now and in fact, every winter, are in bad fix. We have on the one hand, a saving of a five per cent. and upward yearly loss on calves born in winter and their mothers, a material lessening of the range cattleman's greatest source of loss. On the other hand, we have the impossibility of rounding-up in some of the coldest weather, the harm arising from "ginning up" cattle in winter, the increased cost in feeding and caring for the animals taken up, the great danger of accidents in riding or driving over rough and frozen ground and many other objections that will readily occur to anyone who thinks over the matter. Will the returns justify the out-lay? If the recent cold snap is really broken and our winter continues as mild as it has been, the answer must be in the negative. If cattle should enter on a hard winter in poor condition, it certainly would pay. But right here, as we are met by the almost total impossibility of rounding-up in severe weather, the question remains as far from solution as ever. There is no question, however, that it would pay to ride the ranges more constantly than is now done and in case a cow and calf need help and are not too far from the ranch, they can be driven there and cared for. We have seen many cows with calves this winter on the range, which were near their owners' home ranches and which would have been greatly benefitted and in several cases have had their lives saved, by being cared for. The calf round-up could certainly be worked profitably to this extent.

Some time last year the Journal kindly permitted me space for a little article under the above caption.

Since then I have witnessed some successful "broncho busters" handle a lot of unbroken colts, and I will endeavor simply to describe what I saw.

The band of horses which they were breaking are well proportioned, active, and about the average weight and size, universally admitted to be the finest, most carefully selected lot of western saddle horses ever unloaded at Miles. Among them are the usual proportion of "hard buckers" and vicious ones found in every band of horses.

There were two "busters," each having a "helper."

Two bronchos were quietly cut out and left in a moderately close corral, one for each breaker. A broncho was roped (on foot) by the front feet and thrown. Instantly a "leading rope" was put on. This consisted simply of a small rope about 30 feet long, having at one end a loop about 7 or 8 inches long. This loop was forced into the broncho's mouth, so that it was at once a sort of rope bit and curb. Then the long end of the rope was passed over the head and through the off side of the loop; then it was brought over the head back again and through the near side of the loop, making a sort of headstall.

This done, the broncho was permitted to rise and run around the corral at will till he became perfectly used to the trailing rope and entirely indiffernt to it.

Then came the first lesson. The breaker approached the rope quietly, picked it up, and if the broncho started to move off, gave the rope a strong pull (not jerk) to teach it that it could not escape, and that the loop would hurt its mouth every time it tried to pull loose.

In a few moments the breaker could approach the broncho at will and pet and caress it. It was no longer afraid of him, and stood always head toward him.

Very slowly he pulled it around, first to the right then to the left, only a step or two at a time. Again as soon as the broncho knew what was wanted it made this move quickly. Then it was led forward slowly a few steps at a time. Again, as soon as it knew what was wanted, the broncho led up. In a very little while it would lead easily and quickly anywhere.

Then a lariat loop was reeved around its middle and the lariat given sharp jerks. This made the broncho buck in every instance, but the jerking was continued till the broncho no longer bucked. It was then let run at will with the rope around its middle and dragging against its legs till the broncho had examined it by smelling at it and was entirely indifferent to it.

The saddle and saddle cloth were then passed to it and it was permitted to smell at and examine both until it learned there was nothing in either to hurt it. Then slowly and quietly the saddle was placed on its back and latigoes reeved. Then quickly and quietly the cinches were tightened and buckled. In some cases the blind was necessary to do this, but in most, not. Then the broncho was given its liberty to run around the corral. If it was quiet, the saddle was soon removed. If it bucked it was permitted to run and buck around the corral till it quit bucking, quieted down and seemed perfectly indifferent and careless about the saddle.

Then a doubled rope was fastened by the middle to the saddle horn and the ends permitted to drag, one under each hind leg and flank. Again the broncho was let have the freedom of the corral until it found these ropes would not hurt it and cared nothing for their dragging over its flanks and between its hind legs.

The broncho was then unsaddled and unhaltered and let to stand to hay in the corral all the afternoon. Next morning it was ridden either with hackamore or bit, in the usual way for colts. The majority moved off quietly without running or bucking a single lick, and in no instance was a blind required in mounting.

At each obedience the broncho was petted and caressed. It was never scolded or struck angrily. Perfect quiet was preserved around the corral.

Before freeing from the "leading rope," some of the bronchos were made to stand perfectly quiet while a lariat was swung under their noses or flung at will over their heads, and they were so afraid of that jaw loop that they trembled violently, but dared not move.

After being ridden once or twice, the horses broken in the above manner have proved gentle and quiet, do not buck, and are not afraid of a rope dragging between their hind legs.

We do not know if the above is a "system," but we commend the method, for we saw it worked successfully, and we gamble on success every time, you bet.—[Pony Bill in Stockgrowers' Journal.

The young maverick savant could take a [kindergargarten?] course in the study of cow-brands. Here a wide field opens up to the scholar. The adult steer in the great realm of beef is now a walking Chinese wash-bill, a Hindoo poem in the original junk-shop alphabet, a four-legged Greek inscription punctuated with jim-jams, a stenographer's notes of a riot, a bird's eye view of a premature explosion in a hardware store.

The cowboy who can at once grapple with the great problem of where to put the steer with "B bar B" on left shoulder, "Key Circle G" on left side, "Heart [illegible] Heart" on right hip, left ear crop, wattle wattle, and seven hands round, with "Dash B Dash" on right shoulder "vented," wattle on dewlap "vented," and "[illegible] D Q," "C O D" and "N G" vented on right side, keeping track of transfers, range and postoffice of last owner, has certainly got a future which lies mostly ahead of him.

Perhaps I have said too much on this subject, but when I get thoroughly awakened on this great porter-house steak problem, I am apt to carry the matter too far.—[Bill Nye.
The Burleigh county commissioners have sent a bill to Morton county for $2,600, the cost in De Mores' trial.

Fred Willard started for Deadwood Tuesday morning. He will go in by way of Chadron.

N. A. Thayer and his bridge crew are here repairing the bridge which was drawn out of shape by the cold weather.

F. I. Ellison of Mandan, came in from the east Friday evening and after a brief visit with his brother, C. F. returned Saturday morning.
J. C. Fisher is getting to be such an expert polishing horns that admiring friends are said to pay fabulous prices for his work and to place them on exhibition as souvenirs.
Mr. and Mrs. J. N. Maxwell are now living in St. Paul. Mr. Maxwell takes a position as messenger for the Wells-Fargo, with a run between St. Paul and Fargo.
Geo. A. Cole returned Saturday night from St. Paul, where he closed the office of the N. P. Ref. Car Co. The headquarters of the company will hereafter be in Medora.

W. D. Williams, who has been here for some time looking up a chance to invest in stock, left for the east last Sunday morning. The weather was too cold for him to look around much during his stay and he expects to return.

Supt. Green was in Medora Tuesday morning. He has sent his family to Puget sound for the winter and will go for them in the spring. His duties on the Missouri division have prevented him from ever going west of Glendive personally.

Chas. Cook has started a drug store in the Red Mountain mining district north of Helena. The Helena Herald is a strong advocate of a railroad from Helena to Rimini, the supply point of the district and the place where the "four-eyed blonde" is now in business.

Willis Eaton and Harry Tarbell came down from the Logging camp and Horse ranch yesterday. They report seeing only one dead animal so far and that a through Texan of last year's drive, but that the recent cold snap had a very weakening effect on the cattle.

Charley C. Conley, well known to Montana and Dakota cowmen, died Jan. 9. at the Hot Springs, Arkansas. He had formerly been an inspector for the Wyoming stock association and of late years worked for the Hashknife and E6 outfits. He leaves a widow in the Black Hills.

W. H. Merrifield and "Sylvane" Ferris started for Chicago last Friday morning on receipt of a telegram from Theodore Roosevelt inviting them to meet him there. The boys anticipated a first-rate time and are probably now enjoying it. "Sylvane" will return in a few days but Merrifield will make a longer stay "in and about" St. Paul.

Again has there come a time for congratulation. Some time yesterday in New Brunswick, Joe. Ferris was made happy by taking unto himself a better half. We must postpone the publication of particulars or draw on our imagination, so we can only wish the newly married couple all manner of prosperity. They will probably return the last of February.

W. Aug. Fonda is being shown up in good shape by the Mandan Pioneer. In some mysterious way he was appointed post-master at Stanton to replace a lady whom every one liked. W. Aug. left a very unsavory reputation here but by all who knew him, was excused on account of a supposed mental weakness. Go to him, Bro. Tuttle.

A chinook came down on us in full force yesterday and the snow began to disappear rapidly. Last night the thermometer went down again, forming a slight crust on the snow. To-day, the weather is milder, being 12 above at twelve o'clock. The recent cold snap humped the cattle up considerably and they will need some warm weather in which to recuperate.

We wish to call especial attention to our offer of Huffman's round-up views. They consist of thirty-six handsomely finished photographs of the most prominent round-up scenes and are well worth double $5 for which they invariably have and will be sold. To subscribers, however, we offer the complete set and the Cow Boy for a year for $6 cash. This is really getting the paper for $1 a year, as the views have not and will not be sold for less than $5. Call at our office and examine the photographs.

Roby Bros. and Heegaard & Hoke were burned out in Mandan, Monday morning. The loss to both firms was $15,000. Insurance, $10,750.
The Dawes' bill for the opening of the Sioux reservation passed the Senate without a dissenting vote anp will probably pass the House easily as soon as it can be reached.

Jacob Wertheimer, proprietor of the Merchants' Hotel in Deadwood, died on January 27, of bronchitis. No one who has ever been to Deadwood was unacquainted with the genial "Jakey" and many will mourn his loss.
Of all the imbecile staggers at poetry that were ever perpetrated on an unoffending public, those in the railroad column of the Glendive Independent are the chief. For Heaven's sake, Widmyer, let up!

Gladstone, after defeating Lord Salisbury the English Premier, by very doubtful means, is again forming a cabinet and will again take up the burden of government where he laid it off a few months ago. It is almost certain that Gladstone's success is due to a combination with Parnell by which Ireland is guaranteed home rule.

Since Theodore Roosevelt gave his lecture on ranch life, he has received about 100 applications for places on his ranch. They have come from clerks, salesmen, professional men, mechanics and laborers, and the evident desire of each one was for an opportunity to lead an easy and careless life, away from the hard work of the city. The professional men asked for superintendencies, and the clerks wanted a chance to do a little figuring, but the mechanics had but faint ideas of how they were to make themselves useful in a log or mud hut, or among the herds.—[Bismarck Tribune.

Will the editor of the Mandan Pioneer go back to the time when the writer of this article was condemning the Mandan water-works system in the Bismarck Tribune and the editor of the Pioneer was lauding them in his paper? The total loss in Mandan's late destructive fires has caused the Pioneer to sing the same tune the Tribune sang over two years ago. It would have been a blessing to Mandan if the Pioneer had joined the Tribune in condemning what it and every citizen in Mandan recognized as a swindle, pure and simple.

We do not think there is a person in the county why has paid his tax levied by Stark county and we think more strongly than ever that a test case will show the law to be unconstitutional. Howard Eaton has secured the opinion of an able lawyer on the subject, who coincides with the authority we published last week and goes deeper into the discussion. He proves conclusively that the tax levied for school, road and bridge purposes is taxation without representation and consequently unlawful. The taxation for territorial purposes might hold if embodied in a law by itself, but coupled with the others, makes the whole law unconstitutional. Stark county will undoubtedly fight the matter and Billings will be organized none too soon to protect the interests of her citizens.

MEDORA, DAK., Feb. 1.—Some time ago a petition was circulated, asking that the county of Billings be organized. It is now affixed to Morton county for judicial purposes and is taxed seven mills on the dollar. Many oppose the organization of Billings county, because in that event, taxation would be twenty-five or thirty mills on the dollar.—[Bismarck Tribune.

What earthly object inspired the writer of the above, besides ignorance, it is hard to tell. Morton county levies no tax whatever on Billings county, much less seven mills on the dollar. If there is a solitary opponent to the organization of the county, we have yet to hear him express his opinion. There are now not more than two voters in the county who refused to sign the petition for organization, which was signed by more than 170 voters. Finally, we wish to state, that provided we receive $4,000 rail-road tax, there will never be an honest tax of twelve mills on the dollar at the present rate of assessment, except to meet some extraordinary expenditure, which must first be voted on by the people.

In another column will be found the notice for the election of county officers and a county seat for Billings county. It was a long time in coming but has now gone beyond the power of any outsider, or insider for that matter, to stop. In spite of politics, shyster lawers, wind or weather, Billings county will be organized on the second Monday in April. And now it behooves our citizens to drop entirely such log-rolling as characterized a few weeks of political discussion last fall and all unite on men who are qualified for the different offices. It should be agreed by all that in the first place, the stockmen name two of the three commissioners. This can be done by them in a caucus pre-vious to the one in which the balance of the ticket is nominated and their nominees can be approved by the mass convention or nominating caucus.

We have no especial favorites to bring forward for the different offices and provided good men are nominated will work and vote for the caucus nominees. Every man, however, who wants an honest administration of the county affairs should make up his mind that only men known to be capable and honest are nominated and elected. There is plenty of good, sound timber in Billings county ont of which to make candidates and it should be used in every case.

It will require time and trouble for every man to attend both the nominating convention and the election, but each man owes it to himself and his neighbors to take that trouble.

It might have been better to have had three polling places instead of one, but it was found impossible to define voting precincts distinctly and the governor thought it better to have only the one at Medora for the first time and to have the precincts defined before the next election.

As it is no one's duty in particular to call a nominating caucus, we suggest Monday, March 1, as a good day. We have no particular reason for naming this day except that it is far enough away to give every one notice in the county and as it is a month from the election, two trips can be arranged by some living at a distance which would be difficult if the times were nearer together. Provided there is no opposition to the day we will publish the call in our next issue.

The average of cattle receipts for the last three weeks at the Chicago stock yards, has been 41,500 head. A large part of these have been undesirable beef cattle which made a decided decline in prices in their classes, while on the other hand, good to choice cattle were "scarce and high." About a hundred Texas cattle, averaging 806 lbs. were on the market Monday and sold at $3.25

The large purchase by Col. J. N. Simpson of Dallas, president of the Texas live-stock association, of the Goddart ranch, and 16,000 head of cattle on the Pecos, involving an expenditure of about $250,000, indicates that the colonel has faith in Texas investments. It looks, too, as though he prefers buying to leasing at six cents. The purchase was made by Col. Simpson just prior to the meeting of the cattlemen's convention in Austin.—[San Antonio Express.

The National range convention, in session at Denver, adjourned last Saturday to meet the second Monday in February, 1887, at Denver, which will be the permanent headquarters of the association. The officers for the ensuing year are: president, Col. R. G. Head, of Colorado; secretary, J. C. Leary, of New Mexico; treasurer, Hon. J. L. Routt, of Colorado and senior vice-presiden, Thomas Sturgis, of Wyoming. Much good will follow the organization of this association as it is the first attempt by rangemen from all quarters to combine for their own protection.

We have before had occasion to allude to the Western Rural's ideas of the range industry. The last issue especially contained a mass of twaddle that it seems scarcely possible could find a medium of publication. It says: "It is a great wrong to our breeders upon the farm to compel them to compete with those who are breeding and fattening cattle upon the people's lands without paying a penny for their use." The Rural should know, whether it does or not, that nine acres out of ten occupied by range attle are totally unfit for cultivation. In the case of the tenth acre, we defy the Rural or any other paper to show a solitary instance where there has been opposition to have it cultivated. In many cases, especially in Texas and Colorado, ranges that were formerly occupied by cattle have been entirely given over to small farmers. Moreover, ranch associations have repeatedly petitioned Congress to settle the matter of leases in some way, so that the cattleman may have some kind of a tenure to his land. As it is now no cattleman in the north has a defined range of his own and other cattle are as free to graze on his range as his own cattle are. It seems to be the universal sentiment among cattlemen, as expressed in conventions, that they wish to have some title to their ranges and that they are willing to pay for the same. The Rural article shows a dog-in-the-manger policy that shames an Indian. Eastern breeders cannot use the western ranges and consequently, according to the Rural, it is an outrage for them to be used at all. The gist of the whole article, however, is in the fact that range cattle have lowered the price of beef so that there is not as much profit in it as hitherto for eastern breeders. What do the laboring constituents of the Rural think of this? It would put down a perfectly legitimate industry that has reduced the price of beef to a point where all can use it. That is, it would compel the masses of the people to pay millions of dollars more for their beef than they do now all for the sake of a disgruntled lot of kickers who are attempting at the same time to make a living out of the very industry they are trying to crush, by selling their pedigreed and almost useless cattle to rangemen. Consistency holds no place among the jewels in the Rural diadem. And now will the Rural turn its arrows to that Congress which refuses to lease land to cattlemen who are perfectly willing to pay for the same, and put the blame, if there is any, where it belongs. As an answer to the whole phillippic of the Rural, we ask: How are the cattlemen to pay for grazing their cattle on the public domain, when the government will not receive their money and in what respect they are to blame when they have repeatedly offered to pay.

The large bunch of cattle that drifted down below Dickinson have been driven back into the Bad Lands. They are not much the worse for their stay on the prairie, the steers especially being in good condition. Some of the pilgrims, however, are looking pretty thin.

The Fargo Insurance company has adjusted and liquidated some $50,000 of losses during the year 1885. On its hail insurance business its adjusters in the field made their returns from eighteen to twenty-five bushels to the acre, subject to the approval of the board of directors. At their meeting, the final adjustment reduced the amount less than twenty-five per cent, and the paid losses average on the hail business about sixteen bushels of wheat to the acre. It is said that the production of wheat on the average in the territory was less than fifteen bushels to the acre, and this would look as though the Fargo Insurance company had been exceedingly fair in its settlement with policy holders. The officers have gone on, in a quiet yet effective way, and have met the disasters of the season's work as befitting men who have gone into the business with the determination to fulfill their obligations. They have made no special effort to attract attention, and in a quiet and and business like manner have met the demands of their patrons without a murmur. The company does not pretend that it did not lose money on the hail business during the year 1885, but having liquidated all claims against it, feels that in retiring from that branch of the insurance business it has a right to expect credit for meeting its obligations honorably and fairly, and now the Fargo proposes to push a legitimate fire insurance, and asks of the public a fair share of patronage.—[Fargo Argus.

In a recent lecture in New York, Theodore Roosevelt gave additional evidence of his admiration for the cowboy and his contempt of the Indian. Here is an extract:

"I suppose I should be ashamed to say that I take the western view of the Indian. I don't go so far as to think that the only good Indians are the dead Indians, but I believe that nine out of every ten are and I shouldn't like to inquire too closely into the case of the tenth. The most vicious cowboy has more moral principle than the average Indian. Turn 300 low families of New York into New Jersey, support them for fifty years in vicious idleness, and you will have some idea of what the Indians are. Reckless, revengeful, fiendishly cruel, they rob and murder, not the cowboys, who can take care of themselves, but the defenseless, lone settler on the plains. As for the soldiers, an Indian chief once asked Sheridan for a cannon. "What? do you want to kill my soldiers with it?" "No," replied the chief. "Want to kill cowboy; kill soldier with a club." Ranch life is ephemeral. Fences are spreading all over the western country and by the end of the century most of it will be under cultivation. I, for one will be sorry to see it go; for when the cowboy disappears one of the best and healthiest phases of western life will disappear with him.—[Mandan Pioneer.

Capt. Moore and son Frank, left Sunday morning for Minneapolis. Frank expects to obtain the post-tradership at Ft. Mead.

Last Saturday, L. C. Hunt bought out Frank Moore's interest in the KC ranch and will hereafter be the manager of the KC herd. We congratulate Mr. Hunt on his prospects, which, with a good range, ranch and herd all point to a financial success.

Rassie Deffebach returned from the E6 ranch last Thursday evening. He reports the E6 cattle and those in Cave Hills as being in tip-top condition, better even than those in the Bad Lands. The E6 will start a horse-herd on the South Moreau, having bought out Macy's ranch, and Rassie will manage it.

Bob Roberts will leave for Buffalo Gap and the railroad south of the Black Hills as soon as the weather moderates sufficiently. He will engage in contract work on the railroad extension to Ft. Fetterman. Dick Carr will accompany him and a number of others will also go. They will probably start about the first of March.

Again have the merry wedding bells pealed forth and again are two hearts made happy. This time, Miss Jennie Macbeth of Mankato, Minn., and W. H. Merrifield of the Maltese cross ranch are the subjects of congratulation. Both are too well known and liked here to need any remarks except the universal wish for the happy married life which they are sure to enjoy. The marriage took place in Mankato, Tuesday night.

If any further reason in favor of organization were necessary, the delay of Stark county's alleged deputy in serving his warrant on Bill Jones is sufficient. Such tardy justice is a shame and a mockery. It matters not whether the warrant was issued on account of the brutal shooting of a dog or a man, the probabilities are that there will be the same delay and subsequent failure in obtaining justice, as long as our affairs are governed by another county. We cannot be too thankful that Billings county will soon dispense her own justice.

Last Saturday produced the largest number of "drunks and disorderlies" that Medora has seen for many a day. The wind-up came in the shooting of a valuable dog by Bill Jones. The dog was a large, affectionate creature, owned by Miss Helen Wade and the shooting was an outrage that cannot be sufficiently punished. A warrant was sworn out in Dickinson for Jones' arrest and a deputy came up Monday night. We are informed that he was several times in Jones' company and at least once engaged him in conversation. Tuesday morning he returned to Dickinson with the report that he could not find Jones anywhere, but that he would get him if it took until next summer. This has no other meaning than that he will make as many trips as possible so as to triple or quadruple his fees.

Mandan Water Works.

The Mandan Pioneer makes a characteristic answer to the charge made in our last issue against the Mandan water works system. The article occupies a column in the Pioneer; most completely begs the question and while showing to every one that our position, as published in the Bismarck Tribune was right, as clearly shows that the Pioneer lacks the backbone to come out boldly and acknowledge it.

The controversy, if carried on according to the plan of the Pioneer, would be as endless as it would be uninteresting to our readers. We merely ask the Pioneer to deny the following statements and that the history of the Mandan water works shows great negligence, if not actual fraud, for the following reasons:

1. There never was a contract let, nor did the council vote on the question. The proposal of a former partner was accepted by the Mayor.

2. Other proposals were not considered. Notably the one of a perfectly responsible company who offered to erect necessary buildings and constantly supply Mandan with water for domestic and fire purposes. Their bid was only a few thousand, two or three, we think more than the accepted proposal, which only offered water for fire purposes.

3. Full price was paid the contractor, although he put in cheaper and inferior water pipes to those mentioned in his proposal.

4. The supply of water came only from the Northern Pacific tanks and only a verbal agreement was had with an officer of the company that they would furnish the town with water in case of fire.

5. There has been at no time a guarantee of sufficient water even for fire purposes.

The above and twenty other minor charges were the points we urged two years ago against the Mandan water works. There is no use asking the Pioneer to deny them for they are absolute facts, known to all. That the Pioneer begs the question in its answer to our article is shown by the fact that its strongest point is made on the supposition that the present water works in Mandan are thought to have kept the fire from spreading and thus saved a loss of $60,000 or more. We are almost ashamed to answer such a statement, which we will do, however, by a question: "Would not the better system we have advocated saved as much as this poorer system."

In conclusion we will add that a system of water works which would have furnished water in abundance for domestic and fire purposes, would have paid for itself already in actual cash in a reduction of insurance rates and by the collections for water privileges.

We beg pardon of our readers for having taken up space for the discussion of a question that in no wise interests them or us and as we know the Pioneer cannot answer our statements, leave the matter for the Mandanites to fight out among themselves.

The anti-Chinese agitation at Seattle has reached the culminating point. Sunday morning a large body of men raided the Chinese quarter and compelled them to go bag and baggage on board a steamer bound for San Francisco. The city officers attempted to stop the eviction but were powerless.

Edward Payson Weston on last Saturday night, finished his long tramp of 2,500 miles in fifty-four days. It was a test case wherein Weston represented total abstinence and Dan O'Leary the whiskey men. Temperance won and Weston is to receive a purse of $2,000 from his prohibition friends in New York.

Mr. S. Pelton of Dickinson, recently gave a correspondent of the Mandan Pioneer some useful information relative to the thermometer and the correspondent waxed wroth thereat. We don't like to mix in such family jars, but we suggest as a good subject for the correspondent's next effort the following words which recently appeared in one of Mr. Pelton's letters; "My thermometer is placed where it is sheltered from the wind." This is the first intimation we have had that wind effects a thermometer.

As mentioned in our last issue, we to-day issue the call for a nominating convention. We have spoken to a number of citizens and all agreed that March 1 would be the best time to hold the convention as sufficient notice can be given to all and it leaves nearly five weeks between the nominating convention and April 5, the day of election. Although every one spoken to, agreed that March 1, was the best date to hold the nominating convention, it was thought unnecessary to obtain signatures to a call, for the reason that no man or body of men had authority in the matter and the list must of necessity be incomplete unless it contained the name of every voter in the county.

There seems to be perfect unanimity of feeling in regard to the stockmen nominating two of the commissioners. We suggest that it would be a good plan for the cattlemen to hold a caucus before the nominating convention on March 1 and then present the names of their nominees to the convention for confirmation. It could be easily arranged in the afternoon of March 1, or in the evening before the convention.

General Hancock died Tuesday afternoon on Governor's Island. His death was a great shock and surprise to his family and friends, being [entirely?] unexpected. He died of kidney disease. Gen. Hancock was one of the most gallant soldiers of the rebellion and an unsuccessful candidate for the Presidency in 1880. His successor as Major General will be one of Generals Schofield, Terry or Howard.

The true reason why President Cleveland refuses to give reasons for removals from office, appears to be that he is protecting politicians who in many instances have trumped up false charges against perfectly honest and competent officials. To be true to his civil service principles, he must give reasons, and good ones, for every removal. It looks as though any reason had been accepted whenever a ward striker wanted a position and that the President has placed himself in a bad situation. Either he must give up all pretension of civil service reform or expose the lies of his political friends.

It seems scarcely necessary to remind every one of the duty they owe themselves and the county to attend the nominating convention to be held here March 1. In spite of all that can be said or done there will be those who will stay away from the convention and then kick against the ticket or a portion of it. It is every voter's duty to attend both the convention and the election and he fails just that much in performing his duty if he stay away from either. No perfectly representative ticket can be nominated without the attendance of all or nearly all of Billings' voters.

Cattle in good condition and weighing over 1,200 pounds hold their price well, but prices on poor animals are totally demoralized. According to the Inter Ocean, there have been 5,000 steers sold at $4 and below, to every one sold over $5.50.

In a note to the editor, Mr. Stafford, our representative at the Denver convention, writes of the subject of branding cattle:

"Mr. Light's paper on branding cattle was very good, but in talking with the cattlemen I learn their position is that they do not feel it incumbent upon them to tear their tunics over a change in the present system of branding till there is more difference in the price paid for hides with brands and hides without brands, and that whenever the distinction is made in price that Mr. Light claims exists in value of the hides, they are ready to pay some attention to proposed changes in branding. A prominent Southwest Texas cattle owner told me that he shipped a large lot of hides from the Indian Territory, some with very light brands, and others burned all over and that there was no distinction."—[Texas Stockman.

There is a style of cow boy very rare, let it be said to the credit of the guild, who think it smart to "shoot up" a town, though of late several of these smart Alecs have had their cowardly carcasses punctured with cold lead, and this amusement is not so popular with them as of yore. Of late, terrorizing passenger trains is a favorite pastime with them, and there it is, among women, children and unarmed men, that their peculiar style of bravery (?) finds full scope. There they can insult ladies, frighten children, terrorize train men to their heart's content, and who is there to make them afraid. Some time they will make one of these plays in the presence of a sure enough cowboy, one of the sort that attends to his own business, takes off his hat to ladies even in a smoking car, and if he wants a row, hunts up some one in the same humor, and then these bad men from away high up on Bitter Creek will receive a deposit of more cold lead where it will do the most good, and a jury of decent citizens will say amen.—[Texas Stockman.

How to Break a Broncho.

"How do you break bronchos?" asked a reporter of a well-known horseman.

"Why, sometimes we use an axe and sometimes a stone-crusher," replied the horseman, who was real funny when he felt good natured.

"No, but seriously, how is the work of getting a broncho into the state of being, whereby he becomes like an every-day gentle horse accomplished?" asked the reporter, who was searching for information on an important subject, rather than for gems of American humor.

"Well, sir," said the [horseman as he?] closed one eye and looked critically at a thoroughbred bull pup, "when you come to that, a broncho never becomes like a well-behaved horse until he is ready to drop into his grave or the hands of the rendering works people.

"When a broncho gets so that he behaves himself decently all the time, if you own him, you had better sell him, for you can bet your life he has his will made and is going to croak soon. A broncho is only a pony, a kind of small horse and so we try to break him in the same way we use in breaking a colt. But the difference between the two animals is that a colt will always be wild and more or less mischievous at first, while a broncho is always vicious and full of deviltry that can never be taken out of him.

"All bronchos," continued the horseman in a meditative tone, as he slowly scratched the bull pup's head with the end of a whip-stock, "stand toward the common horses very much as the Devil does toward mankind.

"You know that all men and women and kids have more or less wickedness in 'em, but Old Nick is just chock full of cussedness. Once in a while Beelzebub may pretend to show a little bit of goodness, but it's just for a blind. He's always got some scheme in it. And that's just the way with the bronchos."

"A mule is an angel of light alongside a broncho, chimed in a hostler, who had been listening to the conversation.

"That's so," agreed the horseman, "I used to own a pair of the handsomest mules that ever set foot in Colorado, and they were pretty well-behaved for mules too. Well, I've known one of those mules, when I was driving 'em double, to kick out and hit a dog in the road twelve feet behind him and never lose step with his mate. Do you want to buy a broncho, Mister?"

The visitor jingled two lonesome nickels in his pocket and modestly replied in the negative.

"Because if you did," the horseman continued, "I've got the only broncho in this stable that ever really was broken and he's a pretty little beast too. But if you only want to know for the curiosity of it, I'll tell you how we break them.

"The first thing is to catch one. You know they run wild like other colts until we get ready to try and use 'em. Unless you use a lariat, you'll find that catching a broncho in the field or even in a corrall, is no spiritualist's picnic. When you've got him you must mount him and that ain't no coming home from the picnic by moonlight, neither.

"He will dance and kick and kick and dance like all posessed. If you are patient he will stop still enough for you to get near enough to get on, after a little while, say about an hour. Of course he's got no idea what you want to do, for nobody ever tried that on him before."

"So as soon as you make a jump he'll jump sideways about eight or ten feet, and if you've got him by a halter or a lariat he'll jerk you about twenty feet unless you let go. If you do let go you'll not catch him again for about a week unless you've been doing all this in a brick building. If its any other kind of a building he'll kick the side of it out and get away."

"Suppose that you get on him finally, you won't need a bridle the first time; just grab him by the hair and lay down. If you can, get your feet locked underneath him at the same time. If you were nailed onto him, he'd get you off in a few minutes anyway, but you have to give him as much of a tussle as you can."

"The first thing he'll do is to run like lightning, and shake himself from side to side. A part of the time he'll run sideways, and a part backwards, and now and then he'll go a little ways straight ahead. If you keep on all this time he'll stop suddenly when he's going full tilt, with all four legs stiff as iron bars. If that dont throw you off his back, it'll jerk your entrails into your mouth. I've seen a man thrown twenty or thirty feet off a broncho's back before now."

"For the first lesson all you can do is to try and keep on him as long and as often as possible. After you've done this several days you can try and get a bridle on him and bits into his mouth. You'll have a circus getting them fixed, and another one when you try a saddle, and a side show attached when you try to hitch him to a wagon, but all you've got to do is to make him know that you intend to be boss, and in time, if you are patient enough, you'll get your broncho as [near?] broken as it's possible to break one of the nasty little cusses."—[Denver Tribune-Republican.

Vol. III, No. 1, of the COW BOY, appears this issue. As a three-year-old, we hope to put on more (financial) fat, than has come to our lot in the yearling and two-year-old periods and our readers can be certain that the COW BOY will strive harder than ever to give value received.

A flood came down the river very unexpectedly yesterday, reaching Medora a little before twelve. To-day it has gone down but little, if any and it is impossible to ford it. Large cakes of bottom ice are seen occasionally and it would not be surprising if the annual break-up should begin any time.

Saturday and Sunday were two as perfect days as could be imagined. The thermometer ranged about sixty degrees above, and Saturday it reached seventy-five. The warm weather extended far south, as is shown by the immense volume of snow water now pouring down on the ice.

Lloyd Roberts and Tommy Skinner started for Cave Hills Tuesday night. Lloyd will start east soon to buy cattle on contracts he has already secured and may buy for Aleck Connell, who has bought out Gallup's Cave Hills ranch and will stock it this season. Tommy Skinner will again go to "cow-punching" in Aleck's employ.

It appears that the Rev. Schaffner was allowed to leave the country, in spite of the fact that he was sentenced to six months in the penitentiary. He was said to have chopped a large amount of wood north of Dickinson for his son to sell this winter and then bade good-bye to the banana belt and returned to his beloved Canada. The ways of justice in Dakota are sometimes very dubious.

The local officer had the thief in his eye, but when he undertook to place him in limbo the fellow wouldn't have it and drawing his gun, escaped.

The above article, taken from the Rapid City Republican, is a meagre report of the attempted capture of "Calamity Joe." It seems that the deputy who tried to make the arrest is generally so full of whiskey that he dont know the difference between a pair of handcuffs and a search-warrant and while fumbling in his pockets for the former, "Calamity Joe" drew a revolver and stood the deputy off.
