In some parts of Massachusetts, notably in Boston and Roxbury they are having destructive floods.

One hundred and fifty delegates attended an anti-Chinese congress at Portland, Oregon, last Saturday. Although the feeling of the entire west is against the Chinese, the mob-law used in driving the Chinese out will lose the movement many friends.

In another column will be found a communication written in answer to a letter making inquiries about alfalfa. From the answers, we see no reason why alfalfa should not be grown extensively in the Bad Lands, enough at least to make each cattleman independent of the native hay crop for ranch use. It is undoubtedly worth the trial.

Lieut. J. M. T. Partello and wife of Ft. Keogh, returned from their European trip about a month ago. We notice in the last Western Rural, an article from the Lieutenant's gifted pen, describing the exciting experience of being chased by wolves. As before mentioned in the Cow Boy, the Lieutenant takes almost a corresponding rank among literery men that he does among marksmen.

In view of the way horse-thieves are being cleaned out of the country and the almost absolute certainty of the capture of the thief and the recovery of the stock, it seems that a person must be either perfectly reckless or almost a fool to indulge in the pastime of running off another man's horses. Detection and capture are far more certain in the west than in the east and the punishment is more severe. Within the last two years especially, there has been good work done in clearing the country of these criminals or fools, and the good work is still going on so merrily that we can almost feel the time when horse-stealing will become a lost art. We have not heard of a white man's horse being stolen west of the Missouri in Dakota, for nearly a year.

Several Billings county tax-payers have paid their taxes to Stark county. The vast majority, however, remain unpaid. To avoid difficulty, we advise by all means that an injunction be issued on the treasurer of Stark county, enjoining him from collecting the tax until the constitutionality of the law can be passed upon. There is no doubt whatever that at least part of the tax is uncollectable and a test case will show the unconstitutionality of the whole law. As the matter stands at present, the treasurer of Stark county has authority to compel payment of taxes, together with his fees and mileage which will amount to over $80 for each trip.

Alfalfa.

Denver, Colorado, Feb. 9, 1886.

A. T. Packard,

Dear Sir:—

Your favor of Jan. 30, to Mr. J. W. Hill, Las Vegas, was sent to us by that gentleman for reply as there is no Alfalfa seed raised in N. M. That territory is supplied by Utah and Colorado. Now we will answer your questions.

1. Alfalfa will grow on dry land without irrigating, but will not yield as heavy as when irrigated.

2. It will yield perhaps three to four tons of hay per acre.

3. It will furnish two cuttings of one and a half to two tons each, and should be cut when it just comes in bloom.

4. It is a perennial clover and will last a life time without reseeding.

5. We are not positive whether it will stand such severe frosts as fifty degrees below zero but feel convinced that it will, as it is the hardiest of the clover family.

6. It requires about twenty-five to thirty lbs to sow one acre of ground, it can be sown either broadcast or with a drill, in the latter case it is advisable to drill it both lengthways and crossways to procure an even stand.

7. Best quality of seed is selling at $14 per 100 lbs. It weighs sixty lbs. to the bushel.

8. The cutting, baling etc. is the same as with Red Clover.

9. Alfalfa hay is in every respect superior to Red Clover or Timothy hay as to fattening qualities.

10. It is sowed and cut like other hay.

11. It will grow if sown on sod, but the ground should be loosened a little, and after seeding, well harrowed, thus preventing the seed from being blown away. However, we recommend to sow it on plowed ground.

12. It thrives best on a sandy, loam soil. Wet underground is fatal to the plant. The proper time for sowing is about April 1. Any further information will be cheerfully given.

Yours Truly,

Barteldes & Patch.

The spring meeting of the Montana Stockgrowers' association begins at Miles City, April 19.

At least a week before the meeting in Miles City, there should be a meeting of the Little Missouri river association, to arrange for the round-up and other matters of general interest. The time above all others then for holding this meeting is April 12, the day of the election for county officers. The reason for this is too manifest to need any urging. It will be an additional incentive for every cowman especially to be in attendance at the election and a far larger vote will be polled than would be possible if some other day were set for the meeting. We hope the officer issuing the call will bear this fact in mind.

We have received several inquiries as to the per cent. of loss among cattle in the Bad Lands. To one familiar with the range cattle business, it is manifest that a definite answer to this question is an utter impossibility. It is certainly less than it was last year when the highest estimate of loss was three per cent. Cattle entered on this winter in much poorer condition than they were at a corresponding time the previous year, but we have had less real winter weather so far than we had in any month of last winter. Cattle have fully or more than held their own and it must be severe weather that will make much of a loss.

Heavy losses of cattle occurred in Kansas, Wyoming, Montana, Dakota and other states during the recent terrible blizzard. Many have been found frozen to death standing on their feet. Colorado and New Mexico have suffered comparatively little, while Arizona had no loss to speak of. In many cases of death, the cause may be attributed to cattle drifting against wire fences.—[Arizona Hoof and Horn.

Outside of the remarkable fact that the frame-work of the above article has appeared in nearly every one of our cattle exchanges extending from the Gulf of Mexico to Canada, with appropriate changes in making its own state or territory most free from loss and outsiders suffering terribly, there is nothing in the above article but pure "filling." There has been no genuine blizzard in either Dakota or Montana this year and "the recent terrible blizzard" alluded to, came no nearer us than Colorado and at that very time, we were having the pleasantest weather we have had this winter. We might add that we never saw or heard of a wire fence either in Dakota or Montana that was long enough to harm cattle in any way. Such articles, aside from the absolute untruth of their statements, throw discredit on all its articles in particular and the entire range press in general. There is too great a tendency among cattle papers to exaggerate and it is time to call a halt.

Nine-tenths Bogus.

We asked an extensive and fashionable grocer of this city a few day's since what proportion of the product sold in Chicago as butter was butterine. He replied without hesitation: Nine-tenths! Nine-tenths of the stuff sold as butter is not butter. We asked him if he sold it? He replied: Not intentionally, but I presume I do for it is impossible to tell it from butter unless one is an expert. Here is plenty of food for thought, without stopping to consider whether or not the grocer told the truth when he said he did not intentionally sell it. It is not very clear from what he said that he believed nine-tenths of what he sold for butter was butterine. It is very clear that he did not care if it was, and therefore, if he knew what it was he purposely bought it to impose upon his customers; and if he did not know what it was then he was imposed upon by somebody else. In either case the stuff is being sold as butter, a rank fraud. Now what is to be said about such a state of things? Is it not incredible that people will submit to being swindled in this way and to this extent? Is it not incredible that butter-makers will submit to such an injustice when it is within their power to compel legislatures and law-officers to protect them? And yet, notwithstanding that nine-tenths of the butter sold in Chicago is nothing but an imitation, we are told over and over again that bogus butters do not hurt the sales of genuine butter if it is good butter. Suppose this nine-tenths of imitation butter was not made, does it require any argument to show that pure butter must be had to supply the deficiency, and if there was not enough to supply it that the price of butter would quickly rise.

According to the statement of this grocer, nine-tenths of the people of this city are eating bogus butter. Yet at the very time he was telling us this, creamery butter was worth in this city forty cents a pound, at retail, and this bogus stuff was being sold as creamery butter at that price. If the imitations had not been filling the market is it unreasonable to suppose that creamery butter would have been much higher than forty cents? A little common sense in the matter is quite as good as figures.—[Western Rural.

Overstocking the Range.

Let me warn the amateur cowman that in the great grazing regions it takes a great many acres of thin grass to maintain the adult steer in affluence for twelve months, and the great pastures at the base of the mountains are being pretty well tested. Moreover, I believe that these great conventions of cattlemen, where free grass and easily acquired fortunes are naturally advertised, will tend to over-stock the ranges at last, and founder the goose that now lays the golden egg. This, of course, is none of my business, but if I didn't now and then refer to matters that don't concern me I would be regarded as reticent.—[Bill Nye.

No distinct breed of horses, it is thought, had its origin in this country. The broncho or mustang is a peculiar type of horse, but it is a sort of uncivilized descendant of the horses brought over by the first Spanish settlers of this country, crossed with other breeds which have escaped from civilization, perhaps during the early wars. These little horses, though, have bred and raised their young of the same peculiar type so long, perhaps for over a century, and their traits are so distinct and well established that they may now be considered a distinct breed, peculiar only to the western and southwestern plains of America. These horses may now not only be considered a well established breed, but they have many excellent qualities which might be engrafted upon the breeds in common use with evident advantage. These qualities are their proverbial hardiness, toughness and powers of endurance. Perhaps no other breed posesses these most desirable qualities in a horse in a greater or even in an equal degree, and it is very desirable that they be perpetuated in a larger and more [useful?] [illegible] by crossing the mustang mares with stallions of the large breeds.—[N. M. Stock Grower.

The Arabian Horse.

The Arabians profess to trace the ancestry of their horses back to the time of Solomon, yet in the light of authentic history, their horses before the Thirteenth century were not of a character worthy of special notice. The horse of the desert receives the personal care and affection of his master. To the Arab the horse is not only a companion in solitude, but is also his only means of locomotion in arduous and perilous journeys. It is not strange, therefore, that these nomads of the desert should bestow much care upon the breeding and rearing of their horses; and during the past seven centuries such care has been bestowed. The Arabs did undoutedly understand the true principle of breeding, care, feeding, selection and training, at a period when Arabia was the seat of learning and all Europe was enveloped in the gloom of the dark ages, or was just beginning feebly to see the dawn of the revival of letters.

Arabian travellers of the last century do not agree as to the number of distinct breeds of horses in that country. A Mohammedan writer who seems to have had candor, and a good opportunity for gathering facts, divides them into six tribes, as follows:

The Dgelfe, found chiefly in Arabia Felix, seldom seen in Damascus, but common in Anaze. Horses of this breed are of lofty stature, have narrow chests, but are deep in the girth, and their ears are long. They are remarkable for spirit and fleetness, but are extremely tractable, and their ability to endure hunger and thirst is a remarkable feature.

The Secaloni, a breed from the eastern part of the desert, somewhat inferior to the Dgelfe, though resembling him in most points.

The Mefki, is a handsome horse, but not so fleet as either the Dgelfe or the Secaloni. In figure he has the resemblance to the Spanish or Andalusian stock.

A fourth breed is called the Sabi, similar to the Mefki but seems to posess no specially useful or striking qualities.

The Fridi. This breed is very common, but they are often vicious and untrustworthy, and lack some of the excellent qualities posessed by the best of the others.

The Nejdi, found chiefly in the region of Bussorah. These are said to be at least the equals of the Dgelfe and the Secaloni. Some judges assert there is no horse to be compared with them, and they stand very high in the market. The Dgelfe and Nejdi are reported to be the most valuable. They are known to be the favorites of the horse fanciers of India, many fine animals of these stocks have been carried thither by the sportsmen of that country.—[Pictorial L. S. Cyclopedia.

Relying on an authority we suppposed to be good, the Cow Boy of two weeks ago contained a statement to the effect that W. H. Merrifield had taken unto himself a wife on his eastern trip. On his return, we found that our informant, laboring under the delusion that it was funny, had made up the story out of whole cloth. This is as far from our idea of fun as black is from white and we cannot appreciate the sentiments of anyone who can even see a funny side to it.

"Calamity Joe" was captured last Saturday at Glenullin, by Sheriff Sebastian and Deputy Goudy, of Stark county. He came in from Rapid City to Glenullin, when word was immediately sent to the Stark county officers. He was found in the post-office and on seeing the officers, started to escape, running through the back door. The officers ordered him to stop but he refused to obey. As he was armed with an ugly looking six-shooter, the officers were compelled to fire on him, bringing him down with wounds in the left side and fleshy par of the hip, the shot in the side breaking a rib, but neither wound being serious. On receiving the wounds he dropped and attempted to return the fire, but his revolver refused to work and he wisely gave himself up. He was taken to Dickinson, where he will lie in jail until he is able to undergo his preliminary examination; probably in a week or ten days. It is amusing to read in eastern papers that he was one of the most notorious desperadoes and horse-thieves in the entire west. He was known here as a quiet, peaceable man, perhaps a trifle weak in the upper story, but with nothing of the criminal about him naturally. This weakness is shown by his coming back to the scene of his crime, where everyone knew him, when he knew that officers were searching everywhere for him. If it had not been for his intimacy with horse-thieves, we doubt if he would ever have stolen a horse.

It seems that we are on the eve of one of the greatest railroad wars the United States has ever known. Through rates from Chicago to San Francisco have been reduced to $30, first class and $20, second class. All the Pacific roads have been interested except the Canadian Pacific. Now, by a combination with the Manitoba, they will begin on June 15, to run through trains from St. Paul via the Manitoba and Canadian Pacific to the Pacific terminus of the latter. This will make an important factor in the fight and we very much doubt if any of the Pacific roads make money this summer.

There is at least one poliiician who dares state what he knows to be the facts concerning the hypocrisy over civil service reform. Witness the following from Robert G. Ingersoll:

"If the president feels that he is bound to carry out the civil service law, ought not the senate to feel the same way? Is it not the duty of the senate to see to it that the president does not, with its advice and consent, violate the civil service law? Is the consent of the senate a mere matter of form? In these appointments the president is not independent of or above the senate; they are equal, and each has the right to 'honor bright' with the other, at least. As long as the foolish law is unrepealed it must be carried out. Neither party is in favor of civil service reform, and never was. The republican party did not carry it out, and did not intend to. The president has the right to nominate. Under the law as it is now, when the president wants to appoint a clerk, or when one of his secretaries wants one, four names are sent, and from these four names the choice has to be made. This is clearly an invasion of the rights of the executive. If they have the right to compel the president to choose from four, why not from three, or two? Why not name the one, and have done with it? The law is worse than unconstitutional, it is absurd".—[Col. Ingersoll.

NEW YORK, Feb. 22.—The Marquis de Mores has not yet started for his cattle ranch in the west. He has been delayed here to perfect a scheme which will probably have considerable effect on the price of meats in this city. A Tribune reporter met him incidentally up town last night and although the project is not yet fully ripe, he explained the principal features of it. "We propose" he said, "to stop the expense of middlemen and send meats direct from the producer to the consumer. I have discovered that in the practical working of the cattle business as at present conducted, there are eleven middlemen, each of whom must have a profit before the meat reaches the consumer. The wholesalers are eating us up. We propose to start retail shops in all the tenement-house districts of the city, where our meats will be sold on account of the company. The cattle will be killed at our abattoir. The beef will be shipped in refrigerator crrs. It will be delivered to a central market, and from there distributed to the different shops. We shall have the scheme at work in about sixty days. The details are now being perfected. The advantage to the consumer will amount to from 2 to 4 cents per pound all around. We think we might as well give the consumer the benefit of this profit which now goes to the middlemen."

Range cattle, especially cows with sucking calves, are far from being in good condition. The small loss, almost nothing so far, is not by any means on account of the good condition of the animals, but because of the unusual mildness of the winter. Had there been as many cold snaps as there were last winter, the loss now would probably have reached five per cent. or more. The only danger of severe loss now is in a protracted cold snap, before another snowfall; a danger that we are happy to state is very remote.

In their last year's shipments, Ferris & Merrifield brought in several Polled-Angus cattle. It is a pleasure to see them now, brought into sharp contrast with the other cattle by their plump condition. They are not only in good fix, but are rolling in fat. The position of the Cow Boy for two years past that the black doddies are by long odds the best range cattle, has been abundantly proven by experience.

This winter, more than ever before, has the necessity been shown, of keeping cattle back from the river and creek bottoms. Rides over the ranges disclose the facts that a large number of poor cattle stay constantly on creek bottoms, where their existence is a slow starvation, owing to the almost total lack of feed. In almost every instance, the weakest cattle are found here, and although we have not yet seen a dead animal on the range, we are much mistaken if there is no loss among them. Back from the creeks, cattle are found to be in far better condition, having for the most part, plenty of feed. Many places were also found where no cattle had been all winter and where there is plenty of feed for the cattle now on the creek bottoms. It would require considerable extra work and expense to keep them back, but a look at the cattle ought to convince anyone of the advisability of the plan.

The flood in the river has brought[?] out a plan by which horses at least, can be transferred from one side of the river to the other in perfect safety, during high water. The plan is to nail six inch boards on each side of the two boards already laid. Of course it would be better to take up the old boards and lay new two-inch plank. Strikes all over the United States are so numerous that it is almost impossible to keep track of them. From the street car employes in New York city to the men on the Texas and Missouri Pacific roads there is a constant chain of strikes stretching clear across the United States. We think a low estimate of the present number of strikers in the country is 30,000, representing a loss to them in wages of over $50,000 per day.

There seems no chance now of Dakota being admitted to the union this session of congress, unless the Democrats conclude to compromise on all the bills and admit the territory as a whole. This is a remote contingency however, and the most that will be done will probably be to submit the question of division and admission to the people at the November election. This will put the matter off another year at least.

Three members of the Newark, N. J. colonization society were here Tuesday, having returned from an exploring trip and hunt up the river. The three are Wm. Germayne, well-known in this country as a hunter and who guided the Rufus Hatch party through the Yellowstone park, Wm. Huenemann and F. Ruhnke. The party started Tuesday evening for Sentinel Butte and Beach, near one of which places they think of starting a colony of several hundred families. They will make a thorough investigation of the country and the intending colonists will be guided by their decision. We will publish their report in a future issue.

A characteristic point in western politics is clearly shown in our nominees for office. This is the fact that in selecting candidates for office, their being Democrats or Republicans had no weight whatever. The question as to which political party the candidate belonged to was not only never asked, but we believe never thought of. We doubt if there is a person in Billings county who knows or for that matter cares to which party any three candidates for county offices belong. The fact that they are good men is alone sufficient. Their party politics are not considered of sufficient importance to be even asked. These facts are a guarantee of better officials than could possibly be elected if party lines were closely drawn, and no matter whether Dakota is admitted or not, we hope that the political question will never effect the choice of Billings county's officials. On national questions where the success of a party is at stake it is well to take sides. In county affairs where one political party may greatly overbalance the other, honesty and capacity are the only things to be considered.

The Republicans of New York are so badly demoralized that they have solicited Conkling to again lead them to victory. Whether or not he assumes the leadership, the fact of his being asked, is the highest compliment that could be given him. Although he committed the greatest political blunder of the nineteenth century in resigning his seat in the Senate and not being sure of re-election, he is head and shoulders above any Republican leader in New York.

A curious trait of states' cows is that of "caching" their calves. For several days after birth, they generally keep their calves hidden in some secure place, visiting them once or twice a day and perhaps getting their own feed a mile or more away. Strange as it may seem this practice is much more common among gentle states' cattle than any other class.

M. Wadsworth of the Bad Lands cattle Co., intends sowing several different kinds of grass seeds this season, and in the future, sowing the one giving the best satisfaction, in a hay meadow. A Branded Bear.

A gang of Colorado cowboys the other day found a grizzly bear in a favorable location, surrounded and lassoed him and then branded him in half a dozen places with the ranch mark. Bruin was then turned loose and by the law of the stock regions, will be recognized as the property of the men whose brand he carries around with him. The leader of the cowboys who played the prank was Webb Cross, a young fellow well known in Nebraska and a graduate of the Journal establishment.—[Nebraska State Journal.

Is Old Beef Tough?

I wish here to protest against the prevalent idea that old meat is tough. Never was there a greater fallacy. The age of the animal has nothing whatever to do with it and the fact is, the toughest and most tasteless meat is that of a two-year-old steer, kept fat from birth and then shipped to market where he will arrive in a shrinking condition. On the contrary, the most tender, juicy and highest flavored meat is that of an old animal, a cow or even a work steer, no matter how old, if fattened rapidly and killed when in a thriving condition. All meat is more or less tough when the animal is losing flesh and the opposite, tender and juicy if the animal is gaining rapidly, and if all your meat is killed when the animal is losing flesh, you never get any really good meat. The change can be noticed in the meat before the eye detects it in the animal's condition.—[Drover's Journal.

A number of our stock exchanges contain editorial comments on the International range association which must be prompted by petty jealousy or spite. They entirely ignore the fact of the universal good such an organization will be to the range industry and allow themselves to criticize the association harshly on account of small defects that may not take away the least from the good the association will do. The International association stands in exactly the same relation to local associations that these associations do to the individual cattlemen. Individually, almost nothing can be accomplished. United, no one will dare do them an injustice. The International association has "taken the bull by the horns" in the outset, and if backed up properly by the state and territoreal associations will effectually prevent the introduction of infectious diseases and see to it that the price of range cattle is not manipulated to suit the taste of three or four Chicago packers. It is utterly impossible for local associations to cope with these tasks successfully. The International range association, backed by all local associations, will be in a position to demand and command justice. We earnestly hope that no narrow-minded policy will cause associations to be luke-warm[?] in their allegiance[?] to the International association. Business principles should prove to all, that the new organization is worthy of their warmest assistance.

Origin of Native Cattle.

The origin of the so-called native cattle on this continent is credited to a small herd brought by Columbus on his second voyage. Other Spanish navigators brought small herds from time to time, while in 1553 the Portuguese landed both cattle and hogs in Nova Scotia. Cattle are said to have been introduced into Canada in 1608, and Virginia was reported to have 500 head of cattle in 1620. At that time stringent laws prohibited the killing of any domestic animals. Cattle were introduced into New England in 1624. It is said that in those days the red color depreciated the price of cattle, a red calf being more likely to be mistaken for a deer by the wolves and killed than a black one.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.

"The loss of cattle on the ranges in western Kansas and eastern Colorado by the terrible cold weather is beyond almost any comparison heretofore made. A report received here a few days ago makes an estimate of 25,000 head as being large enough to cover the losses. In a trip from Emporia to Syracuse, sixteen miles this side of the Colorado line, your correspondent is positive that he saw dead bodies and hides enough from the car windows to almost make that amount. In one place a bunch of 100 were found together, all dead, while in the hollows passed, where the snow had been heavily drifted, hundreds of horns, heads, and parts of bodies could be seen protruding from the snow as it was being rapidly melted away from the carcasses. And this is not all, for thousands of animals may be seen tottering along, partly frozen, and so thin and gaunt that it seemed the wind could almost blow through them. Cattlemen are evidently desirous of making as light of the matter as possible, but, in the language of a citizen of western Kansas 'there will be a big stench when warm weather comes."—[Emporia, Kan. telegram.

Owing to the withdrawal and changes in the "Stockmen's Ticket" it was thought best to drop it and make the changes as seen in the list of candidates published. This is done with the approval of as many of the stockmen as have been seen and because the printing of both tickets in full doubles the expense of publication to almost all the candidates.

Arthur Smith has declined to run for office of surveyor and it will be necessary on election day to vote for some one else in his stead. His name will be kept on the ticket, as there does not appear to be any other available candidate at present.

That there is pressing need for work on the bridges and roads of Billings county, no one at all acquainted with the Bad Lands can doubt. That there is strong objection to the county paying out any large sum for these purposes and that there will be a vigorous kick should it be attempted, is also beyond doubt. Any plan by which the county can be spared expense and still have the work done, will consequently be hailed with delight. The best plan that has been proposed is to vote on additional day's work on poll tax, at the coming election. Instead of the one day's work that is required let each voter state his preference as to whether he wishes two, three or four day's work to be done on the roads by each voter in the county. If the number should be settled at four days, every road and bridge in the county can be put in first class order and new roads made where needed. In addition to this nearly every ranch in the county would furnish extra work with teams and men. This matter should be thoroughly agitated before election.

Word has been sent by the treasurer of Stark county, that legal measures will be taken for the collection of the taxes from Billings county, if they are not paid by April 1. We scarcely think this notice will enrich the treasury of Stark county a solitary cent. Tilden R. Selmes has been retained as attorney for the tax-payers of Billings county and he will take immediate steps toward restraining the collection of the tax and deciding the constitutionality of the law authorizing it. The more this law is studied, the more unjust and unconstitutional does it appear. The railroad tax due Billings county, is abundant to pay all the amounts taxed against us by Stark and Morton counties. Only the actual cost the junior counties are to the senior counties, can be collected. This cost as we have said, is more than covered by the amount of tax raised from the forty miles of railroad running through Billings county and of which sum not even an act of Congress could deprive us. Enough of this tax is and has been paid to Stark and Morton counties, to cancel all our debts. Where then is the constitutionality in a law, compelling us to pay for what has already been paid? But even this is not all. The law, as construed by Stark county, gives the right to tax us for county, school and bridge purposes. It would be as just to make us help pay the county expenses of any other county in the United states, or New Jersey either, as it is to ask us to help out the financial standing of Stark county, which is already equal or superior to that of any county in the Territory. The taxes for school and bridge purposes are as unjust if not more so, than the county tax. Not a solitary cent has ever been spent for either bridges or schools in Billings county, except what has been raised by private subscription from our own citizens. Stark county has never contributed a nickel to us for either of these, or for any other purpose, whatsoever. In fact, the law is on its face unconstitutional, as it is nothing less than taxation without representation, an odious doctrine that died in the United States when our fore-fathers won their independence from England. As a matter of principle, the payment of this tax should and will be, resisted to the last ditch.

Only a few have so far paid the tax, and these only did so to avoid the penalty, or not knowing that a combined effort would be made to oppose its collection. If we are not mistaken, only four or five outfits have paid the tax, and all have signified their willingness to help fight it. Of course Stark county cannot be blamed for attempting to collect this tax and the only way to test the matter is to have the constitutionality of the law settled as soon as possible.

All here will remember the excitement created by the murder of Lenz, near Bismarck, the large reward offered for the supposed murderers, Mills and Gilbert and the subsequent arrest of Gilbert. His trial came to an end last Saturday in Bismarck, resulting in acquittal. Public opinion does not seem to agree with the verdict.

Sitting Bull is now at his camp near Standing Rock and it is thought that he has not long to live. His voice is no longer the chief guide of the Sioux. He is now old and feeble, and younger braves are taking to themselves the power the old man formerly possessed alone. This state of affairs is an encouraging one for those who have been fearful that the Indians would again give trouble. Sitting Bull is too old and powerless to ever again combine the Sioux nation and lead the Indians to war and there is no young chief who can ever secure the power once held by Sitting Bull. The backbone of the great Sioux nation will be broken when he dies.

We have written to the proper source to learn about the disposal of the railroad tax that would have been paid to Billings county in case we had been organized. This tax is raised from an assessment by the territory, on the gross earnings by the company within the territory and is then divided by the total number of miles of road and then divided proportionately among the counties through which the road passes, provided these counties are organized. When they are not, the expense they are to their senior county is paid. Since the Northern Pacific was built, there must have been several thousand dollars more raised from railroad taxes in Billings county than we have cost our senior countiys and the territory. It is in reference to this surplus that we have written. If we do not mistake, we stand, before organization, in exactly the same relation to the territory, that an orphan does toward his guardian. Now that we are coming of age, it is interesting for us to know whether the old man left us any money.

J. A. VanEeghen has sold his bunch of horses to B. F. Lamb. "Van." will start in afresh, by investing $40,000 in horses and ranch improvements this summer. This will give him one of the best horse herds in the whole country. He will make a specialty of fine riding horses of the Morgan breed.

The House committee on Agriculture last Monday instructed Representative Hatch to report favorably to Congress a bill amending the act to establish a bureau of animal industry by providing means for the suppression of contagious diseases. Twenty employes are authorized for the bureau and every means will be taken to advance American cattle interests.

The call of Chairman Roosevelt, issued above, should secure the attendance of every stockman who is anywhere near Medora. Whether he is a member of the association or not, makes no difference. He should attend the meeting and join the association. Except for some unforeseen item of general importance, there is no tax on the members. It is a working association and a branch of the Montana one. To the stockmen with headquarters in Mingusville and Dickinson, it is of especial importance to join at this meeting. The date is one of the best that could have been selected, coming as it does, the day after election. We hope not only to see a large attendance, but to have many new names added to the membership roll.

A. N. Jeffries, who returned from Texas last Wednesday and went to his ranch down the river, Saturday, reports that his company will drive about 10,000 head of cattle this year. He also reports that the loss in western Kansas and eastern Colorado, as published in the last Cow Boy, is not exaggerated. The long wire fences, extending for hundreds of miles and against which the cattle drift, are responsible for the most of the loss. In many cases, fifty per cent will not begin to cover it.

Link Lee, well known here as one of the best "broncho busters" who has been in the Bad Lands is now in "durance vile." He left here last fall and went to Montana, on the Rosebud. With a branding iron and a gall of the same metal he attempted to start a herd. His neighbors soon tumbled and Lee skipped to Wyoming. Here he was arrested and brought to Miles City by Stock Inspector Billy Smith. He plead guilty to the charge of stealing cattle and was sentenced to $100 fine and three years in the penitentiary. We knew that Lee did'nt have any more sense than to try to ride anything that had hair on but we certainly did credit him with more sense than to fool with the detective end of the Montana Stockgrowers Association.

The new edition of "Wonderland" published by Chas. S. Fee, contains the following about the Bad Lands. "Just as the sun was going down we entered that marvelous region, Pyramid Park, popularly known as the Bad Lands. If the most gifted writers acknowledge the impossibility of conveying an adequate idea of the extraordinary appearance of the country when describing it in detail, how can I expect to do it in the few lines that I can devote to it? That it is worth coming all the way from England to see is saying very little. The easiest way to describe anything is to compare it with something else and then you can say how far it surpasses and in what respect falls short of what you are comparing it with. But when there is nothing else like it in the world what are you to do? Well, the country owes its singular appearance to the combined influence of fire and water, which have united to produce the most fantastic forms and startling contrasts of color that the most disordered imagination could conceive. I should think there is more outline to the square mile than anywhere else in the world, and the mounds, and domes, and pyramids, and towers, and spires would constitute it a perfect Wonderland if even the whole were characterized by the dullest monotone of color. So also would the marvelous colors, if the extraordinary variety of outline were absent. Judge, then, of the combined effect. I felt, a- I have felt since, here in the Park, that, as in real life, truth is stranger than fiction, so, in nature, neither my childish dreams of fairy-land nor any conception of the genius of a Dore could paint such pictures as are unfolded in this true Wonderland. These pyramids, and turrets, and battlements, varying in height from a few feet to about three hundred feet, extend for many miles, and the surface of a single one will be black, and gray, and blue, and red, and green, not just a shade, or tinge, but the most decided and, not infrequently, the most brilliant of colors. The gray and blue are, I suppose, the natural colors of the clay, the black is coal, the green the short grass of the country, and the red the lovely terra-cotta into which the burning of the coal has turned the clay. If there were no signs of activity, the scene would be weird and awful enough. If all were cold and dead, and the power by which it was produced mere matter of speculation, I, at least, who never had much patience with scientific jargon, should be inclined to take refuge in the theory of supernatural agency, so appalling to the senses is the effect produced. But the process is still going on. Every day the burning coal is converting the gray and blue clay into the red terra-cotta, under the blue sky, and with the beautiful green grass all around. You can not only see the smoke, and from that, by a well known piece of logic, argue the existence of fire, but you can see the fire itself."

J. H. Bruem of Taylor, Stark county has, according to the Mandan Pioneer, shown his dishonesty by trying to buy counterfeit money and then shown that he is a consummate fool by kicking, when he found that he was swindled. It appears that he went to New York to buy the "queer" and the man of whom he bought it, put it in a satchel and in Bruem's presence expressed it to Philadelphia, where Bruem wished to stop off to see Independence Hall; a beautiful illustration of a patriotic criminal. When he claimed his satchel in Philadelphia, he found nothing in it but stones. It is beyond doubt that Bruem intended to pass this money among his freinds and neighbors. Stark county's "3-11-77" should give him about two hours to leave the country.

Again has Glendive received a "baptism by fire." This is the fifth fire that has occurred there in the last few months and according to report, was the most destructive of any. It completely swept the only business block remaining and now there are only a half dozen business houses and no hotel building left standing. This last fire especially is a crushing blow to Glendive and it is doubtful if she has recuperative power to recover from it. It seems that every new town must pass through this fiery ordeal, and it is only a matter of time when it strikes Medora. With the wind in the same quarter and as strong as it was yesterday, a fire starting on Main street, anywhere between Mrs. Malloy's hotel and Bob. Roberts' saloon, would make a clean sweep of the whole block. It might also jump to Fitzgerald's hotel and from there, burn clear to the Catholic church. This would be a catastrophy which, although not probable, is possible on any day such as yesterday.

Saturday, the twenty-fourth day of April, has been named by the Governor as Arbor day. This holiday has hitherto been "more honored in the breach than the observance" throughout the Territory; a state of things we hope no longer to see. Although we, in the Bad Lands, are fairly well supplied with trees, there is no one thing that Dakota stands more in need of. In Medora, there are no shade trees except those that grew naturally and there is abundant room for improvement in this respect. There need be little or no expense incurred in planting the trees, as each can dig his own. To help along the movement, if those interested in planting trees will dig them within a reasonable distance of Medora and guarantee to care well for them after being transplanted, we will bring them into town, free of charge. As this will reduce the cash outlay to nothing, we hope to see our offer generally accepted. It will improve the appearance of our town more than any other one thing.

Theodore Roosevelt arrived last Thursday evening and Friday morning started down the river to the Elkhorn ranch. He will remain in the Bad Lands the greater part of the summer. In reference to national politics, he is as outspoken as ever and has effectually cleared himself from any charge of mugwumpery. He thinks that Secretary Garland is in a bad mess through his connection with the Pan-Electric business, as the unadorned fact is that Garland received an immense amount of the stock for no other valuable consideration than that of his influence as a senator and prospective attorney-general, when the only thing that would give value to the stock was a decision of the United States, through the latter office, in its favor. Mr. Roosevelt regards Conkling's re-entry into New York politics as probable, but is by no means in love with that statesman's despotic rule as a leader. Politically, he divides all men into slaves and enemies and the "By Godfrey, I'll never be a slave," was snapped out with a determination that showed there will be strong opposition to Conkling again being the autocrat of the New York Republicans. Mr. Roosevelt is in love with the northwest and were it not for the business and social ties that bind him to New York, would probably reside here permanently.
Predictions as to when the Big Missouri will break up range between April 5 and 10.
Judging from the increase of cattle between 1870 and 1880, there must be nearly or quite 55,000,000 at present in the United States; more than one each for every man woman and child.

The Northern Pacific railroad threatens to again open up the case against the Wells-Fargo and try to prevent them doing business on the road. It is doubtful if the case will come to trial, as several of the heaviest holders of Northern Pacific securities are also deeply interested in the American and Wells-Fargo express companies.

A report was published in the Bismarck Tribune, apparently reliable unless Bro. Quinn happened at the time to be short of copy, of a fight between cowboys and horse thieves about 200 miles above Bismarck on the Big Missouri. Eight cowboys were engaged in a running fight with the thieves and finally brought them to bay on the bank of the Missouri. Here two of them were killed and the other four started across the river on horseback. Two of them broke through and were drowned and the last two surrendered. Coming to shore, they were bound on horses and carried back into the country. If the story is true, there are just six less horse thieves in the west.

Green grass has already begun to show, and last Monday we picked several new blades over an inch long. On the old grass, the fresh green was found in numerous instances to extend up two or three inches. This will soon set the cattle to wandering.

Although the loss in the Bad Lands has been very slight, less than ever before, the average condition of the cattle is probably as poor as it has ever been at this season. There are good fat beeves at present on the range, but they are not as numerous as formerly, while the cows are still further from being in good fix. They will soon begin to pick up rapidly after the second or third week on grass.

Owing to the impossibility of gaining perfectly accurate information concerning cattle losses, we have always been reasonably sure of the per cent. of loss in the Bad Lands before publishing the estimate. Even now it is difficult to be exact, but from conservative statements from range riders between the Custer Trail and VI camps, a distance of seventy miles, the whole well-stocked with cattle, the loss cannot exceed two per cent. and it is more likely to run under one per cent. In this district, we have this winter seen thousands of cattle on the range, and have not seen one solitary animal that died during the winter, except two at the Big Plateau bull-camp. This estimate is certainly within bounds and is doubtless a fair one for the whole Bad Lands, as it comes from the most thickly stocked part of them.

Bismarck, Dak., March 22, 1886.

A. T. Packard:—

In reply to yours of March 20: The railroad taxes are divided into three parts, two of which remain in the territorial treasrry, and the other is paid to the organized counties theough which the respective lines run, the share of unorganized counties being retained by the territory. The rate per mile, based upon gross earnings has been as follows for that position of the Northern Pacific west of the Missouri rives since its construction there: 1881, $13.18; 1882, $89.92; 1883, $153,70; 1884, $198.88; 1885, $176.65. There is now no provision for the share obtained from that portion in unorganized counties, to be delivered to them upon organization. It would require the enactment of a statute in order that it could be done.

The same state of things exists regarding taxes upon personal property in unorganized counties, assessed amount levied by nearest organized county. The law is found in section 2, chapter 22, laws of 1995, "shall be subject to taxation in the nearest organized county." The way the statue stands now, the relation of an unorganized county to the territory is not that of ward to guardian, but rather of garden to gardener to be cropped without recompense.

If there is anything further which you would like to know in regard to the matter, we would be glad to furnish the information.

Yours to command,
E. W. Caldwell,
Auditor.

Estray Law.

Although we published the estray law Dec. 24, 1885 we find that its provisions are generally misunderstood. The law on the subject is rather complicated but no more so than seems necessary to avoid dishonesty. In this country especially, an animal cannot be considered an estray and subject to being taken up and sold as such unless it is several hundred miles at least from the home ranch. Even then, it is generally a very simple thing to find the owners name by the brand on the animal and no one interested in the cattle business would take up and advertise an animal as an estray unless he was postive that the owner was not in the country. The law takes into consideration the fact, that range animals may wander far from the home ranch and consequently throws every obstacle it can in the way of persons wishing to take an unfair advantage of loose laws on the subject. The very fact the law is so strict and that it is so difficult to obtain ownership of estrays according to law is one of the greatest protections cattlemen have. The following is a synopsis of the full law on the subject.

"Under United States laws, estrays can be taken up only by house-holders and claim-holders and when such estray is found in the immediate vicinity of his or her place of residence in the county where he or she resides, except when the estray is found ten miles from any habitation, in an uninhabited part of the territory.

Estrays cannot be taken up between March 1, and October 1, unless found trespassing.

Whoever takes up an estray, must within fifteen days, give notice of the taking up or finding three times in a weekly newspaper printed in the county where the estray is taken up.

If the estray is not claimed within twenty-two days after the first insertion of the notice, the finder must go before a justice of the peace of the county where he resides and make oath to the facts of the case.

The justice must issue a warrant to three house-holders of the county to appraise the estray, and report a description of the animal and the name and place of residence of the finder to the justice in writing, under oath.

The justice must immediately publish the report and appraisment according to law.

Register of deeds must keep a book entitled 'Estray Register,' and record such reports.

When claim is made for the estray, both the claimant and finder must go before a justice, the claimant make oath to his name, residence and description of property, after all fees and reasonable chargs have been paid the estray must be delivered up.

At the end of one year after the finding if the finder has had the estray advertised and appraised and the appraisment does not exceed fifty dollars, the animal shall belong to the finder.

If the estray is worth more than fifty dollars, notice must be given the justice or his successor who must appoint a day of sale, the sale to be made by the justice at the county seat. The notice must be published three times in a weekly newspaper published in the county. The justice after paying the cost of advertising and all legal costs and charges, pays the residue to the county treasurer and takes his receipt therefor.

If the money is not claimed within six months and proper proof made, the county treasurer shall pay it to the school fund.

The justice must also file with the treasurer a certificate giving a description of the estray, marks and brands and the name of the finder.

The fees of the justice, advertising and appraising must be paid by the finder and be a first lien on the animal.

Any person not authorized, taking up an estray failing to advertise it or imprudently working or failing to feed it properly, shall forfeit to the owner $25 which can be recovered by action for debt before any justice of the peace.

If any estray, after being taken up and advertised, be lost or injured without negligence on the part of the finder, he is not liable to the owner.

Bradstreet's Journal says; "It is given out that the new trunk line rates on fresh meat are to be reconsidered. The last Stockgrower's Journal gets at the meat of the matter in the live-stock vs. dressed-meat rate war in good shape. A commission man from Chicago, Capt. S. R. Reed, in a speech at the annual meeting of the Northwest Texas Live Stock association declared that Phil. Armour was virtually the only buyer on the Chicago market and explained how the prices were manipulated. It seems that a pool would be formed and a medium price offered for a shipment of cattle. The shipper would refuse this price, say five cents, and go to a second buyer who would offer four, while a third would offer three. The seller would then try to sell to the man who had offered five cents and be told that he had changed his mind. The four cent man would say the same and finally the cattle would have to be sacrificed to the man who offered three cents. The live-stock shippers are now raising a disturbance on account of this monopoly and except for the point brought up by the Stockgrower's Journal have had the argument in their favor. This point is that there is no reason why the live-stock shippers should not bid for the the cattle, irrespective of the monopoly. There is no law that compels them to take a back seat and allow the dressed-beef men to carry off cattle at their own price. If their chief aim, as they say, is to break the monopoly and pay cattlemen higher prices, what in the world is to prevent them doing it by offering fair prices when the combination has forced the price down? The amount of the matter is that the dressed-beef men have been making constant inroads on the profits of the live shippers and the latter are trying to work up a sentiment against the former so that it may influence the rail-roads to make a wider difference in rates. The way out of the difficulty is for the live shippers to pay for cattle what they are worth, irrespective of a pool to lower prices or drop out of the business entirely. This, moreover, is only a question of time as dressed meat men can and do land beef in the eastern markets in better condition and can sell it cheaper that the shipper. A few years will see the virtual extinction of live stock shipping east of Chicago. The slaughter-houses now in operation and those that will soon be built will use up the most of the range cattle of the future.

Now is the time that stockmen should be on the alert. A full force of range riders should be kept in the saddle from now until the branding season begins. Young heifers in dropping their first calves often need assistance, and the presence of range riders not only frequently saves a calf but the mother also. The percentage of loss in the spring of the year may be greatly lessened in this way. One can scarcely ride a half a day on the range in any direction without seeing an opportunity of rendering assistance to some animal in distress; either a young heifer needs assistance with her first born, or an unlucky calf has dropped into a ditch or hole where it must die if not helped out. Cows that are very old are also generally low in flesh at this season, no matter what the winter has been, and frequently need care as well as the heifers. Then in a few weeks from now stock will be constantly getting into the mire and will need to be helped out, and it will pay better to have men in the saddle at this season of the year than any other. Instead of counting the cost of these range riders, cattle owners should consider that in justice to the men they should furnish them employment the year round, and should reckon their expenses on this basis. There is no economy in just employing a force of cowboys at branding time and letting the herd shift for itself the rest of the year, as is practiced by so many owners Men are needed on the range at all seasons of the year, and more especially in the spring, and if they were employed by the year they could earn their wages right along. We, therefore, urge owners if they have not a good force riding daily among their stock, to lose no time in putting men in the field. It will be economy in the end, and it is far better for the owner, better for the country and for the cowboy to give him employment every day that he can earn his wages than to let stock die of wanton neglect. Give the boys a show, and save your herds by giving them the necessary attention.—[Rocky Mountain Husbandman.

Bad Lands Cow Boy, By A. T. Packard.

"STICKERS"

122 votes polled.

The judges and clerks had the hardest work of any. Their siege of fourteen hours, with no intermission, was harder than sawing wood.

Mr. McGinness made a good supervisor. In case any of his decisions had not given satisfaction, a glance at his frame would have discouraged the average objector.

There were three different kinds of tickets used. There being a chance for four or more stickers on the regular ticket, the result in some cases, was unexpected.

J. R. Grymes made a good run for constable. He didn't stay with the leather long enough, though.

When one of the judges makes a man who is swearing in his vote show up his teeth to decide his age and then remarks that his statements are "tooth in," it calls for gore.

The fact that no one could vote whose name was not registered, until he had sworn his vote in, caused several to believe that their vote was challenged.

Gill Kennnedy deserves and has the everlasting thanks of the officers of election for a large pail of delicious lemonade.

John Warn was again remembered by one of his Medora friends. "Alaska John" would have "got there, dead or alive" if he had been present.

The way Mike Coleman's name bobbed up for constable, knocked calculations "galley west for election."

Some good hits on Democrats would not have been mede in the poll room, if all had known that Supervisor Mc Ginness was one of the strongest Democrats in Dakota.

The danger of one person depending on others to do what he should do himself, was well illustrated in the election of surveyor. Arthur Smith refused to run under any circumstances. He is not a citizen and would not have accepted the office if he had been. Consequently he resigned in favor of D. O. Sweet, who consented to run more as a matter of accommodation than anything else, as it is doubtful if there is anything in the office except the empty honor. As it was so well understood that Arthur would not serve if he could, everyone expected that Sweet would get the highest number of votes and consequently neglected to substitute his name for Smith's, whose name appeared on the ticket as the nominee of the convention.

The spring meeting of the Montana Stockgrowers' association begins at Miles City, April 19.
Lloyd Roberts will arrive in Medora about the 25th., delivering at Dickinson Aleck Counell's herd for his Cave Hills ranch.

The Ref. Car Co. and Bad Lands Cattle Co. will start an outfit about the 17th. to work the Grand river country, probably from its source to its mouth. The outfit will probably work in connection with one from the E6.

Wm. Dantz arrived this morning with 300 two-year-old heifers and unloaded at the stock yards. The lot is a fine one, probably as good as has ever been brought in at this season. They are all from Minnesota. Dantz will start back east in the morning to receive another lot of 350, which have already been purchased in Iowa.

We are in receipt of a book entitled "A Texas Cowboy," written by C. L. Siringo, and printed by Siringo & Gibson, Chicago. It has not, nor does it pretend to have any claims of a literary value, but it is written in cowboy language and is descriptive of many phases of cowboy life. The author's description of the manner in which herds were started in early days, with a pony and a branding-iron is especially interesting. Looked at from the cowboy point of view, it is a truthful account of the hardships a cowboy voluntarily or involuntarily endures.

Meeting of the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association.

The fourth semi-annual meeting of the above association was called to order by Chairman Theodore Roosevelt, at the town hall, last Monday morning at half past ten.

The roll being called by Secretary J. L. Truscott, nearly all members answered to their names.

The minutes of the last meeting were read and approved.

W. A. Merrifield proposed the name of L. C. Hunt for membership. The chairman stated that unless there was objection he would decide that as membership in the Association was by firms and as E. W. Casey & Co. already held membership, there was no necessity of electing Mr. Hunt, he being representative of E. W. Casey & Co. There being no objection, it was so held and Mr. Hunt's name was enrolled as a member.

The report of the secretary was read, showing the association to be free from debt and a cash balance in the treasury.

Willis Eaton moved that John Goodall be elected foreman of the spring round-up. There being no further nominations the motion was unanimously carried.

On motion of Willis Eaton, it was decided to start the round-up on or about June 1. at the mouth of Box Elder. Working down the Little Missouri to the mouth of Beaver, thence up Beaver to its head.

On motion of J. L. Truscott, it was decided that the committee appointed to go to Miles City, be instructed to recommend the above at that meeting.

It was moved by J. L. Truscott and carried that J. N. Simpson and Theodore Roosevelt be appointed the committee to represent this association at the Miles City meeting. These two members also to have power to choose a third. Also that the committee be instructed to recommend that J. N. Simpson and Henry Boice be the members of the executive committee from Dakota.

As moved by Willis Eaton and amended by J. L. Truscott a motion was made and carried, that mavericks be given to the owner of the range on which they are found. In case of dispute, the matter is to be left to arbitration, each party in dispute choosing a representative and these to choose one, two or three more.

On motion of D. K. Wade, this resolution was ordered embodied in the by laws of the association.

W. A. Merrifield brought up the subject of branding cattle between Dec. 1 and the spring round-up.

On motion of Willis Eaton, a resolution was carried to the effect that members shall not be allowed to work cattle between Dec. 1 and the spring round-up and that in other respects our rules should conform to those of the Montana association on the subject.

J. L. Truscott moved that the association stand by Jos. McCoul and others in their action in reference to an animal in dispute between them and the Bad Lands Cattle Co. On calling the roll, there were found to be eight yeas and seven nays. The chair stated that on account of the peculiarity of the vote and that as it was a subject to demand greater unanimity and without in any manner expressing an opinion on the merits of the case he should vote nay and declare the motion lost.

Association adjourned.

In the BAD LANDS COW BOY this week will be observed the advertisement of Lyman's gun sights, which are probably about as near perfect as will be reached in this century. His rear sights are universally used by hunters and riflemen throughout Europe and America, and, when used with his new ivory bead front sight which is here illustrated, an ordinary marksman can bore the bulls-eye with astonishing accuracy, and kill running game with ease. The American Field recently published engravings of targets made with these sights, showing that out of seventeen shots, all struck within the bulls-eye but one, which struck the line between bulls-eye and center. We have received a sample of the sight, and will take pleasure in showing it.

If he who makes two blades of grass grow where only one grew before, is a public benefactor, then whatever will cause the soil to grow more fodder and extend the season of growth six or eight weeks is also a benefactor.

Alfalfa will do this. It is a clover nearly related to red clover. It is as hardy, if not hardier. Rooting deep it is quite independent of the rain fall. It starts earlier in the spring than the grasses and continues to grow after they are dead.

Mr. J. R. Lowe, of Bijou Hills, Dak., writes me that five years ago he received from the Agricultural Department a package of alfalfa, which he scattered thinly over a patch of ground that had been worked two years and paid no more attention to it. Naturally the weeds took possession but the alfalfa caught. For three years the weeds had the upper hand and being an eyesore he mowed them. But the following year being very dry the alfalfa gained ascendency, and in the spring of '85 every plant was in its place alive and vigorous and showed its color three weeks before anything else started, and was full six inches high before cattle could live on the prairie. He is absolutely certain that not a plant has died from any cause, that it extends the time of green feed at least two months in the year, early frost not killing it down; that it is worthy of trial, and he has great hopes that it will prove a success in Dakota.

There is ample proof that it will stand our cold winters. At Highmore, Dak., there are five acres, sown last spring, that made a good growth. It was visited by a hail storm, but being a tough stalk was not cut as badly as the wheat. Specimens I have from the field, in fact show no effects of the hail.

It was a standing temptation to the pigs of the neighborhood, and whenever they got out they took a near way to the alfalfa. At Blunt, Mr. Zollers pulled from his patch a plant whose root measured twenty-two and a half inches, the growth of one season. At Miller, Hand Co., an eighth of an acre sowed on sod last spring made a splendid growth. I observed reeds on the stalks which were left standing to help it through the first winter. It was alive and in good condition the 8th. of February when examined. At this place, an experimental patch, by its growth enthused us with a belief in its future.

I hear some one ask what if it does yield eight or ten bushels to the acre yearly after it is well set, what is it good for?

It is relished by all kinds of stock; it takes the place of corn; alfalfa fed beef resembles corn fed; pigs riot in it, and grow fat during the mild months by having portable fences on different lots, as it will not stand constant feeding; it will enable Dakota to compete with the corn states in raising stock; it will produce an abundant yield every year in spite of hail, frost or drought; it will renew the soil. Dakota cannot always grow small grain. It is only a question of time when the present culture will exhaust the soil. I look to alfalfa as the stepping stone to profitable stock raising, a sure foundation to any country's prosperity.—[Northwestern Farmer.

Freight conductor M. Linsley, who was run over last week in Dickinson is now in the hospital at Brainerd. His leg had to be amputated, but he is now resting easily and will recover.
Editor M. H. Jewell, of the Bismarck Tribune, came down Tuesday evening and went back Wednesday morning. The last time he was here, Medora consisted of sage-brush and a dug-out.

The N. P. Ref. Car Co. has also had an injunction issued, restraining Stark Co's. treasurer from collecting taxes of Billings county. George Cole, as representative of the Co. had the papers served yesterday.

There were numerous complimentary remarks at Mr. Roosevelt's method of conducting the stock meeting. Useless or irrelavant discussions were brought to a sudden stop and close attention was held on the business before the meeting.

C. R. Kelsey, of J. S. Collins & Co., has appointed J. A. Ferris the sole agent for the Collins' goods in Medora. A full stock is now on hand at Ferris' store and they will be sold at the same prices as goods ordered directly from Miles City.

We are in receipt of a telegram from Tilden R. Selmes, stating that he has procured an injunction on the treasurer of Stark county preventing him from collecting taxes of Billings Co. By this time the injunction has been served on the treasurer by the sheriff. This will make a stay of proceedings until the constitutionality of the law can be properly decided.

We received last evening a copy of the injunction, issued through Attorney Selmes by Judge Francis. It restrains the treasurer of Stark county from ever collecting taxes from Billings county, provided the charges made are proved. It might be well to state that there are several new charges made and if they are proved it will render the assessment null and void, whether the law authorizing it is constitutional or not. Mr. Selmes will be in Medora in a few days.

Theodore Roosevelt returned Monday from a successful chase after the men who stole his boat about three weeks ago. Sewell and Dow accompanied him on the trip and they overtook the thieves about a hundred miles down the river. Mr. Bad Man Finnegan tried some of his old tactics and refused to return but such sound arguments were advanced that he concluded to change his mind. The prisoners were brought across the country to Dickinson and from there were sent to Mandan for trial. They will be sent up for as long a time as the law allows.

There are still several tax-payers who have not signed the agreement to pay their pro rata in contesting the legality of the law under which we are taxed by Stark Co. The paper was left with us by Howard Eaton for additional signatures and we hope to see every tax-payer represented on it. This contest is something in which every tax-payer is interested and the only fair thing is for each tax-payer to pay his share of the expenses. The pro rata to be fixed by the amount assessed against each tax-payer. This will make the share of each insignificant. This being a matter of such public concern, no one should depend on his neighbors' paying his share.

The most scurrilous libel that even long-suffering Medora has ever endured, is contained in the following Bismarck telegram to a Chicago paper, dated April 16: "At Medora last evening, (1) the cowboys of the Bad Lands (2) indulged in a dance at a leading hotel and although no one was killed, the event was worthy of notice.(3) The Marquis de Mores, having returned from the east, has started operations at his Medora ranch(4) and the cowboys were rejoicing over their source of financial supply.(5) The hotel was filled with transients,(6) most of whom were called to the place by business relationships with the Marquis.(7) The dance was at its height at midnight. The female population of the Bad Lands was present and the cowboys were determined to show their mettle and worth.(8) At midnight, revolvers were drawn(9) and from that time until morning,(10) the fusillade drowned the music of the orchestra.(11) Every bed-room in the hotel was shot into(12) and that no one was killed, is looked upon as a miracle.(13) Dr. Williamson of this city, occupied a room near the ball-room(14) and his door was perforated(15) so that it resembled the lid of a pepper-box.(16) In the morning, he picked up numerous bullets in his room, (17)—enough, according to one story, to fill a quart cup(18)—and he believes that his life was saved by the mattress, under which he remained during the night.(19) Every guest was paralyzed with fear(20) and from the number of bullets shot into their rooms(21) all feel grateful that they escaped with their lives.(22) Not once during the night did the dancing cease,(23) women and men cheering and yelling,(24) as each volley was fired.(25)" Whether the author of the above was actuated by malice or a craving for the sensational, it is hard to decide. Certain it is that there are in the above article, twenty-five separate and distinct lies. It might be best to show them by mentioning the exact facts. The ball was held on the evening of April 12, and was managed by Fred A. Willard and Moses Ryder, sufficient guarantee, if there had been any need of it, that there would be no disturbance whatever. The dance was not given in honor of the opening up of any new work here, for the season's work has not as yet opened up in any of its branches, but was given in honor of the stockmen who were present for the purpose of attending the election and the stockgrowers' meeting. The dance was attended by the stockmen and citizens, with their wives and daughters and the low-minded flings at the "female population of the Bad Lands" who were "cheering and yelling as each volley was fired" are enough to make the blood of every man who knows the facts, boil with indignation. Nowhere can be found truer or more perfect women than are found right here in the Bad Lands. To intimate that they would in any way approve of such a ruffianly trait as the discharging of a revolver inside of a house, or any "bad man" shooting outside, is an insult hard to be borne by the husbands and fathers in the Bad Lands. There was one shot and one only, fired in the hotel that night and for that matter, the only one that has been discharged there since Mr. Boyd assumed the management. This one was fired by some drunken tenderfoot in the hall in front of Dr. Williamson's room, which by the way, was the farthest removed in the hotel from the dining-room, which was used for dancing. Although no one at the dance was in the slightest degree intoxicated, we say that this man was drunk because he made considerable noise in the halls by colliding with Dr. Williamson's door, before discharging his revolver. That the man was a tenderfoot is shown by the fact that his was a 38-calibre revolver, which made so little noise that only a few who were in the office of the hotel, heard the discharge and after discussing its probable whereabouts, concluded that it was fired near the depot. From extensive inquiry, we are satisfied that this was the only shot fired in Medora during the evening. The bullet went through the plastering in the hall and rebounded from the brick to the floor, where it was picked up in the morning by Dr. Williamson on coming out of his room. Not a shot that or any other night, ever went through a door in the hotel. If the Bismarck perjurer will come here and show us a solitary hole shot through Dr. Williamson's or any other guest's door, we will fill it with diamonds and give to him in token of the clearness and beauty of that truth which he so rarely stumbles upon. The most of the blame for this criminal libel on Medora is now laid to Dr. Williamson, who undoubtedly took a highly colored account of the affair to Bismarck. We think we can put our finger on the man who sent the telegram to Chicago and who will probably be called on in a suit for libel to explain his version of the matter. Our columns are open to Dr. Williamson to vindicate himself from connection with what he knows to be an entirely unjust commentary on Medora, a slander on the citizens of the Bad Lands and an insult to every woman here.

There is no disguising the fact that there was some foundation, though ever so slight, for the above article, in the discharging of a revolver. Sheriff Willard is in earnest in the article published in this issue, stating that the law in respect to the discharge of fire-arms will be strictly enforced, and we look for the practice to fall into "innocnous desuetude."

T. W. Gordon wishes us to announce that the sale advertised in this issue is a genuine one and that it will afford an unprecedented opportunity to buy cheap goods.
George Frazer and Riley Brooks left this morning for the Hashknife camp, where they will represent the Ref. Car Co. in the round-up which starts from there about the 17th.

The Marquis is now in Milwaukee, making arrangements with the brewers to supply them with malt and to receive from them the refuse, which is the basis of the new fattening food, called "brewers' grain."

The Commissioners' ideas of the way to run the county, cannot be too highly praised, and bid fair to be carried out to the letter. In brief, they propose that the same rules shall guide them as do in the conduct of any business.

The citizens of St. Paul are entertaining the committee sent there to discuss the matter of establishing stock-yards, to make a market for western cattle. This committee will stop at Medora on its return, to look over the plans of the Marquis for establishing a fattery here. They were to arrive to-night, but it is doubtful if they will be here before Sunday.
Wm. Benson of Dickinson, day before yesterday shot a very large silver-tip bear, on Knife river.

A letter from Charlie Galligan, foreman for the Hashknife outfit, states that that company will drive 40,000 head of cattle to their northern range this summer. They will come in thirteen herds. He also states that there was considerable unexpected loss among the cattle during March.

The inaugural address of Chairman of the Board Truscott is too good to be lost. It ran as follows: "Mr. McKenzie proposed me for chairman and I proposed Mr. McKenzie. Whereupon we compromised on me. I therefore declare myself duly elected and call the board to order."

Willis Eaton will probably begin assessing on Saturday of this week. Under the new rules by which everything is to be assessed at its full value, and the railroad tax of over $5,000, we confidently expect that the rate will be under six mills. If so, we will have the lowest rate of any county in Dakota.

Lloyd Roberts went through Medora to Glendive, Sunday morning, where he delivered several cars of cattle to Mr. Bangs. He returned Monday and left this morning again for St. Cloud, where he has contracted for more cattle. His daughter Lizzie went with him, to attend school in Minnesota.

A cousin of J. A. VanEeghen is now visiting at the VE ranch. The last word received from VanEeghen was that horses were scarcer in Washington Ter. than he expected, but that he was making fair progress. He expects to buy at least four hundred mares and more, if he can buy them right. He has not yet decided whether to drive or ship.

We have an over-stock of 3½ Studebaker wagons that the Studebaker M'f'g. Co. have instructed us to close out at $75 each. These wagons have never turned a wheel under a load, are new and first-class in every respect, have the Co's. full guarantee for 5,000 pounds, according to old freighters are the best ironed and easiest running wagon of its size in the world, and cost at the factory, $87 each in car lots. There never has been and never will be again such a bargain in wagons in this country. The $75 rate is cash of course and holds good for one or more.
