J. H. Gordon and wife and Joseph Hanauer of Glendive, were here Sunday, on a visit to T. W. Gordon.

Dr. Stickney of Dickinson, was here last Saturday. Hereafter, he will be in Medora twice a week. The Dr. is now the railroad surgeon, taking the place of Dr. Robarts, who now has charge of Hunter's Hot Springs.

To-day's showers are a perfect god-send to the stockmen. Although the grass was well started a week or ten days ago, it has grown but little, if any, since that time. It will now get a good permanent start.

It will make Assessor Eaton rustle hard to get through his work by July 1. He must, according to law, assess from Cave Hills on the south, to the Missouri river on the north and to Stark county on the east, making a territory in round numbers 200x50 miles. Our assessor's cowboy training will stand him in good stead.

Charles Eaton and bride returned Monday evening from their bridal trip, being accompanied by Mrs. Eaton's mother. The party is now visiting at the Logging Camp, before going home to the SOHO ranch. Mrs. Eaton and mother are warmly welcomed to the Bad Lands, which is to be their future home. They are both accomplished musicians and we look for many a happy social gathering at the SOHO ranch.

So much has been written and said lately on the subject of ensilage and silos, that it has attracted especially the attention of small stockmen to the benefits to be derived from their use. To anyone wishing a ready means of fattening cattle or who have any number of milch cows, silos undoubtedly would prove a profitable investment.

From "A Practical Treatise on Ensilage and Silos," by E. W. Ross & Co. of Springfield, Ohio, we learn many points of interest. The work consists almost wholly in letters, written by farmers and others who have tested the value of ensilage and all are loud in their praises of it.

As is to be expected, opinions differ widely as to details, but we publish as nearly as possible, the substance of the letters.

Like most other things, silos cost almost any amount the owner wishes. Aside from the lumber, or stone and cement required, the item of labor is the only expense. Thus, good silos for feeding a few animals, have been built for from $30 to $50. More elaborate ones, for feeding a larger number of animals, could easily cost thousands of dollars. The only requisites seem to be: water and air-tight sides and bottom and a movable top that will fit inside the walls as perfectly as possible. Sometimes the top consists only of hay or straw. The silo is usually built partly underground, as it is then handier, both to fill and empty. Common dimensions for a silo are twenty feet long, ten feet deep and twelve feet wide. Such a one, built of lumber in this country, with double walls filled with dirt, would cost about $250. Figuring at fifty pounds to the cubic foot, such a silo would hold about sixty tons. This will last twenty cows for six months.

Opinions vary as much in ensilage as they do in silos. Clover of different kinds, pea vines, etc., are highly recommended, but the vast majority seem to be in favor of corn. This is cut when the corn is in the milk, the ears and stalks are cut into lengths about an inch long and the silo is filled as quickly as possible. The ensilage is tramped thoroughly and the top is then put on. Over this is spread earth or rocks, about a foot thick. There must be a constant and heavy pressure and the top of the silo must be movable, so that it will follow the ensilage, which shrinks a third or more. The ensilage ferments and is ready to be fed at the end of two or three months. As to its relative value, we quote an estimate from one of the letters. "With one hundred fresh milch cows, feed for six months will take 250 tons of timothy hay, worth at least $7 per ton, $1,750. It will take at the same time 132 tons of bran and meal, at $14 a ton, $1,850. This makes a total cost, under the old system, of $3,600. Now, for the same time and number of cows, with ensilage; 450 tons of ensilage, cost in silo under the press, $450; fifty tons of timothy hay, at $7 per ton, $350; seventy-two tons of bran and meal, at $14 per ton, $1,000, making a total of $1,800. We feed fifty pounds of ensilage, seven to eight pounds of mill-feed and five pounds of hay per day to each cow. Here is a gain of $1,800 in favor of ensilage. And not only this, but we gain in milk from one and one-half to two quarts a day from each cow, which will make about $1,000 more to add to the gain in feed." Of course the feed which makes milk in a cow, would make fat in a steer. A fair to good crop of corn ensilage ranges from fifteen to twenty tons to the acre.

We predict that before many years, silos will be built numerously, throughout the range country. An ever-occurring possibility of fire, either before or after mowing his hay, the liability of that feed being extremely scarce and of poor quality, and the impossibility of any more than keeping an animal in condition on hay alone, will inevitably turn the ranchman's attention to ensilage. It is a sure crop, costs but little, if any, more than hay, is three times as valuable as hay and cannot burn, either before or after cutting.

The project of the establishment of a fattery here by the Ref. Car Co., is now approaching realization. Every one of the sixteen members of the committee from the Montana association, agreed individually to put in cattle of their own and as a body, agreed to report the matter favorably to the Association. The details of the plan here have not been fully worked out, but in the rough, are as follows: The plant will consist of a barn, capable of holding 2,500 cattle or upwards, besides outside ranches, for holding the cattle, a large farm for raising a root crop, etc. Between September and December, 18,000 cattle will be delivered here for fattening. Fifteen or sixteen thousand of these will be distributed to the different ranches, to be held ready for the fattening process. From two to three thousand will be fattening all the time. Over 250 acres of land on the river bottom will be cultivated for a root crop, which will be fed not only to keep the cattle in condition, but it will also be a constituent of the fattening food. The boiled roots, costing only a few cents a hundred pounds will take the place of corn-meal costing a dollar a hundred. The analysis of brewers' grain is as follows: Fat, 6.57; Albuminoids, 20.92; Carbo hydrates, 56.33; Cellulose; 12.12; Mineral matter, 4.06; Total, 100. Under very unfavorable circumstances last winter, such as being fed in a nearly open shed, exceptionally cold weather and several mistakes in feeding, made by new men, three steers were fed twelve quarts of the brewers' grain and five pounds each of hay per day and averaged a gain of three pounds each per day between January 7 and March 6. The last week of the experiment, when the weather had moderated, the cattle gained five pounds a day. From careful estimates, it is found that brewers' grain can be put on the market for about half a cent a pound. It will, if the supply of grain holds out, revolutionize the feeding system of the United States. Prof. Mott of New York, after a careful test, pronounces the new food to be practically and scientifically correct and highly recommends its use. There seems now no reason to doubt that the fattery here will be a great and constantly increasing success. The Northern Pacific railroad is joining actively with the Marquis in the fattery enterprise and gives rates on the brewers' grain which are merely nominal.

From a Galveston, Texas, press report, we learn that "Thousands of beef cattle are being brought to Galveston by rail, to be started on the trail. There are thousands of cattle and a thousand head of horses leaving every day, the cattle for Dakota and the horses for Kansas. Water and grass are exceedingly scarce in western Texas, owing to the drought and cattle that passed a good winter, are going to market in very poor condition. The trail is now virtually open and fully 45,000 head of cattle are going northward. Heretofore, most of the cattle from the ranches, struck the trail in the southern or western part of the state. This year, the long drought in the Pecos valley, has forced cattlemen to send their herds as far as possible by rail, before starting them on the trail. This had never been attempted before, as cattlemen thought it would cost too much. The reverse has been the case. Instead of the customary losses of cattle on the trail before they get out of the state, there is none at all. Leading cattlemen here, looking after the interests of their herds, express the opinion that there will be no national trail in a few years, as railroad transportation from Texas to Dakota, Montana and Colorado will be found cheaper."

The Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association at its last meeting, passed a resolution adopting the Montana law in respect to the time of branding cattle. As the law seems to be little known, we publish it in full: "It shall be unlawful for any person to brand or mark any calf or other cattle that are running at large during the first day of August and the first day of September of each year, and between the fifteenth day of November and the fifteenth day of the month of May following. Provided, that the owner of any stock may brand, on his own premises, at any time, in the presence of two responsible citizens:

Any person violating the provisions of this act shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and, on conviction before any court of competent jurisdiction, shall be punished by a fine not less than twenty-five dollars, nor more than one hundred dollars, for each and every animal thus branded, or by imprisonment in the county jail for a term not exceeding six months, or may be punished by both such fine and imprisonment, in the discretion of the court."

Of course the penalty in the above law cannot be inflicted in Dakota, but it is a good law, the breaking of which would cause more disputes and hard feeling than almost anything else in the cattle business.

Charlie Rowe and Miss Bentley, both of Beaver creek, were married at Dickinson, May 2. We join in hearty congratulations to the newly married couple. We prophecy that this union will cause renewed activity to the social life of the Beaver valley.

Arnett & Thomas are making some valuable additions to the AHA herd. Already they have driven on their range, about thirty head of full-blood Hereford bulls. Two thousand two-year-old Montana steers have also been bought and will be added to their herd this summer.

The largest barn in the world is situated at Papilion, Neb. It covers five acres of land and shelters 3,750 cattle. It is said to be the intention to enlarge this stable to accommodate 8,000 cattle. The object is to take range cattle and finish them into fine beef. This great barn is said to have a complete system of waterworks and is thoroughly washed, twice every day. The cattle are fed on cooked meal. One man feeds the whole herd by turning on a large faucet, thus letting the feed run to them from tanks.—[Hoof and Horn.

Lieutenant Partello of Fort Keogh, has not lost his grip a particle on shooting. With a military gun and plain open sights he recently made a perfect score of fifteen consecutive bull's-eyes at 500 yards and seventy-three out of a possible seventy-five at 600 yards. The target-practice of his company is also improving rapidly. They made seventy qualifying scores a few days ago, where a good average is fifteen. The Lieutenant will make the Bad Lands a visit in a few months.

The average importation of horses from Canada into the United States for some years past has been about 22,000 head. A few years ago, the average value of horses so imported, per head, was $95; whereas last year, it was $140. This shows not only a rapid improvement in the quality of the supply, but the fact that the demand requires just as many, is evidence that it is at least just as easy, and in many cases far easier, to find purchasers for the better class of animals. The difference to Canada, represented in these values, is over $1,000,000 annually.—[Hoof and Horn.

We just want to rise up long enough to ask whether, in spite of senator Edmunds and the vigilance of the reporters, president Cleveland has not committed bigamy. We have a collection of newspaper pictures of Mrs. Cleveland, ranging all the way from Bismarck with his mustache cut off and old Mother Bendor to the Venus de Medici. One picture of the collection resembles another about as much as a maverick resembles a hondoo. We don't want to cause any trouble, but either the president has started a harem in the White House or some newspapers are lying about "their remarkably faithful likeness of the President's bride."

According to recent telegrams, the average reporter's enterprise is only exceeded by the capaciousness of a car platform. We read in the Pioneer Press that "the President thought he had outwitted the reporters in leaving the White House grounds by an almost unused gate to talk a special train for Deer Park, but a Pioneer Press reporter was watching every move the bridal couple made and on his trusty bicycle followed the carriage to the train, which steamed out at 10:55 with a Pioneer Press reporter on the hind platform." Here we thought, is a reporter that will make his mark in the world. Sure enough either he or another one did for the New York World contained exactly the same article, except that in this case it was a World, instead of a Pioneer Press reporter. Here then, are the two rustlers for news who will in time occupy the top notches of journalism. Someway we began to doubt the reporter's veracity when we found that a St Paul Globe repersentative also had a reserved seat on the hind platform. We had scarcely recovered from our surprise when we found that an Inter Ocean reporter was also on the list and the hind platform. By this time the platform must have been rather crowded but a Minneapolis Tribune reporter edged his way on, only to be elbowed by a news friend from the Cincinnati Enquirer. This must have shoved some of them up on the brake wheel but they had to make room for representatives from the Boston Herld, the New York Times, the Indianapolis Journal and the Detroit Free Press. After reading these veracious accounts of the news gathers, we came to the conclusion that either that back platform had a crowding capacity equal to a Chicago street-car or that the reporters were lying. The latter proved true for the special correspondent of the BAD LANDS COW BOY rode on the front platform all the way from Washington to Deer Park and has sent us affidavits that he was the only occupant of that airy perch and that not even a tramp decorated the back platform with his presence.

If Mose. Ryder doesn't take care, he will bring a case against himself for malicious maiming. We heard him try to get a man to ride his broncho on a bet of $50 that he couldn't ride him four rods. As we publish no obituary notice this week, the fact speaks for itself that the bet was not taken.

The round-up was at the 777 camp Tuesday night, making fast and satisfactory progress. The boys think they will finish by the 15th. Both riders and horses are better than those of any previous round-up here, everything has so far worked to perfection and the general verdict is that this is, as it should be, the best round-up the Bad Lands have yet had.

We have received several requests for the publication of the official list of the calves branded on the round-up. We find that this is impossible, as each man keeps a count on his own calves and no general list is kept. There is also quite a rivalry among the cow-men as to who shall brand the greatest number of calves; the per cent. not being brought forward as it should be. This fact adds to the difficulty of getting a correct list, as a man hates to say that he only branded two hundred calves while his neighbor has branded five hundred, although the former's per cent. may be much higher than the latter's. We can only say in reference to the general calf crop of the Bad Lands, that it seems to be the universal opinion of the boys on the round-up, that the spring and fall round-ups will show a considerably larger per cent. of calves than we have yet had. The present round-up shows a slight increase over the average, while the prospects are that the showings of the fall round-up will be a decided improvement.

The total drive from Texas this year has been carefully computed by some of our southern exchanges at 171,000. Of these, the Hashknife company is only credited with 21,000, whereas they now have 36,000 on the trail, for their Little Missouri and Box Elder ranges. According to report, Driskill, Blocker & Davis have 35,000 on the trail; E. S. Newman has 5,000; Mabry & Pryor, 3,000 and Reynolds Bros., 10,000.

Last week when the round-up was at Pierre Wibaux' ranch on Beaver creek, Bronson Rumsey offered five dollars to the cowboy who roped and tied down a steer in the shortest time. Some quick work was done, the prize being taken by Henry Williams who works for Gregor Lang. Time 2:38. Link Gates was second but had bad luck, his rope breaking or he would have rustled Henry, who is one of the best ropers that ever came to the country.

Opinions as to whether the rain of Monday will start the grass to growing again, are divided. The majority think that the feed will be materially increased, but that it will make a person rustle hard to find hay. Some go so far as to say that there will be no further growth of grass while others think that it is scarcely hurt at all. In Colorado, last year, the ranges had all turned brown by June 20, but rains started the grass again in good shape. We hope to see more rainy weather very soon and as the grass is now manifestly getting a fresh start, all scarcity of feed may be avoided.

The question is being earnestly discussed as to whether it would not be better for the cattle-raisers of the west to erect shambles and do their own butchering, sending dressed beef to market instead of live beef. It was once thought necessary to send all beef on foot to the point where it was to be consumed and have it butchered there. This was before the days of refrigerator store-houses. Already the practice once thought necessary is partially superceded. Dressed beef is shipped from Australia to England, and from this country to our English cousins. Western beef is sent to the eastern states for consumption, and just now Chicago dressed beef is creating considerable excitement in the great cities of the east and southeast, where it comes in competition with that slaughtered by the local butchers. Those who favor the adoption of this method make the following claims: 1. The saving of an untold amount of suffering; 2. It gives healthier meat to consumers; 3. It gives cheaper meat; 4. It gives tenderer meat; 5. It gives better meat in every respect; 6. It gives better prices to the producer; 7. Both the producer and the consumer have the right to the benefits of the age; 8. Hence, no man, or small set of men, have any right to intervene; 9. It is against public policy for common carriers to be so controlled as to sacrifice the public good for the few.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.
The Flocks of the United States.

The Department of Agricultural in a recent report gives the average valuation of sheep per head in several eastern and western states and territories as follows: New Jersey, $3.75; Rhode Island, $3.75; Vermont $2.68; New York, $3.06; Maryland, $3.08; Ohio, $2.00; Texas, $1,70; New Mexico, $1.60.

From the same report it appears that over three-fourths of the sheep in the United States are owned in the following States and Territories; the numbering each being over 1,000,000, disturbuted as follows: Texas, 6,802,615; California, 6,069,698; Ohio, 4,753,034; New Mexico, 4,323,755; Oregon, 2,469,551; Michigan, 2,269,607; New York, 1,595,825; Missouri 1,285,078; Wisconsin, 1,218,800; Kansas, 1,190,163; Pennsylvania, 1,189,481; Colorado, 1,126,647; Indiana, 1,088,157; Illinois, 1,005,653. In these states the average valuation is $1.88 per head, it being the lowest as a rule, where the largest numbers are, Ohio and Michigan being the only states owing over 2,000,000 that show a valuation above $2.00. The states and territories not above enumerated in which about one-fourth are owned showed an average valuation of $2.00. The grand total of the flocks of the United States is, in round numbers, 50,000,000,000, vauled at $95,000,000.—[Journal of Agriculture.
The Daily Journey of the Horse.

According to Hon. John E. Russell, secretary of the Massachusetts board of agriculture, the regular daily journey of the horse should not exceed twelve or thirteen miles. This is as great a distance, he thinks, as can be economically alloted a horse as a day's journey for every day in the week. If he has a longer daily journey, he must have a day or two off each week. This day's work of the travelling horse is based on the experience of stage and car companies. For the stage, where most speed is required, ten miles have been found the limits of an economical day's journey. But a great deal depends on the speed. Give the horse plenty of time and he can do a longer daily journey than he can if he is urged beyond an easy gait. In emergencies, a good horse can do fifty or sixty miles in a day. Seventy-five and eighty miles have been driven. But such long, fast journeys are very trying to the [illegible] and he needs to be managed with great care and judgment to prevent harm from such violent, continued exertion. Such driving cannot be repeated often with safety. The regular day's journey should be lengthened or shortened according to the condition and character of the road and the weight of the load. Then there is a difference in individuals, and what one horse does with ease, may be very hard for another. Feed and care are also factors in the problem not to be overlooked.—[Hoof and Horn.

BY WILL VISSCHER.

Well yes, I'm fum Wyoming—
Ain't 'shameed to say so, nuther—
An' I'd ruther be fum that place
En almos' any other.

The mountains is the highest
An we've got the broadest plains;
We irrigate the valleys—
Don't bother atter rains.

Thar's a world of gold and silver,
An' soda 'oil an' coal,
An' cattle on a thousan' hills
Ez fat ez they kin roll.

The sun shines thar the brightest,
An' stays the hull year 'round
An' the climate is the healthiest,
That ever has been found.

The women vote at 'lections,
Ar' wise about it too,
An' they've got a better right to vote
En any dude like you.

I'm a statin' that a woman
Ez is had a half er chance
Allers makes as good a citizen
Ez camps about the ranch.

An' when I make a statement,
An' know it to be squar',
'Tain't safe to go to doubtin' it,
Out here er anywhar.

We've got the broadest set er men
Upon the bloomin' earth,
An' manhood's what we measure by,
An' not the'r blood an' birth.

Thar's room fur 'bout er million—
Er some the rise er that—
An' room enough to all git rich,
An' healthy, strong an' fat.

But they'd orter be the best thar is,
Fur littleness don't pan
In the gorjus territory
That's adjacent to Shyann.
—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

A man afflicted with deafness took a prescription to a druggist, who filled it with care and in the latest style. The deaf man asked the price, when the following talk occured:

Druggist (leaning on the counter and smiling in a won't-you-pay up sort of a manner)—"The price is seventy-five cents."

Deaf Customer—"Five cents? Here it is."

Druggist (in a louder voice)—"Seventy-five cents, please."

Deaf Customer—"Well, there's your five cents."

Druggist (in a very loud voice and very firm manner)—"I said seventy-five cents."

Deaf Customer (getting angry)—"Well, what more do you want? I just gave you five cents."

Druggist (sotto voice)—"Well, go to thunder with your medicine; I made three cents, anyway."—[Drug Record.

In Judge Seaton's court last Saturday, Mr. A. 1. Stiff was brought up under the vagrant act. A jury of our most reputable citizens was impanelled after considerable difficulty, juror Garver firmly refusing to serve or render a verdict until his fees, amounting to two bits, had finally compromised on a pipeful of tobacco, donated by Judge Seaton. Prosecuting attorney Gordon presented the case for the Territory and handled the subject ably. He ransacked ancient and modern history to furnish examples of the worthlessness of mankind and for pure, unadulterated, cussed uselessness, pronounced the prisoner at the bar "facile princeps." (We don't know what that means and disclaim any responsibility for any hidden meaning or dynamite lurking about it-Ed.) Attorney Wadsworth for the defence, acknowledged that "my clint may be a laverick, with no regular grazing gorunds and no brand on him except the stamp of genius, but, gentlemen of the jury, examine him carefully, look at the ear-marks of talent that crop out all over him, take a look at his eyes, unbleared by anything except budge, notice the hidden mine of wealth he would be to our saloon-keepers if his pocket-book were not a personification of emptiness and turn him loose to pick a living from eastern tenderfeet." The attorney's eloquence was here interrupted by juror Gar[ver?], whose pipe had gone out. After relighting this source of inspiration, the jury retired and agreeed on a verdict immediately, but refused to bring it in unless a bottle of lubricant was furnished. Pending a discussion of Ways and Means committee as to how this could be provided, a freight train came in and Mr. A. 1. Stiff went sailing out of town on a break beam.

Referring to the Cow Boy account of the shovel-nosed fish caught recently here by Billy Reach, the Billings Gazette says: "The fish caught by Billy was undoubtedly the shovel-nosed sturgeon, which was, in the early days of Miles City and Billings, a staple article of diet. The Custer Trail outfit will take their she cattle out on the prairie for the summer.

The Montana brand book is now being circulated and is the best one of the kind ever published. It reflects great credit on its compilers and will be of great value to the stockmen of the Montana Stockgrowers' Association.

Hough & Dustin of Miles City, expect to open their slaughter-house to-morrow. They have facilities for killing from seventy-five to a hundred head a day. Their limited cold storage capacity will confine them to about fifty a day however.

War has begun on rates between St. Paul and Chicago. The rate some time ago was $14.25, which has now been rereduced to $3.00. This is owing to the fact that the Northwestern and Milwaukee roads have put on fast trains, making better time than is possible for the Rock Island which has 130 miles longer haul. To meet the reduced time, the Rock Island has cut rates, which are now met by the other roads. The fight will probably be a long one, as the other roads will combine to freeze out the Rock Island. This road is a stayer though and we look for it to secure its fair share of the travel.

Stories of skill in the use of the lariat are numerous but one told by Harry Bennett as seen by him on his return from McGinness, makes a big bid for first place. Harry struck a round-up party north of the Yellowstone and camped with a wagon run by Jess Reeves, well known as one of the best cow-punchers in the Yellowstone country. In the morning as they started out, Jess jumped up a jack-rabbit. Hastily grabbing his rope he threw it and heeled Mr. J. Rabbitt as neatly as the operation was ever performed on a steer. Of course there was considerable luck in the throw, but all who know Jess, swear that he could do it if any one could.

The rains of Friday, Saturday, Sunday and Monday have put an entirely different complexion on the feed question. In themselves, they guarantee that there will be sufficient grass for grazing purposes, but the hay question is still far from being settled. The grass has undoubtedly taken a fresh start, but whether there will be enough for hay is doubtful. In some favored localities we have a good crop, but these spots are less than an acre generally in extent and are widely scattered. These facts bring forward more prominently than before, the question of raising tame hay for ranch use. As we have often said, there is no avoiding this issue. There are getting to be so many cattle in the Bad Lands, that the grass is not given a chance to attain its full growth. Hereafter, even a moderately dry season will show a shortage or total lack of hay. This summer and coming winter are good times for our cowmen to carefully ponder this subject.

The St. Paul stock-market scheme seems to be entirely a thing of the past. The Cow Boy did not see at the time the plan was first brought up how it could possibly be a success and stated fully its reasons for its belief. The real origin of the whole plan, we firmly believe, was a land speculation. Several interested persons had a block of land that would bring a good price for stock yards and wished to make a sale. Hence their solicitous care to relieve the stockmen from the Chicago monoply. But there happened to be other blocks of land near St. Paul, with owners equally anxious to make sales and as the matter was getting to a question of bidding and a consequent reduction in price, the original movers are beginning to think that they will let the cattlemen struggle on a while longer. Humanity is all right as long as it is a money-making scheme but it lacks lots of being popular when it is not.

It is seldom that we sympathize with a movement in which private citizens take the law in their own hands to punish offenders, but we wish to be put on record right here as approving in every way with the action of the citizens of Mingusville in flogging a sneak-thief there recently. It appears that the thief had brought in some cattle to deliver and had stolen some small articles, such as a slicker, quirt, chapps &c., intending to clear out of the country with them. He was detected and according to the article from our Mingusville correspondent, published in another column, it must be extremely uncomfortable for the "quirtee" to sit down even now. Had the man been arrested and taken to Glendive, he would have been fined a small amount and then turned loose. As it is, he will have such a wholesmoe remembrance of the result of his thieving, that he will propably not engage in it again. The effect on other offenders will also be far greater than if the thief had been arrested and we can almost guarantee Mingusville immunity from petty thieving for some time to come. Small frontier towns are always great losers from the operations of this kind of robbers and nothing will so arouse public spirit against them as summary punishment of this kind.

A cattle and sneak-thief named James Harrison alias "Buckskin" has been arrested south of Mandan. He will doubtless get the full benefit of the law. Last fall he butchered and sold in Bismarck, six animals belonging to different owners.

The New Mexico Stock Grower is urging the advisability of digging wells for the cowmen of New Mexico. Provided the Sioux reservation is opened, it will need no urging for cowmen to sink artisian wells all through the old limits of the reservation. It is destined to become a great cow country.

The cattle are in far better condition than could possibly be expected. At least thirty per cent. of four-year-old steers would now make prime beef and in three weeks this per cent. will be increased to eighty. Instead of the beef being later this year than last, it will probably be two weeks earlier.

Outfits will be immediately made up both north and south of the track to round-up all the country east, going as far as the Missouri river if necessary. They will probably start inside of a week. The country to be rounded up is an immense one, extending from the Killdeer Mts. to Cave Hills and from the Bad Lands to the Missouri; in round numbers about 170 miles square.

The Chicago stock market shows a gain in prime cattle and a drop to $1.00 per 100 for scalawags. Compared with a year ago, Texas cattle are fifty cents lower, owing to their inferior condition. There were about 7,000 of these cattle on the market during last week, cows and bulls selling at $2.25 @ 3.25 and steers at $[3?].80 @ 4.90. Grass Texans generally sold under $3.40. In Liverpool, the best American dressed beef sells at 13½c. per lb.

M. Wadsworth, of the Bad Lands cattle Co., has experimented with several different kinds of grasses this year. Alfalfa and millet bid fair to do the best, but our recent dry spell killed nearly all of the latter. It started well and with all the way from twelve to twenty stalks to the seed but as stated, was badly nipped by the drouth. The alfalfa, on the other hand has done splendidly from the start. It started out well and has kept green and growing through the dry weather that even browned the native grasses. Of course the experiment is not yet conclusive, but it goes a long way to prove all that the advocates of alfalfa have claimed for it. As before stated in the Cow Boy, in at least ten cases throughout Dakota, alfalfa has been a gratifying success. In not one case coming to our notice has it proved a failure. This season will finally decide the matter, as all over Dakota, alfalfa is now growing and we certainly expect that it will prove to be all that is claimed for it; the forage plant par excellence.

To-day is the last day of the round-up, the work being finished at Sully creek ranch. Only twenty-two days were consumed in the work; a shorter time than any Bad Lands round-up has yet taken. The boys all worked well and the only rest they had was one day off on account of a pouring rain. Five hours' sleep was a rarity, the average being nearer four. On several occasions dinner, or at least the second meal of the day, was served at seven o'clock in the morning. There was not a moment's waste time except at meals and working hours were from seventeen to eighteen hours a day. The most of the boys, having so little use for their beds, wanted to trade them off for lanterns. At least they said they did. It has long been recognized as an impossible task to make a perfectly clean round-up of the Bad Lands. Cattle will hide away in the dense brush of out-of-the-way coolies, especially cows with calves. The last week there has been further difficulty that water was abundant everywhere and very few cattle came down on the river and creek bottoms. The figures on the calf crop are as hard to obtain as ever. The round-up has not shown a present increase of over thirty per cent. When the fact is taken into consideration that there may have been ten per cent. of the calves missed and that the fall round-up will show as great or greater per cent. than did this round-up, the result is more encouraging than any the Bad Lands has yet had. Steers are generally in very good condition, a large per cent. being now fit for beef. Taking into consideration the amount of hard riding done, the horses are in far better condition than could be expected. As a whole, the work done was very satisfactory.

Sheriff Sebastion of Dickinson, was here Saturday.
Bronson Rumsey came in from the round-up last night and left for his home in Buffalo this morning.
A dance will be given by Arch Boyd at the Northern Pacific hotel this evening. All are invited.
School will open the first of July in Wm. Van Driesche's building, formerly owned by John Kiefer.
Mr. E. Elmer was thrown from a wagon last week and considerably bruised. She has now nearly recovered.
In Justice Copeland's court, the case of J. A. Ferris vs. Mrs. P. Malloy, which came up last Thursday, was postponed eight days.
The recent drouth badly nipped the wild cherries and plums. The crop of each will be unusually small, if it is not an entire failure.
Fishing is now attended with good success in the Little Missouri. Numerous cat-fish of from two to five pounds in weight are caught.
Some time ago, word was received that Dick Carr had lost his team of mules south of the Hills. We learn that they have not yet been recovered.
The people of Dickinson are making preparations for a grand celebration on the 4th. of July. If possible, they will get Theodore Roosevelt to deliver the oration.
S. E. Grindall, deputy-sheriff at Mingusville, was in town last Thursday. He reports cattle as doing well in the Beaver valley, but that the grass needed rain as much as it did here.

H. S. Boice has gone to the Northwest Territory, to look up the stock ranges there. The Canadian government is offering great inducements to Amerian cowmen to range their cattle there. Long time, low-rate leases and free entry into Canada are the bait used to catch them.

Harry Bennett returned Saturday from his trip to Fort McGinness after Johnny Goodall's horses. He found them, eight in all, about sixty miles west of the fort. On his return, he picked up one belonging to Wall Osterhaut, near Miles City. Harry reports that cattle are doing better in the Bad Lands than they are further west, owing to the superior feed. He made the round trip of over 1,000 miles in twenty-one days. Going, he only had one horse to ride and returning, he drove eight and nine horses. Altogether it is good enough time to go on record.

A man named Landrum from Glendive, borrowed a saddle and outfit here recently from Dan. McKenzie and E. G. Paddock and started to Mingusville. He sent word that he had shipped them back but it was learned that he had taken them to Glendive. Mr. Paddock went up to Glendive and found Landrum there with the goods and after a vigorous use of the King's English, brought them back with him. No criminal case can be made out against Landrum, or he wonld propably suffer for his action.

Sheriff Sebastian of Stark county and L. N. Cary of Mandan, returned Monday from locating the scene of the murder of Dode Straugh in the year of 1883, by Dave Lee. It was a point of dispute whether the murder was committed in Daketa or Montana. Messrs. Sebastian and Cary surveyed the ground and found that the scene of the murder was in Dakota, five miles from Montana, on the line between Ewing and Bowman counties, at the mouth of the Box Elder, where the Hash knife cattle company now have their home ranch. Straugh was a buffalo hunter from Spearfish and Lee was a cow-boy. In a dispute over a game of cards, the murder was committed. There is said to be abundant evidence to convict Lee.

Mingusville Mont., June 14, 1886.
Editor Bad Lands Cow Boy:—

Mingusville takes the cake in the way of reform movement. Our patient but long-suffering people have tired of the too effective work of the sneak-thief and at least one of that fraternity will ever remember us. This one made himself very busy taking quirts, slickers, leggins etc., but was caught and after being compelled to deliver each article to its rightful owner was taken to the platform at the depot, bent over a convenient spool of barbed fence wire and given an energetic application of five lashes each by some half a dozen healthy men. We understand that blood was drawn. Perhaps the thief was too severely punished, yet he deserved some attention and received it in a way much less expensive than by arrest and law proceedings and doubtless more effectively; without it costing the tax payers of Dawson county a cent. There are people here who seemingly propose to make sneak-theiving much more of a rarity than it has been.

There are in the United States, 14,160 newspapers. In Canada and Newfoundland, there are 679. Of those in the United States, New York state has the most, 1,577. Dakota has 309; Nevada the fewest of the states, 28, and Indian Territory, the fewest of the territories, six.

Of all the states and territories in the Union, only California and Texas have a greater area than Dakota. Texas has 262,290, California has 155,980 and Dakota has 147,700 square miles. Dakota is more than 2,460 times as large as the district of Columbia, which has only sixty square miles.

The Stockgrowers' Journal advocates the creation of the office of chief stock inspector; a proposition that we think will meet favorable consideration at the hands of the legislature. The inspectors are new under the direct authority of the stock commissioners; a body of men selected more for their business ability or their standing among cowmen than for their ability as officers or commanders of a body of men whose duty it is to see that laws are obeyed. In other words a man who would make a first-class commissioner, might be the poorest man in the country to organize a raid on a gang of horse thieves. The Montana stock inspectors are a very able body of men, whose work has given eminent satisfaction, but we certainly think their efficiency could be largely increased by being in charge of one competent man who has made a record of his ability on dealing with violators of the law.

We have received several letters lately from persons interested in the tax suit between Stark and Billings counties. Briefly, the matter stands as follows—At the last session of the Dakota legislature, a bill was passed, authorizing any organized county to tax for all purposes, adjacent unorganized counties. Also it gave authority to the organized county to tax any unorganized county which was nearer to it than to any other organized county. Under this law, Stark county assessed and taxed Billings county before we were organized. The tax amounted to nearly thirteen mills of which three mills was territorial tax. All the rest was for school, bridge and road taxes &c., for Stark county. Our tax-payers readily conceded the justice of the territorial tax and have stood ready at any and all times to pay it, if it could have been separated from the other subjects for taxation under the bill. They can in no wise, however, see the justice of being taxed to pay for the schools, roads or bridges of Stark county. Naturally our tax-payers, seeing the unjustice of the law, refused to pay the tax. Stark county, being authorized by the law, as naturally took measures to collect the tax. Our citizens then met and decided to fight the collection and appointed T. R. Selmes of Mandan as attorney. Mr. Selmes gave his opinion that the law was unconstitutional and had an injunction issued on Stark county, restraining the further collection of taxes from Billings until the constitutionality of the law could be decided by the courts. This is the present status of the matter. Stark county has given every evidence of desiring fair play and will readily acquiesce in the decision which we confidently believe will be adverse to the constitutionality of the law. The case will come up at the August term of the circuit court and no matter which side wins, it will doubtless be appealed. It can then come before the supreme court in October in Deadwood or in November in Bismarck. We do not think that the case will then be appealed to the supreme court of the United States, as the territorial supreme court undoubtedly has sufficient jurisdiction over the acts of Dakota legislature. We will keep our readers constantly informed if any new points in the case that may arise.

Some of the Texas drives are in a bad fix at present. There is not enough grass and water on the trail provided by Congrass and new trails are being sought. To this the neighboring cowmen are naturally objecting. They will even prevent driving on a new trail by force of arme. One of the Hashknife drives under charge of Col. Simpson was stopped near Springer, New Mexico, and there was no way out of the difficulty except to ship. The cattle were in poor condition when started and the delay on the road is likely to be serious.

Grass is growing as well as it has this year since the first week or two it started. This does not mean an abundance of hay, but with a good deal of rustling, it probably means that enough can be secured to feed a few horses and cows on each ranch.

The Ref. Car Co. has so far gathered about 3,200 of the 4,800 steers turned loose last season. As all of the eastern and southern and one or two of the western round-ups are yet to be heard from, the figures indicate that almost all will be gathered.

The eastern round-up north of the track is now at work and finding large numbers of cattle. The report comes in that one round-up on Green river contained 4,000 head. This may be exaggreated but is an indication of the large number that have strayed off to the east.

The round-up on Reynolds Bros'. range only lasted three days. It was understood that it was to extend to the Big Missouri if necessary. There are undoubtedly some cattle in that district which have never been rounded up and it would be advantageous for our regular round-up No. 6 to have this territory included in its boundaries.

The Chicago correspondent of the Texas L. S. Journal, estimates that there will be 325,000 Texas and 210,000 northwestern cattle on the Chicago market this year. Last year there were nearly 300,000 Texans and a few over 200,000 from the northwest. 1884 saw the largest shipment, there being then 358,374 from Texas and 231,879 from the northwest.

Beginning to-day and lasting for three days, Devil's Lake will treat itself to a blooded stock show. The tributary country has probably been filled up more rapidly with pure blood stock than any corresponding district in the west. Many wealthy farmers have gone extensively into the business of raising blooded cattle and J. J. Hill's liberality has put pure bred animals upon almost farmer's land. It will probably be as fine a stock show as the northwest has yet seen.

J. A. Van Eeghen and Joe McCoul returned yesterday from their western trip after horses. "Van" bought between two and three hundred mostly mares and Joe about twenty. The horses are of all kinds and a few of them are for sale. They were bought in Beaverhead Co. Montana, on the Idaho line and have been on the trail for six weeks. There was good feed and water the last of the way and they arrived here in better condition than when they started.

"Spearfish," one of the Maltese Cross horses took a trip Tuesday evening that may shorten his days considerably. He jerked away from his rider, Mike Seitz, and ran along the railroad track to the approach of the bridge. Here he tripped on his rope and as he was going at full speed, a somersault off the approach was the result. He lit square on his back on the ground beneath, a distance of over twenty feet. He was immediately ridden to the ranch and apparently did not suffer much from his fall.

There are plenty of strange cases in the catalogue of every doctor's personal experience. I ran across several some years ago in one af the mountain camps of Colorado, all fatal, and which while bearing a certain degree of resemblance, have not been to my knowledge described as a type in any of the medical journals. At the post mortem we discovered in every instance a hard, foreign body directly in the rear of the right external iliac fossa or outer surface of the hip bone. The foreign body extended downward and varied in length from six to eight inches, the end being tubular in form and terminating in a round, honeycombed structure containing from five to seven separate cells. Singular, wasn't it. By the way, each one of these cells contained a 45-caliber, center-fire cartridge, and the entire foreign body was technically known as a Colt's revolver. These cases were very common in Colorado and the mortality resulting from them was considerable.—[Dr. G. P. Reynolds.

Your outfit, or bed, clothing or equipments, will cost you about half your earnings, and if you smoke freely and do not try to same your money, the end of the season will leave you neither richer nor poorer. You will often have a wet bed, and thank heaven for getting to it, wet as it is. You will always be up before daylight, and generally two hours out of the night as well; you will eat [coarse?] food—everything [fried?] in lard; [you?] will be in the [saddle?] from twelve to eighteen hours every day; you will often suffer for the want of food and water during a long day's work in hot sun; you will expose yourself to some peril of life and more of limb; you will be for much of the time as absolutely cut off from the civilized world as if you were only a vessel in mid-ocean. You will vow three times a day that when you strike the ranch again you will quit. You will be sore and bruised, cold at night, and scorched by day, wet to the skin one hour and parched with thirst the next, and for the rest of your life you will look back to your life on the range, with longing thoughts of its charms. Very few men are rich enough to indulge the taste for riding by keeping more than two saddle horses. A 'puncher' often rides a dozen, and does much of his work at full run. He breathes the finest air on earth, eats beef as freely as an ordinary workingman eats cabbage and potatoes, and fancies tne class to which he belongs are the aristocracy of labor. He is generous, always quick to appreciate pluck and kindness in others, chivalrous to the few women he sees, ever ready to help hang a horse thief, and undergoes more hardship and danger than a dozen soldiers.—[San Francisco Chronicle.

This clover, which goes under several names, is decidedly the coming forage plant of the west, not only on account of its nutritious properties either green or cured, but on account of its adaptability to any soil and climate.

It loves water and grows best when supplied with a liberal amount, but it hangs on with a pertinacity during a long drouth that throws Aunt Jemima's plaster in the ground.

In our valley the usual time for planting is in August, which gives the young plants time to become well rooted before the cold weather comes on. Others prefer to plant in the spring after all danger of frost is over, but they do not expect to reap any benefit from the first year's crop, whereas the fall planting gives a very nice return. The third year, however, is the time we expect the best results, but as intimated above, its staying qualities are immense, and after eight and ten years of neglect, if ploughed with light plows and watered, it will come up in the most sprightly manner. You would think it had been making use of the "bloom of youth."

In preparing the land it should be well ploughed with two strong mules or horses, well harrowed and then thoroughly irrigated, and as soon as the land is dry enough sow your seed, about twelve or fifteen pounds per acre, and harrow in.

The first crop will be light and pretty full of weeds, but they never make a second attempt to outgrow their competitor, but throw up the sponge in despair, and once alfalfa becomes well rooted it will not brook any opposition, but smothers out everything else. The depth the roots will go down into mother earth in search of moisture is something marvelous, often fifteen to twenty feet, and will grow as large as a man's wrist. It is, therefore, rather hard to eradicate from your garden and orchard, and should not be allowed to seed, as it springs up wherever a seed is dropped, even after having been used as food by our domestic animals. It can be easily killed, however, when it is desired, by being flooded with water for a few days, and then the full force of a July or August sun soon kills it.

The first cutting is usually about the 10th or 15th of May owing to a late or early spring, and if there is plenty of water to irrigate during the summer one can safely rely on three, and often four, cuttings during the season. From three-fourths to a ton, and on our best lands a ton and a half, can be had at each cutting. The ground can then be used for pasturage during the winter months. If there should be a rather thin stand it is advisable to allow the clover mature its seed before cutting, as it will give a good stand afterwards, but it is not best to have the plants too thick on the ground, as better results are obtained where only a good stand is on the ground. The usual time for cutting is when the plant is in full bloom.

Alfalfa is so hardy that many have obtained the best results by simply sowing the seed broadcast in among the corn in August or September, and simply by cutting down the corn stalks with a hoe and leveling the ground when very uneven and irrigating afterwards.

We propose in our next to give some information as to the method of curing, price, baling and our market for alfalfa, and land best adapted to its growth.—[The Two Republics.

School will begin next Monday with Miss Alice Ellison, sister of C. F. Ellison, as teacher.

Willis Eaton has finished his assessment and will make his returns to the commissoners next Monday.

The Marquise de Mores and a hunting party are down the river. Bear hunting is the principal object of the trip.
Miss Jennie Morton of South Heart, was married last week to a fireman whose name we are unable to learn.

Tom Mathews, stock-inspector at Glendive is taking Fred Willard's place as inspector at the slaughter-house, during the latter's absence.

Frank Foster and wife arrived in Medora last Thursday evening. With them came a force of butchers, including "Shorty" and Cranston of last year's men.
Four-year-olds are considerably livelier than threes, as is evidenced by the fact that two steers jumped the eight-foot corral fence, a feat that has hitherto been deemed impossible.
At four o'clock yesterday afternoon the [thermometer?] stood at 118 in the sun. The rain of the morning barely wet the ground and did but little to relieve the intense heat.
C. A. Quigley, representing Studebaker Bros. M'f'g. Co., stopped off in Medora Wednesday. He reports sales of $50,000 on the N. P. between St. Paul and Helena for the last eight months.
Word comes from Mingusville that Mr. and Mrs. John Munro are rejoicing over advent of a lively infant who will go through this world's trials and tribulations under the name of William.

Dick Carr has not as yet recovered his mules, which strayed away from south of the Black Hills about two months ago. A sharp lookout by our cattlemen may bring them to light, as they are liable to come back to the Bad Lands.

Dr. Jorgens and Johnny Fitzgerald started the first of the week for the Doctor's Cave Hills ranch, with two loads of supplies. They will return in a few days. The Dr. and his family will spend the most of the time until fall on the ranch.

Eli Mickelson returned Tuesday from his trip to the Hills. He was in Rapid City the most of the time and reports that there was plenty of work, but about seven men for every job. All the boys who went from here have secured work, however.

There may be no connection between Fred Willard's departure for Spearfish and the threat of the Stockgrowers' Journal to come down with a deputy sheriff, a double barrelled shot-gun and a yellow dog to collect Fred's advertising bill for the editor of that paper, but we look for gore on his return.

The story of the shooting affray at the [E6?] ranch in which a cowboy named Chadwick was killed, was exploded by Russ Wilson on a recent trip to the Hills. He said that Chadwick and his alleged murderer were a hundred miles apart on the day the shooting was said to have occurred and that Chadwick is now alive and well.

A baby boy was born to Mrs. John Goodall last Thursday. Johnny don't say much, but feels about seven inches taller than usual. We happen to be one of the few unfortunates who were absent at the general distribution of cigars. This may be considered as an item of news or a hint, at the pleasure of the reader, however.

Work began at the slaughter-house promptly on time this morning. The beef is in far better condition than it was this time last year; in fact it will sell readily anywhere. Layers of fat in most cases, completely cover the carcasses. The coolers have just been filled with 300 tons of ice and under the able superintendence of Frank Foster, everything is running as smoothly as at the end of the season's work last fall. About fifty head will be slaughtered to-day.

We have an over-stock of [3⅛?] Studebaker wagons that the Studebaker M'f'g. Co. have instructed us to close out at $75 each. These wagons have never turned a wheel under a load, are new and first-class in every respect, have the Co's. full guarantee for 5,000 pounds, according to old freighters are the best ironed and easiest running wagon of its size in the world, and cost at the factory, $87 each in car lots. There never has been and never will be again such a bargain in wagons in this country. The $75 rate is cash of course and holds good for one or more. For further particulars, call at or address the Cow Boy office.

The "Two Republics" of El Paso, Texas is a new and promising condidate for honors among our stock exchanges. That Geo. B. Loving is editor, is sufficient guarantee that it will keep up to the high standard of excellence that its opening numbers show. Success to the "Two Republics."

The entire plant of the Miles City Dressed Beef Co. was destroyed by fire Tuesday. The loss was $15,000. No insurance. We are unable to learn anything of the plans of the company but as there was considerable difficulty about their cattle contracts it seems probable that they will not rebuild.

The long continued hot weather has about dried up the green feed that was to be used at the experimental fattery here but feeding will begin very soon on twenty or thirty head. In the series of experiments in New York, one yearling increased in one hundred days from 840 to 1120 pounds and was then sold at a top price for beef.

Last Saturday, a hail storm east of Dickinson did severe damage to the crops. Beginning a few miles east of Dickinson and extending beyond Glen Ullin, it is estimated that over a thousand acres of standing grain was completely ruined. The most of it was insured. The evening passenger train met the storm near Hebron and over seventy-five panes of heavy window glass were broken out.

We have before had occasion to allude to the weak arguments employed by the Western Rural in its articles against the range cattle industry. It was one of the leaders of the eastern agricultural press a few months ago in an endeavor to compel range cattlemen to lease the land they occupied. As any reasonable man should have foreseen, the selfish animus of the crusade was so manifest that it fell of its own weight. There were no arguments in right or justice to support it. Now, however, the Western Rural speaks of cowmen as "interlopers." An interloper is one who meddles in business in which he has no concern. The only possible way in which this term can apply to rangemen is that their product, by coming into competition with stall-fed cattle, makes them "interlopers." Grant that in this sense they are interlopers and what does it prove? By the Rural's own words they are interlopers because they compete in open market for business. An argument then, based on such a foundation, would totally destroy all business principles. Competition is not only the life of trade, but in this case, competition is the greatest boon imaginable to the poorer classes of the United States. There is no need of an array of figures to prove that the range cattle industry has decreased the price of meat so that it is now a regular food for poor men, where an advance of a few cents a pound would put it in the list of luxuries, seldom or never to be tasted. Suppose that the Rural's expressed wish should be realized and that "our farms produce all the cattle for which there is such a demand." The utter folly of such a statement and wish is so apparent as scarcely to need explanation. If eastern farmers could supply the beef demand, why in the world don't they do it? The Rural's answer would be "they can't do it at the cheap price of the range beef." They couldn't possibly do it anyway, but take the Rural's answer as final and we have an astonishing boomerang of a social science argument that an industry should be annihilated for the benefit of a small number of men, which, by its existence, saves millions of dollars a year to consumers. But to prop up its argument, the Rural would say, this business is made possible because it is conducted on land that belongs to the United States. Would it be better to stop this food supply, to the detriment of every man, woman and child in the country, because rent is not paid for for the use of land that no one else wants? The Rural's arguments are too narrow and selfish to find many adherents. It argues for a small class against all the rest of the people, a position perfectly untenable under a republican form of government. In conclusion we would tell the Rural that the very fact of its existence is one of the strongest points in its favor. No such abuse as the Rural claims the range industry to be, could keep its footing in the United States. It would long since have been annihilated by legislative enactment.

After some protracted experiments in cattle feeding at the Illinois State university, Prof. G. E. Morrow says: Bearing in mind that it is not wise to draw final conclusions from single trials, the fact concerning these cattle suggest or illustrate, among other things, that:

1. The difference in animals of like breeding, and under like treatment is often greater than those in typical animals of different breeds.

2. Under the prevalent methods of wintering steers in the western states, little or no gain is made in weight during winter.

3. It is difficulty, if not impossible, to secure under good conditions, gains in winter which shall nearly equal those made in summer.

4. The largest gains may be expected from animals in thin flesh, if in good health. It is difficult to secure rapid gain in weight during continued feeding.

5. Under like conditions young animals make largest gain in proportion of food eaten.

6. A fair profit can be made at present low prices by grazing, and then grain feeding for two or three months, cattle which have been judiciously bought or economically reared, to be sold when from 30 to 36 months old.

7. Economy of production is quite as important as maximum product, especially in times of low prices. It is not clear that it is profitable to give full grain feeding to steers, designed for the general market, during the best of the grazing season. It is not proven that it is most profitable for western farmers to fatten and sell steers as yearlings.

As considerable alarm exists throughout the country at the present time concerning the spread of glanders, a brief history of its cause, and the best method of prevention may be valuable to horse-owners.

The principal cause of this incurable disease, says Dr. Pelton, is tight, foul stables. It is contagious by inoculation. Farcy is a different form or stage of the same disease, and the horse never dies of either until both forms are fully developed. But if farcy appears first it may be cured by correct and prompt treatment.

Mr. Hinds, an English veterinary writer, cites an instance where three hundred cavalry horses were put below decks during a storm at sea, and the hatchways closed, and when taken out thirty-six hours afterwards, all were found to have taken either glanders or farcy, and they were all thrown overboard.

Glanders first shows itself by staring coat, and slight discharge (thin and glutinous from the left nostril, and never from the right nostril. Small white blisters soon appear a little upon the membranes of the left nostril, and the glands of the under jaw on that side become somewhat enlarged and hard. Let no man handle such a case unless his hands are sound and free from any scratch or sore, for the matter coming in contact with a raw place, or membrane, will communicate the disease to man as readily as to a horse. But if the hands are sound, put your finger up the left nostril to make sure it is a white blister on the membrane, and if it proves to be so, destroy the unfortunate animal at once. But it must be remembered, that nasal gleet is often mistaken for glanders. It is readily cured by a skillful veterinarian, and is not contagious. It is caused generally by out-door exposure, and the discharge, in bad cases, is very profuse from both nostrils, usually a light straw color, often streaked with blood, when running to grass.

Farcy causes a staring coat, and some other symptoms of glanders, but its certain symptoms are what are called farcy buds—small, round, hard swellings on the inside of the legs and thighs, belly, and often about the throat and under jaw; sometimes only in one, and again in all those places. They soon suppurate and become sores, but prompt treatment will cure glanders in this stage, and save the horse.

During the late war, many good horses contracted nasal gleet from exposure and ill usage, and many of them were destroyed under the impression that they were afflicted with glanders, when they might have been saved had the disease been understood.

Horses known to have glanders should be killed at once, and their stables and harness thoroughly disinfected with chloride of lime. A good washing with carbolic acid will add to the means of safety.

Some years ago, three hundred glandered horses were sent to the veterinary college of Edinburg, Scotland, for experiment. All died but two. These two discharged from both nostrils, while those that died discharged from the left nostril only, and the faculty of the college were of the opinion that the two horses saved did not have glanders. They undoubtedly had nasal gleet, which disease was at the time little understood.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

Agreeable to my promise of last winter I will try to tell honest inquirers what I believe to be the difference between Galloway and Polled Angus cattle: Let me say in the outset, I have read most of the articles, pro and con, and after searching and studying nearly five years, conclude that if we go far enough back, say to the Feudal age—we shall find that the wild black and polled cattle owned by the wild men of that period and stolen back and forth from each other at every opportunity, were of the self-same, identical breed that Herodotus speaks of, and that have been referred to as Scythian cattle, and that now we classify as follows: The black Polled cattle raised in what is called the Galloway district by the name of Galloways, and the black Polled cattle raised in the northern or Aberdeen and Angus district, and called Aberdeen or Angus cattle.

But I have not told the difference yet between the Galloway and Angus: Well, let me say that a Scotchman on his native heath is like the laws of the Medes and Persians; he seldom, if ever, changes. The ambition of the boys is to do what their fathers did, and in about the same way. Now the Scotchman in southern Scotland, which is the Galloway district, is raising the same kind of cattle (and with a few exceptions, notably, the Duke of Buccleuch, and a few of the best farmers) is trying to raise them as what is called "store" cattle—(we call them stock cattle) by grazing principally, upon as poor land as any man would wish to see. Being near the Gulf stream the climate is not very severe, but cloudy, misty and rainy. This peculiar climate and running out, browsing for a living, is what makes the hair of the Galloway so shaggy, and with poor care and poor feed for generations is probably what makes him so slow a feeder, and in a measure accounts for his absence from the Smithfield fat-stock shows year after year.

I presume every man has concluded there was a great similarity between the breeds. I know I was struck with that fact when I first saw them, and any man who will take the trouble to examine closely, cattle bred by the Duke of Buccleuch will see how very much like the Polled-Angus they are, especially in head and hair. I want to be entirely fair in what I say, and I record myself here as saying I believe that originally the Angus and Galloway were the same wild breed of cattle, and that the distinctive difference in them to-day is, the more and longer skillful mating, feeding and improving by man. The objectionable features have been bred off the Angus to a far greater extent, and the desirable features have been bred on, until to-day they are known as two distinct breeds, and have two distinct books of records for the pedigreed stock. I may say I think that usefulness will be found in both of these breeds, especially in a country like this, where most of our cattle are scrubs, and right here I want to close by saying, that experience will prove to every farmer and cattleman, that horns are a positive detriment in very many ways, and the reader of this article can keep it, to remember, that I say if any man ever handles cattle one season without horns he will forever banish horned cattle from his place.—[G. W. Henry in Kansas City Live-Stock Indicator.

The first hot wind that Dakota has experienced for three years, was blowing all day Sunday the 4th. The thermometer stood at 118 in the shade at five o'clock in the afternoon. The wind did no damage here except to one's feelings.

A friendly game of base-ball may take place soon between nines from Dickinson and Medora. Either town can well afford to pay the opposing nine's expenses for a game. Our base-ball material is very limited, but we could at least have some enjoyment out of the game.

The Wells-Fargo Express Co. has stopped business on the Northern Pacific, owing to a decision of a Portland judge that one common carrier is not compelled to carry goods for another common carrier. This decision of course did not affect the whole line, but as goods could not be carried over a part of the road, the express company was compelled to refuse all business.

The celebration at Dickinson last Monday was far more of a success than even the most enthusiastic hoped. Except for a strong wind, the day was a perfect one. A procession, consisting of the usual number of riders, both ladies and gentlemen, and a band, a wagon load of goddesses of liberty and a large number of wagons and carriages formed at 9:30. Proceeding to the grand stand at the northern edge of town, several selections were played by the band, "America" was sung and the Declaration of Independence was read by Western Starr. An adjournment for dinner then took place, after which nearly five hundred people assembled at the grand stand to hear speeches from J. A. Rea and Theodore Roosevelt. Mr. Rea was the first speaker and put the audience into a good humor both by his patriotic utterances and quaint anecdotes. Mr. Roosevelt followed with an able discussion on the duties of American citizenship. It was a forcible presentment of high aims a citizen of the United States should keep before him and lacked entirely that spread eagle oratory, with which the speaker said he sympathized deeply. Mr. Roosevelt is essentially a disputant. He gets right at the meat of his subject and in plain, well-chosen words, presents his side of the case in a way that commands attention and wins converts. After the speeches, an adjournment took place to the race track, where the first event was a pony race, Joe McCoul's Blue Jay being barred. Two Indians clothed in little else but modesty took part in the race, one of them "ki-yi-ing" his horse into second place. The next race was a half-mile, free-for-all and was a walk-over for Johnny Goodall's "Splinter." There were about twelve entries of which the most bolted the track, Johnny coming in with a lead of fifty yards, riding side-saddle fashion on a lope and fanning himself with his hat. The next event was the hundred-yard foot race, easily won by a sheep man named Wright, who must spend his spare time running down cayotes. Among the fifteen starters Pat Murn came out a good third. With practice he could make Wright think the tables were turned and the cayotes were after him. In the 200 yard race, Wright again won, Baas of Dickinson second and Murn third.

Later reports state the loss by the burning of the Miles City Dressed Beef Co's slaughter-house at $40,000, on which there was no insurance. The butchers passed through Medora last week on their way to Chicago and report that the intention of rebuilding, has been abondoned. The firm intends now to either hire or rent a building in Chicago and ship cattle there alive. They have about 5,000 contracted for that they will dispose of in this way.

Word comes from T. R. Selmes that those who have not already done so, should immediately send certified checks to the Frst Nat. Bank of Mandan, for the amount taxed against them by Stark county. This is not in payment of the tax, but is to be held in trust by the bank, until the suit is decided. It is understood that any other person or firm taxed by Stark county whether residing in Billings county or not, can thus send in a certified check and escape taxation unless the case is decided against us. The above plan is simply another way of putting up a bond for costs. It is undoubtedly a fairer plan, as each then assumes the full measure of his own responsibility, instead of putting it on the shoulders of bondsmen. Our case looks as promising as ever and we see no reason why we should not win. We learn that there are still a few tax-payers who have not joined in the agreement to fight the case, but will be equally benefited in the decision. This is doubtless owing to the fact that they do not realize that this case involves the right of taxation by Stark county, of all outsiders assessed by it and consequently all are interested who come under this head. All who have not yet done so should express a willingness to stand their share of the expense.

To the average reader, it must seem absolutely impossibe that the soldiers who are after the Apaches in Arizona, can be brave men. We have continually seen articles in eastern papers, drawing unfavorable comment from the fact that a thousand soldiers have for more than a year been chasing a hundred Apaches and have virtually accomplished nothing. When we think that the Bad Lands are almost a level prairie in comparison with he country in which the Apaches are fighting, that they know every inch of it, that they are as well or better armed than the soldiers, that they can on foot run clear away from a troop of cavalry in a day, that they leave almost no trail, that they are constantly subdividing into bands of from three to twenty and striking where they are least expected, that they can live in luxury where soldiers would starve and that man for man there is no body of troops in the world a match for them on their chosen battle ground, the results of the campaign are more easily explained. About the only feasible way now seems to be to furnish a sufficient number of troops so that every water hole could be guarded and the Apaches kept moving so that exhaustion would finally compel them to surrender.

As shown by our report, the cattle market about holds its own, with no particular increase or decrease. There does not seem, however, to be that shaky feeling which characterized last year's market at this season. Prices bid fair to hold up well and there will probably be no long depression. It can be set down as a maxim that good cattle will always bring good figures. Poor cattle will only by accident bring a good price. For instance, Monday, some Colorado and Nebraska grass cattle averaging 1,200 to 1,300 lbs., brought $4.75@$5.00. On the other hand some big, horsey, raw-boned Washington Territory cattle weighing 1,200 lbs., brought only $2.50. Texas cattle are generally very poor and averaging the different grades, did not bring over $2.65. Very few Montana and Dakota cattle have been shipped, but they have brought good prices.

Bill Lundy of the 13 outfit, has left the country with no enviable reputation behind him. He has for some time been worming himself into the confidence of other boys in the outfit and borrowing what he could of them. He also drew his pay in advance from the 13 company. Some time ago, he drew more money on the plea of paying some bills in Belfield and started for there. He landed in Medora and with a plausible tale, induced T. W. Gordon to trust him for a suit of clothes. He then boarded the cars and the last heard of him was at Miles City. He came here from the Judith Basin and it is supposed he returned there. The boys of the 13 outfit are especially angered over the actions of this dead beat and want him shown up in all the cow papers of the west. It is just this kind of a rascal that hurts the reputation of cowboys as a class and each should feel it his duty to bring him to justice. Range papers will confer a favor by copying the above.

Mingusville July 8th 1886.

Editor Cow Boy.

A terrible wind storm accompanied by rain and hail visited this place yesterday afternoon doing great damage to crops. The water raised five feet in Beaver creek. It also washed out a bridge fifteen miles west of here and delayed No. 1 about eleven hours at Mingusville.

It is rumored that one of Mingusville's cattle men is about to round up one of Glendive's fairest about the 12th. We all give him our best wishes.

The newest thing in Mingusville is that new pool table of Powers & Gidley that they just received from the east.
