There are some parties here who think seriously of starting a dog ranch, they have a stock of four now on hand.

The American Agriculturist recently had an article on alfalfa in Colorado in which the writer said the plant was first seeded eight years ago. To our certain knowledge, Major Jacob Downing had alfalfa sowed in his door yard as early as 1863, and the next year L. K. Perrin sowed five pounds of California seed in his field. The seed was furnished by Mr. Perrin's brother, who had made a great success of it in the Sacramento valley. As far back as 1872—fourteen years ago—the colonists of Greely were sowing alfalfa, and some of the original meadows still produce fine stands of it.

In this connection it may be said that alfalfa will hold its growth in ordinary soil for at least a period of forty years—in fact no man of our acquaintance has ever tried it long enough to tell exactly how many years it will remain in perennial rotation.

The writer once interviewed an old native ranchero on his hacienda in the state of Chihuahua, Mexico. The old don had a grand vega of hardy alfalfa on the second bottom, and the writer was informed that it had been growing there for fifty-two years. The plant was healthy and vigorous, and had been subject to cutting every six weeks of its growth. This trip to Mexico was two years ago, and we suppose the stand is still growing, as it showed no signs of decay. It may last seventy-five, a hundred or two hundred years for all we may know of its probable longevity.

It pretty much depends, we may conclude, that the age of alfalfa depends largely on the condition of the under soil. This must neither be too wet, least it rots the lower roots, nor too dry else it will not obtain healthy root and die a "borning." The low river bottoms are not the place for alfalfa, as the rot is very apt to take it off after a year or two of struggle. The extreme high places are generally too sterile for successfull propagation—so then we have solution: We must plant on the intermediate lands, watch it closely in season and out of season until it gets well in root, when it will take care of itself, and forever yield forage in great abundance.

When we wish to learn of alfalfa, or any other Colorado product for that matter, we do not want to look in an eastern agricultural paper for reliable information. In fact the Colorado farmer should have no use for the eastern agricultural papers—they are "no wano" for the west.—[Field and Farm.

In Camp, San Miguel county, N. M. June 26, 1886.—For the past few weeks I have been working, part of my time, in a field that brought me in contact with a number of parties who have been negotiating with capitalists east for the sale of ranch properties, and having seen the correspondence in relation to the same, I am convinced that the cattle business has had a heavy setback, owing to the way many new companies have been run for some time past. All investors seem to write in the same discouraging manner, which is the result of many parties having invested in the business and as yet received no returns from their investments, except in the way of a detailed report from the secretary and treasurer, with vouchers attached. This is an undisputed fact in the case of many cattle companies, and more particularly with those largely composed of foreign capitalists.

Having noticed a good number of old cattle men perfectly contented with their business, I have been more than solicitous to find out the true cause of such a state of affairs, and the most practical illustration that I know of, was given in the following conversation had this week with one of New Mexico's oldest stockmen. I have gone over the above ground pretty thorougly with said stockman, and asking his theory as to the cause of so much dissatisfaction among those who have of late years invested in the cattle business, he replied by telling an experience which he had recently gone through with the company of which he is now manager.

He stated that some years ago he started with a small bunch of cattle, and after a number of years of hard work and close application to his business, he sold his herd to a company composed of eastern capitalists, at a fair market price, and "counted out" at the time of delivery, some 18,000 head of stock cattle. He hired himself to the said company at a good salary as their manager. Things went along nicely for a season or two; they sold some beeves during the time, but not near enough to pay expenses and an interest on the capital invested; stockholders and directors meetings were held, and a general dissatisfaction arose; so one day said manager was forwarded a telegram requesting him to report at once to the headquarters office, and a committee which was authorized by the directors, met him with the interrogatory, why was it that the business did not pay them so well as it had him in the past? To which he replied by saying: "Gentlemen, you have officers of your company, and you pay them salaries of, (per year.)

President at a salary of....................$5,000.00
Secretary and treasurer at a salary of 2,500.00
Bookkeeper and cashier " .. 1,200.00
Manager (and manager only in name) at a salary of.......... 2,500.00
Range foreman at a salary of........... 1,200.00
Trail boss at a salary of.................. 1,000.00

"You also have bought fine thoroughbred bulls, paying as high as $1,000 for one or two, and then any number of grades at from $50 per head up to $100; you have built good camp houses, barns and stables; you buy the best of flour, canned goods, and a quantity of other "Delmonico eatables," with everything else in like proportion, whereas I was my own president, secretary and treasurer, bookkeeper and cashier, manager, range foreman, trail boss, and besides making a d—d good $50 hand myself. Instead of fine camp houses, I lived in "dug-outs," which I made during my spare moments; made ropes out of the hides of dead animals; instead of a "chuck-wagon" filled with fancy eatables, I used a packhorse, carrying a little corn meal and bacon; for branding irons I used bent wire; for bulls I kept trading with my neighbors, and everything else I did in a like manner. Now, if you will do away with a great deal of this unnecessary help and expense, curtail your expenses right and left, or let me be manager in fact, instead of only in name, I will promise to report to you all as often as you desire, and will take for my work or salary, twenty-five per cent, of the profits, after paying all expenses and ten per cent per annum on the capital invested in your company.

The above tells its own story, and without further comment, save that it is like unto [an?] old rubber shoe, it can be made to fit a great many feet at the present day.—[Col. Kansas City L. S. Indicator.

The oldest citizen is at last cornered. In all his Dakota experience there is nothing like the continued hot weather of the last three weeks. In all this time there has not been a day that the thermometer has not stood over 110 degress in the sun and once it climbed over the 136 degree fence and smiled cooly at sweltering humanity. There has scarcely been a public question since the war broke out, that has been given such attention or the discussion of which has been characterized with more bitter feeling than the question of the manufacture of oleomargarine. The prime difficulty has been that in all legislation and attempted legislation on the subject, each side claims that it is entirely right and the opposition is entirely wrong. A conference of the leading men on both sides should be able to formulate legislation that will be at least fairly satisfactory to all concerned. Such a conference never has been held and it is doubtful if it ever will be. The chief points brought against oleomargarine are that it is a fraud to sell it as butter, that it is driving pure buttery out of the market and that it is unhealthy. The first point is undoubtedly the best one and all fair-minded people will agree that oleomargarine should be sold under its true name. The market does not show any decrease in price on good butter for several years and oleomargarine really only comes into competition with the poorer grades of butter. That it is unhealthy is as yet unproved, except in cases where diseased animals have been used; these being cases for health officers to rule upon. The oleomargarine people should be willing to sell their product under its true name, and in this way we believe that nine-tenths of the discussion would be stopped. We do not, however, see the justice of putting a tax on the manufacture of oleomargarine. If it is sold under its true name and the consumer knows what he is buying, it would be as sensible to put a tax on any newly-discovered, low-priced article that comes into competion with a high-priced article. For instance, if it is right to tax oleomargarine, manufactured and sold under its true name, it would be right to tax the telephone up to a point where they must charge the same as the telegraph. There is certainly competition, but competition drives monopoly to the wall and lessens prices to consumers. We hope the only national legislation to be passed on the subject will be to compel oleomargarine to be sold under its true name.

Talking of roping, by the way, a cowboy by the name of Henry Williams, in the employ of the Neimmella cattle company on the Little Missouri, accomplished a feat on Wednesday last with a grass rope which heads the record. He was hunting saddle horses, and had come across two or three head of the missing animals drinking at the river. He rode down to turn them out, when a full-grown wild goose flew up from under a bunch of undergrowth on the bank of the river and passed straight in front of him. He had his rope uncoiled and ready for use with which to secure the horses out of the river, and quick as thought as the bird flew past him he pitched the rope at it and succeeded in catching it by one wing. He took the bird home to the ranch and it will be kept and tamed if possible. So far, nothing with four feet has been considered safe from being ensnared by the treacherous lariat, but a bird on the fly, even though as big as a wild goose, has hitherto been considered safe from any such mode of capture. The man who accomplished the above is well known as one of the most skilled ropers in the Little Missouri country, and to those who have witnessed him swing the lariat the feat does not seem so surprising.—[Stockgrowers' Journal.

The above article makes a pair with the feat of Jess. Reeves in catching a jack rabbit with a [lariat?] published in the Cow Boy, t[he f]irst of June. Either seems imposible until one sees what an expert can do with a rope.

The demand for beef is growing more rapidly than the herds are increasing. In the year 1860 there were 814 cattle in the United States for every 1,000 of our population. To-day there are only 775 head of cattle to each 1,000 of population, a very considerable falling off in the relative supply, notwithstanding that during this period the whole of Montana, Dakota, Idaho, eastern Oregon, Nevada, Wyoming, Colorado, Arizona, most of New Mexico and nearly one-half of Texas have been withdrawn from the domination of the Indian and filled to overflowing with cattle. The increase in these states and territories alone, since 1860, has been over 15,000,000 head of cattle. Still, with this wonderful extension of the business into new fields, and the saving of every she animal of the bovine race for breeding purposes, the increase of population has been so rapid and continuous that we have not been able to keep up our beef supply. No one will for a moment dispute the statement that the population of this country will go on increasing at a proportionate rate, and that in consequence in the year 1910 we will have 100,000,000 people to eat beef. Where is this supply to come from? There is no more unoccupied country. As a general proposition [the?] country is full of cattle. With our [population?] doubled the demand for beef will be doubled. How can this demand be met? Only by producing double the amount of beef on the same ground now occupied. This condition can only be reached in a small area of the country, for the reason that the larger per cent. of the arid region, or permanent range country, has no adequate water supply and no greater number of cattle can be raised than can gain their subsistence from the range in its present condition. Then it is a safe and reasonable conclusion that year by year the beef supply will grow less per capita, and that there will be a gradual advance in prices in proportion as the supply is short.

If then, there is no danger of an over-supply, and a consequent lowering of prices, as a business proposition it is safe to spend money in the development of a country where increased supplies may be had, so long as you keep those expenditures at a point below which you can secure a present return. The future will guard itself.

There is yet another advantage. By the production of hay the ranchman is put in virtual control of the market. The beef market of the east has for years been regulated by Chicago. The vast numbers of grass Texans thrown upon that market in July and August lower prices from one to two cents a pound. During the two and a half months following the great runs of northwestern beef from the ranges still further reduce prices. But all range beef must go to the market, for they cannot be held on the open range. In consequence the shipper must take such a price as he is offered. But with great stacks of alfalfa in the fields the fat steers may be held over until the demand creates satisfactory prices.

A fat three-year-old steer, weighing 1,100 pounds off the range in October, may be put in an open lot anywhere on the valley lands, and fed hay through the winter with an absolute certainty of gaining 200 pounds gross, and a probability of seventy-five pounds more if judiciously handled. It is always profitable to feed a beef steer if he is thriving and "doing well," as feeders say, provided the feed is secured at a reasonable price. He is laying on fat that has a commercial value greater than the raw material that was converted into fat.

To back up this alfalfa feeding idea the writer has taken great pains to secure facts and figures, some of which are herewith presented. Two years ago a gentleman living near Ogden, Utah, fed a bunch of steers for several months, weighing the hay fed out each day and the steers every week. The result showed that 2,240 pounds of alfalfa put on an even hundred pounds of flesh or growth. Another gentleman living fifteen miles from Salt Lake City brought fifteen three-year-old steers out of pasture seven miles distant, drove them to his pens and weighed them, paying therefore at so much a pound. They were weighed on the first day of November. On the 31st of December they were sold to a Salt Lake butcher, driven fifteen miles to the slaughter-house and weighed, having again been purchased at so much a pound. They had gained 120 pounds, or two pounds a day, and during the time had been fed nothing but alfalfa hay in an open lot.—[Nevada Letter Cheyenne Journal.

T. Martin is the weather prophet of this country and justly so as he has a tri-daily report of the weather extending back many years. A comparison of the first half of July with other periods shows that there has never been known such a warm spell as the first sixteen days of July. For all that time, the weather averaged 102 degrees in the shade and 114 in [the sun?] between six in the morning and six in the evening.

The present drought has brought out a number of experiences, encouraging to stockmen. There has only been one year in Montana that compared with this for dryness and that was early in the '70's. There was almost no rain until the middle of September. Then the ground received several good soakings and there has not been better grass, except in size of the blades, before or since.

In spite of the large numbers of horses that have been brought to the Little Missouri ranges the last three years, the price holds up better than in almost any other part of the range country. This is probably explained by the facts that there is a constantly growing demand among the farmers east of us for work horses and that the horse ranches on the river have taken all the good mares that have been brought in. In any event, the price of good horses is as high as it was three years ago and there seems no immediate prospect of there being any break in the market. Within three years, however, the horse ranches here will be able to supply a large demand for first-class heavy work horses as well as the best quality of cow-horses.

The special delivery system goes into effect on Oct. 1, in every post-office in the United States. Hitherto, only first and second-class post-offices, were special delivery offices but after Oct. 1, as said, the rule applies to all offices, large or small. The post-office under this system, guarantees the immediate delivery of letters upon which an extra ten cent stamp is affixed.

The United States is placed in a rather embarrassing position in its present difficulty with Mexico. To begin with, the man Cutting, whose arrest has caused the difficulty, is such a notorious fraud that the trouble has many of the elements of a farce. In the second place, a war between the United States and Mexico, would be such an exaggerated case of "big dog eat little dog," that the Government will probably decline to begin a war from very shame. The honor of the nation is at stake, however, and it compels her to demand satisfaction from Mexico for an outrage on even such a citizen as Cutting. Altogether, the affair is so perplexing that it has caused Secretary Bayard to fall into a state of chronic exasperation.

Mandan and Bismarck were visited Sunday afternoon by a violent wind storm which lasted for three hours and did considerable miscellaneous damage. In Mandan, the worst damage was done to George Peoples' building, the tin roof being blown off and furniture, walls, carpets etc., being soaked with water; the total amounting to about $1,500. The Northern Pacific bank building, the new court house and many others buildings were damaged. Probably the whole will amount to $5,000 in Mandan. In Bismarck, the loss is estimated at less than $2,000. The Tribune's signal service report states that the wind blew forty-eight miles an hour. July 13, 1883, it blew fifty-six miles an hour as it did also on April 22 of the same year. On April 18, 1876, was the hardest storm Bismarck has probably ever experienced, the rate at that time being seventy-four miles an hour. The storm of Sunday extended far into Minnesota and altogether did about $25,000 worth of damage.

Among recent facts of literary and popular interest, is the announcement of a new illustrated biography entitled "The Every-Day Life of Abraham Lincoln," written by "Those who knew him." The plan of the work is that of an exhaustive biography, giving not only the general facts of his life in chronological order, but incidents, anecdotes and every day facts minutely personal, such as could only be given by those in closest intimate and confidential relations, during the various periods of his life. These were, in pursuance of the plan, enlisted for the work, embracing those who knew him as a boy, as a flatboatman, a rail-splitter, a clerk in a country store, a law student, a lawyer, politican, President—every period of his eventful and most interesting life. Each author writes of the facts of his life during the period in which he knew him—facts and incidents that came under his own observation and within his own knowledge. A book thus written, and so exhaustive in fact concerning one of so enduring a place in the hearts and admiration of his people, is assured of an enthusiast welcome and a lasting place in popular esteem. We are told that the last literary work performed by the late Judge David Davis, Lincoln's lifetime friend, was one of the many contributions to this volume, in which he took a deep personal interest.

It is a grand career and character that is thus so minutely delineated. What lover of simple worth and homely virtues is not touched by the story of Lincoln's pure and manly life? In what other country could it have been possible to produce a character and career like his?

The work is rendered further attractive by nearly 100 superb engravings from original designs made especially for this book, illustrations scenes and incidents in his life. It is sold at popular prices within the reach of all.

The canvassing agent for such a work will find the latch-string out; a welcome and patronage that will make his business both pleasant and profitable. N. D. Thompson Publishing Co., St. Louis, Mo., and New York City, are the enterprising publishers.

The Indian Territory, said Colonel Taylor in reply to a question, had been lost sight of almost as a cattle country, or rather that portion which was formerly so prominent and gave so much cause for discussion; the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservation. The cattlemen had shown no disposition to break over the orders of the government in reference to those sections and now a traveller can ride a day in either one of the reservations without seeing more than a dozen cattle. Numerous outfits have been sent in to gather up the stragglers and now there were very few left. The Choctaw and Cherokee strip still offered very good ranges and there also were probably 100,000 cattle on the Comanche grounds, but they gave no trouble and no fear was entertained that they would be removed. Some of the cattlemen who had herds on the strip in the name of squaw men; thus grazing their cattle at less cost than if they leased direct from the Nation; experienced a great deal of trouble on account of an order made by the Nation taking away some of the rights of the squaw men, directing that they should take no herds except on payment of $3 a head. But that trouble was settled by the cattlemen acquiescing, where they had to, on the real owners of the herds becoming known to the Indian officials.—[Globe-Democrat.

In the construction of artesian wells the experience of the pioneers is of value to those who have yet to solve the problem. The true artesian vein is a white sand rock, which lies, at Yankton 600 feet below the surface. Northward from this point the depth of this rock increases, and the in Alexandria neighborhood it probably lies not less than 700 down. To reach the artesian basin it is necessary to pass the drill through chalk, shale, stiff clay, iron pyrites, quicksand and various conglomerates, most of the formations being difficulty to overcome and requiring patience, skill and experience on the part of the well maker. Every foot of the distance between the surface and the water-bearing rock should be tighly cased and it will be found that heavy salt water casing is the most economical in the end, though it is more expensive than the lighter grades. Perfect casing is the most important part of the work. If a portion of the bore is neglected the artesian water when reached sends a considerable portion of its volume off through the loose overlying formations and the defcet is created which constantly increases in magnitude. In searching for the true artesian vein numerous minor veins are generally encountered which produce flowing wells. The discharge from these veins is much less than from the lower veins, and an inferior quality of water is given forth. So it is best to resist the temptation to stop when a tolerable flow is encountered and go down to the artesian sand rock, which has never yet failed to give a spouting well. In the city of Yankton and in its suburbs there are now telvew flowing wells. These vary in depth from 350 to 600 feet. In only the deepest of these was the white sand rock vein reached, and that one is yielding water of the best quality at the rate of 1,500 gallons per minute. the others have a flow of from 30 to 100 gallons per minute. Most of the smaller wells were made for private use and answer the purpose for which they were constructed. But for public uses the deepest is the only one of the dozen which gives a satisfactory flow.

There is reason to believe that almost every Dakota village, city and farm can enjoy the luxury of a spouting well.—[Press and Dakotaian.

The wonderful two-year-old Tremont has had a remarkable career. He has started twelve times, and has never been forced to anything like an exertion by the best horses that have been pitted against him. He has won his owners in stakes and purses this year something over $30,000, and will duplicate that amount before the end of the season. He cost $1,600 as a yearling. This splendid colt is jet black, and the only mark on him is a little white star in the forehead, about as big as a silver half dollar. The youngster seemed to be proud of the attention shown him, and moved about the stall, occasionally coming up to take a nip at his master's coat sleeve.

"He is the greatest two-year-old that ever lived," said Captain Conner, and both the Dwyers nodded assent. Philip said: "Yes, he can beat any horse now on the turf for three-quarters of a mile and carry just as much weight as his competitor. He is a good disposition horse also."

Miss Woodford is, in many respects, the most phenomenal race horse I ever knew of. The fact is, she is the only one I have ever known that was just as good at six years old as three. It is really singular how she holds her power.

The splendid mare came up to her master, rubbed her nose against him lovingly, and there was such a beam of intelligence in her eye that it almost seemed as though she understood the praise her owner was giving her and the depth of the admiration he has for her. As he patted her long and beautifully-arched neck Mr. Phil. Dwyer said:

"She has won us $150,000 in stakes and purses—what is known in racing parlance as public money. No race horse in this country has ever yet equalled her performances—that is, been beaten so few times in an equal number of starts."
—[Philadelpha Times.

T. W. Gordon's future address will be at Glendive, where he will be pleased to meet any of his Medora friends.
The railroad commissioners of Dakota made a trip to Medora last Saturday in Supt. Green's private car.
Mr. and Mrs. Delamatre of Meadville, Pa., left Monday morning. They have been visiting at the Custer Trail ranch.
Z. Gilbert's photograph gallery was shipped back to Mandan yesterday. A first-rate business was done here and some fine views taken.

M. C. Conners is to-day shipping forty-eight cars of cattle from Mingusville. The Montana cattle Co. yesterday shipped thirty-two cars from the same point. Mingusville is now in the full rush of the shipping season.

Wm. Van Driesche and Frank Foster took advantage of the expiration of the law Tuesday and beat the record on chicken shooting. They bagged thirty-three in less than two hours' shooting. The samples they left with us were enough to make an epicure's mouth water.

Mike Finnegan and partner, who stole a boat at the Elkhorn ranch last spring, were brought up before the court at Mandan Tuesday, and pleaded guilty to grand larceny. They were sentenced to twenty-five months imprisonment each. The Mandan Pioneer in commenting on Finnegan's appearance, did not seem to be especially struck with his manly beauty.

Mr. Carleton of Port Huron, Mich., was in town Monday and Tuesday. He is a prominent Michigan Democrat but "lacks lots" of being a friend of the present administration. He has twenty-five hundred acres of land near South Heart, five hundred being under cultivation. The crop this year will not pay expenses and he is thinking of putting cattle on the land.

The case of the Territory vs. Joseph Meyer, for horse-stealing, came before the grand jury at Mandan and they failed to find an indictment against him, the evidence not being sufficiently strong. Judge Francis, however, ordered the prisoner held in bonds of $1,000 to the next grand jury, as he learned that the evidence was deemed insufficient because "Calamity" Joe. was accused of stealing the horse from an Indian.

The hail-storm Friday afternoon was almost unprecedent in violence for half an hour, but its track was so narrow that beyond broken window glass the damage was slight. Its path extended but a mile or two north and south of Medora, by ten miles west and twenty east. An immense body of water fell at the same time. Sixty-eight panes of glass were broken out of the Northern Pacific hotel and others suffered in proportion.

San Francisco has just experienced the worst fire in its history. The loss foots up at least $2,000,000 and may go still higher. The insurance was very light, as the locality was considered a safe one.

The Minneapolis exposition was opened Monday and the machinery was put in motion by Mrs. Grover Cleveland pressing a telegraph key at Upper Saranac lake in New York state. Everything points to a complete success for the expositson.

The commission appointed by the Secretary of the Interior to visit the different Indian reservations has received its instructions. In general, the mission will be to find ways and means to decrease the Indian reservations where it is clearly seen that they are larger than necessary.

On our second page will be found the portraits of the anarchists who were recently condemned to death in Chicago for murdering or inciting others to the murder of the policemen killed on the memorable 4th of May. No verdict has ever been rendered that gave more general satisfaction than the one which condemned these men to death. Their utterances consisted of the rankest kind of treason and all good men will look forward eagerly to the day when they shall expiate their crimes on the gallows.

The hopes of our war-like citizens will be blasted by the news that there is now no chance of a war with Mexico. The Mexicans claim that editor Cutting circulated a libel against Mexican citizens on Mexican soil and for this was arrested and punished in Mexico; a proceeding recognized as legal by all justice and international law. Consul Brigham and Cutting affirm that the libel was only circulated in the United States. Even in this case the Mexicans claim that they would have the right to arrest and convict Cutting; a right which of course the United States will not recognize. Telegraphic reports indicate that Cutting was released yesterday.

The motion made by Willis Eaton at the stock meeting, relative to the back taxes paid on account of Billings county is a good one and was unanimously carried. Between the time the railroad was built and the county organized many thousands of dollars were paid by the railroad to the Territory for taxes on that part of the road passing through Billings county. Subtracting the amount of expense we were to the Territory, there still remains a balance estimated at from $6,000 to $10.000. This amount is of course justly due to us and there seems to be no reasonable doubt that it cannot be secured. The Territorial Secretary's answer to a question relative to the matter that: "An unorganized county stands in the light of a garden to a gardener rather than that of a ward to a guardian," indicates that there may be some opposition to the measure, but its eminent justice stands a good chance of winning the required approval for it.

The round-up camped at Sentinel Butte last night, having worked Andrew's creek yesterday. The OX outfit, which started the round-up, cut out about 600 beeves Tuesday and will probably ship to-day from Dickinson. All the river out-fits have been gathering beeves and the most of them will ship soon. The round-up will work up the river probably disbanding at the Neimmela ranch. The quality of the beef is scarcely as good as was expected.

Clay Leighton, one of the men who stole some horses from the Morton farm near South Heart, two years ago, and after being arrested, escaped from the Dickinson jail, was rearrested at Buffalo Gap recently. Being brought back to Mandan, he was there sentenced to five years and eight months in the Bismarck penitintiory, where he is now "doing time" for the Territory. His partner Scott, who escaped from Dickinson at the same time, has not since been heard from.

Riley Brooks who came in to announce the death of George Fraser yesterday morning, rode about eighteen miles in fifty-five minutes. The hope of doing something to aid his dead comrade lent wings to the errand of mercy.

In a very quiet and unostentations way Miss Lena Eager and Harry Barker were made one at Dickinson last Sunday. The newly married couple have gone to housekeeping at the Cantonment and are nicely settled. They are both well liked and everyone will wish them a happy journey through life.

Rev. Schaffner's case cams up again before the court in Mandan last week and the bondsmen were ordered to pay up the $1,000 bail which the reverred gentleman had jumped. [Since the aboye was put in type, we learn from last night's Mandan Pioneer that Shaffner was seen in Dickinson Tuesday and that instructions have been sent for his arrest.

E. G. Paddock and G. D. Kennedy were the sufferers by a runaway Monday afternoon, that might easily have resulted seriously. They were a few miles from town when the buck-board seat broke and in the confusion a line dropped. In attempting to recover it, the horses started to run and both passengers were thrown forward on the pole Kennedy falling under the wheels and Paddock "staying with the leather" on the tongue. An inventory of damages showed a sprained ankle and countless bruises on Kennedy while Paddock escaped with several scratches and cuts.

The sad news was brought in yesterday morning by Riley Brooks that George Fraser had been killed at eight in the morning by a stroke of lightning and that Ed. Connolly of the 13 outfit, was badly stunned at the same time. Coroner Martin and Moses Ryder started immediately for the scene of the accident and last evening brought in all that was mortal of poor George.

The particulars are about as follows: George and Connelly had started with a bunch of horses from the Ref. Car Co's. lower camp and had gone about five miles when the storm broke. Connelly, who suffered greatly from the shock, says that he scarcely remembers anything except that his horse jumped violently and that he became unconscious. When he came to himself, he looked around for George and saw him lying on his face some distance away. He went to him and after considerable difficulty turned him partly on his back, when he saw that he was dead. His clothes were burning, but Connelly, in his dazed and prostrated condition, found it impossible to put out the fire. He managed to ride into camp and tell the boys where the accident occurred, when he again became unconscious. Brooks started immediately for town to get assistance and a team went from camp to bring in George. It was found that the bolt of lightning had entered his head, bruising it badly. It had then passed through his body into the saddle, which it pierced full of holes, thence through the horse, which was instantly killed and into the ground.

Thus passed away one of the noblest boys that rode the range. Always pleasant, genial and kind-hearted, he was at all times and places a perfect gentleman; one of Nature's noblemen. No one was a greater favorite than he and his acquaintances became immediately his warm friends. We never heard an unfriendly remark about George while the good words spoken for him were legion.

His parents reside at River John, Nova Scotia, and were notified by Dan. McKenzie, who is also a native of the same place.

The funeral took place at two o'clock this afternoon, the services being conducted by Rev. Mr. Boylan of Glendive, who spoke feelingly of the lessons taught by the accident. The remains will be sent to his old home for burial. A fine metallic casket was ordered from Bismarck and in every way possible his friends tried to show their appreciation of poor George's worth.

The total number of cattle received at the Chicago yards last week was 48,312, of which over 20,000 were range cattle. The market during the week fluctuated considarably, but Monday's prices were about the same as those of a week ago. The market altogether presents a more encouraging view than it has for some time. Shippers are bidding largely, a process that invariably raises the price. Montana and Dakota rangers are topping the market.

One of the greatest trials about a cow-ranch is to get the horse-herd "located," so that they will not wander away. When horses haye been raised on a certain range, they can be taken hundreds of miles away and unless watched closely, are liable at any time to return all those hundreds of miles to their native "stamping ground." Instances of this are constantly coming to light, but perhaps as remarkable a one as has ever occurred, happened in the case of a team belonging to John Manning, formerly sheriff of Lawrence county. As narrated by the Black Hills Pioneer, it is as follows:

When John Manning came from Montana to Deadwood he brought with him a span of small bay broncho mares. He drove them in a buggy for a number of years about Deadwood and then put them on his ranch for breeding purposes. They each raised colts for four years which ran on the range with them. A year or so ago the mothers left the range upon which they had been feeding with their progency so long, and returned to their favorite stamping grounds in Montana, many hundred miles distant, and from which they had been absent eight or nine years. Mr. Manning exhausted inquiry for the runaways and then gave them up as lost, thinking they had been stolen. Some time since he received a letter from a friend in Montana, saying his mares were back there on their old range.

Mingusville has been a little upset lately over a dispute in which justice may be meted out to innocent persons. It seems that a cowboy went from Mingusville to Glendive to get a check cashed. While in Glendive he was importuned by a gambler to join in a game of poker. The cow-puncher was altogether too "fly" to enter into any such transaction but the gambler still kept at him and finally followed him to Mingusville. At last the cowboy lost all patience and told the gambler to clear out. Even this hint had no effect and at last it ended in a disturbance on account of which the cowboy and two other good citizens have been arrested. From the facts as we learned them, it appears that the gambler will go free and the others be punished, a state of affairs we hope to see reversed.

Bob. Thompson has "skipped the country" and it is very probable that he will never again show up in the Bad Lands. Last Thursday he shot his revolver off in town and deputy-sheriff Ryder immediately swore out a warrant for him and after considerable difficulty owing to the fact that he would not walk, got him before Justice Copeland. Here he was fined $15 and costs which he paid. Soon after, mounting his horse, he rode up to where Ryder was standing and stated that he had come prepared to kill him, holding him up meantime with his six-shooter. After a parley, he put up his revolver and by a quick move, Ryder got it and turned the tables on Thompson. He was put in irons, awaiting the arrival of officers to take him to Mandan. Friday night he was allowed to sit unironed in front of Jorgens' drug store. While talking, he took his boots off and got up to "streeth his legs," which he did to such good purpose that he has not been seen since. It was a well-planned escape, as no one could expect a man in his stocking feet to get away in the Bad Lands.

The stock-holders of the Northern Pacific will doubtless be well pleased with the report of the earnings for the last month. The passenger as well as the freight business is having a boom, bouble-headers constantly running on the passenger trains.

Mr. Martin's promised weather report appears in this issue and presents as remarkable an array of figures as we have ever seen published concerning the weather. Really the most remarkable point in the whole, is that there was no sickness on account of the heat; a fact attributable to our clear, dry climate. The report is the substance of much work and will well bear careful reading.

In brief, the instructions for the collection of the tax on oleomargarine are as follows: No extra employes are allowed for the collection. A tax of fifteen cents per pound is placed on imported oleomargarine. Unstamped or unwholesome products are to be sold for axle grease. Manufacturers are required to file a bond of not less than $5,000. The factory books are to be open to inspection the same as distillery and brewery books. Manfactures must display a sign on their factory, giving their name, business and number. Each package must have the word "oleomargarine" plainly printed on it in letters not less than one-quarter of an inch square. It is learned that nearly half the oleomargarine made in the United States is exported and that a large share of this comes back in the shape of fancy cheeses.

The Bismarck Tribune of Tuesday has a full table by counties of the Territorial assessment. It has been found that the assessors very generally undervalued property and in some of the counties this will make considerable difference in their rates of taxation. The average levy on the territory at large this year is only two and four-tenths mills; a reduction of from twenty to forty per cent. over anything hitherto levied. Billings county just hits the average, our levy being two and four-tenths mills. Interest at the rate of five-tenths of a mill brings our levy to two and nine-tenths mills. The average valuations for the Territory are: Lands, per acre; $3.87; horses, per head, $51.01; mules, $58.40; cattle, $15.63; sheep, $1.27; swine, $2.24. The rates are based on these figures; any county ranging below getting a higher rate and vice versa. Billings county's valuation was: Horses, $26; mules, $25; cattle, $16., making a very fair average for the whole.

Either the undertaker who furnished the coffin ordered for George Fraser seized the opportunity to turn it into an advertisement or the Bismarck Tribune is guilty of letting a desire for sensationalism run away with its sense of decency. The day after George was killed, the Tribune contained an article to the effect that Sheriff Willard had had a fight with a couple of cow-boys, that he had killed them both and that it was for one of them that the coffin had been ordered. There was not a word of truth in the article and it was so mixed up with an advertisement of a fine line of furniture that it looks as though the man who furnished the coffin is at the bottom of the affair. The people of Medora and the Bad Lands are heartily sick of these lies which are scattered broad-cast about us, generally with no foundation whatever. Especially in the case of George Fraser is such an article looked upon with indignation. We think we are correct in stating that he never had a dispute here of any kind. He was a sober, industrious young man, always had a pleasant word for everyone and was a universal favorite.

The cowmen of the Bad Lands, like those of some of the older ranges, are brought face to face with the fact that there are about as many cattle on the range as it will support in safety. There is room for those already here and their increase, but there will be this year nearly if not quite 40,000 additional head brought in. This increase cannot be repeated with safety to the ranges. There is no disguising the fact that even this year the capacity of the ranges may be tested severely. If there are any extensive prairie fires, there is sure to be a crowding of ranges and consequent loss. Already there is some talk of taking measures, as other districts are doing, to protect the ranges from over-crowding. This can be done in a measure by convincing new-comers that there is no room for more cattle, but it would hardly be consistent when the old outfits are bringing in cattle by thousands. It would be good policy for all to rest on their oars until next spring at least, and by that time the capacity of the ranges will be well tested. The one thing now certain is that thousands of acres of what have been good grazing lands are now absolutely worthless for pasturage. The prairie grasses do not recuperate until at least the second year, when they have been grazed or cut close. This fact, of itself, is enough to make cowmen consider the matter carefully, before adding cattle to what may already be an over-stocked range.

Earthquake shocks were felt Thursday evening in South Carolina, West Virginia, Iowo Wisconsin, Maryland and Alabama. Much damage was done and as telegraphic communication has been cut off from Charleston, South Carolina, it is feared that that city is destroyed.

The cases growing out of the citizens of Billings county refusing to pay taxes to Stark county came up last week in Mandan. In the case of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., the preliminary injunction was sustained by Judge Francis and all the cases will come up at the next term of court.

The latest candidate for journalistic honors is the Montana Democrat published at Miles City. The editors are Putman and Martin, the former well-known under his nomme de plume of "Slade." The Democrat is a tri-weekly and will at all times "strive to be worthy of the confidence of the entire people." We wish it success.

A powder magazine belonging to Laflin & Rand in Chicago, was exploded by lightning last Sunday morning and in all directions for miles an earth-quake-like shock was felt. About 130,000 pounds of dynamite and blasting powder were exploded. One person was killed and five mortally wounded. The loss will be over $75,000 to the powder company. The loss on window glass almost surpasses computation. One pane worth $300 was broken in the Board of Trade building, over seven miles from the scene of the explosion.

If there is one thing more than another that will benefit laboring men, it is in organization. But the very fact of their being organized, when under bad leaders works them the greatest of all mischiefs. A case in point is the strike of 6,000 shoe-lasters in Brockton, Mass., because a poor, old man with a family to support and who happened not to belong to their order, was given work. Alreadly they have lost about $250,000 in wages on account of the strike. With able, cool-headed leaders, even-handed justice will always be meted out to laboring men. The penitentiary for life is too mild a punishment for the man or set of men who ordered this strike.

Chris. Anderson, a northside stockman living on Sunday creek, recently tried a plan of breaking a broncho by tying a dummy on its back. The dummy was made of an old suit of clothes stuffed with straw and somewhat resembled a man. This dummy was tied firmly on the saddle so it could not fall off and the broncho was saddled and turned loose. After some vigorous bucking which [jerked?] off the dummy's head the broncho broke down the corral and ran into a bunch of horses, nearly stampeding them out of the country. While rushing madly along with the limber, flopping, helpless rider on its back, the broncho came in sight of a cowboy returning from recent interviews with Miles City whiskey. Probably the c. b's. vision was none of the clearest then, so thinking to relieve a fellow creature in distress, he jabbed spurs into his horse and flew in pursuit. After a hard and exciting chase he ran up close enough to make a throw with his lariat, and succeeded in missing the horse but caught and stripped off saddle and dummy. Imagine first his horror at finding on the end of his rope a headless man, and a moment after that his relief on learning that it was only Anderson's dummy.—[Montana Democrat.

The first herd of cattle known on the continent of America was brought by Columbus on his second voyage. From these, and from other small herds brought by later Spanish navigators, the wild cattle of South America descended. In 1553 the Portugese took cattle and hogs to Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. The Canadian cattle were introduced in 1608. In 1620 Virginia had 500 head of cattle. The most stringent laws were passed prohibiting the killing of any domestic animal. In New England cattle were introduced in 1624. It is said that for a time, price was regulated by color, a red calf being cheaper than a black one because it was more likely to be mistaken by the wolves for a deer and killed.—[Chicago Stock-News.

This issue of the Record contains a letter from Walter C. Weedon, of Kansas City to the Albuquerque Journal, giving an account of a recent shipment of Arizona cattle in the Burton stock cars, which will be read with interest by stockmen generally. It is really surprising that in such an era of progress the stock car of forty years ago is now in general use, this too, in the face of the fact that they have never been anything but cruel contrivances, which served no other or better purpose than to merely hold stock on the track until the train reached its destination. The railroads have discouraged any innovation on the old method, mainly, of course, on account of the large amount of money already invested in the old-time style of cars, and for the further reason that railroad companies, as a rule, are very slow to adopt any invention which adds anything to their expense account. We believe, however, that the death knell of the old stock car has been sounded at last, and that better facilities must and will be furnished to shippers of live stock. Where competing lines are striving to obtain live stock shipments, instead of monkeying with the tariff and rebate system, improved cars will be offered to the shipper. This will compel other lines to do likewise, and when once the revolution begins it will spread like a prairie fire and improved cars will be the rule.

The Burton car is an undoubted success and is practically a live stock sleeping and dining car. The only reason why it is not generally adopted at sight is the great cost of its construction; but when the railroads generally signify their willingness to take a step forward in the matter, Yankee ingenuity will provide something satisfactory to both the shipper and the railroads, which can be built for a sum not greater than the purpose justifies. The killed and maimed cattle together with the shrinkage directly chargeable to the poorly-fashioned stock cars, have reduced the profits of the range cattlemen millions of dollars, and now that the time has arrived when intelligence and a care for the details must be observed in the range cattle business, the question of better shipping facilities is one that demands careful attention, and there can be no doubt of success if there is unity of action among the cowmen.

The sheepmen have steadily clamored for double-decked cars, and although the railroad companies positively set themselves against the request, the sheep growers were not discouraged, but kept up the fight. They enlisted the stock yard and commission men under their banner, notably Colonel R. D. Hunter, of St. Louis, and their labors have been crowned with success. The Missouri Pacific system and Texas roads have begun the construction of double-deck cars and they will be used by all roads transporting sheep. A like victory awaits the cattlemen if they work for it.—[Colorado L. S. Record.

The people of Charleston, S. C., are sorely afflicted. Four separate times last week they endured violent shocks of earth-quake, and now over 60,000 people there are living in tents or almost any cover, in the parks and streets. About one hundred persons have been killed and wounded by the shocks and a reign of terror is in progress.

The Democrats of Billings county will effect an organization on the 18th., to send delegates to the Aberdeen convention. Party politics will however, have little or nothing to do with county offices and we doubt if the time will ever come in Billings county when a party ticket is run and elected.

The citizens of the county should bestir themselves and hold a convention to elect delegates to the convention which is to nominate members of the Legislature. It is very likely that Billings county's two votes may have some weight in the convention and at any rate must "represent" if we wish to have any weight with the coming Legislature. As the only legislation we will need if any, will be in relation to the stock interest, we suggest that two of our stockmen would make good delegates and can think of no better names for the position than those of Howard Eaton and J. L. Truscott.

Ever since 1878, there have been cases pending, relative to the title to the land in Deadwood. The cases grew out of the filing of mineral claims on land in the business part of the city. The Hawkes claim especially, involving the best of the business part of Deadwood, has been bitterly contested. Numerous decisions have been rendered declaring that the land was mineral and now comes a final decision from Secretary Lamar to the same effect. Of course the title to the land takes the buildings along with it, and the business men will lose all the improvements they have put on the property.

On Tuesday of this week, Frank Mead, well-known in the West-Missouri country and in 1884, Mayor of Mandan, shot and it is feared, fatally injured Frank Farnsworth, a dry-goods merchant of Mandan. The shooting took place in the lobby of the Merchant's hotel in St. Paul and was probably the result of a grudge borne by Mead, though Farnsworth says he does not know what it is. Mead is in jail and declares that the shooting was accidental as he only drew his revolver in sport. He had just before refused to shake hands with Farnsworth, however, and called him several vile names, so that it looks like a cold-blooded attempt at murder.

There has been much talk among Stark county citizens, relative to having Villard county incorporated in their limits. The sentiment in Stark county relative to the stock interests, has repeatedly been shown to be of the kindliest nature, but we doubt if any advantage would be gained by Billings county from such an annexation. If any change is made, the limits of Billings county should be extended so as to include at least all of the Bad Lands and exclusively stock country. At present, our eastern line runs just to the west of Sully Springs, leaving a ragged edge of from three to ten miles of Bad Lands in Villard county. The citizens of Villard have also expressed a decided preference to being incorporated into Billings county, if any change is made. As they are the ones most vitally interested, their wishes should certainly be respected.

Bismarck, Dak., Sep. 7, 1886.

The cattle market remains practically unchanged from last week and the advisability of shipping now is as doubtful as ever. Fowler Bros., who now have a large pork-packing establishment in Chicago, are making preparations to open up one with a capacity of 3,000 hogs a day in St. Paul. At the same time, capitalists are said to be ready to put in slaughter-houses for cattle. This however, is only in the form of a rumor and the completion of a plant in St. Paul, competent to utilize the out-put of cattle from the northwest, seems as far off as ever. Especially to small outfits, such an establishment would be a god-send; saving many dollars on small shipments that must now go to Chicago. The same old difficulty of finding a profitable market, however, stares the promoters of such an enterprise in the face and makes of it a risky speculation. The only way in which we can see that the cattle traffic can be turned from its present channels, is by the adoption of a plan similar to the one now used by the N. P. Ref. Car Co., viz: to establish retail shops in the large cities, to be supplied from western abattoirs. There are now three of their shops running profitably in New York and there is no reason why others should not pay. If this plan is successful in the case of three shops, why should it not be in the case of 300, judiciously placed in eastern cities. As there is no lack of money back of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., we would not be surprised to see it take a leading part in such a move, with headquarters in Medora. At any rate, there seems no further room for new slaughter-houses, unless they do their own retailing.

A man who had amassed a large fortune was asked by a young man to reveal the secret of money getting. "I will give it to you in a nutshell," said Money bags. "Buy when everybody wants to sell and sell when everybody wants to buy."

The "secret" thus disclosed suggests some singular truths. Whenever any particular industry is wonderfully prosperous capital rushes pell mell to get into it, and, although, as a rule, wealth is accumulated by industry and business prudence, those who have, by the exercise of those qualities achieved success, risk their slowly accumulated earnings with astonishing recklessness in schemes which promise unusual returns. The history of the range cattle business illustrates the pig-headed obstinacy of capital on the one hand and its mad recklessness on the other. For twenty years prior to 1880 the range cattle business was carried on with unvarying success. All the men engaged in it began poor and grew rich. Such uniform success and large profits were never before realized in the business. The industry was conducted openly, and its success and profits were generally known, and yet capital was indifferent to the advantages presented, and the stockmen were compelled to pay, and did pay, rates of interest that would have wrecked any other industry. But about the year 1880 the security and great profits of the business stood out so prominently that capital went crazy, and the men who would only risk their money in the business at exorbitant rates of interest with iron-clad security became anxious to become investors, and that, too, without ordinary business inquiry into details. The anxiety to become "cattle kings" became epidemic and the result inevitable. Ranges were crowded beyond their capacity, extravagant and fictitious prices were paid for both ranches and cattle. Many experienced cattlemen caught the infection, and waded beyond their [depth?]. A rigorous winter [depleted?] the herds. The profits realized when the business was conducted on a conservative and common-sense basis disappeared, and disappointment followed. There is nothing in all this which indicates that the range cattle business has changed in any of its essential features, nothing that indicates that it will not, under prudent management, be as safe and profitable as at any time in its history. But it does prove that there must be a return to common-sense methods. That many of those who engaged in the business when everybody was willing to sell are now willing to go out is doubtless true, and, therefore, the time to buy is at hand, and those who secure ranges and stock them within the safety line will realize old-time safety and profit.

It is natural to suppose that capitalists would take this view of it, but it is a historical fact that they don't. They go in when the hurrah is on, get out when disappointment comes and wait for the next excitement, and the men who hang to the willows and control their appetites for gain will go along making money.—[Colorado L. S. Record.

It seems that rangemen, particularly those along the line of the Union Pacific road, are inclined to be discouraged, and are thinking of opening the flood-gates and letting their cattle come to market regardless of condition or prices. At least this is the gist of the conclusions reached by very prominent managers. The reason given is that late rains on the prematurely cured grass has done more harm than good, having washed out much of the essential substance. In view of this fact and the present low prices, a number of cattlemen are said to have decided that there must be a rush of immature beeves to market, and that they had as well gather freely and take low prices early now as later in the season.

In this connection is the following from the Rocky Mountain Husbandman:

The question that presents itself is, shall they gather everything that is marketable or only the prime beef? We unhesitatingly say gather everything that will possibly do for the block. Gather the steers closely, including 3-year-olds and stags, also all the old dry cows. The loss in the winter and spring is largely of the offspring of dry cows, for they calve in early spring or late winter and are almost sure to lose their calves. If the weather is severe and feed scarce they will die also. Beef is low, very low, and prices are tending downward, while the market continues to grow weaker every day. But, for all that, it will be better to sell even at a low figure than endanger the whole herd by having the range overstocked.

The good advice above is not unmixed with evil. It is better to make bad beef of weaklings that could not stand the rigors of winter than to let them die on the range; and every precaution should be taken to prevent overstocking the ranges. But the object of stock raising is to put on the markets products that will bring to the producers the largest possible returns. This cannot be done by indiscriminately crowding forward the very kinds that are in least demand and the kinds which, if forced upon the trade, will injure the market for all below the very finest grades of stock. There are two classes into which range stock may be divided at market. Beef cattle, fat, or at least fleshy, and canning stock. Feeding cattle come in as a sub-class, as they sell inside of the range of prices for canners. Between the best canning cattle and the best range beef cattle there is usually a difference of about $1.00 to $1.25 per cwt. As a general thing, the best Wyoming range steers and good range cows will come in these two respective classes very nicely. But take a shipment of thin and medium steers, and they cannot class as beef cattle and are above the canning grade; thus coming between two classes of buyers and striking neither. Then all depends on the supply. Should such a lot happen here on a very light run and an advancing market, they would be taken by the men and forced to fill the places at good prices. But such conditions, as shippers well known, are only too rare, and [nine?] cases out of ten such cattle have to be sacrificed at about canning prices. The Journal urgently advises rangemen to carefully study and comply with the demands of the trade to avoid forcing "betwix and between" grades of cattle upon an over stocked market. If the rangers need relief, castrate the old bulls, spay the heifers, and place them on feed to fatten, but don't deliberately break down the beef market in taking care of the range, because the latter would be nothing without the former.—Montana L. S. Journal.

Medora seems to be suffering from an epidemic or irruption of skunks. Over twenty-five have been killed in the neighborhood in the last week.
Dr. Jorgens, wife and son Johnny, came in Saturday from the Cave Hills ranch. Cattle are in first-class condition there and antelope, deer and chickens abound.

J. A. VanEeghen returned last night from his trip to St. Cloud. He sold his car-load of horses easily and at good figures. He considers St. Cloud a good horse market, but the demand is almost entirely for broken horses.

The sad news came from Mingusville Sunday night that Sam. Powers of the 777 outfit was killed there that afternoon. No one saw the accident happen but he had roped a calf, when his horse fell on him and he soon died from his injuries.

The Marquise de Mores returned from New York last Thursday night. On Friday evening, the Duc and Duchesse de Luynes and their daughter and Count Suzannet stopped off and visited the Marquise over Sunday. M. de Saulty, who has been here for some time expecting to take a hunting trip to the Rocky mountains, accompanied them on their western trip, Monday evening.

T. W. Gordon came in Tuesday from the west, having been to Helena and Butte. From his report, Butte seems to have recovered from its boom and there is plenty of work at good pay. He also says that judging from the looks of the range from the railroad, the grazing is constantly poorer as one goes west from Glendive. Several outfits are going to move their cattle south for winter feed.

The report comes in from the 13 camp that no horses are missing from there and that as a consequence Bob. Thompson could not have stolen any of them. The charge of horse-stealing is altogether too serious a one in this country to be lightly made and although we heard the matter definitely stated twice we concluded not to publish it. Just before going to press last week, however, we learned from a perfectly reliable source that the report was direct from the 13 camp. Even after the contradiction came in, we were assured that the charge was a true one, but the denial from the 13 camp settles it.

While L. C. and Robert Hunt were loading a bunch of KC cattle at Dickinson, Tuesday, they received word from their sister Bessie at Fort Union, New Mexico, that their father had died there on that day. This death, following so close on that of their mother last winter, is a cruel blow and one which will attract the sympathy of all to the Hunt brothers. Both of them started immediately for New Mexico and will arrive there Saturday. Their father was Colonel in the regular army, stationed at Fort Vancouver, but for the last six months absent on sick leave. Their plans for the future are a little unsettled, but they will probably take their sister to Washington and then return here.

Further shocks of earth-quake were felt in Charleston Tuesday night, which had the effect of terrorizing the already frightened inhabitants, although but little additional damage was done.
The number of acres of public land disposed of in Dakota this year is 3,075,085; nearly as much as Iowa, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Montana, Oregon, Washington and Wyoming put together.
We are just in receipt from J. S. Collins & Co., of one of the new "Letter Sheet Envelopes," the first we have seen. The new departure will be handy in many ways and doubtless extensively used.

In the base-ball contest for the championship of the National League, the Chicagos have a clear lead of seven games over the Detroits, who stand second, while the New Yorks are a bad third. There seems no reason to doubt that the season will be closed in this order by the three leaders.

Although the Mandan Pioneer was very quick to criticize the COW BOY'S action in proposing a candidate for the Legislature; in fact, criticized the idea of our making a choice before we had made one, it has not had the back-bone to commend any candidate to the public. We are at a loss to understand the Pioneer's course, as the very least it could do would be to name the candidates and praise or condemn them alike. Instead of this, it is as mum as an oyster on the subject.

The Republican primary convention of Billings county, made a good choice in its delegates to the Bismarck convention. Neither of them was present at the convention, but they will fully represent Billings county's sentiments at the convention. They are not instructed, but have hitherto expressed decided preferences for Mr. Lyon of Mandan. They will doubtless stick to their choice as long as there is any chance for success, which at present seems a good one.

A report is going the rounds that Stark county was depending on Billings county's delegation, for support at the Bismarck convention. We doubt if this is well-founded, as no effort whatever has been made by Stark county to enlist aid from here. We do not know even that Stark county has a pronounced candidate and even if it had, there is no chance for his nomination. It is far better to unite on some good man who will have a good fighting chance for the nomination.

The Republican congressional convention, now in session at Yankton will probably not get to balloting before to-morrow as there are a number of contests to be settled. Gifford's friends claim that he will be nominated on the first ballot, while the opposition claim that he will go into the convention with only 190 votes to 210 in opposition and sixty-four doubtful and contested. The opposition claim that there is a good chance of nominating Gen'l. Allen of Fargo or Judge Palmer of Sioux Falls, with chances in favor of the latter.

We are in receipt of a "chromio" from Pozzoni's Complexion Powder Co., that in the hints given us as the basis of a laudatory article, is described as "the most expensive and artistic ever published. An ornament to the parlor or the office of the most fastidious." We don't pretend to be a judge of high art, which may account for the fact that we at first took it for a picture of a dashing equestrienne on a circus poster. We morever seriously doubt if a complexion powder company will make its everlasting fortune in the cow country. It is positively affecting to imagine a stalwart puncher in his boudoir, powdering his face in front of his full-length, plate glass mirror, as a protection against the injurious effect on his countenance of the delicate blizzard or the coy chinook. Oh yes, Mr. Pozzoni, bring out a hay rack full and sell it to the boys by the barrel.

Republican Convention.

At a Republican caucus, held in the Court House in Medora, Monday evening Sept. 20, 1886, J. C. Fisher was elected chairman and J. C. Williamson, secretary.

The meeting proceeded at once to the nomination of delegates to the convention at Bismarck, Oct. 3.

The names of J. A. Ferris, D. W. Williams and F. A. Willard were successively proposed and the nominees declined.

The names of Howard Eaton and G. G. Bond being presented they were elected by acclamation.

A resolution proposed by D. W. Williams to the effect that a Stark county man should be supported in the convention at Bismarck, was lost.

J. C. WILLIAMSON,
Secretary.

St. Paul has made an enviable reputation this season as a stock market for small outfits, sales of from two to six cars there bringing prices from fifty cents to a dollar a hundred higher not than in Chicago. It would be a great relief to the cowmen of the northwest if a market could be established there even as large as those at Kansas City or even Omaha. It would at all times act as a kind of check on any attempt to bear the Chicago market and create a healthy competition very beneficial to our cattle industry. We are as much in the dark as ever, though, how yards can be established at St. Paul that will take the whole northwestern output of cattle. The market is too firmly established in Chicago.

The 777 wagons arrived at Mingusville yesterday and the outfit will load a train to-morrow.

M. C. Conners passed through Medora Friday morning, following the first of five trains of his cattle shipped from Mingusville. He said he would feed as long as he could buy hay, before he sold on a low market.

After many inquiries, we learn that the standard rule for determining the blood of an animal is to add the fractions of the parents and divide by two. For instance, five-eighths and three-eighths Shorthorn parents would produce a half-blood Shorthorn calf.

Ex-Senator Dorsey of New Mexico, has a team that he recently drove to a carriage containing three persons, twenty-eight miles in two hours. There were rough places in the road also, that frequently compelled the horses to walk.

Gregor Lang returned last Thursday evening from St. Paul, where he sold his cattle. The steers brought $3.60 and a few dry cows, $2.90. This price was about forty cents higher than the Chicago market, netting at least seventy-five cents per hundred more than if they had been taken through.

From all northern ranges comes the report that cattle were never in better condition in spite of the drougth. We dislike to stand against almost the unanimous voice of the northwestern range press, but It is impossible to truthfully say that cattle are better than in fair condition. They are not in poor condition but are poorer than far several years in spite of the excellent Bad Lands ranges.

Henry Boice has shipped from Townsend, Montana, about 400 head of mares and colts. They will be put on the Beaver creek range of the 777 outfit, and will, in the future, furnish all the cow-horses necessary for the range work of the company. This is a move which could be profitably imitated by almost every outfit in the country. Cow-horses in the north are too high and it will pay much better to raise them than to buy at $50 to $70 each. Many outfits have gone into the business of raising heavy draft and work horses, but no new ones are raising cow-horses. Unless measures like the above are extensively taken, the price of cow-horses will constantly rise.

From articles in our stock exchanges, we think that 30,000 head is a moderate estimate of the number of cattle sent to the Northwest Territory this summer. All seem agreed that the range is not better there and the only advantage is that a man controls his own range and can do as he pleases with it. The exodus shows pretty clearly that the Montana ranges are pretty well stocked, as the expense of moving is considerable and the benefits to be derived would not be sufficient to justify the move, if there was perfect safety in staying on the old ranges. The 30,000 head can then be considered as the surplus of the Montana ranges, which has, so to speak, slopped over into Canada.

A Rise Inevitable.

It has become plain to every student of statistics that no class of meat-producing animals, except possibly the hog, can be increased with a rapidity sufficient to meet the increasing demand for it. There is not only the increase of population to be met but there is an astonishing increase of meat consumption in all the countries of the world. In this country in 1850 there were [814?] cattle to the 1,000 population. Now there are only 772 to the 1,000 population. This decrease has certainly occured during the period of greatest prosperity in cattle raising on a large scale—when the free grasses on the public lands, the vast sums of willing capital, and the skill and energy of the ranchmen and feeders all favored to the highest degree a rate of production above the average of any other period. The total population of the United States doubles every twenty-five years, but east of the Mississippi the increase of cattle has been less than one-third as great. The annual increase of the population of the entire country is to the annual increase of stock as 2¾ to 1½ per cent., or an excess of increase of population over increase of stock of over 55 per cent.

It is easy to see from the above data that our own requirements are more than a match for our own production under even the most favorable conditions. We cannot hasten breeding operations to any appreciable degree but must content ourselves with about a slow 50 per cent. annual increase or a calf for every two she cattle in the land. But our home demand is not the sole absorber of our products. The British population is increasing at the rate of 1,000 per day, which, at the present rate of consumption, would require an increase of 40,000,000 pounds per annum!

In 1840 the consumption of meat in Great Britain per capita was 61 lbs; in 1850 it was 67 lbs; in 1860, 77 lbs; in 1870, 88 lbs; in 1875, 96 lbs, and in 1882, 109 lbs. per annum. Of this 109 lbs, 56 lbs. was beef. From 1840 to 1850 the increase was only 6 lbs. per capita while it was 21 lbs or 3½ times as great from 1870 to 1882, and the population increased in the latter period [2½?] times as fast as during the former. In France the consumption of beef increased from 19 lbs per capita in 1840 to 40 lbs in 1880 There is a felt deficiency in the beef supply throughout Europe. There during twenty-five years previous to 1880, the cattle had increased only 10 per cent., but the population increased 22 per cent. The United States citizens requires 150 lbs of meat per annum.

The demand for our meat products is not only increasing, but this increase is a growing and permanent one. Can it be met? Probably not. Already we lack in numbers of productive stock and from the west the great source of supply—for the last two years has come to us the complaint of overstocking. At first this was received as the cry of some alarmist who was seeking to frighten some timid people into withdrawing from the cattle business and to deter others from entering upon it, but now, after two consecutive winters and one summer of heavy losses it begins to be seen that really many of the ranches are overstocked. There can be no expansion, therefore, in that direction. But an increase can be made in the producing areas by utilizing some of our mountain regions, in dividing some of the large herds and grazing the subdivisions on areas neglected to the present on account of their smallness, and an increase, and possibly the largest increase in our beef feeding capacity, can be made in the farm districts of the country. Our farmers are not producing 50 per cent. of the cattle food that they should and the combined causes of loss probably leave not over 50 per cent. of the entire products to be actually utilized for conversion into meat, but of these cattlemen will take advantage but slowly because in the first the matter will be considered as a utilization of waste places and the second involves a new and improved system of agriculture and enlarged knowledge of the science of feeding that will require time to meet. While production halts at obstacles and speculates as to the probabilities the pace of demand is neither turned nor retarded. It is inexorable and meat must be forthcoming cheaply if possible, but be the price what it may, meat must come. Barring war prices meat is higher now than ever, except possibly during some short period when it has been unwarrantably "boomed," and is sure to continue on its upward tendency. The cattleman has as bright a day before him as anyone. He may not realize during the next six months or even the next twelve, though it is not impossible that he should at once, but let him stay with his herds, the good time cannot fail him. Breeders are not pushing Angus, Galloways, Herefords, Shorthorns, etc., as if the time had [come?] to discard anything so meritorious as even the poorest breed in the list. Instead of advising the pushing out of either breed the Record will urge the pushing of all of them forward to the point of perfection.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.
