The OX round-up will probably pass through Medora to-morrow or Saturday. This will be the last beef round-up of the season on the river.
Tom. Matthews, at present stock inspector at Glendive, has received the Democratic nomination for sheriff of Dawson county, Montana.
Frank Foster has gone to Chicago, where he will meet the Marquis. They will then go to Kansas City to look up a plant where beef can be killed all winter.
Prairie chickens are getting wild and except for the bag of thirty-four killed by Wm. Van Driesche and Frank Foster in two hours, no large killings have been made.
P. S. Bemis who has been "cow-punching" on the river for over a year, will start Sunday for Arizona. He will run a wagon in a large outfit there owned by some of his New York friends.

Fred Willard wants it gently insinuated that the "cooler" is in running order now and that the price of custard pies may come higher. He adds that he would'nt care so much if the pie plates were returned.

C. L. McGee, wife and sister, who have been visiting at the Logging Camp and at Howard and Charlie Eaton's ranches, will start Sunday for their home in Pittsburgh. Mr. McGee is interested in the SO brand.

Although it is a rather malodorous subject to bring up, we would like to inquire for an explanation of the large number of skunks appearing this year. From the Glendive papers we learn that they are unusually numerous there also.

J. N. Maxwell, well-remembered as rail-road agent here, is now running as messenger for the American express Co., on the Manitoba road, between St. Paul and Fargo. His wife is visiting "Max's" parents at Port Byron, Ill.

A wreck occurred at Black River Falls, Wis., yesterday, in which forty head of cattle were killed and many more injured. The cattle are thought to have been shipped from Mingusville, but it is not as yet known who is the owner.

As an illustration of the harm done by hail and drought this summer it is only necessary to state that but eighty-one bushels of oats were threshed in the farms tributary to South Heart. Last year's figures are not obtainable but there were thousands of bushels.

It is a fact that seems not to be well-known that the bite of a skunk is as dangerous as that of a mad dog. Our exchanges have lately mentioned several cases of persons dying from hydrophobia who have been bitten by skunks. In view of this fact they should be killed as relentlessly as rattlesnakes.

The jail cells have been completed at the Court house and we hope will remain in their present empty state for a long time. They are fire-proof but "lack lots" of being warm as there is no way of heating them except perhaps by setting the Court house on fire. Boarders must remember to bring their overcoats with them this winter or they may have a wooden one made for them at the county's expense.

Theodore Roosevelt and W. H. Merrifield returned Saturday from the Bull river mountains, where they have been hunting for the past month. The trip was undertaken for the purpose of killing a white goat. The hunters were completely successful, killing three of this rare kind of game. Their coat is composed of a thick inner layer of wool, through which protrudes a longer growth of a hairy fur, both being snow-white. The horns are about a foot long, taper gracefully to a sharp point and curve backward like those of an ibex.

To close out the stock of Studebaker wagons now on hand, I will make prices for cash that are lower than the wholesale factory rate. The wagons are new and first-class and have Studebaker Bros. full guarantee as to soundness. They will be sold cheaper than any wagons that have ever been sold in this country and cheaper than they can be bought in car lots at the factory. The only reason for making these rates is to close out stock on hand. They must and shall go soon.

A. T. PACKARD.
M. H. Day will be the Democratic standard-bearer in the election for delegate. He may be a very good man but Dakota is too solidly Republican for him to hope to win.

The Indians on the head of the Yellowstone have broken out and killed several persons besides running off a number of horses. The Yellowstone is now being patrolled from Huntley to Billings and troops are in pursuit of the Indians.

The building of the Hudson Bay railroad seems now to be an assured fact. This road will connect the Canadian Pacific with Hudson Bay, whence there is an all-water route to European ports; except when frozen up during the winter months. This congealed fact will make the success of the road rather problematical.

The assessed valuation of all property in Dakota this year, with the exceptions of Emmons and Marshall counties, is $132,063,905. The August Bulletin, published by Commissioner Dunlap, complains that it would have been much higher, had assessors generally followed directions issued by the territorial Secretary.

The special delivery system is now in force in every post-office in the United States. An additional ten-cent stamp is required and compels the immediate delivery of the letter or parcel upon which it is placed, if received between the hours of 7 a. m. and 9 p. m. in all but free delivery offices. In those the hours are extended to 11 p. m.

We publish this week, Governor Pierce's quarantine proclamation, issued against Illinois cattle. For the sake of her stock interests, Illinois ought to kill immediately all cattle exposed to pleuro-pneumonia. Almost all western states and territories have quarantined against her and still the Phoenix and Schufeldt distillery cattle at Chicago are allowed to live. The quarantine is now kept up at a cost of $150 a day, pending action as to their disposal.

It is not generally known, but cattle can be vaccinated against pleuro-pneumonia, as effectively as can human beings against small-pox. The operation has been many times performed on cattle at the Cape of Good Hope, and always successfully. The virus used, comes from the diseased lungs of cattle suffering from pleuro-pneumonia. Healthy cattle are vaccinated on the tail, which soon drops off at the point of vaccination. The animal is then pleuro-pneumonia proof.

Great uneasiness is felt in Chicago stock circles over the future action of packing-house men and their employes. The statement has been circulated that at the annual closing of the houses for repairs and cleaning, they would either start up simultaneously under the old ten-hours-a-day working rules or that they would all remain closed, thus locking out 30,000 employes. Nothing can be learned from the proprietors as to their intentions, but the impression is gaining ground that serious trouble is brewing.

L. C. Hunt returned from New Mexico last Friday. As the weather was very warm and there were no facilities for embalming, it was thought best to bury the remains of his father at Fort Union, and have them removed next winter to Washington. Robert Hunt who went to Detroit from New Mexico, will return in about a week.

D. C. Rowe of Mingusville, was here Monday, having been to Dickinson shipping several cars of DXR cattle. Last spring when here, he thought a new hat's worth that our county tax assessment would be over thirteen mills inside of three years; saying at the time that he never wanted to lose a bet worse. He was naturally much pleased at having to pay only six mills, as he had paid thirteen mills to Stark county and twenty-six to Dawson county. He wouldn't discount his bet on the next two years, which accounts for our still wearing that same old hat.

Marquis de Mores returned last Thursday evening from his eastern trip, and started down the river Sunday with his wife, on a hunting expedition. He has completed contracts with the French government, to supply its soldiers with a newly invented soup. He intends to visit Europe soon to make contracts with western range cattle companies who have their head-quarters there, for the slaughtering of their cattle.

Dan. McKenzie yesterday completed the sale of his blacksmith shop and the rest of his Medora property to Alex. Morton. As soon as Dan. gets the rest of his business straightened up, he will start for his Nova Scotia home, where he intends going into the livery business. We regret exceedingly to lose Mr. McMckenzie, as he has shown himself to be generous, warm-hearted, a faithful county officer and above all, an honest man. There is no loss without a corresponding gain, however, and Mr. Morton is already well enough known to prove that he will be a valuable citizen. He intends bringing his family here and make Medora his home.

A communication was sent us from the west, yesterday morning, containing a well-written account of the adventures of a New Hampshire girl in the range country. The nature of the article was such that we would have hesitated to publish it in any event, but the fact that no name was signed to the article consigned it to the waste-basket; the common fate of all anonymous communications. We hold ourselves personally responsible for every article that appears in the COW BOY and never, under any circumstances, divulge the name of a correspondent, but the rule is equally as strict on all papers, to never publish an article, the source of which is unknown.

To prove that the fools are not all dead yet, the plan has been revived at Washington of allowing Indians to take charge of range cattle on their reservations. At least we can see no other reason for the revival of the plan. As far as getting any cattlemen to put their cattle under Indian management, we would mildly suggest that no such fool cattleman has ever been born. The would-be philanthropists of the east had far better turn their attention to playing "mumble-de-peg" or some other as intellectual a pursuit, than to spring such a crack-brained scheme on the public. Our space is too limited to show why the plan will never be adopted. It is too foolish for discussion.

WHEREAS, it has come to the knowledge of the executive of this territory that contagious pleuro-puenmonia exists among the cattle of Chicago, Illinois; and

WHEREAS, The importation of such cattle will endanger the herds of this territory;

THEREFORE, In pursuance of law, I, Gilbert A. Pierce, governor of the territory of Dakota, do hereby forbid the importation into that part of said territory east of the Missouri river, of all cattle coming from the city of Chicago or the state of Illinois, when unaccompanied by a certificate of health issued from the office of the state veterinarian of Illinois or inspector of the United States board of animal industry.

In testimony whereof, I hereunto set my hand and seal, and cause the great seal of the territory to be affixed.

Done at Bismarck, the capital of said territory, the 30th day of September, 1886.

GILBERT A. PIERCE. [SEAL] Governor.

There seems to be no reasonable doubt that Etherington's herd in Oliver county, north of Mandan, are suffering from pleuro-pneumonia. Stock Inspector Willard and John Goodall, foreman of the Y (cross) outfit, started Tuesday morning for Mandan, taking horses with them, for the purpose of thoroughly quarantining the herd. As soon as it is positively determined that the disease is pleuro-pneumonia, the cattle will be killed and burned.

Through criminal carelessness or maliciousness several papers have alluded to pleuro-pneumonia as being prevalent near Medora. There is absolutely no foundation for such a rumor. For the benefit of these papers we will state that Medora is within ten miles of the eastern edge of the cattle country of Montana and Dakota. Then comes a stretch of 160 miles of farming country before the Big Missouri is reached. On the banks of this river, Etherington's herd of cattle is located. If it is found that they are suffering with pleuro-pneumonia, it will be the nearest the disease has ever come to the range cattle country of the north. There is absolutely no danger that range cattle will be infected, as the diseased herd is now under strict quarantine and 170 miles away.

The Consumers' Dressed Meat company, the New York representative of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., are making preparations for a great enlargement of their New York and Brooklyn trade. They have bought or leased one-half of Manhattan market and are turning it into a head-quarters for their retail trade. The retail stores will be increased to twenty in New York and ten in Brooklyn. They will be supplied in winter from the Kansas City slaughter-house, having a capacity of three hundred cattle and six hundred hogs daily. The policy of the company will be toward a constant extension of their business, until the plan of supplying the leading eastern cities with range beef killed at their own slaughter-houses and retailed from their own stores, is in practical operation.

"Dr. H. W. Coe and Dr. Halloway, the assistant veterinary surgeon for Montana territory, returned late last night from their trip into Oliver county, where they had been to inspect the herd of cattle reported to be infected with pleuro-pneumonia. Dr. Coe was seen this morning by a Pioneer reporter. The Doctor was asked how he found the cattle. He said:

"Twenty or thirty of the cattle are sick and two or three of them look as though they would soon die. There have been no deaths during the past few days. We made a post-mortem examination of several of the cattle and had some sick cattle killed."

"What was the matter with them?"

"Well, Dr. Halloway says that if ten or fifteen government veterinary experts cannot tell what pleuro-pneumonia is in Chicago, he does not propose, right off, on first sight, to diagnose pleuro-pneumonia in Dakota. It is because of the uncertainty in the case that we are going up again to-day. With pleuro-pneumonia and Texas fever in Chicago, any cattle shipped from there to Dakota that develop sickness of any kind, naturally are the source of considerable alarm to all who are interested in the cattle business. It has been feared that the disease with which these cattle are affected is pleuro-pneumonia. It may turn out that the people have been unnecessarily alarmed. One remarkable feature of the disease, and one which rather indicates that it is not pleuro-pneumonia is that a number of those that have been quite sick appear to be getting better. These cattle were not very strong when they were shipped from Chicago. They were driven through a section of country where they had a good deal of alkali water, and this may at least in part account for their sickness. Dr. Halloway and myself expect to return north to-day and examine the cattle again and make some more autopsies."

"Did the cattle when being driven from Mandan come in contact with any other cattle?"

"Only a few head belonging to two farmers, were a short distance from this herd as they were being driven north. These cattle have been either tied up in barns or are in pastures. All the cattle in the country along there are kept up very carefully. The nearest cattle to the infected band are eight miles away."

"Have any other cattle been sick besides this herd."

"No."

"What are the cattlemen doing about the matter?"

"The Marquis de Mores and Mr. Theodore Roosevelt, who are members of the executive committee of the Montana stockmen's association, while not believing that this is pleuro-pneumonia are taking active steps so that in case it should prove to be anything serious, the disease will go no further. If we should report it to be contagious, they stand ready, if no other provision is made, to pay for these cattle and have them slaughtered. Fred Willard, cattle inspector of Montana, will be down to-day with some herders and their horses, who will go north and assist in maintaining the quarantine. While they do not know what the disease is, they regard it as being too important a matter to take any chances, and therefore they have taken these extra precautions. We shall deputize them and give them full authority to act the same as our own deputies."

"How do the people up north regard the matter?"

"They are all willing to assist in every way and are taking every precaution to prevent the spread of the disease. I have received a good many telegrams during the last few days from the state boards of health of Illinois and Minnesota and from stockmen in Chicago inquiring about the matter."—[Mandan Pioneer.

Sullivan and Ryan have signed articles to box six rounds in San Francisco, Nov. 25.

The Canadian Blood Indians are crossing the line to give battle to their old enemies, the Gros Ventres. Military forces both from the United States and Canada are hastening to the scene and will put a stop to the proceedings.

Newspapers have, since the surrender of Geronimo and Natchez to Gen. Miles, used up columns of abuse on the General for his alleged lenient terms to his prisoners. It now transpires that the Apaches surrendered unconditionally and can be punished by any authority the government sees fit to recognize.

Spearfish had a fire Sunday that completely burned out about a third of the business portion of the town. Beginning at "Uncle Jimmy" Rogers' hotel it swept everything on the block facing Main street, to and including Williams' boot and shoe store. The total loss is about $75,000. We think Spearfish has sufficient recuperative power to recover from the loss and it will then be of the same benefit that the Chicago fire was to Chicago.

Governor Pierce's annual report to the secretary of the Interior is a carefully worded document in which he deals with facts and wisely avoids any further opening of the division question. He says that the debt of the territory is $568,200; not half the amount authorized by Congress limiting the debt to be contracted by the territories. This fact makes the territorial bonds as good securities as can be found in the market. He estimates the increase in population this year at 85,000. The report ends with an earnest appeal for admission as Dakota does and has for a long time posessed all the requirements for state-hood.

Trouble began last Monday over the attempted return by the Chicago pork packers to the ten-hour-a-day rule. All the pork butchers at the Stock Yards have struck except in one or two houses and in sympathy with them, many of the beef butchers have also quit work. The strike is so far, the most orderly that has been conducted. A special committee appointed by Master Workman Powderly is now in Chicago and a speedy and peaceful settlement of the difficulty is expected. The proprietors very reasonably urge that they cannot pay ten hours' wages for eight hours' work when they come in direct opposition with Kansas City and St. Louis houses paying the same wages for ten hours' work.

At the Morton county Republican convention held Tuesday, delegates were elected to the legislative convention favorable to T. J. Mitchell of Mandan. The fight was between Mitchell and Lyon and was won by Mitchell after a sharp contest. The fight was still further complicated by the nomination at the same time of a full set of county officers. F. A. Briggs was nominated for treasurer, B. J. VanVleck for register of deeds, F. E. Bowen for district attorney, Geo. Harmon for sheriff and H. P. Hillis for auditor. It is hardly possible now to tell how the nomination will turn out at the legislative convention. The west Missouri country will be given a member of the lower house and the fight will again be between Lyon and Mitchell, with chances about even.

There seems but little doubt now that the seven Chicago anarchists will hang. The judge has denied their motion for a new trial and the supreme court, if appealed to, will undoubtedly back up the decision of the lower court. The summing-up of the judge in the case was a wonderfully clear statement of the facts and proved beyond a doubt the correctness of the decision. He quoted a long list of articles from the anarchists' written and spoken words that showed conclusively that for three years they had openly advocated killing the police and prominent men. The murders at the Haymarket last May were the legitimate out-come of their articles and were undoubtedly incited by them. Whether they or any of them threw the bomb that killed the policemen matters not. Judge Gary clearly showed that they advocated the use of dynamite; had set the day when it would be used; and that it was used as fore-told and fore-advised. If seven miscreants ever deserved hanging it is the seven who will assuredly suffer that fate soon in Chicago.

Stock Inspector Fred Willard returned Monday night from Oliver county, where he had been quarantining Etheringtons' herd of cattle. Dr. Halloway, assistant territorial veterinarian of Montana, returned on the same train. The Dr. pronounces that the disease is undoubtedly pleuro-pneumonia. A long trench eight feet deep was dug on the ground where the herd had been quarantined and yesterday every animal in the herd, whether showing symptoms of the disease or not, was shot and thrown into the trench. One hundred barrels of lime were then thrown on the carcasses and they were then buried deeply. There never was a more perfect case of the complete stamping out of a disease and stockmen are congratulated on their escape from what threatened to be a vital danger. The disease was located a long way from the range country but if one animal had strayed away from the infected herd it might in the course of time have spread the disease here. The Montana Stockgrowers' Association, through Marquis de Mores and Theodore Roosevelt two Dakota members of the executive committee, are to be thanked for the prompt action taken.

It is at last learned that "Bobby" Adams, one of the most notorious and successful burglars in the world, robbed the Minneapolis post-office of the $15,000 worth of stamps recently. He has been arrested and will doubtless be convicted as the evidence is said to be conclusive.

There are several of our county officers who cannot or will not run again, but aside from these, the sentiment seems to be in favor of the re-election of the old ticket. The county has certainly been run an a very economical basis; a sure guarantee of the honesty and efficiency of the county officials. They have earned a re-nomination.

We have several times had occasion to refer to the Butchers' Advocate of New York and its attacks on western dressed beef.

The Advocate was started as the organ of New York retail butchers and for the expression of their opposition to western dressed beef. No one denies the right of any corporation or set of individuals to establish a newspaper to represent them in all their interests and to lawfully oppose anything detrimental to those interests. The establishment of the Advocate for these reasons was not only right but was a good move on the part of the New York butchers.

But there is a limit to the lawful opposition of the Advocate in its crusade against western dressed beef and that limit it has not only reached but passed. No untruthful statements are lawful in backing up a position no matter how right that position may be.

In its last issue, the Advocate step-father's the report that pleuro-pneumonia has broken out near Medora and insinuates strongly that the diseased cattle were killed here and sent to New York to be sold in the Co.'s retail shops.

If the above were the truth in either of its parts, the Advocate or any sensible man knows that the Co. would be criminally liable in a large amount. If they were liable, the Advocate would be the first to take steps to have the Co. punished. No such steps have been or will be taken, because the Advocate knows the statement to be untrue. The nearest the disease has come to Medora is 160 miles away. The infected cattle were immediately quarantined and have now not only been killed but buried in a trench eight feet deep and the carcasses covered with lime and dirt. And this work was done by money guaranteed by Marquis de Mores and Theodore Roosevelt. The former is the head of the Company which the Advocate intimates slaughtered the diseased cattle for their retail trade and the latter is one of the prominent raisers of the "sage-stubble" beef, whom the Advocate accuses of selling diseased carcasses to confiding eastern purchasers. This article will reach the eye of the editor of the Advocate and we call upon him to right the wrong he has done range interests by stating that pleuro-pneumonia had broken out near Medora. The infected district is as far practically from Medora as is Australia. Over 160 miles of farming country lie between, across which the disease could scarcely have passed and certainly never will now that every animal in the infected herd whether diseased or not has been killed and buried.

The Advocate has a way of denying articles by saying that they are the work of the Co. That it cannot resort to such subterfuge in answering this article we will say that we have had no word of correspondence in any form with any member of the firm directly or indirectly on the subject; that we are in no sense in their pay and that we are now and for some time have been paying them more for rent alone than we have been receiving from them.

The facts as to the location of the disease are easily learned and a manly retraction from the editor of the Advocate is the only course left open for him.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 13.—Commissioner Coleman, of the Agricultural Department some time ago sent Professor George Vasey, the botanist of the department, to make an investigation of the grasses of the arid region of the west, in accordance with an appropriation for that purpose, to ascertain if there were other native grasses and forage plants which would probably be more productive than those now prevailing in that region. Vasey has just returned from his trip, and having made a very thorough investigation of the country included in northeastern New Mexico, eastern Colorado, western Kansas, and western Nebraska, is full of interesting information on the subject.

He says: The native grasses occupying this great tract are numerous, but those which constitute the great [proportion?] of the vegetation, and are the main [reliance?] for the support of stock, are but two kinds, namely, gramma grass and buffalo grass. These are botanically of different genera, but by the greater part of the people are both called buffalo grass. They are grasses of low growth, forming patches of greater or less extent, having spaces of bare soil between the patches. The leaves are very short and much crowded close to the ground. When not too closely cropped by cattle slender, flowering stems are sent up in July and August bearing at the summit one or two short banner-like spikes, which are rather conspicuous, as they stand out horizontally, and are swayed by the breeze. The true buffalo grass (buchloe dactyloides) formed extensive cushion-like beds, covering the ground closely with its short compact foliage, which is of a lighter green color than the gramma. Thess two grasses, in varying proportions, constitute generally 60 per cent of all the grass product. In most localities the gramma grass is much the more abundant of the two. There are several other kinds, which in some localities form a considerable amount of forage. One of these is the Colorado blue-stem or blue grass, very different from the

BLUE GRASS OF THE EAST.

This is a great reliance for stock in winter, and often cut and cured for hay.

Another frequent grass is the blue-joint of Kansas and Nebraska, botanically a species of audropojon. It grows with rather a tall, coarse stock and long leaves, and although somewhat coarse is a valuable grass and everywhere cut for hay. In the bottom lands and in alkaline soils a grass prevails which is called alkali or salt grass. It often forms extensive beds, with the appearance of Kentucky blue grass, and is eaten by horses and cattle, and is said to be nutritious. There can be no doubt that the gramma and buffalo grasses have a very high nutritious value, but they grow so sparsely that cattle require an extensive range in order to obtain proper support. When we come to inquire as to the number of cattle that can be supported on a square mile or on a quarter section we shall realize that there is great poverty as to the amount of grass.

There is a surprising difference in the estimates as to the supporting ability of the plains of these States, some stating that it requires forty or fifty acres to support one animal, others giving twenty to thirty, and still others ten to fifteen acres. All these estimates are correct as to certain localities, and over the entire region it may be considered probable that the average amount required would be about fifteen acres to the head. The inquiry will naturally arise, can not the grazing capacity of this region be greatly increased by substituting more productive grasses?

The results of Professor Vasey's investigations on this subject show that this may undoubtedly be done. So long as the old system of keeping cattle on ranches of vast extent, without providing winter feed or shelter, continued no improvement could be expected, for

NO CHANGE CAN BE EFFECTED

without cultivation of the land. But the cattlemen have mostly evacuated Kansas, and are rapidly removing their herds from Nebraska to occupy Wyoming and Montana, and the vacated lands are now being rapidly occupied for homesteads by incoming settlers, notwithstanding the risks to be encountered from scarcity of water and possible droughts. From the results of farming experiments in various sections during a few years past very sanguine expectations are entertained as to the value of the land for general farming purposes. Admitting the possibility of moderate success in that line, there can yet be no doubt that the country is naturally a pastoral one, and that it can by proper means in the future be made to sustain a much greater number of cattle and sheep than it has in the past. This will be done by holders of limited quantities of land, from a quarter section up to a section or more, who will provide fodder for their stock in the winter and give them suitable shelter, and at the same time break up their land and lay down pastures of new and more productive grasses. What these grasses shall be is yet an open question, and can only be settled by carefully-conducted experiments. It is highly desirable that the government should establish a central and characteristic location, an experimental grass station, where all the commonly cultivated grasses and forage plants and also the more promising native ones could be thoroughly tried under various conditions of culture, and the results given to the public. Undoubtedly a properly conducted and well continued series of experiments in this direction would result in important discoveries of great value to the future residents in this arid district.—[Inter Ocean.

Notice is hereby given that on the 25th day of October, at two p. m., a convention will be held in the Town hall for the purpose of placing in nomination a full county ticket for the coming election. A full turn-out is desired.

MANY VOTERS.

Theodore Roosevelt was recently nominated by the Republicans of New York city as their candidate for mayor and has accepted the nomination. New York is and has been strongly democratic, but the County and Tammany Democrats are at swords' points and there are already five or six candidates for the office. The Republicans are heartily united on Roosevelt and it would not be strange if business as New York's mayor would prevent him from being present at our spring round-up. If the Bad Lands "cow punchers" could help him out with their votes, he would go in with a rush.

The candidacy of Supt. Green on the democratic ticket for the legislature is a conundrum to every paper in the district. When a rail-road man is running for office, the cry is always raised that the rail-road has a job it wants to push through. In this case, however, it would have been far easier for the rail-road to have nominated an outside man on the Republican ticket and no cry of jobbery would have been raised. Mr. Green is an ardent Democrat and it looks as though he has consented to be sacrificed for pure love of party. The break in the Republican ranks, owing to the enmity caused by the Bismarck convention, may make some difference on the vote, but we do not think that even Mr. Green thinks he stands any chance of election. He would make an able representative, but if elected, his railroad position would badly handicap him in any legislation he desired.

There is much uncertainty as to the precinct boundaries and probably will be until the lines are better known. The county has been divided by the commissioners into three voting precincts, by east and west lines. The northern precinct is No. 1, and at the coming election elects a commissioner for one year. It begins on a line running east and west near the Co.'s horse corrall below Lamb's ranch and extends to the northern boundary of the county. All voters within these limits will vote at Tompkins' ranch. Precinct No. 2 is the Medora district and extends from the south line of precinct No. 1, to a line running east and west through a point about a quarter of a mile north of the Logging Camp. It elects a commissioner for two years. All voters in this precinct will vote at the Court House in Medora. Precinct No. 3 elects a commissioner for three years and includes all the county south of precinct No. 2. The polling-place is the home ranch of the Little Missouri Horse Co. In the above, concerning the election of commissioners for different terms in the different precints, it should not be constrned that each precinct nominates and elects its own commissioner. All candidates are nominated and elected by the county at large, but a commissioner must be chosen from each precinct. The terms of office were decided by lot.

The Bismarck convention for the nomination of candidates for the legislature, was an eye-opener to those not acquainted with the arts of the wily politician. The west-Missouri country has been allotted a member of the lower house heretofore, a representation that our population demands. It was thought then, that the only contest would be as to the candidate nominated by the west-Missouri country. This was decided at Mandan by the nomination of Maj. T. J. Mitchell, who, although not Billings county's first choice, would probably have made a good representative. At the legislative convention held at Bismarck last Saturday, the claims of the west-Missouri country were entirely ignored and Alexander Hughes of Burleigh was nominated for the council and E. A. Williams of Burleigh and W. F. Steele, were nominated for the house. The manner of bringing these nominations about displayed the finest piece of political wire-pulling that Dakota has ever seen. There were thirty-five delegates to the convention and although Burleigh county voted for Mitchell, he was defeated by a vote of eighteen to seventeen. The Morton delegates objected strongly to this vote and openly charged Burleigh with treachery. On the face of things, Burleigh had acted in a perfectly honorable manner and her delegates pointed to their vote to prove it. But he who judges politics and especially Dakota politics, by outward signs, shows himself the rankest kind of a political tyro. It is well known that Bismarck is by no means secure in her possession of the capital and that a determined effort will be made this winter to remove it to some point in central or southern Dakota. To oppose such a measure, Bismarck wants to be represented by her ablest workers and the three chosen are absolutely the three best men in the district to work for Bismarck's interests. These are the actual facts in the case and one is not long in seeing the fine Italian hand of the Burleigh county ring which used the outside counties as a cat's paw with which to draw its chestnuts out of the fire. The matter does not affect Billings county particularly, except that it practically disfranchises the whole west-Missouri country, leaving us without a representation which rightfully belongs to us. The scheme was a good one, but Burleigh county will some day be sat on hard by Morton county, whether she is guilty of treachery or not.

The name of Howard Eaton has been prominently mentioned as a candidate for commissioner from precinct No. 1. He absolutely declines however, and favors D. C. Rowe strongly for the position. The Beaver creek country deserves a representative and Mr. Rowe will undoubtedly be nominated and elected.

A new scheme for county division is being broached which, if urged at the coming session of the legislative, will probably be carried. For several years the western part of Morton county has been fighting the eastern and the same is true of the eastern and western parts of Stark county. It is now proposed that a new county be formed from the western part of Morton and the eastern part of Stark, with Sims probably as county seat. The rest of the plan is to extend the western boundary of Stark county to a line east of Belfield and include the rest of Villard county in Billings county. There would seem to be no serious cause of objection to this plan, if carried out as proposed, but we scarcely see the animus of the plan, unless it is to curtail the power of Morton county. In any event, the residents of the counties should be consulted about the changing of their boundary lines and the most feasible plan would be to have an expression of their opinions on it at the November election.

The story comes from Washington that the law officers of the General Land Office are elaborating a plan by which it is hoped that the Northern Pacific will lose its entire land grant from Duluth to Puget's Sound. The Secretary of the Interior lately decided that no land grant road had earned its grant unless a completed plot of the whole road and the land donated had been filed. With this decision for a starting-point it is hoped to declare the whole grant forfeited. This plot is only a continuation of a long persecution to which the Northern Pacific has been subjected and which has been of incalculable harm to the northwest. The government has for several years allowed the Northern Pacific the right of posession and it has, except for a few technicalities, earned the land granted it. The matter should be settled finally and in favor of the road.

The stockyards strike in Chicago ended Monday by the return of the old men to the ten-hour rule. Tuesday, the 300 or 400 new men employed by Armour concluded that they did not want to stay if the old men came back and a train was sent out to the yards to take them away. The butchers were in the front of the train and Pinkerton's police in the rear. A stop was made outside of the yards and a crowd gathering around, Pinkerton's men fired and it is supposed mortally wounded two men. Telegraphic reports say the crowd was quiet and that the shooting was unprovoked, although the men claim that the crowd fired first. The event is much regretted, as it is the first difficulty of any moment that has been caused by the sfrike. The strikers returned unconditonally, Armour declaring that he would not yield them a point. After their return he voluntarily raised their wages fifty cents a day all around.
The Plague, And How to Escape From it.

The animal industries of the United States are in imminent peril from the ravages of an insidious, contagious and incurable disease in cattle commonly called pleuro-pneumonia or lung plague. Many years ago it obtained lodgment on the Atlantic seaboard from imported cattle, and notwithstanding repeated warnings of the danger to be apprehended from its spread, based upon the experience of European countries that have suffered severely from it, our people blinding themselves to their peril, and by spasmodic and half way measures simply averting the disease for a time in particular localities, have allowed it to spread until it has now obtained a firm foothold in the western States, as well as in a number of the eastern ones; and and it is only a question of a very short time when it will find its way to the immense herds on the western and southwestern ranges, unles radical measures are at once adopted to exterminate it where it already exists, and prevent its communication to other parts of the country. This is a matter that affects not only the raisers and dealers in cattle, farmers, dairymen, and butchers, but every man, woman and child in the country, for it strikes directly at the source of supply of [animal food?]. Allow this disease to spread in [the future?] as it has in the past, and the day is not far distant when the animals affected can be counted by the million and not by the hundred as at present, and it is easy to perceive the effect this will have upon our markets and the scarcity of beef that must be the natural result. For years back efforts have been made in some of the States to stamp out the disease, and some light attempt has been made by Congress to give National directions to these efforts, but unfortunately it has been on the penny-wise and pound foolish principle. Owners of cattle naturally object to having their animals killed without receiving full compensation for them, and the government, both State and National, has failed to make provision to pay for the animals that should be slaughtered to eradicate the contagion. As a consequence temporizing measures have been adopted, animals apparently recovered have been permitted to live and mingle with healthy cattle. A partial quarantine has been established about infected herds that has been so loosely enforced as to be practically of no effect, and numerous experiments of inoculation have been tried. It has been very difficult to educate the people of this country to believe that pleuro-pneumonia was contagious, and harder still to convince them that it was incurable. Many animals that had been but slightly affected, apparently recovered, and to outward appearance to the unprofessional eye, were restored to their normal condition of health, and yet these very animals have been the means of spreading the disease all over the country, and while apparently healthy themselves, were centres of contagion that disseminated the seeds of the plague to hundreds of healthy animals. While acting as an Inspector of the United States Government in 1881, in my report to the Commissioner of Agriculture, I recommended as an ultimatum, without which the disease could never be eradicated, "the killing of all chronic cases no matter how apparently healthy they might be." I arrived at this conclusion from careful observation of the operations of the disease not only in this country, but in England, where I had considerable experience in examining its development and spread. Since that time I have carefully watched the progress of the disease in this country, and have communicated with some of the most eminent scientists and experts in England and the United States, who fully agree that the greatest danger to be apprehended is from these chronic or apparently recovered cases. Prof. G. T. Brown, Royal Veterinary College, London, professional adviser to the British Government on contagious diseases of animals, in answer to an inquiry I addressed to him, says, under date of October 21, 1884: "It is quite impossible to tell at what period recovered animals cease to be capable of communicating pleuro-pneumonia, but we have ample evidence to prove that they are the cause of numerous outbreaks of that disease in various parts of the country; in fact, you may take it to be a matter of absolute certainty that it is quite impossible to stamp out pleuro-pneumonia in any country where the so-called recovered animals are allowed to remain alive." In the face of this testimony, and taken in connection with our own actual experience of the constant spread of the disease and its steady march westward, can we afford to longer close our eyes to the danger that threatens us, and allow all our cattle to be affected, before we awaken to the fact that action, prompt, heroic and effective is needed at once, to avert this dire calamity. See to it then that the laws already in existence are rigidly enforced and new ones enacted to meet the exigencies of the case. Have every animal killed that is or has had the slightest contact with diseased animals. The carcasses of healthy or apparently healthy animals killed by reason of contact can be sent to market after proper inspection to prove that they were not injuriously affected, while those that were infected should be buried or entirely destroyed.

In this way and in no other can the plague be checked, and effectually stamped out. While the present outlay of money to accomplish this may be considerable, yet it will save millions of money in the future, protect the food supply of our country and open the foreign markets which have been closed against us for seven years, by reason of the existence of the disease in this country, and in the end as a matter of investment alone prove of incalculable benefit to the cattle interests of the country, and indirectly be of advantage to all consumers of animal food.

JOHN W. GADSDEN,
M. R. C. V. S. Eng.

Remember the nominating convention next Monday.
Sheriff Sebastian of Dickinson, has been very sick for some time.
Things at the tank-house look more natural with Jas. Riley at the helm.
Moses Rider and Robert Nugent are expected soon from their St. Cloud trip.
W. D. Knight of the Yellowstone Journal passed through Medora yesterday morning.
The recent rains have caused the river to rise until it is higher than it has been this summer.
Probate Judge Ed. Simmers left Tuesday morning for Chicago, where a business opening awaits him.
A brakeman named Ed. James was killed at Glendive Tuesday night, by falling between the cars.
E. G. Paddock returned from Wadena Saturday night. He brought a car of vegetables and supplies with him.
W. F. Van Driesche is becoming the acknowledged Nimrod of Medora. He has been very successful lately in killing deer.
Dr. Cunningham arrived Tuesday night and has been busy with dental work since. He will probably leave tomorrow night.
Mrs. Lloyd Roberts came in yesterday from the Sloping Bottom ranch and reports that Lloyd is now in Cheyenne instead of St. Cloud.
Howard Eaton met with a serious loss early this week by the burning of fifty tons of hay, a barn and some fencing near the VI ranch.
Col. W. F. Steele was in Medora Tuesday night. He is the Republican nominee for the legislature from Kidder county and was here looking after his fences.
Harry Tarbell, one of the managers of the HT horse brand, has decided not to return to the Bad Lands. The beath of an uncle recently probably influenced his decision.

Word has been received from T. R. Selmes, attorney for Billings Co.'s taxpayers in the suit resisting taxation by Stark county for county purposes, that the case will be decided by the supreme court not later than February.

Marquis de Mores and wife are still down the river on their hunting trip. Up to yesterday, they had killed six mountain sheep, two elk and several antelope and black and white tailed deer. A bear was seen within twenty or thirty feet, but it was too dark to tackle it.

In spite of the fact that every one anticipated a shortage of hay, more has been put up in the Bad Lands this year than ever before. The Ref. Car Co., have 240 tons, E. G. Paddock about 200 tons, Munro & Lehmicke about 300 tons and every ranch on the river from fifteen to one hundred tons.

The snow came down in a perfect cloud Tuesday and the ground was covered to a depth of four inches. There is no record of such a storm so early in the season, but it furnishes no basis by which to judge the weather of the coming winter, for if the temperature had only been a few degrees warmer, we would have had a fall rain instead of a snow storm.

Tommy Smith came in last Saturday from a season's work on the trail and in the British Possessions. He reports that there was plenty of work at good prices. On his return he saw the beginning of a fight between two bands of Indians but as he hadn't lost any Indians he didn't stop to enquire their names. He will winter in Deadwood and return in the spring to the British Possessions.

Car Co.'s office, at Ferris' store and at the drug store. These copies are for correction and it will be a kindness if all would take an interest in making the list as nearly perfect as possible.

Chief Crazy Horse of the Rosebud agency and some of his braves are on a sheep-stealing excursion on Tongue river. A battalion of infantry left Ft. Keogh yesterday morning to put a stop to the depredations. The Indians complain of a scarcity of government rations, which is probably a fact.

The report comes from Bismarck, that Supt. Green, in his candidacy for the legislature, has been up and down the road in his private car, telling all the railroad men that they must vote for him. We are no champion of Mr. Green's, but we do not believe in this way of fighting the candidate of an opposition party. While here, Mr. Green told several railroad men that they ought to vote as they thought best and that no pressure of any kind would be brought to bear on them. This was not said publicly or for effect, but personally to different railroad men.

At the coming session of the legislature, a bill will be introduced from Billings county for a rebate of the railroad taxes paid into the territorial treasury on account of its mileage in Billings county while it was yet unorganized. The Cow Boy has several times mentioned this matter and a full discussion only shows the more plainly that we should receive the back taxes. We see no difference in our relations, while unorganized, to the territory than there is between a ward and a guardian. The taxes are simply held in trust for us by the Territory until we reach our majority by organization. This we have done and now of course we want a settlment from our guardian. The amount involved is about $10,000; enough to pay our county expenses for two or three years.
The post-office at Sentinel Butte, Patrick Tammany post-master, is now opened.
J. R. Grymes is in New York city and will soon begin work as draughtsman on the Manhattan elevated railroad.
John W. Buster of the Hashknife Co., passed through Medora this morning on his way to Dickinson and the home ranch at the mouth of Box Elder.
G. M. Woodman who has been spending the summer at the HT horse camp, left for his home in Boston, Tuesday morning. He will return in the spring.

Marquis de Mores started for New York yesterday morning. He will return about the twentieth and the force of men at the slaughter-house here will then be moved to Kansas City, where work will begin Dec. 1.

The Powder River cattle company will ship thirty cars of steers and dry cows from here in the morning. They are in poor flesh now and will be taken to the company's feeding establishment at Duluth. About nine hundred others will be turned loose here until barns can be built in Duluth for their reception. Messrs. Langham and Kennedy are here to oversee the shipment.

A New York syndicate now has agents in the field who are negotiating for the purchase of the whole Cherokee strip. It consists of over 6,000,000 acres and the price offered is $3 per acre. The Cherokees are holding off for a higher price which will doubtless be offered them. The syndicate wants the strip for grazing and agriculture.

There is no question that the present pool rate established on both live and dressed beef between Chicago and New York is exorbitant and will call for general discussion at all the meetings of the cattle associations. In spite of the fact that beef is selling lower than for several years, these roads have increased the freight rate to a higher point than it has ever been since there was any competition. This of course, affects stockmen directly, as it costs from $1 to $1.25 more to market a steer than it has hitherto. This applies whether the animal is sold in Chicago or New York. In short, should the present rate continue, stockmen can figure that they will lose at least a dollar a head on all their beef cattle. This matter is worth looking into and remedy ing.

The fact that it pays to feed cattle is abundantly demonstrated in the case of the Powder River cattle company. For several years they have been running large feeding pens near Duluth and they state that it nets them from $10 to $12 on every animal they have fed. This makes a splendid margin and applies to all classes of cattle not in the very best condition. The feed consists principally of wheat screenings, ground and boiled. Oat straw and prairie hay are also fed. The animals are tied in rows in large barns and are seldom liberated before being sent to market. When a shipment arrives, the animals are tied up as rapidly as possible, for they get exceedingly wild if allowed to stand in the yard more than a day or two. After the second day in the stable, they eat ravenously and often get as gentle as barnyard cows. When liberated, however, they become as wild as ever. This company has now fed so long and with such unifom success that it has entirely passed the experimental stage. There are occasionally animals that do not fatten well but they are only the exceptions that prove the rule; they have averaged over $10 a head on all the animals they have ever fattened, the feeding extending over a period of several years. We expect to see the example of the Powder River cattle Co. largely followed by range stockmen. There is no reason why it should not be a success for all, as well as one.

There is no business on the face of the earth which depends so entiely on providence and honest neighbors as the cattle business. There is no business that covers such an area for every operator and none in which there are so many chances for leaks to foot up large totals. In spite of these facts, there is no class of men who place such implicit reliance in final results and certainly no class of men, taken as a class and not individual who are so utterly careless of their vital interests as are cowmen. Time after time, important measures need to be adopted and fail, either from lack of unanimity or because the most of the stockmen are too careless or lazy to look after their own interests. There is no need in specifying particular instances. A score will come to the mind of any one in the range country. Now however, the most vital question touching the stock interests is the threatened spread of pleuro-pneumonia. The stockmen should rise as one man and demand that not alone should every diseased animal be killed in the United States, but that hereafter and forevermore, not a solitary animal should be imported from any country not absolutely free from the disease. A feeble cry comes up occasionally from isolated stock associations, protesting against the free or virtually free importation of cattle, but this has done and will do no good. The united demand of every stock-grower in the United States will compel Congress to take action and it is doubtful if anything short of this will. Why can't stockmen see that "in union there is strength." and that by united action they can compel recognition for their just claims.

The experiment of growing alfalfa or California clover in the western portion of this State by our farmers and stockmen, has met with most flattering results. They have met with such excellent success that others are induced to seed down large tracts of land with this valuable hay and feed-producing range plant. The seeding may be done in early fall and about 30 pounds of seed should be used to the acre, which would insure a thick stand for the first season. The yield of alfalfa is enormous, as much as eight or ten tons per acre, which on good soil, such as will produce corn, can be cut four times a year. If cut for hay it should be cut just before it turns to seed or while in bloom. It may be cut twice for hay each year and the third time for seed. Alfalfa may be grazed until late in the fall and winter, then again in the spring and still make a fair seed crop. The roots of this plant go down into the soil to a depth of ten or fifteen feet, and in some instances have been known to go even deeper, to a depth where, as a rule, it would strike water. We would advise all who can to put in a field of alfalfa.—[Dodge City, Kan., Globe.

It is to be hoped that Congress will before long become sufficiently intelligent in regard to the public land system and the condition of life and business in the far west to see that some legislation is urgently needed concerning the ownership and occupancy of land in the great central grazing zone, where agriculture is not feasible, and where the only value of the soil is its capacity of furnishing pasture to stock. The existing land laws, adopted when Illinois was the remote west, have little applicability to Montana or Wyoming. Only very limited areas of the Territories can ever be occupied under the homestead and preemption acts, for the reason that not one acre in a hundred is good for farming, and those acts contemplate settlement by farmers only. The stockman is not considered at all. He can do nothing with the 320 acres which is all that he can get title to under the statutes now in force. That amount of land would not pasture enough cattle to support a family a single month. It takes about thirty acres to feed a steer the year round. What would the stockman do with ten or a dozen animals as his only resource to make a living? He cannot farm because the rainfall is not sufficient to raise crops. He must have more cattle, or more sheep, and to subsist on them he must use land that belongs to the government.

Now if the government gives farming land in the rich prairie regions to the settler who will homestead it, handing over a patent to 160 acres, and selling 160 more for $1.25 to $2.50 per acre, why should it not make some equally just and liberal provision for the settler in regions where the land is worth nothing except for grazing and not more than 25 to 50 cents an acre for that use? The settler asks no more than land enough to support his family as comfortably and with as much labor as will a quarter section in the agricultural regions. He is willing to buy this land, but the government will not sell it. The government, by virtue of its present stupid land system, makes the stockman a sort of Bedouin, for it refuses to give him the ownership of a fixed abode where he can make a living for his family.

The cattle king, with his vast herds, does not complain of the present system, for he takes posession of as much land as he needs, turns his stock upon it and employs his cowboys to look after it. The small stockman who has only a few hundred head cannot put his little band of cattle out on the public range, for in a few months they would be scattered far and wide among the herds of many different owners. He cannot afford to go to all the different round-ups and identify his animals. What we want is the right either by purchase or rental from the government to fence land enough for all his needs so that his cattle can be kept at home. What is greatly needed for the prosperity of the entire grazing belt is an expansion of the present homestead and preemption laws to adapt them to regions essentially unfit for farming. The new legislation might provide that in such regions a homestead should consist of four sections (2,560 acres), with the right of preemption and purchasing as much more. This would give permanence to the stock industry and would make it to the interest of the herdsmen to preserve the grass on the great natural pastures.—[The Northwest.

It will be remembered that at the last meetings of the National Cattle Growers' Association and the National Cattle and Horse Growers' Association, committees were appointed from each to arrange for a union of the two associations. This union was accomplished under the title of Consolidated Cattle Growers' Association of the United States and the next meeting will be held in Chicago, Nov. 16 and 17. It seems that now is the accepted time for every cattle association to represent at this convention and together, as one man, adopt measures that will finally and forever stamp out pleuro-pneumonia from the soil of the United States. Time is too precious now to indulge in factional or sectional fights. The battle against pleuro-pneumonia and other diseases can best be waged through the medium of the Consolidated association. Each association, if working by itself, can accomplish little or nothing. All should unite in the larger association and protect themselves and their neighbors from the imminent danger of contagious diseases on the range.

The St. Paul stock-yards scheme is having another boom by the formation of a company with a capital of $1,500,000 for the purpose of erecting immense feed stables, slaughtering and packing houses to utilize as much as possible of the range product of the northwest. This move is closely watched by stockmen of this country and a long sigh of relief will go up from them as soon as the yards are in successful operation.

The Miles City Dressed Beef Co's slaughter-house was closed last week by the action of numerous creditors levying attachments on the works. The outstanding accounts in Montana aggregate about $95,000 and the backer of the concern, L. M. Dustin of Lincoln, Ill., is a financial wreck. His bank at Lincoln is also closed, owing to a run on it. In what ever light this matter is placed it cannot but be a misforture to the range country. There is no denying the fact that cowmen are being underpaid for their live beef and large slaughter-houses in the range country are one of the feelers put out to find a good road for the cattlemen out of present "slough of dispond" of low prices. As far as the feeler in Miles City is concerned, it did not live long enough to prove anything besides the incompetence of the management. It is to be hoped that some practical ranchmen can form a partnership with a practical butcher, to thoroughly test the matter of slaughtering beef on the range for the wholesale trade. Should the attempt prove unsuccessful, there seems no other way than that rangemen should pool together to raise prices or to adopt the Medora plan of killing on the range and retailing in large cities.

Six thousand of Swift & Co's and Nelson Morris' beef butchers struck Monday morning sooner than return to the ten-hour-a-day rule. Two or three hundred canners from Libby, McNeal & Libby also struck as their firm was getting beef from the above firms. This will undoubtedly be the last stand made in Chicago against working ten hours a day. If all employes in the United States of any one trade should work eight hours a day, there would probably be no trouble except for the fact of machinery and capital lying idle a fifth longer than was expected when the works were erected. This difficulty could doubtless be remedied, but that of one or more firms working on the eight-hour plan with ten hours' pay while all other firms work ten hours places the first at a disadvantage that will soon find the bottom of the best-filled pocket. It is simply a financial impossibility for a firm in any business to pay twenty per cent. more for their employes than do other firms. Since last May, this is exactly what the Chicago packers have been doing and they now find that they must either stop it or close up their works. If the butchers all over the United States were well enough organized to all demand eight hours' work, the plan would be successful and after things were adjusted to the new order, entirely satisfactory. Until the butchers are so organized, however, it is folly to ask any one employer or the employers in any one town to adopt a plan that places them at such a disadvantage that a proffitable business is impossible.

A cattleman remarked the other day in our presence that "bad ear marks make bad cattle." In answer to the inquiry why? he said he did not know, but that he had observed in handling range cattle that animals with their ears gone or badly disfigured were ugly and difficulty to drive.

The remark caused us to philosophise as follows. The ears were given to animals for a certain purpose and the law of adaptation was faithfully carried out in the matter of construction. Without going into the details of the formation of the bovine ear it is sufficient to say that it is so shaped as to catch the slightest vibration of sound and lead it directly to the organs of intelligence or instinct, as the reader may see proper to class that intellectual power our dumb animals process. The cutting off the ear destroys the natural conduit of sound and throws it upon the inner organs with such violence as to produce an abnormal effect and very rapidly destroy them. So to, does the carving of the ear into many parts by slits, crops or bites destroy the approach of sounds and give exaggerated notions of danger. All this tends to make an animal nervous, and very practical cowmen knows that this means trouble when he attemps move cattle on the range or road. One or two nervous animals in a bunch of beef steers on the way to the shipping point cause a shrinkage in the herd of more than the value of one or even a dozen, in many instances, by stampeding or causing unnecessary excitement.

The ear mark is really of little value, so long as brands are used, in determining the ownership and they might be dispensed with. At least such marks should be used as will effect in the least the hearing of the cattle, and these will be those that do not greatly disfigure the ear.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
Cattle Feeding on a College Farm.

CHAMPAIGN, Ill.
Eds. The Farmer:—On October 15, at the regular weighing of cattle on the farm of the [University of?] Illinois, a lot of six choice steers, averaging a few days less than 30 months in age, and 1,603 pounds in weight, were found to have made an average gain of 89 1-9 pounds in 45 days (from September 1) and of 27½ pounds in the last 19 days.

A lot of four good steers, averaging a little over 30 months, and 1,455 pounds had made average gain of 150 pounds in 45 days, and of 58¾ in the 16 days.

A lot of 24 steers of poorer quality and probably of not much less age, averaging 1,118 lbs., had made an average gain of 118½ pounds in the 45 days, and of 44 pounds in the 16 days.

The lot of six have been on a full grain feed during all the summer and last winter—four of them also during the preceding summer. The lot of four were well fed last winter, but had no grain from May 1 until August 15—on full feed since September 1. The lot of 25, with one exception, were purchased in the spring and summer, and had been poorly fed during the winter. Since August 15, they have had same treatment as the lot of four. The average gain of the 24 purchased since June 12, when most of them were bought, has been 242½ pounds.

These cattle have all been on pasture and have been fed on corn in the ear, averaging about one-half bushel per steer daily. They are fed three times a day—generally from the wagon as it comes from the field. The lot of six best steers have not had so good pasture as the others and have eaten a little hay. Pigs "follow" all the cattle and have grown rapidly from the corn left undigested by them. The variations in the rate of grain are partly explainable from the poorer quality and smaller size of the larger lot of steers and from the longer feeding and much higher degree of fatness of the lot of six.

The facts concerning these cattle are in accordance with our experience year after year on the university farm, which seems to show that, under present conditions in Central Illinois:

1. Increase of weight in cattle is most cheaply secured by pasturage without any grain during the best part of the season.

2. Feeding whole corn in the autumn months to cattle on the pasture is the most economical method of fattening cattle. The feeding is done with the least labor. When hogs follow the cattle there is very little waste. The manure is saved and distributed without cost. While comparatively low prices are to be expected for cattle marketed in the autumn or early winter, a fair profit has been made annually. Even with the prevailing exceptionally low prices, sales have been made (for November delivery) of most of the cattle purchased last spring at a price which gives fairly satisfactory profit.

3. After three or four months of full grain feeding a considerable decrease in rate of grain may be expected.

4. Apparently, from 30 to 36 months are the most profitable ages at which to sell cattle fattened on this system—unless those of a little greater age can be bought at a price which gives no profit to the grower.

5. It is not profitable to feed grain to yearling steers on good pasture, if it is designed to keep them another year and fatten for the general market.

6. Calves reared on skim milk, with addition of some meal may make entirely satisfactory growth and beef animals of good quality. A high grade Short-Horn steer now on the farm weighs 1,470 pounds at a few days over 29 months, and with less than two months full grain feeding. He has gained 185 pounds in the last 45 days.

The four steers recently put on grain averaged 153 pounds less than the six which have been kept on full feed—or comparing them with the four of the latter lot of like breeding, and almost exactly the same age, the difference in average weight is 172 pounds. Two steers of the lot of six, which were not grain fed in summer of 1885, lack, the pair, only 115 lbs. of the weight of their mates which were full fed that summer.

Pure bred or grade Ayrshire, Hereford, Holstein and Short-horn cattle, aside from some "common" stock, are in these lots, but not in sufficient number to enable one to dogmatize as to merits of the breeds. The heaviest cattle are half-blood Holsteins. The greatest weight is 1,785 pounds for a steer not quite 31 months old. The steer of best quality is a three-quarter Hereford. A pure bred Ayrshire weighs 1,525 pounds at 32 months. The steer of best form is a pure bred Short-Horn, but a local trouble has reduced his weight 200 pounds or more.

G. E. MORROW,
Prof. of Agriculture.
University, Champaign, Ill.

It seems proper to give an explanation of the defeat of A. T. Packard as justice of the peace. He had absolutely and unqualifiedly refused to run for any office and returned the same answer when urged to run for justice of the peace by Messrs. Willis Eaton and Gregor Lang and many others. He even went so far in his refusal as to say that he would not even run for an office for ten times the combined salaries of all the county officers. Messrs. Eaton and Lang finally put the matter on a basis of pure personal obligation, urging that he was the stockmens' choice and that he should throw aside personal feeling and oblige them to that extent. This was the reason which impelled him to accept a nomination which he not only did not want, but which under any other circumstances he would have refused. As a consequence of the manner of his nomination, he was perfectly free in saying, when the matter was brought up, that he should, in case of election, follow consistently the path he has so clearly marked out, of opposition to the "ba-a-d man" idea and would give every such offender the extreme limit the law allowed. This remark was the direct cause of his defeat. One of the men who heard it, immediately spread it where it would do the candidate the most good or harm, depending on the light in which the matter is looked at. He then scratched all the tickets at hand, substituting the name of F. D. Foster for that of the regular nominee. The defeated candidate has no reason to be ashamed of the remark that caused his defeat and in that light his defeat is one of the highest compliments that could be paid them. Of course he does not relish the defeat itself, but he would far sooner be defeated than have it supposed that he would renounce the opinions he has always upheld. Frank D. Foster, the elected candidate knew nothing of the matter until after the election and freely expresses his opinion that it was a contemplible trick.

A Proclamation by the Governor.

During the season that has passed, the people of this territory have been abundantly blessed with health and freedom from distressing calamities;

The hand of justice has not been stayed;

The laws have been observed;

No social disturbance has afflicted us;

No angry turmoil has rent communities in twain or called for force to maintain order.

Though the fullest fruits of American citizen-ship have not yet been attained, no people are less burdened with legal restrictions, and no freer breath is drawn than that enjoyed by the citizens of this commmon-wealth. Safe in his home! Safe in the enjoyment of his conscience and his God!

For these and for kindred blessings it is becoming that we raise our voices in gratitude to the Almighty.

Therefore, in conformity to the president's proclamation, I commend to the people the observance of Thursday, the 25th day of November, as a day of thanksgiving and prayer. "With malice toward none, with charity for all," remembering the needy and afflicted, and beseeching the Divine blessing on the future of this land, let us meet in church and home and celebrate this annual festival—a season associated with sacred memories and hallowed by the custom of our fathers.

"Under God the people rule."

Witness my hand and the great seal of the Territory, this 4th day of November, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and eignty six.

GILBERT A. PIERCE.

The Cherokee syndicate, formed in New York for the purpose of buying the Cherokee strip of the Indians, comes out with the cool statement that they intend getting up a corner on grazing lands. The coolness of this claim is refreshing. In the first place, the government has the first option on the purchase of these lands and it is not at all likely that it will wave its rights in the interest of a set of land-grabbers. In the second place, the Cherokee Strip is only an insignificant part of the grazing area of the west and a hundred times its 6,000,000 acres would hardly corner the range territory. The brains of the syndicate, if it has any, had better come west and see some of the country before they begin talking of cornering the western ranges. They are nearly as bad as Griffins' Irishman who wanted the earth—and some of the outside.

A case decided recently in Wyoming, declared it to be unconstitutional for a stock association to sell mavericks for its own benefit. This maverick question gives rise to more disputes than anything else in the cow business but the plan adopted by the Little Missouri association seems to give better satisfaction than any other. Here all mavericks are branded with the marks of the owner of the range on which the maverick is found. In case of dispute, the matter is left to arbitrators, whose decision is final.

Col. C. C. Slaughter of Texas is busy at work on a scheme whereby the value of all range cattle will be raised $10 to $25 per head. The plan is to pool all range cattle- growers, the total number of cattle represented, being 10,000,000. Each owner is then to contribute a dollar a head and the $10,000,000 thus raised is to be used in building immense stock-yards in St. Louis and Chicago. Each owner is also to agree not to sell any cattle to outside buyers for less than six cents a pound, Providing all rangemen will adopt the plan it will be a success, but on this same plan farmers could combine and force wheat up to two dollars a bushel. They never have done this and never will. Enough will stay out to break the pool. Something should certainly be done to raise the maret price of cattle but it must be a more feasible plan than the above. If a few men would put up the requisite $10,000,000 for the good of their fellow stock-raisers, the plan ought to succeed. It never will if each owner is required to chip in a dollar a head on his cattle.

The present strike at the Union stock yards in Chicago, bids fair to be desperately fought out to the bitter and bloody end by both sides. The packers have positively declared that they will not under any circumstances employ Knights of Labor in the future. Any member who is employed by any of the packers must first resign and place his resignation in the hands of his employer. This is a move against the Knights of Labor as a body and the strikers claim that their cause must now be championed by the general assembly of the Knights. They declare that a boycott on all Chicago dressed beef will be declared and that they will not yield an inch. About 20,000 men are now striking and the packing houses are employing new men as fast as they apply for places. Pinkerton and Town of Lake police, 350 deputy sheriffs and two companies of state militia are now camped at the stock yards and will enforce order. The packing houses are all short handed but the proprietors say they will close before yielding a point to the strikers. Shots have been exchanged frequently but up to yesterday, no one had been killed.
